articles.text: On Friday, March 25, eight Piedmont teens participated in the Youth vs. Apocalypse rally and protest in San Francisco with other young climate justice activists. The non-violent march protested those profiting from the destruction of the planet and sought to amplify the voices of the youth concerned about the future of the environment. There were no classes in Piedmont that day, meaning students choose to take BART to the Embarcadero for the 10:00 a.m. gathering on their own volition. The march headed to Howard Street to protest at the headquarters of BlackRock Investment Management and then to Sansome Street outside a federal government office to protest I.C.E. (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) policies. articles.text: The Piedmont Community Pool project is $6 million over budget according to a hard cost estimate, necessitating that the conceptual design be trimmed. Piedmont City Council discussed the matter at a March 21 meeting, and approved the modifications proposed by city staff and ELS Architecture and Urban Design, the firm chosen to lead the design process. The city council approved a design on January 18 after considering feedback received in three community workshops and reports from five publicly-held Pool Advisory Committee meetings held between October 2021 and February 2022. ELS completed the schematic design process on March 4 and sent a schematic design package to City Council, including construction cost estimates. The Emeryville-based construction management and consulting firm Mack5 analyzed ELS’ design elements and provided the City with a cost estimate; it far exceeded the city’s target budget. “Mack5’s analysis of the design elements resulted in a ‘hard cost’ construction cost estimate of roughly $25 million which far exceeds the city’s target of $19 million. We are faced with a $6 million gap as we move toward design development,” Lillevand said, adding that the extraordinary cost estimates will necessitate a reduction of the original design. “These modifications, while significant and disappointing, do continue to meet the aquatic needs of the community,” Lillevand said. The primary reason for higher-than-anticipated costs is hyperinflation, Lillevand explained. Construction industry experts also advise that construction costs will rise at a rate in excess of 1% per month. Modifications to design Clarence Mamuyac, President of ELS, provided a design update to city council on March 21. ProRendering by ELS Architecture and Urban Design Due to escalating construction costs, the Piedmont Community Pool will have to scale down in size and eliminate the second floor of the aquatic facility.
articles.title: Cost estimates soar to $6 million over budget

articles.text: The City of Piedmont hosted a virtual community workshop on March 24 to seek suggestions from the public on appropriate Housing Element sites. At least 80 members of the public tuned in, and were able to explore a new interactive tool called the “Piedmont Puzzle.” Stakeholders have until May 1 to submit suggestions via “Piedmont Puzzle.” The state requires that each city make a draft of the housing element available for public comment for at least 30 days before submittal to the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD). Piedmont is working toward releasing a draft Housing Element update by the April 19 Housing Advisory Committee meeting. A refined draft will be reviewed by the California Department of Housing Community Development (HCD) in July. This gives the city approximately three months to review, revise, and refine a draft with sufficient public comment. The HCD does not review any first draft submittals that have not demonstrated adequate public outreach. Since 1969, California has required that all cities and counties plan to meet the housing needs of the entire community. articles.text: The following letter was sent to the Piedmont City Council. Editor: Whichever decision you make with regard to how the pools will be heated, you can expect issues to come up during construction, with a subset of problems having to be brought to your attention. Sleep loss is inherent to the fate of people who build real stuff! If you select an all-electric solution, it is likely that the number of headaches will be higher, given that Piedmont will be innovating in deploying a proven technology for a new use (for sure in California). But our community will have the satisfaction of showing other municipalities the way to create aquatics facilities as green as possible: an important case study for our State. I am confident that given the quality of the City staff, the contractor and consultants involved that you will make an informed decision weighing technical considerations, capital and operational expenses, environmental issues, the uncertainty of the relative future costs of different energy sources and inflation. As Piedmonters, we elect you to make the tough decisions, and regardless of the way you choose, taking a prudent approach, a trailblazer one, or something in-between, I encourage our community to support your decision. I certainly will. –Bernard Pech For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

articles.text: Join the League of Women Voters of Piedmont tonight, Wednesday, March 30, for a discussion with Dr. Fiona Hill, Senior Fellow at The Brookings Institution at Stanford. The Zoom episode will explore the current state of democracy, from both domestic and international points of view. Dr. Hill is the Robert Bosch Senior Fellow at the Center on the United States and Europe in the Foreign Policy program at the Brookings Institution and member of the Council on Foreign Relations. Her most recent book, There is Nothing for You Here, draws on her personal journey out of poverty, as well as her unique perspectives as a historian and policy maker, to show how we can return hope to our forgotten places. From 2017 to 2019, Dr. Hill served as deputy assistant to the president and senior director for European and Russian affairs on the National Security Council. From 2006 to 2009, she served as national intelligence officer for Russia and Eurasia at the National Intelligence Council. She has researched and published extensively on issues related to Russia, the Caucasus, Central Asia, regional conflicts, energy, and strategic issues. Co-author of Mr. Putin: Operative in the Kremlin and The Siberian Curse: How Communist Planners Left Russia Out in the Cold, she holds a master’s degree in Soviet studies and a doctorate in history from Harvard University and a master’s in Russian and modern history from St. Andrews University in Scotland. This event is part of the League’s 2022 Defending Democracy Speaker Series and is co-sponsored by local Leagues in California, Oregon, Colorado, and Florida. This talk will be held live on Zoom and YouTube and will include an audience question and answer session. Visit the website Dr. Fiona Hill is the guest speaker of a League of Women Voters discussion on Russia tonight, March 30. lwvpiedmont.org to learn more about the series and register for this event. Once you have registered, you will receive the Zoom link by email. The event is free and open to the public.
articles.title: LWV Defending Democracy talk with Russia expert Fiona Hill tonight

articles.text: The City of Piedmont will host a virtual discussion on equitable real estate practices that support an inclusive community on April 7 via Zoom. The event, entitled “Welcome to Piedmont: Real Estate Practices in Support of an Inclusive Community,” is co-sponsored by the Piedmont League of Women Voters (LWV), Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC), and Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC). The discussion will be moderated by Carol Galante, a Piedmont resident and founder of the Terner Center for Housing Innovation at UC Berkeley. The panelists include retired Piedmont real estate agent Maureen Kennedy, a former member of the Clinton Administration; Chief Diversity and Equity Officer at California Association of Realtors Farrah Wilder; and Ashley Gardner, Community Outreach Coordinator for California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA). Residents and real estate professionals who tune in will learn about what the current context for real estate practices and its impact on the demographics of the Piedmont community. A moderated discussion between the above professionals will focus on the benefits of an inclusive community and how Piedmont residents can help affirm the city’s commitment to be a more welcoming and diverse community. “Real estate transactions and the interplay between sellers, real estate professionals and potential buyers is one piece of a complex puzzle we are striving to solve... how to bring more diversity to Piedmont,” said City Administrator Sara Lillevand. “We look forward to an engaging dialogue focused on evolving practices and new ideas to help shape the Piedmont of the future.” In September 2021, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed into law over 30 affordable housing bills that focused on cutting red tape and holding cities accountable for providing their fair share of housing. When signing the legislation, he said “[the] bills, plus [last] year’s historic budget investments in affordable housing, will directly lead to more inclusive neighborhoods across the state. Creating denser housing near jobs, parks and schools is key to meeting our climate goals as well as our affordability goals.” To participate in this event, use the Zoom Registration Link at https://piedmont-ca-gov. zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_ zGnJ-AWnT4KFzrNxe2mKlg.
articles.title: Zoom discussion on equitable real estate practices on April 7

The updated design presented to city council last week was just above $19 million in estimated costs, he added. Mamuyac explained that modifications this early in the design process are not unusual. “This is how you meet the marketplace,” he said. “We want to get our bid package together in four months, in early August. We’re hoping to pull together another [cost] estimate in two months, and another right before we go out to bid. These are a lot of ‘checks’ in a short span of time, and that’s how we’re managing our risk.”

Councilmember Betsy Andersen said she was pleased to see that there are still two pools, and that the competition pool is still 27 meters with the proposed modifications. “The water polo community has been supportive throughout this process, so I’m glad we get to keep a body of water [that is appropriate] for that sport,” she said. Both Councilmembers Conna McCarthy and Jennifer Long commented that the design was still aesthetically pleasing despite the modifications. Andersen questioned how the modifications would impact operational costs. Lillevand noted that the elimination of recreation pool lanes may be a benefit to the city in terms of operating costs. “It may be a benefit to us from a recreational standpoint. Adding deck space may make it a more attractive place to spend more time. Shorter [recreation pool] lanes, from a teaching and programming perspective, is not a loss,” Lillevand said. Mayor Teddy Gray King added that her initial reaction to the conceptual design approved by council earlier this year was that the design needed more deck space. Now with the elimination of conference and meeting rooms on a second floor, deck space would be even more valuable, she said. Andersen noted that she was concerned with the possibility of having only one family changing area, and that she anticipated “more demand than [the facility will] have ability to meet.” Moving forward With now rising costs, the City Council discussed whether or not to ask the community for help. “As a community, we excel in public-private partnerships. Every great project we’ve done in the past has included some potential for fundraising,” Vice Mayor Cavenaugh said. “It doesn’t seem like we have the ability to squeeze the design anymore. I’m wondering if there is a point in the not-too-distant future that we think about reaching out to the community to find out what kind of support there might be to bring this design to life.” Lillevand said that community fundraising, in her experience with recent projects such as Hampton Park and the Corey Reich Tennis Center, has been successful. “We’ll be thinking a lot about that, talking weekly – if not daily – with the design team about costs,” she said. “There will be an opportunity for the community to support what will be a fabulous facility. I think people will be upset if we didn’t ask, and if we just made decisions unilaterally.” have reached an understanding [of its housing needs] and the Piedmont City Council will make a decision of whether or not to send the draft review to HCD to review and ensure compliance with state law,” Slama said. More than 875 Piedmont community members provided public comment since April 2021 through voluntary submission and survey initiatives. A range of input was received at the first community workshop meeting, explained Dave Javid, founder of Plan to Place, a firm that specializes in communication and outreach efforts related to community planning and housing goals. Its clients include Sausalito, Berkeley, Oakland, Mill Valley, and numerous other Bay Area cities. Key takeaways, Javid said, included a community desire for dense housing other than single-family homes, affordable housing for those in the public service and education industry, and affordable housing located close to public transit opportunities. “Across the board, [the survey showed] there seemed to be good support for housing and for a diversity of housing types,” Javid said. Chris Adams, president and co-founder of Balancing Act, presented an interactive community planning tool called “The Piedmont Puzzle.” “It’s meant to give a glimpse into what the challenges are, and ways to provide input,” Adams said. The Piedmont Puzzle was introduced to attendees at the March 24 meeting, allowing participants to “click” on zones in the city and submit suggestions on where 587 new housing units could exist in Piedmont. People were given 10 minutes to explore the tool. The tool can be viewed at https://piedmont.abalancingact. com/housingsim. The deadline to use the tool and submit suggestions is May 1. In conjunction with Arbor Day festivities, Piedmont Park Commission will present a screening of the 2016 documentary Intelligent Trees in Piedmont Park on April 28. The 2016 film explores how trees communicate with one another. Intelligent Trees features Suzanne Simard, Forest Ecology Professor at the University of British Columbia, and Peter Wohlleben, the bestselling author of The Hidden Life of Trees. The two have observed and investigated for decades the communication between trees and its relevance to humans. The film reveals their scientific findings on how, and to what extent, trees have intelligence. At least half of the film’s revenue goes toward Simard’s ongoing research. Her studies are currently housed in the Forest and Conservation Science Centre at the University of British Columbia. The documentary is directed by Julia Dordel and Guido Tolke. articles.text: The inaugural Piedmont Food Fest is coming to town. On Sunday, April 24, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., in partnership with the City, schools, local businesses, community partners, and the fiscal sponsor Social Good, Piedmont Food Fest will welcome visitors and showcase a family-friendly event. It will include food, the stories of the people behind the food, as well as multicultural stage performances, locally sourced beer and wine, and a kid activity zone. Event organizers are hoping this event may become an annual tradition the community can look forward to year after year. A central mission of Piedmont Food Fest is to showcase the many diverse offerings of the broader Bay Area community that help enrich the community and neighbors. The event will feature food from Curry Up Now, Ceviche & Co, Swahili Spot, Kiss My Boba, Piedmont’s Robert Dorsey Catering, and others. Live music will be provided by the mariachi duo Son Nuestro, the Great Wall Youth Orchestra, a Black Music Incubator Showcase, and the Oakland Samba Revue. Piedmont Food Fest is open to the public in the broader Bay Area. To register or volunteer, please visit www.piedmontfoodfest.org. articles.text: This past Saturday, March 26, Piedmont families gathered to show their support for struggling families in Ukraine at a fundraiser and bake sale hosted by the Wildwood community to benefit the 1K Project (https:// www.1kproject.org/). This established, volunteer-driven project passes donations directly to Ukrainian families in need, with each $1,000 raised supporting a single family. “Already, funds are supporting a single mother of three named Viktoryia from Snigurivka. She is using this funding to buy food and medicine for her family. We look forward to raising more funds to support others like her,” said Xenia Meyer. Families from across Piedmont participated by contributing baked goods, flowers, crafts for sale, and direct donations totaling $5,600. That’s tantalizingly close to directly helping six Ukrainian families who are facing situations we shudder to imagine. We are deeply grateful to Piedmonters for their support and care for these families. To continue this initiative, the Piedmont community has banded together to establish a dedicated sponsor page with a $10k goal to support ten struggling families. See https://1kproject.org/piedmont for more details on how to make your tax-deductible donation. articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Advanced Acting class will perform William Golding’s Lord of the Flies in five performances from Thursday through Sunday, March 31 to April 3. The novel Lord of the Flies, adapted for the stage by Nigel Williams, is part of Piedmont’s freshman year English curriculum. Williams’ stage adaptation follows the plot of the novel – a group of British boys get stranded and are forced to face horrifying beasties on an island after their plane crashes on the island. Acting students of all genders will perform roles as the English boys, including speaking with a British dialect. What happens when young boys are left alone on an island with no structure? “The answer is pretty terrifying,” said cast member PHS junior Chloe Kibarian. The production is rated PG-13 for violence. The cast features Advanced Acting juniors and seniors Theo Arenstam (Simon-Sat, Sun 6pm), Liam Gordon (Simon-Thurs, Fri, Sun 1pm), Milani Juarbe (Robert), Sarone Kelete (Henry), Chloe Kibarian (Perceval-Fri/ Sun), Molly McWeeny (Piggy), Fernanda Meagher (Roger), Izzy Rosselli (Maurice), Erik Stenstrom (Eric), Joyce Stern (Ralph), Katherine Stormer (Perceval-Thurs/Sat), Holden Temple (Jack), John Gross Whitaker (Sam), and Charles E. White (Henry). Director Kimberly Taylor said, “I am grateful that the class is able to perform at the Piedmont Center for the Arts once more after the last successful collaboration there for the production of Lisa Loomer’s Roe immediately prior to the pandemic shutdown in March 2020. The Piedmont Center for the Arts allows us the flexibility to create unique seating configurations. For this show, audience members will be close to the action and will feel like they’re on the island, too,” she said. Lord of the Flies performances are Thursday through Saturday, March 31 to April 2 at 7:00 p.m., with two performances on Sunday, April 3 at 1 p.m. and 6 p.m. Tickets are $10 for students and $17 for general admission. The Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue across the street from the high school. All events at the Piedmont Center for the Arts require audience members to present proof of full vaccination plus booster, as well as proper masking inside. articles.text: On Friday, March 24, this reporter received an invitation to Ted Scherman’s 7th grade core class for an Inside the Classroom story. Instead of sitting in the back of the class to take notes for a story on the students studies, I was asked to stand at the front and take the microphone. The students were studying about the Protestant Reformation, and they had decided to create a newspaper. So I donned my press pass, and arrived with a recorder, camera, and typewriter to encourage all the budding journalists. I placed my Royal Safari typewriter, a DSLR camera, and copies of the Post on a desk for everyone to see, touch, and use. The students were attentive, polite and seemed genuinely interested in writing and journalism. I did my best to impart to them how much I enjoy getting to meet new people doing extraordinary things every week, and added a few secrets of the trade. We talked about the importance of receiving consent for recording audio, the California laws on paparazzi, and fair use for taking photos in public. I pointed out the press box in the paper, the proficiency of the Post’s city editor Allyson Aleksey, and we discussed why a writer might want to use a pseudonym (pen name). Scherman asked about the state of print journalism versus digital. I suggested that online publications are still in a wild west-like stage, and looking for ways to charge for content. During COVID, despite news being consumed at a high level, the number of newspapers that went out of business increased by the hundreds. However, I shared my observation and belief that there is a nostalgia for printed newspapers. Now it was time for the students to be part of the story I would be writing, so I turned the camera over to a couple of Piedmont Post delivery kids in the class, Henry Call and Colby Hong, hoping they were as good at photography as they were at chucking a paper to front doors. After describing the camera’s features, they took a few photos to get photo credits for this article. After handing out copies of the Post I asked for observations and received some of the following questions: What is the difference between a feature and a news story? How did the author get these photos? Do you ever get writer’s block? What do you do to get rid of it? The last question gave me the opportunity to introduce my typewriter, a somewhat ancient relic, a Royal Safari, circa 1965. There is something rewarding about seeing your words instantly in print, hearing the clickity clack of the typebar’s anvils hitting the paper, and the ding of the bell at the end of each line being typed onto a page. Another strategy to tackle writer’s block relies on far more contemporary technology, using Photos by Henry Call, Colby Hong, and Ted Scherman Daniela Lucaccin (left), Elsa Wallway, Claire Aubrecht, Thomas Moision and Colby Hong try their hand at writing poetry. the voice-to-text feature on a phone. (I am of generation Y, after all.) Students found that strategy more palatable than anything involving the 40-pound keyboard in front of them, a machine older than most of their parents. After the talk, students came to the front to try it out and learn how a typewriter ribbon works. After a few failed attempts by students, I explained the keys had to be pressed down much harder than on a computer and introduced the “hunt-and peck” two-finger typing style to some of them. When it looked like the typebars were jammed and the machine broken, the students learned about the “margin release” key. They were impressed that the typewriter ribbon had two colors, red and black. If they weren’t so well-mannered, they might have called me crazy when I explained that I had to re-ink the ribbon with a paint brush and stamp pad ink, one inch at a time. After gathering my stuff and saying goodbye, the students turned their attention to their daily lesson, watching a current events show and then creating their own fake Instagram or Facebook pages of someone from the Renaissance era. With the class back in the hands of the veteran teacher, I returned to my comfortable post at the Post, with a renewed appreciation for teachers and the remarkable curiosity of Mr. Scherman’s students. Back to the future: Ted Scherman looks over the work of Chloe Toyama (left) and Nora Trombi. Seventh graders Claire Aubrecht (left), Thomas Ero, and Colby Hong discover a dinosaur in the world of journalism, a manual Royal typewriter. Jay Russell adjusts the platen knob on a typewriter for students in Ted Scherman’s class. Jeannie Choi (left) watches reporter Jay Russell describe the Piedmont Post.

I pointed out the press box in the paper, the proficiency of the Post’s city editor Allyson Aleksey, and we discussed why a writer might want to use a pseudonym (pen name). Scherman asked about the state of print journalism versus digital. I suggested that online publications are still in a wild Students in Ted Scherman’s class learn about typewriters west-like stage, and looking for ways to charge for content. During COVID, despite news being consumed at a high level, the number of newspapers that went out of business increased by the hundreds. However, I shared my observation and belief that there is a nostalgia for printed newspapers. Now it was time for the students to be part of the story I would be writing, so I turned the camera over to a couple of Piedmont Post delivery kids in the class, Henry Call and Colby Hong, hoping they were as good at photography as they were at chucking a paper to front doors. After describing the camera’s features, they took a few photos to get photo credits for this article. After handing out copies of the Post I asked for observations and received some of the following questions: What is the difference between a feature and a news story? How did the author get these photos? Do you ever get writer’s block? What do you do to get rid of it? The last question gave me the opportunity to introduce my typewriter, a somewhat ancient relic, a Royal Safari, circa 1965. There is something rewarding about seeing your words instantly in print, hearing the clickity clack of the typebar’s anvils hitting the paper, and the ding of the bell at the end of each line being typed onto a page. Another strategy to tackle writer’s block relies on far more contemporary technology, using Photos by Henry Call, Colby Hong, and Ted Scherman Daniela Lucaccin (left), Elsa Wallway, Claire Aubrecht, Thomas Moision and Colby Hong try their hand at writing poetry. the voice-to-text feature on a phone. (I am of generation Y, after all.) Students found that strategy more palatable than anything involving the 40-pound keyboard in front of them, a machine older than most of their parents. After the talk, students came to the front to try it out and learn how a typewriter ribbon works. After a few failed attempts by students, I explained the keys had to be pressed down much harder than on a computer and introduced the “hunt-and peck” two-finger typing style to some of them. When it looked like the typebars were jammed and the machine broken, the students learned about the “margin release” key. They were impressed that the typewriter ribbon had two colors, red and black. If they weren’t so well-mannered, they might have called me crazy when I explained that I had to re-ink the ribbon with a paint brush and stamp pad ink, one inch at a time. After gathering my stuff and saying goodbye, the students turned their attention to their daily lesson, watching a current events show and then creating their own fake Instagram or Facebook pages of someone from the Renaissance era. With the class back in the hands of the veteran teacher, I returned to my comfortable post at the Post, with a renewed appreciation for teachers and the remarkable curiosity of Mr. Scherman’s students. Back to the future: Ted Scherman looks over the work of Chloe Toyama (left) and Nora Trombi. Seventh graders Claire Aubrecht (left), Thomas Ero, and Colby Hong discover a dinosaur in the world of journalism, a manual Royal typewriter. Jay Russell adjusts the platen knob on a typewriter for students in Ted Scherman’s class. Jeannie Choi (left) watches reporter Jay Russell describe the Piedmont Post.

articles.text: At the onset of the COVID- 19 pandemic, many pediatric services such as tutoring, counseling, physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy and other health care and educational services, switched from in-person to virtual formats. Initially, this transition was necessary due to quarantine conditions as we tried our best to support kids and families while unable to see them in-person. But now that practitioners have had a few years with this service delivery model, and are now presented with options: what does the future look like for pediatric services? Has teletherapy (via real time video conferencing) proven to be successful enough to sustain learning success and comparable to face-toface support? A review of the initial research reveals that teletherapy may be as effective as face-to-face interventions, across disciplines and for a variety of clinical outcomes. While there is more research to be done in this area, we are encouraged that the studies thus far do not demonstrate inferior outcomes with virtual vs in-person scenarios. The teletherapy studies examine 3 teletherapy models. First, teletherapy was shown to be successful in terms of providing educational information (written material, videos, etc.) directly to parents. Second, teletherapy was shown to be effective as a method of providing parent mediated support known as parent coaching in which, for example, the parent is Initial research indicates that teletherapy is effective. coached on how to implement a particular instructional or therapeutic program. And third, teletherapy was shown to be an effective platform for direct therapist/ child real-time treatment which shares many of the underlying principles as face-to-face therapy. There are obvious logistical advantages of teletherapy, such as reducing family stress during the busy after-school hours by cutting down on the amount of travel time needed to access the services and allowing children access to specialists who may be outside of the family’s geographic area. And there are obvious logistical elements, such as access to quality technology and physical home set up, which must be in place to ensure a successful virtual session. Taking into account these, and other logistical elements, can we develop a roadmap which allows service providers to maximally leverage the advantages provided by technology into our clinical practice ongoing, and provide families with increased access, options and convenience? Since the research is showing us that teletherapy is generally an effective service delivery model for educational and therapeutic services for children, perhaps over the next few years clinicians can focus on further exploration of questions such as for whom and under exactly which conditions is virtual vs in-person indicated. Katie Pengilly, MA, CCC, SLP, is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn. pengilly@speechinc.com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C .

articles.text: Scouting volunteers will be recognized at the Piedmont Council’s Annual Recognition Dinner to take place on Thursday, April 7, at the Guild Hall in Piedmont Community Church. “Our volunteers support our local youth development, and provide service to the greater community as well,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “They are guiding these youth through service projects that impact our community right now, such as Scouting for Food, creek clean ups, and more. But their impact also continues for decades, as today’s Scouts carry the ethic of service throughout their lifetime.” The Silver Beaver recognition is the highest recognition a council can give a volunteer. This year’s honoree is Seth Hilton. The selection committee was chaired by Sue Smegal, and included many longstanding Piedmont leaders. Hilton was chosen for his calm and steady leadership as council president through uniquely challenging times. As he settled into the second year of his tenure, he helped the council navigate COVID, social distancing impacts on program, challenges faced by the National council, and the selection of a new executive director/Scout Executive. In his professional life, he is a partner with Stoel Rives LLP. His practice includes advising independent energy produccouncil made it through these challenges in the best shape possible.” At the dinner, the council will also recognize other volunteers who have stepped up, in some cases for many, many years. Principal awards include: Silver Beaver: Seth Hilton District Award of Merit: Michael Bandrowski and Lisa Gros William Peterson Youth Award: Mollie King and Jack Gros President’s Award: Lisa Reynolds Distinguished Scouter awards will go to volunteers who have contributed strongly to the Scout program in their own Packs, Troops and coed units over the past year. The dinner is open to community members. Tickets are available online at www.piedmontbsa. org. For more information, call the Piedmont Scout office at 547- 4493. articles.text: Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) has announced that the annual Spring Fling gala, titled “Under a Piedmont Sky” this year, will be held in person on Friday, May 6 on Magnolia Avenue outside the Piedmont Center for the Arts and the new school theater. “We decided to have a blockparty style event this year,” said PEF Executive Director Heather Frank. “Piedmont has three years’ worth of elementary parents who haven’t experienced an in-person Spring Fling. We wanted to be able to share the fun with as many people as possible, as safely as possible.” Though the event hasn’t been held in town in many years, the foundation was determined to find a way to do it as part of building the elementary school community while showcasing Piedmont itself. The event will feature snacks, cocktails, a silent auction, and a set by Piedmont’s own Russell Simon, with popular bluegrass band Rusty Stringfield. “Spring Fling brings people together to share memories of the year that was, and to look forward to the year ahead, all over music, wine, and snacks,” said former Spring Fling Chair Amber Brumfiel. Andrea Horvath and Lisa Peters have been working closely with the City, police, fire, and school district to get the appropriate permits, keeping safety a priority. The January camp auction was successful, and there are a few parent theme parties being planned. An online auction will be available in April. Comings & Goings – portraits of students when they were in 1st grade and fifth grade – are on sale now at PiedmontSpringFling.org. This year’s fund-a-need will support PUSD’s Diversity, Equity and Inclusion programming. Funds raised through Spring Fling auctions and events directly support Beach, Havens, and Wildwood elementary schools. Visit PiedmontSpringFling.org to learn more about sponsorship and volunteer opportunities. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community. tel: 510-658-2588 www.piedmontfuneralservices.com 5000 piedmont ave., oakland, ca (fd#2210)

articles.text: Members of Highlander Robotics with their Engineering Inspiration Award. Twenty-five students from Highlander Robotics, Piedmont High School’s robotics team, traveled to UC Davis last weekend for the FIRST Robotics Competition’s Sacramento Regional Tournament and won an award that will take them to the FRC World Championship in Houston in three weeks. The FIRST Robotics Competition announces a new game in January each year to be played by two alliances of three robots, built by 9th to 12th grade students, in an arena about the size of a basketball court. An entirely new robot must be constructed for each season, and competitions begin 8 weeks after kickoff. In this year’s game, called Rapid React, robots up to 120 pounds score points by collecting and shooting 9.5-inch-wide tennis balls into an 8-foot high 4-foot wide funnel before climbing a set of inclined monkey bars. Teams can win a number of awards based on the performance of their robots; the quality, innovation, and creativity of their designs; and the impact they make on their communities. In their first in-person regional tournament, the Highlanders competed with a 109- pound, 30-inch-square robot named “Selkie”. The tournament included 42 other teams who had come from as far as Mumbai and Taipei. After finishing 11 qualifying matches with a 7-win 4-loss record, the Highlanders ranked 5th, behind three former world champions and a veteran team from Orange County. After advancing to the playoffs as the third seeded alliance captain, the team won two straight quarterfinal matches before being eliminated in the semifinals by the second seed team captained by 2019 world champions, The Greybots, from Atascadero. In addition to bids to the world championship given to members of the winning alliance, two awards are given with the most prestigious judged awards, so some small hope remained. “It’s been a dream since 7th grade. I knew there was still a very slim chance but we’d been waiting through the awards and hadn’t gotten any”. When [they announced] we won the Engineering Inspiration Award, we were extremely surprised,” said team captain Charlie Lambert. The Engineering Inspiration award celebrates outstanding success in advancing respect and appreciation for engineering within a team’s community. This recognized their contributions in advocating for Piedmont High School’s new Fabrication Lab, supporting Piedmont Makers fundraiser for the lab, efforts towards gender parity on the team, and mentoring other local robotics teams. In addition to qualifying the team for the world championship, the team also had its $5000 registration fee sponsored by NASA. Selkie was operated by Vaughn Khouri and Asha Byers and supported by drive coach Charlie Lambert, technician Valentina Prieto Black, and human player Arun Brahma. Alex Ware led the pit crew which kept the robot running smoothly through 15 full contact matches with turnarounds as quick as 30 minVaughn Khouri, Asha Byers, and Charlie Lambert of the drive team perform last-minute checks before competing. Selkie (left) climbs using tape measures and a carbon fiber hook alongside its alliance partner. Beck Peterson and Alex Ware of the pit crew do routine maintenance to keep Selkie running between matches. utes. Jasper Tripp and Charlie Clowes ran scouting operations with a team of 11 which informed alliance selection for the playoffs. Chloe Kessinger and Lewy Seiden acted as team ambassadors, answering questions, building connections with other teams, and representing the team to FIRST Judges. Highlander Robotics was founded in 2019 by brothers Henry and Charlie Lambert and now is comprised of 31 students from Piedmont High School, College Preparatory School, Las Lomas High School, and Head Royce Upper School. For more information contact Kevin Clark at kevin.clark@gmail.com.

articles.text: Piedmont Scouts in Troop 6, based at Corpus Christi Church, held their 2nd annual plant sale over the last two weekends to a resounding success. The Troop has been propagating plants from seeds since the beginning of January and successfully raised over 2000 seedlings, with an amazing variety of plants. There were 30 varieties of tomatoes, 10 varieties of pepper, many varieties of squash, cucumbers and herbs, all grown from seed. articles.text: Piedmont’s tennis team continues to power through its league schedule with a 6-1 victory over San Leandro at the Pirates’ home courts on Thursday, March 24. The match brings Piedmont’s overall record to 8-1 and 5-0 with league opponents. “The boys played well with our only loss at number one singles. Ben Breber started out strong but started to have trouble with his serve in the middle of the first set against a very good opponent. Kai Baudendistel, who usually plays doubles, played almost flawlessly [at No. 3 singles],” said coach Jim Landes. Piedmont has a critical opponent today, Wednesday, March 30 in San Francisco against University. The Red Devils won the last two North Coast section team championships (2018 and 2019) and beat Piedmont 4-3 in 2018 for the title. University also defeated PHS 5-2 in April last year. “We’ll see how University is; they seem to have a strong team. They’ll be a good measuring point for us,” said Landes. Against a weaker opponent in San Leandro, Piedmont was able to shuffle the lineup and give No. 1 Charlie Lambert and No. 2 Lenni Burchardt the day off. In singles, Breber took the team’s lone loss, 6-3, 6-0, to Elijah Cho. Breber usually plays at the No. 3 spot. Monte Imburg, bumped up to No. 2 singles, won 6-2, 6-2. Baudendistel had a double-bagel victory at No. 3, 6-0, 6-0, and Charlie Sullivan won 6-0, 6-1 at No. 4. In doubles, Piedmont swept the field. Oliver Maxwell and Brady Colbert won 6-2, 6-2 at No. 1, Carson Hicks and Jacob Hsia won 6-0, 6-0 at No. 2, and Graham Alban and Nick King won 6-0, 6-0 at No. 3. Tuesday vs. Berkeley The Highlanders hosted Berkeley last night, March 29. See next week’s Post for match details. Kai Baudendistel shut out his San Leandro opponent, 6-0, 6-0. Ben Breber, playing No. 1 singles, lost against San Leandro.

articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team is coming off of two consecutive wins against upper Foothill Division opponents, defeating San Leandro 5-3 on Wednesday, March 23 at Humphries Diamond, and Castro Valley 3-1 at the Trojans’ field on Friday, March 25. The Highlanders won both games behind strong pitching performances of Tobin Cantrill and Alex Tafapolsky, who each recorded a complete game. Cantrill struck out seven San Leandro batters with two walks and hits allowed, while Tafapolsky also struck out seven in the game with Castro Valley, with four hits allowed and two walks. “They are throwing strikes and making the hitters feel uncomfortable, which is what we’re trying to do as a pitcher. Tobin has solidified himself as our number one guy. To carry a no-hitter into the sixth is a great feather in his cap,” said coach Eric Olson. Both seniors, it marked both pitchers’ first complete games. Cantrill carried a no-hitter heading into the top of the sixth inning. “I love playing with a lead and having that all the way to the sixth was great. My curveball was feeling great, so I knew Davis [Alazraqui] was going to call a bunch of first-pitch curveballs. It was hitting the spot,” said Cantrill. Piedmont’s league schedule in the Shoreline Division opens with games with Hayward, San Lorenzo, Mt. Eden, Tennyson, and Encinal. The teams will play twice, with a home and away game. Through 10 games, Alazraqui, the senior catcher, leads the team with a sterling .379 batting average. “I’m just hitting with confidence, knowing that if I hit it, it’s going to go far. I’ve put on some weight and that helps the ball travel,” said Alazraqui. 5-3 win vs. San Leandro Piedmont scored three runs in the bottom of the first inning and another two in the bottom of the second to jump ahead 5-0. Photo by Mark Aikawa Tobin Cantrill pitched a complete game with seven strikeouts versus San Leandro. Staff Photo Alex Tafapolsky pitched a complete game against Castro Valley with seven strikeouts and four hits allowed. San Leandro gained some steam in the top of the sixth with three runs, but that was the only time they would score. In the bottom of the first, freshman centerfielder Markos Lagios got the game started in the right direction with a single, then stealing second base. With one out, Peter Krumins smacked a single to bring Lagios around to score, followed by Alazraqui’s double to score Krumins. Nico Defazio hit the first of his two doubles to push Alazraqui to third. He then scored on a wild pitch. Piedmont’s two runs in the bottom of the second came with two outs. Aikawa got on with a Staff Photo Markos Lagios leaps to make a catch in centerfield. single, followed by Krumins who hit a ground ball that resulted in two throwing errors, bringing Aikawa in and advancing Krumins to third. Alazraqui hit an RBI single for a 5-0 lead. Final stats: Alazraqui was 2-for-3 with a double, two RBIs and a run scored. Defazio was 2-for-3 with two doubles. Lagios was 1-for-3 with a run scored. Krumins was 1-for-3 with two runs scored and an RBI. Cantrill pitched a complete game with seven strikeouts, two hits allowed, two earned runs, and two walks. 3-1 win vs. Castro Valley Piedmont scored all of its runs in the top of the second inning and Castro Valley scored its only run ;ate in the game – in the bottom of the seventh. In the top of the second, Evan McConathy launched a three-run homerun on the first pitch. Final stats: Evan McConathy was 1-for-3 with his homer, three RBIS, and a run scored. Ryan McConathy was 1-for-3 with a run scored. Alazraqui, Aikawa, and Lagios all were 1-for-3. Tafapolsky pitched a complete game with seven strikeouts, four hits allowed, one earned run, and two walks. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-4) hosts Hayward today at Witter Field, Wednesday, March 30 at 4:00 p.m. They head to Hayward on Friday, April 1 for a 4:00 p.m. game, and travel to Oakland Tech on Saturday, April 2 at 2:00 p.m.

articles.text: Photo by Mike McConathy Piedmont’s defense sets up against Encinal, a Shoreline Division team. As time continues to push toward the summer, more answers regarding the Piedmont High varsity football team are becoming firm. What we know is that the school will continues its historic 101-year varsity program. What we don’t is how the schedule will be created, or when, and with what teams. On March 15, Piedmont High principal Adam Littlefield announced at a virtual meeting with parents that four of the six teams in the Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division voted to not revise their schedules to accommodate Piedmont. this means that PHS will not be eligible to schedule league opponents, win a league championship, or earn any All-League recipients. “San Lorenzo, Kennedy, Newark and Alameda said no. What I did was reach out to the principals we haven’t heard from, and my message for them was to have those principals nudge their athletic directors to connect with Bradley [Smet],” said Littlefield during the meeting. Smet also spoke at the virtual meeting and confirmed Piedmont would be ineligible for a league title in the WACC in 2022. “The downside in not being attached to the WACC is no league championship or league awards… Yes, it’s correct we’re not currently in the Shoreline. We could force a vote on the 17 total schools to let us in the Shoreline, but if everyone is saying ‘No’ in our league, is it the right thing to force a vote on the other schools,” asked Smet. Littlefield said that he has been working with WACC commissioner Dave Kiesel to find alternative options so Piedmont could have a standard 10-game schedule. He indicated that Kiesel is working with him to identify teams in the North Coast Section, Northern Section, Central Coast, and San Joaquin Sections that would be willing to play Piedmont. Littlefield added that PHS athletic director Bradley Smet is focusing on schools within the Central Coast (where he is from), Northern, and Sac-Joaquin sections and is hoping to schedule four home games and six away. This could mean a lot of driving for parents. PHS would be eligible to qualify for a postseason by finishing with a .500 overall record. Teams are typically eligible to qualify for the playoffs base on a number of factors. Without options in the Shoreline Division of WACC or North Coast Section, Piedmont must finish with a positive overall win-loss record. Littlefield confirmed that the high school will arrange and provide all transportation for away games. Piedmont’s non-league status also means that the Junior Varsity team must revise its schedule to fit with the varsity game plan. The school is now 12 days into the hunt for a new head football coach after officially posting job opening on Friday, March 18. Mason Kimball with a forced fumble against former league opponent Bishop O’Dowd. Markos Lagios rushes for yardage against Mt. Eden.
articles.title: After 101 years, no league games for PHS football

articles.text: The PHS girls’ lacrosse team got its first league win in a big way. Playing before a home crowd at Witter Field on Friday, March 25, the Highlanders throttled the Washington Huskies 15-0. Piedmont led 13-0 at halftime and took its foot off the gas. PHS is 1-1 with league opponents, and has a favorable WACC schedule in the future, including Newark on April 1, Moreau Catholic on April 5, and Berkeley on April 22. With expected victories, Piedmont would qualify for the North Coast Section playoffs. “When I first set up the schedule, I wanted the girls to feel challenged and ready for league. I think we played great against our league opponents so far this year. The girls are having a lot of fun. Our record doesn’t show it (2-7), but they aren’t looking at records,” said coach Carlton Chan. The Highlanders prepare for a busy week with hosting NCS Division 2 opponent Miramonte on Thursday, March 31, league opponent Newark on Friday, April 1, then two game at Witter Field, Monday, April 4 vs. Tamalpais, and Moreau on April 5. Smet also spoke at the virtual meeting and confirmed Piedmont would be ineligible for a league title in the WACC in 2022. “The downside in not being attached to the WACC is no league championship or league awards… Yes, it’s correct we’re not currently in the Shoreline. We could force a vote on the 17 total schools to let us in the Shoreline, but if everyone is saying ‘No’ in our league, is it the right thing to force a vote on the other schools,” asked Smet. Littlefield said that he has been working with WACC commissioner Dave Kiesel to find alternative options so Piedmont could have a standard 10-game schedule. He indicated that Kiesel is working with him to identify teams in the North Coast Section, Northern Section, Central Coast, and San Joaquin Sections that would be willing to play Piedmont. Littlefield added that PHS athletic director Bradley Smet is focusing on schools within the Central Coast (where he is from), Northern, and Sac-Joaquin sections and is hoping to schedule four home games and six away. This could mean a lot of driving for parents. PHS would be eligible to qualify for a postseason by finishing with a .500 overall record. Teams are typically eligible to qualify for the playoffs base on a number of factors. Without options in the Shoreline Division of WACC or North Coast Section, Piedmont must finish with a positive overall win-loss record. Littlefield confirmed that the high school will arrange and provide all transportation for away games. Piedmont’s non-league status also means that the Junior Varsity team must revise its schedule to fit with the varsity game plan. The school is now 12 days into the hunt for a new head football coach after officially posting job opening on Friday, March 18. articles.text: Staff Photos Wilson Wong had a productive game with seven aces against Hayward. The PHS boys’ volleyball team defeated Hayward, 3-0, on Thursday, March 24 at Binks Rawlings Gym, with game scores of 25-12, 25-12, 25-14. The team was still without setter Shunji Higashi, meaning the bulk of the roster had to step up. “Coming into this game, we knew that losing would put everything on a downhill slope. Hayward has had its program one year longer than us. It’s great to test how we are. We dominated and played strong,” said junior captain Wilson Wong. Piedmont did well in getting its serves in against Hayward, recording 12 aces on the night including seven from Wong, four from John Champion, and one by Kai Lambert. “I’ve been working really hard on consistency and my top-spin serves. John and I have really been working hard on our topserves, we want to build consistency,” said Wong. Piedmont’s front line was also productive with middle blockers Mason Kimball and Felix Broach, often getting their hands on spike attempts to block shots. “We really focused in practice on blocking. We figured it out; we’re a good defensive team,” said Kimball. The Highlanders opened the first set with a 5-0 lead thanks to four consecutive aces by Wong. The Highlanders then won another four consecutive points before a service error, 9-2, then five of the next six points for a 14-3 lead. Hayward inched back to 17-8, but Piedmont’s work in front of the net continued to limit attacking options. Broach had two blocks in the remaining points, and Kimball had a kill for set-point. In the second set, Piedmont started similarly with the first five points to jump ahead 5-1 PHS’ first seven points were thanks to errors from the Farmers when either defending or trying to create an attack with nearly all of their spike attempts sailing out of bounds. Kimball had two spikes to put PHS ahead 11-4, and had another three kills to help win the set, 25-12. Piedmont closed the third set with another 10-plus point victory, 25-14. This time, the Farms jumped out to a 6-3 advantage and increased it to 10-6. However, PHS scored the next five points to go ahead 11-10. The Farmers gained the next two points to re-gain the lead at 12-11, but the Highlanders scored the next 10 points with the help of a Kimball block and spike, and three aces by Champion – putting PHS up 21-12, with Wong finishing it off with two aces. articles.text: Diego Rivera’s massive mural “Pan American Unity” will be on display on the main floor at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art through summer 2023. On June 17, 2021, Diego Rivera’s colossal fresco “Pan American Unity” was carefully moved from San Francisco’s City College to SFMOMA. The priceless 4,000-pound mural, created in 1940, is arguably one of San Francisco’s greatest art pieces of the 20th century. Rivera’s mural was the centerpiece of the Art in Action exhibit, which featured different artists engaged in creating art pieces while the public watched. The fresco on plaster is 670 by 2,260 centimeters and was created on 10 steel-framed panels bolted together and weighing about 21 tons. It was designed to be portable and was moved to the college campus from its original location on Treasure Island. It is the largest of the artist’s works, and completely spanned the narrow lobby of the Diego Rivera Theater at City College. A four-year, multimillion dollar undertaking resulted in its careful removal and transport across the city to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, where it is now on display through 2023, when it will return to City College to be installed in a new performing arts center. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/pan-american-unity/ to learn more.
articles.title: Diego Rivera’s historic “Pan American Unity” mural on view at SFMOMA

articles.text: At the close of its 2022 season, San Francisco Ballet will honor the 37-year tenure of Artistic Director Helgi Tomasson with a gala performance. Tomasson has hand-selected ballets from the more than 50 works he choreographed and directed for San Francisco Ballet. The program includes The Fifth Season, Two Bits, pas de deux from Romeo and Juliet, and an excerpt from Harmony. Tomasson was a distinguished dancer before assuming artistic leadership of San Francisco Ballet in 1985. Under his direction, the Ballet became a company widely recognized as one of the finest in the world. Diego Rivera’s historic “Pan American Unity” mural on view at SFMOMA By Allyson Aleksey Diego Rivera’s massive mural “Pan American Unity” will be on display on the main floor at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art through summer 2023. On June 17, 2021, Diego Rivera’s colossal fresco “Pan American Unity” was carefully moved from San Francisco’s City College to SFMOMA. The priceless 4,000-pound mural, created in 1940, is arguably one of San Francisco’s greatest art pieces of the 20th century. Rivera’s mural was the centerpiece of the Art in Action exhibit, which featured different artists engaged in creating art pieces while the public watched. The fresco on plaster is 670 by 2,260 centimeters and was created on 10 steel-framed panels bolted together and weighing about 21 tons. It was designed to be portable and was moved to the college campus from its original location on Treasure Island. It is the largest of the artist’s works, and completely spanned the narrow lobby of the Diego Rivera Theater at City College. A four-year, multimillion dollar undertaking resulted in its careful removal and transport across the city to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, where it is now on display through 2023, when it will return to City College to be installed in a new performing arts center. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/pan-american-unity/ to learn more. articles.text: Jim Callahan’s Piedmont Piano Company is hosting a benefit concert tomorrow, Thursday, March 31, for humanitarian efforts in Ukraine. The concert, entitled “My Ordinary Family,” is presented by the non-profit organization Jazz at the Ballroom. Music will be set to the true story of August Paszkudzki, a lover of American jazz and native of Ukraine. Paszkudzki’s grandson, pianist Konrad Paszkudzki, will be joined by vocalist Olivia Chindamo and jazz artist Carmen Bradford. The program includes a collection of songs between the 1930’s and 1940’s. All proceeds from the concert will go to the International Rescue Committee (IRC) in Ukraine. The concert begins at 7 p.m. and live stream access will be available beginning 6:45 p.m. Visit https://www.piedmontpiano.com/calendar/2022/3/31/benefit-for-ukraine to obtain tickets to either live-stream or in-person access. “My Ordinary Family” is a benefit concert for victims of the RussoUkrainian conflict. ®

articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir hosted its Making History Concert on Saturday, March 19 at First Congregational Church of Berkeley. The concert, which celebrated voices of Black, Indigenous, and people of color (BIPOC), was filled with energizing performances from PEBCC’s four performing choirs and featured two world premieres, four student conductors, and one dance group reflecting the diverse East Bay community. A highlight of the night was Ecco’s Conducting Scholars, Tomo Takeuchi, George Mouratoff, Khoa Sands, and Anna Klein, conducting their peers in Estonian Lullabies. This was especially meaningful as Artistic Director, Eric Tuan, got his start conducting when he was a singer with the Choir. While each of the conductors had a different style, they demonstrated their ability to lead their peers through their interpretation of Veljo Tormis’ Estonian folk melodies with grace and expression. Ancora performed the World Premiere of A Portrait in Greys by local composer Jens Ibsen. Ibsen, who attended the concert, shared advice for young people about composing. “Own that you have something to say. I started as a singer and thought composing would be a hobby. I never could have dreamed I’d be doing things with my original music like I’m doing now…Composing means having something to say. You have to put that out there. Do yourself that kindness and go ahead and say it. The world is going to be better with more good music out there.” Ancora’s performance blended beautiful, haunting expressive vocal lines and crystal clear, well blended tone to bring this piece and the other selections to life. As the penultimate song of the evening, Ensemble performed a new piece, When I Sing, composed by Artistic Director Eric Tuan and commissioned by Yonchu Jenkins and Toshi Takeuchi. It was commissioned “to give back to the wonderful choir community and to show the beauty in music and the joy of singing as we emerge from these difficult times,” explained Tuan. Audience members couldn’t help but smile as the singers enveloped the concert hall in melodies of joy and optimism as they moved from singing to unison and ending the song in four-part harmony. The concert closed with Bolo Bolo Sab Mil Bolo, a collaboration between Ensemble and Kali Futnami’s youth bharatanatyam dancers. “The song is a well-loved devotional song to Shiva,” explained Futami. “Bharatanatyam dance is a very ancient South Indian classical dance form that is very rhythmic. The dancers helped to create the choreography. This is about Shiva, who is a dancer. The first sound of the universe is the sound of his drum, so the dancers show this and the little drum he carries. It was a full sensory experience as the dancers added movement and body percussion to Shiva Bhajan’s devotional song.” Bolo Bolo Ensemble and Kali Futnani dancers perform with Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir in a March 19 concert titled Making History. articles.text: Robert Redford and Nick Nolte star in A Walk in the Woods. A Walk in the Woods, released in 2015 and now streaming on Netflix and Prime, is a humorous geezer flick that is essentially a long hike on the Appalachian Trail, one in which two old friends renew an almost forgotten bond. Once the two central characters – Robert Redford as Bill Bryson and his out of shape bud, Stephen Katz, played by Nick Nolte – step off the parking lot tarmac and begin their journey, there’s not a lot to do other than put one foot in front of the other and engage in yearbook conversation. Nevertheless, this story has more than a few comic moments that made me smile and laugh out loud. Nolte as Katz is a hoot. When Bryson hit the trail, and later wrote the hugely popular novel of the same name, he was 47. Redford was heading toward 80, give or take, and Nolte was 74. These are not two guys having a midlife crisis, but perhaps hoping to encounter an epiphany in the backwoods while hiking the length of the Appalachian Trail, 2200 miles, from Georgia to Maine. In essence, they’re two codgers who’ve convinced themselves that a change of scenery (or a splash of adventure) might give than a fresh outlook on life. The film could have taken artistic license with the book and written lots of dialogue, even voice over, about how old guys just don’t casually sling a 60-pound pack over their aging shoulders and spend weeks walking through the Smokey Mountains, sleeping on the ground in their tent. When you’re 70+, the body has long ago begun to signal that “the golden years” was a slogan invented to sell cruise ship jaunts and never intended to indicate that you should be spending hours debating the efficacy of a hiking boot or a backpack with a kid in his early twenties who works at REI. A Walk in the Woods involves old dude conversations, but not how mortality haunts each day. Instead, they sit around a campfire and have friendly chats, and who better to do that than Nolte and Redford. There are more than a few gags, most taking place in small towns, off-trail. Katz has a conversation in a laundromat with a friendly, plus-size lady whose panties get caught in spin cycle and happens to have a jealous husband. Or the funny moment when they stop at a trail youth hostel, where Katz breaks the top bunk slats and lands on the bottom bunk on top of Bryson. One other thing: At the start of the hike, Katz and Bryson are almost like strangers. It’s been decades since they’ve hung out. But they work at what becomes an unforgettable reunion. Last point: Redford and Nolte are two actors who have demonstrated for decades that they can move across a wide spectrum of characters. Initially, Redford wanted to do this film with Paul Newman; instead, it remained on his shelf far too long. But as it turned out, that’s part of its charm. A Walk in the Woods. Directed by Ken Kwapis. Starring Robert Redford, Emma Thompson and Nick Nolte. 1 hr., 44 min. Rated R. Streaming on Netflix and Prime. Originally published in the Post in 2015.
articles.title: A Walk in the Woods a gem with Redford & Nolte

articles.text: The Boy in the Striped Pajamas, released in 2008 and now streaming on Prime, is a heart-rending film, adapted from the young adult novel by John Boyle. This film is for middle school kids, teens and adults, and ideally should be watched with parents and discussed afterward. It captures the atrocities of the World War II Holocaust from the perspective of an 8-year-old boy, Bruno. The boy’s father is a high-ranking Nazi officer, Ralf (David Thewlis), who is promoted to be the commandant of what is euphemistically referred to as a “farm” somewhere in Poland. What this this means to Bruno is that he must leave Berlin, his familiar home and friends, and move to a remote countryside mansion where he feels suddenly isolated, lonely. Upon arriving, he is told by his mother, Elsa (Vera Farmiga), that he must not wander beyond the backyard wall or into the dense woods beyond. As an aside, it is evident that Elsa accepts the term “farm” without questioning her husband about his duties, initially basking in his prestigious position, and enjoying her large new home. Bruno and his older sister, Grete (Amber Beattie), instead of attending school are provided with a tutor, Herr Listz (Jim Norton), who fills his lessons with anti-Semitic propaganda. Grete covers the walls of her bedroom with posters of Hitler and Hitler youth. She is also enamored with a young, sadistic Nazi lieutenant, Kurt Kotler (Rupert Friend), his father’s adjutant. Bruno, soon feeling bored, begins to wander the compound, and though he has been admonished to remain within the walls, he finds a gate and ventures into the dense woods. He soon discovers a barbed-wire fence that encloses an expansive camp. On the other side of the wire he sees a boy his own age, wearing striped pajamas, and playing in the dirt. Sitting down on the other side of the fence, Bruno asks him his name. The boy stares through the fence, and finally says Shmuel (Jack Scanlon). Bruno, hungry for companionship, in all his innocence, begins what becomes an almost daily visit and conversation (he often brings the boy food), never suspecting that Shmuel is a prisoner and that the “farm” is, in reality, a death camp for Jews. Never revealing to his parents that he leaves the house grounds, or that he has found a new friend, Bruno, curious, does ask his mother about the smoke coming from the farm, and about the old man, Pavel (David Haymon), who works in their kitchen and is dressed in the same pants and shirt as is Shmuel. The answers to his questions are always vague. But unbeknownst to his father, Bruno does happen to watch him and a group of Nazi officers watching a propaganda film wherein the camp is shown to be a happy, almost joyous place for all those living inside the fence. One day Shmuel mentions that he can’t find his father, and Bruno offers to help find him. And so the boys devise a plan. Shmuel will bring a set of pajamas and cap (to hide Bruno’s unshaved head) the next day, and leaving his own clothes behind, Bruno crawls under the wire, dresses in the striped clothes, and the two will set off into the camp to locate the father. Watching the two walk together across a field, and toward the barracks in the distance, creates a chilling tableau. What awaits them is a truth beyond their comprehension. And it is a truth that Elsa has only recently come to suspect. And when she can’t find her son in the house or in the yard, she and Elsa begin a search w that is terrifying (she later calls Ralf), as is the conclusion of this powerful film. The Boy in the Striped Pajamas. Directed by Mark Herman. Released in 2008 by Miramax Films. Starring Asa Butterfield, Vera Farmiga, and David Thewlis. 1 hr., 34 min. Rated PG-13. Now streaming on Prime.
articles.title: The Boy in the Striped Pajamas a powerful reminder of the Holocaust

And it is a truth that Elsa has only recently come to suspect. And when she can’t find her son in the house or in the yard, she and Elsa begin a search w that is terrifying (she later calls Ralf), as is the conclusion of this powerful film. articles.text: Rango, released in 2011, and now streaming on HBO MAX/ Prime, is pure enjoyment to watch. Kids, say, eight and above, will enjoy this animated feature for its clever, comedic, western motif. At the outset, Rango (Johnny Depp) isn’t a gun slinging cliché. He’s a pet chameleon riding along in the back of the family station wagon, comfortably ensconced in a glass terrarium. The car has an accident and Rango’s container bounces out. He finds himself stranded on the side of a highway in the Mojave Desert. It’s hot, and he’s thirsty. After taking the advice of an armadillo named Roadkill (Alfred Molina), who caused the wreck, Rango heads out into some very forbidding territory. He eventually reaches a small western-looking town called Dirt, a place filled with talking animals such as badgers, toads, owls and possums. The mayor of Dirt is a slow-moving turtle (Ned Beatty), and the most fearsome gunslinger in town is a dude named Rattlesnake Jake (Bill Nighy). He also meets an attractive desert iguana (soon to become his love interest) named Beans (Isla Fisher). When asked who he is, Rango tells the town folks that he is a tough drifter, and he embellishes his reputation by explaining that he has killed a dangerous gang called the Jenkins Brothers with A scene from Rango. just one bullet. And thus Rango reinvents himself from being a household pet into a hard case Sergio Leone, Clint Eastwood type hombre. Before long Rango meets up with Bad Bill (Ray Winstone) a local, swaggering Gila monster. On the verge of a shootout, Rango is saved by a swooping hawk that terrifies Bad Bill. During the mayhem, Rango knocks down a water tower crushing the bird. Mayor turtle is so impressed by Rango that he appoints him town sheriff. But the denizens of Dirt still worry about the possible return of Rattlesnake Jake. As sheriff, gun-totting Rango embarks on a number of adventures, to include facing down a gang of bank robbers led by a mole named Balthasar (Harry Dean Stanton). He even organizes a posse, and searches for the cause of Dirt’s awful drought (something nefarious is happening to the town’s water supply). Consider the water issue a way that director Gore Verbinski pays homage, however indirectly, to the film Chinatown. Of course, there are more adventures for Rango (he and Bean get locked in the bank’s vault). But in the end, consider it a fun, sophisticated, sometimes over-the-top spaghetti western with a swashbuckling spirit that will entertain kids of all ages. Rango. Directed by Gore Verbinski. Animated. With the voices of Johnny Depp, Isla Fisher, and Abigail Breslin. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG. Released in theaters 2011. Now streaming on Prime/HBO Max.

articles.text: Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen (aka T-2), released in 2009 like its precursor is a kid magnet. This big tent franchise is loud, kinetic and superbly stylized. It is based on Hasboro toys, those plastic robots (Autobots and Decepticons) that can be transformed into machinery and were featured in television cartoons and comic books. The first film, T-1, directed by Michael Bay, grossed $708 million worldwide, won three awards for visual effects and was nominated for three Academy Awards. The story was original (if a bit convoluted) and a veritable buffet of CGI and surround sound. At the center of the original Transformers is Sam Witwicky (Shia LaBeouf) and Mikaela Barnes (Megan Fox), high school seniors, who find themselves caught up in an ancient struggle between the evil Decepticons (Megatron, Blackout, Scorponok, Frenzy, Barricade, Devastator) and the good Autobots (Optimus Prime, Jazz, Bumblebee, Ironhide, Ratchet). Though it’s more a ride than a story – more action than introspection – embedded in the movie is a coming of age, first car, first girlfriend narrative that is sweet and compelling. The challenge for the T-2 sequel was how to recapture those jaw-dropping moments when, for the first time, filmgoers watched in stunned silence as incredible pieces of machinery were transformed into Bots, good and bad, followed by sounds of metal tearing, and orange volcaA scene from Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen. nic explosions. Regrettably, T-2 is unable to fulfill the visceral excitement of T-1. The magic of the Bots transforming is now familiar. The Bot battle scenes, still a ballet of destruction, seem almost predictable. The chemistry between Sam and Mikaela is well established and reduced to whether they will actually say to one another, “I love you.” Is it a cinematic spectacle, a ride to be enjoyed for the sheer, overwhelming special effects and visual artistry? Indeed. But the story – the resurrection of the Decepticons (Megatron, buried in the Laurentian Abyss, in particular) and their search for the All Spark – has grown even thinner. The screenwriters, likely sensing their own lack of inspiration, attempt to jack up the script with comic relief. John Turturro’s role as Agent Simmons in T-1 is reprised only to descend into silliness. Most egregious is the stereotyping of two new Autobots, Skids and Mudflap, two trashtalking Bot-homies from the hood. The only thing they’re not wearing is black face. Though meant to be funny, they are simply evidence of the obvious cultural and racial myopia of the writers and the director and a failure to find something to write about that is fresh and gripping. Putting all that aside, T-2 earned its keep at the box office. There are fans of the franchise as loyal as those Potter heads who, like the Transformer crowd, believe not in the destination but in the journey. Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen. Starring Shia LaBeouf, Megan Fox, Josh Duhamel. Directed by Michael Bay. 2 hrs., 29 min. Rated PG-13. Reprinted from 2009.
articles.title: Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen not the same as the original

articles.text: Guitarist John Scofield and bass player Dave Holland will perform together live in Miner Auditorium at SF Jazz on April 15. Scofield and Holland are considered two of the most influential instrumentalists in modern jazz; Scofield performed with numerous small combos, trios, and quartets, and Holland has performed publicly for more than five decades. The two jazz stars started working together a few years ago and have created an impressive portfolio together. They both have contributed original compositions to a duo repertoire that will encompass a wide selection of jazz standards. All SF JAZZ members are welcome to visit the Leaders Circle prior to the performance for complimentary drinks and refreshments. The performance will begin at 7:30 p.m. Visit https://www.sfjazz. org/tickets/productions/johnscofield-dave-holland-2122/ to obtain tickets. John Scofield Photo by Nick Suttle

articles.text: Archaeologists continue to make some of the most marvelous discoveries. While we look into the deepest recesses of humanity, we find that we are able to look at ourselves in the mirror. Pictorial art dates back to Neanderthal days; approximately 64,000 years ago. Homo sapiens left cave paintings in Chauvet and Lascaux. Less is known about prehistoric musical instruments. Logic tells us that music must have played an important part from the beginning. Children do not need to be taught to clap their hands. Early humans surely must have learned to sing simply by discovering their own voices or listening to the howl of animals. There is an Italian saying: “anyone who has a voice can sing”. Instrumental music developed later. The earliest musical instrument discovered was a Neanderthal flute made of bone some 50,000 to 60,000 years ago. Early humans made flutes of bone and wood. Early trumpets were made from the horns of animals. The earliest stringed instruments developed at the same time as the bow and arrow. With civilization came the development of music notation. The Sumerians used music notation and the Greeks were past masters of the musical art. These were the inspirations for modern opera. Somewhat akin to opera is the Requiem. For sheer drama, nothing tops the Requiem by Verdi. The Stabat Mater by Dvorak probes the human soul. This past weekend I discovered another great work, this one a German Requiem by Johannes Brahms. In two performances under the inspired direction of David Morales, both concerts featured Morales’ Cantare Chorale, a full symphony orchestra, spoken reflection by six young poets, and professional vocal soloists soprano Shawnette Sulker and baritone Torlef Borsting. If memory serves me correctly, Morales has been an inspiration in the East Bay community for some 50 years. He exemplifies the best of the unification of humanity. The chorus and orchestra are all ages, ethnicities and abilities. They all come together to express the highest ideals of humanity. And now a word about the PCO The same can be said of our own Piedmont Chamber Orchestra. Let us hope that the difficulties of the COVID pandemic are waning. The 4 p.m. concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday afternoon, March 26, was a festive event. A large audience was enthusiastic in its response. And the orchestra responded and played its heart out. It also helped to have Martha Stoddard as the conductor and Stuart Gronningen as manager. The Piedmont Chamber Orchestra is a community effort – the city’s hometown orchestra. It includes professional musicians playing alongside amateurs both old and young. Former Mayor McBain was there, but current members of the Piedmont city Council were notable by their absence. The general public knows that the Piedmont Center for the arts is the gem in the crown of Piedmont‘s cultural arts. A large festive crowd attended the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra concert on Saturday afternoon, March 26, at the Piedmont Center for the Arts.
