articles.text: Local pottery makers and ceramicists will discuss their artistry this Sunday, April 3, in an event hosted by Oakland Museum of California. Oakland Museum of California will host an informational discussion with Bay Area potters and ceramicists this Sunday, April 3, in the James Moore Theater. Featured local artists include Rosa Dorantes, Viviana Matsuda, and Chinzalee Sonami. The discussion will be held in conjunction with the museum’s ongoing exhibition, Edith Heath: A Life in Clay. The event will be moderated by Dorantes, Head of Ceramics at the Crucible, in a discussion with Sonami of Pala Ceramics in Oakland, and Mutsuda of Mud Witch in San Francisco. The event, titled “What Does it Mean to Endure?”, reflects on artistry and entrepreneurship. The three female artists will discuss Heath’s legacy in pottery and ceramics, and her uses of materials that are sustainable and easily found in California. Her love of natural landscapes shaped the quality of her designs and inspired her to seek clays from California rather than traditional white clay for dinnerware. The James Moore Theatre is located in the museum at 1000 Oak Street. Masks will continue to be required for all visitors, regardless of vaccination status. Adults must show proof of vaccination along with photo identification. Capacity is limited. The event will be held from 2 p.m. to 3:30 p.m. Visit ht t ps://museumca. org/2022/what-does-it-mean-endure-conversation-bay-area-potters to obtain tickets.
articles.title: Oakland Museum hosts pottery-making discussion this Sunday

After David Morales’ Sunday afternoon concert of the Brahms Requiem at the First Presbyterian Church in downtown Oakland, a number of us went to Marzano Restaurant on Park Boulevard. At the adjoining table were a number of young musicians, who told us about the Young People’s Symphony Orchestra concert tour planned for Europe this summer. It always amazes me how conductor David Ramadanoff is able to arrange memorable concert tours like these. The YPSO will perform concerts in Berlin, Leipzig, Prague and Vienna. This brings up other possibilities. Music in the summer Parents… If you are looking for things for your kids to do this Summer, please consider music camp. At this time of year, I always offer a few suggestions. The La Honda Music Camp is conveniently located in the San Francisco Bay Area. It is a beautiful place and the quality of the instruction is very high. If you happen to be in Europe, you should take advantage of the music festival in Narnia, Italy, directed by our good friend Cristiana Pegoraro. The festival combines many aspects of vocal arts such as opera and musical theater. There is also a very lively instrumental music program. Another high-level instrumental music program is the Altschuler Summer Music Institute in the Italian resort of Rimini. I found out about this program recently and was very impressed. Please note… and this is very important. Registration deadlines are fast approaching. Check out music camps as soon as possible. Musical life is not merely artistic. It contributes greatly in other ways. While some highly vocal factions in our society are bent on vituperation and divisiveness, music really does bring us together. articles.text: Nº 51 in a biweekly series I first met Terrance Gelenter when Guy and Jeanine Saperstein invited Michael and me to a club date at the Hotel Madison to hear him sing music from the American Songbook. They had heard him perform before Christmas holidays, and Terrance was back on the microphone last weekend, and was even better. He had proved to the Hotel Madison that he could fill the place and keep the wait-staff busy serving drinks. The club had a great vibe and the tunes flowed, ballads of the 1940s to 1960s, along with the 1939 jewel, Somewhere Over the Rainbow. Accompanied by Sheldon Forrest on keyboard, Terrance started with Chances Are, originally recorded by San Francisco native Johnny Mathis, As I closed my eyes, I was back in Teen Town, dancing cheek to cheek. As Sheldon played the first few notes, anticipation hung in the air, then the audience sighed in recognition. Terrance’s resonant voice filled the space, transforming a hotel breakfast room into a New York City jazz club. He deftly channels the greats of musical song, taking us a world away from Brooklyn, where in a prior life, he was a schmatta salesman in the New York garment trade. His story is not so different from many of us expats who left the good life for the shores of faraway places. At age 60, he recast himself to become a Parisian and brought along his musical gifts of song, openheartedly sharing the gem-like lyrics with emotional clarity as crisp as salty chips. Terrance likes to include the preludes to songs from a time when lyricists wrote more good verse than put to music. He morphed into Tony Bennett and Because of You, where he playfully parroted Bennett’s Queens accent for a moment. Then, Fly Me to the Moon, at ringside with Sinatra. Then, Johnny Mathis, When Sunny Gets American vocalist Terrance Gelenter at Café Les Deux Magots at 6 Place Saint-Germain des Prés, a favorite of his. Blue, and Side-2 of Wonderful, Wonderful. He sang Smile in Nat King Cole’s original arrangement and reminded us that Charlie Chaplin is given credit as composer (it was in his 1936 movie Modern Times). Playing the cards we’re dealt The gig economy is not what is normally associated with retired people. In the U.S., the hard boundary between “work” and “retirement” and even the touchstone of retirement age of 65 has blurred as people write a second act to their work life. Employer-paid pensions, except government jobs, fell out along the way, and older adults feel pressured to keep working. Not Terrance, he had too much talent and too many passions that were not being utilized. Terrance’s second act shifted into new territory. He wrote movie reviews, ran a broadcast series on World Radio Paris called Your American Friend in Paris, and has recently premiered a Zoom show interviewing authors and inviting in listeners. He also leads tours of Paris and the regions of France: Normandy, Loire, Burgundy, and the Dordogne. His social media covers the bases: Twitter, Facebook, Linked-In, Amazon, YouTube. articles.text: Many expenses in life are unpredictable. But there are two things you know you’ll have to pay for: medical bills and retirement. You’ll probably need to take a variety of steps to meet these costs, but one financial instrument that can help is a health savings account (HSA). If you’re not familiar with an HSA, here are the basics: • Eligibility – If you are enrolled in a qualified high-deductible health plan (HDHP), you can generally contribute to an HSA. While HSAs are typically offered through employers, you can still open one if your employer doesn’t provide it, or if you’re self-employed, although you must have HDHP coverage. You also can’t be enrolled in another health insurance plan, other than those permitted, such as dental, vision, long-term care and disability insurance, and you can’t be enrolled in Medicare. Also, you can’t be claimed as a dependent on another person’s tax return. • Contribution limits – In 2022, you can put in up to $3,650 to an HSA if you have single coverage, or $7,300 for family coverage. And if you’re 55 or older, you can put in an extra $1,000 per year. • Tax benefits – An HSA has triple tax advantages: Your contributions are made with pre-tax dollars, so they can reduce your taxable income for the year; your earnings grow taxfree; and your withdrawals are tax-free, provided the money is used for qualified medical expenses. (Withdrawals taken before age 65 that aren’t used for qualified medical expenses are taxable and subject to a 20% penalty; once you reach 65, the penalty no longer applies, although withdrawals are still taxable.) In addition to its providing tax benefits, an HSA can help you in other ways. Perhaps most significantly, your HSA can be an additional financial resource for your retirement. That’s because the money in your HSA can be carried over from year to year – you aren’t obligated to “use it or lose it.” So, the money not spent on annual medical expenses can continue to grow tax-deferred. Plus, an HSA is “portable” – it moves with you when you leave a job. Furthermore, unlike a 401(k) or a traditional IRA, an HSA does not require you to begin taking withdrawals once you reach 72 – you can leave your account untouched for essentially as long as you’d like. And while you may need to use your HSA funds to meet your medical expenses in retirement – which can be considerable, even with Medicare – you can use what you don’t spend on medical costs for your other needs without penalty, once you reach age 65. (As mentioned above, any HSA withdrawals not used for qualified medical costs are taxable.) Here’s one other point to keep in mind: Your HSA likely contains investment options, along with a cash account. If you put all your funds in the cash account, as many people do, you might be depriving yourself of the growth opportunities provided by the investment options. On the other hand, of course, these investments generally carry more risk. One possible way to benefit from both parts of your HSA is to keep enough cash to cover your health insurance’s out-of-pocket maximum and invest the rest. As you can see, an HSA can help you in numerous ways. If you have access to one, consider taking advantage of it. articles.text: Wednesday Walkers view the tulip garden of the Reich family on King Avenue. Pictured are: Martin Levy, Noemi Alvarado, Priscilla Wanerus, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Mike Henn, Ken Young, Helen Dong, Quincy Dong, Elizabeth Richter, Brenda Ferrero, Jim Kellogg, Melba Yee, Judy Wang, SiowFang Tan, Adrienne Hamlin, Wenny Young and sister Jessica Lee, Stella Houston, Edith Lee, Sherry Jacobs, Renee Goldhammer, Jo Normington with K-9 best friend Penny Lane, Alan Goldhammer, Jim Kuo, Alicia Rivera, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome first-time walkers Cheryl Stanton, Sharon Ho, and Lynn Richmond. Last Wednesday, March 23, was the first Wednesday of spring, and another beautiful day for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group’s weekly walk. There was a solid turnout of 30 walkers and one K-9 best friend. Noemi Alvarado announced that the group’s official Piedmont Heritage Tree submission had been sent to the city. It is the large redwood at the entrance to Wildwood Gardens. Winners will be announced at the City Arbor Day festivities on April 28. Spring brings with it beautiful flowers which adds to the enjoyment of walking Piedmont’s streets. The group headed off, going up Highland Avenue past the trees with wonderful, white blossoms in upper Piedmont Park, and then went down to the crosswalk at Sheridan Avenue. They crossed the street and saw the house on the corner had gotten a head start on another type of hunt. On its front yard lawn were about a dozen very large, different colored, plastic Easter eggs. At the corner of with Lakeview and Sheridan the houses on both sides of the street have large dogwoods with delicate, white flower petals. Going up Lakeview, they saw the very tall, old redwoods that shade the street. The story was told that over a hundred years ago the man who built the beautiful home, a little further up the hill at the corner of Sea View and Lincoln Avenues, was a lumber baron who loved redwoods and he planted them around his estate. On their way up Lakeview, the group saw an opening between a set of redwoods in a front yard. During the windstorm in January, one of the redwoods came crashing down, taking out trees on its way, and falling into the street. At the top of Lakeview the group went on Sea View. At its corner with Lincoln Avenue, they saw the home built by a lumber baron and owned for many years by Senator William Knowland, the U.S. Senate majority leader during the Eisenhower Administration in the 1950s and owner and publisher of the Oakland Tribune. The group went down Lincoln one block to King Avenue and down King to Crocker Park, were the walkers enjoyed seeing the azaleas, fruit tree blossoms, dogwoods, calla lilies, and other flowers. The walkers emerged on Hampton Road and went onto Sea View where they were treated to the sight of a veritable forest of different colored tulips in the front yard of the Reich family. The walkers made their way back to King with a one-block walk up Farragut Avenue, and then continued down King to La Salle Avenue. Along the way, there was a wonderful, exotic front yard garden to see. On a past walk the group had met the homeowner who told them the story of the garden’s creation. It was originally a typical Piedmont front yard, but he had an inspiration. A neighbor was doing an excavation and had a truckload of dirt that he was willing to trade for a case of beer. The mound of dirt provided the base for this large garden of tropical plants. Jim Kellogg and Mike Henn were on the Piedmont Planning Commission at the time and told the group about the challenging approval process for the unusual landscape design, which turned out to be wonderful. Crossing Crocker Avenue they came to a yard with two gorgeous dogwoods and more beautiful spring flowers. Further on, red buds and striking red leaf maples added even more color to this spring walk. The walkers turned down Woodland Way where it meets La Salle. They noted that repair work was being done on the roof of a home that had been damaged when a large tree fell on it during the January windstorm. Further up Woodland the walkers were charmed by wisterias on the two sides of a garage and the purple f loral frame around its entrance that the plants made. Even though the group was a little behind schedule for a noontime return to the center of town, they couldn’t resist taking a side trip onto secluded Wistaria Way loop. They returned by way of Wildwood Gardens, where passed the group’s redwood Heritage Tree submission. It had been over a three-mile tour of Piedmont’s beautiful spring trees, plants, and flowers; and felt like a walk in a big, wonderful park during the first week of spring. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome by registering with the Piedmont Recreation Department at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.
articles.title: Like a walk in the park on a beautiful Spring day

articles.text: On the weekend of March 12-13, Piedmont Scouts in Troop 15 trekked into Tahoe National Forest for an overnight snowshoe trip. At the trailhead, Scouts and adults layered up, strapped on their snowshoes, and put on their packs. Snow covered everything on the two-mile trek up 600 feet of elevation on the south flank of Castle Peak. Sebastien Swain said “Snowshoeing was my favorite part of the trip – the scenery as we wound through the trees was really spectacular. It was quiet and pretty”, added Romi Bhatia. Scouts and adults got to work at the campsite – pitching tents and digging their snow caves. Danny King said, “My favorite part of the trip was building an igloo.” Landon Heppner added, “I was surprised at how well an igloo is formed using compact blocks of snow.” As Scouts finished preparing Troop dad James High was ready for a snow adventure. Zachary Barber is at ease traveling across the snowy forest floor. The beauty of Tahoe National Forest. A brightly-lit forest beckons Scouts on snowshoes on a sunny Saturday. Parent Aaron Barber holds a form packed with snow to make blocks for building an igloo with Landon Heppner (rear) and Theo Barber. Scoutmaster Glen Tripp set a good example in making a tidy tent site. Scouts set ground cloths under their tents to keep drier and warmer. Scout Theo Barber delivers snow from his shovel into the block form held by his father Aaron Barber. Landon Heppner stays warm in a cozy igloo. Assistant Scoutmaster Robert Barbosa shares in the satisfaction of completing an igloo with Danny King (left), Landon Heppner, Theo Barber, and Thomas Moision.

articles.text: To keep your body running at peak performance, it needs regular maintenance: a spring tune-up, so to speak. The lovely spring days we are experiencing now encourage us to exercise by getting out and walking or taking an aerobics class. In our haste to firm up our body by heading to the gym, let’s not forget the need to exercise our brain as well. Did you know there are few things that stimulate the brain the way music does? Researchers at Johns Hopkins Medicine have found that listening to music can reduce anxiety, blood pressure, and pain. Plus, they found that music can help improve sleep quality, mood, mental alertness, and memory. If you want to keep your brain engaged throughout the aging process, it seems like listening to or playing music is a great tool. It can provide a total brain workout. So just how does music do this? Music can activate almost all brain regions and networks. Thus, music can help us keep our brain pathways strong, including networks that are involved in well-being, cognitive function, quality of life, and happiness. In fact, studies show there is only one other situation in which you can activate so many brain networks at once, and that is when you participate in social activities. Here at The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, we firmly believe in the benefits of music. As a social activity we have an active Glee Club because the act of singing lowers stress and releases endorphins that help make us happy. Research also shows that choir singing releases an antibody which boosts our Members of The Lake Merritt Glee Club, Laura McGee (left), Pat King, and Diane Livingston singing “Give My Regards to Broadway.” immune system. Further, singing has been shown to enhance the memory part of the brain. With the pandemic waning, The Lake Merritt is happy to welcome back live music into our community on a weekly basis. The Jazz Therapists, featuring local jazz performer Anna de Leon, performed in The Terrace Room just last week. This seven-member band plays in communities for older adults throughout the Bay Area. Our residents enjoy the music and many also take to the dance floor in the Terrace Room, which overlooks Lake Merritt. If you are interested in some everyday brain boosts from music, you may want to try these ideas. Try listening to what your kids or grandkids are listening to. New music challenges the brain in a way that old music does not. It might not feel pleasurable at first, but that unfamiliarity forces the brain to struggle to understand the new sound. You can also increase brain power by listening to familiar music and recalling a memory. Does listening to a certain Frank Sinatra song bring you back to the first moment you laid eyes on your spouse? Listening to music can help you decompress or motivate you. Pay attention to which kinds of music stimulate or soothe you. I’ve heard it said that our brain loves music like Willy Wonka loves chocolate. articles.text: It’s one thing to ask for a little help with daily activities in the home, but getting 24-hour care can be intimidating at first. Around-the-clock care can be needed for the following reasons: • Post-surgery recovery • Support of hospice and palliative care • Chronic conditions such as dementia that may include symptoms such as wandering • Increased fall risk A trained caregiver can help with bathing assistance, grooming, meal preparation, toileting, medication reminders, transportation to medical appointments, and more when 24-hour care is needed. Whatever the need, there are benefits to receiving 24-hour care in the home for yourself or a loved one, either temporarily or for an extended period of time: • Family caregivers can get much-needed rest when there is a professional caregiver as part of the team. This is called Respite Care, and it allows friends and family to take care of themselves when a loved one needs overnight care as well as daytime assistance. • • • As the saying goes, “You can’t pour from an empty cup,” and a caregiver cannot truly be helpful if they are not getting good sleep and exercise to recharge. When a person becomes more confined to their home due to age or illness, a companion caregiver can lift their spirits. Loneliness does not need to be added to illness and people can truly benefit from a kind smile and friendly conversation. There can be give and take in a care partnership, where someone who is in need of care can still feel valued and share their experiences and knowledge with their caregiver. Call it peace of mind, being reassured, having a safety plan, whatever you prefer, but it comes down to the fact that a compassionate and trained caregiver can provider more security. Illness and age can create vulnerability and someone who is in a weaker condition may need the eyes, ears, and extra set of hands for improved well-being. When someone is transitioning from a hospital to home or from a rehabilitation center to home, it can be reassuring to have a caregiver • • who is with them through all of it. This caregiver can observe any changes and share concerns with the family to communicate to the health care provider. Something as simple as making sure medications are taken at the correct times and doses can be the difference between a trajectory of getting better or being readmitted to the hospital. A caregiver can stay on top of medication reminders as well as meal preparation to encourage rehabilitation. Not all forms of care can come to the home so that’s why it’s beneficial to have a reliable caregiver who can provide transportation to and from medical appointments, whether to a physical therapist or primary care provider. In order to fully heal, follow-up appointments and adherence to prescribed therapies are critical. The lovely spring days we are experiencing now encourage us to exercise by getting out and walking or taking an aerobics class. In our haste to firm up our body by heading to the gym, let’s not forget the need to exercise our brain as well. Did you know there are few things that stimulate the brain the way music does? Researchers at Johns Hopkins Medicine have found that listening to music can reduce anxiety, blood pressure, and pain. Plus, they found that music can help improve sleep quality, mood, mental alertness, and memory. If you want to keep your brain engaged throughout the aging process, it seems like listening to or playing music is a great tool. It can provide a total brain workout. So just how does music do this? Music can activate almost all brain regions and networks. Thus, music can help us keep our brain pathways strong, including networks that are involved in well-being, cognitive function, quality of life, and happiness. In fact, studies show there is only one other situation in which you can activate so many brain networks at once, and that is when you participate in social activities. Here at The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, we firmly believe in the benefits of music. By Cookie Segelstein Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear Macmama: I just bought a new laptop and it has Monterey as the operating system. I know each operating system has new features. Can you tell me what some of the new features are for this one? I also bought a new phone. –Mel, Rockridge Dear Mel: Each operating system comes with some new features, that seem to more and more be meant to help us sync all of our devices and be able to use them together. Monterey is no different. Here are some of the newer features that I really like. 1. You can now stream media from your iPhone or iPad directly to your Mac’s screen. Your phone must be running iOS 15, and if you are using airplay, you will see your Mac now as a usable choice. You can have videos or pictures stream picture in picture or full screen, and you can have music from your iPhone play in the background on your Mac. 2. Many users have noticed and complained that when transferring pictures from your iPhone they come in an HEIC format. With Monterey, you can convert your pictures from HEIC to JPEG with a right click. If you have, set up a right click in your mouse/ trackpad preferences), or a control-click (hold the Control button on your keyboard and click with your mouse or trackpad). When you right or control click an image that you’d like to convert, choose Quick Actions, and then choose Convert Image. 3. You can also change the color of your cursor, by going to System Preferences/Accessibility/ Display/Pointer/Pointer Color. This feature can be useful if you have a dark Desktop Picture on your Mac. 4. You can now save pictures to your Photos library directly from the Messages app on your computer. When someone sends you a picture and you open it on your Mac, there is a little box with a downward pointing arrow. If you click this, you will be given the option to save it in Photos. 5. Erasing and resetting your Mac’s data is now as easy as it is on your iPhone or iPad. Open System Preferences, go up to the top left of your screen, click on the word System Preferences and choose Erase All Content and Settings. 6. One of the most important features in Monterey is called Digital Legacy, which lets you securely pass down your data to trusted family and friends. This feature can be a real benefit when you pass away, so your surviving family members can access your documents, photos, etc. To enable this, follow these steps: Open System Preferences. Click on Apple ID in the top right corner, then select Password & Security/ Legacy Contact/Manage. Select Add Legacy Contact and select the desired contacts (your Mac will suggest any contacts that are part of your Family Sharing). You will then see an access key for this contact, which you can download and share. This will be shared through iCloud to your other devices. Cookie Segelstein is the MacMama, an Apple Certified Service Professional who provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. articles.text: On a beautiful day in March, the Piedmont Seniors visited the historic McConaghy House in Hayward on a monthly outing. When Scottish-Irish immigrant Neal McConaghy built his home in 1888, his youngest son, John, lived there until he passed away at age 100. After John’s death, there were plans to demolish this historic home for retail space. Fortunately, concerned citizens halted ideas for demolition in 1972, and the property was purchased by the Hayward Area Recreation District (HARD). It reopened as a museum, curated and managed by employees and volunteers in 1976. This stately Victorian has authentic period pieces of furniture, floor and wall coverings. Due to its age, the McConaghy House is not ADA compliant, but the house was so interesting the Seniors found the nine exterior stairs easily worth it. There are two parlors, one for family and one for visitors. This is an interesting concept as the house was considered “middle-class” in its day. Located at 18701 Hesperian Boulevard in Hayward, it is open on some Saturdays or by appointment. Donations are welcome to help maintain the integrity of the home. After the house tour, the Piedmont Seniors collectively satisfied their appetites with lunch at a wonderful Italian restaurant, Buon Appetito. The restaurant could rival any of the best dining spots in San Francisco, and with much more reasonable pricing. All agreed that the tiramisu was the most delicious we have ever tasted and is made on site daily. The outdoor dining made for a very pleasant dining experience. To finish off the day, the Seniors went to a little-known oasis in Hayward, the Japanese Gardens, the oldest Japanese garden in California. It is also managed by the Hayward Recreation The Piedmont Seniors recently visited the historic McConaghy House in Hayward. Pictured are (front): Mona Jamieson (left), Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Patti Singer; (2nd row): Janet Epstein, Irene Westler, Larry Singer; (3rd row): Rick Luciano, Ann Morales, Margaret Brownell, Gregory Jurin; (4 row): Jim Ayotte, Havillah Kapellias; (top): Fred Pemberton. District. This garden is situated next to Hayward’s Senior Center and adjacent to the Douglas Morrisson Theatre. The garden follows the Japanese principles of design, while using California native stone and plants. This 3.5 acres of serenity is the perfect place for weddings, or simply to meditate in a beautiful environment. It is also free for visitors. Though many of the Piedmont Seniors have lived in the East Bay for years, no one from the group had ever previously discovered this hidden gem. To find out more about the Piedmont Seniors and their activities, including monthly meetings, and to receive a quarterly newsletter, contact Seniors’ Coordinator Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov, or call the Piedmont Recreation Department at 510-420-3070. The Japanese Gardens are one of Hayward’s many jewels. They are a tribute to Hayward’s long history and kinship with the Japanese people and culture. A must-see for visitors and locals alike, the gardens are open from 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily.

articles.text: The remarkable Robert (“Bob”) Kingsbury Lane, a loving husband, father, grandfather, brother, and friend, passed away on February 19, 2022, at the age of 77. Robert spent his last day surrounded by family and the beauty of nature on a sunny and secluded Santa Cruz beach, soaking his feet in the Pacific Ocean and delighting his grandkids with treasures he’d sifted from the sand. Robert was born September 1, 1944, the first son of Jack and Trudy Lane of Los Angeles and older brother to Christopher. A 3rd generation Californian, he was raised in Pacific Palisades and received his high school diploma from Harvard School. A life-long learner, Robert attended the University of California in Berkeley where he pursued many academic passions, including architecture and photography. While there, he made many of his enduring friendships as a member of the Psi Upsilon fraternity. After graduating with a Bachelor’s degree in history, Robert returned to Los Angeles to earn his Juris Doctor at Loyola Law School. Prior to beginning his legal career, Robert heeded the call and served in the United States Army as a First Lieutenant, stationed in Baltimore, Maryland. Though he served during a time of social and political turbulence, Robert remained guided by his personal ethos and completed his service honorably as a conscientious objector. It was in Baltimore where Robert met his wife, Reiko. While on day-leave from military assignment, Robert wandered into the historic Peabody Institute in the city’s Mount Vernon neighborhood, drawn by the 19th century architecture. There, Robert discovered Reiko playing the pipe organ in an out-of-the-way practice room. Returning weekly to listen to her play, Robert and Reiko eventually married in California and moved to Piedmont to live, work, and raise their family. They were married for 50 years and had three daughters. Fiercely principled, staunchly free-thinking, and endlessly engaged, Robert was a vigorous advocate for his clients, friends and loved ones, and as a global citRobert Lane izen. Over the many decades that Robert practiced law under his own banner, R. Kingsbury Lane, Inc., he never had to market his services. Referrals and long-held contacts made up his loyal client list. As “Dad” to his daughters Nysa, Mari, and Lindsay, he was a coach, tutor, musical troupe manager, camp leader, Fourth of July fireworks scofflaw, “party favor” distributor, constant champion, and life-long trusted advisor on things great and small. Perhaps above all, Robert instilled in his daughters the importance of independent thinking, self-reliance, and fighting for what you believe in. He modeled these values himself as a vocal and action-oriented proponent of social and environmental justice. Robert viewed the world through the lens of an artist. His poetry captured the emotion and essence of its subject; his camera seized the candid, the wild, the unexpected, the golden hour moments; his sketches were never constrained by what was, only what could be. In the family’s overwhelming grief at losing him, we try to see his life as he would - beautifully, and uncommonly well-lived. Robert is survived by his wife Reiko, daughters Nysa, Mari, and Lindsay, five beloved grandchildren, his brother Christopher Lane, cousins John Hogle and Barbara Clement, and many nieces and nephews. A celebration of life will be held on Sunday, May 1st at 2 p.m. at the First Unitarian Universalist Church of San Francisco.
articles.title: Robert Lane dies February 19 at age 77

articles.text: The City of Piedmont will host a virtual Housing Element Community Workshop, the second in a series of community workshops, on Thursday, March 24 at 5:30 p.m. via Zoom. The workshop will focus on the 2023-2031 Housing Element update, and will feature an introduction to the Housing Element draft, which will set forth the city’s goals, policies and actions that address the need for all housing types at various income levels. A complete review and revision of the existing Housing Element must be adopted by Piedmont City Council by December 2023. A highlight of tomorrow’s workshop will be a presentation of a new, interactive digital tool called “The Piedmont Puzzle,” which operates on Balancing Act software. Chris Adams, president and co-founder of Balancing Act, will lead a demonstration on how to use the community tool. It will allow users to pick locations in Piedmont that would be suitable for housing and what that housing might look like. Community members can access the Housing Element workshop by joining the Zoom meeting by computer or smart phone at bit.ly/piedmonthousingpuzzle. You may also call in to the virtual meeting, by dialing (669) 900-9128 and enter webinar meeting number 870 3457 5751. The City installed banners in the center of town and on Grand Avenue in anticipation of upcoming community workshops related to housing equity and the draft Housing Element.
articles.title: Virtual Housing Community Workshop tomorrow at 5:30 p.m.

pages.text: Volume 24, No. 22 Piedmont, California March 23, 2022 91¢ ✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ ALL CITY EDITION ✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ Piedmont Post Piedmont Post A Community Newspaper Serving the Citizens of Piedmont Virtual Housing Community Workshop tomorrow at 5:30 p.m. By Allyson Aleksey The City of Piedmont will host a virtual Housing Element Community Workshop, the second in a series of community workshops, on Thursday, March 24 at 5:30 p.m. via Zoom. The workshop will focus on the 2023-2031 Housing Element update, and will feature an introduction to the Housing Element draft, which will set forth the city’s goals, policies and actions that address the need for all housing types at various income levels. A complete review and revision of the existing Housing Element must be adopted by Piedmont City Council by December 2023. A highlight of tomorrow’s workshop will be a presentation of a new, interactive digital tool called “The Piedmont Puzzle,” which operates on Balancing Act software. Chris Adams, president and co-founder of Balancing Act, will lead a demonstration on how to use the community tool. It will allow users to pick locations in Piedmont that would be suitable for housing and what that housing might look like. Community members can access the Housing Element workshop by joining the Zoom meeting by computer or smart phone at bit.ly/piedmonthousingpuzzle. You may also call in to the virtual meeting, by dialing (669) 900-9128 and enter webinar meeting number 870 3457 5751. articles.text: The world knows about the horrors happening in the beautiful country of Ukraine. The world knows of the shelling and the bombing. The world knows of the bullets and blood. Ukraine knows of the war tearing its country apart. But Ukraine also knows of her citizens fighting back against those who invade her country. Ukraine knows the brave souls who give their lives to keep her safe. For the past weeks Ukraine has been defending its territory against the invading Russian forces. With shelling happening all hours of the day and night, many Ukrainians have been forced to take shelter underground – in parking garages, theater basements, and subways – to keep themselves and their loved ones safe. The Ukrainian army, though heavily outnumbered, is holding its ground against the invading Russian forces. Ukraine and Russia have coexisted for centuries without conflict. As a first-generation Russian-American, I remember growing up and watching cartoons based on old Russian legends, always based in Kyiv. I remember when my grandmother who lives in Moscow would come to visit, we would always watch a popular TV show together. The producer of that show is actor-turned Ukrainian president Vladirmir Zelensky. I remember my mother making me Ukrainian borscht and vareniki (dumplings). My life has been influenced by Ukraine in more ways than I can possibly imagine, and I am beyond grateful for it. My parents would always tell me about Russia’s famous writers who hailed from Odessa, Ukraine, and how their works of literature were prized by the entire world. My Jewish father’s grandparents were born near Odessa, and lived there before moving to Moscow. My mother’s Russian relatives still live there. I had always believed that Ukraine and Russia only differed in their language and borders. I still believe to this day that Russians don’t want a war with the people they call their brothers and sisters. I believe it’s the Russian government and its goons who use propaganda and TV to stupify the country. But I speak for myself. I don’t want a war to rip apart countries who are separated by a line drawn on a map.
articles.title: To Ukraine with love, from a Russian-American

To the brave souls fighting back with everything they have and the brave souls who have left in fear, I stand on your side. To the men and women who have picked up a weapon for the first time to defend their home. To the children who have been separated from their families. To the business owners converting their shops to help the war effort. To President Zelensky for staying with his people. Every day and night the Ukrainian flag flies is another day that the Ukrainian people have fought for and stood their ground. It is another day of battle and death, but each day, has hope. Hope that when the sun rises the next day the Ukrainian flag is still proudly displaying its yellow-and-blue colors. Another day of the country’s famed sunflowers blooming. Another day of the Dnieper River rushing through Kyiv. Another day of Mount Hoverla standing tall. But most importantly another day that the Ukrainian spirit lives on. articles.text: Join the League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWV) on Wednesday, March 30, for a discussion with Dr. Fiona Hill, Senior Fellow at The Brookings Institution at Stanford. The Zoom episode will explore the current state of democracy, from both domestic and international points of view. Dr. Hill is the Robert Bosch Senior Fellow at the Center on the United States and Europe in the Foreign Policy program at the Brookings Institution and member of the Council on Foreign Relations. Her most recent book, There is Nothing for You Here, draws on her personal journey out of poverty, as well as her unique perspectives as a historian and policy maker, to show how we can return hope to our forgotten places. From 2017 to 2019, Dr. Hill served as deputy assistant to the president and senior director for European and Russian affairs on the National Security Council. Central Asia, regional conflicts, energy, and strategic issues. Co-author of Mr. Putin: Operative in the Kremlin and The Siberian Curse: How Communist Planners Left Russia Out in the Cold, she holds a master’s degree in Soviet studies and a doctorate in history from Harvard University and a master’s in Russian and modern history from St. Andrews University in Scotland. This event is part of the League’s 2022 Defending Democracy Speaker Series and is co-sponsored by local Leagues in California, Oregon, Colorado, and Florida. This talk will be held live on Zoom and YouTube and will include an audience question and answer session. Visit the website lwvpiedmont.org to learn more about the series and register for this event. articles.text: In the week of March 12-18 only one student COVID case was reported in Piedmont School District, and none by staff members. This was the first week of the new mask policy which highly recommend that they be worn indoors, but no longer requires them. Although Piedmont schools have been very progressive with their vaccination policy and the city of Piedmont has some of the highest vaccination rates in the nation, there have been varying opinions on wearing masks. APT (Piedmont teachers’ union) President Elise Marks teaches English at the high school. She offered the following observation about the first week with the new policy. “I’m not seeing much tension between individuals. People are being respectful [of individual’s choice to wear a mask or not].” “At the same time, I’ve heard from several students who didn’t want to see the mask mandate lifted, that they’re quite uncomfortable having to be in classrooms all day with unmasked people. I’ve had a couple of students choose not to come to school for all or part of this week,” she added. She estimated half to 2/3 of students in her classes are still wearing masks, mostly the N95 or KN95 types. At a school-wide pep rally inside the Binks Rawlings gym on Friday, this reporter observed more than half of students not wearing masks. One week ago, March 16, marked the two-year anniversary of the first COVID stay-at-home order in California. Many in the community are ready to move forward and see mask removal as the next logical step. “I think something that is underserved in our community in Piedmont is the mental health aspect of the pressures we have placed on the children to do things like wear masks, comply with other Covid policies, and be away from schools. As parents, my wife and I do take notice of our kids’ mental welfare as much as their physical welfare and we have concerns there,” said Piedmont alum and parent Jonathan Essner. Alameda county continues to enjoy low COVID numbers, since March 4. The seven-day average since then has hovered between 173 and 113 confirmed daily cases. In the same time period, the seven-day average of daily case counts in the U.S. has decreased from 50,000 to 29,000 daily. Elsewhere, the new subvariant of Omicron BA.2 has caused spikes in case counts across western Europe, a region that has typically been a couple of weeks ahead of the US in showing new COVID trends. On March 18 Germany recorded 300,000 cases. Some scientists are raising the alarm since the number of Americans with booster shots is around 30% while 50-60% of western Europeans have had a booster. On the other side of the world, India’s Bharat Biotech, a vaccine manufacturer, leads the way in the production of a COVID nasal spray vaccine. The argument in favor of this type of vaccine is that it would create antibodies at the point of infection, the nose. In theory this would stop infection before it happens, Piedmont’s Dr. George Rutherford warns of cautious optimism. “It’s a good idea; they may get there someday in the not too distant future. But for right now, I think it is far out on the edge of the horizon.” Rutherford, pointed out that the only current nasal vaccine in the U.S. is for the flu and it doesn’t work for people over 50. It may be hard to administer for very young people since the patient has to breathe in at the same time. “It is not going to do anything unless we can get more than 70% of the population to get it. There is still all the vaccine hesitancy that goes on.” Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Children’s Fairyland is bringing back its premiere fundraising gala, Once Upon a Time in Fairyland, to the shores of Lake Merritt on May 25. Single tickets are now available. Once Upon a Time in Fairyland is a rare and coveted opportunity for adults to experience the park without their children. The 8-acre property is kid-centric in every sense of the word; but on May 25, it will transform into an elegant evening space for food, wine, and costumes. The fundraiser makes magical programming at Children’s Fairyland possible for Oakland and Bay Area families. articles.text: A trip to Disneyland, which begins tomorrow, March 24, is a reward for three years of cookie sales by Piedmont Girl Scouts in Troop 33587. The Scouts, most of whom attend Wildwood Elementary, have sold close to 10,000 boxes of Thin Mints, Samoas and other varieties or cookies since 2020. That volume qualified them for a VIP guided tour of Magic Kingdom. “They’ve been so driven,” said Carolyn Pan, one of the troop leaders. “It’s just amazing how they’ve maintained focus on their goal for so long.” Troop 33587 has been together since 2017 and first set its sights on Disneyland in 2020. They sold more than 5,000 boxes that year before COVID-19 cut the selling season short. Last year, they were only able to sell 1,100 boxes amid pandemic restrictions. Sales have been brisk this year, however. The troop has set up stands throughout Piedmont and Oakland with people lining up to buy in some cases. They also built online stores to take remote orders and knocked on countless doors. “People haven’t seen us for two years,” Pan said. “They’re hungry for cookies.” The 11 girls in the troop have sold an average of 326 boxes each, a number that would be even higher if it wasn’t for supply constraints that limited the number of cookies the Scouts could get. This year, Pan has been struck by how confident the girls are, noting how they project their voices, engage with strangers, and guide customers to flavors with more inventory. “I’ve learned how to manage money and connect with people,” said 10-year-old Junie Waters Worthen, a troop member for the last three years. Cookies are still available online at bit.ly/troop33587, and the Girls Scouts will ship for free any orders over $50 placed on March 26 and 27. To learn more, see their video at https://youtu.be/EOAwwxO7RPo. Lilly Curran sells Girl Scout cookies from the comfort of her car. Savannah Sears and Charlotte Phung had a great day selling their inventory of Girl Scout cookies.

articles.text: The inaugural Piedmont Food Fest is coming to town. On Sunday, April 24 from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., in partnership with the city, schools, local businesses, community partners, and fiscal sponsor Social Good, Piedmont Food Fest will welcome visitors and showcase a family-friendly event in Piedmont Park. It will include food, the stories of the people behind the food, as well as multicultural stage performances, locally sourced beer and wine, and a kid activity zone. If all goes well, this event may even turn into another annual tradition the community can look forward to year after year. A central mission of Piedmont Food Fest is to showcase the many diverse offerings of the broader Bay Area that help enrich the experiences of community and neighbors. The event will feature food from Curry Up Now, Ceviche & Co, Swahili Spot, Kiss My Boba, Piedmont’s own Robert Dorsey Catering, and others. There will also be live music from the mariachi duo Son Nuestro, the Great Wall Youth Orchestra, a Black Music Incubator Showcase, and the Oakland Samba Revue. Piedmont Food Fest is open to the public and we encourage attendance from the broader Bay Area. To register or volunteer, please visit www.piedmontfoodfest.org. Early bird deals are available now through March 31. The Food Festival Planning Committee includes Roger Tsai, Diana Lee, Abha Kothari, Kala Hale, Kyle Killion, Tien Teng, David Lau, Amy Kelly, Ellen Moon Lee, Lisa Chan Carnazzo, and Michelle Mazzeo.

articles.text: As with most things students do in high school, the point isn’t the subject matter, it’s the skills that underlie the process. Let’s examine what skills can be developed when writing an essay. How do I tell them what I am? Students ask all the time why they have to write essays and not stories. articles.text: Piedmont families are reading A Thousand Splendid Suns by Khaled Hosseini for this year’s community-wide Readmont project, now in its 12th year. The project culminates with an evening event featuring guest speakers on April 21. A Thousand Splendid Suns, a novel published in 2007, was written by Afghan-American author Hosseini following the success of his debut novel The Kite Runner, which enjoyed a 15-week run as the New York Times No. 1 best-seller. A Thousand Splendid Suns chronicles the story of two women living in Kabul, Afghanistan, According to the Piedmont High School’s English Department, the book was chosen “for its beautiful story of love in an unforgiving time, and as a way for our community to discuss the recent events in Afghanistan and the increase of Afghan refugees to the Bay Area.” The book is appropriate for ages 14 and up. For younger readers, the English Department recommends the book I am Malala for ages 10 to 14, and Malala, My Story of Standing up for Girls’ Rights, appropriate for age 6 through 10. Check out a book now at any one of the school libraries. Books are funded through a grant from the Piedmont AppreI Am Malala by Nobel Peace Price winner Malala Yousafzai. Piedmont High School (PHS) English Department Chairperson Beth Black and PHS Librarian Kathryn Levenson will facilitate student discussions beginning April 19. The community read will culminate on April 21 with an evening of guest speakers who soon will be named. The evening event is open to the entire community. articles.text: Primitive Data, a FIRST Tech Challenge robotics team with three members from Piedmont, won first place at the NorCal Regionals held on Sunday, March 13 in Sacramento. The Piedmont team was a key player in a three teams winning alliance. Its alliance partners were Kuriosity Robotics from Palo Alto and Quixilver from San Jose. Primitive Data includes Piedmont High seniors Benjamin Colby, Cooper Downing, and Josh Lee, along with Peter Xu from American High in Fremont. A total of 48 teams from Northern California advanced from earlier competitions to qualify for the regionals. In the final showdown, Primitive data and allies defeated an alliance of two teams from Saratoga and one from Folsom. At the NorCal Regionals, Primitive Data rose to the occasion with an effective defensive strategy, frustrating their opponents and complementing the offensive abilities of their alliance partners. An advanced Swerve Drive drivetrain enabled this unique style of play, which required Primitive Data to introduce a number of hardware and software innovations in their robot development. The Primitive Data team was also named the Northern California winner of the FIRST Tech Challenge Innovate Award. “The Innovate Award celebrates a team that thinks outside the box and has the ingenuity, creativity, and inventiveness to make their designs come to life,” explained FIRST Tech. “This judged award is given to the team that has the most innovative and creative robot design solution to any specific components in the FIRST Tech Challenge game. Elements of this award include elegant design, robustness, and ‘out of the box’ thinking related to design.” This was Primitive Data’s first in-person tournament since winning last summer at the Maryland Tech Invitational, an international competition. Their alliance partners then were from Santa Monica and Fremont. Primitive Data was founded by Downing and Colby for the 2020-21 season. A guiding principle of the team is collaboration across boundaries and leadership from students with no adult mentors. With a team of only four members, Primitive Data has successfully competed against teams four times larger and with substantial school resources and professional adult mentorship. The Primitive Data robotics team holds their first-place trophies. Team members include Piedmont High seniors Benjamin Colby (left), Josh Lee, and Cooper Downing, along with Peter Xu, a senior at American High in Fremont.
articles.title: Piedmont-led robotics team wins NorCal Regionals

articles.text: Piedmont police officer Nicole Casalnuovo was promoted to Sergeant on February 19, and received a formal badge pinning ceremony at the March 7 City Council meeting. Specifically, Casalnuovo transitioned from Acting Watch Commander to Sergeant. In her previous role, she earned “bootson-the-ground” experience that prepared her for the promotion. “The transition is pretty seamless. Of course, there are more responsibilities [as Sergeant], but we’re well-prepared at that point,” she explained. “This department works very hard to make sure we’re led in that [upward] direction.” Casalnuovo was hired by the Piedmont Police Department in 2015 as a patrol officer, and eventually assumed the position of juvenile officer in 2019 working in tandem with the school district. As juvenile officer, Casalnuovo worked with Piedmont youth and served as a conduit between the police department, the school administration and faculty. The position was funded by the California Department of Justice Tobacco Grant program. “Ultimately, Nicole was responsible for doing the real work in terms of setting up a new program that had an immense amount of responsibility tied to it. She did an amazing job,” Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers noted at the ceremonial pinning. Casalnuovo’s service to Piedmont youth extends to her role as Advisor to the Piedmont Explorer Post Program, part of the Piedmont Scout Council, that seeks to provide young women and men with the opportunity to explore their interests and aptitudes in the field of law enforcement. Under her tutelage, many Piedmont youth experienced their first “ride-along,” joining Casalnuovo on duty and observing a day in the life of a Piedmont Police Officer. Although the Explorer Post program had to take a backseat the past two years due to COVID, Casalnuovo sought to engage Piedmont youth in other ways. Recently she helped PPD Administrative Assistant April Fitzgerald install a three-shelf “little free library” specifically for young readers ages 3 through 11. The project was created to encourage kids to stop by and Sergeant Nicole Casalnuovo read or borrow a book from the Police Department lobby. Casalnuovo also serves as National Night Out coordinator, one of the largest events hosted by the Department. The event is a community-police awareness-raising “block party,” traditionally held on the first Tuesday of August. Casalnuovo has over 15 years of experience in military and law enforcement. She served as an intelligence and an analyst for the U.S. Air Force before beginning her career in law enforcement. Casalnuovo looks back at her parents and mentor retired Sgt. Grady Joseph of the Central Marin Police Authority, before she receives her ceremonial pin at a March 7 Piedmont City Council meeting. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team continued its dominant run atop the Western Alameda County Conference’s Foothill Division with a 6-1 win at Castro Valley last Tuesday, March 15. They followed it two days later with a 7-0 shutout of Bishop O’Dowd at the Merritt College tennis courts. The team’s record is now 7-1 overall and 4-0 in league. “We swept Bishop O’Dowd on Thursday without our No. 1 singles starter, Charlie Lambert, who is now healthy and ready to play. The majority of the matches were one-sided,” said coach Jim Landes following the win. Lambert, who has been recovering from a back strain, made his first appearance since FebruBen Breber won 6-3, 7-5 against CV and 6-0, 6-1 with O’Dowd. Monte Imburg, who was named Freshman of the Year by the Post in 2021, won 6-1, 6-4 against O’Dowd and 6-3, 6-1 versus Castro Valley. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 11am-5:30pm 1pm-5pm Benefitting Piedmont Education for 40 Years! dressbestforless.org Staff Photos Lenni Burchardt had a 6-0, 6-2 win against Castro Valley and won his match with Bishop O’Dowd, 6-1, 7-6 (6-4). ary 17 in a 6-2, 6-1 loss to Castro Valley. His return is a good sign of things to come for the team. “For the first time all season, we had our full lineup, and it is formidable. Charlie was still recovering a bit, but having him play was a big boost. Without his usual big serve, he had a difficult time holding, but he played lots of great returns. I know he can do better when we play CV again in a few weeks,” explained assistant coach Corey Reich. The Highlanders have a busy week ahead, facing league opponents San Leandro on March 24 and Berkeley on March 29, followed immediately by a critical match with North Coast Section opponent University on March 30. The Red Devils have won the last two NCS Div. 2 Team Championships (2018 and 2019) and beat Piedmont 4-3 for the 2018 title. “University beat us last year and will be our big competition in NCS, [along with] Head-Royce,” said Ethan Pham. Shutting out O’Dowd Playing No. 1 singles, Lenni Burchardt got Piedmont started with a 6-1 opening set win, and a much narrower 7-6 victory in the second set. It required Burchardt, a German exchange student, to call for a line judge. He wound up winning 6-4 in the tiebreaker. At No. 2 singles, Ben Breber won easily 6-0, 6-1. Monte Imburg won 6-1, 6-4 at No. 3, while Pham won 6-3, 6-2 at No. 4. In doubles, Charlie Olcott and Kai Baudendistel won 6-2, 6-0 at No. 1, and Oliver Maxwell and Brady Colbert won at No. 3 doubles, 6-3, 6-2. But the No. 2 team of Arun Brahma and Charlie Sullivan had to battle through three sets for a 6-4, 4-6, 10-3 victory. 6-1 win vs. Castro Valley Charlie Lambert made his return to the No. 1 spot as he recovers from an injury, but lost 6-2, 6-1 to Castro Valley’s Mason Conlin. Burchardt won 6-0, 6-2 at No. 2, Breber at No. 3 won 6-3, 7-5, and Imburg won 6-3, 6-1 at No. 4. In doubles, Olcott and Baudendistel won easily 6-1, 6-1 at No. 1, and at No. 3, Brahma and Sullivan won in straight sets, 6-4, 6-0. Pham and Maxwell had to work hard to pull out a victory In three sets, 6-3, 6-7, 10-7. articles.text: Piedmont girls’ lacrosse coach Carlton Chan’s suffered his team’s first loss in four years to Bishop O’Dowd, a 7-6 down-tothe-wire match last Friday, March 18 at Witter Field. The Highlanders had won the previous six games with its rival. The Highlanders also took a 10-4 loss to Division 1 school Monte Vista at Witter last Tuesday, March 15. It brings the squad to a 1-5 overall record, but despite the bleak standing, Piedmont should handle the rest of its league opponents in the Western Alameda County Conference, and be able to compete for a league championship game against O’Dowd in April “We will see them again in the league playoffs and l already have a few strategies that would hopefully give us an advantage,” said Chan. “We have a tough schedule, but we’re playing like a team... The girls are stepping up,” Chan said. The Highlanders last lost to O’Dowd 10-9 in the 2017 WACC Championship under former coach Emily Hook. This time the Dragons prevented five of penalty shots by Piedmont. Game Recap The Dragons opened with a quick goal in the first minute of play, and Piedmont had a difficult time finding shooting space. Katherine Kinne scored through contact after six minutes – the team’s first clear look at net. Two minutes later, O’Dowd scored its second goal. Piedmont’s Audrey Mahany had a shot on goal with 8:46 left in the first half. PHS broke the scoring drought with six minutes left when Kinne found Elizabeth Ethington on a cut toward the net for a 2-1 O’Dowd lead. Ethington then scored on a wrap around after starting her run from behind the net to make it 2-2 with 2:47 left in the, half. However, O’Dowd scored on its next possession to go ahead 3-2 at halftime. In the second half, Piedmont made it 3-3 when Ethington found Kinne on a pass from behind the net to Kinne cutting in after just 30 seconds. But, once again, BOD answered on its next possession, to edge ahead 4-3. Ethington had a shooting space attempt saved about a minute later, but Molly Ashton swiftly stole the ball from an O’Dowd defender and scooped and scored at with 22:39 left. The Dragons took the faceoff and turned it into another quick score after just 15 seconds, to remain ahead, 5-4. The Dragons’ goalie then stonewalled another shooting space attempt, this time a penalty shot by Mahany with 20 minutes left. O’Dowd then gained possession and scored after one minute, to take its biggest lead of the game at 6-4. The Dragon goalie then made big stops on two more shooting space attempts, another by Mahany and one by Kinne with 16:20 left in the game. Ruby Guzdar broke Piedmont’s scoring drought after weaving around two defenders, to bring the score to 6-5 with 13 minutes left. O’Dowd scored its final goal with 5:37 left in the game. Katherine Kinne scored a goal and had an assist versus the Dragons.

articles.text: Members of Piedmont’s track team competed in the Dublin Distance Fiesta on Friday and Saturday, March 18-19. It is one of the largest and most popular meets in the state, with thousands of athletes representing more than 100 schools. Seniors Jack Stein and Ellie Black had strong days in both the 1600 and 3200 runs by accomplishing personal records in each event. Senior Cooper Downing also had a PR time and top-10 finish in the 800 meters. “Dublin’s enormity of heats and runners makes it a truly competitive race. Our times are dropping as our seniors are wanting to put a stamp on our program and leave a legacy in 2022 with marks to remember,” said coach Jeanine Holmlund. Stein placed 8th out of 906 runners in the 1600 meters with a personal record time of 4:19.07. He also finished 18th in a field of 420 runners in the 3200 meters with a PR record time of 9:20.56, an improvement of 20 seconds from a race nine days earlier. Black placed 10th in the 3200 meters in a field of 189 runners with a PR time of 10:57.05. She also competed in the 1600 meters and placed 27th out of 515 runners in 5:13.90, also a PR time. Senior Cooper Downing placed 9th out of 722 runners in the 800 meters with a personal record time of 1:57.87. Junior Christian Taylor, whose time was roughly one second slower, placed 15th in 1:58.92. Xander Schulte-Sasse came in 192nd with a time of 2:13.78. Taylor also ran the 1600, finishing in 26th of 906 in 4:27.55. articles.text: Playing at home, Piedmont’s softball team beat St. Patrick 8-5 on Saturday, March 20. “It was overall a good team win. We left a lot of runners in scoring position, but it was a solid win. Everyone stayed in the game. Our defense is getting a lot better, and we put the ball in play offensively in some key moments,” said coach Gene The Highlanders trailed 1-0 after the first inning but piled on five runs in the bottom of the second. The Bruins battled back to tie the game at 5-5 in the top of the fifth, but Piedmont responded with two runs in the bottom of the fifth and one more in the botThe Highlanders were without the big bat of catcher Chiarra Staff Photos Izzie Epstein threw 10 strikeouts in a complete game performance against St. Patrick. Lundin, which forced Piedmont to move centerfielder Leah Bell to take over as catcher. Pitcher Izzy Epstein hurled Morgan Hunt slugged a homerun over the centerfield wall against St. Gretchen Gerhardy was 2-for-3 with a double and two runs scored a complete game with 10 strikeouts and seven hits allowed. She retired 6 of 7 batters in the last two innings and struck out three batters. “Today went up and down. We had some errors, but we came back, got a ton of hits, put up some runs, and hyped up the dugout so when we came back out, we were ready to work. After we put up some runs, we knew we just had to hold them,” said Epstein. Despite being without Lundin, outfielder Morgan Hunt bolstered the offense going 2-for-4 with a solo home run over the centerfield fence. “It’s hard to replace Chiarra’s leadership and offensive production, but it allowed us to play some younger players who need game experience,” said Denard. pages.text: Wednesday, March 23, 2022 15 Highlanders beat St. Patrick 8-5 10Ks and a complete game by pitcher Izzy Epstein By Jonathan Comeaux Playing at home, Piedmont’s softball team beat St. Patrick 8-5 on Saturday, March 20. “It was overall a good team win. We left a lot of runners in scoring position, but it was a solid win. Everyone stayed in the game. Our defense is getting a lot better, and we put the ball in play offensively in some key moments,” said coach Gene Denard. The Highlanders trailed 1-0 after the first inning but piled on five runs in the bottom of the second. The Bruins battled back to tie the game at 5-5 in the top of the fifth, but Piedmont responded with two runs in the bottom of the fifth and one more in the bottom of the sixth. The Highlanders were without the big bat of catcher Chiarra Staff Photos Izzie Epstein threw 10 strikeouts in a complete game performance against St. Patrick. Lundin, which forced Piedmont to move centerfielder Leah Bell to take over as catcher. Pitcher Izzy Epstein hurled Morgan Hunt slugged a homerun over the centerfield wall against St. Patrick. Gretchen Gerhardy was 2-for-3 with a double and two runs scored against St. Patrick. a complete game with 10 strikeouts and seven hits allowed. She retired 6 of 7 batters in the last two innings and struck out three batters. “Today went up and down. We had some errors, but we came back, got a ton of hits, put up some runs, and hyped up the dugout so when we came back out, we were ready to work. After we put up some runs, we knew we just had to hold them,” said Epstein. Despite being without Lundin, outfielder Morgan Hunt bolstered the offense going 2-for-4 with a solo home run over the centerfield fence. “It’s hard to replace Chiarra’s leadership and offensive production, but it allowed us to play some younger players who need game experience,” said Denard. Gretchen Gerhardy smacked a double and advanced to third on a wild pitch against Annabel Castronovo, who brought in Gerhardy on a double as well. It is one of the largest and most popular meets in the state, with thousands of athletes representing more than 100 schools. Seniors Jack Stein and Ellie Black had strong days in both the 1600 and 3200 runs by accomplishing personal records in each event. Junior Christian Taylor, whose time was roughly one second slower, placed 15th in 1:58.92. Xander Schulte-Sasse came in 192nd with a time of 2:13.78. articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team defeated non-league Skyline 5-2 on Tuesday, March 15 at home, but lost on the road to Alameda 4-3 on Wednesday, March 16 and Berkeley 6-3 at home on Friday, March 18. Two Piedmont batters hit their first homers of the year against Skyline, a two-run shot by catcher Davis Alazraqui, and a 3-run homer by infielder Peter Krumins. Michael Aikawa and Nico Defazio, meanwhile, extended their hitting streaks to four games. PHS starts a slate of 10 games in the Shoreline Division of WACC next Wednesday, March 30 against Hayward. 5-2 win over Skyline Trailing the Titans 1-0, Piedmont took the lead in the bottom of the third with a three-run homer by Krumins, who crushed the ball deep over the tall left-center field wall. Liam Campbell led off by reaching first on an error by the first baseman, and Aikawa singled through the middle to center, setting up Krumins’ 3-run homer on the first pitch. Skyline crept closer with a run in the top of the fifth, but Piedmont responded swiftly with two runs in the bottom of the inning. Krumins got on base after being hit by a pitch, and Alazraqui drove him home with a two-run homer and a 5-2 lead. Starting pitcher Scott McKenzie went five innings and had four strikeouts. Senior Cole Garcia entered in relief for the final two innings, retiring all six batters he faced, striking out one. Final stats: Alazraqui was 3-for-3 with a home run, two RBIs, and a run scored. Krumins went 2-for-3 with three RBIs and a run scored. Aikawa went 2-for-4 with a run scored, Tobin Cantrill and Defazio were both 1-for-3. 4-3 loss to Alameda Piedmont scored a run in the top of the first inning, but the Hornets went ahead 2-1 in the bottom of the first and took a 4-1 lead in the third inning. PHS added runs in the top of the fourth and fifth but couldn’t get the tying or winning runs home with two runners on base in the top of the seventh. In the first inning, PHS scored on an error with two outs when Alameda misplayed a fly ball to Staff Photos Davis Alazraqui smacked a two-run home run in Piedmont’s win against Skyline. right field, enabling Alazraqui to reach second and have Krumins score. In the top of the fourth, PHS scored when Ryan McConathy led off with a double and older brother Evan McConathy singled him in. The squad crept closer in the top of the fifth when Krumins drove in Markos Lagios on a sacrifice fly. Lagios was on base after leading off with a double. Final stats: Evan McConathy went 3-for-3 with an RBI. Ryan McConathy was 1-for-3 with a run scored. Krumins went 1-for-2 with a run scored and an RBI. Defazio went 1-for-3 with a double. Lagios went 1-for-3 with a double and run scored. and run scored. Aikawa went 2-for-3 with an RBI. Will Sprague went 2-for-2 with a run scored. Sprague also pitched five innings with four strikeouts in relief. Alex Tafapolsky started, going two innings with one strikeout. NEXT UP Piedmont (4-4) hosts San Leandro today, Wednesday, March 23 at 4:00 p.m. at Humphries Diamond. 6-3 loss to Berkeley Berkeley opened with a run in the top of the first and made it 5-0 by the third inning. PHS added two runs in the bottom third and closed the score to 5-3 by the sixth inning. The Yellowjackets scored one more in the top of the seventh. Final stats: Defazio went 1-for-4 with a triple. Evan McConathy was 1-for-4 with a double Michael Aikawa has five hits in the last three games and extended his hitting streak to four games. Nico Defazio hit a triple against Berkeley. He’s also on a four-game hitting streak.

articles.text: Photo by Mike McConathy The boys’ volleyball team is soaring with a 3-1 record. The PHS boys’ volleyball team, now 3-1, has matched its win total from last spring’s shortened 2021 season when its record was 3-5. On Wednesday, March 16 in the Jets’ home gym, Piedmont swept Encinal 3-0, with games scores of 25-20, 25-12, 25-18. The following day the squad lost to Bishop O’Dowd 3-0 (25-14, 25-18, 25-15). “It was a pretty decent victory over Encinal and a tough match with O’Dowd,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. “Against the Jets, we noticed during warm-ups that their team did not hit down the line, so we knew right away that we needed to take away all angle swings.” “We play to our opponents pretty well. We were a bit surprised to beat Encinal the way we did. Last season was really a development year and we knew just about everyone would be returning. We know we have the roots to create a good team,” said captain Wilson Wong. Piedmont gets ready for a threegame home stand over the next week, including Hayward tomorrow, March 24, Berkeley on March 29, and Arroyo on March 31. 3-0 win over Encinal The Highlanders cruised to a 3-0 win over Encinal in the Jets’ home gym. Final stats: Mason Kimball leading with 10 kills, Kai Lambert and John Champion had three kills, Wong and James Manguyen had two kills, while Eric Olaru-Hagen and Adel Sahuc each had one spike. 3-0 loss to O’Dowd The Dragons typically compete for the league title. Game scores were 25-14, 25-18, 25-15. Final stats: Manguyen led with four kills, Wong and Kimball each had two spikes, while Wong logged two aces. Olaru-Hagen had one spike, while Champion also notched two aces. Tuesday vs. Berkeley The Highlanders traveled to Berkeley on Tuesday, March 22, resulting in a RESULT. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-1) hosts Hayward tomorrow, Thursday, March 24, for a league match at 5:15 p.m. They also host Berkeley on March 29 for another 5:15 p.m. match. Staff Photos Wilson Wong goes up for a spike against Bishop O’Dowd. Staff Photos Mason Kimball (left) and Wilson Wong go up for a double block. Kimball had 10 kills against the Encinal Jets.

articles.text: The tide seems to have changed in the world of lacrosse. With Greg Gately and other former lacrosse stars now in college, the Piedmont boys’ lacrosse team suffered a 13-7 loss to Bishop O’Dowd on March 18 at the Dragons’ home field. It marked O’Dowd’s first win over the Highlanders since April 2017, a string of six games. “O’Dowd had a really good defense, they are hyper aggressive with a lot of seniors. They took it to us in the first and second quarter. We made a good push in the third, and never stopped trying. We showed a lot of heart, but it was atypical of Piedmont lacrosse,” said first year coach Alex Yu, who was an assistant with BOD when they last defeated PHS ’17. O’Dowd’s defense performed as good as advertised with frequent pressing and forcing a wide field to keep an eye on Piedmont’s cutters moving toward the net. “We had a lot of solo-dodges into multiple defenders and never got settled. Give credit to them and their defense,” said Yu. The match was Piedmont’s first league game of the season. The Dragons were very physical with checks and shoulder chargers, committing 10 penalties. PHS was able to score only three times on penalty plays. Prior to the game, O’Dowd seniors could be heard reminding teammates of last spring’s 9-8 overtime Piedmont win. “O’Dowd has a tough defense and they like to push out a lot. Next game, I think we need to capitalize with off-ball movement and more cutting, that’s the one thing we can counter with when they are pushing us out. We can do better in transition as well,” said junior leader Jack Nelson. “They had more ground ball possession than us and it took a while to figure out what worked. We [need to] get more consistent and get more ground balls,: said junior Soren Dixon. Game Recap The Dragons opened with four consecutive goals until Nathan Fredericks flicked a pass to Soren Dixon for a goal with 2:42 left in the first quarter on a 2-man advantage. Dixon made it 4-2 while up a man as well with 1:25 to go, when he stole the ball from BOD goalie Alex Sproul, who charged out of net after recording a save against Dixon. The Highlanders also started the second quarter with a man-advantage, but Dixon and Fredericks were stonewalled by the goalie. BOD then scored four consecutive goals again to jump ahead 9-2 with 42 seconds left until halftime. Rylan Nelson launched in a goal with 10 seconds on the clock for a 9-3 halftime score. In the third quarter, Piedmont drew a penalty 30 seconds in and attempted a wrap-around shot by Dixon, but his shot was saved. O’Dowd committed another penalty with 6:59 to go and Fredericks fired another shot on target, but the keeper was there to thwart his attempt again. At the 5:45 mark, Fredericks found the net on a low-arching shot to make it 9-4, but O’Dowd scored 19 seconds later, 10-4. From there, PHS added three consecutive goals, but the die was cast. Spencer Settlemier scored after scooping a ground ball in the attacking area and quickly flicking it into the net with 4:45 left in the third, 10-5. The Highlanders then converted a man-advantage with 52 seconds to spare when Dixon found Jack Nelson for a goal, 10-6. In the fourth quarter, Fredericks fed Rylan Nelson for a goal with 9:45 left in the game to make it 10-7. O’Dowd scored three more times for the 13-7 final. Final stats: Dixon had two Staff Photos Soren Dixon had two goals and an assist against Bishop O’Dowd. Nathan Fredericks scored once and had two assists.

articles.text: Members of the Block C flag football team: (front) Ben McMurtry (Havens Elementary, left), Ryan McMurtry (Havens), Will Harris (Wildwood), Gael Fierro (Wildwood), Gabriel Gurney; (back) Kellin De Verney, Aidan Shartsis (Wildwood), Coach Kaleb Elarms-Orr, and Angel Fierro (Coach and parent). Not pictured: Finn Salyk. On Sunday, March 13, the Next Level Flag Football program at Cal Berkeley held its own Super Bowl. The Block-C White team made up primarily of Piedmont 5th graders won their age group, 47-13. The team was led by 5th and 4th graders from Havens and Willdwood, Ben McMurtry and his brother Ryan, Will Harris, Gael Fierro, and Aidan Shartsis. Other members of the team not from Piedmont included Finn Salyk, Gabriel Gurney and Kellin De Verney. Players who contributed during the season included Ari Moskovitz, Clemens Conrad and Henry Ven Den Bos. The team, which finished with a 6-2 record, was coached by Cal football player Kaleb Elarms-Orr and parent Angel Fierro. The Super Bowl win was a rematch against a team that beat the Block-C White team the second week of the season. Will Harris and Ben McMurtry wowed the crowd as quarterbacks with a combined 7 touchdowns. Ryan McMurtry, Gael Fierro and Finn Salyk caught touchdown passes, and Gabriel Gurney, Aidan Shartsis, and Kellin De Verney moved the ball down the field with several key receptions. Ben McMurtry led the team in rushing. The key to the team’s success was its defense led by Kellin de Verney who was matched against the opponents’ best receivers all season. De Verney and defensive players Gabriel Gurney, Aidan Shartsis, Ryan McMurtry, Will Harris, and Finn Salyk helped hold their opponent to two touchdowns, and Ben McMurtry and Gael Fierro had interceptions.
articles.title: Piedmont-led flag football team wins Next Level Super Bowl

articles.text: The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team raced in its second race of the season the weekend of March 19-20 at Fort Ord, near Monterey. A total of 14 high school and seven middle school riders competed in the two-day meet. Junior Andres Roberts earned a podium finish of 5th place in the JV Boys D1 category. Senior Kurt Wilson, coming back from an injury, and starting at the back of the pack, charged to a 13th place finish in the JV Boys D1 Category. Sophomore Matteo Scanu earned a podium spot with a 4th place finish, and classmate Matteo Scanu (left) earned a 4th place finish in the Sophomore D1 Category. Photo by Matteo Scanu Andres Roberts finished 5th in the JV Boys D1 Category. Schuyler Sawicki slotted a 7th place finish in the Sophomore Boys D1 Category. “It’s a fast course that keeps you on your toes,” said Sawicki, “You have to stay alert and stay aware. It’s a grippy track where a balance of speed on the flats and steeps is key.” The team will compete on a new course, the Modesto Flow at Beard Brook Park in Modesto, on April 9. To join the Mountain Bike Club or for information, contact coach Sally Aldridge at sally. aldridge@mac.com.

Ben McMurtry led the team in rushing. The key to the team’s success was its defense led by Kellin de Verney who was matched against the opponents’ best receivers all season. De Verney and defensive players Gabriel Gurney, Aidan Shartsis, Ryan McMurtry, Will Harris, and Finn Salyk helped hold their opponent to two touchdowns, and Ben McMurtry and Gael Fierro had interceptions.
