articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) is hosting an exhibition of artist Tauba Auerbach’s interdisciplinary works. Auerbach, born in 1981 in San Francisco, creates work that considers the ways that structure, pattern, and gesture function from intricate to vast scales. A life-long student of mathematics and physics, she uses a variety of media, ranging from painting and photography to book design and musical performance. In her first solo exhibition, Auerbach showed a series of text-based drawings that explored various linguistic systems that included calligraphy, Morse code, semaphore signals, the Ugaritic alphabet and Alexander Melville Bell’s visible speech. The title of the exhibition, “S v Z”, is a reference to the close yet indeterminate relationship between form and meaning that surfaces throughout the artist’s materials. SFMOMA’s Auerbach exhibition on view through May 1 Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/tauba-auerbach-s-v-z/ to learn more and to plan your next visit to SFMOMA.

New exhibitions include David Huffman: Terra Incognita, the first museum exhibition surveying the Oakland artist’s Traumanaut series; Elegies: Still Lifes in Contemporary Art, a group exhibition of international artists, including Njideka Akunyili Crosby, Sadie Barnette, Awol Erizku, Deana Lawson, and Rashaad Newsome, who have appropriated the still life painting genre to create work that reflects on Black diasporic identities, histories, and collective experiences. Guests will be able to see the latest in MoAD’s “Emerging Artists Program” series. Sam Vernon’s installation Impasse of Desires, which debuted in fall 2021, will continue to be exhibited in the museum lobby through September. Visit https://www.moadsf.org/ event/spring-exhibitions-opening-day to learn more and to obtain tickets. The museum is located at 685 Mission Street in San Francisco. articles.text: Celebrating its 50th year, Berkeley Symphony will perform a concert this Friday, March 25 at 7:30 p.m. at First Congregational Church of Berkeley at 2330 Durant Avenue. The program includes a uniquely Berkeley retelling of Sergei Prokofiev’s Peter and the Wolf, narrated by illustrator and graphic journalist Wendy MacNaughton, and Maurice Ravel’s Mother Goose Suite. Audio descriptions will be provided for Peter and the Wolf, as three local illustrators bring the music and story to life through live drawings during the performance. MacNaughton has a long history of combining the practice of deep looking, listening and drawing to create stories of often overlooked people, places and things. As the creator and host of “DrawTogether,” a participatory drawing show for kids, she helps others use art to bolster social-emotional skills, self-confidence and connection. Tickets that include audio descriptions of Peter and the Wolf are $30 and are available at berkeleysymphony.org or by calling the box office at 510.841.2800. Please mention ACCESSWOLF30 when booking. A special feature will be the appearance of Hindustani singer Saili Oak and soprano Maya Kherani performing Indian-American composer Reena Esmail’s Meri Sakhi Ki Avaazi, a cross-cultural journey that explores family and community. Esmail works between the worlds of Indian and Western classical music. Berkeley Symphony requires proof of vaccination and masks to be worn at all in-person events. articles.text: Fefu and Her Friends premieres tomorrow in an ACT production at the Strand Theatre. American Conservatory Theatre will produce Fefu and her Friends, a comedy-drama written by Maria Irene Fornes, a Cuban-American playwright, beginning March 24 at the Strand Theatre in San Francisco. The story is a dialogue of eight women gathered at a New England country home in 1935. The production stars Stacy Ross, with Catherine Castellanos, Cindy Goldfield, Maria Gomez, Jennifer Ikeda, Leontyne MbeleMbong, Sarita Ocon, and Lisa Anne Porter. The multi-storied, multi-roomed Strand Theater will be used as a non-traditional production stage, where audience members will be divided into four groups that independently tour Fefu’s home. The show will be directed by Pam MacKinnon. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/20202122-season/fefu-andher-friends/.
articles.title: ACT’s Fefu and her Friends premieres tomorrow

articles.text: Some dining traditions have served us well over the years. Anyone from New Orleans knows that Monday is reserved for red beans and rice. In many places, tamales are served on Tuesdays. And Fridays were reserved for fish. You might think that this was entirely a Catholic tradition, but that is not entirely correct. Both Catholics as well as other Christians, and Jews avoided meat on Fridays. The reasons were completely different, but the result was identical. In both cases, Friday was a holy day. This word was spelled “haly”. The species of flat fish were termed “butte”. By combining these two words we get halibut. Here is a festive fish recipe from Liguria, Italy which you can enjoy on Fridays or any other day. It combines fish, any type of pasta and fennel. I tried the recipe with potato gnocchi, but I would suggest using some type of spaghetti. For four people, make a circle with your thumb and middle finger. That is enough pasta for four people. Plan on a quarter pound of fish per person. The traditional recipe uses lobster tails but you can also use crab claws. I used rock shrimp and it was terrific. Do not use clams or mussels. If you want to avoid shellfish, I would suggest using a firm fleshed fish such as Corvina sea bass or rock cod. Swordfish is also a good choice. articles.text: If you happen to have kids hanging out at your house and you walk by a room and see a youngster/tween/teen stretched out on a bed or sofa reading a comic book, take a moment and consider what that means. Begin with the word “reading.” Then pause and see if you can get a look at the cover. What’s the art look like? What or who is the title character? Then with all the humility and approbation you can muster, ask, “Whatcha reading?” With that question, mom or dad, you’ve entered hallowed ground. When I was a youngster, I yearned to learn to read. I spent time with my “cousins” who were slightly older and had stacks of comics in their rooms, magazines that I paged through but couldn’t decode. .I soon read comic books voraciously, willingly suspending my disbelief, spending countless Saturdays in comic book trades with other comic book fans. All of us were collectors of a sort and each of us had a favorite superhero. Keep in mind that we arrived at the tail end of what is now thought of as the “Golden Age” of comics. Superman, for example, was created in 1938 and had already established a legacy of fighting for truth and justice and the American way. Ditto Captain Marvel, though later. Each comic – most by created DC and Marvel Comics – was made up of sequential panels with text in boxes and dialogue in balloons, highlighted by drawings that were vibrant, kinetic, and compelling In the aggregate they told a story of peril and adventure. And there were, of course, the characters that included the world of Disney (Mickey, Donald, Pluto, Goofy and so on) as well as a sprawling cast of superheroes such as Superman, Batman and Robin, Spider-Man, Aquaman, and Wonder Woman. It was a world of richness, imagination, and endless permutations. It wasn’t until the 1970s when Marvel Comics created a stable of superheroes, assembled by the hugely creative team of illustrators Stan Lee and Jack Kirby. They were initially called the Fantastic Four: Ant-man, the Hulk, Iron Man, and Thor and later the Wasp and Captain America. Gradually the Marvel Universe of superheroes grew deeper and wider, with a rotating roster. Soon came The Avengers, whose motto was that the Avengers “fight the foe no single hero can withstand.” In 2012, Marvel Studios (now owned by Disney) created the first live-action feature titled Avengers and introduced to worldwide audiences this rich cast of superheroes. It had a seismic opening box office weekend. In 2015 came Avengers: Age of Ultron, and, in 2016, the cohort made an appearance in Captain America: Civil War, followed by Avengers: Infinity War in 2018. The number of characters has expanded exponentially, and when the sequel to Infinity War, Avengers: End Game, opened, super fans (and parents sitting several rows back), likely needed a program for the mind-numbing layers of characters. Keep an eye out for a genetically engineered raccoon called Rocket who is one smart, highly verbal bounty hunter. Keep in mind that all of the ideas began with a pulpy magazine called a comic book that appeared in 1933, based on humorous panels (comics) that were lifted from newspapers. The rest is history. And in the world of comics, “reading” is still the operative word. Buy a few and leave them in the living room and see what happens... Just a suggestion.
articles.title: Deconstructing the Comic Book

articles.text: All public events at Piedmont Center for the Arts require photo ID and valid proof of full vaccination including booster shot, as well as proper masking while inside. Wednesday, March 23, 7 p.m. Lisa Riddiough book launch Lisa Riddiough brings fellow children’s book authors Aimee Lucido and Joanna Ho to a discussion about writing illustrated books for children, moderated by Piedmont author Cynthia Nooney. As a children’s book author, Lisa strives to make her books accessible to the type of reader she remembers being as a child. In her opinion, it is perfectly OK to choose a book that is short, has a large font, and has plenty of illustrations. The book is dedicated to Piedmont Middle School science teacher Ted Greenebaum. Recently published books of the authors will be available for purchase and are currently available at A Great Good Place for Books, an independent bookstore in Montclair. The event is free to the public. Saturday, March 26, 4 p.m. Piedmont Chamber Orchestra Concert Returning after the long pandemic hiatus, the community orchestra will perform a concert including Mendelssohn’s Hebrides (Fingal’s Cave) Overture, Fauré’s Masques et Bergamasques, and Beethoven’s Symphony No. 8, conducted by Martha Stoddard. Admission is free but donations to the non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts are welcome. COVID safety protocols will be in place (vaccination cards checked, masks required). This 28-member volunteer orchestra will help celebrate Spring with style. The 75-minute concerts will be followed by light refreshments and an opportunity to interact with the musicians. Thursday–Sunday, March 31–April 3 Lord of the Flies – PHS Drama As an extra-special Spring treat, the PHS Drama Department’s Advanced Acting Class under the direction of Kim Taylor will present five performances of the stage play adapted by Nigel Williams from the 1954 novel Lord of the Flies, by Nobel Prize-winning English author William Golding. Lord of the Flies performances are Thursday through Saturday, March 31-April 2, at 7:00 p.m., and two sows on Sunday, April 3 at 1:00 and 6:00 p.m. Tickets are $10 for students and $17 general admission and should be purchased in advance at https://www.showtix4u.com/ events/LOTF. Support the programming of Piedmont Center for the Arts by donating generously to the Tip Jar at these events.

And there were, of course, the characters that included the world of Disney (Mickey, Donald, Pluto, Goofy and so on) as well as a sprawling cast of superheroes such as Superman, Batman and Robin, Spider-Man, Aquaman, and Wonder Woman. It was a world of richness, imagination, and endless permutations. It wasn’t until the 1970s when Marvel Comics created a stable of superheroes, assembled by the hugely creative team of illustrators Stan Lee and Jack Kirby. They were initially called the Fantastic Four: Ant-man, the Hulk, Iron Man, and Thor and later the Wasp and Captain America. Gradually the Marvel Universe of superheroes grew deeper and wider, with a rotating roster. Soon came The Avengers, whose motto was that the Avengers “fight the foe no single hero can withstand.” In 2012, Marvel Studios (now owned by Disney) created the first live-action feature titled Avengers and introduced to worldwide audiences this rich cast of superheroes. It had a seismic opening box office weekend. In 2015 came Avengers: Age of Ultron, and, in 2016, the cohort made an appearance in Captain America: Civil War, followed by Avengers: Infinity War in 2018. The number of characters has expanded exponentially, and when the sequel to Infinity War, Avengers: End Game, opened, super fans (and parents sitting several rows back), likely needed a program for the mind-numbing layers of characters. Keep an eye out for a genetically engineered raccoon called Rocket who is one smart, highly verbal bounty hunter. Keep in mind that all of the ideas began with a pulpy magazine called a comic book that appeared in 1933, based on humorous panels (comics) that were lifted from newspapers. The rest is history. And in the world of comics, “reading” is still the operative word. Buy a few and leave them in the living room and see what happens... Just a suggestion. articles.text: Renée Zellweger as Judy Garland in Judy. After a brief flashback in which Louis B. Mayer is lecturing young Frances Gumm (later to be known worldwide as Judy Garland), the film Judy, released in 2019, opens with Judy and her two children returning late at night to her L.A. hotel where – her suitcases at her feet, her exhaustion palpable – she is told that her suite has been released to someone else and her things have been put in storage. Her line of credit, she’s told, has been cancelled. Desperate, broke, with bills in arrears, she takes the children to their father, Sid Luft (Rufus Sewel), where she leaves them and quickly signs to do a series of shows in a London nightclub, Talk of the Town. Its owner (Michael Gambon), has warily made a bet that the audience will indeed turn out to see this still famous entertainer and that Judy will perform as promised. Just to be sure, however, she is assigned an assistant (Jesse Buckley) to shadow her days and remind her of the daily schedule, for they are ever cognizant that this once huge talent may have reached her nadir. And so, all those who satellite the show’s preparation watch and wait for any hint of Judy faltering. The movie audience knows her story all too well known, if only in outline form. The London performances represent a fragile opportunity, desperate to find something to slow her fall from the limelight. The film walks a precarious tightrope. In every scene and with every decision, the heartfelt wish is that she will prevail. But simultaneously, we know that this will not end well. And yet we hope, even when she refuses to rehearse, when she washes down pills with alcohol, when she suffers chronic insomnia, when she shows up late, often overcome with a stage fright, as her audience waits. These emotions are not simply the result of a known foreshadowing, but testimony to the transcendent performance by actress Renée Zellweger. Absent from movies for almost a decade, she embraces the character of Judy as if she stepped into a holographic figure and uses all of her own gifts to bring Judy back to us. Zellweger is that good. It is her voice we hear. It is her commitment to this performance that she offers without hesitation. And as she sits at the end of the stage and the lights wash over her, singing “Somewhere Over the Rainbow,” she heartbreakingly dazzles. It’s a breathtaking moment. Using flashbacks, we observe young Judy (still Frances) following a yellow brick road, every stone laid by cynical and avaricious adults, such as Louis B. Mayer, and most certainly her uber-stage mother who plied her with stay awake/diet drugs and relentless admonishments (“look at the birthday cake, don’t eat it”), while obliterating her youth. From the first frame of this remarkably well-told story, it is a tragedy in the making. And it is also a window into the price of fame and those pursuing it know how imperfect that yellow brick road can be. One of the final lines, part of the ending credits, tells us that six months after Judy left London she died. She was 47. Zellweger did win an Oscar for Best Leading Actress for her outstanding portrayal Judy. Directed by Rupert Goold. With Renée Zellweger, Jessie Buckley, Finn Wittrock, Rufus Sewell, and Michael Gambon. Released in 2019. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated PG-13. Now streaming on Prime. Review originally published in the Piedmont Post in 2019.

articles.text: In its many extraordinary films over the years, Pixar (now Pixar/Disney) has focused on countless emotional issues: in Inside Out it emphasized that sadness was necessary to experience joy; in Coco it examined how love can prevail after death; and in WALL-E how greed can overwhelm humanity. But it’s in the wonderful, coming-of-age animated feature Turning Red that Pixar courageously, and with sensitivity, tackles the issue of female puberty. Re-released this year (2022), the story, set in Toronto, has at its center a 13-year-old girl named Meilin Lee (Rosalie Chang). She plays the flute, is an eighth grade honor student, and in all respects an ideal girl on the cusp of becoming a young woman. But despite all of her accomplishments, she finds herself rebelling against the strict rules of her over-controlling mother, Ming (Sandra Oh), the quintessential helicopter mom. We soon learn that when Meilin becomes emotional (some teens might describe this as getting your freak on), and is overwhelmed by feelings that seem beyond her understanding – perhaps set in motion by, well, a boy-band, or a store clerk that she’s crushing on – she turns into a very large red panda, a character that is symbolic of the stress and roller coaster ride known as adolescence. The repercussions of Meilin’s first period, an example of all the changes she’s going through, are handled with sensitivity, certainly within the parameters of the film’s PG limits, and there’s not a gratuitous moment in this nicely told tale. The story does convey that puberty, this tumultuous rite of passage, is a beast, a composite of seemingly unbearable stress and self-conscious emotions that define this time in an adolescent female’s life. Meilin quickly learns that all she has to do is calm down, and she will revert from the giant red panda back into herself, the ideal student and newbie teen that her parents so warmly love. But we also see that Meilin struggles with her feelings of ambivalence regarding being the compliant and obedient daughter or pushing back against her mother, however timidly. The question posed throughout is, does she want to conform to the rules? She is surrounded by Chinese culture and caring parents. But despite her supportive family, Meilin’s ultimate preference is her influential peer group, composed of Miriam (Ava Morse), Priya (Maitreyl Ramakrishman), and Abby (Hyein Park) who are never put off by Meilin’s alter ego panda. In fact, they devise a plan to sell tickets to their school classmates, which will allow them to watch her transform into the giant red panda. The girls’ plan is to use the proceeds to attend a concert by their favorite boy-band 4*Town, whose songs are reminiscent of boy-bands like ‘N-Sync. When Meilin asks permission to go, her parents are, naturally, hesitant, knowing that such concerts create intense, even frenzied emotions, and Ming is fearful that her daughter will “go all red panda.” But Meilin comes to understand that her red panda is an integral part of who she is, however disconcerting those moments might be. Turning Red is filled with teachable moments in the best Pixar tradition, with one overriding lesson: be yourself. Pixar nails it. Turning Red. Directed by Domee Shi. A Pixar animated film. Released in 2022. With voices of Rosalie Chang, Sandra Oh, Ava Morse. 1 hr., 40 min. PG-13. Now streaming on Disney.
articles.title: Turning Red a sensitive Pixar coming-of-age film

articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors group is hosting a CHP-led Safe Driving presentation at Piedmont Community Hall from 9:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. on Wednesday, March 30. The “Drive Safe and Smart” seminar returns after an absence of three years. It will include: • Compensating for age-related changes, • A tune-up of your driving skills • Rules of the road • Nutrition and strength • Safe driving tips Senior members of the community are encouraged to take advantage of this traffic safety seminar. You may be entitled to an auto insurance discount, and certificates will be provided to participants. Pre-register with Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. Space availability is limited, with priority to Piedmont Seniors’ members. in each section of the concrete sidewalks on the length of St. James Drive. The walkers took a short side trip up Cambrian Avenue so hey could walk down a 104-foot, hidden path between Cambrian and St. James. It is an old short cut between the streets and doesn’t have handrails. At the end of St. James is Corpus Christi Church at the corner of Park Boulevard. The walkers decided to continue onto Leimert Boulevard. On the Leimert bridge that spans a canyon is a plaque that tells its history. Its official name is the Sausal Creek Arch Bridge which was completed in 1926. George Posey, Alameda County Surveyor and engineer of the Posey Tube between Oakland and Alameda, designed it. It is 257 feet long and 118 feet high. The Park Boulevard Company, which was owned by Walter and Harry Leimert, was responsible for building it and running a Key System streetcar line across it. The Leimerts wanted to develop an Oakmore Highlands neighborhood on the other side of the canyon. The bridge, with distant views of San Francisco, spans Dimond Canyon far below, and was originally part of Antonio Maria Peralta’s land grant. There was once extensive lumbering in the area with great redwoods cut and floated down the creek to Lake Merritt and the Bay. The walkers explored the retail block beyond the bridge, where Rocky’s Market, is the centerpiece. It was founded in 1961 and sells local, organic produce and other items. Noemi Alvarado also shared that at the end of the block, up Arden Place, is a trail that goes up to Highway 13. It was getting close to noon, and time for the walkers to return to Piedmont’s town center. It ended up being almost a five-mile walk, one of the group’s longer walks, but on a beautiful morning with unexpected history. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.

It was noted that the next day was St. Patrick’s Day. A little research had found that Saint Patrick was a fifth-century Romano-Christian missionary and bishop in Ireland and is the primary patron saint of Ireland. Saint Patrick’s Day is observed on March 17. The walkers felt they could walk St. James Drive, the only Piedmont street that references a saint. Research showed that St. James was one of the Twelve Apostles of Jesus, and was one of the first disciples to join Jesus. He and his brother John were with their father by the seashore when Jesus called them to follow him and be “fishers of men.” St. James was also the first to be martyred according to the New Testament. He died in 44 AD and is the patron saint of Spain. Piedmont’s St. James Drive was named after St. James Woods, an early, very large Piedmont neighborhood development. St. James Drive is .7 of a mile and is lovely, flat, and easy to walk. Additionally, at its end on Park Boulevard, there were options for the walkers to continue on. They could either see Cavendish Lane, an Oakland street with four homes with Piedmont addresses, or cross Park Boulevard to the Leimert Bridge and a few retail stores. They went past Crocker Park on Hampton to its intersection with St. James Drive, where this street starts. One block further at La Salle Avenue are two large columns that marked one of the entrances to the St. James Woods development. The group noted that the columns are still missing lanterns on their tops. Mike Henn remembered a few years ago the neighbors wanted the City to install new ones, but the City didn’t have the money to do it, so it never happened. articles.text: One of the great things about walking around town is discovering the many different sculptures, statues, and garden art placed by homeowners and/or their designers. These ornaments reflect the personality and design sense of the inhabitants. Even if they came with the house, if after a number of years they are allowed to remain, they receive the imprimatur of the owners. The variations are numerous, with many different types, styles, and characters possible. They can be playful and even humorous, or more formal and serious. And while it is necessary that they harmonize with the main architecture and landscape architecture, there is still plenty of room for originality and creativity. One of the most common examples of this ornamental type of site feature is the use of lion statues “guarding” entrances. Used all over the world since Different examples of lions guarding the entries to homes in Piedmont. The single one on the left seems to express a welcoming attitude with the lifted paw (like my cat asking for a pet) while the classical pair on the right indicate a calmness and tranquility. But there is also an underlying sense of strength and “guardian” quality evident in both postures. Like many “hidden” sculptures in backyards around town, this contemporary iron sculpture by artist Roger Miller at the end of a new stone path adds subtle punctuation to the garden of Kirk and Christina Miller. One of a number of kinetic art (art that moves) pieces around town that are subtle and understated, blending in well with the surrounding garden planting. articles.text: Dear Jim: Now that we are working from home full time, and one of our adult children is moving in after college, we are considering digging out our basement for more space. Is this a good option for our home? With the new post-pandemic work-at-home reality, coupled with the explosion in home values, our company has seen a marked increase in requests for basement projects in the past few years. These jobs are proving to be great solutions to create new space, but there are several things to consider before turning this dream into a reality. Is it the best option for creating new space? Most homeowners have three possibilities to add new living space, each with advantages and disadvantages. A new addition behind your home is the simple, more affordable approach but requires sufficient space to do it, limited by an (average) allowed lot coverage of less than 50% and property line setbacks. A second-floor addition will add possible warmth, light, and views, but will likely require structural work below, neighbor buy-in and is pricier. A new basement offers cooler living space and is easiest to permit. However, potential lack of views, windows and light need to be considered. Basement renovations can lead to unexpected work Basement jobs typically consist of three elements-the structural work and dig out, the remodel, and what I call the infrastructure project. New foundations, drainage and digging down to create an 8’ ceiling are basic considerations. Then, often a substantial portion of the utilities need to be upgraded since they are outdated, insufficient for the increased space and need to be placed in a centralized location to accommodate the new floor plan. If you have an old foundation, drainage and seismic issues, plus outdated utilities, this may be the perfect fit. What are the limitations on what new spaces can be added? Access and windows are often the two most important things to consider. Depending on the slope of your property, the location and size of windows can be limited. 12-foot tall ceilings on this project required significant rebar and waterproofing. If you are looking for internal access, you will need to carve out the space upstairs to add a stairway- otherwise you would be limited to an outside entrance. For added bedroom spaces you will need enough height for an egress window (usually around 4’ minimum), so that may be a consideration. Conversations with Your Local Contractor is a feature by Jim Gardner, owner of Jim Gardner Construction Inc. He is a long-time Piedmont resident and has been doing structural repair and basement renovation in local neighborhoods since 1983. articles.text: Sign at entrance I have been enchanted by Tiki style restaurants since my family frequented one called The Islands in my childhood in Phoenix, Arizona. Twenty years ago when I moved to the Bay Area, we celebrated our relocation with a family dinner at Trader Vic’s in Emeryville. So here I was all these years later being escorted into the small private dining room in the back of the restaurant to have lunch with General Manager Faith Nebergall and conduct an interview. Faith relocated to the Bay Area from Chicago and got her first job here as a cocktail waitress at Trader Vic’s. She worked her way up through the organization and is now General Manager of the Emeryville flagship restaurant. Trader Vic’s has deep roots in the East Bay. The chain had its beginnings when “Trader” Vic Bergeron started a restaurant in the 1930’s called Hinky Dinks on San Pablo Avenue in Oakland. Inspired by the success of Don the Beachcomber tiki restaurants in LA and Chicago, he changed the name to Trader Vic’s and opened a location in San Francisco on Cosmo Place that became one of the city’s iconic restaurants. In 1972 Bergeron opened a new spacious restaurant right on the water at the marina in Emeryville. The company expanded rapidly with restaurants in Seattle, Chicago, Atlanta, Beverly Hills, Scottsdale and many more including their first international location in London. While today there are only three Trader Vic’s in the U.S. – Emeryville, Atlanta and the San Jose airport – the company began franchising locations in a number of exotic locations and now have restaurants in Dubai, Qatar, United Arab Emirates, Oman, Bahrain, Jordan and the Seychelles Islands. Vic Bergeron was a pioneer, and it can be said that it was the first “fusion” restaurant decades before that style became trendy. To this day the menu blends Polynesian, Chinese, Thai and European elements. We started with the Cosmo Tidbits which is a pupu platter of assorted appetizers – crispy shrimp, braised marinated pork, crunchy wontons and BBQ spareribs. We also sampled the Trader Vic’s salad with Javanese dressing and the tuna poke made with big chunks of fresh ahi. In addition, we had fried rice with shrimp, chili coconut chicken which was a fresh tasting stir fry, and a Hawaiian Cubana sandwich which had the original sliced pork and cheese plus fresh pineapple. It took me right back to the delicious Cuban spots I used to haunt when I lived in Miami. The menu changes several times a year but the classics remain. (Bongo Bongo soup has fallen out of favor). One of the most distinctive aspects of TV’s culinary style is the use of two huge Chinese wood-fired ovens. They sit in the middle of the restaurant behind glass to protect from the smoke but so everybody can see the cooks lowering big racks of spareribs and whole ducks into the ovens. The item I have ordered most over the years is the oven cooked Chinese duck. It has delicious crispy skin and tender succulent meat with aromas of hoisin and Chinese 5 spice powder – totally delicious. (The ovens don’t operate during the lunch shift.) But Trader Vic’s is more than about the food – it’s the experience. Here is how Steve Siegelman, author of “Trader Vic’s Tiki Party” describes it. “You walked out of your life and into that swank, clubby Polynesian fantasy world, blinking as your eyes adjusted to the dim light, and slowly took it all in. There were carved tiki heads, spears, and tribal drums competing for space with ship’s bells, fishing nets, shark jawbones, and harpoons. Overhead, outrigger canoes floated among the rafters above a jungle of bamboo, palms, and Technicolor flora. “Here and there purple flames flickered under platters of pupus. Over by the massive clay oven, a chef was fishing meat from the roaring fire with a long iron hook. The Hawaiian-shirted bartenders were turning out concoctions of equal parts rum and Hollywood spectacle – a Kamaaina in a ceramic coconut, a two-quart Rum Keg with four impossible long straws, a hurricane glass sporting a garland of island fruit and flowers crowned with a winking plaster parrot. “And all of it – the drinks, the food, the laughter, the carefully crafted chaos of the tropical Trader Vic’s dining room. The bar at Trader Vic’s. Manager Faith Nebergall and the Potted Parrot. décor – came together to create an irresistible mix of excitement, sophistication, and over-thetop fun. From the moment you walked in, you felt like you were on vacation on a faraway island somewhere outside of time, at a perfectly orchestrated party.” Now we come to the most important thing about Trader Vic’s – THE DRINKS! Vic Bergeron is most famous for inventing the Mai Tai. One day he was behind the bar and he grabbed some J.Wray and Nephew rum, lime juice, sugar syrup, orange curacao and a little French orgeat, mixed them together with ice and handed one to some friends visiting from Tahiti. After a sip they declared “It’s mai tai roa ae!”– Tahitian for “Out of this world!” And thus, the Mai Tai was born. It is to this day the most popular drink at Trader Vic’s and they have two versions – the Original, and the “SF” with an extra float of rum on top. Faith Nebergall informed me that one of the most popular drinks is not even on the menu, but insiders know to order the Tiki Puka Puka cocktail. Why so popular? It is the strongest drink they make, using four different rums. I followed that with the Suffering Bastard, a drink from the Sheppards Hotel in Cairo. Another popular tiki drink is the Zombie, hyped by the fact that the menu used to warn customers that only two per person were allowed. Also recommended are the Potted Parrot “when it’s time to go home the parrot goes with you,” the Samoan Fog Cutter “strong enough to cut through any fog and later put you in one!” and Tiki Grog “warning more than one may result in a temporary tiki face.” The restaurant also carries a Founder Vic Bergeron pretty good wine selection but oddly the Cabernet-heavy list is more appropriate for a midwestern steak house than a tiki joint. But to me the wine list is beside the point. You can get good wine anywhere …where else can you get great tiki drinks like these? The bottom line is 85 years after Trader Vic started his little restaurant on San Pablo Ave. in Oakland the brand is going strong. On a recent Friday evening when I stopped in with friends for a drink, I was delighted to find the large dining room packed with diners and the bar equally hopping. So it looks like this venerable institution has made it through the pandemic and is heading into the future in search of the next million Mai Tais.
articles.title: Trader Vic’s – standing strong after all these years

articles.text: Dear Abby: We found a small pug wandering around the parking lot of Trader Joe’s in Emeryville. We took her to the Vet but she was not chipped and was not wearing a collar. The Vet said she was only a puppy, under a year old, less than 15 pounds. We’ve named her Noqui which is Spanish for Gnocci. So far no one has responded to the Lost & Found post that we put online on Craig’s List and Nextdoor. We’d love to find her owners. Come over and meet her, or I’ll come to you. -Natalia noqui2022@gmail.com Dear Natalia, The Pug Queen tells me that you should post ASAP on Pug Rescue of NorCal at Pugpros.org. It is a non-profit which many pug owners know about and search. It is also smart to call the Piedmont and Emeryville Police Departments and let them know you found a Pug pup. Petfinder.com and Pawboost. Thanks Natalia. We honor you with the Paws of Honor Badge. -Abby Dear Abby: Have you heard that someone is still stealing roses from the Morcom Rose Garden? Hundreds of plants have been stolen and the Oakland Police do not have the time to watch the garden because they’re pretty busy. Please tell all your dog buddies to be on alert if they’re in the neighborhood and out for a walk. In this day of turmoil, we need our rose garden to restore us. We need help, -Cheryl Dear Cheryl: There’s nothing we like more than a spring walk through any garden but we are not allowed inside to sniff at the lovely Morcom Rose Garden. Maybe if we all keep a firm lookout, we can end this bad behavior. Those thieves are barking up the wrong rose tree, -Abby Dear Abby: Have you noticed that there are a lot of aggressive dogs in the dog park lately? I live right next to Crocker Park. Our dog is big but very friendly and many people warn us that their dog is not. Don’t get me wrong, com are other sites many people use to search for dogs of all breeds. Perhaps you can print a photo of her and put a sign up at that Trader Joe’s? Sweet Noqui is lucky that you found her.
articles.title: Aggressive dogs should avoid dog parks

pages.text: Wednesday, March 23, 2022 27 Dear Abby A pet column compiled by Piedmont pets Aggressive dogs should avoid dog parks By Abby, a Bernese Mountain Dog Dear Abby: We found a small pug wandering around the parking lot of Trader Joe’s in Emeryville. We took her to the Vet but she was not chipped and was not wearing a collar. The Vet said she was only a puppy, under a year old, less than 15 pounds. We’ve named her Noqui which is Spanish for Gnocci. So far no one has responded to the Lost & Found post that we put online on Craig’s List and Nextdoor. We’d love to find her owners. Come over and meet her, or I’ll come to you. -Natalia noqui2022@gmail.com Dear Natalia, The Pug Queen tells me that you should post ASAP on Pug Rescue of NorCal at Pugpros.org. It is a non-profit which many pug owners know about and search. It is also smart to call the Piedmont and Emeryville Police Departments and let them know you found a Pug pup. Petfinder.com and Pawboost. Thanks Natalia. We honor you with the Paws of Honor Badge. -Abby Dear Abby: Have you heard that someone is still stealing roses from the Morcom Rose Garden? Hundreds of plants have been stolen and the Oakland Police do not have the time to watch the garden because they’re pretty busy. Please tell all your dog buddies to be on alert if they’re in the neighborhood and out for a walk. In this day of turmoil, we need our rose garden to restore us. We need help, -Cheryl Dear Cheryl: There’s nothing we like more than a spring walk through any garden but we are not allowed inside to sniff at the lovely Morcom Rose Garden. Maybe if we all keep a firm lookout, we can end this bad behavior. Those thieves are barking up the wrong rose tree, -Abby Dear Abby: Have you noticed that there are a lot of aggressive dogs in the dog park lately? I live right next to Crocker Park. Our dog is big but very friendly and many people warn us that their dog is not. Don’t get me wrong, com are other sites many people use to search for dogs of all breeds. Perhaps you can print a photo of her and put a sign up at that Trader Joe’s? Sweet Noqui is lucky that you found her. Years ago when I grew up in Piedmont, dogs that weren’t friendly were not walked in the dog parks. I think that’s a better plan. Happy Hounds Only, -Sam and Tucker Dear Sam and Tucker: Dogs that do not get along with other dogs should steer clear of dog parks, especially the smaller parks. Some owners may make the case that visiting any dog park will help those dogs become less aggressive, but what if it was a child came up to pet them? Or an older adult? One sunny day not too long ago, I was in Piedmont Park, sitting under my Mom’s legs as she was on a bench talking with a girlfriend and a Golden Retriever came up and ripped the heck out of my leg and neck. I had to have dozens of stitches and wear a cone of silence for weeks so that I wouldn’t lick the stitches. The Golden was on a leash but the owner couldn’t hold her back. The owner confessed it had happened before. The legal ramifications of dog bites is daunting. Owners can be held responsible. Dogs that want to be the boss and don’t want to be near or sniffed by other dogs should stay in bigger spaces where they have more room to roam. Head Halters or Mouth Leashes can also help owners control those aggressive behaviors. Now they make them in all sizes and shapes so they can be comfortable. Happy dogs, happy life. -Abby E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at MSJ312@ aol.com. articles.text: Old World elegance and a modern lifestyle come together in the 1918 Jacobethan Revival estate at 456 Wildwood Avenue in Piedmont. Recently refurbished, this 6++ bedroom, 7++ bathroom grand estate was designed by Albert Farr with a wealth of architectural details. As you pass through the wrought iron gate and stone pillars, the prominent parapeted gables topped with finials and tall angled bays with leaded glass windows dominate the façade. The stone driveway encircles a fountain and brings you to the richly paneled entry doors, recessed in a Tudor arch. In true Albert Farr fashion, the wood paneled foyer opens to handsome rooms. Farr’s one slogan in designing a building was, “Do the job right. Please the client, but do it right.” Many would agree that Farr designed this house “right.” The grand foyer with its gleaming gumwood paneling extends from a spacious living room on the west to the elegant dining room. The tones of the ornate Italianate ceiling set the color for adjacent rooms. Paneled walls cleverly conceal the doors to the powder room, coat closet and elevator, now a closet. Oak flooring in a herringbone parquet pattern runs throughout the main floor. Three sets of leaded glass French doors open to a rear terrace, overlooking lush gardens and pool. Balustrades line the terrace and the steps down to the lawn. The swimming pool was replaced by a pool with an integrated spa. Leaded glass French doors open to the spacious living room which fills the western end of the house. Four bay windows bring in natural light, and French doors open to a terrace. The blue walls relate to the blue of the ornate ceiling in the foyer. Mirrored French doors open to the dining room with its chandelier, decorative plaster ceiling, and bay window overlooking the terrace, lawn and pool. The red tinted walls recall the red of the ceiling in the foyer. The façade of the home at 456 Wildwood Avenue designed in 1918 by Albert Farr, the architect who designed Piedmont’s City Hall and Piedmont Community Church. A newspaper clipping from Architect and Engineer magazine shows a photo of the Albert Farr designed house at 456 Wildwood Avenue in 1918, the year it was built. In 1930, the house was owned by industrialist Bert Scott, who had a Christmas Tree by the fountain in the entry courtyard. The wood-paneled grand foyer at 456 Wildwood Avenue extends for much of the ground floor. The chef’s kitchen has been enlarged and remodeled with new slate counter tops, coffered ceiling, and a large central island. French doors open to the pool area and nearby outdoor dining area. The breakfast room offers a pleasant space for casual family dining. The grand staircase fills the two-story, leaded-glass bay and is accented with shields of colored glass, a grand chandelier and polished wood. This staircase accesses the three main floors of the house. A second, utility stairway extends to all four floors. Upstairs, the four bedrooms are generously sized with ensuite bathrooms and bay windows that overlook the gardens. The primary suite fills the western end of the house and offers a gas fireplace and two walk-in closets. The ensuite bath has a built-in soaking tub in one bay window and marble floor with inlaid design. Down the hall, two sizeable bedrooms, one with a fireplace, have angled bays facing south, and ensuite bathrooms. The substantial suite to the east has a marble fireplace, balcony, free-standing soaking tub, and pedestal sinks. A charming sitting room overlooks the front garden. A full-height attic adds two large bedrooms and one smaller bedroom, a full bath with double sinks, three bonus rooms and many closets. The lower floor, originally a ballroom, is now a family room with fireplace, entertainment center with surround sound, wet bar, wine cellar, pantry, half bath, laundry room, and storage. The former chauffeur’s quarters over the three-car garage is a studio apartment with kitchen and full bath. The plumbing, electrical, heating, security, entertainment, irrigation, and drainage systems have been upgraded throughout, and a new well supplies water for the gardens. A rch it e ct A lbe r t Fa r r designed this house in 1917, and contractor Alfred Peterson built it in 1918 for John Spohn, president of a wholesale food manufacturing and distribution company. Spohn may have built the house on speculation. He and his wife and two sons lived in it only three years. Businessman Bert C. Scott, of the Hall-Scott Motor Company, was the long-term resident. He and his wife Trubee, sons Kenneth R. and Edward B. (Bud) and daughter (Kathleen) lived there from 1920 to 1963. Scott partnered with engineer Elbert J. Hall and manufactured high performance internal combustion engines for aircraft, marine and truck engines. The Scotts were active socially and entertained frequently. In 1930, they won first prize for their outdoor Christmas tree decorated with silver tinsel and reflected in their front pond. Gail Lombardi is an architectural historian and President of the Piedmont Historical Society.

articles.text: Piedmont Scouts in Troop 6 had a couple of amazing adventures recently, with service projects and camping at Kirby Cove in the Marin Headlands and Angel Island. Both trips were centered on San Francisco Bay and the iconic Golden Gate Bridge. Troop 6 Scouts, based at Corpus Christi Church in Piedmont, value community service and actively look for opportunities to help in different ways. On February 26, they had the opportunity to help prepare campsites at Kirby Cove, located in the Marin Headlands and part of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area. It is a small site just west of the Golden Gate Bridge and includes five campsites as well as an old artillery battery from World War II. Since the site was closed during the COVID pandemic, there were two years’ worth of weeds and overgrowth to clear. The gravel pathways are designed for wheelchair access, so clearing them of debris and ivy was the top priority. The campsites had already been leveled with raised boxes for tents, but plants were encroaching onto the sites. With hoes, shovels, and brooms, a total of 15 Scouts and seven adults made good progress in rescuing the paths and sites from Mother Nature. In total, the troop was able to: • clear 700 feet of accessible trail • uncover eight buried campsite boundary markers • remove over 100 square feet of weeds from the campsites • sweep 380 square feet of pavement • remove five gallons of trash • clean two campsites of fallen debris After a hard day’s work, the Scouts drank in the spectacular views, spent time on the secluded beach watching cars cross over the bridge while ships crisscrossed below. After dinner, they hiked over a ridge to the Golden Gate Bridge, walked under the bridge, and enjoyed the moonlit views of Alcatraz and Angel islands. Alcatraz and the Zombie Hike The weekend of March 5-6 Troop 6 Scouts camped on the largest natural island in San Francisco Bay, Angel Island, known for its 740 acres of pristine parkland, picnic areas, hiking trails and its rich history as an immigration station from 1910 to 1940. The trip started at Corpus Christi Church on Saturday afternoon with 12 Scouts and three adults. After loading their camping gear, they boarded a ferry from Oakland to San Francisco’s Ferry building. From there, the group relaxed for the 50-minute ferry ride to Angel Island and then hiked about a mile and a quarter to a campsite close to the beach. This trip was aimed at teaching beginning backpacking skills. Scout patrols were given a “just add water” directive, which essentially meant that Scouts had to plan and prepare meals that only required water. The meals were rated on taste, use of ingredients and originality. As an extra twist, there was a “Pack it in, pack it out” challenge. Each patrol received a one-quart Ziploc bag to fit all the garbage they created including all packaging and any uneaten food. The patrols carried their Ziplocs out on Sunday to have them weighed at the next Troop meeting. After dinner and clean-up, the Scouts prepared for a Zombie hike. Armed with headlamps and flashlights they strode off into the dark. They hiked along the Troop 6 Scout Terry Pierre and Cub Scout Nicholas Pierre. articles.text: Gabriel Pierre, Alex von Komarniki, Martin Gustavson, and Alex Mante. perimeter road to Four Corners and took the fire road to Ida Trail. While on the hike the Scouts had constellations pointed out in a clear night sky by the father of a Scout, The Ida Trail took them to the highest peak on the island, 788-foot Mount Caroline Livermore. The sights along the way and at the top were amazing, with a 360° panoramic view of the Bay and bridges lit up and reflecting off the water. On the way back, the Scouts took the Sunset Trail to the perimeter road and returned to camp from the opposite side. It was then that they discovered that some food had been left in a backpack only to be found by raccoons. Luckily, the raccoons were polite. They only moved the backpack to help themselves to the food and there was no damage. Another important lesson a Scout learned! Hiking to the Kirby Cove campsite in the Marin Headlands. Just Add Water Cooking Challenge Meal - Couscous with veggies and chicken made by just adding hot water and letting it sit. Yum! Benji Calceon, Nick Castro, and JD Sellman enjoy oatmeal by just adding water. Getting ready for the Just Add Water Challenge: Nico Salvadei, Alek von Komarniki, Benji Calceon, Matthew Goldweber, Brett Bacheller, Gabriel Pierre, RJ Grace, and Sammy Do. After breakfast on Sunday morning the Scouts broke camp, completed a line sweep (campsite clean-up) and loaded up for the hike to the ferry. On the way to the ferry they saw a brick hospital built in 1904. After enjoying a quick lunch at Ayala Cove, they proceeded homeward by way of the SF Ferry Building, and then another ferry to Jack London Square. Angel Island is truly the hidden gem it is claimed to be. The weather was as close as you get to perfect. The two Troop 6 adventures make everyone appreciate all that there is to explore in the Bay Area. It’s no surprise that when Dr. Rutherford received a call from Committee member Kathy Kelleher asking if he would be the parade Grand Marshal, he assumed it might be a news station. “I didn’t recognize the number at first. I thought it might be a press call, so I stepped out of a meeting,” he said. “I was flabbergasted - utterly flattered and couldn’t wait to tell my wife and kids.” Dr. Rutherford recalled that his six children - Alicia (43, American University), Will (PHS 2000, Merritt), Alexandra (AKA Bunny, PHS 2004, University of Vermont), Anne (PMS 2003, Stanford), Hugh (PHS 2009, Cal Maritime), Amanda (PHS 2013, Princeton) - were as excited as he was to hear of the nomination. “It’s the highest honor in town, next to getting a sandwich named after you,” he said with a smile. “My kids and grandkids are jockeying on who will get to ride along. I had to explain to them that the car won’t fit all of them.” Dr. Rutherford moved to Piedmont in 1988 and can recall many fun parades in past years. Some of his favorite mainstays of the parade are the Balloon Platoon, the Brass Band-style music, and dancing in the park afterwards. He is looking forward to seeing the classic car that will be dedicated to this year’s Grand Marshal - and confirmed that he is already practicing his “Queen Elizabeth” wave. game. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has caused the largest refugee crisis in Europe since World War II, with reports of over 3 million Ukrainians fleeing their country. Brasfield chose Red Cross Ukraine and the Come Back Alive Fund, both of which provide vital aid to Ukrainians affected by armed conflict; including blood collection, mobilization of volunteers and resources, and emergency outreach. The Come Back Alive Fund was launched in 2014 when Russia annexed Crimea, largely considered the onset of the Russo-Ukraine conflict. Brasfield works for Grammarly, a cross-platform cloudbased typing assistant that uses artificial intelligence to review and correct spelling, grammar, and punctuation in digital writing. The company is based in San Francisco but was founded in Ukraine 12 years ago by Max Lytvyn, Alex Schevchenko, and Dmytro Lider. Grammarly Inc. maintains offices in Kyiv, the capital and most populous city of Ukraine that has experienced an extreme mass exodus due to the Russian invasion. Brasfield said that about 250 The sales table donned blue and yellow flowers and was set in front of a large Ukrainian flag. Mo’s chocolate chip cookies, a community favorite available at Mulberry’s Market. of her team members at Grammarly are currently fighting for their country or being forced to leave their homes in Ukraine. She described the first-hand accounts as heartbreaking, which prompted her to search for ways to help from across the globe. “I’ve seen the support for Ukraine firsthand in Piedmont; Ukrainian flags proudly wave throughout my neighborhood, and bake sales are popping up right and left. Our bake sale took the guesswork out of properly vetting organizations,” she said. Brasfield noted that kids donated their ‘tooth fairy’ and birthday money, and parents bought cookies for entire soccer teams. She added that the bake sale’s success was a true testament to the generosity of Piedmont. “It was heartwarming to see the outpouring of support,” she said. “When I shared the fundraiser details with my colleagues in Ukraine, they cried. They said they could have never imagined that a community half a world away would care so deeply about people they’ve never met. articles.text: San Francisco and Berkeley lifted their proof-of-vaccination requirement for patrons of indoor commercial spaces on Friday, March 11. It is unclear when Alameda County will follow suit. The City and County of San Francisco announced on March 9 that it will no longer require people to provide proof of vaccination or a negative COVID-19 test to enter certain businesses. Businesses may decide to be more restrictive than local guidance. For example, a restaurant owner in San Francisco may still require that patrons show proof of up-to-date vaccination status and wear masks indoors. The health order requiring proof of vaccination was made in San Francisco on August 20, 2021 - six months before the same order was issued in Alameda County. San Francisco was the first city in the nation to make such a requirement. Berkeley followed suit soon after, making a similar requirement in September. The Health Order in San Francisco was authored and recommended to city officials by the San Francisco Department of Public Health (SFDPH), and approved by San Francisco Mayor London Breed and Director of Health Dr. Grant Colfax. In Berkeley, the order came from the city’s own public health department. The timeline of when Oakland’s (and other Alameda County cities excluding Berkeley) requirement will be lifted is unclear. That’s because most cities in Alameda County align with directives from the Alameda Department of Public Health, but that agency will not be providing directives on when to lift the requirement - in the situation of Oakland, it will come directly from Oakland City Council. Guidance will come when the City of Oakland’s Declaration of Local Emergency is lifted by Oakland’s City Council, a decision that will not be directly influenced by the Alameda County Health Department (ACPHD), confirmed Communications Specialist Sonia Painda. In Oakland, the requirement went into effect on February 1 under a directive by Oakland’s City Council, based upon an ordinance sponsored by Councilmember Dan Kalb. Councilmember Kalb did not immediately return request for comment. “The city of Oakland does not have a public health department. We have aligned with Alameda County [Public Health Department],” Oakland Citywide Communications Director Karen Boyd confirmed. “The City Council would have to take action to reverse that ordinance. There is no timeline, because we are still in the midst of the COVID emergency.”
articles.title: SF and Berkeley end proof-of-vax requirement

articles.text: The weekend of March 12-13 was a boon to Piedmont teens. Piedmont Community Church held its annual Treasures Sale and raised $19,000 for its annual Youth Service Trip during Spring Break to build homes in Mexico. The youth and adult leadership are excited to be able to plan for the trip the week of April 11-15. The church-sponsored trip was canceled the last two years due to COVID. The large fundraiser at the church venue was sized down this year for safety precautions. In 2019 the sale raised more than $38,000. The 2020 sale was one of the last events to happen in Piedmont before the shelter in place was ordered on March 15, 2020 and raised $30,000, although the 2020 trip in April was canceled at the last minute. The funds pay for the supplies needed to build the houses in Mexico, allowing the construction to be done at no cost to the recipients. Funds also are used for scholarships for students to take part on the six-day trip service project. “We were very fortunate to raise $19,000, because last year we could not have the sale,” said Rev. Scott Kail, the church’s Youth Minister. “We had a meeting Sunday in our church sanctuary with everyone involved in the Mexico trip. Everyone was thrilled and very excited about going.”
articles.title: PCC Treasures Sale raises $19,000 for teen house-building project in Mexico

articles.text: Piedmont Community Church named Dr. Steve Schibsted as its new Senior Pastor on Sunday, March 6. He has served 14 months as the church’s Transitional Pastor following the retirement of Rev. Dr. Bill McNabb who served as Senior Minister for 20 years. He was selected following the recommendation of a Pastor Nominating Committee, co-chaired by Eric Behrens and Zookie Todd, and by consensus vote by parishioners in the church on March 6. He gave his first sermon as the church’s new Transitional Minister on January 3, 2021. Rev. Schibsted has over 20 years of experience working in churches much larger than Piedmont Community Church. A Southern California native, his first experience with the Presbyterian Church was as a youth intern in Santa Barbara, which led to leadership roles in youth ministries at Mount Hermon near Rev. Dr. Steve Schibsted In-person voting at Piedmont Community Church among the congregation on March 6 showed overwhelming support for Dr. Schibsted as new Senior Pastor.
articles.title: Piedmont Community Church names Rev. Dr. Steve Schibsted as Senior Pastor

articles.text: The City of Piedmont will host a virtual discussion on equitable real estate practices that support an inclusive community on April 7 via Zoom. The event, entitled “Welcome to Piedmont: Real Estate Practices in Support of an Inclusive Community,” is co-sponsored by the Piedmont League of Women Voters (LWV), Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC), and Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC). The discussion will be moderated by Piedmont resident Carol Galante, founder of the Terner Center for Housing Innovation at UC Berkeley. Panelists will include retired Piedmont real estate agent Maureen Kennedy, a member of the Clinton Administration; Chief Diversity and Equity Officer at California Association of Realtors Farrah Wilder; and Community Outreach Coordinator for California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) Ashley Gardner. Residents and real estate professionals who tune in will learn about what the current context is for real estate practices and its impact on the demographics of the Piedmont community. articles.text: Join the League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWV) on Wednesday, March 30, for a discussion with Dr. Fiona Hill, an expert on Russia and a Senior Fellow at The Brookings Institution at Stanford. The Zoom episode will explore the current state of democracy, from both domestic and international points of view. Dr. Hill is the Robert Bosch Senior Fellow at the Center on the United States and Europe in the Foreign Policy program at the Brookings Institution and member of the Council on Foreign Relations. Her most recent book, There is Nothing for You Here, draws on her personal journey out of poverty, as well as her unique perspectives as a historian and policy maker, to show how we can return hope to our forgotten places. From 2017 to 2019 , Dr. Hill served as deputy assistant to the president and senior director for European and Russian affairs on the National Security Council. From 2006 to 2009, she served as national intelligence officer for Russia and Eurasia at the National Intelligence Council. She has researched and published extensively on issues related to Russia, the Caucasus, Central Asia, regional conflicts, energy, and strategic issues. Co-author of Mr. Putin: Operative in the Kremlin and The Siberian Curse: How Communist Planners Left Russia Out in the Dr. Fiona Hill is the guest speaker of a League of Women Voters discussion on Russia on March 30. Cold, she holds a master’s degree in Soviet studies and a doctorate in history from Harvard University and a master’s in Russian and modern history from St. Andrews University in Scotland. This event is part of the League’s 2022 Defending Democracy Speaker Series and is co-sponsored by local Leagues in California, Oregon, Colorado, and Florida. This talk will be held live on Zoom and YouTube and will include an audience question and answer session. Visit the website lwvpiedmont.org to learn more about the series and register for this event. Once you have registered, you will receive the Zoom link by email. The event is free and open to the public.
articles.title: Russia expert Fiona Hill to speak at LWV event March 30

The Zoom episode will explore the current state of democracy, from both domestic and international points of view. Dr. Hill is the Robert Bosch Senior Fellow at the Center on the United States and Europe in the Foreign Policy program at the Brookings Institution and member of the Council on Foreign Relations. Her most recent book, There is Nothing for You Here, draws on her personal journey out of poverty, as well as her unique perspectives as a historian and policy maker, to show how we can return hope to our forgotten places. From 2017 to 2019 , Dr. Hill served as deputy assistant to the president and senior director for European and Russian affairs on the National Security Council. From 2006 to 2009, she served as national intelligence officer for Russia and Eurasia at the National Intelligence Council. She has researched and published extensively on issues related to Russia, the Caucasus, Central Asia, regional conflicts, energy, and strategic issues. articles.text: Piedmont’s annual Arbor Day celebration will take place on Thursday, April 28, the day prior to National Arbor Day. Arbor Day was held virtually in 2021 due to the COVID pandemic, but all the usual festivities will return live this year. The Piedmont Park Commission will host “gratitude trees” in Crocker Park and Piedmont Park. During the week of April 24-29, residents and kids are invited to write messages on tags to place on trees. Tags can be picked up at City Hall and at the Recreation Department. The Park Commission will sponsor a movie in Piedmont Park, a documentary entitled Intelligent Trees to be shown at 8:30 p.m. on April 28 in the Main Park. There will be popcorn and refreshments for the film. Special additions this year include more kid-friendly activities. At its most recent meeting, the Park Commission discussed plans to revive last year’s tree-related sidewalk chalk art, which will again be hosted by Piedmont’s Public Works Department. Young participants will choose their favorite public tree and include the name of the species in their drawing. Those who would like help identifying trees should contact Parks and Projects Manager Nancy Kent at nkent@ piedmont.ca.gov. “It’s a fun and creative way for young residents to get involved in Arbor Day activities,” Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap said. “[Arbor Day] activities have been more geared toward adults. With [Park Commissioners] Robin Wu and Amber Brumfiel’s push, we’re reaching a different level of residents,” said Commissioner Betty Goodman. There will also be a kidfriendly scavenger hunt. With more than 80 species of public trees in Piedmont, the city’s urban forest will make for an excellent and challenging hunt. “We’re going to have the community thinking about trees for at least five days – hopefully longer,” Dunlap said. Will, Finn and Max Brumfiel participated in last year’s sidewalk chalk art displays celebrating Piedmont’s many tree species on Arbor Day. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: As a way to showcase the diversity that exists in the Bay Area and here in Piedmont, a few Piedmont families pulled together some ideas, time and talents to bring to town its inaugural food festival. On Sunday, April 24, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Piedmont Food Fest will be launched in Piedmont Park. In partnership with the City, schools, local businesses, community partners, and sponsor Social Good, the Food Fest will welcome visitors and showcase a family-friendly event. Stories of the people behind the food will be shared, with multicultural stage performances, locally-sourced beer and wine, and a kid activity zone. If all goes well, this event may even turn into another annual tradition our community can look forward to year after year. What started as wishful thinking between a few Piedmont residents during the heart of Covid lockdown last year has blossomed into a broad community-led effort. In just over two months, the Food Fest has not only raised capital to make this event happen, but also designed a holistic program that will offer something for everyone. A central mission of Piedmont Food Fest is to show the many diverse offerings of the broader Bay Area community that enrich the experiences of our neighbors. To that end, the Piedmont Food Fest will include chef stories (personal stories from our food vendors themselves), community partner tables (local organizations making the Bay better), and even art and writing samples by local students. Piedmont Food Fest is open to the public and invites attendance by residents in Piedmont and the broader Bay Area. To register or volunteer, please visit us at www.piedmontfoodfest.org. The Food Fest planning committee includes Roger Tsai, Diana Lee, Abha Kothari, Kala Hale, Kyle Killion, Tien Teng, David Lau, Amy Kelly, Ellen Moon Lee, Lisa Chan Carnazzo, and Michelle Mazzeo.
articles.title: Starting a new tradition in Piedmont?

articles.text: Health services company Curative continues to offer COVID-19 testing in Piedmont in the Community Hall parking lot five days a week. Testing is available Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. in the Community Hall parking lot at 711 Highland Avenue. The test offered is a self-collected nasal PCR test, with results available within 48 hours from receipt of the sample at the lab. There is no cost to the person being tested, and insurance is not required. PCR testing is accepted as required testing before air travel in the United States according to the Center for Disease Control. At this time, appointments are encouraged but not required. To schedule an appointment and for more information, call 888-702- 9042 or click on https://cur.tv/ piedmont.

articles.text: Wildfire season hit California hard this year. Climate-change-fueled fires are burning across the state in record size and number, devastating communities and turning the skies red with smoke. During these times, it is easy to feel helpless, especially when the underlying causes of these crises are so monumental. What can ordinary people possibly do to address each other’s health and survival? The Common Humanity Collective (CHC) might have the beginnings of an answer. CHC came together at the beginning of the pandemic as a small group of friends, neighbors, and UC Berkeley graduate students to create alternative ways to produce and distribute hand sanitizer and high-filtration face masks in the Bay Area when these basic resources had disappeared from store shelves. CHC’s momentum grew as more people joined the effort, eventually to over 300 volunteers. They coalesced into decentralized groups across the Bay to build PPE and slow the spread of COVID-19. So far, CHC has distributed over 60,000 DIY “N80” face masks and over 7,000 gallons of sanitizer – all for free. Efforts to make CHC’s masks continued in 2022 and even spread across the country to organizations who heard about CHC from the It Could Happen Here podcast. Recognizing the harmful effects of smoke and air pollutants during the wildfire crisis, the collective has also built high-quality Do It Yourself (DIY) air purifiers so individuals and families can filter the poisonous air that billows into their homes. Since the first signs of smoke in the summer, community members, students, teachers, organizers, tenants, and workers of the East Bay have come together every other Saturday to build these air purifiers and deliver them to the most Elaine Qian distributes an air purifier to a community member in East Oakland who has asthma. affected parts of their communities. More than 130 people from 10 different Bay Area organizations have participated in these builds. The effort has grown to include members of the tenant union Tenant and Neighborhood Councils, the East Bay and SF chapters of the Democratic Socialists of America, the Sunrise Movement, Mask Oakland, other mutual aid groups, as well as friends and families. The DIY purifiers are comparable to significantly more expensive commercial purifiers and can filter a room full of smoke and particulates down to healthy levels within a similar period of time as commercial products. CHC distributes purifiers to the most polluted and least-resourced communities in Oakland and Berkeley, occasionally in partnership with organizations such as East Oakland Collective and Tenant and Neighborhood Councils. The group also makes a determined effort to recruit the recipients of the purifiers to participate in future builds and personally distribute purifiers they assemble to neighbors. Traditional nonprofits that act as a stopgap measure against government austerity often have a demobilizing effect on the beneficiaries of their goodwill. This can perpetuate a cycle of alienation. By urging people to assume ownership of the processes of production and distribution of these essential tools, the work of mutual aid increases their autonomy and their participation in decisions that affect their survival. The attendance at each build event has increased each week with over 1,300 high-quality purifiers assembled and given out so far. What can we do when faced with smoke in our skies from wildfires? Common Humanity Collective says: come together. One person can make a difference, but a community can make a vastly greater difference. We can exercise our collective agency and grow strong together, in the process forging the social relations necessary for the fight toward a better future. Elaine Quian is a PHS class of 2014 graduate and former president of the Piedmont Community Service Crew. Visit https://www. biointeractive.org/classroom-resources/covid-19-sparks-community-action to watch a Documentary CHC from the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. CHC volunteers teach community members in East Oakland how to make air purifiers and then give the purifies to residents.
articles.title: Grassroots group provides free air purifiers to East Bay residents

articles.text: Theodore Markopoulos joined Cub Scouts in 2011 as a Wolf with meetings at Beach Elementary School and made it through to Arrow of the Light. After joining Troop 1, Theo was a Den Leader, participated in NYLT, elected to Order of the Arrow, and Assistant Patrol Leader. In December he completed all requirements to attain the rank of Eagle Scout. A Court of Honor ceremony will be scheduled in the Spring. “I began my Eagle project as a way to give back to the Milo Foundation, a non-profit no-kill organization, to promote a healthier lifestyle for stray animals. My vision was to create a shade structure in the Milo Foundation’s dog lot. Due to local extreme weather conditions, many volunteers were choosing to stay indoors to take care of the dogs, which was not the ideal environment for these animals. However, after my shade structure was built, it has Theodore Markopoulos, Eagle Scout in Troop 1. provided a shaded area for volunteers to shelter under during harsh weather, encouraging volunteers to spend more time outdoors with the dogs.”
articles.title: Theo Markopoulos achieves rank of Eagle Scout

Since the first signs of smoke in the summer, community members, students, teachers, organizers, tenants, and workers of the East Bay have come together every other Saturday to build these air purifiers and deliver them to the most Elaine Qian distributes an air purifier to a community member in East Oakland who has asthma. affected parts of their communities. More than 130 people from 10 different Bay Area organizations have participated in these builds. The effort has grown to include members of the tenant union Tenant and Neighborhood Councils, the East Bay and SF chapters of the Democratic Socialists of America, the Sunrise Movement, Mask Oakland, other mutual aid groups, as well as friends and families. The DIY purifiers are comparable to significantly more expensive commercial purifiers and can filter a room full of smoke and particulates down to healthy levels within a similar period of time as commercial products. CHC distributes purifiers to the most polluted and least-resourced communities in Oakland and Berkeley, occasionally in partnership with organizations such as East Oakland Collective and Tenant and Neighborhood Councils. The group also makes a determined effort to recruit the recipients of the purifiers to participate in future builds and personally distribute purifiers they assemble to neighbors. Traditional nonprofits that act as a stopgap measure against government austerity often have a demobilizing effect on the beneficiaries of their goodwill. This can perpetuate a cycle of alienation. By urging people to assume ownership of the processes of production and distribution of these essential tools, the work of mutual aid increases their autonomy and their participation in decisions that affect their survival. The attendance at each build event has increased each week with over 1,300 high-quality purifiers assembled and given out so far. What can we do when faced with smoke in our skies from wildfires? Common Humanity Collective says: come together. One person can make a difference, but a community can make a vastly greater difference. We can exercise our collective agency and grow strong together, in the process forging the social relations necessary for the fight toward a better future. Elaine Quian is a PHS class of 2014 graduate and former president of the Piedmont Community Service Crew. articles.text: In Piedmont School Board’s March 9 meeting, school administrators and teachers reported the results from the February social-emotional health screener. The survey was given to students in grades 3-12 and showed the same percentages of students in each mental health risk category when compared to the survey in September. Based on answers to 28 questions, students scores put them into one of three levels of risk for mental health: “normal risk,” “elevated risk,” and “extremely-elevated risk.” In the fall and in February 86% of students in the district were classified as normal risk, 11% at elevated risk and 3% at extremely-elevated risk for social-emotional health concerns. SEPTEMBER 2021 FEBRUARY 2022 Students at Millennium High School took a field trip in February – their first in two years – to repair a transitional housing facility in Oakland. Principal Shannon Fierro said the project was an example of a school activity boosting students’ mental health. “We are within the normal range, but we know some students in the normal [risk] range are having challenges,” acknowledged curriculum Director Cheryl Wozniak. The test administered was the BASC-3 Behavioral and Emotional Screening System (BESS), first given to Piedmont students in September of 2020 due to concerns over mental health during distance learning. The test results can be further broken down into the following separate indexes: • Internalizing Risk: Locus of control, social stress, anxiety, depression, and sense of inadequacy. A sample question is “I worry but I don’t know why.” • S el f- Re g u l a t io n R i s k : Self-control, hyperactivity and attention problems. A sample question is “I have trouble sitting still.” • Personal Adjustment Risk: Relations with parents, interpersonal relations, self-esteem, and self-reliance. The data is reviewed by principals, counselors, and school psychologists, and is shared with the parents and teachers of students with elevated scores. Middle school students who have been in the elevated or extremely-elevated risk categories for a second iteration of the survey are offered group counseling. Teachers of students falling in one of these categories for the first time are instructed to provide additional attention, and positive reinforcement. Piedmont Principals agreed that the most effective aspect of the survey was that the results allowed them to identify students individually. PHS Principal Adam Littlefield identified some of the limitations of the survey. “We have had some students in the ‘normal risk’ that were hospitalized for self-harm, so it is one of those things that is a piece of information, but is not the end all,” said Littlefield. Littlefield also noted that some students were answering the questions in a way to avoid talking with an adult, essentially bypassing intervention. Millennium High Principal Shannon Fierro expounded to the board what was being done
