articles.text: In its March 9 meeting the Piedmont School Board approved issuing advance layoff notices to classified employees due to a lack of work or lack of funds. The position most affected is that of Health Clerk, with the equivalent of approximately four full-time salaries being reduced. “In 2021-22, the District hired several health clerks and instructional aides with one-time grants. The funding is not available for the 2022-23 school year, requiring [the] Board [to] reduce the positions so that lay-off notices can be provided,” said Superintendent Randy Booker. The district currently employs eight health clerks. “Of that total, six are regular employees who will receive notices for part or all of their [salary],” said district CFO Ruth Alahydoian. The other two Health Clerks were already on short-term contracts. These notices must be delivered earlier than in the past due to a change in California Education Code 45117. California schools are now required to give layoff notices for the following year by March 15 to Classified Employees. Previously schools gave 60-day notices. The layoffs are projected. Official notices will be delivered in May. The district is required to give this advance notice telling employees that they likely will not be employed. “In May we will determine whether or not there will be different funding for the following year, or if different work [is] needed. We don’t know where we will be with COVID in May or August, so this just gives us flexibility,” Booker explained. School Board Vice President Megan Pillsbury attended a meeting with Classified Employees and was heartened by the communication the district provided. “I was grateful to hear that the district is making good efforts to find other areas to employ some of these people. Hopefully that can happen with some of the staff that is being laid off,” she said.
articles.title: School District gives advance layoff notices to classified employees

articles.text: In a letter dated March 2, 2022 to parents of Piedmont Middle School students, middle school Principal Ryan Fletcher wrote: It is with mixed emotions that I share with you that I will not be returning to Piedmont Middle School next year. My wife Laura and I have decided to relocate our family to Denver, Colorado. We will be joining a wonderful network of friends and family there, and I will be taking on the position of principal at a small middle school in a suburb outside of Denver. I am so grateful for all that I have learned and gained during my time at PMS. As I begin this next chapter and enter a new school community, I can only hope to feel as embraced and supported as I have been throughout my time in Piedmont. While Laura and I are excited to plant new roots in Colorado, we are sad to end this chapter in Piedmont and will forever feel connected to our time and our experience as part of this special community. I want to assure you that in my final months at PMS I will remain committed to the site goals and initiatives that are currently underway, and I will dedicate my time and energy to supporting the transition to Piedmont Middle School’s next principal. This move is truly bittersweet, and I will carry with me all the wonderful moments, memories, and people who have made my time here so meaningful. I am grateful for all that we have accomplished together, and all the ways we have grown as a community. PUSD is beginning its search for Piedmont Middle School’s next principal immediately. The position will be posted this week, and the PMS community will be invited to participate in the process. The District will update families on next steps and will keep you updated throughout the process. With gratitude, Ryan Fletcher Principal Piedmont Middle School
articles.title: Ryan Fletcher reflects on nine years as PMS Principal

articles.text: The Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award will be presented by the Piedmont School Board at its meeting on May 11. Nominations for the award are now being sought. The deadline is March 18, 2022. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who also will receive the gift of a work of student art. The student will receive a monetary award and commendation from the Board. The award, a de facto Volunteer of the Year Award, is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered over a period of time and have made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. Art Hecht, from 1970 to 1982 was a tireless community volunteer and was dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He was very active with the Piedmont Continuation High School (now Millennium High School). In 1998, the Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established by school board member Dewey Watson in memory of Mr. Hecht. articles.text: The Garden Fest Foundation has been working for six years to build community and raise money for charitable organizations making change in the Bay Area. To date, the Foundation has raised over $32,000 and has impacted the lives of more than 3,500 people through its fundraising. Some of the organizations that have received support are Mercy Brown Bag, Lavamae, and Heifer International. The founders are now looking for the next team of students to take the organization forward. The Garden Fest and its annual dinner event was started in 2016 by Toby Jacob and Anabel Loucks as a bat-mitzvah project. Once that event was over they decided that doing the event was a passion that they wanted to pursue and made the organization an official 501c3 non-profit foundation. Every year the events have been sold out, bringing the community together for a gourmet multi-course dinner, with local wines, hand-crafted cocktails and local entertainment – all served by Piedmont high school and middle school students. The pandemic did not stop Garden Fest from happening either. In May 2020 Toby and Anabel partnered with Oliveto restaurant and Market Hall to deliver a gourmet 4-course dinner to more than 150 diners, The event raised $11,000 for Mercy Brown Bag. Now seniors, Toby and Anabel are looking for another Piedmont student team who are interested in carrying forward the Garden Fest Foundation. articles.text: Nancy Rowland has been named as Orinda Academy’s next Head of School, starting on July 1. She will succeed Dr. Susan Eva Porter, who also was a regular contributor to the Piedmont Post. Rowland will arrive with 28 years of progressive independent school career experience at the prestigious Lab School in Washington D.C., a prominent arts-centered school for bright students with dyslexia and other language based learning differences. “It will be my privilege to continue the school’s legacy with the faculty, staff, administration, parent body, and Board of Trustees,” Rowland said. Rowland connects deeply with Orinda Academy’s mission and vision for the future and in “the value of a high school experience that recognizes and supports the unique needs of each student.” Rowland is a Master Teacher and has advanced through the Lab School with various leadership roles. She also created and directed the popular Summer Project at Lab, a cross-curricular program applying academic skills through art, theater, music, set design, and simulations. For the past 10 years Rowland has been Associate Director of Admissions, and in that role initiated relationships with the Black Student Fund and the Latino Student fund and was a leader on the steering committee which developed Lab’s first DEI strategic plan. Founded in 1982, Orinda Academy is an independent, private high school serving grades 9-12 in Orinda, California. Orinda Academy’s personalized approach to learning ensures that rigorous curriculum is accessible to all students, including those who learn differently. Combined with academic support, executive Nancy Rowland will be the new Head of School at Orinda Academy starting July functioning skill development, and social/emotional balance, every student reaches their full potential. The school is located at 19 Altarinda Road in Orinda. (925) 254-7553 www.orindaacademy. org

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Advanced Acting class will perform William Golding’s Lord of the Flies in five performances from Thursday through Sunday, March 31 to April 3. The novel Lord of the Flies, adapted for the stage by Nigel Williams, is part of Piedmont’s freshman year English curriculum. Williams’ stage adaptation follows the plot of the novel – a group of British boys get stranded and are forced to face horrifying beasties on an island after their plane crashes on the island. Acting students of all genders will perform roles as the English boys, including speaking with a British dialect. What happens when young boys are left alone on an island with no structure? “The answer is pretty terrifying,” said cast member PHS junior Chloe Kibarian. The production is rated PG-13 for violence. The cast features Advanced Acting juniors and seniors Theo Arenstam, Liam Gordon, Milani Juarbe, Sarone Kelete, Chloe Kibarian, Molly McWeeny, Fernanda Meagher, Izzy Rosselli, Erik Stenstrom, Joyce Stern, Katherine Stormer, Holden Temple, John Gross Whitaker, and Charles E. White. Director Kimberly Taylor said, “I am grateful that the class is able to perform at the Piedmont Center for the Arts once more after the last successful collaboration there for the production of Lisa Loomer’s Roe immediately prior to the pandemic shutdown in March 2020. The Piedmont Center for the Arts allows us the flexibility to create unique seating configurations. For this show, audience members will be close to the action and will feel like they’re on the island, too,” she said. Lord of the Flies performances are Thursday through Saturday, March 31 to April 2 at 7:00 p.m., with two performance on Sunday, April 3 at 1 p.m. and 6 p.m. Tickets are $10 for students and $17 for general admission. The Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue across the street from the high school. All events at the Piedmont Center for the Arts require audience members to present proof of full vaccination plus booster, as well as proper masking inside. Piedmont Center for the Arts will host Piedmont High School’s Advanced Acting Class in a production of Lord of the Flies from March 31 through April 3.

articles.text: What are the chances of an asteroid or a comet impacting Earth? Chabot astronomers have received a lot of questions on the topic after the recent release of the Netflix film Don’t Look Up, centered around an Earth-ending comet. Here’s the good news: there is no known asteroid big enough to cause a global impact that is estimated to hit Earth in the next 100 years. An asteroid would need to be larger than 460 feet to have significant global effects upon impact. Okay, so a big asteroid is likely not coming anytime soon. But how often do small asteroids impact Earth? It turns out, bits of asteroids and comets hit Earth’s atmosphere and burn up all the time. Approximately 80-100 tons of space dust and small meteorites fall on Earth each day. This is what causes “shooting stars”. Recently, a very small asteroid (estimated at less than 7 feet) made impact near Iceland on March 11. Named asteroid 2022 EB5, it was discovered 2 hours before impact by the Konkoly Observatory and became the 5th asteroid to be found before impacting Earth. Did the asteroid land in the ocean? Probably not. Asteroid 2022 EB5 was estimated to be moving about 11 miles per second. When plummeting against the Earth’s speed of 18 miles per second, it likely burned up into a fireball. Some people in Iceland said they caught a bright flash of light or heard a boom. Asteroids like these and comets that can pass within approximately 30 million miles of Earth’s orbit are categorized as Near Earth Objects (NEOs). How many Near Earth Objects are out there now? NASA is currently tracking more than 28,000 and reporting detailed information on Original reporting and mapping by Bill Grey at Project Pluto. their locations. While there is no known global asteroid threat, tracking remains key to understanding and planning for any possible scenario. It is estimated that only about 40 percent of asteroids 460 feet and larger have been found to date and we find around 500 large NEOs like these per year. In fact, around 30 new asteroids are discovered each week by NASA’s NEOWISE spacecraft and ground telescopes around the World. In fact, Chabot Space & Science Center helps with asteroid tracking using our most powerful telescope, Nellie. In July 2008, Chabot Space & Science Center’s 36-inch telescope, Nellie, was officially designated Observatory G-58 by the International Astronomical Union’s Minor Planet Center (MPC) and selected to contribute to its Near Earth Object (NEO) detection and tracking program. To get involved with asteroid tracking, look at The International Astronomical Search Collaboration (IASC). This program puts high-quality data into the hands of citizen scientists around the World, creating opportunities for original astronomical discoveries and hands-on astronomical exploration. Mary Catherine Frantz IS Marketing and Communication Manager at Chabot Space & Science Center is a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth.

articles.text: Piedmont Adult School is offering two new classes for the spring semester. Fiction and Creative Nonfiction Writing The class is designed for beginners and experienced writers alike. It will focus on the components of effective writing and strategies to maintain a writing practice. There will be short readings, writing exercises, discussions, and the opportunity to participate in workshops. The six-week class will be taught by Caitlin McCarthy, who currently teaches at Corpus Christi School and is a published author. She is also a private writing coach and teaches writing workshops for all ages. Art from the Heart Art from the Heart will focus on drawing techniques that encourage students to observe closely and let creativity take over. Students will look at the works of famous artists for ideas and inspiration, and classwork will include contour drawings and portraiture. Novices are welcome. Art from The Heart is a six-week class being taught by Kathleen Deyo, a graduate of Syracuse University’s School of Fine Arts. Deyo has taught Illustration at Bridgeport University and Interior Design at the College of New Rochelle. To register for these and other classes, visit Piedmontadultschool.org or call (510) 594-2717. Classes are open to all adults age 18 and over.

pages.text: 8 Wednesday, March 16, 2022 PHS actors to perform Lord of the Flies at PCA Piedmont High School’s Advanced Acting class will perform William Golding’s Lord of the Flies in five performances from Thursday through Sunday, March 31 to April 3. The novel Lord of the Flies, adapted for the stage by Nigel Williams, is part of Piedmont’s freshman year English curriculum. Williams’ stage adaptation follows the plot of the novel – a group of British boys get stranded and are forced to face horrifying beasties on an island after their plane crashes on the island. Acting students of all genders will perform roles as the English boys, including speaking with a British dialect. What happens when young boys are left alone on an island with no structure? “The answer is pretty terrifying,” said cast member PHS junior Chloe Kibarian. The production is rated PG-13 for violence. The cast features Advanced Acting juniors and seniors Theo Arenstam, Liam Gordon, Milani Juarbe, Sarone Kelete, Chloe Kibarian, Molly McWeeny, Fernanda Meagher, Izzy Rosselli, Erik Stenstrom, Joyce Stern, Katherine Stormer, Holden Temple, John Gross Whitaker, and Charles E. White. Director Kimberly Taylor said, “I am grateful that the class is able to perform at the Piedmont Center for the Arts once more after the last successful collaboration there for the production of Lisa Loomer’s Roe immediately prior to the pandemic shutdown in March 2020. The Piedmont Center for the Arts allows us the flexibility to create unique seating configurations. For this show, audience members will be close to the action and will feel like they’re on the island, too,” she said. Lord of the Flies performances are Thursday through Saturday, March 31 to April 2 at 7:00 p.m., with two performance on Sunday, April 3 at 1 p.m. and 6 p.m. Tickets are $10 for students and $17 for general admission. The Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue across the street from the high school. All events at the Piedmont Center for the Arts require audience members to present proof of full vaccination plus booster, as well as proper masking inside. Piedmont Center for the Arts will host Piedmont High School’s Advanced Acting Class in a production of Lord of the Flies from March 31 through April 3. articles.text: Nº 50 in a biweekly series The French are proud of the females who are recognized Impressionists. Art historian Henri Focillon, a professor at Académie Beaux Arts, wrote in 1928 that he deemed three women to be serious Impressionists, les trois grandes dames, Berthe Morisot, Mary Cassatt and Marie Bracquemond. The works of the three females were “revolutionary,” according to Artnet, bringing the feminine sensibility by portraying the real lives of ordinary people. One of the women, the American expat Mary Cassatt, lived most of her life in France and was extraordinarily successful both critically and commercially. Her themes of “mother and child” were universal and insightful forays into women’s inner life. Another of the trio, Marie Bracquemond was a gifted artist who lived “under the thumb” of her artist-husband Félix, the chief saboteur of her art legacy. Their son Pierre later wrote about his parents’ relationship, calling out Felix’s jealousy of his wife’s talent and the successes she enjoyed at Salon and the Louvre. Balcony, Édouard Manet, 1868. Berthe (left) sat for the artist. Déjeuner sur l’herbe, by Édouard Manet, 1863, the artist’s provocative painting. A 2018 retrospective of Marie’s work reintroduced her to the French public as a major artist. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, March 16, 2022 AMERICANS IN PARIS The Women of French Impressionism By Patricia Forsyth Nº 50 in a biweekly series The French are proud of the females who are recognized Impressionists. Art historian Henri Focillon, a professor at Académie Beaux Arts, wrote in 1928 that he deemed three women to be serious Impressionists, les trois grandes dames, Berthe Morisot, Mary Cassatt and Marie Bracquemond. The works of the three females were “revolutionary,” according to Artnet, bringing the feminine sensibility by portraying the real lives of ordinary people. One of the women, the American expat Mary Cassatt, lived most of her life in France and was extraordinarily successful both critically and commercially. Her themes of “mother and child” were universal and insightful forays into women’s inner life. Another of the trio, Marie Bracquemond was a gifted artist who lived “under the thumb” of her artist-husband Félix, the chief saboteur of her art legacy. Their son Pierre later wrote about his parents’ relationship, calling out Felix’s jealousy of his wife’s talent and the successes she enjoyed at Salon and the Louvre. Balcony, Édouard Manet, 1868. Berthe (left) sat for the artist. Déjeuner sur l’herbe, by Édouard Manet, 1863, the artist’s provocative painting. Berthe at Easel, by Edma Morisot They worked together at Havilland, creating porcelain dinnerware and pottery bowls. A 2018 retrospective of Marie’s work reintroduced her to the French public as a major artist. In comparison, the life and work of Berthe Morisot is well known to the French, but The Paris Review noted that Musée D’Orsay’s ushered Berthe Morisot into the collection many decades later than the male artists. The Morisot sisters Édouard Manet was already a cause celebré when Berthe Morisot and her sister Edma were introduced to him by a mutual friend, painter Henri Fantin-Latour who had intimated the sisters were noticeably promising painters. Édouard wrote to Fantin-Latour that, “they’re delightful sisters,” but “what a pity they can’t be men.” He was clearly annoyed by the waste of art training on women. To date, no women had been recognized as serious artists, and yet he was astounded by their confidence and ambition. Edma and Berthe enjoyed all the advantages that the Victorian era could possibly provide. They were intelligent and educated. Their father was an architect in government service and their mother was a distant relative of the rococo Jean-Honoré Fragonard and supported their daughters’ enthusiasm for art instruction. The parents built a studio at home and enlisted A-list artists, especially the Barbizon trailblazer Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot who praised the girls for their quick learning and skills. Berthe qualified for the annual Impressionist exhibition at age 23, and as she matured, she exhibited her work yearly for more than a decade. Her painting style was loose with fast brushwork radiating confidence, but she was shadowed by self-doubt. The year after her older sister Edma married a military officer and moved from Paris, Berthe, unhappy with her work, threw out all of it, and See Americans in Paris on page 11 Woman at her Toilette, by Berthe Morisot, 1875 Eugène with Julie, by Berthe Morisot, 1881.

She could not refuse this dashing man, whose paintings were the talk of Paris. Accompanied by her mother who sat quietly and knitted, Berthe agreed to weekly sittings. Over the next four years, they forged an intimacy, and the sessions were clearly important to Édouard. Berthe became his favorite model. She sat for eleven Manet paintings. Their romance Berthe at Rest, Édouard Manet, 1870 was a love affair, exciting, and flirtatious, though he was a married man with a child to raise, and unavailable. Berthe was the one female in the Manet tribe of artists, and her parents graciously extended their home as Salon for the tribe to gather and banter about art and politics. The Morisot and Manet families grew close. Édouard’s younger brother Eugène joined the gatherings, and in time, Berthe noticed his attentiveness and accepted Eugène’s proposal. She married him at age 33, an age more typical of a widow. Eugène was a wonderful husband, supporting Berthe’s work and proving to be a caring father to Julie, their only child. From a young age Julie began to model for her mother. When Berthe died of pneumonia in 1895, Julie, age 17, was already showing art talent and a desire to follow her mother’s vocation. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team continued its strong start to the season, defeating University of San Francisco 20-11 at Witter Field on Friday, March 11. The Highlanders are undefeated at 4-0 and have scored at least 18 goals in each game. “Overall, it was a very good game for us. We’re improving every game. Our offense is very potent for a young team. We’ve seen a lot of improvement across the board and we’re going to need it. We’re going to play some very difficult opponents in the coming weeks. The boys have really gelled together as a family,” said first-year coach Alex Yu. PHS has now scored 74 goals and allowed 35 through four games. A plethora of scoring options was on display Friday Staff Photos Jack Nelson had a 3-goal hat trick, including a behind-the-back shot in the fourth quarter. Freshman goalie Gus von Metzsch had 15 saves against the Red Devils. Soren Dixon scored eight goals and had two assists and one ground ball recovery in Piedmont’s 20-11 win over University. night. University entered with a 4-1 overall record and is a strong Division 2 team. It faced Piedmont in the 2019 North Coast Section Semifinals, which PHS won 10-5 and went on to win the NCS championship. This year’s team may have more scoring options than in 2019; perhaps proving THAT Piedmont deserved its promotion to Division 1 with large-enrollment schools. “We try to preach selfless ball. The teams that go far in the playoffs are the ones who share the ball. We call it ‘finding the onemore,’ the one extra pass to find the person who is open. They are very good at that,” said Yu. Soren Dixon led the scoring with eight goals against the Red Devils; Nathan Fredericks had six goals, and Jack Nelson had a hat trick (3 goals) including a flashy, no-look goal in the fourth quarter. “It was a beautiful pass when I was running across the field. It was too late for me to do an overhand shot, so I had to go around the back. It just happened in the moment,” explained Nelson. Piedmont freshman goalie Gus von Metzsch continued to impress with 15 saves. “Gus came out tonight. He probably had his best game of the season. Some of his saves were up-close and point blank. His clearing has been stellar as well. I couldn’t be happier to have him, he’s a great teammate,” said Yu of the freshman. University Recap Piedmont jumped ahead 6-1 after one period and led 9-3 by halftime. It outscored the Red Devils 3-2 in the third quarter, and added eight more goals in the fourth for the 20-11 victory. Final stats: Dixon had eight goals, two assists, and one ground ball recovery. Fredericks had six goals. Jack Nelson had three goals, one assist, and one ground ball. Rylan Nelson had two goals, two assists, and two ground balls. Logan Huh scored once, Andrew McLaughlin gained an assist. Tuesday vs. Marin Academy Piedmont traveled to Kentfield to play Marin Academy yesterday, March 15. See next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP Piedmont (4-0) heads to archrival Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland this Friday, March 18 for a game at 7:00 p.m.
articles.title: Piedmont bashes University 20-11 to remain undefeated

articles.text: Staff Photos Izzy Epstein pitched Piedmont to a 7-1 win over San Leandro. Piedmont’s softball team defeated San Leandro 7-1 on Tuesday, March 15, but was shut out 1-0 by Skyline on Friday, March 11. Both were non-league games. It was a strong hitting display on Tuesday when Piedmont, accumulated eight hits against the Pirates. Chiarra Lundin had a double and scored two runs. “Chiarra is one of our seniors and is the No. 3 hitter in the order. We hope for big things for her this season,: said coach Gene Denard. On the mound, Izzy Epstein pitched a complete game, striking out 11 batters while holding San Leandro to 3 hits and one walk. Annabelle Castronovo pitched a complete 7-inning game against Skyline with five strikeouts. “Izzy is our workhorse this year; she’s maybe the best pitcher in our league. Annabelle is a quality No. 2 for us. She won’t throw as often but we’re confident in her when she does,” said Denard. 7-1 win over San Leandro Piedmont scored its first run with two outs in the bottom second when Morgan Hunt smacked a single to centerfield to bring in Epstein from third. PHS added three runs in the bottom of the third when Castronovo led off with a single and Lundin cracked a double to the left field wall. After a fielders’ choice that advanced Castronovo to third, Miya Fujimoto reached on an error to score Castronovo. Gretchen Gerhardy then brought in Fujimoto and Angelina Wu on a sacrifice fly that was dropped by the outfielder, giving the Highlanders a 4-0 lead. In the bottom of the fourth, Wu reached on another error to score Leah Bell with two outs, 5-1. The final two runs were scored in the bottom of the sixth inning with Fujimoto singling in Castronovo, and Lundin stealing home on a hit-and-run. Final stats: Lundin was 1-for-3 with a double, two runs scored, and a stolen base. Bell went 1-for-4 with a run scored, Castronovo was 1-for-3 with a run scored, Fujimoto went 1-for-4 with two RBIs and a run scored. Loss to Skyline PHS allowed the winning run in the top of the third in a game that was close start to finish. Each team had 4 hits. The Highlanders had a chance to score in the bottom of the third with two runners on and one out, but Fujimoto and Julia Banuelos were stranded on first and second. Final stats: Banuelos went 2-for-2 with a walk. Fujimoto went 1-for-3, Wu went 1-for-4. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-1) hosts St. Patrick this Saturday, March 19 at Witter Field at 11:00 a.m. Annabelle Castronovo had a complete game against Skyline, striking out five. Chiarra Lundin had a double and scored 2 runs in Piedmont’s win against San Leandro.
articles.title: Epstein strikes out 11 in 7-1 win against San Leandro

articles.text: The Highlander baseball team sustained two losses last week against non-league Foothill Division opponents, losing 7-5 to Bishop O’Dowd on Wednesday, March 9 at Humphries Diamond, and getting trimmed 7-2 by Arroyo in San Lorenzo on Friday, March 11. Piedmont used six different pitchers in the pair of games. “That’s the way it’s going to be for a while. We have a lot of [pitchers] that we’ll be able to use in different ways,” said Olson. Despite the losses, it was a strong hitting display for two first-year varsity starters against the Dragons. Sophomore first baseman and pitcher Dmitri Papahadjopoulos went 2-for-4 at the plate with a double and run scored, and freshman outfielder Markos Lagios went 2-for-3 with a double and one RBI. 7-5 loss to O’Dowd The Dragons scored the opening two runs in the top of the second inning. Piedmont closed it to 2-1 in the bottom of the fourth, but the Dragons exploded for four runs for a 6-1 lead In the top of the fifth inning. The Highlanders tacked on one run in the bottom of the fifth but allowed one run by O’Dowd in the top of the sixth. PHS rallied for two runs in the bottom half and added one more in the bottom of the seventh. Peter Krumins scored PHS’ first run on a fielder’s choice. Lagios made it 6-2 with a one-out double in the bottom of the fifth, but PHS stranded two runners on base to close the inning. In the bottom of the sixth, Papahadjopoulos and Defazio doubled with one to score Liam Campbell from third, Papahadjopoulos scored on an error by BOD’s shortstop after Evan McConathy hit a hard groundball to him. With two outs, Lagios hit a ground ball to the shortstop and beat the throw to first base. Piedmont sent Defazio all the way from second base to home on the throw to first, but O’Dowd threw him out at the plate. PHS scored its last run on a two-out error. Ryan McConathy reached first base on an error by the Dragons’ third baseman. Tobin Cantrill started on the mound for Piedmont and threw 4 innings, striking out three. Will Sprague pitched one inning, striking out one and allowing one hit. Scott McKenzie pitched the last inning with 1 strikeout and no hits allowed. Final stats: Papahadjopoulos was 2-for-4, a double and run scored. Lagios went 2-for-3 with a double and one RBI. Defazio went 1-for-3 with a double, RBI, run scored, and a stolen base. Mike Aikawa with one run scored and two stolen bases. 7-2 loss to Arroyo Tied at 0-0, Arroyo scored three runs in the bottom of the fourth inning. PHS responded with one run in the top of the fifth, but allowed one the following inning and another three in the bottom of the sixth. PHS scored its final run in the last inning. Davis Alazraqui had both RBIs got Piedmont, despite not having a hit. He brought in Will Sprague from third on a long fly ball in the top of the fifth. In the top of the seventh, he reached on an error to score Lagios from third. PHS loaded the bases with one out in the last final inning, but the game ended on a strikeout and ground out. SOFT Tennyson H 4:00 ------ KEY: H = Home BASE = Baseball LAX-B = Boys’ Lacrosse TRACK = Track & Field TEN = Boys’ Tennis A = Away SOFT = Softball LAX-G = Girls’ Lacrosse SWIM = Swimming BAD = Badminton GOLF = Boys’ Golf VB = Boys’ Volleyball Piedmont loses 2 to non-league opponents O’Dowd prevails 7-5; Arroyo wins 7-2 By Jonathan Comeaux The Highlander baseball team sustained two losses last week against non-league Foothill Division opponents, losing 7-5 to Bishop O’Dowd on Wednesday, March 9 at Humphries Diamond, and getting trimmed 7-2 by Arroyo in San Lorenzo on Friday, March 11. Piedmont used six different pitchers in the pair of games. “That’s the way it’s going to be for a while. We have a lot of [pitchers] that we’ll be able to use in different ways,” said Olson. Despite the losses, it was a strong hitting display for two first-year varsity starters against the Dragons. Sophomore first baseman and pitcher Dmitri Papahadjopoulos went 2-for-4 at the plate with a double and run scored, and freshman outfielder Markos Lagios went 2-for-3 with a double and one RBI. 7-5 loss to O’Dowd The Dragons scored the opening two runs in the top of the second inning. Piedmont closed it to 2-1 in the bottom of the fourth, but the Dragons exploded for four runs for a 6-1 lead In the top of the fifth inning. The Highlanders tacked on one run in the bottom of the fifth but allowed one run by O’Dowd in the top of the sixth. PHS rallied for two runs in the bottom half and added one more in the bottom of the seventh. Peter Krumins scored PHS’ first run on a fielder’s choice. Lagios made it 6-2 with a one-out double in the bottom of the fifth, but PHS stranded two runners on base to close the inning. In the bottom of the sixth, Papahadjopoulos and Defazio doubled with one to score Liam Campbell from third, Papahadjopoulos scored on an error by BOD’s shortstop after Evan McConathy hit a hard groundball to him. With two outs, Lagios hit a ground ball to the shortstop and beat the throw to first base. Piedmont sent Defazio all the way from second base to home on the throw to first, but O’Dowd threw him out at the plate. PHS scored its last run on a two-out error. Ryan McConathy reached first base on an error by the Dragons’ third baseman. Tobin Cantrill started on the mound for Piedmont and threw 4 innings, striking out three. Will Sprague pitched one inning, striking out one and allowing one hit. Scott McKenzie pitched the last inning with 1 strikeout and no hits allowed. Final stats: Papahadjopoulos was 2-for-4, a double and run scored. Lagios went 2-for-3 with a double and one RBI. Defazio went 1-for-3 with a double, RBI, run scored, and a stolen base. Mike Aikawa with one run scored and two stolen bases. 7-2 loss to Arroyo Tied at 0-0, Arroyo scored three runs in the bottom of the fourth inning. PHS responded with one run in the top of the fifth, but allowed one the following inning and another three in the bottom of the sixth. PHS scored its final run in the last inning. Davis Alazraqui had both RBIs got Piedmont, despite not having a hit. He brought in Will Sprague from third on a long fly ball in the top of the fifth. In the top of the seventh, he reached on an error to score Lagios from third. PHS loaded the bases with one out in the last final inning, but the game ended on a strikeout and ground out. articles.text: Photos by Todd Marshburn Katherine Kinne (13) scored six goals and had two assists against Dougherty Valley. As Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team continues to work through its early-season slate of matches against upper Division 1 competition, it beat Dougherty Valley in San Ramon 13-11 for its first victory of the season on Friday, March 11. “The first three games were against some really tough opponents, Cal High, Redwood and Marin Catholic are all big-time lacrosse programs; the girls finally clicked in the Dougherty. I set up the schedule against tough opponents to ramp up their lacrosse IQ. I think they finally are seeing each other and playing like a team,” explained coach Carlton Chan. Senior attacker Katherine Kinne tied a career-high six goals against Dougherty Valley, and goalies Sofia Ethington and Lindsay Kottle split duties, combining for 9 saves. In the first half, while down 3-0, Kinne got PHS on the board after nearly five minutes of play at 20:19. Elizabeth Ethington made it 3-2 at the 18:14 mark, while Molly Ashton tied it after another three minutes. Kinne put PHS ahead 4-3 at the 13:59 mark, but DV tied it 30 seconds later. At 4-4, Ruby Guzdar scored at 11:54 to put PHS back ahead, but DVHS scored once again just seconds later. Ashton scored again and Kinne scored her third goal 15 seconds later for a 7-5 lead. DV scored again and the teams went into halftime with Piedmont holding a slim 7-6 lead. Dougherty Valley came out firing in the second half, tying it at 7-7 in the first minute of action and then going ahead 8-7. Kinne tied the game after a minute, and then Ashton bagged her third goal with 13:52 on the clock for a 9-8 led. One minute later DV tied the game again. Piedmont’s defense then shut down Dougherty Valley, holding them without a goal for eight minutes. Meanwhile, Kinne and Elizabeth Ethington scored, and Kinne added another goal for a 12-9 lead. DV inched closer , 12019m with 4 minutes left, and scored once more with 1:50 left in the game. However, Piedmont got an insurance goal from Charlotte Theut for the 12-10 final and a hard-earned win. Final stats: Kinne with six goals, two assists, and three ground balls. Elizabeth Ethington and Ashton each had three goals and an assist. Guzdar and Theut had individual goals. Tuesday vs. Monte Vista Piedmont faced Div.1 Monte Vista last night at Witter Field and lost 10-4. See next week’s Post for game details. articles.text: Piedmont hosted its first league track & field meet of the season on Thursday, March 10 at Witter Field with Hayward, San Leandro, and Tennyson. PHS also brought its distance relay team to Skyline High in Oakland for the Titan Twilight on Saturday, March 12 while pole vaulter Parker Terrill competed at the K-Ball Classic at Westmont HS in Campbell on the same day. In Thursday’s event at Witter Field, PHS had a strong showing, winning 15 of 30 events. Some fields were composed entirely of PHS athletes. Ellie Black was the star of the day, winning three events, She won the 400 meters in a field of 10 runners, posting a time of 1:07.78, a personal record by nearly three seconds. Her winning time of 10:59.20 in the 3200 smashed her previous personal record by more than 2-1/2 minutes. PHS sophomore Jamie Schwartz, the only other runner, was second in 13:06.17. Competing with three other runners, two of whom were Highlanders, Black won the 1600 meters with a time of 5:58.16. Violet Lemley placed 2nd in 6:14.92, and PHS freshman Caroline Taylor was 3rd in 6:22.27. Schwarz won the 800 in a field of eight with a time of 2:33.96. Lemley was timed in 2:47.95, and Molly McWeeny in 2:48. Sara Govert won the shot put with a distance of 25-feet, 7.5-inches against a field of seven. Junior Brie Sotelo finished 3rd at 23-feet, 10-inches. Ellie Black won the 400, 1600, and 3200 meter runs in a league meet last week on March 10. Also pictured is Violet Lemley (right) in the 1600. Sotelo also won the discus in a field of seven with a distance of 63-feet, 2-inches. Govert was 2nd at 59-feet-1, and senior Ana Romanczuk third with 58-10. Sophomore Breah Bell won the long jump with a leap of 15 feet, 7.75 inches. Zenobia Pellissier-Lloyd was second at 14-feet, 10.5-inches, and Zoe Saldanha was third at 13-feet, 5.25- inches in a field of nine. Bell also placed 2nd of 16 sprinters in the 100-meter dash in 13.25 seconds. Stein wins 1600 and 3200 Jack Stein won the 3200 meters against eight other runners with a personal record time of 9:40.17, lowering his previous best time by six seconds. Christian Taylor placed 2nd in 9:59, and Parker Long clocked a time of 10:04.92. Stein also won the 1600 against 14 other runners with a time of 4:28.38. Long placed 2nd in 4:51. Cooper Downing won the 800 meters in a field of nine with a time of 2:00.04, narrowly beating Christian Taylor at the line, 2:00.42. Parker Terrill won the high jump with a height of 5-feet, 6-inches. Weekend events Piedmont’s distance relay team of Taylor, Alex Aubrecht, Parker Long, and Stein traveled to Skyline High in Oakland for the Titan Twilight on Saturday, and won their event with a time of 10:55.96 in a field of 17 teams. They defeated the 2nd place Skyline by 20 seconds. The event includes distances of 1,200, 400, 800, and 1,600 meters. Also on Saturday, Terrill competed in the pole vault at the K-Bell Classic in Campbell. In a field of 19 vaulters, he placed 3rd with a height of 13 feet, more than one foot below his recent school record vault. St. Ignatius’ Logan Lehnert won at 14-0, and Bellarmine’s Justin Vigna was 2nd at 13-6. NEXT UP Piedmont athletes will compete in the Dublin Distance Fiesta on Friday and Saturday this weekend, March 18-19. The event typically attracts over 160 high schools and 3,000 student athletes. PHS will also compete in the San Leandro Track and Field Invitational this Saturday, March 19. Sara Govert won the shot put with a distance of 25 feet, 7.5 inches.

articles.text: Photos by Shari Fuji Piedmont’s boys’ volleyball team is off to a 2-0 start its season. Pictured are (front) Coach Mariah Cardenas (left), Wilson Wong, John Champion, Shunji Higashi, Eric Olaru-Hagen, Kai Lambert, Atom Rognuson, Owen Kelly; (back) Adel Sahuc, Mason Kimball, Brayden Day, and Felix Broach. Piedmont High’s boys’ volleyball team began its season on a strong note, beating Alameda 3-1 in the opener on Tuesday, March 8 in Binks Rawlings Gym, and shutting out Tennyson 3-0 on Thursday, March 10 in Hayward. This will be the first full season of boys’ volleyball in 20 years. The game scores with Alameda were 25-23, 25-20, 16-25, and a narrow 27-25 win in extra points to clinch it. Piedmont swept Tennyson in 3 straight games, 25-18, 25-22, and 25-15. “Our hitting has really leveled up this year. We have more time to sync up with our setter Shunji (Higashi), we’ll be able to really put the ball away quickly,” explained team captain Wilson Wong. It is the first season for head coach Mariah Cardenas after accepting the role on short notice when former coach Leslie Blakely moving out of the country. “I’m so proud of them and how they started this season strong. We struggled a bit to get into the rhythm in the first game against Tennyson but were able to win it easily,” said Cardenas. Cardenas brings a fiery flare to the court. She was promoted from the junior varsity team, and has previously coached Piedmont’s girls’ team. “Coach Mariah has a different approach than some my past coaches; she has been really, really supportive. She yells with us to fire us up, and that really improves the game atmosphere. It allows us to play smarter and less emotionally,” said Wong of the new coach. The team is made up of Wong and John Champion as outside hitters, Brayden Day as their Libero, opposite hitters Eric Olaru-Hagen, Owen Kelly, and Kai Lambert, middle blockers Mason Kimball and Felix Broach, defensive specialists Atom Rognuson and Adel Sahuc, while Shunji Higashi is their setter specialist. “We have a new roster of middles this year and our double blocks on either side need to sync up. Seniors Mason (Kimball) and Felix (Broach) are huge and great blockers. We’re a very scrappy bunch and many of us have played together since middle school,” explained Wong. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-0) travels to Encinal today, Wednesday, March 16 for a match at 5:15 p.m., and will host Bishop O’Dowd tomorrow in Binks Rawlings Gym, Thursday, March 17 at 5:15 p.m. Felix Broach (26) goes up for a spike.

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s swim team is back after a two-year halt due to the COVID-19 global pandemic. The squad competed in the Head-Royce Invitational on March 3 at Mills College in Oakland, and had its first league meet of the season at Castro Valley last Friday, March 11. Both the boys’ and girls’ teams on at the Head-Royce Invitational. The boys came out on top in a field of seven teams, and the girls won in a field of six. The girls’ team also won their league meet with Castro Valley. Colby Price has returned as head coach In the absence of a pool in Piedmont as a new $19 million facility is being designed, the team will be training at Mills College. “We started with a preseason invitational that we took really seriously and wound up winning, which is fun,” said Price. “We are doing everything we can to get the kids involved. We’re one of the biggest teams at Piedmont High. This year, we have really focused captains who are doing a lot of work outside of the pool.” The boys’ team is led by junior Simon Lins, who has committed to the University of Virginia. Lins has already achieved a North Coast Section consideration time in the 50 freestyle. “Simon is our sprinter; he makes gaining points a lot easier. He already has an NCS cut and is working towards more times he wants to swim at NCS. You can ask him to do anything; he’s going to win it for you,” said Price of the junior who will be entered in the 50 free, 100 free, 100 fly, 100 back, and relay teams this season. The girls’ team will be led by senior Kate Aubrecht, sophomores Taylor Rolefson and Josie Oesterer, and freshman Sonja ten Grotenhuis. They will make up the relay team, which won the 200 medley relay and 200 freestyle relay at Castro Valley. “Our girls are our best shot at finishing well against a lot of schools. We have some really strong swimmers. They are each clocking strong times,” said Price. HRS Invitational results The PHS women won with 460 points in competition with six other schools, and the boys’ team won with 386 points against five other schools. Though it was a preseason meet, all times count toward North Coast Section and CIF qualification. Lins’ winning time of 21.30 in the 50 free in a field of 20 is already an automatic qualification time to the NCS Championship meet, and he has a consideration time for CIF. To automatically qualify for state, he must swim a time of 21.09. Lins also won the 100 backstroke in a field of eight with a time of 56.06 Both boys’ relay teams won, including Lins, Ryan Stokes, Chuck White, and Farris Saffouri, who posted a time of 1:42.59 in the 200 Medley relay and 1:38.41 in the 200 freestyle relay. Taylor Rolefson, a member of the A relay team, won the 200 IM and 100 butterfly against Castro Valley.

articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir’s Ensemble singers performed with the Oakland Symphony on Friday, March 4 in a program titled Fountains of Rome. The concert honored the memory and life of one of the choir’s most ardent champions and a passionate supporter of the arts and social justice, Bonnie Bonetti-Bell, who died November 20. The loving and personal program celebrated the Oakland Symphony conducting debut of the choir’s Artistic Director, Eric Tuan. Tuan led the singers and orchestra in sensitive and exquisite performances of Claude Debussy’s Salut Printemps (“Greetings to Spring”) and Einojuhani Rautavaara’s Lapsimessu (“Children’s Mass”). Rautavaara is perhaps the best known and most frequently performed Finnish composer who composed eight symphonies, nine operas, and 12 concertos, as well as numerous vocal and chamber works. “This was our most artistically substantial collaboration with the symphony,” remarked Tuan. “The audience and collaborators were impressed by Ensemble’s skill, sound, and musical sophistication. I enjoyed having the opportunity to conduct the welcoming and incredibly skilled musicians of the Oakland Symphony for the first time,” he said. Under Tuan’s assured direction, singers and orchestra created a breathtaking and engaging performance. Founding Artistic Director Robert Geary expressed the impact: The performances of the Debussy and the Rautavaara rose to the highest artistic standards. Ensemble (flagship group of the Choir) demonstrated again why it has been so successful on national and international stages. Complex musical structures and harmonies were performed effortlessly, intonation was impeccable, and the French and the Latin expertly handled. Maestro Tuan was masterful conducting both the Oakland Symphony and Ensemble. Guest conductor Kalena Bovell led the Symphony through Respighi’s Fountains of Rome with warmth and grace, bringing the listeners on a journey to Rome and the joy and energy of its signature fountains at varying times of day. Bringing the audience to its feet for a third time in the evening’s program, Meng Su delivered a stirring and passionate rendition of Rodrigo’s Concierto de Aranjuez. Throughout the evening, Tuan, Bovell, and representatives of the Oakland Symphony musicians and administration shared loving memories of both Bonnie Bonetti-Bell and the late Oakland Symphony conductor Michael Morgan, who designed the program with Bonnie’s husband, PEBCC Board Treasurer James Bell. “This [was] Bonnie’s playlist. Bonnie’s family name is Bonetti, and she [was] immensely proud of her Italian heritage. Bonnie found her Italian voice in Respighi. Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir joins Oakland Symphony in Eric Tuan’s triumphant conducting debut Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir’s Ensemble singers performed with the Oakland Symphony on Friday, March 4 in a program titled Fountains of Rome. The concert honored the memory and life of one of the choir’s most ardent champions and a passionate supporter of the arts and social justice, Bonnie Bonetti-Bell, who died November 20. The loving and personal program celebrated the Oakland Symphony conducting debut of the choir’s Artistic Director, Eric Tuan. Tuan led the singers and orchestra in sensitive and exquisite performances of Claude Debussy’s Salut Printemps (“Greetings to Spring”) and Einojuhani Rautavaara’s Lapsimessu (“Children’s Mass”). Rautavaara is perhaps the best known and most frequently performed Finnish composer who composed eight symphonies, nine operas, and 12 concertos, as well as numerous vocal and chamber works. “This was our most artistically substantial collaboration with the symphony,” remarked Tuan. “The audience and collaborators were impressed by Ensemble’s skill, sound, and musical sophistication. I enjoyed having the opportunity to conduct the welcoming and incredibly skilled musicians of the Oakland Symphony for the first time,” he said. Under Tuan’s assured direction, singers and orchestra created a breathtaking and engaging performance. Founding Artistic Director Robert Geary expressed the impact: The performances of the Debussy and the Rautavaara rose to the highest artistic standards. Ensemble (flagship group of the Choir) demonstrated again why it has been so successful on national and international stages. Complex musical structures and harmonies were performed effortlessly, intonation was impeccable, and the French and the Latin expertly handled. Maestro Tuan was masterful conducting both the Oakland Symphony and Ensemble. Guest conductor Kalena Bovell led the Symphony through Respighi’s Fountains of Rome with warmth and grace, bringing the listeners on a journey to Rome and the joy and energy of its signature fountains at varying times of day. Bringing the audience to its feet for a third time in the evening’s program, Meng Su delivered a stirring and passionate rendition of Rodrigo’s Concierto de Aranjuez. articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse will produce Water by the Spoonful opening March 16 and running to April 23. Winner of the 2012 Pulitzer Prize for Drama, the play written by Quiara Alegría Hudes is a heartfelt meditation on lives on the brink of redemption. Set in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, Eliot has returned from Iraq and is working at a Subway sandwich shop while simultaneously trying to jumpstart his acting career. “Quiara Alegría Hudes’s masterful Pulitzer Prize winner speaks even more profoundly to our world today,” said Bill English, San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director. “Separated from friends and loved ones by the pandemic, we, like the characters in Water by the Spoonful, celebrate our human resourcefulness, which will overcome any distance to build connection and hope.” The play is directed by Denise Blasor, with performances on the main stage through April 23. Proof of up-to-date vaccination is required to attend. To obtain tickets, visit https:// w w w.sf playhouse.org /sf ph / upcoming-plays/ Playbill cover for San Francisco Playhouse production of Water by the Spoonful. ®

articles.text: The UC Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) will highlight the work of four contemporary Bay Area artists in a collective exhibition beginning March 19. The exhibition is entitled “The Artist’s Eye,” and features the work of Tammy Rae Carland, David Huffman, Lava Thomas, and John Zurier. The four artists were chosen by BAMPFA to “guest-curate” an exhibition that draws from the museums 18,000-work collection. Each artist has been featured at BAMPFA in the past. “We’re delighted to work with Tammy Rae Carland, David Huffman, Lava Thomas, and John Zurier, who brought their instinctive curiosity to exploring, curating, and critiquing the collection,” said Curatorial Assistant Claire Frost, who worked with the artists to organize the exhibition, along with Associate Curator Stephanie Cannizzo and Collections Engagement Associate and Academic Liaison Lynne Kimura. Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Fine Archive. “The project required close collaboration on many levels and has resulted in an exhibition that illuminates their work and lived experiences as it intersects with the museum.” The name of the exhibition is a nod to an iconic program at London’s National Gallery during the 1980s, which invited one artist at a time to curate an exhibition from that museum’s collection. Among the artists featured in the exhibition are: Zarouhie Abdalian, Diane Arbus, Francis Bacon, Yamamoto Baitsu, John Baldessari, Sadie Barnette, Jean-Michel Basquiat, Romare Bearden, McArthur Binion, Yosa Busan, John Cage, Tammy Rae Carland, Theresa Hak Kyung Cha, Constance Chang, Sarah Charlesworth, Barbara Chase-Riboud, Robert Colescott, Willem de Kooning, Erica Deeman, and Jay DeFeo. To learn more and to obtain tickets, visit www.bampfa.org.

articles.text: Mila Kunis and Justin Timberlake in Friends with Benefits Friends With Benefits is not your grandfather’s movie. In the 1939 film Gone With the Wind Vivien Leigh asks Clark Gable, “What shall I do? Where shall I go?” He turns and says, “Frankly my dear, I don’t give a damn.” That singular word, “damn,” evoked gasps from audiences and represented a sea change in movies. It was the beginning of a gradual loosening of film censorship regarding not only language but the interaction between men and women (physical and verbal). Until the late 1950s, Ozzie and Harriet slept in separate beds and everyone had a robe handy. Decorum and restraint ruled. But that was then, and this is now. Romantic comedies such as Friends definitely represent another change in terms of language and physical contact. True, “FWB” has outstanding portrayals by Mila Kunis as Jamie, young NYC based headhunter, and Justin Timberlake as Dylan, online art director from LA, who arrives in New York for an interview with GQ magazine. And true the exploration of benefits is taken to the edge of that well-worn envelope and beyond. “FWB” is randy and profane and funny, even if it’s a runaway cliché. You know the drill: cool guy and hot girl like each other and swear they can be friends even if they have sex. Neither is looking for a commitment. They have tons of chemistry, hangout well, text, and even find themselves in the middle of a Manhattan flash mob, doing what flash mobs do. It’s all kinda cool. But not to forget: benefits signify benefits. No matter the steam on the windows and their amazing mutual attraction. What Jamie and Dylan refuse to acknowledge – and the story moves from pillar to post in terms of narrative – is what everyone in the audience already knows: they’re in love. Denial (or sustained dissembling when confronted) is not a river in India, but in rom-coms of this ilk it’s a familiar refuge. The tension is nicely developed, compounded by Jamie’s conviction that she’s damaged in some vague way and Dylan’s certainty that he’s emotionally unavailable. Both have been told this during past breakups. As romantic comedies go, and there have been a spate of them in the last several years, “FWB” is the exception, meaning it’s really good. The writing is sharp, the pacing is engaging, and both Jamie and Dylan are smart and interesting, especially Jamie. Kunis is wonderful, and if she is an example of the young, metro woman who is confident and fearless, in a funny, quick, and intelligent way, that’s all to the good. “FWB” is light years from It Happened One Night with Clark Gable and Claudette Colbert (1934), and way better than anything that has appeared recently, including No Strings Attached. Friends With Benefits. Directed by Will Gluck. Starring Mila Kunis, Justin Timberlake, Patricia Clarkson, Richard Jenkins and Jemma Elfman. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated R.
articles.title: Friends With Benefits a lightweight romantic comedy

articles.text: Surely it was tempting for the filmmakers to portray an elderly woman who permanently parks her weathered and much lived-in van in a tony neighborhood in North London, as charmingly eccentric. All she needs is an umbrella and wide-brimmed straw hat. While she’s decidedly pungent, dressed in frayed, castoff clothes, she’s also educated. Behind the layer of grime and rags is a fiercely independent, termagant, tart-tongued “bag lady.” Her name is Mary/Margaret Shepherd and as portrayed by Maggie Smith in Lady in the Van, she’s not simply local color, nor does she provide comic relief for the locals. There is more to her than she is willing to tell. She arrives with a history that is only briefly revealed in flashbacks, mere glimpses into her past. But at first glance she seems a harmless vagabond. One of the neighbors, Alan Bennett (Alex Jennings), a playwright and a bit of a recluse himself, grudgingly and against his better judgment, invites Mary to park her van in his driveway – for just a short time while she sorts herself out. As it turns out, Mary stays for 15 years. What Bennett learns as the years slip by is that Mary is not simply a determined gypsy but a deeply damaged human being who is suffering from gradual dementia, abiding health issues, and a sense of overwhelming isolation. She is a mass of contradictions and continues to surprise Bennett as he adjusts to her presence (her van is soon surrounded by plastic bags of garbage and personal detritus). His head-shaking tolerance turns not into anger or regret, but into concern and then affection. He learns that she was once a pianist, a failed nun, and has a brother living just outside of London. She had a life and then lost track of it. And as a writer he can’t help but view Mary as possible material for his work. The Lady in the Van is particularly English, meaning it is a quiet, careful character study of Mary and Alan, and a close depiction of their relationship (a plot is barely discernable). The film is adapted from a memoir published by Bennett in 1989, which became a stage play starring Maggie Smith in 1999, and recently brought to the screen. Smith was the obvious choice for the movie. She brings to the role all of her talent and ability, to include the hauteur of the dowager so central to Downton Abbey, combined with elements of her marvelous portrayal as professor McGonagall in Harry Potter. Maggie Smith is a treasure and is in essence the reason to see this film. It does have an embedded question that has more to do with Bennett than with Smith and that is when confronted with a homeless individual like Mary, what is the right thing to do? His neighbors take an interest in her welfare but always from a distance. Though Alan offers his driveway and gradually his support, he never tries to overcome her choice to live as she does. He takes her as he finds her. His decision keeps the movie from being sentimental or maudlin. And in the end he does tell Mary’s story, such as it is. The Lady in the Van. Directed by Nicholas Hytner. Starring Maggie Smith, Alex Jennings, Roger Allam. 1 hr., 44 min. Rated PG-13. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 11am-5:30pm 1pm-5pm Benefitting Piedmont Education for 40 Years! dressbestforless.org
articles.title: The Lady in the Van another treasure with Maggie Smith

In the 1939 film Gone With the Wind Vivien Leigh asks Clark Gable, “What shall I do? Where shall I go?” He turns and says, “Frankly my dear, I don’t give a damn.” That singular word, “damn,” evoked gasps from audiences and represented a sea change in movies. It was the beginning of a gradual loosening of film censorship regarding not only language but the interaction between men and women (physical and verbal). Until the late 1950s, Ozzie and Harriet slept in separate beds and everyone had a robe handy. Decorum and restraint ruled. But that was then, and this is now. Romantic comedies such as Friends definitely represent another change in terms of language and physical contact. True, “FWB” has outstanding portrayals by Mila Kunis as Jamie, young NYC based headhunter, and Justin Timberlake as Dylan, online art director from LA, who arrives in New York for an interview with GQ magazine. And true the exploration of benefits is taken to the edge of that well-worn envelope and beyond. “FWB” is randy and profane and funny, even if it’s a runaway cliché. You know the drill: cool guy and hot girl like each other and swear they can be friends even if they have sex. Neither is looking for a commitment. They have tons of chemistry, hangout well, text, and even find themselves in the middle of a Manhattan flash mob, doing what flash mobs do. It’s all kinda cool. But not to forget: benefits signify benefits. No matter the steam on the windows and their amazing mutual attraction. What Jamie and Dylan refuse to acknowledge – and the story moves from pillar to post in terms of narrative – is what everyone in the audience already knows: they’re in love. Denial (or sustained dissembling when confronted) is not a river in India, but in rom-coms of this ilk it’s a familiar refuge. The tension is nicely developed, compounded by Jamie’s conviction that she’s damaged in some vague way and Dylan’s certainty that he’s emotionally unavailable. Both have been told this during past breakups. As romantic comedies go, and there have been a spate of them in the last several years, “FWB” is the exception, meaning it’s really good. The writing is sharp, the pacing is engaging, and both Jamie and Dylan are smart and interesting, especially Jamie. Kunis is wonderful, and if she is an example of the young, metro woman who is confident and fearless, in a funny, quick, and intelligent way, that’s all to the good. “FWB” is light years from It Happened One Night with Clark Gable and Claudette Colbert (1934), and way better than anything that has appeared recently, including No Strings Attached. Friends With Benefits. Directed by Will Gluck. Starring Mila Kunis, Justin Timberlake, Patricia Clarkson, Richard Jenkins and Jemma Elfman. 1 hr., 49 min. articles.text: Chris Evans as Captain America in a scene from Captain America: The First Avengers. Who are these pulp fiction superheroes and why do they resonate with our children? Whatever the answer, Hollywood is in love with the comic book genre, especially with tales from the archives of DC and Marvel Comics Summer big tent blockbusters are often defined by the superhero: “Thor”; “X-Men: First Class”; “Green Lantern.” And not to forget “Transformers.” Plus “Harry Potter,” a superhero to be sure. Just ask Voldermort. An example is the 2011 film, Captain America: The First Avenger. Consider the setup: a 90-pound weakling, Steve Rogers (Chris Evans), is desperate to join the Army and fight the Nazis (“I hate bullies” he says), but he can’t pass the physical. He is recruited and transformed (using Super-Soldier serum) into a totally ripped G.I. Joe, aka Captain America, replete with shield, mask and tights. What 90-pound kid wouldn’t love to suddenly have the washboard abs of Captain America, an all-American hero who goes off to fight not just the Nazis, but evil doers in an outfit called Hydra, led by Red Skull (Hugo Weaving), someone who also possess some serious weaponry. This first Captain America was an origin film (begins in 1942), and act one is devoted to how Rogers morphs into his present incarnation. It’s all nicely done, albeit with holes in the logic, requiring serious suspension of disbelief as well as a huge assist by Computer graphics. But then, that’s what defines these wonderfully imagined movies. “No way” some literalists might say. Response: a chorus of kids saying, “Yes, way!” Captain America fights for truth and justice, which means serious combat with the Hydra. Sequel to follow. Captain America: The First Avengers. Director Joe Johnston. Starring Chris Evans, Haley Atwell, Tommy Lee Jones, Hugo Weaving and Stanley Tucci. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: Captain America – kids will love it

articles.text: Old Yeller is a classic, family friendly film, released in 1957, and now streaming on Disney+ and Prime. Set in 1869 in post-Civil War frontier Texas, it has at its center a relationship between a boy, Travis Coates (Tommy Kirk), and a stray dog that he names Old Yeller. In the opening scenes we see Travis’ father, Jim (Fess Parker), about to leave for Kansas to buy cattle. While he is gone, Travis and his younger brother, Artiss (Kevin Corcoran), work the cornfields and it’s there that Travis encounters a stray Black Mountain cur. Initially, he tries to chase the dog away, but when it saves his brother from a bear that is defending her cubs, he changes his mind about the courageous dog, and the brothers bring it home, not realizing the impact it will have on their lives. One evening, a neighbor, Bud Searchy (Jeff York), and his granddaughter, Lizbeth, come to dinner and Lisbeth, close to Travis in age, tells him that Old Yeller has been stealing food throughout the county. Hearing this, Travis, concerned, scolds the dog. One day, Old Yeller’s previous owner, Bud Sanderson (Chuck Connors), stops by, looking for the dog. Realizing that the boys have grown attached to the dog, he agrees to swap Old Yeller for a good home cooked meal. Bud also warns the boys that there is a plague of hydrophobia in the area and to keep an eye on their animals, including the dog. Not long thereafter, Old Yeller is attacked by a feral pig and wounded. Concerned, his injury is treated by Travis’ mom, Katie (Dorothy McGuire), and the boy insists that the hog is not rabid. But the threat of rabies remains as a subplot throughout the story. Early one morning, Travis spots their cow, Rose, stumbling about the yard, its mouth foaming, and he is forced to get the family rifle and shoot Rose. Katie and Lizbeth, who is visiting, burn the body; but while disposing of the cow, a wolf comes on the property and attacks them. Old Yeller fights the wolf off, but in the process, is bitten. Katie is certain that the wolf was rabid, and regretfully insists that Old Yeller must be shot. Travis pleads for the dog’s life, suggesting that they put him in a pen and wait to determine if he has any symptoms of the disease. Reluctantly, Katie agrees, and so they wait. The tension builds, and Travis visits the pen daily with hope and food. How the final act turns out is what makes this fine Disney film compelling. Kids, 8 and older and older, will be captivated by the story, made in stunning color with just the right amount of action and heart-rending moments. Old Yeller. Directed by Robert Stevenson. Starring Dorothy McGuire, Tommy Kirk, Fess Parker. 1 hr., 28 min. Rated G. Currently streaming on Prime and Disney. Beverly Washburn, Dorothy McGuiren and Tommy Kirk in Old Yeller.
articles.title: Old Yeller a sweet story of a boy and a dog

articles.text: It sure is hard to find any joy in the world these days. Maybe I can do something about that. After all, tragedy and comedy exist…one next to the other. In the history of music, drama came first. Comedy was a second thought… the intermission entertainment between the drama. It was readily apparent that audiences loved the comedies. And that’s how comedic opera was born, and with it all the other musical comedies. After reading this article, you may be inspired to do a little research on your own. Let’s take a quick look at different aspects of musical comedy. Rap and hip-hop take themselves far too seriously, and as a result I can find no humor or parody in them. Country and western music is a lot better; mainly because they enjoy making fun of themselves. He-Haw star Roy Clark is a perfect example. There is no doubt in my mind that he was a great musical talent. Clark also had a great gift for humor. Be sure to check him out, and then check out some of the other people from classic country music. Weird Al Yankovic is the biggestselling comedy recording artist of all time. When people think of funny music, cartoons always come to mind. Almost every classic cartoon was an artistic treasure. For example, if you want to learn about opera, the classic Bugs Bunny cartoon “What‘s Opera, Doc?“ is required research. Bug’s final line in the cartoon says it all and will whet your appetite for more research. That’s your homework. The heyday of classic radio was also the battleground for comedy. Vaudeville comedians who were used to visual comedy had to adapt to spoken comedy. In this way, visual comedy gave birth to what we know as standup comedians.
articles.title: Now, more than ever

articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) will host an engaging and unique event next month. The Museum’s Soapbox Derby returns to San Francisco for the first time since 1978 and will be held on April 10. In the spring of 1975 more than 100 Bay Area artists built 75 ‘cars’ and made 32 trophies for an artists’ soapbox derby. Designed as a fundraiser, it generated $20,000 for the museum. This family-friendly event builds on legendary artists’ derbies held in 1975 and 1978. Both events attracted a crowd of thousands of spectators. This year, residents, local artists, educators, students, and community organizations will cruise down the curving hill of John F. Shelley Drive in McLaren Park. Each racer will descend one-by-one in their custom-made, gravity-powered vehicles. The Soapbox Derby event in 1975 brought thousands of spectators. Artists, educators, and students will compete for trophies at the SF MOMA Soapbox Derby in San Francisco’s McLaren Park. Trophies will be designed by artists and derby alums, including Chip Lord and Mike Henderson, as well as new participant artists Liz Hernandez, Leah Rosenberg and Matt Goldberg. Announcers for the event are Pendarvis Harshaw, the host of KQED-FM’s “Rightnowish,” and Kumasi Aaron, ABC7 News Bay Area Morning Anchor. This event is free and open to everyone, with music, food, and family-friendly activities in and around the newly renovated Jerry Garcia Amphitheater. The festivities begin at 10 a.m. To learn more about the tradition of the derby and directions to its location, visit https:// w w w. s f m o m a . o r g /e x h i b i - tion/2022-soapbox-derby-at-mclaren-park/.

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, March 16, 2022 The Musical Gourmet Curiously, classical music The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet offers the most opportunity for parody. There are so many examples of ethnic humor that it’s hard to know where to start. Just about every culture has enjoyed making fun of itself. The simplest form of comedy were laughing records. The music would begin and then one of the players would make some foolish mistake. The members of the band would start to laugh and so would the people listening to the record. Many famous musicians made party records. Some of them were issued by major record companies and sold commercially. Other recordings were made during actual parties. These recordings are revealing artistically and are often extremely expensive to purchase on the market. About 20 years ago one of Jascha Heifetz’s party records was offered for sale at $1000. I can think of three great artists who made some outstanding party records. Enrico Caruso made one where he holds a high note forever. He did it as a joke and did not permit the record to be released commercially. The German tenor Richard Tauber recorded “my curly headed baby” and his behavior is really silly. He clears his throat a number of times, coughs, miss-pronounces his words and sings in a very unpredictable way. Some ethnic comedians knew how to evade the censors. Benny Bell’s classic “shaving cream” is a perfect example. articles.text: Annually the Civic Projects Committee of the Piedmont Garden Club donates $5000 to the Parks Commission of Piedmont to use for special projects in Piedmont. The last several years their emphasis has been to provide funds for native plant materials in and around the community parks. This year Patty Reed and her committee presented a check to Patty Dunlap, the chair of the Parks Commission, for the monies for two projects. The first project is for the Linda Park Lawn Renovation which is located near the Linda Dog Park. This area above the walking path will have all of the invasive ivy, lawn on the slope, and the low chain link fence removed. The club’s donation of $2500 will be used to partially cover the cost to install native plants, ground cover and trees to the area. The second $2500 will help pay for a new hedge in front of the Community Hall. The existing hedge was removed to repair water leaks in the lower level of the building. The new hedge will be coffeeberry, a native plant. This project was chosen because the Community Hall is near and dear to the garden club members; it is where they meet each month. Founded in 1923, Piedmont Garden Club has been part of the Garden Club of America since 1926. Piedmont Garden Club members meet monthly to learn about garden-related topics including garden and floral design, garden photography, horticulture and environmental conservation. Other activities include hands-on workshops, field trips and work projects. The Civic Project committee members of the Piedmont Garden Club are Patty Reed, chair, Lori Adams, Molly Ashford, Lisa Cole, MJ Dodds, Roxanne Gault, Barbara Giuffre, Cathy Glazier, Susan Hill, Dana Low, Conna McCarthy, Judi Mckee, Margy Pengilly, Cindy Rafton, Patty Siskind, Karen Sullivan, and Jamie Totsubo. In recent years the Garden Club has made donations to the Hall Fenway renovation of the landscape, lighting of the Bufano bear sculpture in Crocker Park, planting of native plants in the Ramona-Ronada Triangle, and the re-design of the park entrance at Highland Avenue and Guilford Road. Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap (left), receives a check for $5000 from Piedmont Garden Club members Patty Reed, Molly Ashford, Cathy Glazier and MJ Dodds.
articles.title: Piedmont Garden Club donates $5000 for 2 city projects

articles.text: Napa Valley, the nation’s most famous wine growing region, is divided into 16 different agricultural areas called AVA’s. Many of the names like Stag’s Leap, St. Helena and Mount Veeder have become almost as famous as Napa itself. You could also add the Rutherford AVA to that list. The Rutherford AVA is centered around the town of Rutherford in the flat center of Napa Valley and is famous for its high-quality Cabernet Sauvignon. The appellation of 6600 acres consists of gravel, loam, sand and volcanic soils. Rutherford is home to some of Napa’s most historic and iconic wineries such as Inglenook and Beaulieu Vineyards. In February the Rutherford Dust Society, a group of wineries and growers dedicated to promoting the Rutherford AVA, held a tasting at Peju Winery for Trade and Media. Most of the region’s wineries showed up to pour one or more of their wines. Of the many excellent wines poured that day the wines selected below were the cream of the crop – the best of Rutherford AVA. wine’s deep ruby/purple color is followed by sweet, full-bodied flavors, copious quantities of black fruits and a long, lusty finish. A job well done. The Chaix family is in the heart of the Rutherford AVA. • 2018 Chaix Cabernet Sauvignon For many years the Chaix family has been farming grapes in Napa Valley and is now bottling wine under their own name. Their 2018 Cabernet Sauvignon is deep garnet-purple colored and opens with notes of blackberries, plums and cigar box with flavors on the palate of raspberries, currants and black pepper. Davis Estates Cabernet Sauvignon This is my first opportunity to taste from this producer. The 2018 Cabernet is dark-ruby colored with aromas of toast, smoke, spice box and currants. This is followed by a full-bodied wine with ample sweet blackberry fruit and lovely elegance. It has the structure to evolve for several years and should drink well for two decades. • 2018 Beaulieu Vineyards Cabernet Sauvignon Rutherford We all owe a great debt to Beaulieu Vineyards as they were Napa pioneers who helped establish the international reputation of Napa wines. This bottle proves they are still going strong after all these years. It is deep garnet-purple colored and displays chocolate and licorice scents over a core of cassis, black soil and plum preserves with a touch of dried herbs. Full-bodied, concentrated and packed to the gills with ripe, rich black fruits, it has a firm frame, good freshness and finishes long and spicy. • 2018 St. Supery Merlot This Rutherford Merlot blended with 10% Cabernet Sauvignon has a spicy nose of cinnamon, cloves and pepper over a core of warm blackberry preserves and plums, plus notes of vanilla and tobacco. Medium to full-bodied, the palate reveals generous plums and blueberry layers with a plush texture and spicy kick to the smooth finish. • 2017 Wm. Harrison Cabernet Franc Cabernet Franc is often thought of as the lighter, fresher little sister to Cabernet Sauvignon. This little sister is delicious.
