Piedmont Garden Club donates $5000 for 2 city projects Annually the Civic Projects Committee of the Piedmont Garden Club donates $5000 to the Parks Commission of Piedmont to use for special projects in Piedmont. The last several years their emphasis has been to provide funds for native plant materials in and around the community parks. This year Patty Reed and her committee presented a check to Patty Dunlap, the chair of the Parks Commission, for the monies for two projects. The first project is for the Linda Park Lawn Renovation which is located near the Linda Dog Park. This area above the walking path will have all of the invasive ivy, lawn on the slope, and the low chain link fence removed. The club’s donation of $2500 will be used to partially cover the cost to install native plants, ground cover and trees to the area. The second $2500 will help pay for a new hedge in front of the Community Hall. The existing hedge was removed to repair water leaks in the lower level of the building. The new hedge will be coffeeberry, a native plant. This project was chosen because the Community Hall is near and dear to the garden club members; it is where they meet each month. Founded in 1923, Piedmont Garden Club has been part of the Garden Club of America since 1926. Piedmont Garden Club members meet monthly to learn about garden-related topics including garden and floral design, garden photography, horticulture and environmental conservation. Other activities include hands-on workshops, field trips and work projects. The Civic Project committee members of the Piedmont Garden Club are Patty Reed, chair, Lori Adams, Molly Ashford, Lisa Cole, MJ Dodds, Roxanne Gault, Barbara Giuffre, Cathy Glazier, Susan Hill, Dana Low, Conna McCarthy, Judi Mckee, Margy Pengilly, Cindy Rafton, Patty Siskind, Karen Sullivan, and Jamie Totsubo. In recent years the Garden Club has made donations to the Hall Fenway renovation of the landscape, lighting of the Bufano bear sculpture in Crocker Park, planting of native plants in the Ramona-Ronada Triangle, and the re-design of the park entrance at Highland Avenue and Guilford Road. Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap (left), receives a check for $5000 from Piedmont Garden Club members Patty Reed, Molly Ashford, Cathy Glazier and MJ Dodds. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, March 16, 2022 Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers tour the city’s Heritage Trees By Dick Carter It was another sunny, beautiful day last Wednesday and the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group responded with 33 members and one K-9 best friend. Siow Fang Tan had shared information about the city’s Heritage Tree program, and the walkers thought it would be fun and informative to go see some of the past Heritage Trees, and also submit a tree candidate of their own. The first past Heritage Tree was an easy one for the walkers to see. They just had to look up at the Highland poplars that surround the Exedra. This is a deciduous tree with a shapely oval form. They are considered to be drought tolerant. Their large, serrated, heart-shaped leaves turn yellow in fall. They are fast growers and will grow to be about 50 feet tall at maturity with a spread of 30 feet. They can live for 60 years or more. The next Heritage Tree was a short walk to the Community Hall to see a Yulan Magnolia in the rotunda in front of the building. This tree is native to China and is also called Lilly Magnolia. It was probably the first magnolia cultivated about 4,000 years ago. It has pure white, elegant flowers, and was regarded as far back as 650 AD by Buddhist monks as a symbol of purity. The tree in front of the Community Hall was planted by former Piedmont Public Works superintendent Dave Frankel. Nearby was a set of Japanese maple next to the Japanese Tea House. Unlike many other Piedmont trees, their leaves had not yet emerged. These maples are prized for their delicate and colorful foliage throughout the growing season and autumn. This tree is a smallish and slow growing, with mature heights up to 30 feet. Their leaves offer striking color throughout the growing season, becoming even more beautiful with their fall color change. The next tree was the very tall California redwood just inside the old columns of Frank C. Havens’ Wildwood Estate in Wildwood Gardens. This is a massive tree that has been watered by an underwater creek for decades. This is an evergreen species that can live 1,200 to 2,200 years or more. They are among the oldest living things on earth and also the tallest trees, reaching up to 379 feet in height without the roots and up to 29 feet in diameter. The species is monoecious, with pollen and seed cones on the same plant. The walkers loved this tree and stopped for a group photo in front of it. The walkers then went to the Hall Fenway at the corner of Wildwood and Crocker Avenue to see a set of European white birch trees. This is a short-lived species native to northern North America. Its thin, white bark peels in paper like layers from the trunk. The wood is often used for pulpwood and firewood. It is a medium-sized deciduous tree typically reaching 66 feet tall, and exceptionally to 130 feet with a trunk up to 30 inches in diameter. This tree is a typically short-lived species, but in colder-climate regions can grow for more than 100 years. Its fall color is a bright yellow. The next tree was a Monterey pine across the street in Crocker Park. This tree is native to the Central Coast of California and Mexico. It is an evergreen and is a versatile, fast-growing, medium-density softwood, suitable for a wide range of uses. It is the most widely cultivated pine in the world, and is also the most widely planted tree for choose-and-cut Christmas tree farms in California. Its root system can extend 30 to 39 feet. They grow to between 50 and 100 feet in height in the wild, and up to 200 feet in cultivation. They attain full size in 80 to 100 years, but rarely live beyond 150 years. Some walkers remembered one of these Crocker Park pines coming down a few years ago in a windstorm and falling onto Hampton Road. The next tree was a grove of huge eucalyptus trees on Hampton where St. James Drive ends. Eucalyptus trees are also known as gum trees, and are native to Australia, which has almost 900 species of them. They are found throughout California and have become invasive along the coast. They grow rapidly, and many species attain great height. The giant gum tree is one of the largest and can grow to about 300 feet and have a circumference of about 25 feet. A eucalyptus tree can grow six feet each year. They can have long lives with most species able to survive 250 years. Their wood is sometimes used as a less expensive and more easily and sustainably farmed hardwood. Eucalyptus leaves are also poisonous to most animals and humans. Eucalyptus trees got here as seeds on ships coming to California from Australia in the 1850s during the Gold Rush. Within a few decades of them being planted on the West Coast, many Californians grew disenchanted with them. The trees proved to be terrible for woodworking, and the wood often split and cracked, making it a poor choice for railroad ties. The trees were also thirsty and drained wells. They are filled with aromatic oil, which makes them highly combustible. In the East Bay firestorm of 1991, vast swaths of eucalyptus burned, and the fire left 25 people dead and thousands homeless. The walkers had now seen all their Heritage Tree candidates and it was time to vote. The California redwood won in a landslide. It received all but one vote. With the voting done it was time for return to the town center. Noemi Alvarado and Siow Fang Tan volunteered to make a Walking on Wednesdays’ submission for a Heritage Tree. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the Group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Members of the First Mondays Reading Group on the deck at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park: Bella Almanzan (left), Ken Young, Adrienne Hamlin, Carol Long, Lois Price, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Sarah Johnson, Karin Fetherston, Darby Gragg, Mike Bandrowski, Jerry Gragg, Melba Yee, Pat McMahon, Laura Goldman, Mike Henn, Albert Chen, and Priscilla Wanerus. Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group met again outside the Tea House in the Piedmont Park on March 7. It was another warm, sunny afternoon and 18 members of the group were on hand for the discussion without the need for masks. Carol Long continued to spoil the group with candy and fruit, which were of light blue and yellow colors to honor the Ukrainian people. The group was there to discuss their March selection, Matt Haig’s The Midnight Library. a fantasy best-selling novel published in 2020. Haig’s protagonist is Nora Seed, a young woman who is unhappy with her life choices and is filled with regrets. Everything possible in her life is bad, including a lost job and a dead cat. During the night she tries to kill herself but ends up in a library managed by her old school librarian. The library is between life and death with millions of books filled with stories of different versions of Nora’s life. She can visit as many as she wants to find out what her life would have been if she had made different decisions. She gets to find her perfect life and finally be happy. But none satisfies her. The things that are making her unhappy in her “root life” go with her to other lives. However, in this process she eventually finds that her existence really does matter. She has significant, often unintended, positive effects on others. Additionally, she has the potential to build a brighter future with her actual life. She doesn’t need a new life, she just needs to realize that her own life has potential, and she could keep reinventing herself until she achieves happiness. The Midnight Library turned out to be a surprisingly good book group selection because some readers loved it, and others didn’t like it at all. This made for a good conversation. Those on the positive side appreciated the moral that life does matter. You have the ability to affect others, and you have the potential to keep working towards happiness for yourself and others. It was noted that at the age of 24 Haig experienced severe depression and an attempted suicide, so his writing seems to be an attempt to help others work through difficult times. Those who did not care for the book found the character of Nora to be shallow and gave up too easily on her loves and lives. Learning of Haig’s personal history led to a discussion of how much a reader should know about the author before reading the Matt Haig’s The Midnight Library work. It was agreed that a book needs to stand on its own. With their discussion complete the group turned to future book selections. They had previously picked the non-fiction Destiny of the Republic by Candice Millard as their April book and The Lincoln Highway by Amor Towles for May. The next discussion will be Monday, April 4 at 1:30 p.m. with plans to meet outside the Japanese Tea House in the park. New readers are welcome to join the group and there is no fee to participate. Registration is required by calling 510 420-3070 to register.

articles.text: Where can women over the age of 50 find young, sexy men who are interested in them? Try a bookstore, under fiction. A lot of pro basketball players have shaved their heads. Doesn’t that prove that baldness is sexy? Absolutely – and its effect on women may be intensified if you’re also under 30, over 6-feet-6, incredibly athletic, and wealthier than many Eastern European nations. What sort of people show up at a mixer for singles over 50? A: People over 60. What’s the most insulting word to describe a 50-year-old man’s flirtations? She has significant, often unintended, positive effects on others. Additionally, she has the potential to build a brighter future with her actual life. She doesn’t need a new life, she just needs to realize that her own life has potential, and she could keep reinventing herself until she achieves happiness. The Midnight Library turned out to be a surprisingly good book group selection because some readers loved it, and others didn’t like it at all. This made for a good conversation. Those on the positive side appreciated the moral that life does matter. You have the ability to affect others, and you have the potential to keep working towards happiness for yourself and others. It was noted that at the age of 24 Haig experienced severe depression and an attempted suicide, so his writing seems to be an attempt to help others work through difficult times. Those who did not care for the book found the character of Nora to be shallow and gave up too easily on her loves and lives. Learning of Haig’s personal history led to a discussion of how much a reader should know about the author before reading the Matt Haig’s The Midnight Library work. It was agreed that a book needs to stand on its own. With their discussion complete the group turned to future book selections. They had previously picked the non-fiction Destiny of the Republic by Candice Millard as their April book and The Lincoln Highway by Amor Towles for May. The next discussion will be Monday, April 4 at 1:30 p.m. with plans to meet outside the Japanese Tea House in the park. New readers are welcome to join the group and there is no fee to participate. articles.text: Shopping in the Atrium of the Concord Plaza Hotel The Walnut Creek Bead & Design Show has returned and will be held March 25-27 in the ballrooms and meeting space at Concord Plaza Hotel. This three-day event brings together a diverse group of independent artisans, beadmakers and tradespeople with 150 artisan exhibits and hands-on workshops. Makers and designers will find a great line-up of high-quality bead merchants, and suppliers, with trade beads, gold and silver findings, seed beads, gems, cabs, unusual components, and more, all at great prices. Interactive workshops are offered throughout the show and let you get creative and learn new skills. Try your hand at mixed media and jewelry-making techniques, including beadwork, chainmaille, pearl knotting, soldering, kumihimo, wire work, and Peyote beading. pages.text: 26 Wednesday, March 16, 2022 Girl Webelos advance to Scouting Webelos is the most-advanced level of Cub Scouting. On February 8, the six 5th-grade girl Webelos based at Havens School transitioned to Scouting in a ceremony called Arrow of Light. New Scouts Charli Hale, Dani Hale, Lauren “Mai” Levy, Ashlan Mitchell, Willow Thomas and Molly Tulloch crossed over to the Bobcat Patrol in Piedmont Council’s Troop 15 during a Court of Honor. Other Webelos to join Troop 15 in the past year include Kai Hsu, John Bunje, Quinton Cole, and Rafael “Rafa” Rajan. After just one month in Scouting, Molly Tulloch said, “Troop 15 is really fun. I’m looking forward to camping trips and working on merit badges.” Patrol Leader Christiane Zuber was recognized at the Court of Honor for her leadership to the Bobcats. She, too, was once a Webelo in Pack 3 at Havens. “Bobcats like camping and learning new skills”, she explained. “For Summer Camp, we are going to Emerald Bay on Catalina Island from June 18-25. I’m going to learn to canoe and kayak on the sea.” Girls and boys ages 11 and up and their parents with an interest in spending time in nature and improving leadership skills can learn more about Scouting by attending the Troop 15 Open House on Tuesday, March 22 at 7:30 pm at Havens School, 325 Highland Avenue. For more information, contact Scoutmaster Glen Tripp at Glen@Galileo-learning.com. articles.text: could do about it. Many musical comedians used implied scatological humor. Mad Magazine issued a record and in promoting it declare, “it’s a gas”. When it comes to this form of humor, the champion was a French comedian who was known as “Le Petomane.” Composers like Mozart and Beethoven were more subtle in their use of scatological humor. A few composers found comedy in animals. The first one that comes to mind is St.-Saens in his Carnival of the Animals. The Italian Scarlatti wrote “The Cats Fugue.” The great violinist Paganini played a piece where he imitated all kinds of barnyard animals. If he didn’t like the behavior of his audience, his final variation was an imitation of a jackass. This was his way of thumbing his nose at a rude audience. Speaking of violinists, be sure to see Jascha Heifetz on YouTube imitating a bad violinist. Type in “Jascha Heifetz Audition”. Heifetz made other party records. The name he used on these recordings was Joseph Hague – same initials but different name. Some people tried to prove that there actually was a Joseph Hague. All you need to do is take a look at the photograph of the supposed Joseph Hague. The violin in the photo is the Guarnerius violin owned by Heifetz. The hands and torso are Jascha Heifetz, but the head of someone else is attached, Finishing the day was sophomore Monte Imburg, who won 6-1, 6-2 at No. 4 singles. In singles, Burchardt won 6-3, 6-2 at No. 1, Breber won 6-3, 6-2 at No. 2, Imburg was a 6-2, 6-3 victor at No. 3, and was steady with a 6-3, 6-3 win at No. 4. articles.text: On Sunday afternoon, March 6, a man brandishing, what turned out to be a replica gun, in the Trestle Glen area led the Piedmont police to issue a shelter-in-place notice to nearby residents and the deployment of an Oakland police helicopter. The first call to police occurred at 3:20 p.m. about a man wearing a black hooded sweatshirt, red Chicago Bulls jersey, and dark pants waving a gun while walking on Trestle Glen Road. The man was initially scared off by a barking dog before walking up the steps to Sandringham Road. Three more calls to police came in from St James Drive, Cambrian Way and Sandringham Road about a man mumbling to himself and entering a resident’s backyard. Piedmont police issued a shelter in place order to residents in the area. Alameda County Sheriff’s Office and Oakland Police provided additional support and an Oakland Police Department helicopter was seen in the area, trying to locate the man. The suspect unlawfully entered a garage on St. James Drive and was confronted by the homeowner as he was rummaging through cabinets. The suspect, identified as Miguel Mejia, 31, of Oakland, was taken into custody by police and the gun was determined to be a replica. Piedmont Police’s investigation found that Mejia pointed the replica weapon on three different occasions at three separate residents. The shelter-in-place lasted approximately 90 minutes. Mejia was arrested and transported to Santa Rita jail. He was on a felony probation with a full search clause and was charged with home invasion, burglary, brandishing a weapon, trespassing and probation violations. March 15. See next week’s Post for game details. CRIME REPORT By Jay Russell Man brandishing replica gun draws helicopter On Sunday afternoon, March 6, a man brandishing, what turned out to be a replica gun, in the Trestle Glen area led the Piedmont police to issue a shelter-in-place notice to nearby residents and the deployment of an Oakland police helicopter. The first call to police occurred at 3:20 p.m. about a man wearing a black hooded sweatshirt, red Chicago Bulls jersey, and dark pants waving a gun while walking on Trestle Glen Road. The man was initially scared off by a barking dog before walking up the steps to Sandringham Road. Three more calls to police came in from St James Drive, Cambrian Way and Sandringham Road about a man mumbling to himself and entering a resident’s backyard. Piedmont police issued a shelter in place order to residents in the area. Alameda County Sheriff’s Office and Oakland Police provided additional support and an Oakland Police Department helicopter was seen in the area, trying to locate the man. The suspect unlawfully entered a garage on St. James Drive and was confronted by the homeowner as he was rummaging through cabinets. The suspect, identified as Miguel Mejia, 31, of Oakland, was taken into custody by police and the gun was determined to be a replica. Piedmont Police’s investigation found that Mejia pointed the replica weapon on three different occasions at three separate residents. The shelter-in-place lasted approximately 90 minutes. Mejia was arrested and transported to Santa Rita jail. He was on a felony probation with a full search clause and was charged with home invasion, burglary, brandishing a weapon, trespassing and probation violations. articles.text: This year’s trip has been scaled back due to COVID precautions, despite immense popularity and desire for participation. This spring the church is anticipating 160 students and 40 adult volunteers traveling to Tijuana to build 12 homes for families in need. Two years ago, 270 students and 25 adults signed up to build 18 homes before the trip was canceled. Mexico trip volunteers will set up tents and camp between Tijuana and Tecate, four miles south of the U.S. border. The houses are built for the least fortunate residents in Tijuana, many living in shelters made of cardboard. The students forego a typical spring break vacation to serve others, and often return transformed by the experience. Piedmont residents donated over 2,000 items to the church for the Treasures Sale. articles.text: In a nearly five-hour meeting Monday night, March 7, the Piedmont City Council on a 3-2 vote forged ahead with a facility use agreement at 801 Magnolia Avenue that effectively reduces a 10-year lease to a five year use agreement and cuts the use of the Center for the Arts by the citizen volunteers who plan its activities to roughly half the time they have had in the building. In the March 7 meeting in City Hall, City Council members heard public comment from over 20 residents and reviewed over 50 written comments when considering a use agreement between the City and the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The use agreement effectively terminates a previous month-to-month lease agreement between the two and prohibits the Center from leasing its office space, forcing the eviction of the city’s hometown paper, the Piedmont Post. The lease was on a monthto-month basis since April 2021, when a 10-year lease between the City as leaser and PCA as tenant expired. PCA, a non-profit and independent arts organization, 801 Magnolia Avenue.
articles.title: In marathon meeting, City Council cuts PCA to 5 years; use of Center cut by 55%

articles.text: Piedmont resident Brett Byers proudly flies a large Ukrainian flag over his garage, but his efforts to support the country and people under attack don’t stop there. By preserving Ukrainian culture, writing to elected officials, making donations, and helping promote effective boycotts, Byers has taken up a humanitarian cause which requires hours of effort each day. Byers toured Ukraine and Russia in 1992 and 1994 with the Yale Russian Chorus. During the trips he sang in Kyiv, which included a performance for monks within the Kyiv cave monasteries. The monasteries were built underground to keep the monks safe from many wars in Ukraine over hundreds of years. From his choral music experience in Ukraine, Byers used his contacts to preserve over 500 pieces of sheet music from the Dudaryk Choir’s music library on files from a web server in Lviv. “This music ranges from hundreds of years old to modern choral music. Ukrainian choral music ranges from sacred to traditional folk,” he said Byers is also now working to see if he can help preserve the sheet music of the Kyiv Chamber Choir, which has the largest Ukrainian choral music library in the world. Byers’s past personal experience has driven him to preserve Ukrainian culture in a way specific to him through music. articles.text: Piedmont School Superintendent Randy Booker recently announced that masks would no longer be required inside schools regardless of vaccination status. As previously indicated, Piedmont School District aligned with Alameda County’s policy. On February 28, the state of California dropped the requirement of indoor masks and allowed counties to follow suit. “I believe Piedmont has been ahead of the curve since the start of the pandemic, providing a fine example to the County of what can be accomplished when a community works together to keep its residents safe. That hard work is now showing results,” said Booker. Booker’s initial announcement used the terms “mask-optional” and “mask-optional environment,” and due to some confusion in the community he attempted to clarify the district’s policy on March 8. “The terms [‘mask-optional’ and ‘mask-optional environment’] were used solely to convey that as of next Monday, students and staff would have the option to not wear a mask indoors - if they so choose - and does not represent an overall ‘mask-optional’ policy. PUSD is firmly aligned with the state and Alameda County’s decision that indoor masking is ‘strongly recommended’ for all individuals while on campus,” Booker stated yesterday. Piedmont teachers will not be allowed to require masks in their classrooms. That decision is up to each individual student and staff member. articles.text: After nine years as Principal of Piedmont Middle School, Ryan Fletcher will be stepping down at the end of the school year. He and his family will be relocating to Colorado where he will take on the role of Principal for a middle school in suburban Denver. “I am so grateful for all that I have learned and gained during my time at PMS. As I begin this next chapter and enter a new school community, I can only hope to feel as embraced and supported as I have been throughout my time in Piedmont.” Fletcher said in a letter to the school community on March 2. Fletcher began his journey in education while still an undergrad at the University of Vermont, as a student-teacher in 2000. Upon moving to California in 2003 he taught 4th, 5th and 6th grade in Palo Alto until 2008. After earning a Master’s degree at Santa Clara University, he became Assistant Principal at J.L. Stanford Middle School in Palo Alto from 2009 until 2013. Since then, Fletcher has been the Principal in Piedmont. Accomplishments under his tenure include providing computers for all students, equitable grading practices, late start bell schedule, an updated homework policy, and a comprehensive 6th grade Orientation Program. Fletcher also faithfully guided middle school students and staff through COVID and the transition to distance learning, a hybrid schedule and the return to in-person classes. “Ryan loves working with and knowing the students at ‘his’ school. He is committed to ensuring that all students feel supported,” said veteran 6th grade teacher Ted Scherman. “I have always found Ryan to be a man of strong character and principle. I consider Ryan a colleague and a friend, and I will miss him greatly,” Scherman added. Piedmont resident does more than fly Ukrainian flag By Jay Russell Piedmont resident Brett Byers proudly flies a large Ukrainian flag over his garage, but his efforts to support the country and people under attack don’t stop there. By preserving Ukrainian culture, writing to elected officials, making donations, and helping promote effective boycotts, Byers has taken up a humanitarian cause which requires hours of effort each day. Byers toured Ukraine and Russia in 1992 and 1994 with the Yale Russian Chorus. During the trips he sang in Kyiv, which included a performance for monks within the Kyiv cave monasteries. The monasteries were built underground to keep the monks safe from many wars in Ukraine over hundreds of years. From his choral music experience in Ukraine, Byers used his contacts to preserve over 500 pieces of sheet music from the Dudaryk Choir’s music library on files from a web server in Lviv. “This music ranges from hundreds of years old to modern choral music. As previously indicated, Piedmont School District aligned with Alameda County’s policy. On February 28, the state of California dropped the requirement of indoor masks and allowed counties to follow suit. “I believe Piedmont has been ahead of the curve since the start of the pandemic, providing a fine example to the County of what can be accomplished when a community works together to keep its residents safe. That hard work is now showing results,” said Booker. Booker’s initial announcement used the terms “mask-optional” and “mask-optional environment,” and due to some confusion in the community he attempted to clarify the district’s policy on March 8. “The terms [‘mask-optional’ and ‘mask-optional environment’] were used solely to convey that as of next Monday, students and staff would have the option to not wear a mask indoors - if they so choose - and does not represent an overall ‘mask-optional’ policy. PUSD is firmly aligned with the state and Alameda County’s decision that indoor masking is ‘strongly recommended’ for all individuals while on campus,” Booker stated yesterday. At a dinner at the home of Simon the Pharisee, she washed Jesus’ feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, kissed them and poured oil on them. (see Luke 7:36-50). articles.text: Oakland’s rock star biologist, Damon Tighe is the headliner for the “Topics of Merritt” speaker series on March 10 at 3:30 p.m. at The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living. This freeto-the-public Zoom presentation features Oakland’s charming biotechnologist and urban naturalist who has been featured on local news programs. Tighe will present a talk entitled “Fish and Friends of Lake Merritt’s Waters,” and will highlight the incredible fact that salmon are finding their way back into the Lake Merritt watershed after an absence of roughly 20 years. A public question and answer session will follow his presentation. Since last fall, Chinook salmon have been spotted in East Bay rivers and streams that lead to Lake Merritt, but salmon have not been seen in the lake in over two decades. Tighe reports that they have been showing up this year in the hundreds. In addition, Oakland residents have reported sightings in the lake near Glen Echo where the creek runs alongside the Veterans Memorial Building, by the Laney College football field, as well as a tributary that begins in the hills near Mountain View Cemetery and empties into the northwest branch of the lake, near the intersection of Grand Avenue and Harrison Street. Volunteer groups have been helping provide a healthy fish habitat. The Lake Merritt Institute partners with local citizens and Oakland school students to clean up Lake Merritt’s shoreline and creeks on a weekly basis. Conservationists say these salmon sightings in the lake highlight the much-needed care that goes into conserving Lake Merritt’s amazing, but fragile ecosystem. The return of salmon this year has many people excited and offers proof that we should continue efforts to keep Lake Merritt clean, healthy and Oakland biologist Damon Tighe. well-maintained. Damon Tighe attended Saint Mary’s College in Moraga where he worked on local newspapers while earning a Biology/Chemistry degree. He taught high school in Portland, Oregon and moved back to the Bay Area to work on the Human Genome Project at the National Lab’s Joint Genome Institute. He spent time pursuing an MFA in Natural History and Science Filmmaking in Montana, but returned to Oakland to work on befouls and single cell genomics. He now teaches biotechnology to high school teachers through Bio-Rad Laboratories and is well versed in local fungi, plants and critters of Lake Merritt. The “Topics of Merritt” is a free-to-the-public program of The Lake Merritt – Independent Senior Living. The series is designed to offer interesting and compelling speakers from our community and beyond. An archive of these free talks is available on The Lake Merritt – Independent Senior Living’s website. The public is invited to join us for a free Zoom presentation on March 10, when Damon will share his insights. To register click on: www.tinyurl. com/lakemerrittfish. For further information, contact Tim Johnson at www. thelakemerritt.com. “I can’t understand it...a Stanford MBA, Harvard Law Degree, record test scores, absolutely NO street sense.”

articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont held its third speaker event in its Defending Democracy Speaker Series on March 1, with a discussion on Election Law and the Supreme Court by Berkeley Law School Dean Erwin Chemerinsky. The upcoming events in this series include “Can American Democracy Survive? An International Perspective,” with Dr. Fiona Hill on Mar 30, and Election Subversion and Disinformation with Rick Hasen on April 5. The series is cosponsored by Leagues across the country in Collier County, Florida; Gunnison Valley, Colorado; Oakland, California; The Pikes Peak Region, Colorado; Portland, Oregon; Pueblo, Colorado; Santa Barbara, California; and Solano County, California. Dean Chemerisnky opened his talk by describing an unprecedented event in U.S. history: the first time an incumbent president tried to hold onto power after losing an election. Donald Trump plotted to have his vice president subvert the election and now 70 percent of Republican voters believe that Trump won the election. Since then, 18 states have adopted laws to make voting more difficult for minorities that will have an effect on our elections in 2022 and 2024. Chemerinsky explained partisan gerrymandering, how lines drawn around election districts have long been maximized to favor either Democratic or Republican results. This is not new, but now it’s easier to achieve more favorable results with the aid of computers to analyze populations and draw maps. He stated, “Partisan gerrymandering is illegal when it dilutes the right to vote.” In 2016 and then again in 2018, partisan gerrymandering was found to be unconstitutional, but the Supreme Court reversed this. In June of 2019, the Supreme Court declared challenges to partisan gerrymandering cannot be challenged in federal court because they are political questions. Chemerinsky considers the Voting Rights Act of 1965 to be the most important piece of legislation to counteract our history of Black voter suppression. Chemerinsky made the point that the Supreme Court gutted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act in July 2021 with its decision in Brnovich v. Democratic National Committee. Section 2 prohibits laws that discriminate against minorities. He pointed out the discriminatory effect of moving absentee ballot boxes and other election changes. While partisan gerrymandering cases cannot be heard in federal courts, racial gerrymandering can as it falls under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. Dean Chemerinsky favors increasing the number of Supreme Court justices and having 18-year non-renewable terms for Supreme Court justices. He feels that 40-50 years on the bench is too much power for one person. He thinks Katanji Jackson Brown is terrific and will be confirmed. Also, 2022 will be a momentous year on the Supreme Court with Roe vs. Wade possibly being overruled and with other cases about states funding religious schools and addressing the issues of businesses refusing to serve same sex couples. Chemerinsky closed his presentation with a lively question and answer session with audience members. When asked by Piedmont League President Lorrel Plimier “What can we do?” Mr. Chemerinsky urged people to vote, get others to vote, and work to get congress to adopt new voting rights legislation. This is nonpartisan work to ensure the people get out to vote and that their votes are counted. To learn more about voting rights and the Supreme Court, please watch the recording of this presentation on League of Women Voters’ YouTube channel: lwvpiedmont.org/youtube.
articles.title: Erwin Chemerinsky addresses LWV in its “Defending Democracy” series

articles.text: Join the League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWV) on Wednesday, March 30, for a discussion with Dr. Fiona Hill, Senior Fellow at The Brookings Institution at Stanford. The Zoom episode will explore the current state of democracy, from both domestic and international points of view. Dr. Hill is the Robert Bosch Senior Fellow at the Center on the United States and Europe in the Foreign Policy program at the Brookings Institution and member of the Council on Foreign Relations. Her most recent book, There is Nothing for You Here, draws on her personal journey out of poverty, as well as her unique perspectives as a historian and policy maker, to show how we can return hope to our forgotten places. From 2017 to 2019, Dr. Hill served as deputy assistant to the president and senior director for European and Russian affairs on Central Asia, regional conflicts, energy, and strategic issues. Co-author of Mr. Putin: Operative in the Kremlin and The Siberian Curse: How Communist Planners Left Russia Out in the Cold, she holds a master’s degree in Soviet studies and a doctorate in history from Harvard University and a master’s in Russian and modern history from St. Andrews University in Scotland. This event is part of the League’s 2022 Defending Democracy Speaker Series and is co-sponsored by local Leagues in California, Oregon, Colorado, and Florida. This talk will be held live on Zoom and YouTube and will include an audience question and answer session. Visit the website lwvpiedmont.org to learn more about the series and register for this event. Once you have registered, you will receive the Zoom link by email. The event is free and open to the public. By Tim Johnson Oakland’s rock star biologist, Damon Tighe is the headliner for the “Topics of Merritt” speaker series on March 10 at 3:30 p.m. at The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living. This freeto-the-public Zoom presentation features Oakland’s charming biotechnologist and urban naturalist who has been featured on local news programs. Tighe will present a talk entitled “Fish and Friends of Lake Merritt’s Waters,” and will highlight the incredible fact that salmon are finding their way back into the Lake Merritt watershed after an absence of roughly 20 years. A public question and answer session will follow his presentation. Since last fall, Chinook salmon have been spotted in East Bay rivers and streams that lead to Lake Merritt, but salmon have not been seen in the lake in over two decades. Tighe reports that they have been showing up this year in the hundreds. In addition, Oakland residents have reported sightings in the lake near Glen Echo where the creek runs alongside the Veterans Memorial Building, by the Laney College football field, as well as a tributary that begins in the hills near Mountain View Cemetery and empties into the northwest branch of the lake, near the intersection of Grand Avenue and Harrison Street. Volunteer groups have been helping provide a healthy fish habitat. The Lake Merritt Institute partners with local citizens and Oakland school students to clean up Lake Merritt’s shoreline and creeks on a weekly basis. Conservationists say these salmon sightings in the lake highlight the much-needed care that goes into conserving Lake Merritt’s amazing, but fragile ecosystem. The return of salmon this year has many people excited and offers proof that we should continue efforts to keep Lake Merritt clean, healthy and Oakland biologist Damon Tighe. well-maintained. Damon Tighe attended Saint Mary’s College in Moraga where he worked on local newspapers while earning a Biology/Chemistry degree. He taught high school in Portland, Oregon and moved back to the Bay Area to work on the Human Genome Project at the National Lab’s Joint Genome Institute. He spent time pursuing an MFA in Natural History and Science Filmmaking in Montana, but returned to Oakland to work on befouls and single cell genomics. He now teaches biotechnology to high school teachers through Bio-Rad Laboratories and is well versed in local fungi, plants and critters of Lake Merritt. articles.text: Second generation Piedmonter Brian Goodhue, PHS class of 2006, moved back to town after starting a family. Goodhue may sound like an average Piedmont dad until you look in his garage and see his 450 horsepower Infiniti G35 drift car. “Drifting is a motorsport where the object is to drive your car sideways, essentially fishtailing through a set course of corners. Instead of driving for speed, the goal is to get through the corners as sideways as you can, without spinning out, or hitting anyone,” Goodhue explained. What started as a fascination and high school hobby in the early 2000s became a serious endeavor. He now competes in pro-am drift competitions with the aim of winning a podium spot in a Shootout competition. Finishing in the top three in one of the big events is the only way to attain a Formula Drift professional license; allowing him to drive in the Pro-Spec series. Goodhue discovered drifting in the early days of its inception in American culture. While reading a magazine called Superstreet, this new concept swept him off his feet. “Superstreet had this article on drifting and I was trying to make sense of what they were talking about because they were trying to describe drifting in words. This was before Youtube so you couldn’t just watch a video,” he said. You primarily need a rear wheel drive car to drift. The rear wheels will overpower the front wheels, carrying the rear of the car outwards to complete the turn Brian Goodhue (left) and his Crew Chief Joe Pramic. The pit crew consists of 2-6 members who have five minutes between runs in Shootouts to make repairs. in a controlled slide. In most cars if you try to burnout or start to slide, only one tire spins. Hence drift cars have a “positraction” or a welded together differential (the last part of the transmission attaching the drive shaft and the axle), to force the drive wheels to spin at the same rate. Due to the style-based aspect of the sport, three judges score runs on a 100-point system. One judge looks at speed in relation to the capability of the car and motor. Another looks at the line taken through the course of 3-5 turns in which the car is never allowed to straighten out. Finally, a style judge factors in intangibles like initiation, fluidity, and commitment. The sport of organized drifting originally started in Japan with Japanese rear wheel cars, like Nissan Silvias (240SX in US). Drifting slowly migrated to the states by members of the U.S. Navy who had been stationed in Okinawa, Japan. The sport’s popIn Shootout competitions the lead car picks a driveable line and the follow car tries to duplicate the run as closely as possible Brian Goodhue drove a 1997 Mazda Miata Turbo from 2015-2019. Since 2020 Brian Goodhue has been driving a 2003 Infiniti G35 sedan competition car. During left hand drift turns the front wheels are actually turned to the right. ularity moved to Hawaii and then to the mainland U.S. “It was very grassroots, it wasn’t well known at all as a motorsport until 2002,” explained Goodhue. One of the first sanctioned events was in the parking lot at Golden Gate Fields in 2003,” he said. Goodhue recalls heading to the parking lots at the former Alameda Naval Air Base to practice and was surprised to find spectators. “The police would watch or try to do it with you, and a lot of them could. Nobody cared back then,” he said. Highway Patrol officers now attend sanctioned drift events with police cars set up to drift, in an attempt to recruit drifters to join the CHP. On the professional level companies including Toyota sponsor drifters, but for now Goodhue operates as a privateer. He estimates that there are fewer than 20 drifters in the state who support themselves solely with their driving. The payoffs for winning events are not large, but the top pros get paid through sponsors for TV time now that events are becoming nationally televised. Brian Goodhue’s Infiniti G35 has a Japanese Toyota 2.5l Turbo Inline 6 engine. “I think there is a lot of room for branding from things not normally affiliated with drifting. What drifting has done just for production cars is amazing. When you see a new car commercial it is drifting. Even a minivan is sliding into a parking spot,” he said. Goodhue’s previous cars were always stylish, including a Mazda Miata convertible sporting a green Hawaiian shirt pattern. His current car, an Infiniti G35, is a rarity in the drift world, being a sedan instead of a coupe. At 6’1” Goodhue likes it for the cabin room, but said, “It is a unique drift car, so there are not many styling options for it.” Goodhue is teaming up with graphic designer Triple Style to design specific paint schemes and designs. “My goal for 2022 is to bring to market a body effect kit for my car and market it through the year as a product specific to my camp, Team Goodhue,” he said. Sonoma Raceway is set to renew its Wednesday Night Drag and Drift weekly events which run through December, and which Goodhue says has helped grow the motorsport tremendously. To try to attain his pro license he will be at Shootout events around the west coast, which were most recently held at Sonoma’s Annual Winter Jam Drift Festival, Thunderhill Raceway an hour outside of Chico and Las Vegas Motor Speedway. To contact Brian about potential sponsorships, or to just talk cars and drifting, email him at goodhuedrift@gmail.com. articles.text: Since the 1980’s, summer camps have been a staple for cheesy horror films. After all, they provide a plausible reason why a bunch of people would be in a remote, woodsy area with no cell service. Gratefully, most horror plots remain fiction, but fear, discomfort, and nerves are still a very real part of the summer camp experience – but that is a good thing! The scary and uncomfortable parts of camp are often the catalysts for growth in a camper’s life. Consider the idea of a comfort zone, growth zone, and panic zone. Our comfort zones are our standard-operating anxiety-free defaults. Our growth zones start lighting up when we encounter something outside our comfort-zone – new places, people, and experiences can all induce some level of discomfort. We enter our growth zone when we remain open to those challenges and ride out the discomfort in favor of what’s ahead. We enter our panic zone when experiences become too much to handle and we duck into our protective shells. Spending time in the growth zone, while not always easy, makes children (and adults) more resilient and builds a higher sense of self-esteem and self-efficacy. Children need time to learn not only who they are, but what they’re made of. By breaking Far from a horror film, summer at Camp Augusta has its own scary (and inspiring) moments. away from the gentle routine of home and school, kids surprise themselves by how brave, capable, and strong they really are. While moments that push us can come from anywhere, summer camp is often such a novel experience that everything from sleeping in a cabin to climbing a rock wall is pushing campers out of their comfort zones. Those “wow, I can’t believe I did that” revelations build up a tolerance and an appreciation for discomfort, making children ready and excited to take on the next challenge. If the prospect of leaving your child in the woods for summer camp sends shivers down your spine, you’re not alone. Parents
articles.title: The thrills & chills of summer camp

pages.text: Wednesday, March 9, 2022 7 Thinking Outside The Classroom The thrills & chills of summer camp E v e n t C a l e n d a r By Randy Grayson Since the 1980’s, summer camps have been a staple for cheesy horror films. After all, they provide a plausible reason why a bunch of people would be in a remote, woodsy area with no cell service. Gratefully, most horror plots remain fiction, but fear, discomfort, and nerves are still a very real part of the summer camp experience – but that is a good thing! The scary and uncomfortable parts of camp are often the catalysts for growth in a camper’s life. Consider the idea of a comfort zone, growth zone, and panic zone. Our comfort zones are our standard-operating anxiety-free defaults. Our growth zones start lighting up when we encounter something outside our comfort-zone – new places, people, and experiences can all induce some level of discomfort. We enter our growth zone when we remain open to those challenges and ride out the discomfort in favor of what’s ahead. We enter our panic zone when experiences become too much to handle and we duck into our protective shells. Spending time in the growth zone, while not always easy, makes children (and adults) more resilient and builds a higher sense of self-esteem and self-efficacy. Children need time to learn not only who they are, but what they’re made of. Color Me Mine Alameda Alameda.colormemine.com Far from a horror film, summer at Camp Augusta has its own scary (and inspiring) moments. away from the gentle routine of home and school, kids surprise themselves by how brave, capable, and strong they really are. While moments that push us can come from anywhere, summer camp is often such a novel experience that everything from sleeping in a cabin to climbing a rock wall is pushing campers out of their comfort zones. Those “wow, I can’t believe I did that” revelations build up a tolerance and an appreciation for discomfort, making children ready and excited to take on the next challenge. If the prospect of leaving your child in the woods for summer camp sends shivers down your spine, you’re not alone. Winter trip to Mount Shasta In January, Troop 4 ventured to Mount Shasta for winter adventures. They did a nearly full moon snowshoe hike on Sand Flat Winter Trail with Siberian huskies, went sledding at Snowman’s pass, and went skiing and snowboarding. The Scouts also had the chance to do some sledding and build snowmen. Archery in February Just a few weeks ago in February, the Scouts participated in archery at Camp Chesebrough in the Santa Cruz Mountains, where the Scouts not only learned how shoot arrows, but also how to make them. The Scouts were joined by several Cub Scouts as well. “It was nice being able to help the younger Scouts learn about archery. It was also fun for older Scouts since we also got to participate in the archery,” said Senior Patrol Leader Jonah Dupree. “Troop 4 has remained active throughout the pandemic, with regular outdoor gatherings which have allowed Scouts to remain connected and engaged,” explained Scoutmaster Walter Stokes. “We look forward to more great outdoor adventures this spring, including trips for snow camping, spelunking and camping at Pinnacles National Park.” Chocolate fondue featured at Troop 4 Open House Troop 4 is hosting an Open House on Monday, March 14, at 7:30 p.m. at Becker Playfield at Havens School. It recently graduated over a dozen Eagle Scouts and has room for plenty of Scouts to join at any level, individually or in groups of friends. Boys and girls age 11 to 18 or after entry to 6th grade are eligible to join the troop. Troop 4 will be serving chocolate fondue at the open house. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is calling for volunteers to serve on City commissions and committees. Currently, a total of 17 positions will become available. Of the vacancies opening up, eight are guaranteed to be available. The remaining positions potentially will be filled by incumbents. Residents are encouraged to apply to any vacancy of interest. How to Apply The deadline for applications is Monday, March 21 at 5:00 p.m. Interviews will be held the evening of Monday, March 28. Residents interested in volunteering may fill out and submit an application form on the city’s website: https://www. piedmont.ca.gov/government/ city _news_ _ _notif ications/ commission-committee-recruitPlanning Commission 3 vacancies, 3 incumbents; 3-year term The Planning Commission makes decisions regarding proposed modifications or construction to homes. It advises the City Council on issues related to planning and building. It meets monthly on the second Monday at 5:30 p.m. It requires approximately 4 hours per month in addition to meeting time. Appointees to the Planning Commission are required to submit a statement of economic interests. Commissioners still serving active terms include Rani Batra, Yildiz Duransoy, Jonathan Levine, Tom Ramsey, Douglas Strout, and Justin Tucker (Alternate). Recreation Commission 2 vacancies, 0 incumbents; 3-year term The commission advises the City Council on issues regarding the City’s recreation programs, sports field development, allocations of field space and other issues. It meets monthly on the third Wednesday at 7:30 p.m. Commissioners still serving active terms include Dick Carter, Jeffrey Dorman, Vincent Fisher, Lisa Gardner, Rebecca Posamentier, Susan Terrill, and Aamir Virani. Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee 3 vacancies, 3 incumbents; 3-year term The committee reviews and provides comment on five-year projections contained in the City’s annual budget proposal, the proposed funding and expenditures from several long-term funds, and the proposed midyear budget adjustments. It provides a financial review of new programs in excess of $250,000 per year. Commissioners still serving active terms include Andrew Flynn, Cathie Geddeis, Deborah Leland, Robert McBain, Paul Raskin, Frank Ryan, Vanessa Washington and Chris Kwei (Alternate). Public Safety Committee 3 vacancies, 1 incumbents; 3-year term This committee investigates ways to increase public participation in crime reduction; It increases public participation in disaster preparedness, and provides a forum for residents to share comments, issues or concerns regarding public safety issues. The committee meets quarterly. Current committee members are Shanti Brien, Lori Elefant, Jeffrey Horner, Chris Houlder, Lynne Wright (Chair). Corey Smegal is School District Appointee. Alameda County Mosquito Abatement District 1 vacancy; 2-year term This position serves as the City’s trustee on the Board of the Alameda County Mosquito Abatement District. Civil Service Commission 2 vacancies, 2 incumbent; 3-year term The commission deals with personnel issues including classification and serves as the hearing board in disputes between the City and employees. This commission meets as required. Incumbent Commissioners serving active terms are Scott Lawson, Amy Kelly, Laura Isaacs, David Hobstetter, and Claudia Harrison. ment-2022 Applications may be sent by e-mail to the City Clerk’s office at JTulloch@piedmont.ca.gov, or delivered in person to Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue. For more information or to request an application be mailed to you, call the City Clerk’s office at (510) 420-3040. Park Commission 3 vacancies, 0 incumbents; 3-year term The Park Commission makes recommendations to the City Council about improvements to the public parks and manages the street tree improvement program of the city. It meets monthly on the first Wednesday at 5:30 p.m. Commissioners still serving active terms include Amber Brumfiel, Patty Dunlap, Betsy Goodman, Jim Horner, Brian Mahany, Eileen Ruby, and Robin Wu.

articles.text: Staff Photos Natalia Martinez led Piedmont with 31 points against No. 8 Lincoln. Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team, who went farther in post-season playoffs than any other school team, saw its season come to an end on Thursday, March 3, after losing by 7 points, 63-56, to Lincoln at Binks Rawlings Gym in Piedmont. Although the Highlanders walked in with the No. 1 ranking, Lincoln, seeded No. 8, is a school with an enrollment of over 3,000 students, and was the runner-up as a Div. 1 (large enrollment) team in the San Joaquin Section finals. The game included a strange turn of events. With 2:11 left in the first quarter, a power outage in Piedmont forced the suspension of play for one hour. At the time PHS trailed 13-5. “It was tough, but we didn’t quit despite the circumstances. We were down and were turning the ball over; there was a power outage; everything could’ve gone wrong,” said coach Bryan Gardere. But the team was missing a key player, starting guard Maddie Hill out with an ankle injury. “We fought to the end. After the blackout, I think some people thought we’d come out flat, but we came out swinging. I think we all knew that we had to wake up that this could be the end of our season,” said sophomore guard Natalia Martinez, who led the team with 31 points. If you’re wondering how Piedmont got placed in the Division 2 bracket with the top seeding, the California Interscholastic Federation’s decision process is a simple 1-169 ranking system which put 31 teams in order for divisions 1-5 without factoring strength of schedule or section titles. It was a similar promotion made to the boys’ team after winning the 2020 D4 NCS championship and subsequently promoted to Div. 2. PHS fought valiantly and forged to a one-point lead by the start of the fourth quarter, 48-47. Zamora the team’s leading scorer and rebounder fouled out with 1:45 left in the game. “The effort they showed while undermanned was amazing. I told them after the game that it was hard to feel upset because of how well we competed,” said Gardere. Lincoln was led by the combination of Air Force-bound center Faith Shelton with 13 points and guard Junae Mahan, who led with 29. Shelton, a sizeable player, whipped around no-look passes from all kinds of angles and even drew praise from the Piedmont players. “She’s an excellent player, she’s big time. Our game plan was to just stay with the 1-2-2 zone and keep her out of the paint. We knew about her from film and playing AAU-ball together. We were calling her Magic Johnson on the floor, I like to predict where passes are going and those no-looks threw me off. I think being tight on our defense is something we’ll be working on,” said Martinez. PHS concluded its season with a 24-7 record. articles.text: Piedmont High’s baseball team is on a roll to open the season, defeating St. Patrick 3-2 in come-from-behind fashion at Humphries Diamond, and shutting out Lick-Wilmerding 10-0 shutout. With an 8-1 win against St. Helena on February 26, brings Piedmont’s record to 3-0. Coach Eric Olson is got a good look at his pitching rotation in the opening week, using six different pitchers in three games. Senior pitcher Scott McKenzie was credited with the win against St. Patrick, while Alex Tafapolsky started and sophomore Dmitri Papahadjopoulos entered in relief in the top of the seventh. Tobin Cantrill got his second win of the season in the 10-0 rout of Lick, with Cole Garcia pitching two innings of relief. “We couldn’t be more thrilled with how the guys are throwing,” said coach Olson. “This is what we’re going to look like for a while. We have confidence in everyone.” Over the first three games, Piedmont has compiled 21 runs scored and just three allowed. “We have great hitters; they’ve been hitting really well in practice. We lost six seniors from last year’s team, and I think we’ve re-loaded pretty well. We’re going to let the defense work,” said second baseman Michael Aikawa. Against St. Patrick, PHS trailed 2-1 entering the bottom of the sixth. The bats came alive when Ryan McConathy nearly belted a home run on a high fly ball to right-centerfield. The ball hit the top of the wall, resulting in a double for McConathy. He scored on a hit Will Sprague, who then scored the game-winner on a defensive error with two outs. 3-2 comeback vs. St. Patrick St. Patrick got the game started with two runs in the top of the first inning, but it was the final time they’d get on the scoreboard. Piedmont scored their first run in the bottom of the third when Aikawa led off with a double, going to the opposite field on a fly ball to right that dropped in front of the outfielder Aikawa advanced to third base with two outs. Then Papahadjopoulos blooped a single to center field to bring in Aikawa. With Piedmont trailing 2-1 in the sixth inning, McConathy smacked a double, and Sprague brought in McConathy on a seeing-eye single through the infield to leftfield with two outs. Sprague then stole second, then third base, and a throwing error by the catcher enabled Sprague to score. In the top of the seventh, St. Patrick loaded the bases with two outs when Papahadjopoulos entered. With a 1-1 count, the sophomore thrower forced a popup to Aikawa at second. Final stats include: Tafapolsky finished with three innings pitcher and three strikeouts. McKenzie threw 3.2 innings, Staff Photos In relief, Piedmont pitcher Scott McKenzie picked up the win against St. Patrick, with 3.2 innings of work with six strikeouts and no runs allowed. Ryan McConathy had a double off of the right-centerfield wall in the bottom of the sixth against St. Patrick to drive in the game-tying run.

articles.text: Piedmont High principal Adam Littlefield held an online meeting team on Wednesday, March 2 to address the status of the varsity football team. it was the first public declaration to parents that the school is committed to continuing its 101-year tradition of football as a fall sport. “I’ll point it out right now that it is my interest in having a varsity and junior varsity team next year… I didn’t play football in high school, but Friday Night Lights just thrills me, it’s a great opportunity and I appreciate that,” said Littlefield during the meeting. The meeting cleared up some confusion and included a timeline of events on decision making, while offering apologies to parents for allowing rumors to swirl about the possibility of the school not fielding a team in August. Littlefield explained that the school’s Athletic Director Bradley Smet judged that after 11 seniors from team graduated, coupled with injuries, varsity football would not be feasible in 2022. “Player-safety is always our highest priority… This last year we had less than 20 players, where some were playing hurt and some weren’t playing at all,” said Littlefield. On November 12, Littlefield indicated that the school informed other teams in the league that PHS may not field a varsity football team. That resulted in the league forming schedules without Piedmont. A Shoreline Division schedule on December 9 without Piedmont’s inclusion was approved by PHS. “Back in November, Bradley initiated a conversation with the other athletic departments that it was likely that we wouldn’t have a varsity team because we didn’t have enough players. They went ahead with making schedules at that particular time with the caveat that we would be able to field a JV and if we were able to field a varsity team, that was something we could work through as well,” said Littlefield. The principal issued an apology for not sharing that information during the winter months. Moving forward, Littlefield explained that resolving the varsity football situation is now a priority for him ahead of his retirement at the end of the school year. PHS will need the approval of a majority of league teams to be added to the traditional WACC Shoreline schedule. “I can’t undo what has already happened, but I can do my best to move us forward… Two of the teams in the Shoreline Division said they would work with us, while Bradley also reached out to the four teams in the Shoreline which are also aligned in the Mission Valley league, and only one school said that it could not change its schedule,” said Littlefield. Littlefield said that he reached out to WACC Commissioner Dave Kiesel to make sure Piedmont can stay in the league. “I reached out to our WACC Commissioner and I told him there were a few teams who were willing to work with us. He responded that he didn’t want to ‘shut off anything, but it would be difficult based on schedules teams already had,” said Littlefield. Kiesel suggested that Piedmont could fill its schedule with non-league teams, and seemed committed to helping PHS. “There’s also an option that we could schedule non-WACC teams as part of our season. It wouldn’t necessarily be against league members, but Kiesel said he would ‘bend over backwards’ to make that work,” said Littlefield. The next step now is for Piedmont High to hire a head football coach to replace Jerome Johnson. Staff Photo Piedmont High principal Adam Littlefield confirmed publicly the school’s priority to continue to field a varsity football team.
articles.title: PHS confirms its commitment to varsity football in 2022

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team opened the 2022 season with a 6-3 win over North Coast section rival Campolindo and a 7-0 loss to Los Altos, a Central Coast Section team. The Highlanders were scheduled to compete in the top division of the California Tennis Classic in Fresno on March 4-5, but the event was canceled due to rain in the city’s forecast. “The tournament was canceled after they expected rain, so we played Los Altos on Saturday instead. Despite the lopsided score, it was a good match and our boys put up a fight. There was a lot of good tennis against a very strong team and this match will help sharpen us up for the remainder of the season,” said coach Jim Landes. In the match with Campo, Piedmont won four of the nine matches in three seats each, clearly a match that could have been won by either team. Sophomore Ben Breber made his first appearance after returning from the basketball team, winning in straight sets, 6-2, 7-6 (6-4) at No. 2. “We defeated Campolindo in a tightly contested match,” said Landes. “Five matches went to the 3rd set and we won four of them. Ben has not let his long basketball season affect his tennis in the slightest. He played remarkably well, blasting forehands and coming forward to finish points and winning in straight sets.” Campolindo win In singles foreign exchange student Lenni Burchardt lost in three sets at No. 1, 6-4, 1-6, 10-3. At No. 2, Breber won 6-2, 7-6 (6-4). Monte Imburg appeared at No. 3, losing 6-2, 6-4. Ethan Pham played at No. 4 and won 6-0, 3-6, 6-4. At No. 5 Charlie Staff Photo Sophomore Ben Breber won in straight sets as the team’s No. 2 singles player. Olcott breezed to a 6-1, 7-5 victory, and at No. 5 singles, Kai Baudendistel lost in three sets, 3-6, 6-3, 6-4. Piedmont swept all three doubles matches. Playing No. 1, Oliver Maxwell and Nick King won 4-6, 6-1, 6-4; Arun Brahma and Charlie Sullivan at No., 2 won 6-1, 4-6, 6-3; and Carson Hicks and Graham McWeeny won 6-3, 6-4 at No. 3. Los Altos loss Los Altos swept the field in its match with Piedmont, 7-0. In singles, Burchardt lost 6-2, 6-3 at No. 1; Breber lost 6-1, 7-5 at No. 2; Imburg lost 6-3, 6-0; and at No. 4 Pham lost 6-3, 6-4. In doubles, Olcott and Baudendistel lost 6-1, 7-5 at No. 1; Maxwell and King lost 6-2, 6-1 at No. 2; and Brahma and Sullivan lost 6-4, 6-0 at No. 3. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-1) heads to Berkeley today, Wednesday, March 9 for a 3:30 p.m. match. The Highlanders host Alameda on Thursday, March 10 at 3:30 p.m.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team returns to Witter Field after losing its top pair of attackers to graduation, all-time assist leader Sadie Tschider and leading goal scorer Caroline Devine. In their wake, coach Carlton Chan still expects a team that will compete despite some big holes to fill. “On average, we’re a better team than a lot of years, but we’re without those obvious superstars from previous years. The girls haven’t played together for a long time,” said Chan. Piedmont is still the reigning Division 2 North Coast Section champion from 2019. There are a few holdovers from that team The girls’ lacrosse team. who will be starters: Elizabeth Ethington, Charlotte Theut, and Eliza Keville. The leading scorer returning from last season is senior Katherine Kinne, who had 28 goals and seven assists. Chan said that they will need Kinne to fill the scorer’s role, while they also need people to step up around her. “Katherine is mainly an attacker, but we play her in the midfield. Charlotte is a midfielder, but we’ll play her at defense as Photos by Todd Marshburn well. Elizabeth Ethington is an attacker, Eliza Keville will also play defense – those are our four captains,” explained Chan. Chan had high praise for goalies Sophia Ethington, a senior, and junior Lindsey Kottle. “Our goalie is great, Sophia is keeping up in games and helping us establish ourselves. Lindsey Kottle is a returner from last year as well and they split duty, she’s also a really good goalie. We’re really comfortable with them splitting duties. Goalie-play may be where our strength is,” said Chan. “We have a lot of girls who are very unselfish with the ball and we need them to be a bit more selfish. We need someone to take control and become the star of the offense. A lot of this year’s players were secondary players in previous years. Now it’s their time to take over,” said Chan. The run for Western Alameda County Conference title is likely to be between Bishop O’Dowd, Piedmont and Berkeley. Chan is undefeated against O’Dowd at 6-0. The Dragons hired former Highlanders’ assistant coach Lizzy Koehler to the lead job this year. “This will be one of our closest battles, O’Dowd has a good team and they’ve hired our former assistant coach as their head coach. She’s a good friend; it will be a good rivalry,” said Chan. Katherine Kinne scored 28 goals last season. Charlotte Theut is another senior captain. She scored two gamewinning goals last season, including one against O’Dowd.
articles.title: Girls lacrosse team retooling as it eyes WACC title

articles.text: Senior pole vaulter Parker Terrill is starting the spring track and field season with a clear mission in mind – to be the best. The 17-year-old just set a school record in pole vault with a leap of 14-feet, 2-inches at the Clayton Valley Ugly Eagles Relays in Concord on Saturday, March 5. It broke Marshall Wentworth’s 2011 record by two inches. Piedmont’s top five all-time male pole vault records • Parker Terrill 14 feet, 2 inches (2022) • Marshall Wentworth 14 feet (2011) • Irving Moore 13 feet (1940) • Alex Harrison 12 feet, 7 inches (2016) • John Hind 12 feet, 6 inches (1957) Terrill’s 14-feet, 2 inches would have placed him 2nd in the last NCS Bayshore Championship in 2019. The senior now has his sights set on clearing the bar at five meters, 16 feet, 4 inches. “I knew it was a number that was bound to happen. To get the record felt like a good goal to achieve and now I can continue and break it again,” said Terrill. Terrill started the season at the Skyline Invitational on February 26 with a vault of 13 feet, 1 inch. PHS coach Jeanine Holmlund expects big things to happen this year. “It was so exciting to watch, but he is really just getting started. There’s going to be another one (record),” said Holmlund excitedly. Prior to Terrill’s initial vault on February 26, his only official result was at 8-feet, 6-inches at the Del Campo Multi-Event Competition on May 29 last year. Since then, Terrill diligently worked on his craft and bumped up his numbers in training. “It’s been a four-day week of reps since May, all through the summer, and until now. The process has been a lot of work and dedication,” said Terrill. Terrill is focused on being an all-around track and field athlete and developing himself in the decathlon, which is 10 events that typically includes the 100-meter dash, Long jump, Shot put, High jump, 400 meters, 110 meter hurdles, Discus throw, Javelin throw, 1500 metera, and Terrill’s specialty, the pole vault. “My main goal is to just get better at pole vault. It’s my main event, but I really want improve at the decathlon; there are three throws, two sprints, there’s long jump, hurdles, and the high jump... I really want to prioritize developing as an all-around athlete,” said Terrill. In Clayton, Terrill also helped the 4x400 relay team place 2nd of six with a time of 3:38.66. His team included Jack ZirkelPhotos by Steve Zirkelbach Parker Terrill set a school record recently by pole vaulting 14-feet, 2-inches at the Clayton Valley Ugly Eagles Relays on March 5.
articles.title: Parker Terrill sets new school pole vault record

All four of Piedmont varsity teams reached the NCS postseason playoffs, and the boys soccer team won the school’s first North Coast Section Championship. articles.text: The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team began its season on Sunday, February 27 with a trip to Exchequer Mountain Bike park in La Grange, CA. Piedmont had 13 high school and four middle school racers competing, and ended up with Schuyler Sawicki placing 4th place and earning a spot on the podium and Matteo Scanu notching a 6th place finish. Junior Andres Roberts earned a 9th place finish in the JV boys’ D1 category. Next up is a race at Fort Ord, near Monterey. This is a familiar course for returning riders. New riders got to experience it earlier this year with a pre-season race on February 6th.

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse will produce Water by the Spoonful from March 16 to April 23. Winner of the 2012 Pulitzer Prize for Drama, the play written by Quiara Alegría Hudes is a heartfelt meditation on lives on the brink of redemption. Set in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, Eliot has returned from Iraq and is working at a Subway sandwich shop while simultaneously trying to jumpstart his acting career. “Quiara Alegría Hudes’s masterful Pulitzer Prize winner speaks even more profoundly to our world today,” said Bill English, San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director. “Separated from friends and loved ones by the pandemic, we, like the characters in Water by the Spoonful, celebrate our human resourcefulness, which will overcome any distance to build connection and hope.” The play is directed by Denise Blasor, with performances on the main stage through April 23. Proof of up-to-date vaccination is required to attend. To obtain tickets, visit https:// w w w.sf playhouse.org /sf ph / upcoming-plays/ Playbill cover for San Francisco Playhouse production of Water by the Spoonful. Free delivery to Piedmont
articles.title: SF Playhouse’s Water by the Spoonful opens March 16

articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir will perform a concert next Saturday at First Congregational Church of Berkeley. The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) will perform a concert at First Congregational Church of Berkeley on Saturday, March 19, featuring new works by Bay Area composers Jens Ibsen and PEBCC Artistic Director Eric Tuan. The concert will celebrate the voices of Black, Indigenous, and people of color (BIPOC) in the arts. Choreography for the event is provided by Kali Futnani, whose youth bharatananyam dancers will be featured guest artists. Ibsen joins the choir for the world premiere of “A Portrait in Grey’s,” commissioned by PEBCC. Four members of choral group’s advanced singers group will also debut as conducting scholars instructed by Joel Chapman, leading their peers in “Four Estonian Lullabies” by Veljo Tormis. The concert will be held on Saturday, March 19 at 7:30 p.m. All seating will be assigned and tickets may be picked up at Will Call. Advance sales end at noon on March 18. There will be no ticket sales at the door. To obtain tickets, visit https:// w w w.p ie d m o n t c h oi r s .o r g / event-calendar.
articles.title: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir celebrates BIPOC voices in March 19 concert

articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s fourpart 2022 Schwabacher Recital Series begins on March 15 at the Atrium Theatre in the Veterans’ Building next to the Opera House. The recitals offer audiences an opportunity to hear gifted singers in an intimate setting. Since 1983 the recital series has featured renowned artists and has been instrumental in helping launch their international careers. The first of the series features Nikola Printz (mezzo-soprano), Erica Xiaoyan Guo (pianist), and Tatiana Senderowicz (guitar). Winner of the 2012 Pulitzer Prize for Drama, the play written by Quiara Alegría Hudes is a heartfelt meditation on lives on the brink of redemption. articles.text: Featured artists at a show at Berkeley Art Museum are Tammy Rae Carland, David Huffman, Lava Thomas, and John Zurier. The UC Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) will highlight the talents of four contemporary Bay Area artists in a collective exhibition beginning March 19. The exhibition is entitled “The Artist’s Eye,” and features guest curation by Tammy Rae Carland, David Huffman, Lava Thomas, and John Zurier. The four artists were chosen by BAMPFA to “guest-curate” an exhibition that draws from the museum’s collection of 18,000 works. Each artist has been featured at BAMPFA in the past. “We’re delighted to work with Tammy Rae Carland, David Huffman, Lava Thomas, and John Zurier, who brought their instinctive curiosity to exploring, curating, and critiquing the collection,” said Curatorial Assistant Claire Frost, who worked with the artists to organize the exhibition, along with Associate Curator Stephanie Cannizzo and Collections Engagement Associate and Academic Liaison Lynne Kimura. “The project required close collaboration on many levels and has resulted in an exhibition that illuminates their work and lived experiences as it intersects with the museum.” The name of the exhibition is a nod to an iconic program at London’s National Gallery during the 1980s, which invited one artist at a time to curate an exhibition from that museum’s collection. A few artists featured in this exhibition include Zarouhie Abdalian, Diane Arbus, Francis Bacon, Yamamoto Baitsu, John Baldessari, Sadie Barnette, Jean-Michel Basquiat, Romare Bearden, McArthur Binion, Yosa Busan, John Cage, Tammy Rae Carland, Theresa Hak Kyung Cha, Constance Chang, Sarah Charlesworth, Barbara Chase-Riboud, Robert Colescott, Willem de Kooning, Erica Deeman, and Jay DeFeo. To learn more and to obtain tickets, visit www.bampfa.org.
articles.title: Berkeley Art Museum artist collective exhibit opens March 19

articles.text: Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside is preparing for the beauty of its 16 acres of formal gardening grounds in the Springtime. It is home to a vast collection of native and exotic flowers. This year, a record 80,000 bulbs will bloom. Orchids, magnolias, and citrus blossoms are beginning to unfold, and visitors will also catch a glimpse of vibrant Tulips, Irises, Wisteria, Peonies, and wildflowers. The estate and grounds are open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Reservations are required, and unvaccinated visitors will be required to wear masks indoors. To plan your visit, click https:// filoli.org/. Filoli is located at 86 Canada Road in Woodside; phone number is (650) 364-8300. Photo courtesy of Garden Collage Magazine Filoli Gardens will be in full-bloom soon.
articles.title: Spring at Filoli is a sight to behold

articles.text: Oakland Ballet, in collaboration with Oakland Asian Cultural Center, will present its Dancing Moons Festival from March 24 through 26. Tickets are on sale now. The event celebrates Asian and Pacific Islander (AAPI) arts, and features new ballets choreographed by Phil Chan, Michael Lowe, Shannon and Megan Kurashige, and Caili Quan. This year’s event will feature Ballet de Porcelaines (The Teapot Prince), recently commissioned by the Metropolitan Museum of New York. Performances are on Thursday and Friday, March 24-25, at 7:30 p.m., and on Saturday, March 26 at 2:30 p.m. The Festival will be held at the Oakland Asian Cultural Center at 388 Ninth Street, Suite 290, in Oakland. An ID and COVID-19-related documents are required for admission (proof of vaccination or a recent negative COVID test result within 72 hours of arrival). Tickets may be purchased by visiting https://www.eventbrite. com/e/dancing-moons-festival-tickets-244713503677.
