articles.text: The Alvin Ailey Dance Company will perform at Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall beginning March 29. Cal Performances at the University of California, Berkeley is presenting the Alvin Ailey American Dance Theatre in six performances at Zellerbach Hall beginning March 29, It is the first time they have performed locally in two years. The dance company, now in its seventh decade, has regularly performed at Zellerbach Hall, and has appeared on the UC Berkeley’s campus more than any other place in the world outside of their home base in New York City. This season celebrates Artistic Director Robert Battle and his decade of tenure with the company. Highlights of the performances at Zellerbach Hall include a Robert Battle 10th Anniversary program; the Bay Area premiere of Battle’s For Four; and the West Coast staged premiere of Holding Space by Ailey Resident Choreographer Jamar Roberts, a Cal Performances’ co-commissioned work given its streaming world premiere as part of last year’s Cal Performances at Home online series. Other highlights of the engagement include the return of hip-hop innovator Rennie Harris’ Lazarus; and an All Ailey program celebrating 50 years of Cry, Ailey’s legendary solo dance; and featuring a new 2021 production of the Duke Ellington-inspired Pas de Duke. Tickets are available through the Ticket Office at Zellerbach Hall, at (510) 642-9988, by e-mail at calperformances.org, and at the door. For more information visit calperformances.org/discounts.

articles.text: Tenor Alex Boyer Piedmont Center for the Arts will host Festival Opera’s artist recital series on Sunday, March 20, at 5 p.m. with tenor Alex Boyer and pianist Kevin Korth. Led by Festival Opera General Director Zachary Gordin. the concert will showcase the talents of Boyer and Korth in a concert of music by Pfitzner, Rachmanioff, Schubert, Sibelius, and Tosti. Known for his unique grit and vocal power when inhabiting the great lyric tenor roles, Alex Boyer is in recital alongside pianist Kevin Korth. The program is a decadent and delectable array of vocal showpieces by Hans Pfitzner, Rachmaninoff, Schubert, Sibelius, and Tosti. Front-row intimacy with the power of the tenor voice, as well as with Boyer’s visual storytelling and emotional range will thrill audiences at any stage of their love affair with opera and classical singing. A New York native, Alex Boyer is an alumnus of the Merola and Santa Fe Opera programs. From 2008 to 2013, he was a resident artist with Opera San José where he performed over 13 roles. Most recently, he has been seen as Canio in Pagliacci with Festival Opera, Cavaradossi in Tosca with Hawaii Opera Theatre and as Captain Ahab in Jake Heggie’s Moby Dick with Chicago Opera Theater. Pianist Kevin Korth recently praised by Gramophone for playing that is “superb”, and “full of color and character,” has colPianist Kevin Korth laborated with such legendary artists as Frederica von Stade, Isabel Leonard, Jake Heggie, Nadine Sierra, Anthony Roth Costanzo, Sasha Cooke, Lise Lindstrom, and Deborah Voigt. articles.text: A young Michael Tilson Thomas. The world knows him as MTT. His friends in elementary school called him Mickey. I knew him when we were classmates at USC. He was Mike back in the 1960s. Even at an early age he was regarded as a major talent. The immortal virtuosos Jascha Heifetz and Gregory Piatigorsky engaged Michael as the accompanist in their master classes at USC. A rather amusing thing happened at a Heifetz-Piatigorsky concert on September 29,1963. At the conclusion of the concert, Heifetz and Piatigorsky brought a skinny young kid onto the stage to take a bow. The audience did not know who that skinny kid was nor why he was taking a bow. I found out later that Michael had rehearsed the orchestra prior to the concert. I also found out that Heifetz was very enthusiastic about Michael’s talent. articles.text: After the swing and bebop eras in the thirties and forties, jazz mellowed and became harmonically simpler with cool jazz, west coast jazz, then modal jazz. With arrangers like Gil Evans (Miles Davis’ arranger) and George Russell (author of The Lydian Chromatic Concept), arrangements became clearer and more uniform, making the melody easier to hear. Chord durations were much longer, giving the improviser more freedom to periodically deviate from the current chord. A decade later, jazz fusion guitarists John Scofield, Pat Martino, Scott Henderson, Allan Holdsworth and other jazz fusion guitarists expanded what is aurally acceptable to listeners with innovative harmonic, melodic and rhythmic design. They have all used chromatic drift, where bits of pentatonic scales, diatonic scales, arpeggios and melodic themes can reoccur a half step up or down and return. Chromatic drift establishes brief secondary keys. Voice leading is used to return to the original key with chromatic tones and common tones. Not everyone likes chromatic drift. They tend to love it or hate it. Look at it as an intense spice and use it sparingly and set it up to make sense. Upon first hearing chromatic drift, it may sound out of key or atonal. Once the listener realizes that the accompaniment has not deviated from the current chord, brief instances of chromatic drift can become acceptable and the harmonic deviation seems intentional. John Scofield has played in a diversity of styles, including traditional jazz, funk, rock and blues. He’s performed with Miles Davis, Herbie Hancock, Pat Metheny, Phil Lesh (Grateful Dead) and John Mayer. From all these associations, he picked up ways to play “outside” the key and return while still making sense. Pat Martino and Pat Metheny are among the first guitarists (1970’s) to arpeggiate an interval of a third and move it up or down chromatically. That’s now commonplace for modern jazz guitarists. You can read about various short melodic themes called melodic cells at this web address: http://guitarimprov.com/zc-Melodic_Cells.pdf On the score for the chromatic drift example (link below), there are annotations below the standard notation staff to show superimposed chords and scales that are played. While the main chord is “C7”, the melody may play brief melodic cells to represent Cm7 (darkened C7), Bm7, Bbm7 then Cm7 again. Before becoming to questionable harmonically, the tonality returns to the original key. Use a “two second rule”: if your deviation from the current chord is shorter than two seconds, the listener won’t hear the harmonic disagreement long enough to identify it as too dissonant. Listen to and read my improvised example of for this Chromatic Drift column and my previous columns at: http://www. guitarimprov.com/PostColumns. pdf Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. Call (510)923- 9522, text (510)435-3997 or email jim@guitarencyclopdeia.com for videoconference or in-person lessons. His course is available for free online at www.guitarimprov. com

I contributed the name PDQ Bach. Michael, who is sitting next to me, looked at me and said Michael Tilson Thomas - “Did you ever hear of Professor Peter Schickele?” It didn’t take before he was MTT a mastermind for me to realize I had made a tremendous blunder. I pretended that I knew who he was talking about but, in reality, I had absolutely no idea who Peter Schickele was. Michael was a brilliant student. He devised a system to remember all kinds of things. We were studying medieval music. In order to remember the musical form of a Virelai, Michael used the sentence “Achilles became bald at Athens.” That was his easy way to remember the form, which is AbbaA. One time a group of music students were just sitting around chatting. In the group were noted violinists Michael Foxman, Pierre Amoyal, and a very attractive cellist. The young lady mentioned that she found MTT attractive but mentioned that he never asked her out on a date. Pierre looked at me and said “Joe, explain it to her.” Her eyes opened wide and I don’t think she understood a thing I said. articles.text: A Most Violent Year, released in 2014, is an elegant and beautifully constructed film, one in which the title is unfortunate because the violence, while implied and certainly embedded in the narrative, is never gratuitous. The year is 1981; New York City is in the throes of a hardedged crime wave that is felt in all corners of the city and creates a context and backdrop, contributing to the atmospherics of a taut and cerebral story. At the film’s center are Abel Morales (Oscar Isaac), a seemingly decent and impeccably dressed Colombian immigrant and his elegant but steely wife Anna (Jessica Chastain). Together they own a home heating oil business – a stable of trucks and drivers – based in one of the outer New York boroughs along the East River. They are in the process of acquiring a valuable piece of real estate adjoining their business, have purchased an option from a cohort of Orthodox Jews who have no use for the land or the oil tanks. Abel and Anna have 30 days to close the escrow and need an additional $1.5 million to fulfill the terms of the agreement. If they fail to close, they lose their deposit and the much-coveted property. Writer/director J.C. Chandor nicely inserts a game clock of sorts that gives the film an added tension. From the minute Abel hands the Rabbi a suitcase of cash, events begin conspiring to prevent Abel from meeting the deadline. Most disconcerting (at least at the outset) is that his heating oil trucks, filled with product and on the way to making deliveries, are being hijacked. The question is by whom? His competitors? Abel soon learns from his lawyer, Andrew Walsh (Albert Brooks), that the local D.A., intent on making his bones, is investigating the company and is threatening to indict Abel and Anna for fraud and tax evasion (charges that seem constructed out of whole cloth). Abel’s bank loan of $1.5 million is in jeopardy due to their legal troubles as well as the hijackings. Abel and Anna are caught in a nexus of circumstances that threaten them and their two young girls. It’s a perfect storm of existential events. Compounding their financial situation, they’ve also just bought a new, decidedly modern home in Westchester. The film is ultimately a character study of Abel and Anna, examining intently what they are and are not prepared to do to salvage their situation and what lines they will and will not cross. Abel reminds Anna that he will not become a “gangster” in order to survive in what is a bare knuckles business, one that is, historically, layered with Mob control. A Most Violent Year demonstrates that a film can be a hammer but not every scene need be a nail. It is nuanced and subtle, the tone quietly chilly, the photography often soft instead of hard-edged with wide-angle shots of the Manhattan skyline and snow-covered stretches of land. Violent, when closely watched, is a far more interesting and complex tale when compared to, say, Martin Scorsese’s extreme The Wolf of Wall Street or Goodfellas. One film that it does borrow from in complexity and inherent ambivalence is The Godfather. To quote a line by Michael Corleone “Just when I think I’m out, they pull me back in.” And so it is with Abel Morales. A Most Violent Year. Directed by J.C. Chandor. Starring Oscar Isacc, Jessica Chastain, Albert Brooks. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated R. Reviewed in the Post in 2014. Now streaming on Prime.

articles.text: Frankie Muniz stars in My Dog Skip. The family-friendly film My Dog Skip, released in 2000, is a captivating story that focuses on the touching relationship between a 9-year-old boy, Willie Morris (Frankie Muniz), and his dog, a spunky Jack Russell Terrier that Willie names Skip. The film is set in Yazoo, Mississippi. The year is 1942. Willie, small for his age, is a lonely kid, often bullied by his larger classmates, especially a tough trio who take every opportunity to give him a hard time. He also has a standoffish relationship with his dad, Jack (Kevin Bacon), a gruff man, even bitter, who lost a leg in the Spanish Civil war. His mom, Ellen (Diane Lane), does her best to make Willie happy and often suggests to Jack that a dog would be the perfect companion for their isolated son. Willie of course agrees, pleads for a dog, but Jack firmly resists. Willie is about to have a birthday, and sends out an invitation to his classmates, but on the day of the scheduled party only his grandparents show up. His grandmother gives him a bowtie. But unbeknownst to Jack, his mother brings to the party a small box and inside is a sweet little terrier pup, which delights Willie, and angers Jack. But Ellen prevails. And Willie and the pooch, soon named Skip, form an immediate bond and are soon inseparable. To Willie’s delight, kids who ignored him now pay attention to Skip, especially a classmate named Rivers Applewhite (Caitlin Wachs), a cute classmate that Willie thinks is special. There are, of course, subplots. One involves thuggish moonshiners who use an abandoned burial vault in the local cemetery to hide their illegal hooch. And there’s the bullying trio who dare Willie to stay all night among the tombstones while telling him that he should be on the lookout for a witch who wanders about. There is even an awful moment when Willie, frustrated with his awkward and error-filled performance on the baseball field, gives Skip a hard swat on his nose with his baseball glove. As a result, the dog runs away. Filled with remorse, Willie begins a desperate search for Skip that ultimately involves the moonshiners. My Dog Skip, based on the memoir written by Willie Morris, a noted author and editor, unfailingly finds the sweet spot in this boy/dog narrative, demonstrating that our childhood memories, however dim, remain with us. My Dog Skip is a wonderful example. My Dog Skip. Directed by Jay Russell. Starring Frankie Muniz, Diane Lane, Kevin Bacon. 1 hr., 35 min. Rated PG. Now streaming on Netflix.
articles.title: My Dog Skip a lovely tale of a boy and his best friend

articles.text: If you see the film title of Cinderella (released in 2015) and shrug, feeling the story is all too familiar, wondering what could possibly be new in this narrative, know that you have not seen the story presented in this surprising and beautiful way. Once again it is a Disney production. This is a contemporary version of what is an iconic fairytale, fresh and engaging (with a tweak here and by the writers), but not surprising given that it’s directed by the talented English actor Kenneth Branagh. The story is simple and direct. Unlike those that have come before (the most memorable being the animated version by Disney some 65 years ago), it relies very little on special effects or computer graphics. Of course, there is the scene when Ella’s Fairy Godmother (Helena Bonham Carter) appears and turns a simple pumpkin into a startlingly beautiful, ornate coach, and the house mice slowly morph into six white steeds and two lizards become the coachmen. To its credit this film is character driven, and the wonder of Cinderella can be found in watching each individual revealed – from the very kind and enchanting Ella (Lilly James), to the cruel and sadistic Lady Tremaine (Cate Blanchett). The set up for the movie takes almost all of act one to construct. Ella is living an idyllic life with her mother (Hayley Atwell) and father (Ben Chaplin) in a gorgeous, English countryside mansion. She is embraced by her loving family and secure in her place as a much cared for daughter. Unexpectedly, sadly, Ella’s mother falls suddenly ill and dies, leaving Ella with just her father. Time passes, years slip by, and he decides to remarry, choosing a benign widow (or so he believes), Lady Tremaine, who has two daughters Ella’s age, Drisella and Anastasia (Sophia McShera and Holliday Granger). With their arrival, Ella’s life changes as act two unfolds. At first she is tolerated by her stepmother, but mocked by the sisters. But when her father dies on a business trip, Ella, now orphaned, finds her position in the household one in which she is ostracized and turned into a servant, relegated to the attic, always at the beck and call of the three women. It is they who name her Cinderella, for she sleeps by the fireplace in the den because the attic is too cold in winter. And so the story blossoms in a most compelling and captivating manner. The king (Derek Jacobi) announces that he will give a magnificent royal ball. His young son (Richard Madden), the heir and prince, insists that all of the single maidens of the kingdom must be invited. As it turns out, the prince is about to choose a bride at the ball, whether she is a commoner or titled. Naturally, Tremaine forbids Cinderella from going. That is until there is a magical moment when the fable soars. It is both glorious to watch and touching in its emotions, none of which are disguised behind computer trickery. The visuals – and they are stunning – create a magnetism that transcends and surprises, even though the outcome is solidly based on the Disney concept of living “happily ever after.” It is in getting to that moment that separates this Cinderella from all its precursors (and there have been many, to include a TV special starring Julie Andrews). As an aside, just before Ella’s mother dies, she takes her daughter’s hand and asks her to always have courage and above all else, be kind, a moral principle that Ella tries to live by, and one that is woven with sensitivity into the story. Ella is indeed courageous, and reflexively kind no matter the abuse heaped upon her by the mean-spirited Tremaine. She is also by nature innocent; but also tenacious and someone who, in every frame, is believable as she demonstrates how deeply her decency frames her life. It’s a wonderfully resonant message, brought to you once again by Disney, who has always chosen to see the world not as it is but as it should be. Cinderella. Directed by Kenneth Branagh. Starring Cate Blanchet, Lily James, Richard Madden. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG. Now streaming on Disney..
articles.title: Kenneth Branagh’s Cinderella brings story to life

The visuals – and they are stunning – create a magnetism that transcends and surprises, even though the outcome is solidly based on the Disney concept of living “happily ever after.” It is in getting to that moment that separates this Cinderella from all its precursors (and there have been many, to include a TV special starring Julie Andrews). As an aside, just before Ella’s mother dies, she takes her daughter’s hand and asks her to always have courage and above all else, be kind, a moral principle that Ella tries to live by, and one that is woven with sensitivity into the story. Ella is indeed courageous, and reflexively kind no matter the abuse heaped upon her by the mean-spirited Tremaine. She is also by nature innocent; but also tenacious and someone who, in every frame, is believable as she demonstrates how deeply her decency frames her life. It’s a wonderfully resonant message, brought to you once again by Disney, who has always chosen to see the world not as it is but as it should be. Cinderella. Directed by Kenneth Branagh. For my clients who don’t have two-legged children, four-legged ones often do just fine. If you’ve ever had a pet who became part of your family, you know what I mean. For many of us with pets, we become used to the grime and hassle of keeping a home beautiful with daily wear and tear. It’s to be expected, and we forgive it when these furry friends have stolen our hearts. But what about when we’re exasperated by their bad behavior? Or, when they get sick on the hand-knotted Tibetan carpet you and your designer spent weeks selecting and 8 months to have made? How about the couple whose beloved cats took to the entire suite of furniture with their fierce little claws during a date night, just days after it was installed? These incidents break my heart, and there was a time I’d Huck in his custom dog kennel. Photos by Eric Rorer, Tim Coy, Mo Saito and Laura Bovard, Harvey Milk Bone, may he rest in peace. Charlie waits for her dinner. A custom cat nook for Pele be at a loss with what to do. But with age comes wisdom, and I’ve learned there are certain things you simply avoid – like suggesting a cream rug for a household with small children and a dog, even though the client is in love with it. Sorry, Natalie. My heart is empathetic to our clients who return home from work only to discover that Fido has ripped up a mohair chair, or Fluffy has marked a silk rug. The good news is that you can have the quality and beauty you desire with smart decisions. Here are some tips to extend the life of your home if you have pets: • Make safe purchases. Opt for dark floor coverings. There are rugs made of recycled bottles that look and feel like cotton – yes, such things exist – and they clean easily. Choose wool, tightly woven fabrics, or performance leather, which is wipeable and cleanable. • Cats scratch when they feel anxious, and it’s a natural instinct. It’s how they mark their territory, and it simply feels good. The best foil is to • provide cats a place to scratch that is more appealing. Double-sided sticky tape on furniture corners can deter damage. Even though cat towers can be quite the eyesore, you can do as my client Maggie does, and stash the tower in a side room when she’s throwing a party. Her cat can lounge in its cat apartment happily, and scratch to its hearts content whenever the mood strikes. This makes Maggie – and her designer – very happy. When pets relieve themselves indoors, there are generally clear causes for this. Sometimes, it’s a puppy who isn’t trained yet, or a dog getting back at you for something you don’t know you did. A visiting pet trained at home might not see the wrong in marking a new territory. Or, as in the case of my Harvey, they are sick. Regardless, if you plan on welcoming pets into your home, the best bet is make sure you select cleanable materials. You can’t beat wool. It behaves like hair and washes up well, as long as it’s not over-stripped with stringent cleaners. • Treat your fabrics and furniture, using organic whenever possible. Often, manufacturers can pretreat furniture for you. For retail items or furniture already in your home, DetraPel is a great, non-toxic option that repels liquid and staining. We especially like it because it’s friendly to the planet. For your enjoyment, we’ve included photos of a few pets enjoying customized features designed to include them plus one of our dearly departed fur baby Harvey. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, March 9, 2022 By Will Adams Part 39 in a series One of the most appealing of all landscape installations is the water feature. Water features can include among other things, pools, ponds, streams and waterfalls, either enhanced and displayed in their natural settings, or created, designed, and placed by landscape architects. Probably the most familiar water feature is the fountain. From the small backyard trickle fountains to the popular large immersive fountains, (sometimes called splash pads or wet fountains) seen in many warm weather cities all over the world, fountains are created in many sizes, forms Fountains and architectural styles. The world leader is Rome, Italy, with more than 2000 fountains. Even in a small city like Piedmont we can only guess at the number, as many are hidden in backyards and patios. This all started of course in ancient times when people went to the central town well or fountain for all their drinking and bathing water, often hand-carrying it back to their house. With modern plumbing this functional use is no longer necessary, at least in this country, but fountains are still very prevalent and considered valuable in gardens, plazas and patios. Why do we like them so much? I suppose it’s a combination of things that all contribute to a soothing, tranquil feeling they seem to add to any space of which they are a part. To start with, there is something subliminal about the sound of softly running water that is pretty much universally calming. This ambient fountain water sound also is considered what is called “white noise” that masks or mitigates any other objectionable sounds relegating them to minor background dissonance. There is also the aesthetic contribution of the fountain itself to an outside space. The fountain is a man-made object made of stone or other hard surfaced material that clearly contrasts with surrounding soft, natural green planting to pretty much automatically form a punctuation point in See Walking Piedmont on page 32 Fountains designed and built against walls provide an opportunity to enhance and visually “frame” the water features with wall decoration and/or associated planting. Both at the residential scale on the entry to this Piedmont home or the civic scale like on Exedra Plaza (park side), the effects are impressive and a real asset to the city. pages.text: Wednesday, March 9, 2022 23 The Wine Corner Pierre Gaillard – Gems from the Northern Rhone Pierre Gaillard checking the ripeness of the grapes. By Pierre DuMont In 2015 I made a trip to the Northern Rhone to explore some of the incredible Syrahs and Viogniers that are made in that region. One of the highlights of the trip was the discovery of the wines of Pierre Gaillard. In 1987 he established his winery in the medieval town of Malleval in the appellation of Condrieu. Since then he has expanded by creating estates in the south of France in Banyuls-sur-Mer and in Faugeres. The Northern Rhone appellations of Cote Rotie and Condrieu are some of the most challenging places to make wine in the world. The vines are situated on steep slopes plunging down toward the Rhone. It is only the extensive terracing that keeps the entire hillside from sliding into the river. The soil is made of decomposing schist and granite. In a throwback to earlier days, sometimes Gaillard resorts to plowing the soils between the vines with a horse-drawn plow. This is definitely an old-school traditional estate. The only modern touch seems to be the beautiful watercolor labels on the bottles. If the only Syrahs and Viogniers you have had are from California, you are in for a change of pace. The climate of the Northern Rhone is much colder than California. That results in the wines having more acid and structure. When Viognier The vines of Condrieu roll down to the Rhone river. is grown in a warm climate it often becomes dull and flabby, and Syrah becomes too fruity and sweet. The Rhone versions have incredible balance between fruit and acid, and also have an earthiness and minerality you don’t find elsewhere. The Pierre Gaillard wines are part of the Jack Edwards Collection and are certainly worth searching out. (jackedwardscollection.com) • 2019 Pierre Gaillard Condrieu, $45 I could just swirl and sniff this wine for an hour. It is full and textured with an elegant nose of citrus, honeysuckle, wet stones and peaches. This Condrieu is rich, medium to full-bodied and impeccably balanced with lots of pear and apricot fruit on the palate. This is drinking beautifully, so no need to cellar. • 2020 Pierre Gaillard In Dolio Chardonnay, $20 This wine came as a surprise to me. Chardonnay grapes are not allowed in Condrieu, but are allowed in the adjacent area of Collines Rhodaniennes. This amphore fermented wine has a well-defined citrus-driven bouquet that is nicely controlled and opens in the glass with time. The palate is crisp on the entry with lemon and a touch of orange zest, with a finish that is controlled and refined. While this is an enjoyable wine, my advice to the Rhone winemakers would be to stick with your wonderful native grapes. The world just doesn’t need another Chardonnay. • 2019 Pierre Gaillard Crozes Hermitage, $24 Crozes hermitage is the baby sister of the famed Hermitage hill near Tain. Like Hermitage, it is made from 100% Syrah but has a softer profile. This bottle shows charming floral notes alongside hints of black olives and ripe cherries. It is medium bodied, creamy and fairly concentrated yet silky and fine, with hints of mocha building on the finish. Would be great with a beef stew or braised veal shanks. • 2017 Pierre Gaillard Saint Joseph Clos de Cuminalle, $30 Perfumed, elegant and alluring, Gaillard’s 2017 St. Joseph smells of fresh-cut flowers, blackberry pie and hints of licorice. It builds on the palate and has good richness, but it shines for its elegance and subtlety. Drink over the next decade, preferably serving with a nice roasted leg of lamb. articles.text: Weather forecasts had the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group a little uncertain on Wednesday, March 2, but extra layers of clothes were soon unnecessary. It was a lovely day for a walk. A strong turnout of 36 walkers and one K-9 best friend showed up at the Exedra for some morning exercise. The Post had reported two weeks before that there was a retaining wall project under construction on San Carlos Avenue, so the walkers headed off down Magnolia Avenue, past the new Piedmont High theater. The sidewalk in front of the building was completely cleared and all the fences and construction equipment were gone and the beauty of this new piece of Piedmont High was fully on display. The walkers took a side trip on the 400 block of El Cerrito Avenue which goes directly to Witter Field. The street forms a U as it merges into Jerome, and soon they were back at Magnolia and a short walk later to the lower portion of the divided San CarIos Avenue. At the far end of the block, near Oakland Avenue, they came to the completed, new portion of the wall. It is a hundred feet or so long, and blends in nicely with the rest of the walk. It was agreed that the construction company did a nice job, and they stopped for a group photo with Stella Houston holding the Post. The sheer number of walkers obscured the wall itself (see photo). The walkers carefully crossed Oakland Avenue and continued on San Carlos, observing tree work and house remodeling along the way. San Carlos ends at Blair Avenue, which quickly becomes Ricardo Avenue. Next was Cambridge Way and the group took it to Manor Drive where they went up and down the parallel streets of Manor and York Drive, and Ricardo and Monticello Avenues, with Cambridge Way and Arroyo Avenue providing a bridge between them. On Cambridge the walkers were charmed by a home built in 1925 in a storybook design. It has a “witch’s cap” turret above the front door that the walkers felt Hansel and Gretel would have liked too. The walkers went up Monticello to the Lorita Avenue culde-sac looking for the bottom of a very hidden pathway, but they walked past it without seeing it. The group continued up Monticello and then onto Park Way when the road takes a hard left and Monticello becomes Park Way. They admired the beautiful cedar shake shingle homes across from Dracena Park. Many were built in 1908 by people moving to the area after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake. There was also a huge evergreen tree in the yard of a home near Dracena Avenue that the walkers admired. Near the top of Park was opportunity to visit one more seldom walked street, Waldo Avenue, one-block long with lovely homes and blossoming trees on what was once the back side of the home of Walter Blair, the first European settler of what is now Piedmont. At Blair Avenue they went a half block to Highland and a short walk back to the center of town. In all it had been about a three mile walk with many new and old friends on a delightful, late winter morning. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Dr. Paul Farmer The world has suffered a great loss in the passing of Dr. Paul Farmer, Co-founder and Chief Strategist of Partners in Health (PIH) and Chair of the Department of Global Health and Social Medicine at Harvard Medical School — and a friend to so many of us. There are not enough accolades to describe the life of a man who dedicated himself so completely to solving the world’s greatest problems of poverty, inequality, and global health disparities. Despite a book about his life and work (Tracy Kidder’s Mountains Beyond Mountains), a film (Bending the Arc), his own published works (Pathologies of Power, Partner to the Poor, To Repair the World, Reimagining Global Health, and more), and countless writings, speeches, and awards, it is impossible to fully convey the loss that is being felt around the world. I first met Dr. Farmer when I was a medical student rotating at Brigham & Women’s Hospital in Boston. He was a resident then, and it was during an on-call dinner in the cafeteria when I learned of his work in Haiti. Months later, he received the prestigious MacArthur “Genius Grant,” and yet he would always remain down-to-earth and approachable to medical students. During my residency at the Brigham, Dr. Farmer was the infectious disease fellow who helped us on tough clinical cases at all hours of the day and night. Even then, he was the one who called attention to the unaddressed issues impacting a patient’s medical care. During one memorable conversation about house staff occupational exposures, he pointed out to me the greater challenges faced by less visible healthcare workers, whose choice of profession may not have been as intentional as our own. Photo Courtesy of Harvard University Dr. Farmer’s insights and the life he led by example were an unconscious influence during my formative years of training and may have helped guide my own career decisions that did not follow traditional metrics for success. I was grateful that both my work and the Brigham alumni community afforded me opportunities to stay in touch with him periodically throughout the years. Last year the American Medical Women’s Association was deeply honored to have Dr. Farmer deliver one of our Annual Gala Keynotes. It had been just over a year into the pandemic and eight months after the death of George Floyd, a time which he aptly characterized as one of “awakening and loss… a tectonic level of change.” He reminded us of the importance of resisting a “guild mentality, in order to fight for what our patients deserve and what we need to serve them.” Most importantly, he posed this question, “Where do we go as a healing profession in the midst of all this pain?” His heartfelt answer would become a guiding message for us: “…leadership, allyship, and looking out for each other are a big part of what we most need right now. We are certainly humans before heroes, but many of those gathering virtually for the AMWA meeting are nonetheless heroes to me, working as you do to make medicine truly humane and inclusive but also clearly on the right side of history’s ledger.” At only 62 years of age, Dr. Farmer’s work was far from over. And so, it is left to those of us who remain to follow the path that he forged, to carry on his work to fight inequality on behalf of not only our patients but those less visible in all corners of the world. Dr. Eliza Lo Chin is Executive Director of American Medical Women’s Association and a Piedmont resident.

articles.text: William Joseph Sullivan, 94, passed away peacefully surrounded by his loving family on Saturday, January 29, 2022. He lived a life of service to others and will be greatly missed. Bill was born in Anaconda, Montana on June 16, 1927, the son of Joseph Michael and Alice Marie Peacher Sullivan. In 1945, he graduated from Anaconda High School and enlisted in the United States Army. Bill proudly served as a T-5 Topical Draftsman in Korea with the First Infantry Regiment of the 6th Army Division. Following the Korean War, he returned to his home state and earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Pharmacy and a Master’s of Science degree in Chemistry from the University of Montana. In 1954, Bill married Anaconda native Helen Marie Ryan. They moved to Ann Arbor, Michigan, where Bill continued his studies at the University of Michigan and earned a Ph.D. in Medicinal Chemistry. As a young scientist, he began his career serving as a research chemist for Shell Development Company and moved his family to California where they lived for 60 years. Dr. Sullivan entered into business as a pharmacist and owned and operated various pharmacies, including the Montclair Pharmacy Dr. William Sullivan, the longtime owner of Montclair Pharmacy, passed away on January 29 at age 94. in Oakland. His wife, Helen, joined him in their business pursuits, and all members of their family worked at the stores over a period of 50 years. The Sullivans were generous supporters of many charities and loyal parishioners at Corpus Christi Church. Always active, he enjoyed many painting and construction projects. Together with his son, he built a family vacation home at Lake-of-the-Pines in Auburn, CA. He was a longtime member of the University of Montana’s Grizzly Riders where he earned the “butt buster” award for the most hours in a saddle during their annual horseback rides. Dr. Sullivan retired from the Montclair Pharmacy at age 85 and happily returned to his roots in Montana alongside his devoted wife. He enjoyed the last nine years working on his ranch, following business and political news, managing real estate, and spending time with family and friends. He valued education and endowed scholarships at the University of Montana and the University of Michigan. Most of all, he had an incredible work ethic, was a loyal caretaker, generous patriarch, and devoted Catholic. He is survived by his two daughters, Laurice Salamack (Joe) of Johnstown, NY, and Mary Alice McNeil (Tim) of Piedmont; daughter-in-law Carol Sullivan of Grass Valley, CA; five grandchildren, Ryan Sullivan, Kelly Salamack Casey (Kevin) and Allison Salamack Dodd-o (Joseph), William and Thomas McNeil, and numerous nieces and nephews. He is predeceased by his wife Helen Marie in 2014; son, Joseph Michael Sullivan II in 2020; and sister Shirley Sullivan Kudzia in 2017. A memorial mass will be held at Corpus Christi Church, 322 St. James Drive, Piedmont, on March 19, 2022 at 11:00 AM. In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to Corpus Christi Church.
articles.title: Bill Sullivan, everyone’s favorite pharmacist, dies on Jan. 29

After pulling up to the port we made a beeline for the nearby Boudin Bakery, home of the original (and delicious) San Francisco sourdough bread, where I picked up my preordered lunch. Yummy! At the end of the bridge, I reflected on the hike. Walking the full length of the bridge is something I would never have dared to do alone. Mind you, the last time I attempted to hike this bridge was when I was 5 years old with my family during the chilly, windy winter of 2015. I made it only halfway across then. Since I joined Scouting six months ago, it has dragged me into new and exciting adventures I am experiencing for the first time. We trekked under the bridge to the Marin Headlands where several campgrounds awaited us at Kirby Cove. The view from under the bridge is truly magnificent. After the hike across the bridge many would be tempted to rest, but not Troop 1. The Scouts wasted no time rolling up their sleeves and getting down to business, weeding tent pits and clearing out bear boxes. This service project is just one of the many ways Troop 1 gives back to the community by helping preserve natural and historical landmarks such as Kirby Cove, including an adjacent former artillery battery from World War 2. As the saying goes, give a little, get a little. When we finished with the project the Park Ranger and her intern presented us with a gift for being a returning Troop – collapsible water bottles. This year was the first after a one-year hiatus Troop 1 Scouts in service project at Kirby Cove due to COVID. This was my first backpacking trip and I was completely clueless about several factors, the main one being I had to bring a backpack. I had stuffed all my gear in my school backpack. Functional? Yes. Comfortable? Absolutely not. Scouts transfer ferries. Photos by Bryan Cantrill The underside of the Golden Gate Bridge is an amazing sight. Still can’t have lunch. Scouts head to Crissy Field for lunch. For the first leg of the journey, we took the #33 bus from Piedmont Community Church to Jack London Square for the ferry, which took us to the Ferry Building. In San Francisco we took a connecting ferry to Pier 41. After pulling up to the port we made a beeline for the nearby Boudin Bakery, home of the original (and delicious) San Francisco sourdough bread, where I picked up my preordered lunch. Yummy! But I learned that I couldn’t have it yet. First we had to hike another half hour to Crissy Field for lunch. After lunch, which I thought had been painfully short, we set off once again to hike across the magnificent Golden Gate Bridge enjoying the beautiTroop 1 Scouts Sean Heafey (left), Noah Hildebrand, and Samantha Pell (with French bread) stand triumphant after hiking the length of the Golden Gate Bridge. ful views below us. At the end of the bridge, I reflected on the hike. Walking the full length of the bridge is something I would never have dared to do alone. Mind you, the last time I attempted to hike this bridge was when I was 5 years old with my family during the chilly, windy winter of 2015. I made it only halfway across then. Since I joined Scouting six months ago, it has dragged me into new and exciting adventures I am experiencing for the first time. We trekked under the bridge to the Marin Headlands where several campgrounds awaited us at Kirby Cove. The view from under the bridge is truly magnificent. After the hike across the bridge many would be tempted to rest, but not Troop 1. The Scouts wasted no time rolling up their sleeves and getting down to business, weeding tent pits and clearing out bear boxes. This service project is just one of the many ways Troop 1 gives back to the community by helping preserve natural and historical landmarks such as Kirby Cove, including an adjacent former artillery battery from World War 2. As the saying goes, give a little, get a little. When we finished with the project the Park Ranger and her intern presented us with a gift for being a returning Troop – collapsible water bottles. What a surprise – I was just thinking of buying them the other day. We pitched our tents then headed down to the beach for some views of a gorgeous sunset with the Golden Gate Bridge right in front of us. Those who were willing to take risks and extend radical hospitality to the weary could contribute as well. This Women’s History Month let’s recognize all the women who taught us and teach us still. pages.text: 30 Wednesday, March 9, 2022 PCA lease Continued from page 1 entered into the agreement in May 2011 for $1 a year with the understanding that it would take over all maintenance of 801 Magnolia Avenue. Prior to 2011, the building, which was purchased by the city in 2003, had been left unused and vacant. The new use agreement – as opposed to a lease – gives the Piedmont Recreation Department full control of programming at 801 Magnolia Avenue, a cityowned building, while giving PCA access to program the space for only arts-related events at a $1000-a month usage fee but only 55% of the time. PCA Board President Sue Malick asked city council to approve the use agreement, but added that the non-profit organization will experience financial challenges as it gives up half of its usable hours in the Main Hall, the space used for all concerts, art exhibits, lectures, film presentations and theatrical productions. “We’ve agreed to give up half of our useable hours. We will do so even if this means a significant reduction of income solely used for overhead and keeping the costs for artists and audiences as low as we possibly can,” Malick said. “We will have challenges with this use agreement, but we are up to it.” Based on comments received Monday night, residents seemed divided on the details of the use agreement prepared by city staff. The staff report hoped to remedy the elected body’s conAll-League Continued from page 15 No. 3 seed before losing narrowly No. 2 Branson, 57-55. To get there, PHS defeated No. 14 San Rafael 74-45 and No. 11 Encinal cern “about the landlord-tenant framework as a potential barrier to inclusive community access to the space and achieving the highest and best use of the facility,” according to the report authored by City Administrator Sara Lillevand. Resident Irene Cheng said she believes that the terms of the use agreement does not make the space truly equitable and accessible to all groups in Piedmont because it offered “such a large block of hours to one organization at a reduced cost.” Cheng also suggested that the Center for the Arts building should be explored as a potential site for affordable housing, adding that “no stone should be left unturned.” In the end, City Council did include an amendment to the use agreement that accounted for housing – a termination clause to the use agreement to include statutory requirements related specifically to housing. While the agreement gives the Recreation Department control over calendaring and scheduling, the specifics of programming and use under the auspices of the Recreation Department were unclear. Recreation Commissioner Dick Carter offered public comment during the meeting. “As a member of the Piedmont Recreation Commission, I have developed an understanding of the constraints imposed on recreational activities by the city’s limited facilities,” he said, but added that the city “has not involved the Recreation Commission in this issue.” “This has left me, and I believe almost everyone in Piedmont, with an incomplete understanding of the issue,” Carter said. On prioritization of use, Council member Betsy Andersen pointed out that “if 100 [days on the calendar] are open, 100 groups will want their time.” Currently, there is no definitive prioritization list of programming. Instead, it will be a first-come first-serve basis, and the Recreation Department will decide which groups or individuals may use the facility at what time, and what events will be permitted when. The duration of the agreement was also debated. Council member Andersen said she would not budge from a six-year agreement (down from a 10-year lease), saying that doing so would “be a great disservice to PCA.” Council member Cavenaugh pushed for a one-year tern. The use agreement passed in three separate motions. City Council approved 3-2, with Vice Mayor Cavenaugh and Councilmember Long dissenting, a five-year use agreement, 90-day release, and 18-month good-faith assessment between PCA and the City. The 30-day notice of termination will be delivered to PCA on April 11, meaning the lease will transition into the approved use agreement on May 11. articles.text: At the base of the hillside framing Blair Park is a majestic California bay laurel. This huge tree is part of the Umbellularia californica family. It is a native, evergreen tree found along the western coastline of California and southern Oregon, usually in bottomland sites, along streams, or dry rocky areas. It is a sturdy tree known for its ability to withstand strong coastal winds. Its leaves are oblong shaped with a smooth, leathery texture. When the leaves are crushed, they have a strong, pungent odor. Native American Indian tribes used the leaves for medicinal remedies and to season their food. Today, these leaves are still dried and used in cooking. In the late winter and early spring, the tree blooms with small, yellowish-green flowers. The wood from the tree is highly valued for its beauty and can be made to make wood furCalifornia Bay Laurel. niture and moldings. Additionally, wood carvers often use the burls from California bay laurels to make decorative objects. These burls are rounded outgrowths on the tree trunks and branches Photo by Brian Mahany which are considered beautiful. This California bay laurel was designated as a Heritage Tree in 2021 and was nominated by Marge Blackwell and the Van Slyke family. Go out and explore your Piedmont neighborhood to look for a remarkable tree to nominate as a Heritage Tree. Nominations are due by March 18, 2022 and will be evaluated on their aesthetic, educational, or historical merits by a Park Commission subcommittee. At the April 6 Park Commission meeting, commissioners will vote to approve the selected nominations. This year’s selections will be announced at the City Arbor Day festivities on April 28. Forms are available on the City’s website on its Heritage Tree page at https://www.piedmont.ca.gov/cms/One.aspx?- portalId=13659823&pag eId=17970894. For more information, please contact Piedmont Parks Manager Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov or 510- 420-3064.

articles.text: Starting March 14, masks indoors will no longer be required in California schools, but will be “strongly recommended,” according to a statement on February 28 by Governor Gavin Newsom. Individual counties also must first drop the masking requirement, after which individual school districts can continue or drop the need for wearing masks indoors. Piedmont School District will align with Alameda County, whose decision is expected by the end of this week. In a press release on February 28, the county indicated its approval of changing indoor masks in school from being “required” to “strongly recommended.” “Given continued improvements in local and statewide measures, this is a reasonable change,” stated Alameda County Public Health Public Information Manager Neetu Balram. In a statement to families on February 28 Superintendent Randy Booker confirmed that the district will make masks optional once Alameda County gives the go ahead. He also cautioned, “I want to remind everyone that the wearing of masks will remain recommended for students and staff. Anyone wishing to wear a mask in any setting while on campus will be absolutely permitted and encouraged to do so.” Mask-wearing outdoor on school campuses was made Piedmont students in Beth Black’s AP Literature class shown wearing masks in December as required. The policy may change on March 14.

articles.text: February 27 is known as the Feast of the Transfiguration for the liturgical church – the day when Jesus goes up to the mountain and he meets with Moses and Elijah all glowing in a dazzling white. It is also the day in the Episcopal Church we call World Mission Sunday, where we are reminded, we are part of a bigger church, not just our local congregation here in Oakland. Last year, I remembered this day and spoke about my mission journey to Guatemala. We started a collection for our ministries in Uganda that day. I shared that when you get a chance to go to these places and serve, it is so much different than merely being a tourist. It is transformative. Think back on your life. What are those moments that have transformed you? It was going on a retreat or maybe when you were younger when you went to camp. Those moments give us a glimmer of hope and joy that we can hold onto in dark times. However, we cannot stay on the mountain top forever. I am especially reminded of that this week after Russia began its invasion of Ukraine. As a Christian, to me war is sad. Violence is not an answer. Repeatedly people give into power, and they choose violence for merely more power. When I think back to the message of Jesus, the prince of peace, I am

Jon Owens February 27 is known as the Feast of the Transfiguration for the liturgical church – the day when Jesus goes up to the mountain and he meets with Moses and Elijah all glowing in a dazzling white. It is also the day in the Episcopal Church we call World Mission Sunday, where we are reminded, we are part of a bigger church, not just our local congregation here in Oakland. Last year, I remembered this day and spoke about my mission journey to Guatemala. We started a collection for our ministries in Uganda that day. I shared that when you get a chance to go to these places and serve, it is so much different than merely being a tourist. It is transformative. Think back on your life. What are those moments that have transformed you? It was going on a retreat or maybe when you were younger when you went to camp. Those moments give us a glimmer of hope and joy that we can hold onto in dark times. However, we cannot stay on the mountain top forever. I am especially reminded of that this week after Russia began its invasion of Ukraine. As a Christian, to me war is sad. Violence is not an answer. Repeatedly people give into power, and they choose violence for merely more power. Piedmont Police Department is the first law enforcement agency in the country to launch a transparency portal in conjunction with its ALPR operating system. When presenting the 2021 department year-end report to city council members on February 22, Chief Bowers explained that the police officers made 30 arrests and recovered 34 stolen vehicles with a valuation of $449,500 in activity directly related to the ALPR cameras. The Department has utilized ALPR technology since 2013. The replacement of the city’s ALPR equipment has also afforded an opportunity to use solar-powered units. Flock Safety, in partnership with the Piedmont Police Department, began installing a new set of Automated License Plate Reader cameras (ALPR) throughout town this week. The cameras are able to record images of license plates, and upload and store it in a secure digital “cloud” for 60 days. At a December 20 meeting, Piedmont City Council approved an agreement with new vendor Flock Safety for ALPR equipment for two years. The total cost of replacing the existing cameras is $178,500. In a presentation to council members, Police Chief Jeremy Bowers explained that the previous ALPR cameras had reached the end of their useful life, and that tests of the new camera vendor Flock Safety were successfully utilized in neighboring cities. In addition to the new cameras, the police department launched a transparency portal in partnership with the vendor that allows interested parties to view policies and usage statistics. articles.text: Urban Compassion Project, founded by Vincent Ray Williams, hosts clean-ups every Saturday morning at various locations in Oakland. Piedmont residents have joined Williams in this humble mission since the group’s inception. Urban Compassion Project seeks to build community between the unhoused and housed community through simple acts of kindness, explained Williams. The volunteer-led grassroots effort started under the name Urban Park Cleanup and has since expanded to provide a variety of resources for the unhoused community of Oakland. “I founded it under necessity,” Williams explained. “I wanted to be a part of the solution, from an approach of someone who has lived and experienced the hardships [the unhoused] face for some time.” Williams has lived on the streets of Oakland and San Francisco for over 20 years. Just recently housed, he understands first-hand that dwindling resources and inaction at the city level have exacerbated the problem. “It wasn’t like this when I was growing up,” he said. “It wasn’t at this level. I don’t remember seeing tents as I grew up. Just seven years ago it wasn’t as bad as it is today. That’s a real reflection on both the city and county’s ability to respond in-kind to this crisis we’re experiencing.” The work is not easy. One Saturday cleanup with a handful of volunteers working two to three hours can produce a mountain of trash bags. The individuals who live in the vicinity of the cleanups have limited resources and are infinitely grateful, Williams said. Volunteers range in age and demographic, and there are many methods and ways to help. The group has since moved beyond its regularly-scheduled cleanups, and is now accepting donations of tents, blankets and clothing. The volunteer-led grassroots effort started under the name Urban Park Cleanup and has since expanded to provide a variety of resources for the unhoused community of Oakland. “I founded it under necessity,” Williams explained. “I wanted to be a part of the solution, from an approach of someone who has lived and experienced the hardships [the unhoused] face for some time.” Williams has lived on the streets of Oakland and San Francisco for over 20 years. articles.text: artwork independently with her eyes and then directs her team on how she wants it converted into jewelry, choosing jewelry types, Lilia Munn, a 17-year-old Piedmont student, artist and entrepreneur, creates art in a most unique fashion – solely with her eyes. By tracking her eye movements, a Tobii Dynavox I-12+ eye gaze communication device literally turns her vision into works of art. The unique colors, textures, patterns and digital effects are then turned into jewelry for sale through her business, Lilia’s Eye Candy LLC. Munn has a provisional patent for how she makes her jewelry and 10% of her jewelry sale proceeds are donated to Rett Syndrome organizations that seek a cure and provide support for the rare syndrome. “The pandemic gave me time to think about how I could share my art in a special way. I want to spread light and love to others during a dark time. I want people to be happy when they wear my art as jewelry,” she said in an interview with the Post. Munn communicates much in the same way she paints, by aiming her eyes at words or phrases on a computer screen, or at letters to spell out words with word prediction, which are then spoken. “Remote learning takes away some of the problems of having a physical disability. I can do so much more with my eyes and digital art than with my hands,” she said. Munn is a Piedmont student in an Individualized Education Program (IEP), and loves learning through the computer. She studies jewelry trends, art history, animation and is taking a business course to help expand Lilia’s Eye Candy. Lilia Munn describes her favorite art piece as happy, exciting, and one that brings energy. It is also used in the “Lilia’s Eye Candy” blinking eye business logo. Munn puts in hard work as a committed and dedicated art student, receiving art instruction twice weekly from Professor Jason Hopkins in Chicago. Hopkins holds a Master of Fine Arts from the prestigious School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Professor Hopkins says her works hearken to abstract expressionists like Pollock and de Kooning, but unlike her predecessors working in a tactile world, her art derives from eye gaze and goes straight to a digital world. “Lilia subverts the process of hand-eye coordination [by] ‘willing’ her colors, textures, and patterns into being, pushing pixels around like finger paints in a psychologically more immediate and intimate way. She is a virtual pioneer, championing the liberties of the creative soul, while romantically defying disability and torpor,” Hopkins said. Currently, Munn’s art is available for sale on her website Liliaseyecandy.com. She is also popular on instagram @liliaseyecandy and on Facebook: Lilia’s Eye Candy, LLC where she gives away a piece of jewelry every month. Munn and her mother, Vera Adamovich, plan to expand the business to earrings, rings, cuff links, and keychains, and ideally into retail stores. She’s already making new jewelry for her next 2.0 line with sterling silver, gold, rose gold, glass beads, and crystals. The new line will also include men’s jewelry. Munn is excited to be collaborating with the International Rett Syndrome Foundation Rettsyndrome.org, and will donate 10% of her sales from March 1-June 1 to help raise awareness for Rett Syndrome. From the age of three, Munn has been working with the support of now-retired Piedmont Occupational Therapist Kimberly Bonacum and Assistive Technology Specialist Judy Lariviere. Munn’s art can be seen in person in the Piedmont Art Walk this spring, which raises money to support art in Piedmont schools. Lilia Munn currently sells bubble and bangle bracelets, rad leather charm bracelets, street wear necklaces, and statement necklaces.

articles.text: Jack London State Historic Park in Sonoma County has launched its annual writing contest open to students in grades 6 through 8. The contest will be open until March 31. This year’s theme is “Building Better Communities”. Students are asked to write a fictional story in which the characters create and dwell in a community of their own invention that is unique, or where they overcome something challenging. Young writers are asked to be creative in describing how the community works while telling an entertaining and engaging story. The theme of the story is a nod to famous California author Jack London’s purchased rural land on Sonoma Mountain in Glen Ellen. London modeled “green” farming techniques to create his vision of a cooperative community where all residents would enjoy fair working conditions and great quality of life. It was known as his “garden of good intentions.” To learn more about the backstory for this theme, visit https:// ja ck londonpa rk .com /a n nual-young-writers-contest/. Jack London State Historic Park is run by Jack London Park Partners, the first non-profit to take up management of a state park on behalf of the people of California. Park Partners is an outgrowth group of Valley of the Moon Natural History Association, a citizens’ group established more than 50 years ago to support the needs of three parks in Sonoma County, including Jack London. Judges for the contest are volunteers and are not employed by the non-profit organization. Stories will be judged anonymously by the panel, and cash prizes are awarded for first, second, and third place. Submissions should be in PDF format, typed, double-spaced, and no more than 2000 words. Email all questions on entry format to Kristina Ellis, at kellis@jacklondonpark.com.

articles.text: Storytelling is an important part of early childhood development. School is back in session and everyone is learning their math, science, language arts skills, and hopefully some play. My favorite part of school has always been story time. This activity happens in the classroom at all age levels, from circle time for the littles all the way to Socratic seminars for the bigs. Storytelling is important from the very beginning of life. There is much research stating that storytelling is key for the developing brain including creativity, imagination, vocabulary and communication. This early exposure to letters, words, and structure help children to read and write. Almost more importantly, storytelling and sharing aids children in telling their own stories allowing them to process and understand their own experiences, often reflecting their culture, language and history, contributing to the formation of identity. At Fairyland I watch children enjoying the stories being told at the puppet theatre. So much is manifesting in a short 15-minute show — the recognition of a story with characters, values, emotions, and drama. This is evidenced by laughter, clapping, gasps and questions. As they build language and communication, stories also Children’s Fairyland spark curiosity and engage us in realities other than our own. This trip into another reality gives us valuable perspective on our own experiences. What can you do to support storytelling for your little people? • Talk a lot. For babies and toddlers, narrate what you are doing or what you will be doing and integrate voice inflection to help the story flow. • Share who you are. Tell family histories or stories illustrating who you are as a unit. • Write it down. Take dictation from your young storyteller and read it back to them. It often grows or gets clarified. • Act it out. Help young storytellers dramatize the stories they tell by adding movement. Although the structured environment of language arts in the classroom is crucial, storytelling outside of the classroom is also important. Storytelling directly impacts the development of our children, and the effects have a powerful impact on our community. Reprinted from Piedmont Post on October 6, 2021. Kymberly Miller is the Executive Director of Children’s Fairyland, the mission of which is to spark imagination, learning, and development through the power of storytelling.

articles.text: Girl Scout Troop 31765 set up their Girl Scout Cookie stand on Sunday, February 27, offering cookie sales in person for the first time in two years. The sales booths at the Exedra and in front of Ace Hardware were warmly welcomed by residents eager for the famous cookies – and a return to normalcy. The troop consists of 11 Scouts in the 11th grade, many of whom have been together since 1st grade. The troop has set an ambitious goal of selling 2,760 boxes this year, with the ultimate goal of funding a post-graduation trip to Barcelona with profits saved up from four years of selling cookies. Funds from the sales will also be used for service projects and outings like the Girl Scout Camporee in April. The Camporee is a weekend long event where Girl Scout troops from around the Bay Area practice and compete in outdoor skills such as knot tying, shelter building, orienteering and first aid. “Customers were really excited to see us again. Senior citizens love Girl Scout cookies,” exclaimed Girl Scout Eleanor Lavin. “Parents usually want to try the newer cookies - this year’s new Adventureful, or S’mores that were new a few years ago. The little kids usually go for the boxes that look the biggest, like Samoas, Tagalongs and Trefoil.” This year’s varieties include Troop 31765 Girl Scouts Tyler Knapp (left) and Quinn Reilly help some Girls Scouts cookie customers last Sunday, February 27. Lemon-ups, Trefoils, Do-si-dos, Samoas, Tagalongs, Thin mints, gluten free Toffee-tastic and S’mores. Cookies can also be ordered on the troop’s website: https://digitalcookie.girlscouts.org/scout/ troop31765-636?fpkp=1

articles.text: The Wildwood Dads Club revives a 35-year tradition on April 2 by hosting its popular annual Crab Feed at the Piedmont Veterans Building. All ticket sales support Wildwood School. Doors open at 6:00 p.m. and dinner starts at 7:00, with festivities lasting until 11:00 p.m. A surprise local musical act will perform, and Wildwood Dad Ben Anderson will serve as a DJ to wind down the evening. Inheriting the role of Crab Daddy is Wildwood dad Adam Fishman, dressed as a very large crab. The dads historically have put on comedy skits, recorded short humor films, and even written and performed their own songs with fully scripted shows. (Think Greg Slatoff.) “It was really disappointing when we couldn’t put on the Crab Feed last year. It’s such a great community-building and fundraising event that brings a lot of excitement and pride to our Dads Club meetings,” said Fishman. “I’m going to need to eat twice the crab to make up for last year.” Guests will also be able to purchase a special bottle of wine or spirits for their tables, akin to premium bottle service. The popular event normally draws up to 150 people, and though it’s a month away, more than 60 tickets already have been sold online at Eventbrite.com/e/ wildwood-crab-feed-2022-tickets-222458588627?aff=crabfeedurl. It is a fully vaccinated, adultsonly event. Guests will need to show proof of vaccination at the door. This year the outdoor patio will be available for people who prefer to eat outside. pages.text: 8 Wednesday, March 2, 2022 Get ready... it’s Girl Scout Cookie season By Jay Russell Girl Scout Troop 31765 set up their Girl Scout Cookie stand on Sunday, February 27, offering cookie sales in person for the first time in two years. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is calling for volunteers to serve on City commissions and committees. Currently, a total of 19 positions will become available. Of the open vacancies, five are guaranteed to be available. The remaining positions potentially will be filled by incumbents. Residents are encouraged to apply to any vacancy of interest. How to Apply The deadline for applications is Monday, March 21 at 5:00 p.m. Interviews will be held the evening of Monday, March 28. Residents interested in volunteering may fill out and submit an application form on the city’s website: https://www. piedmont.ca.gov/government/ city _news_ _ _notifications/ commission-committee-rePlanning Commission 3 vacancies, 3 incumbents; 3-year term The Planning Commission makes decisions regarding proposed modifications or construction to homes. It advises the City Council on issues related to planning and building. It meets monthly on the second Monday at 5:30 p.m. It requires approximately 4 hours per month in addition to meeting time. Appointees to the Planning Commission are required to submit a statement of economic interests. Commissioners still serving active terms include Rani Batra, Yildiz Duransoy, Jonathan Levine, Tom Ramsey, Douglas Strout, and Justin Tucker (Alternate). Recreation Commission 2 vacancies, 0 incumbents; 3-year term The commission advises the City Council on issues regarding the City’s recreation programs, sports field development, allocations of field space and other issues. It meets monthly on the third Wednesday at 7:30 p.m. Commissioners still serving active terms include Dick Carter, Jeffrey Dorman, Vincent Fisher, Lisa Gardner, Rebecca Posamentier, Susan Terrill, and Aamir Virani. Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee 3 vacancies, 3 incumbents; 3-year term The committee reviews and provides comment on five-year projections contained in the City’s annual budget proposal, the proposed funding and expenditures from several longterm funds, and the proposed mid-year budget adjustments. It provides a financial review of new programs in excess of $250,000 per year. Commissioners still serving active terms include Andrew Flynn, Cathie Geddeis, Deborah Leland, Robert McBain, Paul Raskin, Frank Ryan, Vanessa Washington and Chris Kwei (Alternate). Public Safety Committee 3 vacancies, 1 incumbents; 3-year term This committee investigates ways to increase public participation in crime reduction; It increases public participation in disaster preparedness, and provides a forum for residents to share comments, issues or concerns regarding public safety issues. The committee meets quarterly. Current committee members are Shanti Brien, Lori Elefant, Jeffrey Horner, Chris Houlder, Lynne Wright (Chair). Corey Smegal is School District Appointee. Alameda County Mosquito Abatement District 1 vacancy; 2-year term This position serves as the City’s trustee on the Board of the Alameda County Mosquito Abatement District. Civil Service Commission 2 vacancies, 2 incumbent; 3-year term The commission deals with personnel issues including classification and serves as the hearing board in disputes between the City and employees. This commission meets as required. Incumbent Commissioners serving active terms are Scott Lawson, Amy Kelly, Laura Isaacs, David Hobstetter, and Claudia Harrison. cruitment-2022 Applications may be sent by e-mail to the City Clerk’s office at JTulloch@piedmont. ca.gov, or delivered in person to Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue. For more information or to request an application be mailed to you, call the City Clerk’s office at (510) 420-3040. Park Commission 3 vacancies, 0 incumbents; 3-year term The Park Commission makes recommendations to the City Council about improvements to the public parks and manages the street tree improvement program of the city. It meets monthly on the first Wednesday at 5:30 p.m. Commissioners still serving active terms include Amber Brumfiel, Patty Dunlap, Betsy Goodman, Jim Horner, Brian Mahany, Eileen Ruby, and Robin Wu.

articles.text: Delacroix is known for three massive paintings hanging in the Louvre, particularly Liberty Leading the People, the most often reproduced painting in French art. He submitted his first painting to the Paris Salon when studying at École Beaux-Arts. The Barque of Dante, a scene from Dante’s Inferno, shows demons attacking the boat as the Roman poet Virgil leads Dante across the River Styx into Hell. It created quite a stir; he was just 24 years-old and an art school nobody. The painting seemed startlingly intense to some but was generally received as a welcome departure from the staid Neo-Classicism works in vogue. The poet and art critic Charles Baudelaire referred to Delacroix as “passionately in love with passion.” Delacroix was a serious student of painting, and a devotee of the 16th-17th C. masters, particularly Rubens and Titian. He dutifully copied their canvases as part of his student work at the Louvre. His style was notably derived from the Baroque style of Peter Paul Rubens. Romanticism had nothing to do with romance in the modern sense; but artists sought to convey human strugMusée Delacroix preserves the atelier and home at 6 Rue de Fürstenberg, 6th arr. gles in desperate situations to evoke powerful reactions. Romanticism valued emotion over logic, and the individual over the collective. Delacroix painted what moved him, taking his themes from religion, literature, history, and societal injustice. By age 40, he had emerged as the leader of Romanticism, though he wasn’t fond of that or any other label. The Barque of Dante, 1822, by Delacroix. Dimensions: 18-in. x 24-in. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, March 2, 2022 AMERICANS IN PARIS By Patricia Forsyth Nº 49 in a biweekly series The wood-frame home and studio of the painter Eugène Delacroix was purchased for preservation a century ago by the Foundation of the Delacroix Museum, and it remains a humble attraction at Place Fürstenberg on the Left Bank. The studio is a separate building behind the simply constructed, spare four-room residence, where the artist lived and worked on his final project – decorating the walls and ceilings of the nearby Church of SaintSulpice. This small museum’s collection consists of prints, writings, memorabilia, and minor oil paintings, takes about an hour to tour. But it’s not murals that Delacroix is remembered for, but the exhilarating, bold canvases he created as a young artist in his twenties and thirties. He was influenced by the great Théodore Gericault who painted Raft of the Medusa (1819). Gericault, only seven years his senior, was part of the Paris art commune; and Delacroix while still in art school posed as one of the corpses sliding off the raft. articles.text: The Death of Sardanapalus, which illustrates a scene from the probably apocryphal legend of an embattled Assyrian king gazing upon the frightful slaughter of his harem and animals before killing himself. The painting is a lurid and confusing work compounded by the swirling red and gold from a tale few people have heard of. The work was not well received. Delacroix’s Liberty Leading the People commemorates the July Revolution of 1830 which toppled the last of the Bourbon kings, Charles X, in the July Revolution. The dispatch of older brother Louis XVI with his Queen Marie Antoinette informed a hasty abdication within days of the uprising. Many view the masterpiece as a call to Revolution, but not Delacroix who painted the bare-breasted Liberty carrying the tri-colored French flag as allegorical to the spirit of Liberty. The French were sympathetic to the Greeks seeing themselves in the revolutionary struggle, and the painting propelled the artist’s recognition and boosted sales. His next colossal canvas was The Death of Sardanapalus, which illustrates a scene from the probably apocryphal legend of an embattled Assyrian king gazing upon the frightful slaughter of his harem and animals before killing himself. The painting is a lurid and confusing work compounded by the swirling red and gold from a tale few people have heard of. The work was not well received. Delacroix’s Liberty Leading the People commemorates the July Revolution of 1830 which toppled the last of the Bourbon kings, Charles X, in the July Revolution. The dispatch of older brother Louis XVI with his Queen Marie Antoinette informed a hasty abdication within days of the uprising. Many view the masterpiece as a call to Revolution, but not Delacroix who painted the bare-breasted Liberty carrying the tri-colored French flag as allegorical to the spirit of Liberty. The painting was so powerful that following its first exhibition, Delacroix was awarded the cross of the Legion of Honor, and Liberty was purchased by the nation and displayed at the Luxembourg Museum for Contemporary Art before moving to the Louvre in 1862.
