I am in awe of his effort, patience, and character,” said PHS counselor Chris Hartford. Hartford stated that he is frequently asked if he would ever become a school administrator. His answer is always no. “It takes a very special person to lead a group of people, with unwavering patience and an ever present positive attitude. Adam has all of that,” said Hartford. articles.text: The way to calculate the years of experience for a nurse’s salary at Piedmont School District was amended in the February 9 school board meeting to include past work performed in both the public and private sector within the nursing profession. If a school nurse had prior experience outside of a school, this change increases their salary by adding years to their placement on the salary schedule. The raises for Piedmont’s nurses retroactively went into effect July 1, 2021. The total increase in salary for all three nurses is around $35,000 for the year. School Board Vice President Amal Smith is an administration at the UCSF School of Medicine, and explained the change. “Before this recently approved change, only very limited types of experience were counted for school nurses when they entered the district. articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont will feature Erwin Chemerinsky, Dean of Berkeley Law School in a discussion on Tuesday, March 1 at 4 p.m. He is a nationally recognized expert on the U.S. Supreme Court and election law. articles.text: Community Church has returned to in-person worship following a two-month hiatus due to the COVID Omicron surge in January. In-person worship at the church returned with live service at 10 a.m. this past Sunday, February 20. The service was led by Don Ashburn, with a sermon by Steve Schibsted. This is the first in-person worship since December 19, 2021. On October 2, 2021, Piedmont Community Church issued an announcement alerting residents of a COVID incident - church staff was informed that a volunteer who was in the Christian Education Building two days prior had tested positive for COVID-19. The person who was infected is fully vaccinated and was double-masked. Online-only worship was available through February 13. “The rapid emergence of the highly transmissible Omicron variant since December has created huge challenges for public health and community. Such a surge comes at a time when we all expected a return to at least a ‘new normal’ with effective vaccines,” said Joan Chow, a member of the Church’s Reopening Task Force. “But instead, we’ve had to make difficult decisions - such as cancelling in-person services from Christmas Eve services through [February 13] to protect the congregation as a whole.” The Reopening Task Force Members include Chow, Pastors Schibsted and Ashburn, Pat Leicher, Steve Senter, Randy Litteneker, Kristin Johnson, Toni Fischer, Leslie Quantz, Jay Foreman, and Tom Walter. The Church’s Reopening Task Force met in the winter months to assist in the planning for resuming in-person worship and advised the public through a emailed newsletter that “if cases and hospitalizations decline sufficiently, [the] proposed target date for in-person worship is February 20,” and that to resume in-person worship, masks would be required regardless of recent changes in County guidance. When attending an in-person service, proof of vaccination or a negative COVID-19 test obtained within 48 hours is required for entry. Masks indoors are required as well. If you do not have a mask, one will be provided to you. Piedmont Community Church

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department provided its year-end 2021 crime report to City Council on Tuesday, February 22. The report found that there was a notable increase in larceny and theft incidents, but a decrease in burglaries. There were 280 reported offenses of larceny, or theft, in 2021, as opposed to 236 reported offenses the year prior. Larceny is described as theft that does not involve trespassing into a structure or vehicle. The major difference between larceny and burglary is the act of “breaking in.” Burglaries decreased from 61 reported incidents in 2020 to 25 reported incidents last year. “While the Police Department conducts proactive patrols to mitigate thefts and other crimes, we cannot overemphasize the importance of residents and visitors employing basic crime prevention actions such as not leaving valuables in vehicles,” Police Chief Jeremy Bowers explained in the Department’s report. There were no home-invasion style robberies in 2021, which Bowers described as a “testament to the outstanding initial response by patrol officers, investigative work by the Detective Unit, and the Department ability to leverage technology.” In the seven robberies that occurred last year, Piedmont Police identified and arrested suspects in four instances. Touting the efficiency of Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) cameras, the report included that officers made 30 arrests and recovered 34 stolen vehicles with a valuation of $449,500 with ALPR assistance; by comparison, 17 arrests and 34 vehicles were recovered in 2020, with a valuation of $167,300. The Department has used ALPR technology since 2013 and is in the process of implementing a Public Safety Camera program, approved by City Council last year. “The current phase of the implementation consists of working with the data fiber provider and utility company to bring the necessary infrastructure to the camera locations. The Department is very appreciative for the assistance of Public Works Director Daniel Gonzalez through this process,” Chief Bowers said. Total calls for service increased last year, from 9,844 in 2020 to 10,636 in 2021. For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken. “He solved the daily bridge hand.”

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California’s popular annual White Elephant Sale will return in-person this year, though with reduced capacity. The Preview Sale will be held this Sunday, February 27, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Instead of one weekend for the regular sale, the museum will have sales throughout March, specifically March 2–5, 9–12, 16–19, and 23–26. A final “blowout” weekend sale will be held on April 2 and 3. Now in its 63rd year, the White Elephant Sale is run exclusively by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board, a group of over 100 members which raises proceeds to support the museum’s art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, and capital improvements. Since the Board’s inception in 1959, it has contributed over $23 million to the Museum. The White Elephant Sale, touted as Northern California’s largest rummage sale, generates a significant amount of funding for the museum. The Sale also boasts many volunteers from Piedmont – most of whom are members of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. Last year, due to COVID-19 Oakland Museum’s White Elephant Sale returns in person this year. and the large number of participants, the sale pivoted to onlineonly for the first time. The event returns this year with in-person shopping experiences that comply with current safety protocols - expect to wear proper masking while shopping and to present your vaccination card. Over the five-week-period of the sale, visitors may browse a range of quality, used goods. Furniture, household items, clothing, artwork, ceramics, sporting goods, music, books, and many other items will be for sale. Visit www.whiteelephantsale. org for donation information and to obtain tickets to the event on a date of your choosing. The White Elephant Warehouse site of the sale, is located at 333 Lancaster Street next to the Cal boathouse on the Oakland Estuary in the Fruitvale District.
articles.title: White Elephant Preview Sale is Sunday

articles.text: Piedmont resident and Russian-born writer Anastasia Edel appeared on CNN’s Saturday morning new show on February 19 to offer her observations on the ongoing Ukraine-Russia crisis. During the interview she explained why Americans should pay attention to the mounting tensions in Eastern Europe and the very real possibility of Russia invading its neighbor, Ukraine. Putin’s comments effectively called two regions in eastern Ukraine, where Russia-backed separatists had been operating since 2014, as sovereign states, and not beholden to being a part of Ukraine. The implication triggered dramatic action from the United States; President Joe Biden condemned Putin for his aggression toward Ukraine and joined other European leaders in imposing economic consequence and sanctions. “It’s a twist of logic,” Edel said. “Putin is saying because Ukraine is so close and related [to Russia], it doesn’t have the right to be independent. It’s classic propaganda. Take some facts: we have centuries of common history, language, and culture. Then mix them with falsehoods, like saying Ukraine is not a ‘real – Anastasia Edel CNN reached out to Edel following an Op-Ed she had written for the New York Times, of which she is a contributing writer. Edel is originally from Kransnodar in southern Russia and moved permanently to America in 1997. Her published work often includes observations of growing up in late-era USSR. Edel explained to CNN anchor Boris Sanchez the relationship between the neighboring countries, describing it as “two separate nations with legally defined borders,” but also with “shared demographic.” “Our blood flows in each other’s veins. pages.text: Wednesday, February 23, 2022 5 White Elephant Preview Sale is Sunday By Allyson Aleksey Oakland Museum of California’s popular annual White Elephant Sale will return in-person this year, though with reduced capacity. The Preview Sale will be held this Sunday, February 27, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Instead of one weekend for the regular sale, the museum will have sales throughout March, specifically March 2–5, 9–12, 16–19, and 23–26. A final “blowout” weekend sale will be held on April 2 and 3. Now in its 63rd year, the White Elephant Sale is run exclusively by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board, a group of over 100 members which raises proceeds to support the museum’s art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, and capital improvements. Since the Board’s inception in 1959, it has contributed over $23 million to the Museum. The White Elephant Sale, touted as Northern California’s largest rummage sale, generates a significant amount of funding for the museum. The Sale also boasts many volunteers from Piedmont – most of whom are members of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. Last year, due to COVID-19 Oakland Museum’s White Elephant Sale returns in person this year. and the large number of participants, the sale pivoted to onlineonly for the first time. The event returns this year with in-person shopping experiences that comply with current safety protocols - expect to wear proper masking while shopping and to present your vaccination card. Over the five-week-period of the sale, visitors may browse a range of quality, used goods. Furniture, household items, clothing, artwork, ceramics, sporting goods, music, books, and many other items will be for sale. Visit www.whiteelephantsale. org for donation information and to obtain tickets to the event on a date of your choosing. The White Elephant Warehouse site of the sale, is located at 333 Lancaster Street next to the Cal boathouse on the Oakland Estuary in the Fruitvale District. Piedmont Russian American writer Anastasia Edel appears on CNN By Allyson Aleksey Piedmont resident and Russian-born writer Anastasia Edel appeared on CNN’s Saturday morning new show on February 19 to offer her observations on the ongoing Ukraine-Russia crisis. During the interview she explained why Americans should pay attention to the mounting tensions in Eastern Europe and the very real possibility of Russia invading its neighbor, Ukraine. Putin’s comments effectively called two regions in eastern Ukraine, where Russia-backed separatists had been operating since 2014, as sovereign states, and not beholden to being a part of Ukraine. articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO) will perform its winter concert at First Congregational Church of Berkeley this Saturday, February 26, at 8 p.m. Six musicians from Piedmont High School are members of YPSO: Violinists Jacob Hsia, Isabella Wu, and Cameryn Kwong; Eleanor Vo, (viola) Caitlin Gong (cello); and Samantha Cheunkarndee (violin). All are seniors except Cheunkarndee, a freshman. This year marks YPSO’s 85th season and 33rd season under the baton of Maestro David Ramadanoff. More than Over 90 young musicians, ranging in age from 12 to 19, will perform. The concert will include the works of Dmitiri Shostakovich, and two living American composers, Jennifer Higdon and Adolphus Hailstork. The first half of the program will feature Blue Cathedral by Higdon and Epitaph of a Man Who Dreamed by Hailstork. Higdon described her piece as “about deciding if life was going to be about living or about death.” In describing his work, Hailstork said “I believe that African Americans deserve to have the same homage paid to their suffering, and to their glories when they occur, as has happened throughout all of Western history.” The concert was rescheduled for Martin Luther King, Jr. Day, January 17, but was rescheduled due to COVID-19 concerns. Tickets can be purchased by visiting http://www.ypsomusic.org/tickets, or calling the box office at (510) 849-9776. articles.text: In the February 9 school board meeting PUSD School District Facilities Director Pete Palmer provided the Piedmont Board with a preview of projects being planned for the summer. When the new theater building is completed, the focus will be on smaller projects including the updating of HVAC systems and the replacement of the turf at Becker Field at Havens School. “I am focusing on the projects that are critical to the health and safety of our staff,” said Palmer. articles.text: The Piedmont Community Service Crew’s “5K Mask Project” is an opportunity for our local community to work together on a simple task that will increase the supply of N95 masks, so urgently needed by health care workers and the general public. Many cannot afford to buy these to protect everyone’s health. On the weekend of March 5th & 6th we plan to have dozens of volunteers working simultaneously outdoors refurbishing N95 masks. The work project will be held at the Dress Best for Less parking lot, 799 Magnolia Avenue, across the street from Piedmont High School. Volunteer hours Saturday, March 5, 12:30 to 4:30 p.m. Sunday, March 6, 10:00 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. This event is being hosted by the Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC), a co-ed Venturing Crew that empowers teens through service and leadership opportunities. PCSC is currently making a big push to get 5,000 refurbished masks completed as soon as we can – precisely why your help at this event is making such a direct impact in helping us reach our goals. This will be a lively event with snacks and music and will be a fun and rewarding way to help others and meet new people. The project is recommended for middle schoolers and older. Anyone younger should come with a parent. For additional information, contact PCSC Vice Presidents Valentina Prieto-Black at valentinaprietoblack@icloud.com or Elena Stevenson at elena.stev@ gmail.com, or Crew Advisor Ken Li at ken.i.li@sbcglobal.com.

articles.text: As we discussed last month, we often neglect the cognitive skills that are used and developed and only focus on the subject matter that is being taught and learned. However, it is often these cognitive skills that have a more lasting benefit to students. Knowing history to avoid repeating it and appreciating literature is valuable. But what are the skills involved in liberal arts classes? The ability to understand another person’s ideas and perspective from their writing is one important skill. There are certainly others, but since this can be so tricky, we’ll just stick to that for today. What are They Trying to Tell Me? I remember I was reading Tom Sawyer in middle school and was going to write an essay on it. My brother was helping me and asked, “Why do you think Mark Twain wrote this book?” “To entertain people?” I asked. “Well partly that’s true,” he told me. “But there is almost always a deeper message about the world.” That message stuck with me and helped me navigate my English and Liberal Arts classes and reading in general for the rest of my life. Where Are They Coming From? Once you have figured out what an author is trying to tell you there is an important second step that we can take: how does this person see the world? This ability to see someone else’s perspective Students gain perspective through reading. is invaluable in navigating our complex and diverse world. Understanding Isn’t Empathy Too often the concept of “understanding” has a connotation of feeling for someone or not hating them. And sometimes this is true. Understanding someone’s point of view can help you see things differently and maybe your anger might dissipate. But feeling for them is not the goal and we can’t avoid seeing someone’s perspective because we don’t believe their perspective deserves our attention. You can never defeat your enemy if you don’t know where he is hiding. Why bother trying to understand how a KKK member sees the world? So that you can turn them or defeat them, not necessarily because I want to heal them. Reading for Perspective Reading to understand someone else’s point of view is not something that comes naturally. When reading it, it requires looking specifically at things that don’t make sense or seem wrong and figuring out what they must be thinking to see things this way. “What the heck are they thinking?!” needs to become a question, not an insult. Paul the Tutor (aka Paul Osborne) runs Paul the Tutor’s Education Services online and on Piedmont Avenue. Thinking Outside The Classroom Reading gives perepctive, not just information By Paul Osborne As we discussed last month, we often neglect the cognitive skills that are used and developed and only focus on the subject matter that is being taught and learned. However, it is often these cognitive skills that have a more lasting benefit to students. Knowing history to avoid repeating it and appreciating literature is valuable. But what are the skills involved in liberal arts classes? The ability to understand another person’s ideas and perspective from their writing is one important skill. There are certainly others, but since this can be so tricky, we’ll just stick to that for today. What are They Trying to Tell Me? I remember I was reading Tom Sawyer in middle school and was going to write an essay on it. My brother was helping me and asked, “Why do you think Mark Twain wrote this book?” “To entertain people?” I asked. “Well partly that’s true,” he told me. “But there is almost always a deeper message about the world.” That message stuck with me and helped me navigate my English and Liberal Arts classes and reading in general for the rest of my life. Where Are They Coming From? Once you have figured out what an author is trying to tell you there is an important second step that we can take: how does this person see the world? This ability to see someone else’s perspective ADVERTISE IN THE POST Students gain perspective through reading. is invaluable in navigating our complex and diverse world. Understanding Isn’t Empathy Too often the concept of “understanding” has a connotation of feeling for someone or not hating them. And sometimes this is true. Understanding someone’s point of view can help you see things differently and maybe your anger might dissipate. But feeling for them is not the goal and we can’t avoid seeing someone’s perspective because we don’t believe their perspective deserves our attention. You can never defeat your enemy if you don’t know where he is hiding. Why bother trying to understand how a KKK member sees the world? So that you can turn them or defeat them, not necessarily because I want to heal them. Reading for Perspective Reading to understand someone else’s point of view is not something that comes naturally. When reading it, it requires looking specifically at things that don’t make sense or seem wrong and figuring out what they must be thinking to see things this way. “What the heck are they thinking?!” needs to become a question, not an insult. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Working with the National Park Service, Piedmont Scouts in Troop 11 scored an end-of-season use of a campsite at scenic Kirby Cove near the base of the Golden Gate Bridge and Marin Headlands. Their mission the weekend of December 4-5 was to help with the overdue maintenance of the trail and campsite. Up until COVID two years ago, the Park Service winterized the campsites by cleaning out the firepits and ensuring that everything is clean and tidy. This year required some long overdue trail work and maintenance on the ADA compliant campsite. “It’s great to see Piedmont Troop 11 out here!” welcomed a park ranger. “We’ll have Piedmont Troop 1 out in the spring to open things up, too.” Scouts and leaders kicked off A view of the Golden Gate Bridge and San Francisco at night from Kirby Cove in Marin County is one of the rewards of being in Scouts. Scouts enjoy a ferry ride from Oakland to San Francisco. Piedmont Scouts from Troop 11 prepare to complete a service project at Kirby Cove near the Golden Gate Bridge. Scouts work to restore trails at Kirby Cover. the weekend adventure by taking the ferry from Oakland to San Francisco. They then hopped on a bus to the Presidio, and then a 5-mile hike across the Golden Gate Bridge and down to Kirby Cove. After dropping off their supplies, the Scouts got to work. After their service work was completed, they set up their campsites and began preparing dinner. Dinners by each Patrol ranged from On the hike across the Golden Gate Bridge, Troop 11 Scouts pause to look at wildlife in the Bay. mac ‘n cheese to sloppy joes, with some tasty desserts to provide a sweet finish. The Scouts enjoyed exploring an old artillery Battery in place since World War II, spending some time on the beach, and watching a classic sunset. On Sunday morning, after making breakfast and packing up, the troop had a closing circle to talk about what was great, what could have been better, and what Scouts are looking forward to. “Dinner was great!” was followed by “Dinner was awful,” from another patrol, highlighting the learning experience Scouts receive when planning and preparing their own food. articles.text: The Piedmont Cub Scout Day Camp, which takes place in Dracena Park the first week that school is out for the summer, is coming up fast. This year Piedmont Cubs and all youth (1st to 5th graders) will be traveling back in time with the theme: Wild, Wild West. With the help of an outstanding camp staff, the Piedmont Scout Council is excited to be offering a wide range of activities, most especially the archery range. Other activities will include Scout skills, games, songs and crafts. The Piedmont Fire Department will highlight the week with the traditional Egg Drop on the last day of camp as parents and families enjoy a picnic while watching the Egg Drop. Returning leadership includes 2021 Camp President Mollie King, Camp Crew Advisor Ken Li and Camp Director Keri Ichimaru. Eagle Scout Jack Gros is new to the team, bringing fresh ideas and energy. Along with other staff and leaders, they’re putting together an ace-high program for the adventures in Dracena Park. “I am always on the lookout for youth who respond positively to opportunities to take charge of what their crew is planning.” said Li. “During the past three years… our annual Cub Scout Day Camp [has] been entirely planned and run by teens.” “It was great to see how well the staff interacted with the younger Cubs,” noted Ichimaru about the 2021 camp. “Day Camp is a highlight of the program year,” confirmed Scout Executive Kate Benson. “Youth get a chance to be outside, bellow through songs, make new friends, and enjoy a week of fun. It’s something we look forward to all year.” Interested youth can register for camp through the Piedmont Recreation Department (piedmont.ca.gov/activityguide). Registration opens on March 1st for Piedmont residents and March 15th for non-residents. Youth interested in joining Cub Scouts, Scouts BSA, Venturing Units, or Exploring are encouraged to contact the Piedmont Scout Council for more information at 510-547-4493 or contact@piedmontbsa.org. For more information, visit the webpage at www.piedmontbsa.org, or mosey down and visit the Scouting staff at the office at 10 Highland Way in Piedmont. Campers test the buoyancy of their aluminum boats. Campers become artists with a rocky canvas.

articles.text: Theatre is back! Yes, across the Bay Area, we are starting to see signs of life returning to our stages. For many companies, it has been over 600 days since we last turned on our stage lights, donned costumes, dusted off the props and welcomed audiences in a traditional way. Yes, we have streamed, zoomed, performed outdoors, created audio plays and musicals and so many other ways that the theatre world has put our innovation to the test, but in the end, we have all missed the specific and unique energy between performers and an audience. Theatre gives us a window into our own hearts and reminds us of the stories of others. Our empathy and imagination muscles are ready to be flexed! For our young people, attending theatre can inspire kids to see beyond the boundaries of their world and dream big, while also stimulating the parts of their creative spirits that are yearning to express themselves. As Bay Area Children’s Theatre returns we are focussing on this aspect of imagination like never before. We have been on a slightly more delayed timeline as some of the adult companies to ensure that at least our 5 and up audience members have the opportunity to be vaccinated. Our new musical, The Imaginaries: An Immersive Musical, opening March 19th in Berkeley, transports the audience to the Imaginary World, where imaginary friends live and train for their work with humans. This production is based on the book “Pocket Guide for Imaginary Friends”, which was written by our writing team and is now available on amazon.com and Photo by Melissa Nigro. A family enjoys a Bay Area Children’s Theater performance. through the BACT website. The book and the show celebrate imagination and creativity as a means to dream up amazing adventures. As we return to the theatre, for both adults and kids, I look forward to the incredible power of storytelling to help us shape a brighter future. pages.text: Wednesday, February 23, 2022 11 16th Annual Summer Camps Edition Wild, Wild West Cub Scout Day Camp this summer The Piedmont Cub Scout Day Camp, which takes place in Dracena Park the first week that school is out for the summer, is coming up fast. This year Piedmont Cubs and all youth (1st to 5th graders) will be traveling back in time with the theme: Wild, Wild West. With the help of an outstanding camp staff, the Piedmont Scout Council is excited to be offering a wide range of activities, most especially the archery range. Other activities will include Scout skills, games, songs and crafts. The Piedmont Fire Department will highlight the week with the traditional Egg Drop on the last day of camp as parents and families enjoy a picnic while watching the Egg Drop. Returning leadership includes 2021 Camp President Mollie King, Camp Crew Advisor Ken Li and Camp Director Keri Ichimaru. Eagle Scout Jack Gros is new to the team, bringing fresh ideas and energy. Along with other staff and leaders, they’re putting together an ace-high program for the adventures in Dracena Park. “I am always on the lookout for youth who respond positively to opportunities to take charge of what their crew is planning.” said Li. “During the past three years… our annual Cub Scout Day Camp [has] been entirely planned and run by teens.” “It was great to see how well the staff interacted with the younger Cubs,” noted Ichimaru about the 2021 camp. “Day Camp is a highlight of the program year,” confirmed Scout Executive Kate Benson. “Youth get a chance to be outside, bellow through songs, make new friends, and enjoy a week of fun. It’s something we look forward to all year.” Interested youth can register for camp through the Piedmont Recreation Department (piedmont.ca.gov/activityguide). Registration opens on March 1st for Piedmont residents and March 15th for non-residents. Yes, across the Bay Area, we are starting to see signs of life returning to our stages. articles.text: Piedmont’s No. 2 seeded girls’ basketball team is set to square off with No. 3 Lick-Wilmerding tonight, Wednesday, February 23 at 7:00 p.m. in the North Coast Section semifinals at Binks Rawlings Gym. The girls powered their way past No. 10 St. Mary’s 76-50 on Saturday, February 19 in the quarterfinals, and demolished No. 15 Swett 74-14 in the opening round on Wednesday, February 16. Should PHS be victorious tonight, they advance to their first NCS finals appearance since 2011. The team has already qualified for the CIF State Tournament. Winning the NCS title would give them a higher seed in the state playoffs. “We’ve been wanting to start strong and compete right from the jump, and the girls have done a really good job of that,” said coach Bryan Gardere. “We’re very excited to be this far. The CIF is the ultimate tournament; it’s the tournament every basketball player wants to be in.” The Highlanders’ 76-50 win over St. Mary’s, a former longtime rival, was never in doubt, though junior forward Trinity Zamora left the game in the third quarter due to leg cramps. Sophomore guard Natalia Martinez picked up the slack with 33 points. “Trinity came out early and I knew what I had to do and what we had to do as a team,” said Martinez. “We can’t always depend on her to score and get rebounds, so we had to step up.” Zamora is fine and returned to practice the next day. She had high praise for Martinez and junior guard Maddie Hill’s leadership in Saturday’s game. Hill finished with 19 points. “Nat has stepped up big-time. She’s really embraced the leadership role and does a great job communicating with everyone. That’s a lot to ask from a sophomore… And Maddie did an exceptional job. We need her,” said Gardere. 76-50 win over St. Mary’s Piedmont led 21-11 by the end of the first quarter and 44-22 at halftime. The Highlanders started the fourth with a 57-39 advantage and finished off with 19 more points for the 76-50 final. Martinez scored 12 of her 33 points in the first half, and then added 21 more after intermission with Zamora not on the court. Thirteen of her points came in the fourth quarter. It was a critical performance and guaranteed that Piedmont would qualify for the NCS semifinal and a berth in the State Tournament. “We’re in the playoffs; we have to keep playing like it’s our last game,” exclaimed Martinez. “It could have been our last game if we lost. I think we had in the back of our minds that if we lost our lead, there would be no more practice after school and no more team lunches. “We aren’t ready to lose that; we had to win,” she added. It was a big game for senior role player Aniya Perine who had Staff Photos Natalia Martinez led PHS with 33 points in Piedmont’s 76-50 win over No. 10 St. Mary’s in the NCS Quarterfinals. 11 points including six in the first quarter, and a big blocked shot in the third quarter. Final stats include: Martinez with 33 points, seven rebounds, four assists, and four steals. Hill had 19 points, eight boards, four assists, and four steals. Zamora had nine points, five rebounds, five assists, four blocks. Perine scored 11 points, four rebounds, two steals and one block. Hannah Govert scored two, had five boards, three assists, and three steals. 74-14 win over Swett The Highlanders’ win was never in doubt against the overmatched team from Crockett, winning 74-14 in a one-sided affair on Wednesday, February 16 in the opening round of the playoffs. Final stats include Martinez with 27 points, Zamora scored 11 with six rebounds, Hill scored 13 points, Govert had eight. NEXT UP Pied mont (22-5) hosts Lick-Wil merdi ng ton ig ht, Wednesday, February 22 at 7:00 p.m. at Binks Rawlings Gym. With a win, PHS will face the winner of No. 1 Marin Catholic vs. No. 4 Gateway on Friday or Saturday, February 25-26. Maddie Hill scored 19 points against St. Mary’s. Aniya Perine had 11 points against St. Mary’s.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team, seeded No. 3, saw its season come to an end last night, Tuesday, February 22, after losing 57-55 to No. 2 Branson in the Division 3 North Coast Section semifinals in Novato. The Highlanders swept to a comfortable 63-33 defeat of No. 11 Encinal in the quarterfinals on Friday, February 18 at Binks Rawlings Gym. The Highlanders needed a victory over Branson in order to qualify for the State playoffs. It would have been their second consecutive NCS Final after winning Division 4 in 2020 prior to the pandemic. Now playing as a Div. 3 team, new NCS rules require Div. 1, 2, and 3 teams to reach the Finals in order to qualify for the State tournament. “Branson is a tough team, they are really well-coached. articles.text: The City of Piedmont has launched an online survey for residents to provide input on the Piedmont Community Pool programming. The pool is set to open in summer 2024; the final design phase was recently approved by City Council. The 15-minute survey is geared toward aquatic programming and focuses on the community’s interest in various programming opportunities at the new aquatic facility. The Piedmont Recreation Department compiled a wide variety of programming to start understanding the community’s interests. Guaranteed programming is listed first, followed by additional options that residents may “rank.” Guaranteed programming includes the yearround Piedmont Swim Team, high school water polo and swim teams, lap swimming, swim lessons, open swim, and lifeguard training. At the completion of the survey, an overall site plan from community workshops is available so that residents may view and provide additional comments or suggestions. To complete the survey, visit https://www.surveymonkey. com/r/Piedmontcommunitypoolprogramming.

articles.text: A retrospective of geometric art by the late Bill Blackwell will be on display at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from noon to 2 p.m. on Sunday, February 27. An architect by profession with a lifelong love of geometry, Blackwell’s art work consists of large collages of geometric shapes painted in bright colors, mounted on Masonite. He was fascinated by the possibilities of combining basic shapes and colors into dynamic art. Before he passed away in November 2021, Blackwell also was working on a book he tentatively titled Explorations in Geometry, which focuses on the mathematical beauty of plain geometry and its multiple uses in the built environment. In the book’s introduction, Blackwell noted, “Galileo was one of the first modern thinkers to clearly state that the laws of nature are mathematical. In The Assayer, published in 1623, Galileo wrote ‘philosophy is written in this grand book, the universe… It is written in the language of mathematics, and its characters are triangles, circles, and other geometric figures.’” Blackwell’s first book, Geometry in Architecture, was published by John Wiley & Sons in 1983. His art was previously exhibited at Piedmont Center for the Arts the day it opened in August 2011. His vivid yellow geometric design was the principal work of art and located above the stage. He earlier had a large art exhibit at the former Metro Center in downtown Oakland. He also exhibited his art at the Mathematical Science Research Institute at UC Berkeley, the Hearst Gallery at St. Mary’s College in Moraga, and a gallery in Pt. Reyes. Blackwell received his undergraduate degree at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and his master’s degree in architecture at UC Berkeley. During his career, he was employed by the architecture firm Skidmore and Merrill, the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency, and the Bechtel Corporation for 20 years. He is survived by his wife Marjorie of Piedmont. This work of geometric art by Bill Blackwell was first shown in Piedmont on opening day of the Piedmont Center for the Arts in 2011. articles.title: Blackwell geometric art exhibit continues on Sunday at PCA

articles.text: Writer and artist Chanel Miller’s exhibit, entitled I was, I am, I will be, is being shown on the exterior wall of the San Francisco Asian Art Museum on Hyde Street and is free for everyone to view. Miller was first known publicly as Emily Doe, the victim of sexual assault by a student at Stanford University in 2015. The victim impact statement she wrote and read at her assailant’s sentencing hearing the following year went viral and was read 11 million times within four days. The case gained international recognition because the assailant, a 19-year-old male athlete, received a sentence of three months in jail. The case influenced the California legislature to require prison terms for rapists whose victims were unconscious. Judge Persky, who handed down the light sentence, was recalled from office by county voters in 2018. Miller’s memoir detailing the tragic event caught the attention of the Asian Art Museum’s head of Contemporary Art, Abby Chen. “Not only is she an amazChanel Miller’s exhibit I was, I am, I will be seen from the exterior of the Asian museum. ing writer, she’s also this visual artist...she’s incredibly young,” Chen said. Chen and museum staff began the process of collaborating with Miller. Growing up in Palo Alto, Miller said she frequented the museum, but never dreamed she would be featured one day. “Whenever I was upset, I’d take a sharpie to the wall and sit for hours and let these ‘creatures’ come to life. I could create landscapes that don’t have narrow borders. That’s the scene that came out of this feeling,” Miller said. Even though the museum’s doors were closed due to the COVID pandemic, Miller’s exhibit was visible without visitors setting foot in the building. At night, Miller’s black and white figures are illuminated and visible from the street. “The whole journey of healing is never linear,” Miller said, adding that she hopes the piece will be seen as universal and not confined to her particular experience.
articles.title: Chanel Millers art on Asian Art Museum exterior

His art was previously exhibited at Piedmont Center for the Arts the day it opened in August 2011. His vivid yellow geometric design was the principal work of art and located above the stage. He earlier had a large art exhibit at the former Metro Center in downtown Oakland. He also exhibited his art at the Mathematical Science Research Institute at UC Berkeley, the Hearst Gallery at St. Mary’s College in Moraga, and a gallery in Pt. Reyes. Blackwell received his undergraduate degree at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and his master’s degree in architecture at UC Berkeley. During his career, he was employed by the architecture firm Skidmore and Merrill, the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency, and the Bechtel Corporation for 20 years. He is survived by his wife Marjorie of Piedmont. Chanel Millers art on Asian Art Museum exterior By Allyson Aleksey Writer and artist Chanel Miller’s exhibit, entitled I was, I am, I will be, is being shown on the exterior wall of the San Francisco Asian Art Museum on Hyde Street and is free for everyone to view. Miller was first known publicly as Emily Doe, the victim of sexual assault by a student at Stanford University in 2015. The victim impact statement she wrote and read at her assailant’s sentencing hearing the following year went viral and was read 11 million times within four days. The case gained international recognition because the assailant, a 19-year-old male athlete, received a sentence of three months in jail. The case influenced the California legislature to require prison terms for rapists whose victims were unconscious. Judge Persky, who handed down the light sentence, was recalled from office by county voters in 2018. Miller’s memoir detailing the tragic event caught the attention of the Asian Art Museum’s head of Contemporary Art, Abby Chen. “Not only is she an amazChanel Miller’s exhibit I was, I am, I will be seen from the exterior of the Asian museum. ing writer, she’s also this visual artist...she’s incredibly young,” Chen said. Chen and museum staff began the process of collaborating with Miller. Growing up in Palo Alto, Miller said she frequented the museum, but never dreamed she would be featured one day. “Whenever I was upset, I’d take a sharpie to the wall and sit for hours and let these ‘creatures’ come to life. I could create landscapes that don’t have narrow borders. That’s the scene that came out of this feeling,” Miller said. Even though the museum’s doors were closed due to the COVID pandemic, Miller’s exhibit was visible without visitors setting foot in the building. At night, Miller’s black and white figures are illuminated and visible from the street. “The whole journey of healing is never linear,” Miller said, adding that she hopes the piece will be seen as universal and not confined to her particular experience. articles.text: The Ambroš Duo, a renowned mother-son music duo coming from Prague in the Czech Republic, will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, March 12 at 5:00 p.m. Sponsored by Sokol San Francisco, the concert will feature works by Mozart, Sarasate, and Czech composers Dvořák and Smetana. The concert will conclude with the lively “Monti Czardas.” Miroslav Ambroš studied violin at the Prague Conservatory of Music and the Hochschule für Musik und Theater in Germany. Ambroš has worked with important musicians, including Pinchas Zukerman and Ruggiero Ricci, and from 2008 to 2011 exclusively took lessons from Maestro Josef Suk, the great-grandson of Czech composer Antonin Dvořák, In his music career Mr. Ambroš has been awarded various prizes, including the international competition “Du Prix des Jeunes Talents Européens de Musique Classique” in Marseille. He received first place in the Competition of Bohdan Warchal, Slovakia, Kocian´s Violin Competition, and Beethoven’s Hradec International Music Competition. He holds a prestigious award from the Yamaha piano company and won the national competition Concertino Praga for chamber ensembles. Mr. Ambroš performs on a violin made in 1734 by the Italian master luthier Camillo de Camilli. The instrument is part of a collection of musical instruments from the Czech National Museum. H i s m o t h e r, Z u z a n a Ambrošová, began her conservatory studies in the city of Košice, Slovakia, and graduated from the Music Academy of Performing Arts in Prague. She also studied piano in Weimar, Germany. At the age of 16 as the laureate of the Smetana Piano Competition and other international competiPhoto by Jakub Ludvik Miroslav Ambroš and Zuzana Ambrošová, the mother-son Ambroš Duo from Prague, Czech Republic, will perform a concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts on March 12. tions, she became a solo artist in the State Philharmonic Orchestra Košice, and made a successful appearance with the Vienna Philharmonic. She taught piano at the conservatory in Košice for 10 years and performed in Slovakia and abroad. Mrs. Ambrošová is a highly sought-after chamber player, performing in international festivals and competitions. articles.text: San Francisco Ballet will present its production of Don Quixote, opening February 26, with the music of Ludwig Minkus and choreography of Alexander Gorksy and Marius Petipa. Don Quixote, based on the classic novel by Miguel de Cervantes, is filled with physical humor and fiery dancing - Artistic Director and Principal Choreographer Helgi Tomasson said one of the production’s most appealing aspects is “the joy it gives you - you could say it’s a bit of a farce, nothing dramatic or psychological. It’s upbeat and fun.” Don Quixote first took the stage at San Francisco Ballet in 2003, and over the years has been updated by Tomasson. In 2012, award-winning costume designer Martin Pakledinaz introduced 19th-century Spanish garb and visually striking scenery. In reworking the classic story, Paklendinaz, who passed away shortly after the 2012 premiere, said “it’s important to drop what you’ve seen and try to make it your original production.” Performances will be at 8 p.m. in the War Memorial Opera House on Saturday, February 26 at 8 p.m., Sunday, February 27 at 2 p.m., and daily through March 6. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfballet.org/aboutdon-quixote/.

articles.text: After being in The Music Man and The Light in the Piazza with Youth Musical Theater Company, Piedmont resident Evie Mitchell, a junior at Bishop O’Dowd, appears in the role of Mrs. Lovett in YMTC’s production of the musical Sweeney Todd, opening on March 18. Also in the show is Ellie Broscow, a 10th grader at Piedmont High. Come see and hear the thrills and chills of one of Stephen Sondheim’s masterpieces, Sweeney Todd, The Demon Barber of Fleet Street, with a cast of the Bay Area’s best and brightest student actors. YMTC is a stellar company which produces captivating musicals with a live orchestra and performing arts students from local high schools, as well as colleges and universities. YMTC’s 17th season opens with the epic Penny Dreadful-inspired revenge tragedy, Sweeney Todd: the Demon Barber of Fleet Street, with music and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim, based upon a book by Hugh Wheeler and the 1973 play by Christopher Bond. In 19th century London, barber Sweeney Todd returns home from serving time for unjust charges trumped up by a cruel judge. Having lost everyone he loves, he teams up with Mrs. Lovett, the proprietress of a meat pie shop, to seek vengeance for his family – and provide the pie shop with plenty of fresh meat. The ensuing morality tale is dark, twisted, gothic, and wickedly funny, set to one of Stephen Sondheim’s finest scores. Performance dates Friday March 18, 7 p.m. Saturday & Sunday, March 19-20, 3 p.m. Friday & Saturday, March 25-26, 7 p.m. Sunday March 27, 2 p.m. Tickets are $36 General Admission, $32 for Seniors. All audience members must show proof of vaccination to enter the lobby and theater. All members ages 5 and up will be required to wear masks in the lobby and theater.

articles.text: Thursday is family day in my home. That was the excuse to have two little kids prepare an elegant dinner for six. My grandchildren are 4-1/2 and seven. All that it took on my part was a little imagination. They made roast chicken with carrots, onions, and potatoes, and it couldn’t have been easier. All you need to keep in mind is that kids love fingerpainting. It is probably best to use a cast iron pan, but you can use anything that’s large enough for the chicken. Preheat the oven to 400°. Take your cast-iron pan and moisten it with some olive oil and sprinkle with a couple of pinches of salt. The chicken should be about 4 pounds. First, let the kids smear the chicken with mayonnaise. While they are fingerpainting the chicken, cut two onions in half and put them in the skillet. Cut up some carrots any way you like and enough potatoes for your diners. Put all the vegetables into the skillet and then put the chicken on top of the vegetables. You might want to add some seasoning - Italian herbs will work. Roast the chicken in the oven about one hour or until it is done. Take it out and let it rest about 10 minutes before carving. Put the vegetables on a platter along with slices of the chicken. That’s about all you need to do. The meal was delicious, and the kids had a great time enjoying the results of their culinary adventure. It couldn’t have been easier. The sensational discovery inspired one of the most popular songs of the time, “Old King Tut” If you listen to the song for its musical value, you’ll also learn a little bit of history. articles.text: Artist Robert Brokl will have an exhibit, “What I’ve Been Up To” at Piedmont Center for the Arts March 5–20. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays, with an artist’s reception on Sunday, March 13 at 2 p.m. The landscape-themed exhibition features recent paintings (oil and gouache), pastel drawings, and woodblock prints, with Brokl’s reflections of trips to the Southern Sierra Nevadas, the deserts of Death Valley and Anza Borrego, and the Mendocino area of California’s North Coast. It is a visual diary of recent travels, from the austere, spare deserts and the flora and fauna that survive temperature extremes. “What’s also become sadly apparent is how vulnerable these places are to the effects of the changing climate,” Brokl said. “My depictions of vast forests, azure lakes, and minimalist, unspoiled, primordial deserts are ‘Befores,’ and serve as records of these areas from before the 2020 Creek Fire.”

Robert Brokl art show opens March 5 at PCA Artist Robert Brokl will have an exhibit, “What I’ve Been Up To” at Piedmont Center for the Arts March 5–20. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays, with an artist’s reception on Sunday, March 13 at 2 p.m. The landscape-themed exhibition features recent paintings (oil and gouache), pastel drawings, and woodblock prints, with Brokl’s reflections of trips to the Southern Sierra Nevadas, the deserts of Death Valley and Anza Borrego, and the Mendocino area of California’s North Coast. articles.text: Review by Jay Russell Wow. Watching The Matrix: Resurrections left me in a state of incoherence. Where do I start with the fourth iteration of the groundbreaking 1995 philosophical sci-fi thriller The Matrix? The original film, starring Keanu Reeves, Laurence Fishburne, and Carrie-Anne Moss, blew my mind at age 12 when I saw it at Jack London Theater. I was drawn into the theater this time expecting to find out what would happen if Neo (Keanu Reeves) took the blue pill and decided to stay in his “illusionary world” instead of taking the red pill, as he did in the original film for the inconvenient truth of the “real”, post-apocalyptic world. After watching the latest version, viewers should be warned that the word plot is a misnomer. The direction of the film felt like a lottery ball drawing, each scene more random with new irrelevant characters assuming desperate roles. It is two and half hours of irrelevance The original movie asked questions such as: What if the things you see are not real? What if you were chained up in a cave and all you knew were shadows on the wall, but never the things making the shadows. The first Matrix film is an allegory to a scenario called Plato’s Cave. The timeless philosophical situation was retold in the first Matrix with modern implications pertinent to religion, the limits of perception and the question of existence. In the new film Reeves plays Mr. Anderson, who did not evolve into the hero named Neo. Anderson is a techie in San Francisco, that designed a video game essentially bringing the world of “the Matrix” to life through video games. He is supposed to feel yearning for Carrie Anne Moss’s character “Trinity,” who lives in an unhappy marriage in this alternate scenario. But there is no chemistry; there are no sparks when they see each other at a coffee shop. The plot failed. Further, why was it filmed in San Francisco throughout the thick of the pandemic? It was pretty much created with computer graphics. I would compare it with the stinker Starship Troopers 2, which used b-roll stock footage from the original 1997 Starship Troopers in the sequel, pawning them off as new scenes. In the Matrix: Resurrections there were many flashbacks to the same footage from the first film. They were mixed in with rehashed scenes that felt like cover band performances. Any original content made little sense. A big mistake was the absence of the great actor Laurence Fishburne as Morpheus. Instead of just letting him be dead from the earlier film, he was “replaced” by two characters, a look-alike and some odd entity, possibly the digital version of Morpheus’ soul? Yikes, just let dead dogs lie. This film cost nearly one fifth of a billion dollars, a whopping $190 million, but earned $157 million at the box office. Perhaps they were lucky to lose only $33 million. Keanu Reeves looks ahead to a fourth movie in the John Wick series, which actually has Laurence Fishburne. Basically the John Wick films take all the awesome gunmanship and action from The Matrix and use a simple but effective plot: a retired hitman’s dog gets killed so he goes on a revenge killing spree. Where The Matrix series crumbles, John Wick succeeds. How many know that Keanu Reeves is actually a competitive marksman? He makes the action scenes in John Wick look real, because he knows what he is doing. But the new Matrix movie hardly ever put a gun in Reeves’ hand. That is like casting George Clooney in a Batman suit and mask so no one could see him. Is The Matrix: Resurrections worse than Batman and Robin (1997) with Clooney? Maybe not. Clooney himself said, “I think we may have killed [The Batman] franchise.” It’s a coin toss which was worse. The Matrix: Resurrections. Directed by Lana Wachowski. Starring Keanu Reeves, and Carrie Anne-Moss. 2 hrs., 28 min. Rated R. Meryl Streep, Steve Martin, Alec Baldwin and Lake Bell in a scene from “It’s Complicated.” Actors in The Matrix: Resurrections (top left Keanu Reeves, bottom left Carrie Anne-Moss, top right Jonathan Groff) probably needed lots of coffee to stay awake during the filming. articles.text: Perhaps it’s time to banish that all too familiar line, “This is a chick flick,” no matter that the genre is still alive and well in Hollywood: young female twenty-somethings in the hunt for that special guy who will complete them. Yet there are also films about women who live very different lives and have very different definitions of what completes them. Case in point would be the recently released “It’s Complicated.” This is a woman’s movie to be sure; however, the target demographic is women 40 and older. Nancy Meyer (“Baby Boom,” “Something’s Gotta Give,” “The Holiday”) has been writing and directing romantic comedies about mature women for the better part of two decades. Her protagonists have had enough life experience to make insightful comparisons (that was then, this is now), bridling when things begin to feel hauntingly familiar. “It’s Complicated” has at its center the incomparable Meryl Streep, portraying Jane Adler, divorced for over a decade from Jake, played by Alec Baldwin. As a middle-aged woman, Jane has it all (well, almost all): a gorgeous, semi-rural home in Santa Barbara; a prosperous, up-scale bakery and café; three grown children; and is an accomplished chef. But still no man in her life. And therein is the rub. At her son’s NYU graduation (the whole family gathers in Manhattan), she unexpectedly has drinks and dinner with Jake with much dancing before and after. Jake is attending the ceremony without his younger wife, Agness (Lake Bell) – buff and demanding and the mother of 5-year-old Pedro. Drunk, swept away by familiar emotions and alcohol, they fall into bed and into an affair resurrecting all kinds of issues that had long ago been if not resolved at least buried. Jane is suddenly the other woman and completely unhinged by events. Jake is energized, captivated and even jealous of Jane’s casual flirtations with her architect, Adam (Steve Martin). The situation makes for engaging comedy. What Meyers does, and does well, is focus on a certain type of woman: mature, professional, once wounded, affluent and feeling she has been sleeping alone for far too long. Jane’s circle of friends, all contemporaries, equally attractive, are at first shocked when told about Jake; yet they remain supportive. Meyer is adept at creating a world that is more fantasy than reality, possessing a bright patina, a bit Disneyesque, lacking any semblance of grit, inspired, it seems, by Crate and Barrel, Architectural Digest and J. Crew. In a nice way. Meyer can easily be forgiven, however, for her movies always possess characters that are exceedingly charming and likable and the world Jane inhabits is deliciously seductive, bathed in a golden glow that brightens every moment. Of course Streep is brilliant, as always. She can actually elicit a laugh from the audience by a single, nuanced expression and she runs the gamut of emotions in the film with consummate ease. Her range and ability as an actress are astonishing. Take note of this year’s Julie and Julia, a role that will certainly result in a nomination. Alec Baldwin is also superb, playing the role of the chunky, aging, well-heeled, roguish husband, suddenly filled with a newly awakened lust and an abiding regret for what he left behind (children, hearth and wife of 20 years) when he wandered off and into the arms of Agness where gravity and age have yet to appear. Both Streep and Baldwin possess excellent comedic timing and make evident their deep well of talent in scene after scene. Though Baldwin is a strong presence in “It’s Complicated,” this is a woman’s film from the first frame and peruses women’s anxieties and issues with a pastiche of honesty and comedy. Meyers also appreciates a tidy ending and manages to find one that seems just right. It’s Complicated. Starring Meryl Streep, Alec Baldwin, Steve Martin, John Krasinski and Rita Wilson.Written and directed by Nancy Meyer. Rated R

articles.text: Kodi Smit-McPhee and Benedict Cumberbatch in The Power of the Dog. Review by Chris Honoré The mythology of the American west is replete with images of men who are symbols of leathery masculinity and independence, two examples, among many, being John Wayne (The Searchers), and Clint Eastwood (Pale Rider). Now comes The Power of the Dog, released in the latter part of 2021, first in theaters and shortly thereafter on Netflix. It has received 12 Oscar nominations, one for Best Picture, and written and directed by Jane Campion. It is based on Thomas Savage’s 1967 novel of the same name. The film is set on a large cattle ranch in the wide expanses of Montana (the picture was actually shot in New Zealand). The year is 1925. The film stars Benedict Cumberbatch as Phil Burbank, Jesse Plemons as his brother George (they co-own the ranch), Kristen Dunst as the widowed Rose, and Kodi Smit-McPhee portraying Rose’s younger brother, Peter, a medical student. Phil is your classic, deliberately unwashed, and unrepentantly blunt rancher who calls George, always well-groomed, even when riding, “fatso.” He also takes cruel exception to Rose’s younger, somewhat effeminate brother Peter, who waits tables at Rose’s small town café, wears white canvas shoes instead of boots, and poses a startling contrast to the ranch’s cowhands – and to Phil’s departed mentor and role model, the quintessential cowboy known as Bronco Henry. He was a man who was the very definition of masculinity, no matter how toxic. As it turns out, George becomes enamored with Rose, and soon returns to the ranch with her as his new bride. For Phil, Rose’s very presence on the ranch fills him with resentment, seemingly for no other reason than she is a woman, and he takes a cruel pleasure in tormenting her. Soon the family (Peter has returned to the ranch from school for the summer) slips into dysfunction, and Rose begins to use alcohol to cope. Phil, of course, continues to play the role of rugged rancher, despite the fact that he graduated Phi Beta Kappa. from Yale University. Surprisingly, he decides to take Peter in hand, hoping to mold him in his own ersatz image. Strangely, Peter simultaneously resists and complies and a bond is unexpectedly created between the two that is complex, suggesting that there is almost a quasi-erotic aspect to their relationship. All of the above begs the question: did I find Power of the Dog compelling? Despite all of the praise the film has received, I found its plot elusive, its tone dark, its characters remote (the deconstruction by Campion of the American cowboy?), even puzzling. Phil, meanwhile, seems damaged beyond understanding, his bullying rage causing me to wonder if he is keeping a secret that to him is unthinkable, and the end of the film borders on the strange. Power of the Dog. Written and directed by Jane Campion. Starring Benedict Cumberbatch, Kristen Dunst, Jesse Plemons. Streaming on Netflix and in theaters. 2 hrs., 8 min. Rated R

articles.text: Small Foot, an animated feature released in 2018, is the name that Yetis, a massive furry creature, has given to humans. The Yeti live in a village, isolated on top of a mountain above the clouds in the Himalayas. The story opens with Yeti Migo (Channing Tatum), who is careful to live by the ancient laws of the stones, which are kept by the Stonekeeper (Common), the village leader. Migo is tasked with the job of hitting a gong each morning with his head, which the Yetis believe causes the sun to rise. One morning, distracted by Meechee, a cute Yeti, and the Stonekeeper’s daughter, upon whom he has a crush, Migo misses the gong and to his surprise lands outside the village where he witnesses a plane crash, piloted by a Small Foot, a human that the Yetis believe is mythical. Astonished, Migo races back to the village to tell everyone what he saw. The villagers refuse to believe Migo and banish him from the village. And thus begins Migo’s adventure, which includes spending time below the clouds, a place he never thought existed. It’s there that he meets a human named Percy (James Cordon), a wildlife documentarian, who has heard the tale of the existence of Migo from the pilot and is eager to film him as proof that such enormous creatures do exist. Percy’s situation is that he has lost his audience and sees filming Migo as a way of regaining his viewers. When Percy does meet Migo, he is initially scared, and in his panic he shoots himself with a tranquilizer gun. Migo puts the unconscious Percy in a sleeping bag and prepares to take him home to his village as proof that he was indeed telling the truth about the existence of the Small Foot. But on the way, above the clouds, the two are hit with a blizzard that freezes Percy solid. Migo tries to thaw Percy over a fire, something that terrifies the human who thinks Migo is preparing to eat him. Percy finally realizes that Migo has saved him, and they keep going, finally arriving at the Yeti’s mountaintop village. Of course, things get complicated and the villagers, especially Meechee, worry that Percy will reveal the location of their secret village and humans will find them. And there’s the difficulty that Percy and Migo and Meechee have communicating with this Small Foot. But finally they manage to find a way which allows them to resolve the misunderstandings that have existed between the Yetis and, well, the Small Feet. Small Foot. Animation. Directed by Karey Kirkpatrick. With voices of Channing Tatum, James Corden, and Zendaya. 1 hr. 36 min. Streaming by Warner Bros.

The story opens with Yeti Migo (Channing Tatum), who is careful to live by the ancient laws of the stones, which are kept by the Stonekeeper (Common), the village leader. Migo is tasked with the job of hitting a gong each morning with his head, which the Yetis believe causes the sun to rise. One morning, distracted by Meechee, a cute Yeti, and the Stonekeeper’s daughter, upon whom he has a crush, Migo misses the gong and to his surprise lands outside the village where he witnesses a plane crash, piloted by a Small Foot, a human that the Yetis believe is mythical. Astonished, Migo races back to the village to tell everyone what he saw. The villagers refuse to believe Migo and banish him from the village. And thus begins Migo’s adventure, which includes spending time below the clouds, a place he never thought existed. It’s there that he meets a human named Percy (James Cordon), a wildlife documentarian, who has heard the tale of the existence of Migo from the pilot and is eager to film him as proof that such enormous creatures do exist. Percy’s situation is that he has lost his audience and sees filming Migo as a way of regaining his viewers. When Percy does meet Migo, he is initially scared, and in his panic he shoots himself with a tranquilizer gun. Migo puts the unconscious Percy in a sleeping bag and prepares to take him home to his village as proof that he was indeed telling the truth about the existence of the Small Foot. But on the way, above the clouds, the two are hit with a blizzard that freezes Percy solid. Migo tries to thaw Percy over a fire, something that terrifies the human who thinks Migo is preparing to eat him. Percy finally realizes that Migo has saved him, and they keep going, finally arriving at the Yeti’s mountaintop village. Of course, things get complicated and the villagers, especially Meechee, worry that Percy will reveal the location of their secret village and humans will find them. And there’s the difficulty that Percy and Migo and Meechee have communicating with this Small Foot. But finally they manage to find a way which allows them to resolve the misunderstandings that have existed between the Yetis and, well, the Small Feet. Small Foot. Animation. articles.text: Troop 6 went on its annual snow camping trip to Lake Alpine the 3-day weekend of January 15-17. Lake Alpine is located east of Arnold on Highway 4, just past the Bear Valley ski resort. The road is closed for the winter and the area becomes a winter playground for outdoor enthusiasts who enjoy snowmobiling, cross country skiing, snowshoeing, and for the Scouts, snow camping. As is the tradition of Troop 6, a total of 23 Scouts and leaders hiked into their camping area, pulling all their gear on sleds. Troop 6 Scouts enjoy a campfire in the snow. Pictured are Peter Ichimaru, Fred Bunkers, Scoutmaster Bill Bruin, Alek von Komarniki, and Jack Throne. Soup’s On. Peter Ichimaru prepared a wonderful Ramen lunch for the Scouts. The campground picnic tables were buried under snow with only the tops of street signs and restroom roofs providing landmarks. Snow camping requires some advance planning to ensure everyone has the clothing and equipment needed to be safe in the cold. Prior to the trip, a Troop meeting was dedicated to reviewing equipment lists and checking to make sure that everything was properly packed. The Scouts had great weather on the trip, relatively warm during the day with blue, sunny skies, and freezing at night. Snow camping presents different challenges than camping in other seasons. Staying warm is one of the key challenges. The temperature ranged from downright balmy in the sun, too cold in the shade, and difficult to Tucker Presnell is shown building a snow fort. articles.text: Wednesday Walkerss on February 16: Marion Lim Yankowitz, Martin Levy, Mike Henn, Linda Brown with her K-9 best friend Champagne, Claudia Lopez, Alan Goldhammer, Jim Kellogg, Peter Persoff, Jo Normington with her K-9 best friend Penny Lane, Renee Goldhammer, Wenny Young, Adrienne Hamlin, Pat McMahon, Helen Dong, Christine Calliste, Priscilla Wanerus, Quincy Dong, Carole Lyons, Sherry Jacobs, Pat Keller, Charlene Louie, Siow Fang Tan, Alicia Rivera, Noemi Alvarado, Jim Kuo, Brenda Ferrero, Melba Yee, Harriette Louie, Carol Long, and Cheryl Papin. It was another beautiful morning and strong turnout for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group on February 16. There were 33 walkers, including Cheryl Papin, a friend of Susan Brown visiting from St. Louis. The warm weather has made for an early spring in terms of trees and flowers blooming early. Longtime locals have noted plants that once bloomed in March are now flowering in February, January, or even late December. Climate change seems to be the reason and is an existential problem. Daffodils made an appearance around town a week or two ago, and “tulip tree” magnolias were in bloom too. White and pink flowering fruit tree blossoms were just starting to pop and a joy to see. Over the weekend it was noted that on Huntleigh Road, just off Hampton Road there was a long line of trees with snow white blossoms on both sides of the street, and that they climbed all the way up its hill. Going to see this once-a-year spectacle seemed like a wonderful destination, so Huntleigh was the group’s destination for the day. The walkers went up Highland Avenue, crossing it to Sheridan Avenue, and down to its intersection with Wildwood Avenue. The home of Jacqueline Davis on this corner has lovely flowers in its garden throughout the year, so the group stopped and enjoyed them before taking the usual shortcut through the Hall Fenway. Crossing the street, the group walked through Crocker Park and enjoyed the large tulip magnolias on its north side; as well as the Benny Bufano statue of a mother bear with nursing cubs in the center of the park. The walkers passed the huge eucalyptus trees on Hampton Road where St. James Drive ends. The group continued on Hampton past Hampton Park, and pressed on up Hampton to Huntleigh. Going through the large, white columns originally marked the main entrance to the St. James Woods real estate development, they admired azaleas and in a beautifully landscaped front yard. Further up Hampton the walkers arrived at Huntleigh Road and caught their first sight of the white, flowering trees lining the street as far as they could see. As they continue up Huntleigh, they were surprised and delighted to see Carol Long. one of the group’s original members. She lives nearby told the group that the City planted flowering plum trees many years ago. The blossoming trees continued on Lexford, and the group followed them down its hill. Further down Lexford, just before Hampton, the walkers came to a unique, brick home built in a storybook architecture style with a brick block maze in the front yard. There is also a circular brick chimney and a wavy brick wall, as well as a terracotta tile roof. Architect Jim Kellogg, a regular Wednesday walker and a former member of the Piedmont Planning Commission pointed out that the house also has a unique brick garage to the right, and that there is a swimming pool in the back. It was then time to retrace their steps and head back to the Exedra. It had been a 3-1/2 mile walk in a little more than 90 minutes with natural beauty that can only be enjoyed this time of year. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday, rain or shine, at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: City of Piedmont 2023-2031 Housing Element Update NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that, as the Lead Agency overseeing this project’s environmental review, the City of Piedmont is soliciting comments on the scope and content of the EIR for the proposed Housing Element Update. The Housing Element is one of the seven state-mandated elements of the local General Plan and is required to be updated every eight years. The City of Piedmont is preparing the 2023- 2031 Housing Element Update to comply with the legal mandate that requires each local government to identify adequate sites for housing to meet the existing and projected housing needs for varying income-levels in the community. It is intended to provide the city with a comprehensive strategy for promoting the production of safe, decent and affordable housing, and affirmatively furthering fair housing during the housing cycle. The Housing Element Update establishes goals, policies, and actions to address the existing and projected housing needs in Piedmont. The project is applicable to the entire City of Piedmont (citywide). Additional information is available on the City’s housing policy website at: https://www.piedmontishome.org/housing-element-update Members of the public and public agencies are invited to provide comments in writing as to the scope and content of the EIR before Friday, March 18, 2022. Please mail your comments to Kevin Jackson, Planning & Building Director, City of Piedmont, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611; or send via email to kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov. A Scoping Meeting will be held by the Planning Commission on March 1, 2022, at 5:30 p.m. The meeting will be held via video and teleconference. Interested parties should check the Planning Commission website for information on how to join the meeting and to confirm the meeting date, time, and agenda: https:// piedmont.ca.gov/government/commissions___committees/planning_commission

articles.text: Former Piedmont resident Mitchell W. Winters, a decorated veteran of the United States Marine Corps and a police officer in Arizona, committed suicide last November. This past Sunday, February 20, 2022, a warehouse full of dedicated fitness enthusiasts came together on a brisk holiday weekend morning to raise money in Mitch’s memory for The National Suicide Prevention Lifeline. The event, called the Winter Warrior workout and held in Phoenix, Arizona, was a rousing success. It raised more than $13,000 and more than 90 people participated. The Winter Warrior workout was the brainchild of James Stratman, the owner and founder of Modern Warrior and Peak Nutrition, which sell curated nutrition supplements to people trying to peak or perfect their physical fitness. First responders and veterans are often part of that community. James didn’t know Mitch and hadn’t even met him. But Mitch took physical fitness seriously, and word of his tragic and untimely death had circulated within that community. When James learned of Mitch’s story, he wanted to do something, through his companies, to help first responders and veterans. “Great companies do more than sell products or services,” James said. “Great companies give back in ways that help to bring about positive change. Awareness around and the damage from suicide in our veteran and first responder communities needs to change.” And thus was the Winter Warrior event born. Because James’ companies underwrote the cost of the event, 100% of its proceeds – every last nickel – will be donated to the Lifeline. The event itself was both fun and grueling. After they signed in and donated, the participants walked to a large open warehouse floor. On it were arranged a deceptively simple array of exercise equipment: attack bikes, boxes for stationary jumps, weights, jump ropes, and mats for burpees. Harmless enough just to look at, but quite taxing once they began to be used for the 20-minute workout. “That was a seriously tough workout. I was panting at the end,” said James, who is very disciplined about his own fitness. James and his team reached out to our family early on, to let us know what they were planning in Mitch’s memory. James said that he was hesitant about asking any of us to participate, because he suspected that we were still raw with grief about Mitch’s death. James was right about the grief still being very raw. But suicide in these communities is a silent and deadly epidemic. Police and firefighters are five times more likely than civilians to suffer from PTSD and depression. And the number of veteran and active duty suicides is more than four times the number of military operation deaths since 9/11. That is a ghastly statistic, and it needs to change. We are so grateful that James and his team reached out. On a personal level, this event was the first thing that has energized me since Mitch’s death. It was amazing that this group of strangers, whom Mitch had never even met, put in the hard work to prepare an event like this. James and his team are big thinkers, and this Winter Warrior event is just the first. James hopes to get ten times the number of participants and donors next year. The Winters family is joining forces with them and will be starting a charitable foundation, the Winter Warrior First Responders Foundation. Each year, it will raise money for the benefit of a family or individual who has been damaged by a first responder suicide or veteran suicide. As with this first Winter Warrior event, the plan is for 100% of the proceeds to go to that family or individual. Not the net proceeds– every last nickel. James and our family have big plans for this, and we’ll have more to report in the coming months. This first Winter Warrior workout was an extraordinary event. Mitch would have loved it. If the event had been in someone else’s memory, he would have happily and enthusiastically done the workout and then cheered others on.
articles.title: Fundraiser in memory of Mitch Winters a rousing success
