articles.text: Piedmont High School alumnus Sara Dosa, class of 2000, premiered her newest documentary, Fire of Love, at the 2022 Sundance Film Festival, selected as one of five films in the documentary category. The documentary was picked up for theatrical distribution by National Geographic following the premiere. Dosa is an Indie Spirit Award-nominated director and Peabody award-winning producer, whose film credits include Audrie & Daisy, available on at-home streaming service Netflix, The Seer and the Unseen, and The Last Season. Fire of Love, Dosa’s documentary chronicling the work of Maurice and Katia Krafft, French husband-wife volcanologists, opened the Sundance Film Festival on January 20. The film contains over 20 years of archival footage and dramatic shots of active volcanoes and explosions. The Krafft couple traveled to volcanic locations in Zaire, Iceland, the Americas and Japan, capturing then-unseen footage of seismic, tectonic eruptions. The footage came into Dosa’s hands when directing The Seer and the Unseen in Iceland in 2019. Finding what the couple captured as “extraordinary and provoking,” she pursued a documentary based solely on the couple. “It was like a puzzle, stitching together over two decades of archival footage, and these incredible moments Maurice and Katia captured,” she said. Under her direction, the team behind Fire of Love weaved the Piedmont documentary film director and producer Sara Dosa. footage together to tell the couple’s love story. The Kraffts spent decades collecting data mere feet away from danger. In 1991 they were killed capturing an explosion on Japan’s Mount Unzen. They left behind a legacy and some of the most dramatic footage humans may ever be able to capture. “I like to think of it as a love triangle. Maurice and Katia were obviously the love story that drove [the narrative], but you also have the volcanoes they chased. In a way they were both in love with this important work they did,” Dosa said. As director, Dosa was involved with every stage of the film, including in the documentary’s clever use of animation and in writing the copy provided to Miranda July, author and independent film screenwriter, who narrates the film. Dosa said she consulted with the Krafft’s contemporaries and colleagues when considering what story to tell - but that the bulk of the narration comes directly from the footage the couple captured, and the Krafft’s own notes, speeches and published works. “I wanted to make something that, if they were able to see it, they would consider an accurate and compelling portrayal of their lives,” Dosa said. Bidding for the film began shortly after its premiere, with streaming giants like Netflix, Sony Pictures, National Geographic, IFC, Universal, and Amazon all included. The deal for Fire of Love closed late last month, with National Geographic Documentary Films closing a mid-seven-figure worldwide rights deal. Volcanologists Maurice and Katia Krafft, the subjects of a documentary film by Piedmont alum Sara Dosa.
articles.title: Piedmont alum Sara Dosa debuts documentary at Sundance

articles.text: Photos courtesy of Columbus Zoo Captain Cal experienced complications stemming from a California wildfire in 2020. Captain Cal, one of three mountain lions rescued from the devastating Zogg and August Complex fires near Redding in September 2020 and transported to Oakland Zoo, experienced additional complications due to burns sustained. On February 4 he had several toes amputated by Columbus Zoo in Ohio, where he has been cared for since November 2020. Captain Cal came to Oakland Zoo in 2020 as a severely burned orphaned male mountain lion cub, and is named after the firefighters that rescued him. He made a promising recovery after 47 days of intensive care at Oakland Zoo’s veterinary hospital and under the care of the California Department of Fish &Wildlife (CDFW). He was transported to Columbus Zoo after receiving roundthe-clock care, daily bandage changes, pain medication, antibiotics, and surgery that partially amputated his toes. Captain Cal recovers from a four-hour procedure that removed several of his toes. Dr. Brittany Carson performs surgery on Captain Cal. Columbus Zoo announced that the cougar, now fully grown, experienced some new complications due to the injuries he sustained from the fire. While he has been doing well overall, his previous injuries from being trapped in the wildlife fires continued to cause challenges. Dr. Brittany Carson, a surgeon at Ohio State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine, said the decision was made to partially amputate the tips of several more of Captain Cal’s toes. The procedure took approximately 4 hours, and he was then transported to the Zoo’s Animal Health Center to be monitored. “WE PAY YOUR SALES TAX”* *On all installed jobs
articles.title: Mountain lion Capt. Cal, a fire survivor, has toes amputated

articles.text: I don’t remember which year exactly it was when I discovered Beekeeper – maybe 10 years ago. I was at the annual Zinfandel Advocates and Producers (ZAP) tasting in San Francisco. In those days this was one of the largest wine tastings in the country – a huge array of big teeth-staining wines. It takes a lot to stand out in an array of so many powerful wines, but at the end of the day there was one wine that truly stood out from the crowd – Beekeeper. The winery was just getting started and founder Ian Blackburn had made only a few cases. Blackburn went on to partner with Clay Mauritson whose family owns some magnificent vineyards in the Rockpile AVA and production today is under 900 cases. The Beekeeper philosophy is simple: treat Zinfandel with the same respect as Cabernet Sauvignon, the king of California grapes. Grapes are selected from only the finest vineyards and yields are kept low. The wines are aged in mostly new French oak barrels which helps explain the prices. In other words – it’s the royal treatment. It doesn’t hurt that Blackburn and Mauritson are talented winemakers who learn and adapt from each new vintage. Beekeeper is able to pull off a tough task. The wines are big, full-bodied and powerful, yet they are not ponderous or tiring on the palate. They possess exquisite balance which keeps them refreshing despite their size. They are also some of the few Zinfandels that actually improve with age, and I recommend a few years in the cellar before serving. The best way to acquire the wines is through the website www.beekeepercellars.com. pull out to serve with leg of lamb or a pork crown roast. • 2018 Beekeeper Zinfandel Montecillo Vineyard, $75 The Rockpile AVA in a remote corner of Sonoma country is a relatively recent appellation but it has proven itself to be able to produce outstanding Zinfandels. This wine is a good example. Deep ruby/purple, with a stunning nose of anise, jasmine, blueberry, blackberry jam and earth, the wine is majestic, full-bodied and an absolute tour de force in Zinfandel winemaking. It should drink well for at least 10 years. • 2018 Beekeeper Zinfandel Hidden Hillside Reserve, $75 This wine is a blend of three vineyards and is made only in select vintages. It is blended with 4% Petite Sirah for added structure. It offers up superb notes of black fruits, licorice, pepper, and flowers. With amazing concentration, an opulent, full-bodied palate, and fabulous length, the wine shows why Beekeeper is in a class of its own in the world of Zinfandel. Would love to drink this with a hearty beef stew or cassoulet. 2018 Beekeeper Zinfandel Secret Stones, $85 This wine from the Rockpile AVA (Sonoma Valley) comes from a vineyard at 1500 feet in elevation. It is blended with 3% Petite Sirah. It sports loads of black raspberry, kirsch liqueur, lavender, anise, and subtle earthy notes in this multidimensional, full-bodied, gloriously decadent and tasty Zinfandel. Cal, a fire survivor, has toes amputated The Wine Corner Photos courtesy of Columbus Zoo Captain Cal experienced complications stemming from a California wildfire in 2020. By Allyson Aleksey Captain Cal, one of three mountain lions rescued from the devastating Zogg and August Complex fires near Redding in September 2020 and transported to Oakland Zoo, experienced additional complications due to burns sustained. On February 4 he had several toes amputated by Columbus Zoo in Ohio, where he has been cared for since November 2020. Captain Cal came to Oakland Zoo in 2020 as a severely burned orphaned male mountain lion cub, and is named after the firefighters that rescued him. He made a promising recovery after 47 days of intensive care at Oakland Zoo’s veterinary hospital and under the care of the California Department of Fish &Wildlife (CDFW). He was transported to Columbus Zoo after receiving roundthe-clock care, daily bandage changes, pain medication, antibiotics, and surgery that partially amputated his toes. Captain Cal recovers from a four-hour procedure that removed several of his toes. Dr. Brittany Carson performs surgery on Captain Cal. Columbus Zoo announced that the cougar, now fully grown, experienced some new complications due to the injuries he sustained from the fire. While he has been doing well overall, his previous injuries from being trapped in the wildlife fires continued to cause challenges. Dr. Brittany Carson, a surgeon at Ohio State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine, said the decision was made to partially amputate the tips of several more of Captain Cal’s toes. The procedure took approximately 4 hours, and he was then transported to the Zoo’s Animal Health Center to be monitored. Beekeeper Cellars – America’s elite Zinfandel By Pierre DuMont I don’t remember which year exactly it was when I discovered Beekeeper – maybe 10 years ago. I was at the annual Zinfandel Advocates and Producers (ZAP) tasting in San Francisco. In those days this was one of the largest wine tastings in the country – a huge array of big teeth-staining wines. The winery was just getting started and founder Ian Blackburn had made only a few cases. articles.text: First Mondays Reading Group members: Mike Henn, Nancy Henn, Ken Young, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Alicia Rivera, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Pat McMahon, Albert Chen, Adriene Hamlin, Bella Almanzan, Dick Carter, Priscilla Wanerus, Carol Long, and first-time participants Darby and Jerry Gragg. The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group met outside the Tea House in the Piedmont Park on February 7. It was a warm, sunny afternoon that had members of the group looking for shade under the park’s tall redwood trees in this beautiful setting. It was hard to believe that cool weather a month before had caused them to have their January discussion as a Zoom call. Seventeen readers were in attendance, one of the group’s largest turnouts. Everyone was in the same boat about the New York Times bestseller The Boys in the Boat by Daniel James Brown. They all loved it and found very little to criticize. The Boys in the Boat is about the University of Washington eight-oared crew that represented the United States in the 1936 Olympic Games in Berlin. It is a true story based on the struggles and sacrifices made by the rowers to compete in the Olympics, and how they narrowly beat Italy and Germany to win the gold medal. The eight young men who won gold had experienced significant hardships in their early lives. All of them came from poorer, rural areas, and started their educations during the Great Depression. However, their determination, rigorous training, and dedicated coaches provide them with the strength and ability to win. Brown’s main character is Joe Rantz. As a youth, Joe was abandoned by his father and stepmother because she didn’t want him in her house. Joe was forced live alone in rural Washington, far from relatives, with no family, and little other support. These hardships reinforced his strong character, and conditioned him to be a successful Washington crewman and Olympic champion. There are two stories within the book. One tells how all nine members of the Washington crew had to struggle to earn their ways through school during the Depression. The second story begins with Hitler ordering construction of spectacular German venues at which the Games would take place. As they proceeded, the Nazis hid the evidence of their inhumane treatment of Jews and created a propaganda showcase for their emerging, brutal regime that won worldwide applause for their Games. After telling all the difficulties Joe Rantz and the other Americans overcame, Brown’s story comes together with his description of the final Olympic race, and the thrilling victory they achieved. Additionally, Brown tells of the bonds they formed during their rowing careers that lasted for their entire lives. After their win, they would come every few years to row together again. The readers found The Boys in the Boat captivating and inspiring. Some members of the group said they were not sports fans, and had reservations about reading a book about a crew; but Brown quickly demolished these concerns. The readers were pulled into his story by the challenges the young men experienced, and also by Brown’s character development and making these people real. The obstacles were huge, but the rowers fought through them, never quit, and preserved. Even though the readers knew the rowers were going to win their Olympic race, Brown created suspense throughout in the rowers’ journeys, and kept the readers enthralled throughout the book. The group felt the rowers were “authentic heroes” and “role models” for today’s youth and our society. Some readers said they enjoyed the book so much they want to learn more about rowing and even go to a crew race. During this 1930s period there were no scholarships or other support for these college athletes, and they had to work hard jobs to earn the money to go to school. This fact led to a discussion of the current state of college athletics. The difference between then and now is dramatic, and made the readers appreciate all the more what these young men accomplished. The only reservation some readers had was the level of detail the author provided. However, this was a minor criticism, and it was also accepted that this information helped readers more fully understand the Depression times, rowing, the characters, and the situations. The Nazis’ use of the Olympics for propaganda and their use of film to support their world view was considered by the readers. It was also noted that the 2022 Winter Olympics were now going on in Beijing, and being used by the Chinese to present an image of their society that they want the world to see and believe. Finally, it was fun to learn that a movie of the book is planned with George Clooney directing it. With the discussion complete, the readers turned to future book selections. They had previously picked the novel The Midnight Library by Matt Haig for March and the non-fiction Destiny of the Republic by Candice Millard their April book. The group selected The Lincoln Highway, the latest work by one of their favorite authors, Amor Towles, for their May read. The group’s next discussion will be Monday, March 7 at 1:30 p.m. Weather permitting the group will meet at the Japanese Tea House I Piedmont Park. However, if the forecast is for cold or rain, the group will have their discussion via a Zoom call. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required by calling the Recreation Department at 420-3070.

articles.text: As you prepare your tax returns before the April 18 filing deadline, you’ll want to be up to date on changes that could affect you. Here are some issues to discuss with your tax professional: • COVID-19-related distributions and recontributions If you took a coronavirus-related distribution (withdrawal) from a retirement account, such as a 401(k) or IRA, in 2020 and chose to spread the amount equally over three years, you need to include the relevant part of the distribution on your 2021 tax return, so you should bring your 2020 Form 1099-R to your tax advisor. You can recontribute your distributions back into any retirement account eligible to receive a rollover for up to three years after you received the initial distribution. So, if you haven’t already done so, you can still recontribute to your 401(k) or IRA up until the April 18 filing deadline – and by doing so, you could reduce your 2021 taxes. (Your tax professional will know what forms and documentation you’ll need for this recontribution.) • Return of RMDs In 2020, the Coronavirus Aid, Relief and Economic Security (CARES) Act suspended the required minimum distributions (RMDs) from retirement accounts that people over a certain age typically must take. But RMDs returned for 2021 and had to be taken by Dec. 31, unless your birthdate is between July 1 and Dec. 31, 1949, in which case your starting date was delayed until April 1, 2022. So, if you had an RMD for 2021, bring your 2020 Form 5498 or your 2021 retirement account statements to your tax professional to calculate the required RMD. You’ll also want to provide your 2021 Form 1099-R to report the amount of RMDs taken. • Charitable contributions The CARES Act authorized a deduction for cash contributions to qualified charities for those who don’t itemize. For 2020, the maximum deduction was $300; this provision has been extended for the 2021 tax year, with a new provision allowing a $600 deduction for joint filers. If you do itemize deductions, be aware that the CARES Act also suspended the 60% of adjusted gross income limit for cash gifts in 2020, a change that has been carried over to 2021. • Child tax credit For 2021, you can claim up to $3,600 for children younger than 6 and up to $3,000 for children ages 6 to 17. This tax credit is refundable, which means you can receive it even if it’s larger than the amount of taxes you owe. The credit phases out at certain income limits. • Child and dependent care credit This credit is more substantial in 2021 – up to $4,000 for one qualifying person and up to $8,000 for two or more. This credit is also potentially refundable, but it phases out differently than in previous years, so you’ll want to go over your dependent-care expenses carefully with your tax professional. And last, but certainly not least, review your IRA contributions. There aren’t any changes for 2022, but you can still fund your traditional or Roth IRA for the 2021 tax year up until the April 18 deadline. to ensure you’ve got everything in order. Staffing shortages at the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), combined with a heavy workload due to pandemic-related programs, may slow down processing of returns, so consider getting your taxes done as soon as possible – especially if you’re anticipating a refund. articles.text: Independence is something that becomes so intrinsic to most people after early childhood that it can be a shock to lose some independence with age or illness. In the United States, in contrast to many other countries, independence is highly valued. The Pew Research Center found that “nearly four-in-ten older adults around the world live with extended family, but those in the U.S. rarely do.” Their study also includes the following details: “In the U.S., 27% of adults ages 60 and older live alone, compared with 16% of adults in the 130 countries and territories studied. In many countries in the Asia-Pacific, sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East, fewer than 5% of seniors live alone.” Simply put, older people live in smaller households. “U.S. adults ages 60 and older also are more likely than their counterparts around the world to live as a couple without young children at home.” The reasons for this choice can be economic and based on government services available to older adults, as well as cultural norms. However, there can be benefits to asking for help as you maintain independence too. How home care can support independence Despite this preference for living alone, as people age and their abilities change, so too does the need for support. In-home care services can help individuals develop a life of interdependence while maintaining independence in their everyday lives. Starting with the idea of “aging in place”, which means living in one’s home and not a facility, a representative from a home care agency can come in to do a falls risk assessment. and reducing the risk of a fall, someone who is living alone at an advanced age might be able to enjoy independence longer. A caregiver can help with light housekeeping, decluttering and removing any tripping hazards, and point out areas of risk to be addressed by a professional electrician, plumber or handyman. For example, the caregiver may be aware that someone is getting up frequently at night to use the bathroom and also observe an absence of nightlights to guide the way. Simply having a caregiver to engage with regularly to provide companionship, assist with recovering from a surgery, do some meal preparation, give rides to and from medical appointments, can help a senior to stay sharp, feel less lonely and therefore able to stay more independent. This Senior Independence Month, look at ways to prolong independence for yourself or a loved one, and also consider embracing interdependence with home care services and caregiving. articles.text: Oakland’s rock star biologist Damon Tighe is the headliner for a free-to-the-public “Topics of Merritt” speaker series at Lake Merritt – Independent Senior Living on March 10 at 3:30 p.m. “We are so happy to offer an encore appearance by this charming biotechnologist and urban naturalist who has been featured on local news programs and articles,” said Tim Johnson. For this “Topics of Merritt” program, Tighe will present “Fish and Friends of Lake Merritt’s Waters.” He will also highlight the fact that salmon are finding their way back into the Lake Merritt watershed. He speaker series is designed to offer Lake Merritt Senior Living residents and a wider audience access to some of the most interesting and compelling speakers from the community and beyond. Since its inception, “Topics of Merritt” has featured Dr. Jill Tarter of the SETI program and the scientist at the center of the movie Contact; San Francisco Chronicle Theater Critic Lily Janiak; international ballerina Stephanie Herman who performed with Nureyev; and renowned chefs explaining how to cook more healthy meals. As for Tighe’s upcoming talk, it seems that Chinook salmon numbering in the hundreds have been seen since late fall in East Bay rivers and streams that lead to Lake Merritt. Oakland residents have reported sightings in the lake near Glen Echo where the creek runs alongside the Veterans Memorial Building, as well as a tributary that begins in the Oakland hills near Mountain View Cemetery and empties into the northwest branch of the lake near the intersection of Grand Avenue and Harrison Street. Chinook salmon have not been Oakland biologist Damon Tighe will speak on March 10 at Lake Merritt – Independent Senior Living, to talk about the wildlife found at Lake Merritt. seen in the lake for more than 20 years. Once prevalent in Lake Merritt, salmon typically don’t survive in the area due to manmade culverts and pollution. Volunteer groups have been helping provide a healthy fish habitat. The Lake Merritt Institute partners with local citizens and Oakland school students to clean up Lake Merritt’s shoreline and creeks on a weekly basis. Conservationists say these salmon sightings in the lake highlight the much-needed care that goes into conserving Lake Merritt’s amazing but fragile ecosystem. A local conservation expert, Tighe attended Saint Mary’s College in Moraga where he worked on local newspapers while earning a degree in Biology and Chemistry. He taught high school in Portland, Oregon before moving back to the Bay Area to work on the Human Genome Project at the National Lab’s Joint Genome Institute. He also spent time pursuing an MFA in Natural History and Science Filmmaking in Montana but returned to Oakland to work on single cell genomics. He now teaches biotechnology to high school teachers through Bio-Rad Laboratories and is well versed in local fungi, plants and the critters of Lake Merritt. The public is invited to join a free Zoom presentation on March 10. To register, click on: www. tinyurl.com/lakemerrittfish. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, 1800 Madison Street, Oakland. For information, call 510-903-3600 or visit www.thelakemerritt.com.

Dear MacMama: I have my photos all over the place! Some on my iPhone, some on my iMac, some on my laptop. My son said that I should use iCloud for my photos. He also said that I should use it for my contacts and calendars and my files. How does that work? Jess G., Oakland Dear Jess: This problem with too much stuff and too many devices holding that stuff is such a common issue, that I would say 75% of my on-site work is helping people synchronize their photos, calendars, and contacts. These days, the current iPhones have such great cameras that we just are inspired to take lots of pictures! Each time we get a new computer or device, we do our best to move our data over from our old machines. So many of us have photos that go back to the early 2000s if not earlier. Wouldn’t be great if there was a way to make all our photos sync with each of our devices? Well of course, there is! If you enable iCloud for Photos on all of your devices, they will eventually sync and be stored in the cloud and show up on all devices with iCloud enabled. So, let’s say you take a picture with your iPhone, it will show up on your laptop, your iMac, your iPad; any device that has iCloud enabled for Photos. Of course, you must be signed into the same Apple ID on all of the devices, have iCloud enabled for Photos on all of them which will then allow all of your stuff to sync. Many clients worry that with so many photos your hard drive will get full too quickly. Especially if you have a small one, like 256 GB or even 128 GB. When you choose to enable iCloud in your photos, you have the option of storing a smaller version of the photos on your device, and then you can always download the full version if you want to print it. I use the word “eventually” it will all sync because if you have a large photo library with videos, let’s say for example on your iMac, it can take quite a while to upload to the cloud. And it all depends on the speed of your Internet. If you haven’t reasonably fast Internet connection, even if you have a huge photo library, it can pretty much all be done within a day. The one caveat is that if you are using the free version of iCloud (5GB), it’s very likely you will have to pay to increase your storage. But I find a price to be very reasonable, up to 50 GB is $.99 a month, and up to 200 GB is $2.99 a month. If you need even more space, you can upgrade to 2 TB of storage for $9.99 a month. You also can also use iCloud to store and synchronize your desktop, documents, bookmarks, keychain (which stores passwords) which allows you to access your files from all your devices. You can even access files on your iPhone that live on your desktop. This can be certainly useful if you need to quickly send or print a document when you are away from your office. Similarly, if you enable iCloud for your contacts, and calendars, if you change details on one device, they will be updated on all of your devices. When Apple first started offering iCloud, there were several issues. It timed out, the syncing was very fussy, and I didn’t use it on my own devices. But for the last few years, I have iCloud enabled on all my devices, so I can access my desktop files on my iPad, all of my photos, contacts and calendars are in sync. Apple is not the only company that offers cloud syncing. If you have a Gmail address, Google also syncs your contacts and calendars. And with Google Drive, you can sync documents and media through Google Photos. Dropbox is another company that allows you to store files in the cloud and access them from all of your devices. They all have a little bit of a different flavor, for example Google is great if you want to work collaboratively with many people through Google docs. Dropbox is great if you have to share big files with colleagues or friends and have a handy cloud back up of your files. And iCloud is a great way to have all your devices in sync. With iCloud, setting up a new machine is much easier. All you have to do is sign in on the new Mac to your iCloud account, and the files just show up in place. Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. Once prevalent in Lake Merritt, salmon typically don’t survive in the area due to manmade culverts and pollution. Volunteer groups have been helping provide a healthy fish habitat. The Lake Merritt Institute partners with local citizens and Oakland school students to clean up Lake Merritt’s shoreline and creeks on a weekly basis. Conservationists say these salmon sightings in the lake highlight the much-needed care that goes into conserving Lake Merritt’s amazing but fragile ecosystem. A local conservation expert, Tighe attended Saint Mary’s College in Moraga where he worked on local newspapers while earning a degree in Biology and Chemistry. He also spent time pursuing an MFA in Natural History and Science Filmmaking in Montana but returned to Oakland to work on single cell genomics. He now teaches biotechnology to high school teachers through Bio-Rad Laboratories and is well versed in local fungi, plants and the critters of Lake Merritt. articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Seniors group are pictured at the Blackhawk Museum in Danville on February 11: (front) Yorkman Lowe (left), Patti Singer, Marianne Gunther-Murphy, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Merilee Hoffman, Mona Jamieson; (back) Larry Singer, Gregory Jurin, Jim Ayotte, Janet Epstein, Rick Luciano, Susan McCreary, Fred Pemberton, Penny Robb, and Irene Westler. On a lovely, sunny day on February 11, sixteen Piedmont Seniors went on an excursion to the beautiful Blackhawk Museum located on the outskirts of Danville. The museum’s essence is about its founder, Ken Behring, a philanthropist who established “The Wheelchair Foundation”, a nonprofit organization to promote the joy of giving and to deliver a wheelchair to every child, teen and adult who needs one, but cannot afford one. The Seniors arranged for a private docent tour, which greatly enhanced the visit and helped them appreciate the value of the individual collections. The museum, which opened its doors in 1988 as the Behring Auto Museum, has an extensive collection of rare vintage automobiles. The variety of 50 historically significant and artistically inspired automobiles begins from the earliest age of motoring to the contemporary Lamborgini automobile. It is a traveling exhibition, so the automobiles in the museum are constantly changing, making every visit unique. Visitors are given the opportunity to see new, interesting vehicles, as well as some old favorites. Its next exhibit, “The Spirit of the Old West”, is a must for every fourth grader studying California history. There are many Indian artifacts, buffaloes and clothing. This exhibition is dedicated to presenting a balanced narrative of both Native Americans and American settlers and the struggles they all made to survive, from the settlers crossing the plains in a covered wagon, to the Indians being forced from their lands onto reservations. There is an impressive diorama on display, which encompasses most of the back wall of the exhibit space. Here you will see the unique animals that populated the West. Viewers are fortunate that this collection once owned by Jerry Fick was appreciated by Mr. Behring, who saw the value of his collection and purchased what visitors see today. The newer exhibits consist of “Intro China”, the “Art of Africa” and the “World of Nature”. The China exhibit assembles handcrafted masterpieces that capture the essence of all that embodies China, past and present. Viewers will see the Great Wall diagram, the Forbidden City on display, as well as the Emperor’s throne. In the “Art of Africa” gallery you will see art created by many indigenous peoples of sub-Saharan Africa – beautiful statues, masks, clothing, and musical instruments. The “World of Nature” exhibit encompasses the Arctic, the desert, North American animals, and rainforests, with mammals, reptiles, fish and birds comprising over 800 members of the animal kingdom. Taking time for lunch After visiting the museum, the Piedmont Seniors were ready for a delightful lunch at Fat Maddie’s, just a short walk away. Sitting outside they could relax and watch the birds and ducks in a nearby pond. No excursion is complete without some shopping, so after lunch the group went to Draegers, an upscale gourmet grocery and dry goods store near the museum. Everyone had a great time and especially relished being able to get together after so much isolation. To find out more about Piedmont Seniors and their activities and to receive a quarterly newsletter, contact Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein at jepstein@ piedmont.ca.gov, or call the Piedmont Recreation Department at 510-420-3070. articles.text: Wednesday Walkers share a group photo on February 9. Pictured are Ken Young, Helen Dong, Albert Chen, Rob Smith, Melba Yee, Quincy Dong, Noemi Alvarado, Jim Kuo, Mike Henn, Jim Kellogg, Wenny Young, Claudia Lopez, Siow Fang Tan, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Priscilla Wanerus, Martin Levy, Brenda Ferrero, Lilly Guardia-Labar, Harriette Louie, Christine Calliste, Pat Keller, Renee Goldhammer, Alan Goldhammer, Elizabeth Richter, Aaron Katzel, Dena Belinkoff, Nancy Henn, John Lenahan, Alicia Rivera, Sarah Johnson, Sherry Jacobs, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome first time walkers Patti Schneider and Jo Normington with her K-9 best friend Penny Lane. The sun was out again to greet the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group last Wednesday. There was a strong turnout of 34 walkers and one K-9 best friend on the sunny morning. The group had not recently been to Sunnyside Avenue on the south side of Piedmont, and there is some interesting history associated with the buildings nearby on Grand Avenue. Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi shared some history of this section of Piedmont. In 1929 the Piedmont City Council adopted an ordinance that allowed businesses from the city line to Linda Avenue on the west side of Grand Avenue, and to Fairview Avenue on the east side. Seven months later voters rejected another zoning ordinance to extend the business district to Oakland Avenue. Today, the business district on Grand Avenue remains the same as it was in 1929. The walkers went off in a long line going down Highland Avenue to the corner of Oakland Avenue. When the group reached Latham Street, they regrouped and shared with new walkers Patti Schneider and Jo Normington that Latham is the only “Street” in Piedmont. All other roadways are called Avenue or Drive or Way or something similar. On Oakland Avenue there were early roses and cherry blossoms to enjoy. It took two stoplight cycles for all the walkers cross Grand Avenue before going up to Sunnyside. They stopped at Linda Avenue and learned some more fun history from Gail Lombardi’s research. In 1892 Axel Gruggel built a restaurant on this corner called A Mon Chateau (My Castle). He also had a beer garden in the back on Linda. Over the years, the establishment had different owners, including three bachelors in 1907 who were denied a liquor license when they became available because neighbors didn’t like all of the restaurant’s noise. However, the bachelors continued to sell liquor, and in 1908 they were arrested and their liquor was confiscated. In 1911 a new owner changed the restaurant into “The Piedmont Casino,” where poker was played. But gambling was illegal, and the casino was raided in 1912. Nine card players were arrested and each was fined $55. Not surprisingly, the casino closed soon after. In 1914 the building became the Grand Avenue Grocery Company. It did well until a Piggly Wiggly supermarket opened down the street at Sunnyside. The competition was too much and it closed in 1935. The building was torn down in 1936 and a succession of gas stations occupied the space until 1987 when Chevron sold the property. The current two-story Piedmont Financial Center was built on the site. The walkers found this history interesting but wished the beer garden was still there. The group turned up Sunnyside and climbed to Olive Avenue, where architect and former Piedmont Planning Commissioner Jim Kellogg pointed out a unique home built and owned by contractor Darryl Rush. It has a circular turret ADU and a waving brick front wall that has a built-in seat. The walkers continued up Sunnyside and crossed Oakland Avenue, then through the Linda Avenue Dog Park. When they came out of the park they saw children on the playground across the street at Beach School. The walkers went down Linda Avenue, returning to the site of the A Mon Chateau beer garden (still closed). They went down Grand and crossed it at the stoplight at Wildwood Avenue. The walkers passed the small, triangular park with 15 tall redwood trees; and continued to a short set of stairs that took them to the foot of Warfield Avenue and the “Five Way Stop” intersection. They stayed on Wildwood, going past the Wildwood School. The group came to the Piedmont Park’s lower entrance and took its upper path to the back of the Community Hall where happy preschoolers were playing in their enclosed yard, with a group of high school senior boys having lunch on the steps below them. There was a realization that the walkers’ visit to Sunnyside Avenue had taken them to all three Piedmont elementary schools. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday, rain or shine, at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.
articles.title: Taking a walk on Sunnyside (of the street)

pages.text: 26 Wednesday, February 16, 2022 Walking on Wednesday Taking a walk on Sunnyside (of the street) Wednesday Walkers share a group photo on February 9. Pictured are Ken Young, Helen Dong, Albert Chen, Rob Smith, Melba Yee, Quincy Dong, Noemi Alvarado, Jim Kuo, Mike Henn, Jim Kellogg, Wenny Young, Claudia Lopez, Siow Fang Tan, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Priscilla Wanerus, Martin Levy, Brenda Ferrero, Lilly Guardia-Labar, Harriette Louie, Christine Calliste, Pat Keller, Renee Goldhammer, Alan Goldhammer, Elizabeth Richter, Aaron Katzel, Dena Belinkoff, Nancy Henn, John Lenahan, Alicia Rivera, Sarah Johnson, Sherry Jacobs, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome first time walkers Patti Schneider and Jo Normington with her K-9 best friend Penny Lane. By Dick Carter The sun was out again to greet the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group last Wednesday. There was a strong turnout of 34 walkers and one K-9 best friend on the sunny morning. The group had not recently been to Sunnyside Avenue on the south side of Piedmont, and there is some interesting history associated with the buildings nearby on Grand Avenue. Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi shared some history of this section of Piedmont. In 1929 the Piedmont City Council adopted an ordinance that allowed businesses from the city line to Linda Avenue on the west side of Grand Avenue, and to Fairview Avenue on the east side. Seven months later voters rejected another zoning ordinance to extend the business district to Oakland Avenue. Today, the business district on Grand Avenue remains the same as it was in 1929. The walkers went off in a long line going down Highland Avenue to the corner of Oakland Avenue. When the group reached Latham Street, they regrouped and shared with new walkers Patti Schneider and Jo Normington that Latham is the only “Street” in Piedmont. All other roadways are called Avenue or Drive or Way or something similar. On Oakland Avenue there were early roses and cherry blossoms to enjoy. It took two stoplight cycles for all the walkers cross Grand Avenue before going up to Sunnyside. They stopped at Linda Avenue and learned some more fun history from Gail Lombardi’s research. In 1892 Axel Gruggel built a restaurant on this corner called A Mon Chateau (My Castle). He also had a beer garden in the back on Linda. Over the years, the establishment had different owners, including three bachelors in 1907 who were denied a liquor license when they became available because neighbors didn’t like all of the restaurant’s noise. However, the bachelors continued to sell liquor, and in 1908 they were arrested and their liquor was confiscated. In 1911 a new owner changed the restaurant into “The Piedmont Casino,” where poker was played. But gambling was illegal, and the casino was raided in 1912. Nine card players were arrested and each was fined $55. Not surprisingly, the casino closed soon after. In 1914 the building became the Grand Avenue Grocery Company. It did well until a Piggly Wiggly supermarket opened down the street at Sunnyside. The competition was too much and it closed in 1935. The building was torn down in 1936 and a succession of gas stations occupied the space until 1987 when Chevron sold the property. The current two-story Piedmont Financial Center was built on the site. The walkers found this history interesting but wished the beer garden was still there. The group turned up Sunnyside and climbed to Olive Avenue, where architect and former Piedmont Planning Commissioner Jim Kellogg pointed out a unique home built and owned by contractor Darryl Rush. It has a circular turret ADU and a waving brick front wall that has a built-in seat. The walkers continued up Sunnyside and crossed Oakland Avenue, then through the Linda Avenue Dog Park. When they came out of the park they saw children on the playground across the street at Beach School. The walkers went down Linda Avenue, returning to the site of the A Mon Chateau beer garden (still closed). They went down Grand and crossed it at the stoplight at Wildwood Avenue. The walkers passed the small, triangular park with 15 tall redwood trees; and continued to a short set of stairs that took them to the foot of Warfield Avenue and the “Five Way Stop” intersection. They stayed on Wildwood, going past the Wildwood School. The group came to the Piedmont Park’s lower entrance and took its upper path to the back of the Community Hall where happy preschoolers were playing in their enclosed yard, with a group of high school senior boys having lunch on the steps below them. There was a realization that the walkers’ visit to Sunnyside Avenue had taken them to all three Piedmont elementary schools. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday, rain or shine, at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. The owner of the residence called the police when the ex-girlfriend of the resident’s son was in the backyard. The resident had previously told Diamond Lopez, a 30-year-old transient, she was not allowed on the property. Police entered the backyard and found her in a wooden structure functioning as a workshop. Through a records search police discovered that she had an outstanding warrant out of San Francisco for narcotics possession. She was also on probation in Alameda County for assault with a deadly weapon, possession of a stolen vehicle, and drunk driving. While attempting to detain the subject, she fled from officers. Officers were eventually able to detain her and placed her in an ambulance for transport to Highland Hospital. When the paramedics slowed at the intersection of Grand and MacArthur Avenue, Lopez jumped out the back of the ambulance. A Piedmont officer was able to detain her and put her back in the ambulance. She was cleared from Highland Hospital at 10:30 p.m. and taken to Santa Rita jail. And all were on hand to celebrate the annual Derby being held in person after not having a Derby race last year due to COVID. “There is something pure and joyful about the race that harkens back to my sense of a ‘golden age’ of childhood,” said co-chair David Cole. “The event feels very nostalgic, with a block of wood, four plastic wheels and some nails – the same materials that have been used on that track for over 50 years. I love the energy in that room during the race.” A sampling of the more than 100 cars that participated in the Piedmont Scout annual Pinewood Derby on Saturday.

articles.text: COVID cases have continued to decrease in Alameda County since the end of the year spike spurred by the Omicron variant. Hospitalizations and deaths from the COVID virus, which lag behind case counts, show signs of having peaked as well. At the end of 2020 cases started to rise in November and did not recede to pre-spike levels until March 2021. Dr. George Rutherford, UCSF Professor of Epidemiology explained what was different this time around. “[Omicron] is much more transmissible, so the timeline is sped up. To use a forest fire analogy, [fire quickly] burns up the dry wood,” said Rutherford in December 2021. Here, Omicron is the fire and the dry wood are those that are susceptible to infection due to being unvaccinated, or due to frequent human contact. The peak daily cases during the end of 2020 was 1,260 cases in Alameda County on January 4. Daily Cases On January 4, 2022, exactly one year after the previous year’s peak, COVID cases peaked in Alameda County at 5990. Data in the last seven days is unreliable and subject to change, so the most recent day of more complete data is January 31, when 1,470 cases were reported in the County. An interesting pattern in the case counts is that Sundays regularly have the lowest case counts and Mondays the high case counts, at least in Alameda County. A likely source of this pattern is labs having reporting delays over the weekend, and catching up with processing cases at the start of the work week.
articles.title: Update on COVID-19 statistics

articles.text: OPL Advocates is a coalition of groups supporting the Oakland Public Library. In June this year, a reauthorization of Measure Q funds will be on the ballot and the Advocates have begun a campaign now to assure libraries receive adequate funding. Measure Q, the Library Services Retention and Enhancement Act, is one of two parcel taxes crucial for the funding of OPL’s budget. Measure Q was first approved by voters in 1994 (as Measure O), and then renewed and amended as Measure Q in 2004. The current measure expires in 2024. Without its reauthorization, some library services, hours and locations will shut down. The Advocates are calling on the public to help to make sure that does not happen. There are lots of ways to help Oakland Public Library and Measure Q including: • Make an individual contribution • Solicit businesses • Solicit individuals • Send thank-you notes • Host a house party • Deliver/distribute lawn signs • Put a sign in your window/on your lawn • Write/design campaign materials • Create/post social-media content • Assist with website • Phone bank • Text bank • Door-knocking Visit and speak at City Council meetings, community groups, house parties, and union meetings. The OPL Advocates will train and provide talking points. You can sign up now to help at: www. opladvocates.org. articles.text: In preparation for African American History Month this year, I read Until I Am Free: Fannie Lou Hamer’s Enduring Message To America by Keisha N. Blane. Hamer’s story is integral to the history of the struggle for Black voting rights, women’s empowerment, economic rights and human rights. Born in Webster County, Mississippi, in 1917, Fannie Lou was the youngest of 20 children, the granddaughter of enslaved people, and a sharecropper for much of her life who became a trailblazing activist and organizer. Her best-known words are, “We have a long fight and this fight is not mine alone. But you are not free whether you are white or black, until I am free.” I find it helpful to reflect on Hamer’s life through the lens of the Exodus, particularly Exodus 5: 1-22, the story of Moses’ first attempt to bring the Israelites out of Egypt. After meeting his brother in the desert at God’s Mountain and gathering the leaders of the people in order to gain their trust and share God’s vision of liberation with them, Moses and Aaron go to Pharoah with a very clear command from the Lord: Let my people go so that they can hold a festival for me in the desert. Pharoah’s reply is predictably dismissive. Who is this Lord whom I’m supposed to obey by letting Israel go? I don’t know this Lord, and I certainly won’t let Israel go. pages.text: 2 Wednesday, February 9, 2022 Opinion Oakland Public Library advocates supporting Measure Q OPL Advocates is a coalition of groups supporting the Oakland Public Library. In June this year, a reauthorization of Measure Q funds will be on the ballot and the Advocates have begun a campaign now to assure libraries receive adequate funding. Measure Q, the Library Services Retention and Enhancement Act, is one of two parcel taxes crucial for the funding of OPL’s budget. Measure Q was first approved by voters in 1994 (as Measure O), and then renewed and amended as Measure Q in 2004. The current measure expires in 2024. Without its reauthorization, some library services, hours and locations will shut down. The Advocates are calling on the public to help to make sure that does not happen. The life of Fannie Lou Hamer and message of Exodus 5: 1-22 By Rev. Jim Hopkins In preparation for African American History Month this year, I read Until I Am Free: Fannie Lou Hamer’s Enduring Message To America by Keisha N. Blane. Hamer’s story is integral to the history of the struggle for Black voting rights, women’s empowerment, economic rights and human rights. Born in Webster County, Mississippi, in 1917, Fannie Lou was the youngest of 20 children, the granddaughter of enslaved people, and a sharecropper for much of her life who became a trailblazing activist and organizer. Her best-known words are, “We have a long fight and this fight is not mine alone. But you are not free whether you are white or black, until I am free.” I find it helpful to reflect on Hamer’s life through the lens of the Exodus, particularly Exodus 5: 1-22, the story of Moses’ first attempt to bring the Israelites out of Egypt. After meeting his brother in the desert at God’s Mountain and gathering the leaders of the people in order to gain their trust and share God’s vision of liberation with them, Moses and Aaron go to Pharoah with a very clear command from the Lord: Let my people go so that they can hold a festival for me in the desert. Pharoah’s reply is predictably dismissive. Who is this Lord whom I’m supposed to obey by letting Israel go? I don’t know this Lord, and I certainly won’t let Israel go. articles.text: Part 1 in a series Do you have a favorite tree or group of trees in Piedmont? How about the grove of European white birch trees growing in the Hall Fenway, the lovely footpath that links Wildwood Avenue to Crocker Avenue near Crocker Park? This unique display features 11 over-arching mature trees growing along the route of a historic rail line that ran through Piedmont. These birches (betula pendula), were designated as Heritage Trees in 2021 upon nomination by Peter and Alicia Fishel. Native to Europe and parts of Asia, these beautiful ornamental trees feature silvery-white bark that becomes marked with irregular black patches as the trees age. Deciduous leaves hang from gracefully pendant thin branches. Varieties including weeping and cutleaf, among others. European white birches have fruiting catkins that ripen and disperse tiny winged seeds into the wind to spread far and wide. These trees are typically planted in groups, as they are in the Hall Fenway. Over the next few weeks, the Piedmont Post will feature a brief article and photo of a Heritage Tree. Other Heritage Trees include a row of seven tall coast redwoods (Sequoia sempervirens), at Linda Beach Field that create an architectural backdrop to the playfield. They were nominated by John Ware with his daughter Sophie, and Betsy Goodman, a member of the Park Commission. Other examples are the grove of Eastern Redbuds at the west end of Piedmont Park off Wildwood, nominated by Lisa Kieraldo; the reclining Coast Live Oak in Piedmont Park, nominated European white birches in the Hall Fenway Photo by Brian Mahany by Will, Finn, and Max Brumfiel; the four evergreen Dogwoods that frame the City Hall entrance, nominated by Bobbe Stehr and Mark Enea; a group of ten Highland Poplars behind Exedra Plaza, nominated by Jim Horner; and a row of seven Dawn Redwoods growing in the former quarry at Dracena Park, nominated by Lyle Gordon. The public is encouraged to seek out these trees to appreciate their beauty, history, and significance. By learning more about the trees that comprise Piedmont’s urban forest, the Park Commission hopes to inspire everyone to seek out special trees in our community and encourage nominations for 2022 Heritage Trees. Submitted nominations will be evaluated on their aesthetic, educational, or historical merits. Nominations are welcome from anyone in the community and trees must be on public property, such as parks, streets, and medians. After vetting by Public Works department arborists, qualifying trees will be forwarded to the Park Commission for review and selection. Nominations are due by March 18 with the winners selected at the Park Commission meeting on April 6. This year’s selections will be announced at the Arbor Day festivities on April 28. Forms are available on the City’s website on its Heritage Tree page at https://www. piedmont.ca.gov/cms/One.aspx? portalId=13659823&pageId= 17970894. There, you can also view an interactive map of the existing Heritage Trees which includes photos of the trees, descriptions, locations, and names of the nominating parties. For more information, please contact Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov or 510-420-3064. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont will feature Erwin Chemerinsky, Dean of Berkeley Law School in a discussion on Tuesday, March 1 at 4 p.m. He is a nationally recognized expert on the U.S. Supreme Court and election law. This event is part of the League’s 2022 Defending Democracy Speaker Series and is co-sponsored by local Leagues in Oakland, Santa Barbara, Solano County, Portland, OR; Gunnison Valley, CO; Pueblo, CO, Pike’s Peak Region, CO; and Collier County, FL. Chemerinsky became the 13th Dean of Berkeley Law School on July 1, 2017, when he joined the faculty as the Jesse H. Choper Distinguished Professor of Law. Prior to assuming this position he was the founding Dean and Distinguished Professor of Law, and Raymond Pryke Professor of First Amendment Law, at the University of California in Irvine. Before that, he was Professor of Law and Political Science at Duke University from 2004-2008, and from 1983-2004 was a professor at the University of Southern California Law School, teaching public interest Law, legal ethics, and political science. Chemerinsky is the author of 14 books, including leading casebooks and treatises about constitutional law, criminal procedure, and federal jurisdiction. His most recent books are Presumed Guilty: How the Supreme Court Empowered the Police and Subverted Civil Rights (Norton 2021), and The Religion Clauses: The Case for Separating Church and State (with Howard Gillman) (Oxford University Press 2020). Erwin Chemerinsky, Dean of Berkeley Law School. He also is the author of more than 200 law review articles. He is a contributing writer for the Opinion section of the Los Angeles Times, and writes regular columns for the Sacramento Bee, the ABA Journal, and the Daily Journal, and frequent op-eds in newspapers across the country. He frequently argues appellate cases, including the U.S. Supreme Court. In 2016, he was named a fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. In 2017, National Jurist magazine again named Dean Chemerinsky as the most influential person in legal education in the United States. In January 2021, he was named President-elect of the Association of American Law Schools. This talk will be held live on Zoom and YouTube and will include an audience question and answer session. Visit the website lwvpiedmont.org to learn more about the series and register for this event. Once you have registered, you will receive the Zoom link by email. The event is free and open to the public. Lic. No. 702138 Scan to book your estimate!

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California is re-introducing its popular White Elephant Sale in person this year with a reduced capacity. Multiple sale dates will be available in March, and the special event begins on February 27 with a preview sale. The sale, now in its 63rd year, is run exclusively by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. The sole purpose of the board, a group of over 100 year-round members, has been to raise proceeds to support the museum in art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, and capital improvements. Since the Board’s inception in 1959, it has contributed over $23 million to the Museum. The White Elephant Sale, touted as Northern California’s largest rummage sale, garners a significant amount of funding for the museum. The Sale also boasts many volunteers from Piedmont – most of whom are members of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. Last year, due to COVID-19 and the large number of participants, the sale pivoted to onlineonly for the first time. The event returns this year with in-person shopping experiences that comply with current safety protocols - expect to wear proper masking while shopping and to present your vaccination card. Over the five week-period of the sale, visitors may browse a range of quality, used goods. Furniture, household items, clothing, artwork, ceramics, sporting goods, music, books, and a plethora of other items will be for sale. The preview sale is on Sunday, February 27, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. March sale dates are March 2–5, 9–12, 16–19, and 23–26. A final “blowout” weekend sale will be held on April 2 and 3. Visit www.whiteelephantsale. org for donation information and to obtain tickets to the event on a date of your choosing. Oakland Museum’s White Elephant Sale returns live this year.

articles.text: Over the past two years, dozens of people have asked how COVID has impacted Mulberry’s, and what has been the hardest. Almost everyone is surprised by my answer. Sure, the initial scramble for toilet paper, flour and other oddly hoarded staples in the spring of 2020 was hectic. Of course we’ve been desperately worried about the physical and mental health of our team members as they’ve slogged through weeks and months and years of working all day in masks, doing their best to avoid getting infected at work and at home, and weathering the less-than-supportive comments of a customer base with increasingly frazzled nerves. And yeah, managing the ever-changing regulations and inspections required by the CDC, the state of CA, and Alameda County has been exhausting. Yet, with all of that, the most difficult and frustrating problem has been one that predated COVID but has amped up considerably this past year: shoplifting. There have always been shoplifters at Mulberry’s. While it stings every single time – why do they miss the fact that they’re stealing from people? – we’ve always considered it part of the territory. Since 2007, Chad has devoted several hours a week to meeting with young people and their parents, sometimes accompanied by PUSD officials or Piedmont Police Department personnel, to explain to them something that shouldn’t require an explanation: why shoplifting is wrong. In the past year, though, the amount of time he’s devoted to this grim task has skyrocketed. In just the past two months he has dealt with dozens of incidents. Here’s what happens when young shoplifters are caught. Inevitably, they deny that they were taking anything. When we point out that a Mulberry’s employee saw them steal, and that it’s on camera, they often pivot to an excuse/argument that they meant to pay, they just forgot, or had to run outside to get money, or needed to tell a friend something right away and planned to return to the register. Also without exception, they always claim that it is the first time anything like this happened. Generally, we take their name and let them know there will be a call home that night. We also encourage them to tell their parents what happened. During that call, Chad asks the parents to come into the store for a meeting with their child. It’s always better when the shoplifter has already broken the news, but only about half of the kids actually fess up. It’s also better when the parents do not suggest that they, too, think that their child probably got confused or distracted and really, really meant to pay. Regardless of their reaction, he has them come in. During the meeting he usually shows the camera footage. Especially if the shoplifter or his/ her parents are leaning toward the “just got distracted” defense. These meetings are not pleasant. Plenty of kids cry, and some parents do as well. Chad yells. Loudly. He explains how serious shoplifting is, and what might happen if you happened to ‘forget’ to pay for an iPhone at the Apple Store or ‘were just messing around’ and end up talking to a security guard at Target with a bunch of surplus merchandise in your backpack. He appeals to the parents to highlight the fact that most small business owners don’t look like Chad, and don’t share his privilege of a lifetime of feeling like the authorities are on his side. The typical owner of a little store like Mulberry’s is a recent immigrant, working a hundred hours a week and barely scraping by. It’s a brutal business and profit margins are miniscule, and many owners don’t feel like they can count on the police. Parents, we are begging you to talk to your kids about how to avoid ever being in one of those meetings. Help them understand that when they steal from Mulberry’s, they’re stealing from families who live in their town and whose kids go to their school. Tell them that shoplifting makes prices higher for everyone. Explain how demoralizing it is to the Mulberry’s employees, who generally don’t live in Piedmont-like neighborhoods, to see kids with a ton of privilege take exactly what they want – and get away with it. Scare them a little bit and let them know there are consequences for bad choices. We need your help! Mulberry’s loves Piedmont’s kids, and we want to get back to making the store an exciting, fun, welcoming place for Piedmonters of all ages.
articles.title: A Pilfering Pandemic

articles.text: As California begins to enter the warmer months, many Piedmonters resume gardening. Water-wise gardening is not only useful in the local climate, but also crucial to maintaining a drought-tolerant garden year round. Also known as smart gardening, water-wise gardening uses landscaping techniques to help conserve water while maintaining a beautiful yard. Some common tactics for a water-wise garden include rainwater harvesting, utilizing low-water plants, and maintaining healthy soils with compost and mulch. Focusing on healthy soils, compost and mulch can be utilized for different purposes when maintaining a water-wise garden. Both compost and mulch use can help to reduce the amount of water required by a garden, and it’s important to know the right uses for each. Since soils are a collection of mineral particles of different sizes, large particles allow water to pass through rapidly, while small particles allow the water to penetrate the soil much more slowly. One solution to both large and small particles is adding organic matter (compost and mulch) to improve the texture and water-holding capacity of the soil. When applied in a 3” layer at the least, organic mulch can cut water needs by blocking weeds and reducing evaporation. In addition to retaining moisture, organic mulches also increase the humidity level around plants, feed your soils, and insulate plants from heat and cold. Although there are many varieties of mulch, East Bay Municipal Utility District recommends organic, weedfree, well-composted mulch with a fine to medium texture. Other aspects to consider when selecting a mulch include the type of plants in your garden and the plants heat preferences, the type of soil your garden already has, and expected weather conditions and our local bay area climate. For purposes of moisture retention, organic matter in the form of compost will improve the texture and water-holding capacity of the soil. For amending soil with compost, working a 4” to 8” layer of compost into the soil provides added benefits when establishing new garden beds or transitioning your lawn into a garden. Topdressing, or spreading a half to two-inch layer of compost on top of the soil once or twice a year, is beneficial to existing gardens. Incorporating at least half an inch to an inch of compost in both the spring and fall seasons can also increase plant growth, reduce the need for chemical fertilizers, and improve soil structure through the addition of beneficial bacteria and fungi. Not all soil and compost are created equally. Piedmonters should generally avoid wood chips, large pieces of bark mulch, and synthetic materials based on the climate of the local area. Similarly, it’s best to avoid weed cloths, plastic, and other weed barriers that prevent the natural cycle of nutrients through soils, which can kill the living organisms in your soil. Fortunately, Piedmonters can obtain free organic matter through various giveaways held throughout the year, including this Saturday, February 12, from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m. at the City’s Corporation Yard. pages.text: Wednesday, February 9, 2022 5 By Laura Pochop Over the past two years, dozens of people have asked how COVID has impacted Mulberry’s, and what has been the hardest. Almost everyone is surprised by my answer. Sure, the initial scramble for toilet paper, flour and other oddly hoarded staples in the spring of 2020 was hectic. Of course we’ve been desperately worried about the physical and mental health of our team members as they’ve slogged through weeks and months and years of working all day in masks, doing their best to avoid getting infected at work and at home, and weathering the less-than-supportive comments of a customer base with increasingly frazzled nerves. And yeah, managing the ever-changing regulations and inspections required by the CDC, the state of CA, and Alameda County has been exhausting. Yet, with all of that, the most difficult and frustrating problem has been one that predated COVID but has amped up considerably this past year: shoplifting. There have always been shoplifters at Mulberry’s. While it stings every single time – why do they miss the fact that they’re stealing from people? – we’ve always considered it part of the territory. Since 2007, Chad has devoted several hours a week to meeting with young people and their parents, sometimes accompanied by PUSD officials or Piedmont Police Department personnel, to explain to them something that shouldn’t require an explanation: why shoplifting is wrong. In A Pilfering Pandemic the past year, though, the amount of time he’s devoted to this grim task has skyrocketed. In just the past two months he has dealt with dozens of incidents. Here’s what happens when young shoplifters are caught. Inevitably, they deny that they were taking anything. When we point out that a Mulberry’s employee saw them steal, and that it’s on camera, they often pivot to an excuse/argument that they meant to pay, they just forgot, or had to run outside to get money, or needed to tell a friend something right away and planned to return to the register. Also without exception, they always claim that it is the first time anything like this happened. Generally, we take their name and let them know there will be a call home that night. We also encourage them to tell their parents what happened. During that call, Chad asks the parents to come into the store for a meeting with their child. It’s always better when the shoplifter has already broken the news, but only about half of the kids actually fess up. It’s also better when the parents do not suggest that they, too, think that their child probably got confused or distracted and really, really meant to pay. Regardless of their reaction, he has them come in. During the meeting he usually shows the camera footage. Especially if the shoplifter or his/ her parents are leaning toward the “just got distracted” defense. These meetings are not pleasant. Plenty of kids cry, and some parents do as well. Chad yells. Loudly. He explains how serious shoplifting is, and what might happen if you happened to ‘forget’ to pay for an iPhone at the Apple Store or ‘were just messing around’ and end up talking to a security guard at Target with a bunch of surplus merchandise in your backpack. He appeals to the parents to highlight the fact that most small business owners don’t look like Chad, and don’t share his privilege of a lifetime of feeling like the authorities are on his side. The typical owner of a little store like Mulberry’s is a recent immigrant, working a hundred hours a week and barely scraping by. It’s a brutal business and profit margins are miniscule, and many owners don’t feel like they can count on the police. Parents, we are begging you to talk to your kids about how to avoid ever being in one of those meetings. Help them understand that when they steal from Mulberry’s, they’re stealing from families who live in their town and whose kids go to their school. Tell them that shoplifting makes prices higher for everyone. Explain how demoralizing it is to the Mulberry’s employees, who generally don’t live in Piedmont-like neighborhoods, to see kids with a ton of privilege take exactly what they want – and get away with it. Scare them a little bit and let them know there are consequences for bad choices. We need your help! Mulberry’s loves Piedmont’s kids, and we want to get back to making the store an exciting, fun, welcoming place for Piedmonters of all ages. White Elephant Sale returns in person Preview sale is on February 27 By Allyson Aleksey Oakland Museum of California is re-introducing its popular White Elephant Sale in person this year with a reduced capacity. Multiple sale dates will be available in March, and the special event begins on February 27 with a preview sale. The sale, now in its 63rd year, is run exclusively by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. The sole purpose of the board, a group of over 100 year-round members, has been to raise proceeds to support the museum in art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, and capital improvements. Since the Board’s inception in 1959, it has contributed over $23 million to the Museum. The White Elephant Sale, touted as Northern California’s largest rummage sale, garners a significant amount of funding for the museum. The Sale also boasts many volunteers from Piedmont – most of whom are members of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. Last year, due to COVID-19 and the large number of participants, the sale pivoted to onlineonly for the first time. The event returns this year with in-person shopping experiences that comply with current safety protocols - expect to wear proper masking while shopping and to present your vaccination card. Over the five week-period of the sale, visitors may browse a range of quality, used goods. Furniture, household items, clothing, artwork, ceramics, sporting goods, music, books, and a plethora of other items will be for sale. The preview sale is on Sunday, February 27, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. March sale dates are March 2–5, 9–12, 16–19, and 23–26. A final “blowout” weekend sale will be held on April 2 and 3. Visit www.whiteelephantsale. org for donation information and to obtain tickets to the event on a date of your choosing. Oakland Museum’s White Elephant Sale returns live this year. articles.text: Piedmont resident Mina Fedor, 13, has been named a top 5 honoree for Time Kid of the Year for her work as an Asian American Pacific Islander (AAPI) activist. Fedor will be recognized along Mina Fedor speaks to a crowd at a rally in Berkeley in March 2021. with the other honorees on the Kid of the Year television special, hosted by Trevor Noah on Nickelodeon tonight, February 9. The second annual Kid of the Year honor recognizes young leaders who have made contributions in a range of fields, including social justice, science, and education. The honor is presented by Nickelodeon in partnership with Time Magazine, following a nationwide search that included thousands of youth. “I was really surprised when I received the email. My family and I were taken aback,” Fedor admitted. “I actually don’t even know who submitted me.” At age 12 Fedor organized a rally at the Berkeley Marina on March 28, 2021 to raise awareness of AAPI hate. Over 1,200 community members attended the rally. Fedor, who is of Korean and Slovakian descent, said she has seen hate against the Asian community even when walking near home with a family member. “I was aware of attacks on the Asian community. As last year progressed, I learned more about AAPI history and wanted to educate myself,” Fedor said. “I wasn’t expecting to hold a large rally at first. [My] friends and I had the intention of hanging signs over a highway that I drive under every day I go to school.” Fedor and her peers made signs that read “I Am Not a Virus,” and “Stop Asian Hate,” while leading a crowd on a march over a pedestrian bridge. Fedor recalls cars honking in support. She expected a crowd would show up in support at the Berkeley Marina but never expected it to grow to over 1000 people. Fedor co-founded the activist group AAPI Youth Rising, comprised of herself and other middle schoolers. They have worked toward a goal of passing state Photo by Jose Carlos Fajardo Mina Fedor legislation that would make the teaching of ethnic studies mandatory in public high schools. That law passed in October 2021. “It’s extremely important to know about other’s stories, and your own. That’s a big part about growing up as an American citizen,” she said. “Representation means everything. When you learn stories similar to yours, or about people who look like you, you feel like your experiences are more valid.” Each of the eight honorees will receive a cash prize and the opportunity to serve as a reporter for Time for Kids, a subsidiary of Time Magazine. Viewers can watch the premiere on the Nickelodeon channel tonight, February 9, at 4:30 p.m.

articles.text: At the January 26 School Board meeting Superintendent Randy Booker presented the board with a report on enrollment capacity throughout the district. The board requested that a survey be conducted to help determine the amount of inter-district transfers that may be accepted for next year. The study found that in grades 1-5 there will be 56 seats available at Beach, 42 at Havens and 35 at Wildwood if the district is at maximum capacity. At the middle school there are an estimated 186 open seats, 75 at Piedmont High and 27 at Millennium High. These numbers do not take into account projected gains and losses after the school year starts, due to students transferring in or out. For example, during a non-pandemic year Piedmont High averages a decrease of roughly ten 9th graders in the middle of the year. Using current numbers for next year, the 9th grade class could add 27 more students. Therefore, considering the midyear exits of 10 students, the district estimates a total of 37 more students that could possibly be added next year before reaching capacity. The current collective bargaining between the district and teachers union limits staffing to student ratio at 1:28 or less. The California Department of Education provides additional funding to districts with a ratio under 1:24 at the K-3 levels. The district plans to limit grades 1-3 to 24 students per class, and the capacity for 4-5 graders is 26 instead of the maximum 28 due to PEF funding. Grades 6-12 have a capacity of 1:28 teacher to staff ratio and Millennium High has a maximum ratio at 1:20. Piedmont School District receives around $9,700 per student from state and federal funds. For every 28 students added, the school district adds approximately one and half fulltime teacher salary. The student increase gives the district around $126,100 and costs the district roughly $124,000 in salary. Booker anticipates competition between Alameda County schools for inter-district transfers. “Absolutely, 100% yes [there will be competition]. Every district in Alameda County is looking for students, except for Dublin,” he said.
