articles.text: Piedmont High School has announced the official launch of Readmont 2022, Piedmont’s annual community read project now in its 12th year. All Piedmonters are encouraged to read A Thousand Splendid Suns by Khaled Hosseini. The book was published in 2007 and chronicles the story of two generations of women, Mariam and Laila, living in Kabul. The story not only portrays the bonds of family and friendship and the endurance of women during Taliban control, but also gives readers a look into the backdrop of the recent history of Afghanistan. We chose this book for its beautiful story of love in an unforgiving time and as a way for our community to discuss the recent events in Afghanistan and the increase of Afghan refugees to the Bay area. The book is appropriate for readers age 14 and older. To encourage younger readers to learn about the topic, the school is also promoting two books appropriate for 6-10 year olds, I am Malala, and Malala - my story for standing up for Girls’ Rights. Books are available for check out at all Piedmont school libraries (high school, middle school, and three elementary schools). The books are funded through a grant from the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee (PADC). A Great Good Place for Books in Montclair is offering a 20% discount on this title. The hope is that this common reading experience will forge positive connections among students, staff, parents and community members, and encourage reading as a medium of collaboration. English department chairperson Beth Black and high school librarian Kathryn Levenson will facilitate student discussions during the week of April 19, and host guest speakers on the topic the evening of April 21. All events are open to the community. More information will follow regarding the community events. If you have questions, contact Kathryn Levenson at klevenson@piedmont.k12.ca.us, 510-594-2781, or Beth Black at bblack@piedmont.k12.ca.us.
articles.title: A Thousand Splendid Suns chosen for 2022

articles.text: The Piedmont School Board approved a first reading of a proposed new class, Film as Literature, to be taught by Mercedes Foster. The first reading serves as an opportunity for Board members to review and discuss the content of the course proposal before it is added to the high school curriculum. It will be a new elective course within the English Department for students in grades 11 and 12. Students will be instructed on how to use literary terminology and analytical techniques learned in their prerequisite English classes to explore films with cultural or societal merit. Students will watch and critically analyze these films, as well as screenwriting choices, sound design, and directional design. “Although the Piedmont High School humanities courses traditionally have included the occasional film or film clip as part of the curriculum, the material is generally used to supplement other material. Rarely is film or video explicitly examined as a piece of art, let alone examined critically as a product of our culture. Exploring film takes time that is not available in the college preparatory English classes,” Foster explained in her course proposal. “We want this course to include relevant experiences that invite fresh conversations, and address the interests and concerns of the students,” Foster said. Students will have the opportunity to use what they learn in the course to produce their own films through online editing software. In addition, the new STEAM building includes a sound booth editing room that will allow students to mix, record or edit overlay audio. Foster noted that many Bay Area schools have a Digital Media class built into their curriculum, notably at Oakland Tech and Palo Alto, or a Film and Media Arts Department like the one at South Torrance High. The School Board unanimously approved the first reading of the course. A second reading will determine whether or not the course will be made available, although School Board President Cory Smegal noted that it will likely get approved. “That’s the most likely thing to happen, unless we hear [opposition] from the public. But the only thing I think we’d hear is that they would really like to take this class,” she said.
articles.title: School Board gives early OK for course on Film as Literature

articles.text: Piedmont Adult School is in full swing, and is offering new courses on climate change and parenting. Classes in progress can still be joined and many have yet to commence. Climate Change 101 Are you concerned about climate change and looking for a way to become better informed? Climate Change 101, a course “by a non-scientist for non-scientists,” is being offered by Piedmont Adult School on March 2 and 3. This two-evening course covers the causes and impacts of climate change and provides students with the knowledge required to make informed decisions. Students will receive useful handouts as well as references for further study. Climate Change 101 is taught by James Stehr, a Piedmont High School graduate in 1960. Stehr graduated with honors from UC Berkeley and went on to a career in architecture. Upon retirement, he decided to pursue his interest in the sciences, and became a project leader for Al Gore’s Climate Reality Project. A man of many interests, Stehr also holds a certificate in financial planning. He will also teach a course at the Adult School in March called Tools and Techniques for Navigating Retirement. Mindful Positive Parenting Austin Lambe returns to teach his popular course, Mindful Positive Parenting starting on March 8. The six-week course is designed to provide parents with a space to share concerns and learn new parenting strategies. The class will focus on behavior challenges that are commonly faced by parents: screen time, work refusal, respectful communications, homework, and friendships. The first four classes will explain the principles of behavior and the last four will be devoted to generating interventions and strategies that can be implemented immediately at home. Lambe lives in Oakland but hails originally from Ireland. He is married and a parent of two teenagers. He is a board certified behavior analyst and he works as the Behavior Analyst for Piedmont School District. He has spent his career coaching students, teachers and parents on challenging behaviors in a variety of settings. Lambe has a background in Clinical Psychology and has a passion for helping others to solve behavior puzzles. For more information and to sign up, visit Piedmontadultschool.org. Classes are open to all adults age 18 and over. Piedmont Adult School offers in-person as well as online classes. In-person classes will be held at Piedmont High School and will follow Piedmont School District COVID-19 guidelines. The Piedmont Adult School office is located at 760 Magnolia Avenue. For information call (510) 594-2655, or e-mail: piedmontadultschool@piedmont. k12.ca.us.

Foster noted that many Bay Area schools have a Digital Media class built into their curriculum, notably at Oakland Tech and Palo Alto, or a Film and Media Arts Department like the one at South Torrance High. The School Board unanimously approved the first reading of the course. A second reading will determine whether or not the course will be made available, although School Board President Cory Smegal noted that it will likely get approved. “That’s the most likely thing to happen, unless we hear [opposition] from the public. But the only thing I think we’d hear is that they would really like to take this class,” she said. Adult School offering class on Climate Change Piedmont Adult School is in full swing, and is offering new courses on climate change and parenting. Classes in progress can still be joined and many have yet to commence. Climate Change 101 Are you concerned about climate change and looking for a way to become better informed? Climate Change 101, a course “by a non-scientist for non-scientists,” is being offered by Piedmont Adult School on March 2 and 3. This two-evening course covers the causes and impacts of climate change and provides students with the knowledge required to make informed decisions. Students will receive useful handouts as well as references for further study. Climate Change 101 is taught by James Stehr, a Piedmont High School graduate in 1960. Stehr graduated with honors from UC Berkeley and went on to a career in architecture. Upon retirement, he decided to pursue his interest in the sciences, and became a project leader for Al Gore’s Climate Reality Project. A man of many interests, Stehr also holds a certificate in financial planning. He will also teach a course at the Adult School in March called Tools and Techniques for Navigating Retirement. Mindful Positive Parenting Austin Lambe returns to teach his popular course, Mindful Positive Parenting starting on March 8. The six-week course is designed to provide parents with a space to share concerns and learn new parenting strategies. The class will focus on behavior challenges that are commonly faced by parents: screen time, work refusal, respectful communications, homework, and friendships. The first four classes will explain the principles of behavior and the last four will be devoted to generating interventions and strategies that can be implemented immediately at home. Lambe lives in Oakland but hails originally from Ireland. He is married and a parent of two teenagers. He is a board certified behavior analyst and he works as the Behavior Analyst for Piedmont School District. He has spent his career coaching students, teachers and parents on challenging behaviors in a variety of settings. Lambe has a background in Clinical Psychology and has a passion for helping others to solve behavior puzzles. For more information and to sign up, visit Piedmontadultschool.org. Classes are open to all adults age 18 and over. Piedmont Adult School offers in-person as well as online classes. In-person classes will be held at Piedmont High School and will follow Piedmont School District COVID-19 guidelines. The Piedmont Adult School office is located at 760 Magnolia Avenue. For information call (510) 594-2655, or e-mail: piedmontadultschool@piedmont. k12.ca.us. Declining enrollment and levels of school capacity By Jay Russell At the January 26 School Board meeting Superintendent Randy Booker presented the board with a report on enrollment capacity throughout the district. The board requested that a survey be conducted to help determine the amount of inter-district transfers that may be accepted for next year. The study found that in grades 1-5 there will be 56 seats available at Beach, 42 at Havens and 35 at Wildwood if the district is at maximum capacity. At the middle school there are an estimated 186 open seats, 75 at Piedmont High and 27 at Millennium High. These numbers do not take into account projected gains and losses after the school year starts, due to students transferring in or out. For example, during a non-pandemic year Piedmont High averages a decrease of roughly ten 9th graders in the middle of the year. Using current numbers for next year, the 9th grade class could add 27 more students. Therefore, considering the midyear exits of 10 students, the district estimates a total of 37 more students that could possibly be added next year before reaching capacity. The current collective bargaining between the district and teachers union limits staffing to student ratio at 1:28 or less. The California Department of Education provides additional funding to districts with a ratio under 1:24 at the K-3 levels. The district plans to limit grades 1-3 to 24 students per class, and the capacity for 4-5 graders is 26 instead of the maximum 28 due to PEF funding. Grades 6-12 have a capacity of 1:28 teacher to staff ratio and Millennium High has a maximum ratio at 1:20. Piedmont School District receives around $9,700 per student from state and federal funds. For every 28 students added, the school district adds approximately one and half fulltime teacher salary. The student increase gives the district around $126,100 and costs the district roughly $124,000 in salary. Booker anticipates competition between Alameda County schools for inter-district transfers. “Absolutely, 100% yes [there will be competition]. Every district in Alameda County is looking for students, except for Dublin,” he said. articles.text: How can we encourage our children to dream? For many of our kids, the last two years have been an experience in limiting – limiting which activities we can do and when, limiting our social engagements, and limiting where we travel or visit. But our kids are at the beginning of their journey. We want them thinking and dreaming as big as the sea and as wide as the sky. The fastest gateway to dreaming big is encouraging imagination. Imagination gives kids permission to see past what is directly in front of them and believe in possibility. Many kids naturally have a huge imagination that are equal parts expansive and detailed. We as parents have the power to encourage their imagination or shut it down. In Improvisation, actors are trained to use the concept of “Yes, and…” to grow a scene or story instead of shrinking it. We call it “accepting an offer” when one actor says something and the other person builds on the idea. For example, Actor 1 says, “I love visiting the zoo with you.” Actor 2 has a choice, she can say, “This isn’t the zoo, it’s an ice cream parlor,” thus limiting the scope of the scene or she can say “Yes, the lions are looking particularly hungry today, should we bring them some ice cream?” And we are off to the races! All of a sudden, we have a really interesting story to tell about two people at a zoo who are going to make an ice cream parlor in a lion’s den. How does this concept apply to parenting? Well, the next time your child starts to talk about an imaginary friend or a crazy Cultivate the power of imagination in your child. dream they had or a story they are making up in their mind, think of “Yes, and..” to encourage them to keep using that powerful imagination! Other ways to encourage that kind of dreaming are all forms of expressive arts including drawing, painting, dancing and singing. Exposing children to great stories through books, movies and theatre is also a terrific stimulation for the mind. As we climb slowly out of Pandemic living, let’s give our kids the chance to dream as big and as wild as they can. With imagination, they have the power to shape the world in ways that we have never fathomed and that gives me hope for the future. Don’t miss out on a show specifically designed to inspire Imagination, “The Imaginaries: An Immersive Musical.” Nina Meehan is CEO and Founder of Bay Area Children’s Theatre and the host of the Creative Parenting Podcast. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. articles.text: Girl Scouts in Piedmont gathered on Saturday, February 5, for the 17th Annual Girl Scout Pinewood Derby, returning to the event live for the first time since 2020 due to COVID- 19. The derby was hosted by Ambassador Girl Scout Troop #31765, a group of Piedmont High School juniors who hosted the derby for the fourth year. The troop is raising money for a trip to Barcelona, Spain for their senior year. On Saturday in Piedmont Community Church’s 2nd floor gymnasium, Girl Scouts, friends and siblings of all ages raced in five groups based on age and rank in Scouting. “It was so great to see everyone in person this year,” said race announcer Eleanor Lavin, an Ambassador Girl Scout. “I loved the excitement on the kids’ faces, and I especially loved seeing the younger Scouts. My troopmates and I started Scouting in first grade, so it’s really fun to see the youngest Girl Scouts who are now starting out.” Julia Banuelos, an Ambassador Scout working at the Nicholas, Charlotte, and James Phung and a friend watch a close finish with their mom Carolyn Pan. Junior racers Mia Thomas with Zoe Schoen (1st place), Sarah Beverly (3rd place), and Maya Evans (2nd place). August Meyer was 1st and Leo Myers was 2nd in the Friends and Siblings race for ages 7 & under. & up race.

pages.text: 12 Wednesday, February 9, 2022 Sports Parents rally to save Piedmont’s 101-year old football program By Jonathan Comeaux As an update on the question of the future of football at Piedmont High, Principal Adam Littlefield said, “The PHS Administration, Athletics Department and football families are working together to offer a safe environment for our student athletes to play at the Varsity level next year. Additional information will be shared as plans are finalized.” The statement appeared to be the first public acknowledgement that the school is planning on continuing with its 101-history of football as its principal fall sport. When the school made the decision to not renew coach Jerome Johnson’s year-to-year contract on December 3, 2021, it set in motion aide speculation about the very survival of the sport. Piedmont had an historic low turnout of students for football with a varsity roster hovering below 20 players, and a junior varsity of roughly 30 players, but primarily freshmen. The school did not publicly announce the firing of Johnson for nearly five weeks. Athletic Director Bradley Smet called a virtual parents meeting in early January, but by then speculation and rumors about the future of football at Piedmont were widespread. Would the school have a varsity team. Would it have enough players for both a varsity and JV team? Would the school even offer football as a fall sport? Without a head coach in place, the rumor mill cranked up and there seemed to be no single source of accurate information. “The goal is to have enough student athletes in the program to have both a JV and Varsity team to allow our student athletes to compete in an environment that is suited to their ability level,” confirmed Smet, the Athletic Director. “A final schedule will be developed once a varsity-level team has been determined,” added Littlefield yesterday. “I feel like we are rebuilding due to the impact of COVID and other distractions over the last couple of years.” – Football parent Sara Kimball Piedmont was not shown on the football schedule pf Western Alameda County Conference in any of the three divisions—Foothill, Mission Valley, or Shoreline. articles.text: Coach Todd Sullivan’s boys got the job done last Friday, February 4, clinching the Shoreline Division boys’ soccer title after defeating Hayward 2-0 under the lights at Witter Field. With three matches remaining, they are in the catbird seat. It is the team’s second official Shoreline title after winning in 2019. Piedmont was undefeated at 10-0-0 in last spring’s COVID-shortened season, but no banner was awarded by the Western Alameda County Conference due to pandemic protocols. “It should be the third [title]” explained Sullivan. “There are a lot of positives in terms of the program. I’m really proud of how the team has progressed over the years and it continues to get better. We’ve had so much positive feedback from so many people who have come back,” said Sullivan. Friday’s win marls’ Piedmont’s 17th consecutive victory against teams in the WAAC Shoreline Division. When reminded of this achievement, Sullivan said, “That’s funny. I didn’t even realize that. I remember saying that after the first league championship it was the start and that we should be competing for a league title every year.” “Clearly, we are,” Sullivan added. Piedmont got its goals quickly against Hayward with Aiden Woolwine scoring in the 9th minute on a breakaway. Two minutes later senior captain Conner Curtis scored on w hat would be the final goal of the game. The 2-0 victory was Piedmont’s fourth consecutive shutout and fifth win in a row. They have scored 20 goals and allowed only one during the win streak. “This is our third time finishing at the top of the table. It’s been amazing; our group of players is something else. Especially Staff Photo Aiden Woolwine (front) celebrates scoring the opening goal of the game with Hayward in the 9th minute. Also pictured is Andre Stankiewicz (left), Ian Work, and Darius Grammer. Staff Photo Russell Tan had three shots on target in the second half. Conner Curtis’s goal pushed Piedmont’s lead to 2-0. this season, we’ve come with a different style of play and we’ve been able to capitalize. We started with high tempo and caught the opposition off guard. It definitely worked for us,” said Curtis. Piedmont has two more league matches on the schedule and one non-league in the season-finale. North Coast Section playoffs get started on Tuesday and Wednesday, February 15-16. Piedmont should be expecting a high seed and should receive a bye in the first round of NCS playoffs. Quarterfinals are scheduled Friday and Saturday, February 18-19. Match Recap The Farmers were in the game early, a shot on target in the 8th minute that was easily saved by Daniel Malecki. But things turned bad one minute later when Piedmont’s defense forced a turnover on a throw-in and played the ball up to Woolwine. The sophomore striker pressed the defensive backline, won the ball, and charged toward the net 1-on-1 with the keeper, slotting home the shot. And two minutes later, Curtis scored for Piedmont after Russell Tan sent a hard pass that ricocheted off a defender and straight to the feet of Curtis running through the back line. He executed a perfect right footed shot to curl it around the keeper for a 2-0 lead, with most of the game still to be played. Although that was it for the scoring, Tan nearly bagged a goal on a free kick just before halftime, Soren Dixon had a shot Photo by Ken DeCrosta

articles.text: Staff Photos Soccer coach Dan Chubbock has two matches left in the season before the NCS playoffs. Hitting something of a dry spell, the girls’ soccer team couldn’t produce any scoring in its most recent pair of gams, losing 1-0 to rival Bishop O’Dowd on Monday, February 7 at home, and being held scoreless in a 0-0 draw with San Leandro at Burrell Field on Thursday, February 3. The results effectively assured Berkeley the league championship among teams in the WACC Foothill Division. “We just didn’t create enough. We need to find a way to open up gaps and create chances,” said coach Dan Chubbock. “We’re not going to change the system this late in the season. We just need to open the gaps and find that end product. The Highlanders have struggled with creating goals since January 21 when they defeated Arroyo 4-1. Piedmont hasn’t scored more than one goal per game in the last six matches, and is scoreless in its last three. “We just haven’t scored enough goals. We don’t have a natural center forward. We have a lot of good players, we move the ball around really well, we just don’t quite create the chances and find that finishing touch,” said Chubbock. Piedmont has two league matches left, hosting Castro Valley for Senior Night tonight, Wednesday, February 9 at Witter Field, and the season-finale at league champion Berkeley on Friday, February 11. North Coast Section playoffs begin on Tuesday and Wednesday, February 15-16. If the Highlanders win the last two home games of the season, they may be enough to earn a top 8 NCS seed, with the possibility of at least one playoff game at Witter Field. 1-0 loss to Bishop O’Dowd Bishop O’Dowd’s goal came in the 31st minute on a fortunate bounce after a corner kick. In the buildup, the cross from the corner went over a leaping O’Dowd forward and fell at the feet of BOD captain Katie Senn for the open shot. Earlier in the 19th minute, Piedmont goalkeeper Morgan Hunt made a big save in a 1-on-1 situation. She came up big again in the 71st minute with another dramatic save. In the second half, the Highlanders came out on the front foot but couldn’t find the finishing touch. Tucker Donahue had a shot trail high in the 42nd, Emily Fitzgerald also had a shot go high in the 57th after Zoe Wolfers played a nice pass in traffic to her. In the late minutes, Fitzgerald had a shot skip wide of the far post after working down the right wing. Cameron Lorin had a shot saved in the 78th which gave PHS a corner kick. Piedmont brought forward Hunt, but the ball in was cleared out. 1-0 tie with San Leandro Against San Leandro, it was a similar story of not finding the finishing touch in the final third of the field. In the first half, Piedmont had five shots on target and seven total shots taken, but a monumental save by the Pirates’ keeper in the 38th minute, diving to her left, deflected a shot from Donahue for what likely would have been the winning goal. In the second half, Piedmont had fewer shots on target. Donahue had a shot on target from distance in the 61st minute and Fitzgerald had a shot ring off the crossbar in the 68th. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-5-4 overall, 4-4-2 league) hosts Castro Valley tonight, Wednesday, February 9 at 6:30 p.m. at Witter Field. PHS plays its season-finale at Berkeley this Friday, February 11, at 6:30 p.m. Emily Fitzgerald had a few shot attempts against O’Dowd and one hit the crossbar against San Leandro. pages.text: Wednesday, February 9, 2022 13 Undefeated in league, PHS clinches title By Jonathan Comeaux Coach Todd Sullivan’s boys got the job done last Friday, February 4, clinching the Shoreline Division boys’ soccer title after defeating Hayward 2-0 under the lights at Witter Field. With three matches remaining, they are in the catbird seat. It is the team’s second official Shoreline title after winning in 2019. Piedmont was undefeated at 10-0-0 in last spring’s COVID-shortened season, but no banner was awarded by the Western Alameda County Conference due to pandemic protocols. “It should be the third [title]” explained Sullivan. “There are a lot of positives in terms of the program. I’m really proud of how the team has progressed over the years and it continues to get better. We’ve had so much positive feedback from so many people who have come back,” said Sullivan. Friday’s win marls’ Piedmont’s 17th consecutive victory against teams in the WAAC Shoreline Division. When reminded of this achievement, Sullivan said, “That’s funny. I didn’t even realize that. I remember saying that after the first league championship it was the start and that we should be competing for a league title every year.” “Clearly, we are,” Sullivan added. Piedmont got its goals quickly against Hayward with Aiden Woolwine scoring in the 9th minute on a breakaway. Two minutes later senior captain Conner Curtis scored on w hat would be the final goal of the game. The 2-0 victory was Piedmont’s fourth consecutive shutout and fifth win in a row. They have scored 20 goals and allowed only one during the win streak. “This is our third time finishing at the top of the table. It’s been amazing; our group of players is something else. Especially Staff Photo Aiden Woolwine (front) celebrates scoring the opening goal of the game with Hayward in the 9th minute. Also pictured is Andre Stankiewicz (left), Ian Work, and Darius Grammer. Staff Photo Russell Tan had three shots on target in the second half. Conner Curtis’s goal pushed Piedmont’s lead to 2-0. this season, we’ve come with a different style of play and we’ve been able to capitalize. We started with high tempo and caught the opposition off guard. It definitely worked for us,” said Curtis. Piedmont has two more league matches on the schedule and one non-league in the season-finale. North Coast Section playoffs get started on Tuesday and Wednesday, February 15-16. Piedmont should be expecting a high seed and should receive a bye in the first round of NCS playoffs. Quarterfinals are scheduled Friday and Saturday, February 18-19. Match Recap The Farmers were in the game early, a shot on target in the 8th minute that was easily saved by Daniel Malecki. But things turned bad one minute later when Piedmont’s defense forced a turnover on a throw-in and played the ball up to Woolwine. The sophomore striker pressed the defensive backline, won the ball, and charged toward the net 1-on-1 with the keeper, slotting home the shot. And two minutes later, Curtis scored for Piedmont after Russell Tan sent a hard pass that ricocheted off a defender and straight to the feet of Curtis running through the back line. He executed a perfect right footed shot to curl it around the keeper for a 2-0 lead, with most of the game still to be played. By Jonathan Comeaux Hitting something of a dry spell, the girls’ soccer team couldn’t produce any scoring in its most recent pair of gams, losing 1-0 to rival Bishop O’Dowd on Monday, February 7 at home, and being held scoreless in a 0-0 draw with San Leandro at Burrell Field on Thursday, February 3. The results effectively assured Berkeley the league championship among teams in the WACC Foothill Division. “We just didn’t create enough. We need to find a way to open up gaps and create chances,” said coach Dan Chubbock. “We’re not going to change the system this late in the season. We just need to open the gaps and find that end product. The Highlanders have struggled with creating goals since January 21 when they defeated Arroyo 4-1. Piedmont hasn’t scored more than one goal per game in the last six matches, and is scoreless in its last three. “We just haven’t scored enough goals. We don’t have a natural center forward. We have a lot of good players, we move the ball around really well, we just don’t quite create the chances and find that finishing touch,” said Chubbock. Piedmont has two league matches left, hosting Castro Valley for Senior Night tonight, Wednesday, February 9 at Witter Field, and the season-finale at league champion Berkeley on Friday, February 11. North Coast Section playoffs begin on Tuesday and Wednesday, February 15-16. If the Highlanders win the last two home games of the season, they may be enough to earn a top 8 NCS seed, with the possibility of at least one playoff game at Witter Field. 1-0 loss to Bishop O’Dowd Bishop O’Dowd’s goal came in the 31st minute on a fortunate bounce after a corner kick. In the buildup, the cross from the corner went over a leaping O’Dowd forward and fell at the feet of BOD captain Katie Senn for the open shot. Earlier in the 19th minute, Piedmont goalkeeper Morgan Hunt made a big save in a 1-on-1 situation. She came up big again in the 71st minute with another dramatic save. In the second half, the Highlanders came out on the front foot but couldn’t find the finishing touch. Tucker Donahue had a shot trail high in the 42nd, Emily Fitzgerald also had a shot go high in the 57th after Zoe Wolfers played a nice pass in traffic to her. In the late minutes, Fitzgerald had a shot skip wide of the far post after working down the right wing. Cameron Lorin had a shot saved in the 78th which gave PHS a corner kick. Piedmont brought forward Hunt, but the ball in was cleared out. 1-0 tie with San Leandro Against San Leandro, it was a similar story of not finding the finishing touch in the final third of the field. In the first half, Piedmont had five shots on target and seven total shots taken, but a monumental save by the Pirates’ keeper in the 38th minute, diving to her left, deflected a shot from Donahue for what likely would have been the winning goal. In the second half, Piedmont had fewer shots on target. Donahue had a shot on target from distance in the 61st minute and Fitzgerald had a shot ring off the crossbar in the 68th. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-5-4 overall, 4-4-2 league) hosts Castro Valley tonight, Wednesday, February 9 at 6:30 p.m. at Witter Field. PHS plays its season-finale at Berkeley this Friday, February 11, at 6:30 p.m. Emily Fitzgerald had a few shot attempts against O’Dowd and one hit the crossbar against San Leandro. Tucker Donahue had a shot attempt against BOD and nearly scored a goal against San Leandro.

articles.text: Coach Bryan Gardere’s basketball team battled to a 3-point victory over Oakland Tech on Saturday, February 5 in the MLK Classic, but rolled comfortably over the Island teams, Alameda and St. Joseph, to remain undefeated in its last nine games. In a busy, successful week, the Highlanders beat Oakland Tech 55-52, ran past St. Joseph 70-14 on in Alameda on Wednesday, February 2, and beat Alameda 52-35 in a home game at Binks Rawlings Gym on Friday, February 4. But in spite of the success, PHS is in a two-way tie for first place with San Leandro, each team at 6-1 in league. Tonight’s game with Bishop O’Dowd and Friday’s season-finale with San Leandro holds title implications. Coach Gardere predicted that the league championship will Aniya Perine scored a career-high 18 points against St. Joes. Natalia Martinez converted two free throws to ice the game against Tech. She scored 20 points. Staff Photos Trinity Zamora knocked down the go-ahead basket in Piedmont’s 55-52 win over Oakland Tech with under a minute to play. come down to the last game of the season. Notably, PHS has not yet won a league championship in the WACC. “It’s going to be a tough finish. We know O’Dowd isn’t going to lie down and that game can go either way. We’re coming in with the mind frame of being ready from the start. Friday’s game is going to be a doozy!” he said. Piedmont’s victory over Oakland Tech required a dramatic comeback. Piedmont trailed by 12 points heading into the last quarter, 47-35. but made a mighty fourth quarter comeback with forward Trinity Zamora hitting the go-ahead bucket in the final minute. “It was a really physical game, but the girls responded. We got into the bonus and began chipping away. Trinity hit a running-floater with around a minute left in the game, then we made the defensive stop. We ended up taking a quick shot and Tech got the ball with nine seconds left. Trinity batted away a pass, and Natalia scooped up the ball and got fouled,” explained Gardere. 55-52 win over Oakland Tech Piedmont trailed 15-9 at the end of the first quarter and was down 27-25 at halftime. Tech held a 47-35 lead heading into the fourth quarter, but PHS scored 20 points in the fourth quarter and limited Tech to nine points for the 55-52 victory. Zamora hit the ho-ahead basket, and Natalia Martinez iced the game with a free throw with nine seconds left Zamora led with 23 points and 19 rebounds. Final stats include: Zamora with 23 points, 19 boards, and three assists. Martinez had 20 points, eight rebounds, three assist, and two steals. Maddie Hill scored six points. Melian scored four points, six boards. Aniya Perine had two. 52-35 win over Alameda Piedmont led 18-6 but Alameda closed the gap 25-19 by halftime. PHS extended the advantage 40-28 to start the fourth before closing out strongly, 52-35. Final stats include: Zamora with 18 points, 18 rebounds, four assists, three steals, three blocks. Martinez had 16 points, six rebounds, four assist, five steals. Melian had 10 points, four rebounds. 70-14 drubbing of St. Joe Piedmont bashed St. Joseph 70-14, after jumping out to a 28-8 lead, and increasing it to 47-14 by halftime. The Pilots were held scoreless in the second half. Final stats include: Melian with 10 points, four rebounds. Martinez scored 16 points, five rebounds, four assist, two steals. Perine scored a career-high of 18 points, to go along with three rebounds. Hannah Govert scored five points, six rebounds, five assists, five steals. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team is on a four-game winning streak after winning three games last week. They defeated Alameda 89-65 at Binks Rawlings Gym last Tuesday, February 1, beat St. Joseph’s in Alameda 69-52 on Wednesday, February 2, and battled Alameda in overtime to a 68-62 win on the road on Friday, February 4. Junior forward A.J. Harris sent the game into overtime when he drained a 3-pointer to tie the game at 60-60. Piedmont then outscored Alameda 8-2 in the four-minute overtime period. “It was a crazy finish, and we knew it would be tough after beating them earlier in the week,” said A.J. Harris. “They jumped on us early, but coach kept preaching that there was a lot of time to come back. We put up a shot with 12 seconds left, but it missed and Adhi [Bornstein] grabbed a huge rebound and kicked it out to JoJo [Murphy], who passed it to me. I pulled up from the left side and was able to connect.” Tonight, February 9, Piedmont looks to avenge its 1-point, 67-66 loss to Bishop O’Dowd on January 24 with a game in the Dragons’ home gym at 7:00 p.m. “The last time we played them was tough. We had them. Every time we play O’Dowd, it’s going to be a battle. We want it bad. It’s always a game that’s circled on the calendar. We’re going to be ready for them,” said Harris. In order for Piedmont to share the league title with O’Dowd, it must defeat the Dragons tonight, have BOD lose to Alameda on Friday, and for PHS to defeat San Leandro. 68-62 overtime win over Alameda Piedmont trailed 16-7 at the end of the first quarter and 36-24 by halftime. The Hornets maintained 53-38 to start the fourth quarter, but Piedmont rallied for one of its characteristic comebacks with 22 points and limited the Hornets to seven points. Trailing, 60-57, they tied the game at 60-60 on Harris’ dramatic 3-point at the buzzer. The defense held Alameda at two points in overtime and won 68-62. Trailing 57-40 with 5:37 left in the game, the Highlander began a 20-3 scoring run. In the final minute JoJo Murphy hit a layup Staff Photos A.J. Harris hit a 3-pointer at the buzzer to force overtime in Piedmont’s 68-62 win over Alameda. He scored a career-high 37 points against the Hornets earlier in the week. JoJo Murphy scored 24 points in an overtime win against Alameda. to cut Alameda’s lead to 60-57, and after a defensive stop, Bornstein nabbed the clutch offensive rebound, fed it to Murphy, then to Harris for the 3-pointer to force OT. Final stats include: Harris with 33 points and 10 rebounds. Murphy had 24 points 11 rebounds, while senior Spencer Settlemier chipped in five points and five rebounds. 69-52 win over St. Joseph Piedmont tied the Pilots 19-19, but PHS pulled ahead 35-29 before the half. Piedmont extended its lead to 55-41 to start the fourth, and closed out the win at 69-52. Final stats include: Murphy with led the way with 24 points Adhi Bornstein made a critical rebound in the final sequence of the fourth quarter in a 68-62 win over Alameda.

pages.text: Wednesday, February 9, 2022 15 Winter Olympics begin The 2022 Olympics Winter Games from Beijing are underway. The 2022 Winter Olympics are underway from Beijing, China, with competition now through February 20. The United States, with five silvers and one bronze medal, is still looking for its first gold medal. Norway leads with four goals, one silver, and four bronze medals through Day 4. This year’s Winter Games includes 109 events in 15 disciplines in seven sports. Here’s a recap of some recent headlines: San Francisco’s Eileen Gu wins Big Air Gold for China Eileen Gu won the Gold medal for China in the Big air event on Tuesday, becoming the youngest Olympic champion in freestyle skiing. She is an early graduate of University of San Francisco and no attends Stanford. She switched from representing Team USA to China in June 2019 to “to help inspire millions of young people in China,” she said. Shaun White’s final Olympics run Shaun White, 35, is appearing in his fifth and final Olympic Games. He holds the most snowboarding Gold medals of all time with three. The San Diego native is only competing in the men’s halfpipe this year. White competes in the Halfpipe finals on Friday, February 11. U.S.’s Chloe Kim looks for Gold in Women’s Halfpipe In women’s snowboarding, 21-year old Long Beach native Chloe Kim was the youngest woman ever to win an Olympic Gold medal for the Halfpipe in 2018. She looks to win her second Halfpipe Gold this Thursday, February 10. articles.text: Piedmont residents Stacey Isaacs and Chuck Wolf have a lot to be thankful for this Valentine’s Day. They will be celebrating almost four years of marriage, but the college sweethearts’ love story begins in 1984. The couple met 30 years ago at UCLA where he was studying history and she was studying communications, both joined Greek Societies and met at a fraternity party. Chuck recalled that he knew Stacey would be the woman he’d marry when he first saw her. “We dated in college, and we were madly in love,” he said. “We fell in love while we were growing up,” Stacey added. But after graduating in 1985, Chuck worked with the military and was transferred to the East Coast. He traveled the world and spent almost a decade working in Virginia and Washington, D.C. Meanwhile Stacey lived and worked in the Bay Area as a business executive with Clorox, Ghiradelli and Diamond Foods, eventually becoming a Realtor with Highland Partners in Piedmont. It wasn’t until a little over three years ago, when Chuck returned to the Bay Area for work, that the couple reconnected and rekindled the love they shared in college. When Chuck settled in Palo Alto, he reached out to Stacey asking her to join him for a cup of coffee. Chuck admitted that he had to press Stacey to meet him after she rescheduled a few times. “I told her to just give me half an hour,” he said. Both acknowledged that at that first “re-meeting” it was as if no time had passed. Since then, the two have enjoyed skiing in Tahoe, camping trips to Lake Shasta, and spending time with their nowblended family. Stacey has lived in Piedmont for 11 years, and after reconnecting, Chuck moved to town, too. The couple even exchanged nuptials in Piedmont. “He sailed his boat from the East Coast to Texas and then shipped the boat to Piedmont. And he’s been here with me ever since,” she said. Valentine’s Day holds special significance for the couple as a time to reflect on their journey to reconnecting and simply enjoying each other’s company. “I think Valentine’s Day is more than just the romance of that day. It’s more of a celebration of your entire life together – a nice mark on the calendar that you should be thankful for the other,” Chuck said. This year, the couple will plan to have an at-home dinner together with teenage son William. Stacey’s favorite Valentine’s Day gift to receive from Chuck are simple and sweet cards. “I would love to get her a dozen roses...but I’m allergic,” he said with a laugh. Stacey Isaacs and husband Chuck Wolf Free delivery to Piedmont
articles.title: Re-connections: Stacey Isaacs and Chuck Wolf

articles.text: Piedmont native Ben Bloom met his future wife Leah online in 2012. At age 27 Ben met Leah in Lafayette for a drink, though both were a little apprehensive over online dating. But quickly the awkwardness fell away over an unlikely common interest: elder care. Later they discovered that that day, July 27, 2012, was the Jewish Valentine’s Day, Tu B’Av. “On our first date we ended up talking about real things. We actually talked a lot about our love of seniors, which is weird. Re-connections: Stacey Isaacs and Chuck Wolf By Allyson Aleksey Piedmont residents Stacey Isaacs and Chuck Wolf have a lot to be thankful for this Valentine’s Day. They will be celebrating almost four years of marriage, but the college sweethearts’ love story begins in 1984. The couple met 30 years ago at UCLA where he was studying history and she was studying communications, both joined Greek Societies and met at a fraternity party. Chuck recalled that he knew Stacey would be the woman he’d marry when he first saw her. “We dated in college, and we were madly in love,” he said. “We fell in love while we were growing up,” Stacey added. But after graduating in 1985, Chuck worked with the military and was transferred to the East Coast. He traveled the world and spent almost a decade working in Virginia and Washington, D.C. Meanwhile Stacey lived and worked in the Bay Area as a business executive with Clorox, Ghiradelli and Diamond Foods, eventually becoming a Realtor with Highland Partners in Piedmont. It wasn’t until a little over three years ago, when Chuck returned to the Bay Area for work, that the couple reconnected and rekindled the love they shared in college. When Chuck settled in Palo Alto, he reached out to Stacey asking her to join him for a cup of coffee. Chuck admitted that he had to press Stacey to meet him after she rescheduled a few times. “I told her to just give me half an hour,” he said. Both acknowledged that at that first “re-meeting” it was as if no time had passed. Since then, the two have enjoyed skiing in Tahoe, camping trips to Lake Shasta, and spending time with their nowblended family. Stacey has lived in Piedmont for 11 years, and after reconnecting, Chuck moved to town, too. The couple even exchanged nuptials in Piedmont. “He sailed his boat from the East Coast to Texas and then shipped the boat to Piedmont. And he’s been here with me ever since,” she said. Valentine’s Day holds special significance for the couple as a time to reflect on their journey to reconnecting and simply enjoying each other’s company. “I think Valentine’s Day is more than just the romance of that day. It’s more of a celebration of your entire life together – a nice mark on the calendar that you should be thankful for the other,” Chuck said. This year, the couple will plan to have an at-home dinner together with teenage son William. Stacey’s favorite Valentine’s Day gift to receive from Chuck are simple and sweet cards. “I would love to get her a dozen roses...but I’m allergic,” he said with a laugh. articles.text: Patty and Carter Dunlap in December. Carter sports one of his festive outfits, a matching polyester sport coat and tie. In 2000, Carter Dunlap and Patty Fleshman were set up by a mutual friend in a matchmaking plot. Their cupid, Mary MacRae, invited both of them to her house, but Patty could not make it. Unperturbed by the missed connection, Carter invited her for drinks in San Francisco that weekend. The targets of cupid’s arrow turned out to make for a classic match. Astrology charts say their union is destined for success. Patty is a Taurus and Carter is a Capricorn, both signs of the earth, with excellent compatibility. With two children each, they were married in May 2003 creating a blended family. Carter’s kids, Wes and Carmel and Patty’s daughter and son, Taylor and Trevor, soon became fast friends and their Piedmont home a place of love and community. This year marks 22 years since they first met, making this Valentine’s Day a special occasion. “We are going to have to step it up this year for Valentine’s Day,” Carter said. “We are still working through this very cute book: The Best Places to Kiss in Northern California, so we might look through that,” added Patty. Their chemistry is obvious upon first sight of the couple. “Most people that know us consider us to be hopelessly romantic, in an endearing but kind of goofy way. Patty has nicknames for me and vice versa. We exhibit public displays of affection,” confirmed Carter. “Yes, we kiss in public,” Patty noted. When asked what quirks of their spouse they particularly enjoy, Patty said, “Almost every day Amazon comes to our house with something new. My husband is a shopper,” she said with a smile. Carter quickly countered with one of his favorite mannerisms of Patty, “When my wife is being silly she combines the behavior of Lucy with Desi Arnaz, she dances around like Lucy but with Ricky’s accent,” Carter said. When they married, Carter promised Patty they would visit a new country every year. For their 15th anniversary in 2018 they went to Paris, for a romantic getaway that was particularly memorable. Carter explained the complexity of “rules” to the travel commitment. “There were no points in France because Patty had been to France before, but had not been to Switzerland, and it was the opposite for me,” he said. Now approaching 22 years, 2022 promises to have many new adventures. What is their secret to love everlasting? “For me, Valentine’s Day gives me a chance to celebrate love in all its shapes and forms, it doesn’t always have to be romantic love. It is love you have for your friends and kids and mom. It is a time to put those sentiments first,” said Patty.
articles.title: Carter & Patty Dunlap nearing 22 years together

articles.text: John and Sue Malick Sue Malick has kept every Valentine’s Day card her husband John has given her – more than 40...and counting. The two met on a blind date in 1972. Sue was an undergraduate at Wheaton College in Massachusetts studying political science and John was a first-year graduate studying architecture at Yale. “I was set up on a blind date by some friends, but he had a family emergency. John was actually the substitute blind date,” Sue said with a laugh. “My friends asked me if I would see him again and I thought if I see him again, that’s it. I won’t be seeing anyone else.” The pair found they had a lot in common from the get-go. Sue admits that, although she majored in political science, her true love was studying architectural art history. “I found what he was studying very compelling,” she said. “My best memories of our courtship was when we were trying to find interesting things to do that were not the ‘sweep-you-off-your-feet moments.’” Sue recalled their third date, when the couple was taking a walk through New Haven. “We were walking around the city, and he was telling me about the architectural style of the buildings. We were both reading the visual arts book ‘Learning to Look’ in college, and John told me to look at the tops of the buildings. The era they were built offered tremendous richness at the top corners. “We both looked up and it was like the world exploded with texture and color,” she said. “To me, that was one of the most eye-opening, wonderful dates.” John remembered one of his favorite dates early on, when he took Sue to East Rock overlooking the city of New Haven. “We have a running joke; we would stand there, overlooking the city, and I’d tell her ‘someday, this will all be yours,’” he said with a laugh. “It’s still a running joke – at the Hoover Dam, the top of Mt. Tam, we look out at the 360-degree view and I say the same thing.” “And that view is really richer than anything you could ever buy,” Sue added. “Seeing the world from that perspective … it did become yours, in that this was a shared experience,” John said. The couple dated for three years before getting married in 1975. Sue and John lived in Portland briefly while he worked for Skidmore, Owings and Merrill, a global architectural and urban planning firm. The couple moved to Piedmont in 1983 for its schools, and laid roots in town raising their three children together. Sue said that her favorite gift on the most romantic of holidays is a hand-written card from John. “I’ve kept every one. They’re funny, they’re romantic, they’re cute, and clever,” she said. “It means the world to me.” “Producing that card is what makes Valentine’s Day unique. It’s not like it’s a weeklong effort. Some years I’m sitting at my desk and think, oh gee, it’s Valentine’s Day, I have ten minutes to make something clever and pithy and meaningful.” “But it’s like if you forced an artist to play Pictionary, he can do something miraculous like that on the fly!” Sue said with a smile. “WE PAY YOUR SALES TAX”* *On all installed jobs

Flash Fiction Forum members will share their original short stories inspired by love, relationships, and Filoli’s expansive gardens. articles.text: Visit the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art now through March 6 to see Rafael Lozano-Hemmer’s exhibition “Unstable Presence.” Lozano-Hemmer’s exhibit was slated to premiere in Spring 2020, but was delayed due to COVID safety precautions. In describing the work, the artist said the title is meant to be a paradox. “Presence is often associated with existence, continuity in time, or material reality. The ‘unstable’ here refers to interaction, improvisation, and performance. The instability brought by participation is welcome, because it allows constant reinterpretation of the work,” Lozano-Hemmer said. With a degree in chemistry, the artist works primarily with media and technology to create artwork. Many of his works include some aspect of interactivity. “Sometimes I think of media artwork as not so much part of the visual arts, but the performing arts,” he said. “You’ve got a score, but that score gets interpreted by different orchestras in a different way. Sometimes we pretend we’re crystallizing a moment in time, when in fact what the artist wants is for the artwork to have, on the one hand, a decent life, and then an honorable death,” he said. To obtain tickets, visit https:// www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/ rafael-lozano-hemmer-unstable-presence/.
articles.title: “Unstable Presence” exhibition at SFMOMA on view through March 6

articles.text: The University of California Botanical Garden will host a virtual tour of its Asian garden on February 17. The University of California Botanical Garden in Berkeley will host a virtual tour of its Asian gardens and blooms on February 17. Horticulturist Eric Hupperts will host the virtual tour, which will highlight the garden’s Asian collection. The collection represents the floral diversity found throughout the large continent, with strong representation from the Himalayas, Western China, and Japan. This year also marks 90 years since the Botanical Garden received rare and noteworthy donations of the rhododendron species. The virtual tour will take place at 1 p.m. via Zoom. All participants are required to sign into their own Zoom account prior to joining meetings hosted by the university. To register for the event, visit https://41780.blackbaudh o s t i n g.c o m /4178 0 / Vi r t u - al-Tour-The-Asian-Collection.
articles.title: UC Botanical Garden offers virtual tour of its Asian Garden

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre (Berkeley Rep) will be showing Swept Away, directed by Michael Mayer, now through March 6 at Peet’s Theatre. Tony Award-winning director Mayer returns to Berkeley Rep with this world premiere musical based on the book by John Logan. Music and lyrics for the production are by roots band the Avett Brothers, with choreography by David Neumann. Swept Away takes place off the coast of New Bedford, Massachusetts, where a violent storm sinks a ship leaving four people stranded. Each character faces a reckoning and audiences will see how far they will go to stay alive - and if they can live with the consequences. Starring in the production are Taurean Everett, Cameron Johnson, Brandon Kalm, Coleton Schmitto, Ben Toomer, Vishal Vaidya, Ryan Watkinson, and Jacob Keith Watson. Peet’s Theatre is located at 2025 Addison Street in Berkeley. Phone (510) 647-2900. To obtain tickets, visit www.berkeleyrep. org/shows/swept-away. Cast members in Berkeley Rep’s current musical, Swept Away.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep’s Swept Away to be performed through March 6

articles.text: After the Berkeley Symphony concert, conductor Joseph Young chatted with the enthusiastic audience. The mood was festive in Zellerbach Hall this past Sunday afternoon. A large and enthusiastic audience cheered the Berkeley Symphony as it embarks on its Golden Jubilee season, exactly two years to the day since its last concert in Zellerbach. The good fortune was to have Joseph Young as conductor. The repertoire was chosen carefully and, as such, could only happen in Berkeley. Considering it as a stream of consciousness concert, it made me wonder: what if James Joyce were a composer or a music director? First he would need to be from Berkeley. He would certainly let his imagination run wild. Music turns on the imagination like a veritable stream of consciousness when one thought becomes many History and the present blend into a panoramic canvas. Then, all of that would be needed to become a word picture. A few words of explanation from the composers Mark Grey and Derek Skye began the concert. The stage and the auditorium were darkened. As the program began, so did the stream of consciousness; somewhat akin to walking in the cosmos unfettered and James Joyce as composer and music director. First came Mark Grey’s Soundscape #1. With the stage darkened and voices of protest emanating as the center of attention, it conjured up a terrifying experience of being an innocent bystander during one of the violent political-social demonstrations near Zellerbach in the ‘60s. The stream of consciousness moved on seamlessly to Morton Gould’s Protest. Not realizing the context of the programming, I was impressed by the Symphony’s brass and woodwind sections. Their resonance was truly impressive. The program moved on seamlessly to Soundscape #2, also by Mark Grey. Once again the feeling of terrible trepidation returned. And then the music moved on to composer Derek Skye’s As Water, Freedom, commissioned Oboist Bennie Cottone (left) and bassoonist Rufus Olivier contributed exquisite solos in Berkeley Symphony’s concert on Sunday afternoon, February 6.

The suite The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet of four pieces was as seamless as it was meaningful. With a brief word of introduction by conductor Joseph Young, the orchestra launched into Finlandia, the masterwork of Finnish composer Jean Sibelius written in 1899. An entire chapter could be written about the importance of this composition. The orchestra played it heroically. Perhaps the soft sections should have been played softer, but my thoughts were directed to Sibelius himself. While I did not know this stupendous genius personally, I have been a friend of his granddaughter for many years. The stories she told me about being with grandfather Sibelius became even more vivid. I vowed to be a grandfather like he was. After intermission the concert resumed with Lollapalooza by Berkeley composer John Adams who enjoys enthusiastic popularity. Once again, the stream of consciousness resumed and I was reminded of the great American composer Charles Ives. As an orchestra, the Berkeley Symphony is at the top of its game. It is quite obvious that the conductor, Joseph Young, is an inspiring influence, and it is fortuitous that Berkeley Symphony was able to engage him as their music director in 2019. The orchestra’s most inspiring playing came at the end with Igor Stravinsky’s evocative Firebird suite. Of particular note were beautiful solos played by oboist Bennie Cottone and bassoonist Rufus Olivier. And once again, the stream of consciousness overcame reality. I remembered what friends who played with the San Francisco Symphony told me about working with Stravinsky. I also remembered the super-human artistry of violinist Jascha Heifetz playing the Berceuse from the Firebird. How I wished the first violin section knew this recording. But then I thought of the beautiful playing of Cottone and Olivier. Joseph Young united everything into a beautiful stream of consciousness. The totality of the program unified so many things. It grappled with the socio-political questions of fate. Needless to say, all who were involved relished the implied connections and reaped the rewards. On the stage and in the orchestra, there had been a steady diminuendo. The waiting multitude stood hushed and still… The tones muted to a murmur. The audience waited. articles.text: Mare Winningham and Alison Lohman in Sharing the Secret. Sharing the Secret, released in 2000, has at its focus teenager Beth Moss (Alison Lohman), who, from all outward appearances, leads a perfect life. She is attractive, popular at school, excels at school and ballet. It’s hard to imagine that she is experiencing anything other than your typical adolescent issues. And yet, we soon discover that she is suffering silently, worried that she is not meeting her family’s expectations and doesn’t feel like she is in control of her life. She is also coping with the conflicting emotions brought about by the recent divorce of her parents – child psychologist Dr. Nina Moss (Mare Winningham), and her dad, John Moss (Tim Matheson). Searching for a way to control her life she turns to the eating disorders bulimia and anorexia, secretly purging after meals and eating far less than she should. Gradually, as a result of this extreme behavior, she becomes symptomatic, beginning with a dizzying misstep in her ballet class, and begging her instructor not to tell her mother. Soon Beth notices that her gums are beginning to bleed. As the story progresses, Beth becomes more and more adept at hiding her symptoms. But one day she passes out in the school hallway. Instead of calling her mother, she asks the school to get in touch with her new stepmother (Mary Crosby), hoping to avoid involving Nina. When her father, John, insists that Beth see the family doctor, he discovers that she is anemic. When he questions her about her diet, she insists that she eats properly and all is well. When Beth returns to school, it is her counselor (Khaditah Karrlem) who confronts her with her suspicions that she is bulimic and tells Beth to discuss this issue with her mother – something Beth has gone to great lengths to avoid, She tells the counselor with conviction that she has no problems. When Beth finally concludes she has no choice, she does speak with her mother, but still denies that anything is wrong. It causes a major conflict between Beth and Nina, who is increasingly concerned, and finds herself in the role as a psychologist first, and mother second. The result is that Beth gets her own psychologist. The film does a fine job of demonstrating the hold that this syndrome can have over young, vulnerable females and how difficult it is to defeat the impulse of denial. Sharing the Secret has been ranked by Disordered Times with its top rating for the portrayal of bulimia and anorexia. It has been praised as one of the best movies made about this deeply disconcerting afflictions, while demonstrating the impact it has on not only the individual but on the entire family. It is a film worthy of analysis and discussion. Sharing the Secret. Directed by Katt Shea. Starring Mare Winningham, Alison Lohman, Tim Matheson. Streaming on Amazon Prime. 2 hrs., Rated PG.

articles.text: No doubt the world of Cormac McCarthy, author of the novel The Road, is bleak and austere. Recall his dark and nihilistic book, No Country for Old Men, which was adapted to the screen by the Coen brothers, garnering four Academy Awards, including Best Picture. This film, made in 2009, is perhaps the most severe of all of McCarthy’s stories and director John Hillcoat follows the novel closely. The film is set during a post-apocalyptic period, one that has caused an ecological disaster, not unlike a nuclear winter. What happened is never made clear. The skies are leaden, a perpetual mist falls, all is grim and gray. A father (Viggo Mortensen) and his son (Kodi Smit-McPhee) are on a road headed to the Pacific Ocean ten years after the catalytic event. Few people have survived the long, torturous decade. Most have starved, been killed or committed suicide. The father and son are faced with overwhelming odds: they are desperate for food and constantly fearful of those they might meet along the way. The fragile patina of civilization has been scraped away revealing the most sinister aspects of the human condition. They hide constantly from predators who will resort to anything to stay alive. Anything. All taboos have been broken. This intersection between order and chaos, between laws and anarchy, intrigue McCarthy, and it’s this that he explores in withering detail in The Road. Know that the post-apocalyptic setting of this film does not resemble Hollywood movies about natural disasters. What is unique about it is that it is unrelentingly stark, with only a glimmer of hope embedded in this harsh tale. The performances of Viggo Mortensen and Kodi SmitMcPhee are impressive. And with the exception of brief backstory on the mother (Charlize Theron), it is the father and son who make the journey. It is their bond of love, their will to survive against all odds, that make for a compelling tale. Some might feel that the story is too forbidding to be enjoyed, but The Road is an antidote to Hollywood’s typical post-apocalyptic storytelling. The Road. Directed by John Hillcoat. Starring Viggo Mortensen, Kodi Smit-McPhee, Charlize Theron and Robert DuVall. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated R. A scene from John Hillcoat’s The Road.

articles.text: Part 37 in a biweekly series One of the most useful ways to form a vision of how we would prefer future development to proceed in our communities is by gathering examples of what we like—and dislike. We can do this by simply being aware of our surrounding built environment, making mental notes and asking the questions: do we like what we see? Do we like the way a neighborhood feels? Do we want to come back to this place? This search for examples should extend as far and wide as we can take it. The world is a big place with many centuries of development. We can still learn from places that were built long ago in places far away just as we can from recent local projects. The “why” we feel the way we do is important as well because no two places are exactly the same. For this reason simply copying examples outright doesn’t work—we are never going to find models that exactly fit our situation, our street, or our city. However if we understand the reasons, the underlying principles of the things and places we like or dislike, we can adapt design solutions accordingly. This is the point where innovation – and hopefully – progress in urban design, architectural design, and landscape design can take place. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, February 9, 2022 Features Development: Models to consider By Will Adams Part 37 in a biweekly series One of the most useful ways to form a vision of how we would prefer future development to proceed in our communities is by gathering examples of what we like—and dislike. We can do this by simply being aware of our surrounding built environment, making mental notes and asking the questions: do we like what we see? Do we like the way a neighborhood feels? Do we want to come back to this place? This search for examples should extend as far and wide as we can take it. The world is a big place with many centuries of development. We can still learn from places that were built long ago in places far away just as we can from recent local projects. The “why” we feel the way we do is important as well because no two places are exactly the same. For this reason simply copying examples outright doesn’t work—we are never going to find models that exactly fit our situation, our street, or our city. However if we understand the reasons, the underlying principles of the things and places we like or dislike, we can adapt design solutions accordingly. This is the point where innovation – and hopefully – progress in urban design, architectural design, and landscape design can take place. This process has been one of my favorite things to do and in my experience, most professionals proceed through the design process just this way as a See Walking Piedmont on page 32 Landscaping plays an important part of any development. Below is my sage advice as you begin to approach your project. Prioritize Teamwork: Construction is not linear, and there is no right or wrong way to launch it. If there is a vendor you already trust – whether an architect, designer, landscape architect, or contractor – start there. See A Life by Design on page 32 Ask Questions: Whether for your established home or a new purchase, it cannot be overstated that the time spent interviewing, vetting, and selecting your team should be done with thoughtful intention. When the going gets tough, you want to understand who and how someone will be under high pressure and trust that they will maintain the momentum. Find out how delays are dealt with, preferred methods and frequency of communication, and how scope creep or scope change is handled. Ask how they handle vendors when work quality is below their standards – or yours. Then listen. If you pay attention, you can quickly discern if you’re in the company of a team player or someone operating from ego. Look out for stories that reflect defensiveness. Trust you’ll be in good hands when interacting with someone who has spent time self-reflecting and taking responsibility for their mistakes. Temper Expectations: You may be stepping in with optimism regarding timelines, unaware of how decimated the supply chain remains due to the pandemic. Good vendors are in high demand, and this is true across the board with professionals in all home industries. If you’re planning a remodel in 2023 and desire custom, high-quality work, it’s not too soon to start your search now. articles.text: On February 2 members of the Walking on Wednesdays group stopped for a photo by a classic Victorian home built in 1896. Pictured are our Wednesday Walkers: Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Rob Smith, Dave DeRoche, Priscilla Wanerus, Bob Gustafson, Peter Persoff, Sherry Jacobs, Quincy Dong, Harriette Louie, Jim Kuo, Albert Chen, Aaron Katzel, Pat McMahon, Lilly Guardia-Labor, Pat Keller, Christine Calliste, Maulshree Solanki, Adriene Hamlin, Mike Henn, Nancy Henn, Brenda Ferrero, Charlene Louie, Sarah Johnson, Elane Rehr, Kat Lang, Alan Goldhammer, Renee Goldhammer, Phil Witte, Jim Kellogg, John Lenahan, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Melba Yee, and Dick Carter. The group was especially pleased to welcome four first-time walkers: Stacy Readal, Nitesh Mehta, Richard Siegel, and Dale Benveniste. Last Wednesday was a cool, breezy morning for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Wednesday Walkers and was windy enough for a kite flyer to test his skills on the grass in Piedmont Park. The pleasant, dry winter weather brought out another large assembly, this time 38 walkers and one K-9 best friend. The walkers enjoy finding Piedmont’s 21 hidden pathways. Gail Lombardi, president of the Piedmont Historical Society, has told us that with Piedmont’s large blocks, these paths have saved countless steps for students going to and from school, and commuters walking to the streetcar lines and bus stops. A primary economic driver of the area before and after the city was incorporated in 1907 has been residential real estate, and people’s ability to get to, around, and through the area has been vital in its development. In 1878 Walter Blair, the first European settler of the area, created a horse-drawn trolley car from the Mountain View cemetery entrance Blair Park along today’s Moraga Avenue, and to the Piedmont Springs Hotel where the Exedra is today. Visitors liked the area and bought land. Frank C. Havens, the area’s most impactful early real estate developer, partnered in 1895 with Francis Marion “Borax” Smith. They formed the “Realty Syndicate” which, among other projects, built the Claremont Hotel and was originally the parent company of the Key System transit company. It operated in Piedmont, Oakland, and the rest of the East Bay as well as San Francisco, and it brought land buyers to the area. Homeowners wanted to be able to easily get to the Key System trains, and pathways were drawn into neighborhood master plans to accommodate them. Many of these paths are still serving Piedmonters and provide fun walks for the Walking on Wednesdays group. The Key System’s No. 12 line went from today’s Jerome and Fairview Avenue down to Grand Avenue and then to downtown Oakland. There are three hidden paths in this part of Piedmont that the walkers chose as their destination for the morning. Off the walkers went down Magnolia Avenue looking for a 246-foot path between the houses at 144 and 200 Magnolia. The parade of walkers got separated briefly as they stopped at the Larmer Court cul-de-sac to regroup. The group continued and found a path that took them down to Palm Drive. It was once Frank Havens’ “Avenue of the Palms” – a grand entrance his Piedmont Park attraction with a hedge maze where Piedmont High’s Witter Field is today. The walkers admired the palms and continued on to where the street becomes Wildwood Avenue. They passed the triangular park with its redwood tree grove and took a right on what is now curiously Nova Drive, not Magnolia Avenue. Three houses layer they came to their second hidden path. This one is 249 feet long and goes up to Fairview Avenue, the street that was once part of the Key System 12 Line. Fairview has upper and lower streets that are separated by a long green space. This was once part of the Key System right-ofway land and the streets are connected by another path. The search for the day’s third hidden path was a little tricky. The walkers went up Fairview to Arbor Drive, then down to the circle where it intersects with Nova Drive and continued up to 112 and 116 Arbor. Between these two homes is 110-foot path with some steep stairs that leads to another cul-de-sac, MacKinnon Place which is connected to Magnolia Avenue. They went down Park View, turned right on Winsor Avenue and left on Wildwood Avenue past Wildwood School and to the lower entrance of Piedmont Park, which now attracts many off-leash dogs and their owners. Rather than take the shorter upper trail, the group took the lower one that runs along Bushy Dell Creek. pages.text: Wednesday, February 9, 2022 25 Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers discover more of city’s hidden paths On February 2 members of the Walking on Wednesdays group stopped for a photo by a classic Victorian home built in 1896. Pictured are our Wednesday Walkers: Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Rob Smith, Dave DeRoche, Priscilla Wanerus, Bob Gustafson, Peter Persoff, Sherry Jacobs, Quincy Dong, Harriette Louie, Jim Kuo, Albert Chen, Aaron Katzel, Pat McMahon, Lilly Guardia-Labor, Pat Keller, Christine Calliste, Maulshree Solanki, Adriene Hamlin, Mike Henn, Nancy Henn, Brenda Ferrero, Charlene Louie, Sarah Johnson, Elane Rehr, Kat Lang, Alan Goldhammer, Renee Goldhammer, Phil Witte, Jim Kellogg, John Lenahan, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Melba Yee, and Dick Carter. The group was especially pleased to welcome four first-time walkers: Stacy Readal, Nitesh Mehta, Richard Siegel, and Dale Benveniste. By Dick Carter Last Wednesday was a cool, breezy morning for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Wednesday Walkers and was windy enough for a kite flyer to test his skills on the grass in Piedmont Park. The pleasant, dry winter weather brought out another large assembly, this time 38 walkers and one K-9 best friend. The walkers enjoy finding Piedmont’s 21 hidden pathways. Gail Lombardi, president of the Piedmont Historical Society, has told us that with Piedmont’s large blocks, these paths have saved countless steps for students going to and from school, and commuters walking to the streetcar lines and bus stops. A primary economic driver of the area before and after the city was incorporated in 1907 has been residential real estate, and people’s ability to get to, around, and through the area has been vital in its development. In 1878 Walter Blair, the first European settler of the area, created a horse-drawn trolley car from the Mountain View cemetery entrance Blair Park along today’s Moraga Avenue, and to the Piedmont Springs Hotel where the Exedra is today. Visitors liked the area and bought land. Frank C. Havens, the area’s most impactful early real estate developer, partnered in 1895 with Francis Marion “Borax” Smith. They formed the “Realty Syndicate” which, among other projects, built the Claremont Hotel and was originally the parent company of the Key System transit company. It operated in Piedmont, Oakland, and the rest of the East Bay as well as San Francisco, and it brought land buyers to the area. Homeowners wanted to be able to easily get to the Key System trains, and pathways were drawn into neighborhood master plans to accommodate them. Many of these paths are still serving Piedmonters and provide fun walks for the Walking on Wednesdays group. The Key System’s No. 12 line went from today’s Jerome and Fairview Avenue down to Grand Avenue and then to downtown Oakland. There are three hidden paths in this part of Piedmont that the walkers chose as their destination for the morning. Off the walkers went down Magnolia Avenue looking for a 246-foot path between the houses at 144 and 200 Magnolia. The parade of walkers got separated briefly as they stopped at the Larmer Court cul-de-sac to regroup. The group continued and found a path that took them down to Palm Drive. It was once Frank Havens’ “Avenue of the Palms” – a grand entrance his Piedmont Park attraction with a hedge maze where Piedmont High’s Witter Field is today. The walkers admired the palms and continued on to where the street becomes Wildwood Avenue. They passed the triangular park with its redwood tree grove and took a right on what is now curiously Nova Drive, not Magnolia Avenue. Three houses layer they came to their second hidden path. This one is 249 feet long and goes up to Fairview Avenue, the street that was once part of the Key System 12 Line. Fairview has upper and lower streets that are separated by a long green space. This was once part of the Key System right-ofway land and the streets are connected by another path. The search for the day’s third hidden path was a little tricky. The walkers went up Fairview to Arbor Drive, then down to the circle where it intersects with Nova Drive and continued up to 112 and 116 Arbor. Between these two homes is 110-foot path with some steep stairs that leads to another cul-de-sac, MacKinnon Place which is connected to Magnolia Avenue. They went down Park View, turned right on Winsor Avenue and left on Wildwood Avenue past Wildwood School and to the lower entrance of Piedmont Park, which now attracts many off-leash dogs and their owners. Rather than take the shorter upper trail, the group took the lower one that runs along Bushy Dell Creek. The creek’s almost constant watering of the trees along its bank has resulted in some huge eucalyptus and redwood trees. A former mineral springs grotto was another point of interest. It was visited by Mark Twain around 1869 when he was on a lecture tour in San Francisco. It had been a morning filled with historical paths, interesting streets, and good conversation with new and old friends. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday, rain or shine, at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation.
