articles.text: Nº 48 in a biweekly series There’s no Welcome Wagon in France, commented my friend Ed recently. I was lamenting the myriad ways we’ve felt tripped up by French bureaucracy for the visa or healthcare and muttering about lost applications that had to be resubmitted resulting in duplicates and causing havoc. We’ve dutifully obtained translations into French of birth certificates, bank statements, and IRS 1040s. We’ve pledged in writing to not take a job while in France. We’ve submitted passports, French identification cards, the lease multiple times, and proof of rent and utility payments. The latest query asks that the rent-payment format be un quittance de loyer, literally a rent demand, not a receipt. Our landlady got right on it, because even the French roll their eyes. The visa required a formal in-person interview to be booked no sooner than 60 days prior to visa expiration. I marked it on the calendar, but that changed. The Ministry’s latest initiative explains how to do-it-yourself sans interview along with new territory for us – geo-photos. Lest we forget, bureau was invented by the French. I wondered what inspires Americans to uproot their lives in the U.S. to make a home in Paris, so I asked some expat friends. Everyone knows that if you own a home in the U.S., you’ve got lots of stuff, entire rooms, closets, and garages full of belongings; and moving out of the country is a decision for strong shoulders and clear eyes. None of us underestimated the monumental task of a transcontinental move. Though the journey starts with one step, as ours did when Michael and I agreed to live in Paris, hundreds, if not thousands, of decisions followed, particularly, the nagging ones. Typically, people devoted two or more years to planning the move. One commonality is the will to make a sharp shift in one’s life. To travel more. To shake things up. To add a life challenge at retirement age. To keep brain cells alive. Those who moved to Paris while the children were still underfoot likely have a French spouse, which undoubtably paves the roadway to getting the notoriously tricky French driver’s license. Speaking French matters, Colorful beads form a cupola at the Metro entry for Palais Royal at Place Colette near Théatre de la Comédie Française. La Cupola at Galeries Lafayette. and when you’re a couple, you both possibly know some French. Michael and I both studied French in school; and by now, we’re reading French passably well. Our vocabulary continues to grow. but comprehension and conversational French will take more work. That we speak English to each other is a drawback. French is a challenge: I fault consonants that are silent at the beginning or the end of words; and vowels skipped in the middle of words, or clustered alarmingly, such as vieille or Montreuil. Remember memorization? Meet irregular verb tenses. Michael points out that French and Saxon birthed English, so therefore, English is based in French, except it’s not, as it’s more accurately based in Latin, and the French language is distinct from Italian. Yet didn’t the Duke of Normandy, William the Conqueror take the English throne in 1066? Saxon England, speaking German combined with French from the Normans, and the dual lingos are the basis for English. Voilà. Our Lake Merritt friends who have enjoyed decades in Paris are fluent in French. Boston friends who 10 years ago came to Paris to “stay a year,” and are still here, are disciplined students who practice French daily. Their go-to is Duolingo. articles.text: Walter Blair’s horsecars at the entrance to Blair’s Park, currently the corner of Highland and Moraga avenues. that “upwards of 400 people rambled through the delightful groves and wooded slopes, enjoying the beauties of nature and the magnificent scenery and views.” With visitors headed for Blair’s Park and the Piedmont Springs Hotel, newspapers soon reported that 700 to 800 passengers rode Walter Blair’s horsecar weekly. The park quickly became a popular spot for Sunday School picnics and school field trips. In the summer of 1882, a reported 5,000 to 7,000 passengers rode Blair’s horsecar per month. At the end of Highland Avenue, a large wooden arch spanned the entrance to the park. Admission was free to those who travelled in their own carriages, but there was a ten-cent fare to ride Blair’s horsecar. Benches near the lakes and picnic tables in shady nooks provided pleasant spots to picnic. There were even swings for children. No refreshments were available at Blair’s Park, and picnickers were encouraged to bring their own baskets. A lively stream cascaded down Moraga Canyon and spilled in a beautiful waterfall into the park. Rustic bridges crisscrossed the falls and stream. The more adventuresome could climb up to Inspiration Point on the knoll above Mountain View Cemetery. Young boys called it “Perspiration Point.” From this 700-foot elevation, hikers were rewarded with expansive views of Oakland, Alameda, Berkeley, San Francisco, the Golden Gate without a bridge, and Mt. They said “Your stinking promises are making us stink with Pharoah. From this day forward keep that stinking talk of liberation to yourself.” Moses was left to cry to the Lord. “The overseers are calling the people lazy. The people are blaming me for their pain. I am blaming you for getting me in to this. Ever since we met at that bush, things have done nothing but go downhill. I don’t think you know what you are doing.” I don’t know all that Fannie Lou went through. Yet, almost certainly, she experienced personal attacks intended to undermine her work. She knew about the poor being blamed for their poverty. She knew about being accused of planting false hope. She knew about being reviled for putting burdens on the backs of the people instead of lifting them off. She knew about wanting to give up on God. In their approach to Pharoah, Moses and Aaron did not seek the freedom of their family and circle of friends alone. They sought the freedom of all the people. Yet, they knew that the people would not be free until they were free themselves. Fannie Lou Hamer shared their understanding. She courageously held on to it. She held onto it so courageously that Vice-President Kamala Harris quoted it in her 2020 speech to the Democratic National Convention as she accepted the nomination to be the Vice-Presidential candidate. Let us not turn our back on the stories of Moses, Aaron and Fannie Lou Hamer believing the lie that some us can be free while others toil in bondage. Freedom, as these heroes make clear, is a proposition of all of us or none. Jim Hopkins is Pastor of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, 3534 Lakeshore Avenue.in Oakland. He became a staff writer for the Wall Street Journal before joining his hometown paper, the Oakland Tribune, in 1979. It was there he spent 17 years on staff as a writer and columnist. Before joining the Tribune, Wong admitted the bulk of his bylines encompassed economic, business, and “hard news” writing. The Tribune offered him a platform to report on items of local, ethnic and societal importance, especially stories that came out of Chinatown, a neighborhood that sits in the shadow of the Oakland Tribune tower but did not enjoy much publicity. “I had a deeper feel from that community than those who weren’t from there. I came up with the idea of writing a column that included Asian American themes. I wanted to bring these missing perspectives and stories into the mainstream journalism menu,” Wong said. “Nine years into my tenure at the Tribune, I began writing the column two to three times a week until I was fired in 1996.” Wong’s tenure at the Tribune ended on March 22, 1996, for reasons still unclear to him. “It was a controversial departure,” he stated. A San Francisco Chronicle article dated March 26, 1996 authored by Benjamin Pimentel and Charles Burress concurred. “Asian American community and media groups are protesting the firing of nationally known columnist Bill Wong, who was ordered out of the Oakland Tribune newsroom Friday,” the lede stated. “Wong’s departure was followed by a spontaneous demonstration in the newsroom during which staff members repeatedly chanted: ‘We want Bill’ [and] reporter’s desks bore signs saying, ‘Where’s Bill Wong?’” “Tribune editors refused to comment on the dismissal,” the article stated. Journalists are expected to work on objectivity and observation; they walk a fine line to balance their professional responsibilities with their humanity and personal experiences. Separating the two will often prove to be difficult, but Wong said he felt a responsibility to tell the stories of communities that were largely invisible. At that time, it happened to be the Asian American community of the Bay Area – one with a complex and rich history – that he sought to cover. Wong is described by the Society of Professional Journalists as “a pioneer among Asian American journalists, and one of the first in the mainstream media to write from an Asian American perspective.” Wong has cataloged his writing and essays in his book, Yellow Journalists: Dispatches from Asian America. standing choice.” Mayor King noted the high level of talent among the original 11 applicants, nine of whom appeared for in-person interviews on Monday, February 7. “We had an embarrassment of riches in the many qualified applicants for the open seat. articles.text: On January 26, Piedmont School District Chief Financial Officer Ruth Alahydoian presented the school board with information on Governor Newsom’s January 8 state funding budget update. State revenue is in good shape and Alahydoian estimated a $600,000 increase in funding for Piedmont School District for 2022-23, an amount that could be increased to $1.9 million. Overall, schools in California will receive more money through Proposition 98, which was passed in 1998 and mandated that a minimum amount of new state revenue go into schools. Currently 38% of new state income must be allocated to schools. Two-thirds of the state’s general fund revenue comes from Personal Income Tax, and half of that comes from the richest 1% of Californians. Alahydoain described this source of income as progressive but unstable since it results from so few individuals. The $600,000 increase results from the Cost of Living Adjustment (COLA) which has been increased to 5.3%, a marked increase from two months ago when it was 2.48%. Concerns over inflation have caused the adjustment to increase. State funding has increased to $9,391 per student. articles.text: Piedmont Shell Auto Care at 29 Wildwood Avenue made the decision last week to close its gas pumps at 10 p.m. following some complaints by a few neighbors. The gas station previously allowed 24-hour access to gas pumps. Residents expressed their concerns about operating hours of the fuel pumps at a Planning Commission meeting on December 13, 2021. However, Planning Commissioners did not recommend changing the hours of operation for fuel dispensing pumps in the revised conditional use permit that City Council reviewed on January 24. Neighboring homeowners called in at the January 24 meeting in opposition to the proposed conditional use permit, and several others wrote letters to City Council prior to the meeting. Although he was not advised to do so by City Council, gas station owner Jeff Hansen volunteered last week to post signs on all gas pumps that they would not operate after 10 p.m. “I’d like to keep a good relationship with the neighborhood,” Hansen said, adding that ceasing fuel pump access at 10 p.m. was a logical decision and likely would not greatly impact sales at the station. Shell Auto Care located at the corner of Wildwood and Grand Avenues. articles.text: My grandmother has this saying in Russian: “И это пройдет”. it means, “And this will pass.” She told me this when I had gotten into a fight with my mother. I had been crying to her over the phone. She had asked me if this was a fight that would result in us never talking again, and I had answered her no. My grandmother told me that of course it wasn’t. And she told me that the old Tsar Solomon wore a ring with “И это пройдет” inscribed on it. She said that she thought of the phrase often whenever she felt as if she was stuck in the past and overcome with sadness. And so, I listened to her. I wrote down the saying on my hand. With tears streaming down my eyes I looked at it. In truth it helped. I didn’t stop crying for a while, but it helped me see past the fog clouding my mind, see past the words, and see the forgiveness waiting for me. The saying made me realize that no feeling ever really stays with you forever. Whether it is happiness, sadness, anxiety. Whatever it is, it will always pass. It taught me that there is always light at the end of the tunnel. It taught me that the darkness and uncertainty of the tunnel was nothing to be afraid of. Instead all you have to do is stand up and follow the light out of the tunnel. My grandmother has taught me many skills throughout my life. She has taught me to sew, to cook, to appreciate opera, and to speak better in Russian, but this has been one of the most important by far. It reminded me that she has lived a long time on this planet, that she has learned things from others and some on her own. The saying she told me that day wasn’t just a temporary fix, or something to comfort me, but to really show me that everything does pass. It showed me that fights won’t last, that things will go back to normal eventually. I have no doubt in my mind that what she said to me will stay with me throughout my life. I also believe that the phrase “и это пройдет” is something that everyone could learn from. It is a phrase that can bring hope to those who think there isn’t any. We live in times when hope is all we are left with. A hope for better times ahead, hope for the dark to end. I know now that eventually everything does come to pass, and that there is no reason to hold onto a fleeting feeling. It has also taught me to never overlook a grandmother’s advice.
articles.title: И Это Пройдет (This too will pass)

And she told me that the old Tsar Solomon wore a ring with “И это пройдет” inscribed on it. She said that she thought of the phrase often whenever she felt as if she was stuck in the past and overcome with sadness. And so, I listened to her. I wrote down the saying on my hand. With tears streaming down my eyes I looked at it. In truth it helped. I didn’t stop crying for a while, but it helped me see past the fog clouding my mind, see past the words, and see the forgiveness waiting for me. The saying made me realize that no feeling ever really stays with you forever. Whether it is happiness, sadness, anxiety. Whatever it is, it will always pass. It taught me that there is always light at the end of the tunnel. It taught me that the darkness and uncertainty of the tunnel was nothing to be afraid of. Instead all you have to do is stand up and follow the light out of the tunnel. My grandmother has taught me many skills throughout my life. She has taught me to sew, to cook, to appreciate opera, and to speak better in Russian, but this has been one of the most important by far. It reminded me that she has lived a long time on this planet, that she has learned things from others and some on her own. The saying she told me that day wasn’t just a temporary fix, or something to comfort me, but to really show me that everything does pass. It showed me that fights won’t last, that things will go back to normal eventually. I have no doubt in my mind that what she said to me will stay with me throughout my life. I also believe that the phrase “и это пройдет” is something that everyone could learn from. It is a phrase that can bring hope to those who think there isn’t any. We live in times when hope is all we are left with. A hope for better times ahead, hope for the dark to end. I know now that eventually everything does come to pass, and that there is no reason to hold onto a fleeting feeling. It has also taught me to never overlook a grandmother’s advice. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Advertise Here! articles.text: The City of Oakland imposed a proof of vaccination ordinance on Tuesday, February 1, which requires all patrons to show proof of up-to-date COVID vaccinations to enter many indoor facilities, including bars, restaurants, clubs, and gyms. In addition, patrons will be asked to show proof of vaccination to enter senior adult care facilities and city senior programs. To enter Oakland City Hall, you may show proof of vaccination or a recent negative COVID-19 test within 72 hours of entry. Patrons will be expected to show their vaccination status at large, indoor events at city and privately-owned facilities. The vaccination requirements for private and public indoor events are in place for events with 1,000 or more attendees. The ordinance is similar to San Francisco’s ordinance in August 2021 which required businesses in high-contact indoor sectors to verify vaccination status. This does not include shopping establishments, department stores, or grocery stores.
articles.title: Proof of vaccination now required for Oakland restaurants, bars

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is currently accepting nominations of noteworthy trees in public open spaces for Piedmont’s fifth year of Heritage Tree designation. Members of the community may nominate trees based on their aesthetic, educational, or historical value. The Piedmont Heritage Tree Program was created by City Council in 2018 upon the recommendation of the Park Commission. The designation recognizes and identifies distinctive trees that are noteworthy for their size, species, location, or historical context in city parks and open spaces. To date, 19 trees or groups of trees are recognized as Heritage Trees in Piedmont. Applications for heritage trees are sought each year, and the program encourages residents to visit City parks and open spaces to find trees eligible for Heritage Tree designation. Nominations will be reviewed by a subcommittee of Piedmont Park Commissioners and Public Works staff. The tree or group of trees selected will be announced at the April 6 Park Commission meeting. To nominate a tree or group of trees, visit https://www. piedmont.ca.gov/government/ commissions_ _ _committees/ park_commission /heritage_ tree_program and download the proposal form. Nominations are due by March 18. Heritage Tree map An interactive map of all Piedmont’s heritage trees is available on the city’s website. Each marker includes the tree or group of trees’ species name, location, year inducted, and the resident who nominated it for the program. Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap created the map, which is powered by Google Maps with populated information that can be accessed on any computer, smartphone or other device. Photos of all trees were taken by Park Commissioner Brian Mahany. The map can be accessed by visiting: https://www.piedmont. ca.gov/gover nment/commissions___committees/park_commission/heritage_tree_program. Photo by Brian Mahany Highland Poplars flanking the Exedra Plaza are among 19 Heritage Trees in Piedmont. hours.

Unclassified service employees would be placed on unpaid leave during this time, while classified service employees will be placed on paid administrative leave. There are a few exemptions to the requirement. Like other California municipalities, there is a religious and medical exemption. Unvaccinated job candidates and current staff must submit a completed certification from their health provider to obtain a medical exemption. Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King announced her intention to mandate vaccinations for all city employees at a City Council meeting on August 16, 2021, citing the emergence of the Delta COVID variant at the time. At that time many California cities and school districts, including Piedmont, had already set forth such mandates for employees. One week after Mayor King’s announcement, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the first COVID-19 vaccine, opening the door for vaccine mandates across various industries. The Piedmont Firefighters Association (PFFA) expressed opposition to the proposed vaccine mandate in September 2021. Over the past five months, the PFFA and the City engaged in meetings to identify how the proposed vaccine policy would be administered. At the onset of those sessions, PFFA President Brian Gidney said, “Union leadership was not prepared to offer support of a directive that was not fully developed into policy. The goals of the City and PFFA with regard to addressing COVID are not at odds,” he stressed. Gidney said that he was pleased with the outcome following Monday night’s policy release. “[The PFFA] was able to voice concerns that we had with the implementation of the policy, [in the interest] of making it as equitable as possible. We had what felt like productive conversations with staff and city, and reached an agreement that we felt comfortable with,” he said. “If aliens come searching for intelligent life, let’s hope they don’t run into you.”

articles.text: The Alameda Countywide Clean Water Program is offering a free Zoom webinar entitled “An Eco-friendly approach to growing healthy roses” on February 10. The webinar will display the variety of roses that can be grown in Bay Area climates, which provide opportunities for year-round blooms. Guest speaker Suzanne Bontempo, a certified Integrated Pest Management Advocate, will discuss how to keep rose gardens free of pests and disease with an eco-friendly approach. Viewers will learn about alternatives to pesticides, as well as receive advice on fertilizing and watering specific to where you live. The Clean Water Program is a consortium of agencies around Alameda County that work to facilitate local compliance with the Federal Clean Water Act. Member agencies include the cities of Piedmont, Berkeley, Oakland, and the Water Conservation District. articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is co-hosting a virtual speaker series entitled “Defending Democracy” covering a range of topics related to elections, voters, and the health of democracy. The next Zoom seminar, to be held on Thursday, February 10, will feature speaker Rob Richie, president and CEO of FairVote. Richie has led FairVote since the organization was founded in 1992. He is a frequent source on voting rights and has appeared on CNBC, CNN, C-SPAN, NPR’s All Things Considered, and more. Richie has been involved with voting development and equity in more than 20 cities and has been integral in voter-access proposals like voter preregistration and automatic voter registration. Audience members will have Rob Richie, President and CEO of FairVote. a chance to ask questions in a moderated question-and-answer session. The Zoom seminar will begin at 4 p.m. To register online, visit www.lwvpiedmont.org. The program will be recorded and can be viewed later.
articles.title: LWV features Rob Richie in Zoom seminar Feb. 10

articles.text: Piedmont Scout Council has announced that Piedmont native and longtime Troop 15 Scout Braeden Turner has been hired as the council’s new District Executive. He will be responsible for overseeing programs for an estimated 750 Scouts, including its five troops, Cub Scout dens and packs, and Venturing Crews. “We’re excited to have Braeden join our team,” said Braeden Turner on a climbing wall. Scout Executive Kate Benson. “He’s already demonstrated a depth of Scouting knowledge that will be helpful in serving our Scouts and volunteers. He’s a quick study and is already working hard to come up to speed on all our program offerings.” Turner comes from a family with deep Scouting experience in Piedmont. His father, Bruce Turner, was Scoutmaster of Troop 15 from 2007 to 2014, and at different times all members of the family were actively involved with Scouting. Older brother Kellan was an Eagle with Troop 15 and Braeden’s twin sister Madeline, earned a Gold Award in Girl Scouts. His mother, Diane, led the Girl Scout cookie sale for many years. An Eagle Scout with Troop 15, Turner, 25, graduated from Piedmont High School in 2014 and earned a degree in Business Administration and Finance at St. Mary’s College in Moraga. After college he moved to Seattle where he worked with a credit union with an emphasis on customer service. “When I heard about the job in Piedmont, I probably wasn’t aware that Scouting had professional jobs,” he said. He interviewed for the job in December and started work in the beginning of January. While in Scouting as a youth, he also participated in the Piedmont Community Service Crew and the Fencing Crew. “I’m looking forward to getting back into Piedmont’s Scouting program,” said Turner. “I grew up in a family that was heavily involved in Scouting, with my siblings taking part in Scouts, and my father serving as Scoutmaster during my time in Troop 15. Getting to return to Piedmont Council as a professional in Scouting is truly exciting, especially after the inclusive changes that Scouting has gone through in recent years.” Turner will be directly involved with most Scouting activities, starting with the Pinewood Derby this weekend, the Camporee for all troops in April, Cub Scouts Day camp at Dracena Park the week after school lets out for summer, and an 8-day summer trip to Northern Tier limited to 16 Scouts. “We’re excited for all the Braeden Turner, a Piedmont native and Eagle Scout with Troop 15, has been hired by the Piedmont Scout Council as its overall program coordinator. events that Braeden will be supporting in partnership with our amazing volunteers,” said Benson. “I’ve been meeting with people in terms of our larger program and learning what their needs are, and what my role might be to assist them,” Turner said. “A lot of Scouts haven’t met much for two years due to COVID, so we have a chance to reinvent some things. We are open to all ideas and suggestions.” One of my biggest goals is to be present with as many troops and packs as possible,” he added. About Piedmont Scouts The Piedmont Council Boy Scouts of America serves youth (not just boys) from kindergarten through age 20, with a variety of programs. Cub Scouts serves youth in Kindergarten through 5th grade, with age appropriate adventures, time with friends, and a chance to build skills. Scouts BSA serves youth age 11-18 with outdoor adventures, leadership opportunities, a wide range of merit badge opportunities, and an advancement program that prepares youth- For Life. Venturing, Sea Scouts, and Exploring serve youth 14-21. The Piedmont Community Service Crew engages youth in service projects ranging from renovating houses to building tiny bathrooms to cooking food to creek clean-ups. Sea Scouts gets youth out on the high seas – or at least on San Francisco Bay and nearby waterways – and offers additional leadership opportunities, planning skills development, and a ton of fun. Exploring is a careerbased program that helps youth understand a career field and learn more about what it takes to be part of the workforce. For more information on how to volunteer and support Scouting activities in Piedmont, call the Scout office at 844-1752 or visit the website at www.piedmontbsa.org. the planet by saving thousands of tons of textile waste from landfill. History of Dress Best For Less Formed in 1982 by Wendy Willrich and a group of forward-thinking Piedmont parents who decided to support the schools by collecting donated household items and clothing to sell to the community, the group was given an unused room at Havens School and grew quickly to form a successful nonprofit, Dress Best for Less. With a storefront on Piedmont Avenue and a donation center on Magnolia Avenue across from the high school, DBFL offers affordable, stylish gently used clothing for the whole family, as well as fashionable home decor.

articles.text: The last two years have been difficult for everyone, and local small businesses have been especially hard hit due to COVID restrictions. Despite the headwinds, Dress Best for Less, the Piedmont non-profit thrift shop, has thrived since its founding in 1982. It has become a vibrant presence in its new home on Piedmont Avenue, drawing a growing and enthusiastic customer base and winning awards for its creative window displays. Strong sales in 2021 enabled DBFL to continue to fulfill its mission of supporting Piedmont schools, and in November last year it presented a check for $50,000 to Piedmont Education Foundation. Since its founding 39 years ago, DBFL has contributed close to $2 million to the Education Foundation and remains its single largest contributor over that time period. DBFL board president Linda Smith Munyan credits the hard work of volunteers and the talent of longtime store manager Julia Kirillova to the store’s success. Smith Munyan also notes the vital role that donors play. “As a resale operation, the success of DBFL is only as strong as the donations it receives. We

Getting to return to Piedmont Council as a professional in Scouting is truly exciting, especially after the inclusive changes that Scouting has gone through in recent years.” Turner will be directly involved with most Scouting activities, starting with the Pinewood Derby this weekend, the Camporee for all troops in April, Cub Scouts Day camp at Dracena Park the week after school lets out for summer, and an 8-day summer trip to Northern Tier limited to 16 Scouts. “We’re excited for all the Braeden Turner, a Piedmont native and Eagle Scout with Troop 15, has been hired by the Piedmont Scout Council as its overall program coordinator. events that Braeden will be supporting in partnership with our amazing volunteers,” said Benson. “I’ve been meeting with people in terms of our larger program and learning what their needs are, and what my role might be to assist them,” Turner said. “A lot of Scouts haven’t met much for two years due to COVID, so we have a chance to reinvent some things. We are open to all ideas and suggestions.” One of my biggest goals is to be present with as many troops and packs as possible,” he added. About Piedmont Scouts The Piedmont Council Boy Scouts of America serves youth (not just boys) from kindergarten through age 20, with a variety of programs. Cub Scouts serves youth in Kindergarten through 5th grade, with age appropriate adventures, time with friends, and a chance to build skills. Scouts BSA serves youth age 11-18 with outdoor adventures, leadership opportunities, a wide range of merit badge opportunities, and an advancement program that prepares youth- For Life. Venturing, Sea Scouts, and Exploring serve youth 14-21. The Piedmont Community Service Crew engages youth in service projects ranging from renovating houses to building tiny bathrooms to cooking food to creek clean-ups. Sea Scouts gets youth out on the high seas – or at least on San Francisco Bay and nearby waterways – and offers additional leadership opportunities, planning skills development, and a ton of fun. Exploring is a careerbased program that helps youth understand a career field and learn more about what it takes to be part of the workforce. For more information on how to volunteer and support Scouting activities in Piedmont, call the Scout office at 844-1752 or visit the website at www.piedmontbsa.org. Dress Best for Less enters 40th year High quality donations, customer loyalty the key By Gayle Sells The last two years have been difficult for everyone, and local small businesses have been especially hard hit due to COVID restrictions. Despite the headwinds, Dress Best for Less, the Piedmont non-profit thrift shop, has thrived since its founding in 1982. It has become a vibrant presence in its new home on Piedmont Avenue, drawing a growing and enthusiastic customer base and winning awards for its creative window displays. Strong sales in 2021 enabled DBFL to continue to fulfill its mission of supporting Piedmont schools, and in November last year it presented a check for $50,000 to Piedmont Education Foundation. Since its founding 39 years ago, DBFL has contributed close to $2 million to the Education Foundation and remains its single largest contributor over that time period. DBFL board president Linda Smith Munyan credits the hard work of volunteers and the talent of longtime store manager Julia Kirillova to the store’s success. Smith Munyan also notes the vital role that donors play. “As a resale operation, the success of DBFL is only as strong as the donations it receives. We Photo Store manager Julia Kirillova inside Dress Best for Less on Piedmont Avenue. would cease to exist without our loyal donors who continue to give so generously,” she said. DBFL accepts high quality donations of new and gently used clothing, jewelry and housewares, and donations are tax-deductible. Growing environ mental awareness and “green” shopping movements have contributed to the success of thrift and resale shops. Buying used clothing helps the planet by saving thousands of tons of textile waste from landfill. DBFL welcomes existing and new donors to their Marking Room at 799 Magnolia Avenue by appointment at: dressbestforless. org. Kirillova encourages high quality donations for maximum impact. “Our best sellers are designer clothing, fine jewelry, original art and small kitchen and home goods,” she explained. Residents can support DBFL by donating quality items and by shopping at its retail store at 4020 Piedmont Avenue next to Piedmont Grocery. History of Dress Best For Less Formed in 1982 by Wendy Willrich and a group of forward-thinking Piedmont parents who decided to support the schools by collecting donated household items and clothing to sell to the community, the group was given an unused room at Havens School and grew quickly to form a successful nonprofit, Dress Best for Less. With a storefront on Piedmont Avenue and a donation center on Magnolia Avenue across from the high school, DBFL offers affordable, stylish gently used clothing for the whole family, as well as fashionable home decor.

Funding is currently determined by Average Daily Attendance (ADA). Declining district enrollment and declining attendance from online classes reduces school revenue. Funding via Average Daily Attendance for 2020-21 and 2021-22 were calculated based upon pre-pandemic levels in February 2020. On February 4, the District will review case rates at PUSD for the period of January 24-February 4, not for Alameda County or the City of Piedmont. “If case rates continue to show a rapid decline within the PUSD community, I will rescind the outdoor mask policy for all students and staff, beginning on February 7,” Booker stated. “I hope the community hears me, I want to remove masks for outdoors, desperately. I really do,” Booker said. No metrics were included to define “rapid decline.” It remains a judgment call by the Superintendent, with guidance from the committee and not up to a school board vote. Outdoor masking has never been required for schools by the state or county. Public comment on the COVID update item lasted for 15 minutes, with many parents voicing strong opinions. Some callers praised the district’s efforts and for keeping schools open, but a majority of callers requested the district to begin following county and state guidelines on outdoor masking instead of frequently changing the policy. “If we just aligned with the state it would make everyone’s lives easier. That way, we are not sitting here debating, and it doesn’t split the community. I would like to see February 7th become a hard stop [to the outdoor mask mandate],” said Havens parent Amy Gurvitz, during public comment. articles.text: Writing can take many forms. The key is practice and fun. Reading and writing are fundamental steps in early learning for young children. Often the focus is reading, which is essential for recognizing that pictures represent symbols, building vocabulary and establishing the context of print. Another essential exercise in building those muscles is writing. Writing reinforces reading and vocabulary development. Emerging writers (ages 2-6) are developing the skills by drawing pictures and symbols that mimic writing. Soon they progress to actually putting together words and sentences that begin to communicate real and imagined concepts. Supporting early writing leads to necessary outcomes such as fine motor skills, building the context of print, phonics and creative expression. Below are just a few ways children of all ages can strengthen their literacy muscles: Draw and write Support young learners in expressing their ideas through pictures and/or words. Ask them to tell you a story through pictures, or drawing a story about their day. Using your imagination Ask children to make up a story. Perhaps they can write about a character in one of their favorite books. As they create, ask questions to keep the juices flowing. Be the scribe Ask your child to tell you a story and you be the scribe, writing what they say word-for-word. Asking questions is the key to keep it moving. Encourage variety Perhaps a child is more interested in poems, or jokes or drawings. Writing takes many forms. What engages your young writer? Collaborate Share a notebook with a child or with the whole family. Perhaps everyone has a daily entry. You could all be writing a story together, or talking about your day or introducing new ideas. Supporting children in their writing also supports their ability to tell their stories. At Children’s Fairyland we host a Young Writers workshop in late winter and early spring. Our desire is to make sure young people have a space to hone their writing skills and provide opportunities to tell their own stories. As they do so, they build the necessary muscles for literacy, confidence in storytelling and expand their creativity. Writing can take many forms. The key is practice and fun. Whatever you do to support your young writer will be adding reps (and fun) to their school-day workout. Kymberly Miller is Executive Director at Children’s Fairyland. 699 Bellevue Ave, Oakland, CA 94610. https://fairyland.org/

articles.text: The current public health crisis has proved that there will always be a need for those who are generous enough to volunteer their time and skills. Piedmont residents have a wealth of opportunities to explore. Thanks to suggestions from residents, Piedmont Post has compiled a list of organizations that are currently seeking volunteers. California Volunteers California Volunteers, in conjunction with the Governor’s Office, is granting vaccine eligibility to residents who volunteer at the Oakland Coliseum vaccination site. Individuals who are interested can sign up at https:// myturnvolunteer.ca.gov/s/landing. Both medical and non-medical professionals are needed, for a variety of activities from educating others about the vaccine to helping your neighbor sign up. It Takes a Village It Takes a Village is an inclusive community of volunteers whose mission is to create and deliver Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) to health care workers serving communities in need throughout the Bay Area. To date, volunteers have delivered over 90,000 masks and 50,000 face shields. The organization is seeking volunteers who can sew masks, wash and press sewn masks, deliver PPE, and assemble face shields. If you would like to get involved, visit https://www. it-takes-a-village.org/. Tax-Aid Tax-Aid offers free tax help from expert Bay Area tax volunteers. The company’s large team of tax professional volunteers handle income situation of all types, and offer free help in a client’s preferred language. There are volunteer opportunities after tax seasons ends, too. Visit https://tax-aid.org/tax-volunteers/ to sign up. Mercy Brown Bag The Mercy Brown Bag program distributes well over one million pounds of food every year, thanks to hundreds of volunteers. The effort was launched in 1982 by residents at the Mercy Retirement & Care Center who saw that seniors in their Oakland neighborhoods were experiencing food insecurity. There are many ways to volunteer, including distributing lunch bags to homebound seniors, helping at distribution sites, and translating written materials. Visit https:// mercybrownbag.org/volunteer/ to sign up. Is there a volunteer effort or organization that you would like to highlight? Interested in expanding this list? Email suggestions to Allyson Aleksey at Allysonaaleksey@gmail.com.
articles.title: Volunteer opportunities open to Piedmonters

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Gung Hay Fat Choy (Gong Xi Fa Cai) means “May you be Happy and Prosperous.” Lunar New Year is the longest and most important celebration in Asia, with over 1.5 billion people across the globe celebrating the new year in China, Taiwan, Vietnam, Korea and Singapore for two weeks. Even during the Vietnam war, the Lunar New Year (a holiday called Tet), North and South Vietnamese forces would traditionally call a truce to allow soldiers to return to their families to celebrate. The Chinese year 4720, the Year of the Tiger, began this week on Tuesday, February 1. The Chinese use a 13-month Lunar calendar which explains why Lunar New Year changes every year. The Tiger is the third animal in the Chinese Calendar 12-year cycle. Did you ever wonder how the animals got their order in the Chinese Zodiac? Legend has it that in ancient times Buddha asked all the animals to meet him on Chinese New Year. But only twelve animals came. In order to decide their order in the Chinese Zodiac cycle, the animals held a very exciting race. The first one to cross the river would be granted the first year, the second to come in would be the second animal in the cycle, and so on. The Tiger, being the “King of Beasts”, thought he would win, but did not count on the strong, hardworking Ox which outpaced him. The Tiger ended up third, the Ox came in second, but the clever Rat jumped on the back of the Ox, which did not even feel the little thing getting a free ride. At the last second before reaching shore, the Rat jumped on land, winning the race. The Ox came in second, the Tiger third, and so it went... The happy-go-lucky Pig took his time and came in last, and the Chinese Zodiac and its twelve signs were born. Buddha named a year after each animal and the cycle repeats every 12 years. He announced that the people born in each animal’s year would have some of that animal’s personality. People born in the Year of the Tiger are active and energetic in work. They are bold to accept new things and decisive to take right actions. They are fully devoted in career and long for success. People born in the Year of the A lunar calendar Tiger art installation at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. Tiger are difficult to resist, for they are magnetic characters and their natural air of authority confers a certain prestige on them. They are tempestuous yet calm, warm-hearted yet fearsome, courageous in the face of danger yet yielding, soft and mysterious. They enjoy a life full of challenges and unexpected events, like visiting unusual places and meeting interesting or outstanding people. Therefore, the most suitable jobs for them are as managers, politicians, actors, police, lawyers, entrepreneurs as well as adventurers. Famous people like Queen Elizabeth II, Sir Richard Branson, Lady Gaga, and adventurer Bear Grylls were born under the year of the Tiger. If you are a tiger, this year you will be either age 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, or 72. Fireworks and Family Feasts At Chinese New Year celebrations people wear red clothes, decorate with poems on red paper, and give children and single people “lucky money” in red envelopes. Red symbolizes fire and good luck, which according to legend can drive away bad luck. The fireworks that shower the festivities also drive away evil spirits. Tangerines and oranges represent prosperity. Families clean their houses, wear new clothes, visit each other, get together for dinner and exchange gifts of food. Year of the Tiger on Parade • The canceled Chinese New Year parade last year left San Francisco with a sudden invention that may end up being an enduring tradition – Lunar New Year zodiac statues installed throughout the city. For the second year in a row, the San Francisco Chinese Chamber of Commerce commissioned a multi-artist Lunar New Year installation public art exhibition, spanning all of the city to ring in the Year of the Tiger. • Six life-sized Tigers will be publicly displayed around San Francisco, from January 17 to February 19 and located in San Francisco’s Chinatown, the Asian Art Museum, Union Square, and Whole Foods at Stonestown Galleria. • The Tiger statues spotlight local artists as well as reflect upon the culture, people, and traditions surrounding Chinese New Year. articles.text: In 2008, the Lantern Festival was listed as an intangible cultural heritage element. The Chinese New Year holiday comes to its climax with the Yuan Xiao (元宵节 / yuán xiāo jié), or Lantern Festival, celebrated on February 15th, 2022. Began over 2000 years ago, the festival has developed many meanings. It celebrates family reunions and society. It features ancient spiritual traditions. Some also call this the “true” Chinese Valentine’s Day. The many activities include moon gazing, lighting lanterns, riddles, lion dances and eating rice balls. According to the lunar calendar, the festival takes place on January 15. Dates of past and future Lantern Festivals using the Gregorian calendar include: 2022: February 15th 2023: February 5th 2024: February 24th 2025: February 12th 2026: March 3rd Cultural Significance of the Lantern Festival The Spring Festival is a time reserved for families. There is the reunion dinner on New Year’s Eve, visits (拜年 / bài nián) to in-laws on the 2nd day and neighbors after that. Stores reopen on the 5th and society basically goes back to normal. But on the 15th, everyone— regardless of age or gender—go out onto the streets to celebrate. Though the Lantern Festival symbolizes reunions (more on that later), it’s also a time of socializing and freedom. In Ancient China, women usually weren’t allowed out the house. But on this night, they can stroll freely, lighting lanterns, playing games and interacting with men. The wild and romantic stories are why some say the Lantern Festival is the true Chinese Valentine’s Day, rather than Qixi (七夕). On a more serious side, the Lantern Festival also has religious aspects. It was important in ancient Chinese paganism, and also modern day Buddhism and ethnic minority cultures. Origins and Histories The general consensus is that the festival began more than 2000 years ago in the Western Han dynasty. Emperor Wu (汉武帝 / hàn wǔ dì) designated this day for worship rituals for Taiyi (太一神 / tài yī shén), one of the universe’s sovereigns. Intense power play and unrest came after his reign. The new emperor was Emperor Wen (汉文 帝 / hàn wén dì). To celebrate the return of peace, he made the 15th a national holiday. Every household would light candles and lanterns. It became known as 闹 元宵 (nào yuán xiāo). “Nao” can be interpreted as having fun, or going wild with excitement. Emperor Ming of the later Eastern Han was a devout Buddhist. He heard that on the 15th, monks would light candles for the Buddha. He ordered the palace and temples to light candles, and for the citizens to hang lanterns. Both events combined and eventually developed into the Lantern Festival we know today. Lantern Festival Celebration The duration of celebrations varied throughout history. Nowadays, the festival technically isn’t a national holiday, so there aren’t any days off. The best period for Lantern Festival lovers would be the Ming dynasty. It lasted around 1 month! There are some holidays that coincide with the Lantern Festival and are now celebrated together. Torch Festival (火把节 / huǒ bǎ jié) The Torch Festival began in ancient times to chase away insects and pests and pray for a good harvest. Children gather firewood and tree branches. Adults then light them. Holding these torches, entire communities dance in fields from dusk to dawn. Even now, it is still celebrated in some parts of Southwestern China. Vegetable Stealing Festival (偷 菜节 / tōu cài jié) This is celebrated by the Miao ethnicity in China. On that day, groups of girls steal Chinese cabbage from someone’s fields. Being caught is totally fine, but it’s forbidden to steal from relatives or friends. Later, everyone puts the stolen Chinese cabbage together to make a feast. The one who eats the most will be the one to marry first. Lighting the Lanterns Lanterns are the most notable part of the festival. Which you can probably tell by the name. In the early days, the Lantern Festival was also called Shang Yuan (上元). It was dedicated to the heavenly palace (天宫 / tiān gōng). People would gather in their yards and give offerings to the gods. The lit lantern near the setup represented a god’s seat. Throughout history, countless variations of lanterns have been created. They can be small globes that fit in your palm, or as large as a parade float. People make lanterns in symbolic designs as well.
articles.title: The significance of Lunar New Year’s lantern festival

articles.text: A famous variation is the Kongming lantern (孔明灯 / kǒng míng dēng). They represent hope, success and happiness. In the past, people used these lanterns to signify they were safe after an attack. Now, they are used for wishes. Also known as the sky lantern (天灯 / tiān dēng), it sounds similar to 添丁 (tiān ding), which means “adding children”. Lanterns would be gifted to newlyweds or couples without children to pass on the blessings. Pregnant women would receive a pair of small lanterns to wish health and safety on both mother and child. Some regions also burn lanterns to determine the gender of their future child from the shape of the ashes. Traditions and Activities Every holiday has its own set of activities. There’s more to this festival than lanterns. In the city of Fengyang, swings play a major role. A popular saying there is, “Swing on the Lantern Festival, no aches or pains the entire year.” One of the festival sights in Hebei are the jǐng xíng lā huā (井 陉拉花) performances. Holding fans and parasol-like props, folks dance to the beat of drums. Lantern riddles (猜灯谜 / cāi dēng mí) The ancient Chinese would often get together with some friends, drink wine and write poetry. Plays on words and riddles were a favorite pastime. Jǐng xíng lā huā (井陉拉花) performances are energetic and colorful dances that hundreds crowd around to watch. Modern riddles dangling from red lanterns.

In the past, people used these lanterns to signify they were safe after an attack. Now, they are used for wishes. Also known as the sky lantern (天灯 / tiān dēng), it sounds similar to 添丁 (tiān ding), which means “adding children”. Lanterns would be gifted to newlyweds or couples without children to pass on the blessings. Pregnant women would receive a pair of small lanterns to wish health and safety on both mother and child. Some regions also burn lanterns to determine the gender of their future child from the shape of the ashes. Traditions and Activities Every holiday has its own set of activities. There’s more to this festival than lanterns. In the city of Fengyang, swings play a major role. A popular saying there is, “Swing on the Lantern Festival, no aches or pains the entire year.” One of the festival sights in Hebei are the jǐng xíng lā huā (井 陉拉花) performances. Holding fans and parasol-like props, folks dance to the beat of drums. Lantern riddles (猜灯谜 / cāi dēng mí) The ancient Chinese would often get together with some friends, drink wine and write poetry. Plays on words and riddles were a favorite pastime. Jǐng xíng lā huā (井陉拉花) performances are energetic and colorful dances that hundreds crowd around to watch. Modern riddles dangling from red lanterns. When you visit a celebration, you might see giant fish, lotuses or dragons. During this festival, people would write riddles on the lanterns. These small games are popular with everyone. They require you to be clever and think outside the box. According to many love stories, you can catch the attention of your crush through this game! Dragon dance (耍龙灯 / shuǎ lóng dēng) Dragon dance has a history almost as long as Chinese culture itself. The performers create impressive formations to the beat of Chinese drums and cymbals. Lion dance (舞狮子 wǔ shī zǐ) Lion dances can be seen in any festive event, from holidays to weddings and store openings. The lion is intricately designed, with movable eyes and mouths. Sometimes, the lion will open its mouth and demand food and red pockets. Other times, they roll around and play like oversized kittens. Stilts (踩高跷 / cǎi gāo qiāo) Chinese stilt performances are an ancient act. They stem from Chinese opera and the performers sing and dance while on stilts. Depending on their character, they have difference costumes and heights. Food and Family The trademark food of the Lantern Festival is called yuan xiao, just like the festival itself. It’s also known as tāng yuan (汤 圆) in the South, and one of the many tasty Chinese New Year desserts. They are glutinous rice dumplings with sweet fillings made of syrup, red bean paste, black sesame paste or more. They can be steamed or fried, but usually boiled and served in hot water. They represent family reunions because tang yuan sounds similar to “reunion” (团 圆 / tuán yuan). Some businessDetails show the dragon’s expression and scales on its body. Each lion is operated by 2 performers, one as the head and one as the body. Yuan xiao resemble full moons and represent reunions. Even on stilts as high as 3 meters, these skilled acrobats can still perform jumps and flips. men also call these balls 元宝 (yuán bǎo), meaning gold or silver ingots. Despite being a night of revelry, the Lantern Festival is also a night for families. Before Chinese New Year finally ends, the family should reunite again. Take a break from the celebrations and relax with your family. Reconnect under the moon. Enjoy firework shows and performances while eating a bowl of yuan xiao. articles.text: Photos by Todd Marshburn Pictured are Cameron Lorin (left), Charlotte Davies, Audrey Lam, and Amy Derr celebrate after a victory. Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team had to settle for a 1-1 tie at rival Bishop O’Dowd on Friday night, January 28 under the lights. On Monday, January 31 they squeaked by San Leandro 1-0 in a home game at Witter Field. The team remains undefeated against Foothill Division opponents. “It was a great game, great fun, high energy, and a good team performance,” said coach Dan Chubbock after the draw with O’Dowd. “It shows how stronger our team is than last year. It’s going to be exciting when we play them again at Witter.” It looks like a tight race to the finish for the Foothill banner, with four teams – O’Dowd, Berkeley, Castro Valley, and Piedmont – all in the mix. PHS has faced each side once, including a 0-0 tie with Berkeley and a 1-0 win over CV. “We brought a lot of energy and wanted to win. It’s always a lot of fun playing O’Dowd,” said sophomore midfielder Hailey Marshburn. ‘Dowd scored the game’s first goal in the 54th minute on a penalty kick, but their lead was shortlived. Two minutes later senior Nina Goldberg rocketed home a free kick from 30 yards for the 1-1 final score. “I thought they would put a wall in front of me, and then they moved everyone except one player. I’ve trained with her and I knew she would duck when my shot came, so I knew I would have an open goal,” explained Goldberg. Game details The two sides went into halftime in a 0-0 deadlock without either team having clear-cut chances on net. Goldberg had an attempt on target from a free kick in the 13th minute, and Audrey Lam took a shot in the 22nd, but both were easily saved. Bishop O’Dowd’s goal in the 53rd minute came moments after a corner kick. After drawing a corner, the Dragons played the ball short with Piedmont’s defense unaware. A Piedmont defender pounced on the attacker to make up for lost ground, but a hasty standing-tackle with the BOD player resulted in a penalty kick. On the PK, Piedmont’s keeper Morgan Hunt got a glove on the ball but couldn’t turn away the shot. Lam drew a foul in the 56th minute, leading to Goldberg sending in her shot from distance to tie the game. Nina Goldberg (middle) launched in a free kick from 30 yards in Piedmont’s 1-1 tie with Bishop O’Dowd.
articles.title: Highlanders beat San Leandro, tie O’Dowd

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team made short work of Bishop O’Dowd on Saturday, January 29, defeating the Dragons 54-34. It marked the team’s second consecutive victory over BOD after closing the shortened spring season in 2021 with a 66-55 win in June. The Highlanders also swatted the Berkeley Yellowjackets 63-39 two days earlier, January 27. The two wins improve Piedmont’s record to 14-4 and puts them in the driver’s seat for the Foothill Division title. But first PHS will need to get by San Leandro to whom they surprisingly lost 50-49 on January 21. O’Dowd struggled with finishing shots, while Piedmont’s defense was instrumental in forcing difficult looks for the Dragon shooters, holding the Dragons to five points in the first quarter and eight in the fourth. “They didn’t shoot it particularly well and our defense was very solid. We used a bit of a zone defense and went from there. It will be an interesting end to the season. If we can continue competing like this, who knows what can happen,” said coach Bryan Gardere. Maddie Hill was electric against Bishop O’Dowd, scoring 17 points with four assists and three steals. Her energy on the floor was a galvanizing presence for the rest of the team. “I wanted to bring a lot of energy and I think that boosted our confidence. It feels great to beat them. O’Dowd has been our rival for over a decade. This game always comes with some pride,” said Hill. Piedmont has won three of the last five games with O’Dowd since a win in 2019. Piedmont has competed in the Foothill Division since 2012 and has competed with BOD for more than 15 years. One member of the team, senior Hannah Govert, has been part of all three victories, putting her in very exclusive company in the school’s history for total wins against its Oakland rivals. Staff Photos \Maddie Hill had 17 points against Bishop O’Dowd and set the tone in Piedmont’s 54-34 win. Hannah Govert now has three wins over Bishop O’Dowd in her high school career. As a freshman, the 2018-19 team won 57-53 in overtime. Last June PHS won 66-55 in Govert’s junior year. The schools will play once more on February 9. “I still remember the first win; we came back after being down and Kristen Seyranian got fouled taking a 3-pointer and hit all of them to force overtime; that was one of the closest games I’ve ever seen,” recalled Govert. “Last year, it was Senior Night for Kai [Johnson], Nat [Natalia Martinez] Trinity Zamora had double-doubles against Bishop O’Dowd and Berkeley.
articles.title: Piedmont romps past O’Dowd 54-34, Berkeley 63-39

articles.text: Do you enjoy spending time outdoors? Is swimming a part of your DNA? Love to get into the water? Do you have fond memories of hanging out with friends and family at the pool? If your answer is Yes to any of these, get involved and have your voice heard. Piedmont Recreation Department and ELS Architects want to learn what activities and programs Piedmont families, youth, tweens and teens want at the new pool. Take part in a survey about programs at the pool that are of importance to residents. Two pools are being constructed at the site, a deep pool (Fast Water) 25 yds x 27 m; and one “Fun Pool” that includes a beach entry and three additional 25-yard lanes. The categories of potential programs include Fast Water, Fun Water, Fun Pool Features, Community Events, and Multipurpose Room. Open the survey on the link shown below, and start providing your ideas and feedback: The Pool Program survey is open to all ages, including youth and teens. https://www.surveymonkey.com/r/Piedmontcommunitypoolprogramming

It’s going to be exciting when we play them again at Witter.” It looks like a tight race to the finish for the Foothill banner, with four teams – O’Dowd, Berkeley, Castro Valley, and Piedmont – all in the mix. PHS has faced each side once, including a 0-0 tie with Berkeley and a 1-0 win over CV. “We brought a lot of energy and wanted to win. It’s always a lot of fun playing O’Dowd,” said sophomore midfielder Hailey Marshburn. ‘Dowd scored the game’s first goal in the 54th minute on a penalty kick, but their lead was shortlived. Two minutes later senior Nina Goldberg rocketed home a free kick from 30 yards for the 1-1 final score. “I thought they would put a wall in front of me, and then they moved everyone except one player. I’ve trained with her and I knew she would duck when my shot came, so I knew I would have an open goal,” explained Goldberg. Game details The two sides went into halftime in a 0-0 deadlock without either team having clear-cut chances on net. Goldberg had an attempt on target from a free kick in the 13th minute, and Audrey Lam took a shot in the 22nd, but both were easily saved. Bishop O’Dowd’s goal in the 53rd minute came moments after a corner kick. After drawing a corner, the Dragons played the ball short with Piedmont’s defense unaware. A Piedmont defender pounced on the attacker to make up for lost ground, but a hasty standing-tackle with the BOD player resulted in a penalty kick. On the PK, Piedmont’s keeper Morgan Hunt got a glove on the ball but couldn’t turn away the shot. Lam drew a foul in the 56th minute, leading to Goldberg sending in her shot from distance to tie the game. See Girls’ Soccer on page 30 Nina Goldberg (middle) launched in a free kick from 30 yards in Piedmont’s 1-1 tie with Bishop O’Dowd. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team made short work of Bishop O’Dowd on Saturday, January 29, defeating the Dragons 54-34. It marked the team’s second consecutive victory over BOD after closing the shortened spring season in 2021 with a 66-55 win in June. The Highlanders also swatted the Berkeley Yellowjackets 63-39 two days earlier, January 27. The two wins improve Piedmont’s record to 14-4 and puts them in the driver’s seat for the Foothill Division title. But first PHS will need to get by San Leandro to whom they surprisingly lost 50-49 on January 21. O’Dowd struggled with finishing shots, while Piedmont’s defense was instrumental in forcing difficult looks for the Dragon shooters, holding the Dragons to five points in the first quarter and eight in the fourth. “They didn’t shoot it particularly well and our defense was very solid. We used a bit of a zone defense and went from there. It will be an interesting end to the season. If we can continue competing like this, who knows what can happen,” said coach Bryan Gardere. Maddie Hill was electric against Bishop O’Dowd, scoring 17 points with four assists and three steals. Her energy on the floor was a galvanizing presence for the rest of the team. “I wanted to bring a lot of energy and I think that boosted our confidence. It feels great to beat them. O’Dowd has been our rival for over a decade. This game always comes with some pride,” said Hill. Piedmont has won three of the last five games with O’Dowd since a win in 2019. Piedmont has competed in the Foothill Division since 2012 and has competed with BOD for more than 15 years. One member of the team, senior Hannah Govert, has been part of all three victories, putting her in very exclusive company in the school’s history for total wins against its Oakland rivals. If your answer is Yes to any of these, get involved and have your voice heard. Piedmont Recreation Department and ELS Architects want to learn what activities and programs Piedmont families, youth, tweens and teens want at the new pool. Take part in a survey about programs at the pool that are of importance to residents. articles.text: Yosemite National Park is currently open for business for the annual Firefall at Horsetail Falls. This year, no reservations are needed for day visitors in contrast to last year when the park limited the number of visitors throughout February. Camping and lodging is available The “Firefall” is a natural phenomenon where the setting sun provides refracted light shining off Horsetail Falls to create a spectacular orange illusion. The event typically occurs between February 10 and the end of the month, and requires sufficient water flowing from Horsetail Falls and clear skies at sunset in order for it to occur. The Yosemite Firefall in 2021. Staff Photo Staff Photo A photo of Lower Yosemite Falls in the winter, an added attraction nearby the Firefall viewing area. Photo courtesy of Yosemite National Park Yosemite is currently open for day visitors without reservations required. Last year the park limited the number of people on a daily basis.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of AllTrails The Methusela Tree, estimated to be 1,800 years old, is located near Highway 35 (Skyline Blvd). Previously closed to the public, you can now walk up for your photo-op with the Big Old Tree. El Corte de Madera Creek Preserve in San Mateo County has some easily accessible features that many more acclaimed destinations around the Bay Area don’t come close to offering. Sitting near Highway 35 (Skyline Boulevard) is a tree that predates the Europeans settling in America, the estimated 1,800- year old Methuselah Tree. It is the only old growth redwood tree in the Santa Cruz Mountains outside of Big Basin State Park. It is known by locals as the “Big Old Tree on Skyline.” The Peninsula Open Space Preserve states that the Methuselah Tree sprouted in 217 AD, experienced Ohlone Native’s bark cultivation in 1,000 AD, was witness to European settlers and Mexico’s independence from Spain in 1821, while lumber mills in the 1870s California Gold Rush likely determined that its massive burl made Methuselah impossible to harvest. The last time we visited, in December 2020, the entrance to the tree was closed due to dry conditions. It has since re-opened to the public, making it an excellent place for a photo-op and a starting point for a day of hiking. You can walk up to the Big Old Tree and sit on its stump. Across the road from the Methuselah Tree is the Sierra Morena Trail, the starting point for a 1.5 mile hike to another historic landmark, the Tafoni Rock Formation. The near 40-foot tall hunk of sandstone is an estimated 30 million years old and progressively deteriorating from wind and rain over time. A platform sits at its base with informative panels of its history and a clear view. The rock formation, Tafoni, is a name to describe the sandstone’s cavernous reaction from weathering conditions. You can spot examples of Tafoni formations along the Pacific coast as wind and waves eat away at shorelines. El Corte de Madera’s represents a prehistoric time, dating back to the middle of the Cenozoic Era when the ocean covered San Mateo County. A half-mile away from the rock formation, continuing on the Fir Trail, is another place of note, the Vista Point overlook. It offers has a narrow view of the Pacific Ocean and has a bench for resting. An interesting memorial to an air wreckage in the 1950s sits at the entrance. The memorial was erected in 2006 to commemorate a British Commonwealth Pacific Airlines commercial airplane bound for Sydney, Australia that crashed in the park in October 1953. One can still find pieces of the wreckage on the park’s Resolution Trail. Continuing back to the parking lot rounds out your day at a mellow 3.6 miles. But continuing past the Tafoni Rock Formation on the Tafoni Trail will provide a 5.15-mile day and slightly under 1,000 feet in elevation gain while being surrounded by redwood trees and stumps from old giants. This loop trail is a hidden treasure in comparison to hiking on Mt. Tam. No dogs are allowed in El Corte de Madera Creek Preserve, and the trails are a common for mountain bikers zooming downhill. To access the area, punch in “Methuselah Tree, Redwood City” on your GPS device. This article was updated from its original publication in the Post on December 2, 2020. The Tafoni Trail past the rock formation is more secluded and is littered with stumps of old growth redwoods. The area is popular for mountain bikers, so hikers need to be on the alert.
articles.title: Area in San Mateo County includes 1,800-year old Methuselah Tree & prehistoric Tafoni rock formation

articles.text: Potter and ceramicist Edith Heath. The Oakland Museum of California opened its highly touted exhibit Edith Heath: A Life in Clay on January 29. The exhibition which celebrates the life and work of the founder of Heath Ceramics, was set to open last year, but was rescheduled due to water damage in the museum during winter rains. A Life in Clay will be on display through October 30. A Life in Clay showcases the legacy of the artist with over 50 pieces of ceramics, clay samples, photographs, and personal memorabilia on display. A documentary video will be shown inside the museum as well. The new exhibition introduces visitors to the artist’s career, which was deeply expressive of California’s land and lifestyle. Heath, who died in 2005, focused on creating dependable and long-lasting products for the home, with a focus on sustainability. articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre (Berkeley Rep) is performing Swept Away now through March 6 at Peet’s Theatre. articles.text: Photo by Erik Tomasson Dores André as Mrs. Robinson and Lonnie Weeks as Ben Braddock in Cathy Marston’s ballet, Mrs. Robinson, performed by San Francisco Ballet. San Francisco Ballet will present a selection of three productions and one world premiere at the War Memorial Theatre now through February 12. George Balanchine’s masterful ballet Symphony in C and set to the music of Georges Bizet, will begin the program, with more than 50 San Francisco Ballet dancers onstage. Composer is Peter Ilyich Tchaikovsky’s Trio follows, choreographed by Artistic Director Helgi Tomasson. Dancers will be adorned in billowing gowns and velvet jackets to present the elegant choreography. The world premiere of Mrs. Robinson will complete the program. The newly composed work by Cathy Marston is a nod to the iconic American novella and film The Graduate, this retelling is from the perspective of the titular seductress. “I immediately thought – this is it,” said Marston, after learning the novella is set in San Francisco. “This is the piece that I need to make for San Francisco Ballet.” “In the film, Anne Bancroft is impenetrable,” explained Marston. “And that’s genius, because it means you project your own feelings onto hers. I suppose that was the inspiration for the ballet. I wanted to get underneath the surface and find out why Mrs. Robinson is as she is, why she does the things that she does, and make specific choices based on those answers.” Music for Mrs. Robinson is composed by Terry Davies, with scenic and costume design by Patrick Kinmonth. San Francisco Ballet now requires proof of updated vaccination status to watch live performances. Patrons are also required to wear an N95, KN95, or KF94 mask to enter the venue; the ballet company will provide these masks to patrons if needed. Food and drinks will not be permitted inside the auditorium. There are multiple performance times between February 1 and 12. To see a full list, and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sf ballet.org/productions/ program-1/. Performances will take place at the San Francisco War Memorial Opera House at 301 Van Ness Avenue across from City Hall. Tickets may also be purchased by calling (415) 865-2000.

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony will open its 50th year with a symphonic concert live in Zellerbach Hall on Sunday afternoon, February 6 at 4 p.m. The opening concert tells a story of rebirth and communal renewal, from Morton Gould’s Protest to Sibelius’ Finlandia to Berkeley composer John Adams’s Lollapalooza. The concert will conclude with Stravinsky’s Firebird Suite, a classic work that celebrates collective reemergence and renewal. Audience members will also enjoy the world premiere of As Water, Freedom by Derrick Skye, a work commissioned by Berkeley Symphony. Skye is a Los Angeles-based composer whose work has been performed by ensembles around the world, including the Los Angeles Chamber Orchestra, Lyris Quartet, Cantori New York, and Super Devoiche Bulgarian Women’s Choir. Artistic Director Rene Mandel explained the change of day and time from the traditional Thursday evening concerts at Zellerbach to Sunday late afternoon. “In an effort to make our conPhoto by Jeff Roman Joseph Young, Conductor for Berkeley Symphony Orchestra certs more accessible to everybody in our community and the entire Bay Area, we made the decision to switch all of our concerts to Sunday matinees,’ he explained. The Symphony’s series of chamber music concerts held at the Piedmont Center for the Arts has been on Sunday afternoons for the past nine years. To purchase tickets, call the box office at (510) 841-2800, ext. 1, visit the website at https:// www.berkeleysymphony.org/ events/symphonic, or e-mail tickets@berkeleysymphony.org.
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony opening concert at Zellerbach on Sunday, Feb. 6

articles.text: San Francisco Symphony is celebrating the Year of the Tiger with a special Lunar New Year performance at Davies Symphony Hall on Saturday, February 5th at 5 p.m. Conductor Yue Bao will make her debut leading the orchestra in traditional Chinese folk music and works by Asian composers. Bao serves as Assistant Conductor of the Houston Symphony alongside Music Director Andres Orozco-Estrada. She has served as both conductor and assistant and has worked with Michael Tilson Thomas, Marin Alsop, EsaPekka Salonen and Oslo Vanska. The program includes music from Chen Gang and He Zhanhao’s The Buttery Lovers Concerto, performed by violinist Guest Conductor Yue Bao will lead San Francisco Symphony on February 5 for the 22nd annual Lunar New Year Celebration. Bomsori, and Tan Dun’s Eternal Vow from Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon performed by Symphony Assistant Principal Cell Amos Yang. The program will also include works by Huan-zhi Li, Texu Kim, Huang Ruo, Tyzen Hsiao, and Liu Yua. The event will mark the 22nd anniversary of the San Francisco Symphony’s signature event that celebrates the beginning of the Lunar New Year, or Spring Festival, one of the most important cultural holidays for many nations in East, South, and Southeast Asia. The annual Blue Moon Banquet will not take place this year due to the surge of the COVID Omicron variant. Proceeds from the Lunar New Year: Year of the Tiger benefit the Symphony’s artistic, education, and community programs. To purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2021-22/Lunar-New-YearYear-of-the-Tiger.

articles.text: Three-time Grammy winner Cecile McLorin Salvant will perform with her quintet at SF Jazz February 10 through 13.
