articles.text: Vin Diesel and Paul Walker reprise their roles in Fast Five, the fifth installment in the Fast and Furious franchise. Fast Five, released in 2011, is a pedal-to-the-metal, rockin’, high octane, high testosterone hottie of a film – perfect for newbie adolescent boys. It uses state of the art film technology to create an experience, a movie in which dialogue is reduced to so much information, used in the main to explain and thus create the next punchy, intense scene. In a franchise which began in 2001 with The Fast and the Furious, this latest incarnation is as good if not better than those that preceded it. Rather than focusing on the chronic gearheads who prowl the backstreets of, say, L.A., driving tricked out rides while setting up match races, Fast Five offers up a nice twist. It borrows heavily from Ocean’s Eleven, and is a flat-out, holdyour-breath heist movie. Yep, there’s ten million bucks stashed in a vault, money that belongs to a kingpin drug dealer, Reyes (Joaquim de Almeida). This ruthless honcho operates out of Rio de Janeiro with its magnificent statue of Christ, arms outstretched as if embracing Rio, with all of its affluence and precariously perched favelas. Brian O’Conner (Paul Walker) and Mia Toretto (Jordana Brewster) are on the lam from the U.S. Federales, hiding out in a favela, waiting for Dom Toretto (Vin Diesel) to arrive. Once he does, the action begins in earnest. Seriously. And just to make sure you’re on board, the opening 20 minutes are a feast of spectacular special effects and very close calls. Of course, you have to suspend your disbelief. The laws of physics play no part in this film. Nor does a tight plot. But no worries, this is pure dash and crash, fast cuts, destruction of tons of property, hand-held cameras capturing some nifty chase scenes, smokin’ hot cars (there’s not a Prius to be found), intense pacing, with only a few moments when director Justin Lin turns down the heat to a simmer for some spare dialogue before stoking the flames once again. Films of this ilk, postmodern types, are not known as talkies. Fast Five was billed as the first film of the summer, and undoubtedly the teen demographic (boys, mostly) will be back in the theaters ready to watch Vin and The Rock, shaved heads gleaming, arms pumped, comparing their hardware, hard stares, and their rides. This franchise pays homage to the growling, rumbling, throaty internal combustion engine like no other. Dude, it’s industrial strength all the way. Fast Five. Directed by Justin Lin. Starring Vin Diesel, Paul Walker, Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson, Jordana Brewster, Joaquim de Almeida. 2 hrs., 30 min. Rated PG-13. This review originally appeared in the Piedmont Post on May 4, 2011.
articles.title: Fast Five a surprising heist film

articles.text: I saw the trailer to The Shape of Water in 2017 more than once and was intrigued by its premise. The year is 1962. The city is Baltimore. The setting, in great part, a sterile, damp, underground government lab where something arrives, called an “asset,” and is kept in a water tank/aquarium. One of the night crew cleaning ladies, Elisa (Sally Hawkins), a plain, mute woman, who, because of her lack of speech is, while friendly, also timid and deeply lonely; yet, atypically, finds she is compelled to explore what is in the tank. To her surprise what she discovers is an amphibious humanoid creature (Doug Jones), covered in luminous scales, looking back at her with large liquid eyes. Captured in a river in the Amazon it is brought back by government agent Richard Strickland (Michael Shannon), a sadistic racist who takes pleasure in torturing the creature with an electric cattle prod and insists it is nothing more than an “abomination.” Strickland’s plan, actually an emphatic recommendation, is to kill the thing and dissect it in order to find anything that could be useful to the military and a bevy of scientists in their efforts to win the Cold War. And so ends act one. But director/writer Guillermo del Toro then takes the narrative in another direction and turns it into an adult fairy tale and love story in which Elisa develops a connection with the amphibian creature that is completely unexpected. She brings it hardboiled eggs, plays music on a portable phonograph, and teaches it rudimentary sign language. Thus begins a tale reminiscent of Beauty and the Beast, replete with scenes, balletic in their coupling, that convey a fearlessness, especially on the part of Elisa, as she expresses her desire (even lust) to consummate her feelings. Having learned about Strickland’s plan, she makes a courageous, life-altering choice. She refuses to yield, devises a plan, having felt no loneliness or isolation whenever with the creature. And so del Toro draws the audience deeper into his allegorical story. It is at this point that he asks the viewer to suspend his or her disbelief and accept what can seem a deeply improbable premise: a love story that is surreal. The question embedded in the relationship, which is beautifully rendered, is whether he asks too much. For some it will be a bridge too far, the fantasy stretching all credibility. Others will be swept away by the resonating contact between this silent woman and her need and an isolated creature conceived in the rich imagination of del Toro. (The amphibian humanoid does bring to mind the 1954 film, The Creature From the Black Lagoon.) I found that I couldn’t accept the core premise of the film and was not moved by Elisa’s reaching out to this strange man-fish. What I did take great pleasure in, however, was watching the stunning performance of Sally Hawkins, a consummate actress who starred in another deeply human film, Maudie, one in which she also faces overwhelming loneliness. She is amazing. But then so is the ensemble cast in The Shape of Water. Richard Jenkins and Michael Shannon are both superb. For me, however, it came down to the story, one that bears the signature of del Toro (Pan’s Labyrinth). His films are high risk, high gain for moviegoers. Yet I wouldn’t be surprised if The Shape of Water wins an Oscar for Best Picture (it has seven Golden Globe nominations) and Hawkins is nominated for Best Actress. I confess that it’s a bit disconcerting when a film is so fully embraced by critics and audiences and I find myself asking what I fail to see that for so many is both evocative and irresistible. But there it is. The Shape of Water. Directed by Guillermo del Toro. Starring Sally Hawkins, Richard Jenkins and Michael Shannon. 2 hrs., 3 min. Rated R.
articles.title: The Shape of Water an intriguing fantasy

Yet I wouldn’t be surprised if The Shape of Water wins an Oscar for Best Picture (it has seven Golden Globe nominations) and Hawkins is nominated for Best Actress. I confess that it’s a bit disconcerting when a film is so fully embraced by critics and audiences and I find myself asking what I fail to see that for so many is both evocative and irresistible. But there it is. The Shape of Water. Directed by Guillermo del Toro. Starring Sally Hawkins, Richard Jenkins and Michael Shannon. 2 hrs., 3 min. Rated R. Vin Diesel and Paul Walker reprise their roles in Fast Five, the fifth installment in the Fast and Furious franchise. By Chris Honoré Fast Five, released in 2011, is a pedal-to-the-metal, rockin’, high octane, high testosterone hottie of a film – perfect for newbie adolescent boys. It uses state of the art film technology to create an experience, a movie in which dialogue is reduced to so much information, used in the main to explain and thus create the next punchy, intense scene. In a franchise which began in 2001 with The Fast and the Furious, this latest incarnation is as good if not better than those that preceded it. Rather than focusing on the chronic gearheads who prowl the backstreets of, say, L.A., driving tricked out rides while setting up match races, Fast Five offers up a nice twist. It borrows heavily from Ocean’s Eleven, and is a flat-out, holdyour-breath heist movie. Yep, there’s ten million bucks stashed in a vault, money that belongs to a kingpin drug dealer, Reyes (Joaquim de Almeida). This ruthless honcho operates out of Rio de Janeiro with its magnificent statue of Christ, arms outstretched as if embracing Rio, with all of its affluence and precariously perched favelas. Brian O’Conner (Paul Walker) and Mia Toretto (Jordana Brewster) are on the lam from the U.S. Federales, hiding out in a favela, waiting for Dom Toretto (Vin Diesel) to arrive. Once he does, the action begins in earnest. Seriously. And just to make sure you’re on board, the opening 20 minutes are a feast of spectacular special effects and very close calls. Of course, you have to suspend your disbelief. The laws of physics play no part in this film. Nor does a tight plot. But no worries, this is pure dash and crash, fast cuts, destruction of tons of property, hand-held cameras capturing some nifty chase scenes, smokin’ hot cars (there’s not a Prius to be found), intense pacing, with only a few moments when director Justin Lin turns down the heat to a simmer for some spare dialogue before stoking the flames once again. Films of this ilk, postmodern types, are not known as talkies. Fast Five was billed as the first film of the summer, and undoubtedly the teen demographic (boys, mostly) will be back in the theaters ready to watch Vin and The Rock, shaved heads gleaming, arms pumped, comparing their hardware, hard stares, and their rides. This franchise pays homage to the growling, rumbling, throaty internal combustion engine like no other. Dude, it’s industrial strength all the way. Fast Five. Directed by Justin Lin. Starring Vin Diesel, Paul Walker, Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson, Jordana Brewster, Joaquim de Almeida. 2 hrs., 30 min. Rated PG-13. articles.text: Jude Law as Dr. Watson and Robert Downey Jr. as Sherlock Holmes. Recall the image of Sherlock Holmes, made famous by Basil Rathbone who starred in some 14 movies featuring the English detective, always accompanied by Nigel Bruce who portrayed Dr. John Watson. Rathbone was long-faced, inscrutable, an ever-present Mahogany Calabash pipe with a meerschaum bowl, and, of course, his signature deerstalker cap, a checked twill, double-brimmed lid that was soon identified as a detective’s hat. Those films, shot from 1939 to 1946, were inspired by the works of Sir Arthur Conan Doyle who preceded English mystery writers such as Agatha Christie, P.D. James and Ngalo Marsh, and who created a panoply of studied whodunits involving the butler in the library with the candlestick, so to speak. Rathbone’s Holmes – always careful and deliberative, never given to emotional outbursts or physical confrontations – has likely shaped the expectations of many moviegoers who turned out to see the more contemporaneous Sherlock Holmes. They are in for a treat. The newly reconstructed Holmes is no longer a detective of the ilk of Agatha Christie’s Miss Marple or Hercule Poirot. Robert Downey’s Holmes is a rogue, dissolute, a master of martial arts, athletic and courageous, given to dark rooms, extreme experiments, harrowing tight spots, a man so keenly observant, so completely aware of his surroundings that he is often tormented. As well, Jude Law’s Dr. Watson has been nicely revisited. No longer is he the bumbling foil; rather, he’s as capable – intellectually and physically – as is Holmes. When together, which is often, they bicker and disagree and yet have been friends for years. So much does Holmes need Watson’s assistance that he is willing to undermine Watson’s pending marriage. This new Holmes is a surprise and far more interesting than any of Holmes’ antecedents, making the film engaging. However, at the center of every Holmes narrative is a mystery: the essential whodunit. And here the screenwriters stumble. Rather than writing a tale that will keep the audience guessing, the villain, Lord Blackwood (Mark Strong), is revealed at the outset, and so it’s never a question of who but how. This Holmes becomes a howdunit, not quite as compelling as a whodunit. Still, the film is rich with close calls for Holmes and Watson as well as Irene Adler (Rachel McAdams), the one woman in Holmes’ life who continues to interest him with her courage, intelligence and insouciance. Suffice it to say that Holmes, in this incarnation, is a man of action as well as a man of incisive deductive reasoning, making for a solidly entertaining movie. Sherlock Holmes. Starring Robert Downey, Jude Law, Rachel McAdams and Eddie Marsan. Directed by Guy Ritchie. 2 hrs., 8 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: Onward, released by Pixar and Disney, brings to bear once again what has proved to be a marvelous engine of imagination that creates, with each film, a special world that beckons kids of all ages to enter and enjoy. The world created in Onward is one of blue-toned elves who live in toadstool houses, a place of dragons, unicorns, magic, spells – and not to forget some engaging wizardry. From the outset, the story is carried by two brothers: shy Ian (Tom Holland), who has just turned 16, and the older Barley (Chris Pratt), a tad different and rebellious. They are the Lightfoot brothers and a study in contrasts. They discover a birthday gift left to Ian by his deceased dad: it’s a wizard’s staff, a rare phoenix gem, and a letter of instructions that will allow their dad to return for just one day. Of course, Ian, with Barley’s help, makes a valiant attempt and only manages to get half-way through the spell, resulting in dad ending up as a pair of pants, socks and shoes. What is needed is a new gemstone to replace the one that fizzled. Barley is certain he knows where to find one. And so the adventure begins. The bros set out on a quest that will take them from place to place, each fraught with obstacles and perilous moments. The part of this hunt that is special is that they take half their dad along, hooked up to a doggy leash so he can’t wander off. Dad, after all, can’t speak or see, hence is what we might describe as high maintenance. Their mode of transportation is Barley’s well-used van, outfitted with some amazing stuff, like blasting air conditioning. Of course the bros bicker about directions, and the ability of Ian to use the staff to create critical magic when needed. What is surprising is that there is a tone of sadness to the story. The bros both are grieving for their dad. Born shortly after his dad died, Ian never knew their father. Barley, however, does have small kid memories and yearns for more. They are convinced once they locate the special stone they will complete their dad’s final transformation and have that one very special day they both hope for. So, onward. There are lots of speed bumps along the way, hence the film is essentially episodic, comedic, and situational. And for good measure, their mom, Laurel (Julia Louis-Dreyfus), is right behind them, certain they are in danger. It’s all in the Pixar wheelhouse, and kids ages six to eight will enjoy the journey and the cast of characters, even ColtBronco, a centaur police officer (Mel Rodriquez), and a strange restaurant, replete with a Manticore (Octavia Spencer). That’s where they find a much needed map to help them find their way on their journey. It’s all a trip to be enjoyed, especially if you’re a kid (or a parent) and relish quality time in elf-land. Onward. Directed by Dan Scanlon. Pixar-Disney animation. With voices of Chris Pratt, Tom Holland, Octavia Spencer and Julia Louis-Dreyfus. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated PG
articles.title: Onward a wonderful adventure film

articles.text: Today is Frederick’s birthday. He was one of the most famous people in history. You might think we are talking about Frederick the Great. That’s a good guess, because THAT Frederick was a great musician in addition to being a great ruler. But this is about another Frederick… Who was also a great musician… Probably the most beloved musician of all time. And that, even though he was a pathological liar… And a fraud to boot! Frederick had the usual early success as a child prodigy. But that did not get him very far. He claimed to have studied art but could only draw stick figures. He decided to pursue another avenue and began medical studies. This did not get him very far, either. He returned to music once again but without success. Frederick was an officer in the Austrian cavalry and saw action in the battle of Tannenburg. It seems that he was injured by a lance wound to the leg. articles.text: San Francisco Opera will present a zoom webinar on Sunday, February 13, as part of the company’s “Opera Aficionado” virtual event series. The upcoming webinar will feature speaker Alla Gladysheva with a discussion of the roots of Russian opera. Viewers will learn about Russian opera, starting with the assimilation of the existing European operatic styles. The speaker will discuss composer Mikhail Glinka, who wrote the music for the first classical Russian opera. Gladysheva is a Music Theory Professor at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. Gladysheva, a Russian native, received her degrees from St. Petersburg State Conservatory. She also served Karelian Radio and Television as a journalist, writing mainly on musicology in Russia. She immigrated to the United States in 1995 and is currently a pianist with the San Francisco Ballet School. The Zoom event will begin at 1 p.m. To obtain tickets to this Zoom event, visit https://sfopera.com/ discover-opera/education/community-programs/aficionado/. Links are emailed one hour prior to the event. Alla Gladysheva, a faculty member of San Francisco Conservatory of Music, will lead a San Francisco Opera webinar on February 13 on the Roots of Russian Opera.

articles.text: Eric Clapton was raised by his grandparents. When his grandfather Jack Clapp found out Eric had been dropped from the Kingston School of Art after skipping classes to play guitar and drink in local pubs, he gave him an ultimatum: “Work with me or get out of the house”. Jack Clapp was a master plasterer, master bricklayer and master carpenter. The work discipline his grandfather emulated was appreciated by Eric and seems to have set a similar standard in his music. No matter what was going on in life, he has always gone to great lengths to prepare styles and pieces for performances and recordings. There aren’t many “bad notes” in EC’s playing. African-American field hollers and work songs have indirectly been a resource for Clapton. They are the source of the 12-bar blues chord progressions and the core melodies for blues. EC particularly studied Robert Johnson and Big Bill Broonzy. He incorporated rhythms from the black fife and drum tradition and from “rival rhythms”. Those rhythms were developed by slaves using Revolutionary War and Civil War instruments and rudimentary drum rhythms, blended with African rhythm. English rock and blues guitar master Eric Clapton. Here are links to my related playlists on Spotify: http://www. guitarimprov.com/FieldHollers. pdf Clapton’s blues style example 1 is based on sixteenths (four notes per beat), Robert Johnson’s style, fife and drum rhythms and revival rhythms. Clapton’s blues style example 2 is an up-tempo triple-time (three notes per beat) blues style that Clapton adapted from Freddie King and B.B. King. Links to notation and live guitar audio are provided near the end of this column. The British blues revival in the sixties was the backdrop for EC’s blues guitar development. He quit the Yardbirds in 1965 because they moved from blues rock to pop rock. He joined John Mayall and the Bluesbreakers, his friend Jimmy Page recommended Jeff Beck as a replacement. While working on the great Bluesbreakers album with bandleader John Mayall, EC was being paid to work eight hours a day on the album. On one of the recording days when they finished well before eight hours, EC asked, “Mr. Mayall, what should I do in the remaining time?” Mayall answered, “Go practice”. He did practice. Eric Clapton was influenced by Robert Johnson, Freddie King, B.B. King, Albert King, and Muddy Waters. He in turn influenced most current blues rock guitarists, including Eddie Van Halen, who influenced Joe Satriani. The roots of the electric blues guitar tradition is now thankfully kept alive by Joe Bonamassa, a great admirer of Clapton. You can listen to recorded examples of my improvisations for this column (Clapton’s Blues) and my previous columns at: http://www.guitarimprov.com/ PostColumns.pdf. Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. Call (510 )923- 9522, text (510) 435-3997 or email jim@guitarencyclopdeia.com for videoconference or in-person lessons. His course is available for free online at www.guitarimprov. com.

Success followed success. Audiences everywhere loved his famous little pieces. And then… And then an inf luential English music critic became suspicious. He demanded to see the manuscripts. Frederick was caught in an international scandal. He was forced to admit that he was the actual composer of those popular little pieces. The public loved him even more. This made the critics furious. Frederick continued on his merry way. He probably played more concerts than any other musician in history. articles.text: The following list is an abridged version of the New York Times 10 Best Books of 2021. Authors across the world have utilized ample time from home to publish books during the pandemic. With both fiction and nonfiction selections, this list can serve as a gift guide for the bookworms in your life looking for the most contemporary literature choices. To view the entire list and description of the books, visit Nytimes.com/2021/11/30/books/ review/best-books-2021.html? age saga, an examination of race and an excavation of American history. It cuts back and forth between the tale of Ailey Pearl Garfield, a Black girl growing up at the end of the 20th century, and the “songs” of her ancestors, Native Americans and enslaved African Americans. ful account of the struggle to reconcile art and life. Yet for all the dramatic twists of her life, these books together project a stunning clarity, humor and candidness. How the Word Is Passed: A Reckoning with the History of Slavery Across America, by Clint Smith. Little, Brown & Company. For this timely and thought-provoking book, Smith, a poet and journalist, toured sites key to the history of slavery and its present-day legacy. Smith holds up a mirror to America’s fraught relationship with its past, capturing a potent mixture of good intentions, earnest corrective, willful ignorance and blatant distortion. Invisible Child: Poverty, Survival and Hope in an American City, by Andrea Elliott. Random House. The book expands on her acclaimed 2013 series for “The Times” about Dasani Coates, a homeless New York schoolgirl, and her family. Elliott spent years following her subjects in their daily lives, through shelters, schools, courtrooms and welfare offices. The book is a searing account of one family’s struggle with poverty, homelessness and addiction. How Beautiful We Were, by Imbolo Mbue, Random House. Mbue’s sweeping and quietly devastating second novel begins in 1980 in the fictional African village of Kosawa, where representatives from an American oil company have come to meet with the locals, whose children are dying because of the environmental havoc (fallow fields, poisoned water) wreaked by its drilling and pipelines. Through the eyes of Kosawa’s citizens young and old, Mbue constructs a nuanced exploration of self-interest, of what it means to want in the age of capitalism and colonialism. Intimacies, by Katie Kitamura, Riverhead Books. His journey to the outermost edges of knowledge offers glimpses of a universe with limitless potential underlying the observable world. The Love Songs of W.E.B. DuBois, by Honorée Fanonne Jeffers. Exploring the racial and social complexities of Texas, her home state, Gordon-Reed asks readers to step back from the current heated debates and take a more nuanced look at history. Such a perspective comes easy to her because she was a part of history – the first Black child to integrate her East Texas school. Determined to rescue the poet from posthumous caricature as a doomed madwoman and Clark aims to “reposition her as one of the most important American writers of the 20th century.” Clark, a professor of poetry in England, delivers a transporting account of a rare literary talent enlivened throughout by quotations from Plath’s letters, diaries, poetry and prose.

articles.text: The winter season is upon us, bringing shorter days, a new wave of COVID-19 cases, and much needed rain and storms to the region. The cooler winter months also occasionally bring poor air quality conditions to the Bay Area, often caused by particulate matter pollution (e.g., wood smoke) that gets trapped close to the ground by an inversion layer (i.e., a layer of warm air above cooler air near the Earth’s surface). Worsening the air quality is the use of gasoline-powered landscape maintenance equipment such as leaf blowers and lawn mowers. This equipment is driven by small off-road engines (SORE), spark-ignition engines rated below 19 kilowatts. According to the California Air Resources Board, the number of SOREs in California (16.7 million) is greater than that of light-duty passenger cars (13.7 million) and is overwhelmingly comprised of residential lawn and garden equipment (77%). The emissions from these small engines are significant. The best-selling commercial leaf blower, during one hour of operation, emits smog-forming pollution comparable to driving a 2017 Toyota Camry about 1100 miles, or approximately the distance from Los Angeles to Denver. In fact, SOREs are on pace to produce more pollution each year than passenger cars. This can be attributed to regulations on car exhaust getting more restrictive over the years, and thus substantially reducing their ozone-damaging emissions. But the same cannot be said for SOREs. Gas-powered leaf blowers expose workers and the public to high levels of toxic and carcinogenic emissions such as formaldehyde, benzene, and particulate matter in equipment fumes, wreaking havoc on local air quality and causing unsafe levels of noise. Across the U.S., hundreds of cities and counties have passed laws restricting or prohibiting the use of gas-powered leaf blowers. Piedmont was the first city in the East Bay and one of the first in California to ban the use of gas-powered leaf blowers, in 1990. Starting as early as 2024, the state of California will outlaw the sale of new gas-powered leaf blowers, lawn mowers, and chain saws. The good news is that electric and battery-powered leaf blowers are simple, light, easy to use, reliable and the cost is decreasing. No more running out of gas, replacing old spark plugs, or cumbersome and heavy equipment. All you need to do is insert a charged battery, flip the switch, and get to work. Lower maintenance costs also mean electric leaf blowers will save you money in the long run. Learn more information about Piedmont’s leaf blower regulations here: https://www.piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ public_works/sustainability_division/leaf_blower_regulations. Alyssa Dykman is the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Program Manager. She can be reached at adykman@piedmont. ca.gov.
articles.title: Reducing pollution with electric leaf blowers

Orange-Scented Olive Oil Cake Adapted from Cook’s Illustrated INGREDIENTS • 1 3/4 cups all-purpose flour • 1 teaspoon baking powder • 3/4 teaspoon table salt • 3 extra-large eggs, room temperature • 1 cup granulated sugar, plus 1 tablespoon to sprinkle atop before baking • 1 teaspoon orange zest, finely grated (I use a Microplane for grating) • 3/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil • 1/2 cup whole milk, room temperature • 1/4 cup orange juice, freshly squeezed after removing the zest, room temperature INSTRUCTIONS Position an oven rack to the mid-oven position and preheat the oven to 350°F. Oil the bottom and sides of a 9-inch round springform pan. A regular 9-inch round cake pan will work too. Line the bottom with parchment and turn it top side up when you remove the cake from the pan to complete cooling. Whisk flour, baking powder, and salt together in a medium bowl. Set aside. Combine the milk and orange juice. Set aside. Using a handheld electric mixer, beat the eggs on medium speed until foamy, about 1 minute. Add 1 cup of sugar and orange zest, and whip on high speed until the mixture is fluffy and pale yellow, about 2 minutes. Reduce speed to medium, and while mixer is running, pour the olive oil in a slow, steady stream. Mix until oil is fully incorporated. On low speed, add half of the flour mixture and mix until barely incorporated. Stop to scrape the sides and bottom of the bowl if needed. Add the milk-orange juice mixture and mix until combined. Add remaining flour mixture and mix until just incorporated. Scrape down the bowl as needed. Be careful to not over mix. Pour the batter into the prepared pan and sprinkle the remaining 1 tablespoon of granulated sugar evenly over the entire surface. Bake until the cake is deep golden brown, about 40–45 minutes. Test for doneness by inserting a toothpick in the center of the cake. It should come out with only a few crumbs clinging. Transfer the pan to a wire rack and cool for 15 minutes. Remove the sides of the springform pan and cool completely before serving. Note: The cake needs no further adornment as the granulated sugar sprinkled on top forms a lovely sparkle and crunch. I decorated my cake with candied orange rind, some dipped in chocolate to fancy it up. This is totally optional. Reducing pollution with electric leaf blowers By Alyssa Dykman The winter season is upon us, bringing shorter days, a new wave of COVID-19 cases, and much needed rain and storms to the region. The cooler winter months also occasionally bring poor air quality conditions to the Bay Area, often caused by particulate matter pollution (e.g., wood smoke) that gets trapped close to the ground by an inversion layer (i.e., a layer of warm air above cooler air near the Earth’s surface). Worsening the air quality is the use of gasoline-powered landscape maintenance equipment such as leaf blowers and lawn mowers. This equipment is driven by small off-road engines (SORE), spark-ignition engines rated below 19 kilowatts. According to the California Air Resources Board, the number of SOREs in California (16.7 million) is greater than that of light-duty passenger cars (13.7 million) and is overwhelmingly comprised of residential lawn and garden equipment (77%). The emissions from these small engines are significant. The best-selling commercial leaf blower, during one hour of operation, emits smog-forming pollution comparable to driving a 2017 Toyota Camry about 1100 miles, or approximately the distance from Los Angeles to Denver. In fact, SOREs are on pace to produce more pollution each year than passenger cars. This can be attributed to regulations on car exhaust getting more restrictive over the years, and thus substantially reducing their ozone-damaging emissions. But the same cannot be said for SOREs. Gas-powered leaf blowers expose workers and the public to high levels of toxic and carcinogenic emissions such as formaldehyde, benzene, and particulate matter in equipment fumes, wreaking havoc on local air quality and causing unsafe levels of noise. Across the U.S., hundreds of cities and counties have passed laws restricting or prohibiting the use of gas-powered leaf blowers. Piedmont was the first city in the East Bay and one of the first in California to ban the use of gas-powered leaf blowers, in 1990. Starting as early as 2024, the state of California will outlaw the sale of new gas-powered leaf blowers, lawn mowers, and chain saws. The good news is that electric and battery-powered leaf blowers are simple, light, easy to use, reliable and the cost is decreasing. No more running out of gas, replacing old spark plugs, or cumbersome and heavy equipment. All you need to do is insert a charged battery, flip the switch, and get to work. Lower maintenance costs also mean electric leaf blowers will save you money in the long run. Learn more information about Piedmont’s leaf blower regulations here: https://www.piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ public_works/sustainability_division/leaf_blower_regulations. Alyssa Dykman is the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Program Manager. She can be reached at adykman@piedmont. ca.gov. articles.text: Photos by Kate Fratar The doorway to City of London Distillery sits below the steeple of St. Bride’s Church, known as the church of the media and press, and just off Fleet Street, once home to a bustling newspaper scene. Aboard the Flying Scotsman – a train, lest the name suggest otherwise – I’m bound for Edinburgh and the second stop on this summer’s spirits trail. The primary focus of this adventure will be on whisky tasting and studying the subtleties of peat and esters. The kickoff to this hard-nosing jaunt came in London, where the emphasis was on gins. Because, well, when in Rome, as they say. Tucked away on an easily missed side alley of Fleet Street is the City of London Distillery. Founded in 2012, the urban upstart is bringing back the tradition of gin distillation to the City of London after a nearly 200-year absence. During the eighteenth century, gin distilleries sprouted in this area, originally the site of a fortified Roman settlement at Londonium, as citrus fruits became available through London’s port. Among the distillery’s gins, The Square Mile is a nod to the two square miles that establishes the City of London as a separate entity, complete with its own mayor and independent police force, within the jurisdiction of Greater London. Its doorway sits beneath the steeple of St. Bride’s Church, known as the church of the media and the press. Down the narrow wooden stairs is the bottle shop, bar, tasting room, and fireproofed, glassed-walled distillery. The cozy setup, complete with dark green paint and plush leather chairs, echoes an era when cigarette smoke might have lingered overhead and the din of clacking typewriters would have overridden conversation (perhaps of the latest news tip?). It’s one-part speakeasy to two-parts journalist hideaway. Jake meets me to host a tour – including the botanicals room, where guests can tinker with their own blends of spices and take the concoction home – and a tasting. The four pillars of the City of London production line are all in the classic London Dry style, with varying levels of citrus. There are also gins infused with rhubarb, lemon and mandarin, respectively, made more as experiments to play within market trends. The City of London Authentic gin won a Double-Gold Award at the San Francisco World Spirits Competition in 2017. The recognition is when the distillery decided to stop any further finessing of the recipe, Jake noted. In 2016, the Christopher Wren, named for the architect of St. Paul’s Cathedral, the more recognizable church-top to overlook the distillery, took home the same award. Where the Christopher Wren carries more undertones of orange, the citrus lacing the Old Tom is primarily lemon zest. The garnishes of orange twist with Christopher Wren and lemon with hibiscus for the Old Tom, along with the choice of tonic, bring variation to the standard G&T on the bar menu. It was a different classic gin cocktail that I wanted to see sampled, however. Perhaps it is due to the pure simplicity of the Negroni that great diversification can be found. Essentially equal parts gin, sweet vermouth, and Campari, variations in any of these ingredients can lead to marked differences. Within the stratosphere of The bar at City of London Distillery, founded in 2012, is well supplied with its gins, which have taken top honors at the San Francisco World Competition. gins, the qualifying factor, by and large, is having some sort quantity of juniper. (Note that gin is not distilled from juniper berries. It is typically grain-based, but it can be made from any fermented base. Locally, Oakland Spirits Company produces gins distilled from grapes.) Today’s gin makers are having fun with the open field allowed to them, leading to more options for consumers. Speaking for myself, I would pull from the Christopher Wren of the City of London Distillery lineup to mirror the orange peel garnish of a Negroni. On to Bar Termini For a real study in the portrait of the Negroni, the place to go is Bar Termini in Soho. Named for Rome’s train station, the place bustles with all the organized frenzy of a terminal, as white-jacketed waiters zip from bar to table carrying trays of coffee and cocktails. American jazz, with Ella Fitzgerald and Frank Sinatra crooning Cole Porter, tries to make itself heard over the hubbub that bubbles out of any proper pub. On the menu are four separate house Negroni options. Classico lives up to its name. The Rosato has a trace of rose petal, the Superiore adds green peppercorn that amazingly doesn’t overpower but adds bite on the aftertaste to the juniper, and the Robusto is aged, doing what aging does. The vibrancy and rougher edges to a Negroni’s bitterness are softened and rounded off, being replaced with deeper, more mature flavors. All four are prepared sous vide, the water bath style of cooking in vacuumed, sealed containers that is known for delivering consistency and integrated flavors. Dry essences are used as part of the mixture in place of fresh garnish. The Negroni is poured tableside from a bottle and served in a chilled glass in a smaller portion that the standard three ounces, without an ice cube that would add dilution. articles.text: Longtime Piedmont resident Marian Smith died on January 26. She was 86. Marian Bamford Smith of Piedmont, California, died January 26, 2022 at home at the age of 86. Her husband, Harold Smith, said she passed away peacefully after a brief illness. Born in North Andover, Massachusetts in 1935, Marian was the eldest of nine children of H. Russell and Marie (Theroux) Bamford. She attended Johnson High School, received a B.S. degree in Physics from Simmons College in 1956, was a graduate student in the Department of Metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology from 1957-59, and received an MBA degree in finance from the Haas School of Business, University of California, Berkeley in 1982. Until 1966, Marian worked as a research scientist at Raytheon, at the Ballistics Research Laboratories at the Aberdeen Proving Grounds, and at UC Berkeley. For the next 14 years, she concentrated on raising her children who were active junior tennis players and who played for their college tennis teams (two at Harvard, one at Yale). While the children were in college, Marian was a full-time student at the University of California (Berkeley) Haas School of Business. Until retirement in 2005, Marian was a principal of the Palmer Smith Corporation, an aerospace management consulting firm. She was appointed trustee of the Board of the Alameda County Employees’ Retirement Association (ACERA) in 1989. She was the first woman to chair the ACERA Board as well as the first woman to chair the ACERA Investment Committee. She was a member of the Executive Board of the Council of Institutional Investors, the Smithsonian Institution Investment Committee, and the Stanford Law School Fiduciary Education Advisory Board. An active genealogist and writer, she documented French and French Canadian ancestors back to 1625 and English ancestors back to 1835. She was a 10th generation descendant of Antoine Terroux who arrived in Quebec in 1693 from Verdun-sur-Garonne. Her ancestor, Augustin Hebert, one of the first colonists of Montreal, emigrated from Caen in France in 1641. Her Bamford and Latham English ancestors emigrated from Rochdale, England in the 1870s to work in the textile mills of North Andover, Massachusetts. A regular golf and tennis player, she was a member of the Claremont Country Club and the Berkeley Tennis Club. Marian and Harold lived an active and eventful life together with many fond memories including a river rafting trip through the Grand Canyon where the attached photo was taken. Marian is survived by her husband, Dr. Harold P. Smith, Jr. of Piedmont, daughters Natalya Marie Smith of La Jolla, and Erika Bamford Smith of Oakland, and son Harold (Peter) P. Smith, III and his wife Patricia McCoy Smith of Oakland. She is also survived by grandchildren Andrew Smith of Oakland, and Harold Gonzalez and Natasha Gonzalez of La Jolla. She is additionally survived by her sisters Roberta Banan of Longboat Key, Florida, and Jacqueline (John) Moran of Little Compton, Rhode Island, and her brothers, Gilbert (Gail) Bamford of Vero Beach, Florida, David Bamford of Sarasota, Florida and James Bamford of Andover, Massachusetts. She is predeceased by her siblings Edith Welch of Longboat Key, Florida, and Susan Sullivan and Stephan Bamford of Andover, Massachusetts. Burial services will be private. A celebration of Marian’s life will be held at an appropriate time. In lieu of flowers the family requests that donations in Marian’s memory be made to the Oak Tree Foundation, c/o Claremont Country Club, 5295 Broadway Terrace, Oakland, CA 94618. The Oak Tree Foundation is a tax exempt non-profit organization with the mission to provide a financial safety net and educational support for Claremont Country Club employees and their immediate families.

While the children were in college, Marian was a full-time student at the University of California (Berkeley) Haas School of Business. Until retirement in 2005, Marian was a principal of the Palmer Smith Corporation, an aerospace management consulting firm. She was appointed trustee of the Board of the Alameda County Employees’ Retirement Association (ACERA) in 1989. She was the first woman to chair the ACERA Board as well as the first woman to chair the ACERA Investment Committee. She was a member of the Executive Board of the Council of Institutional Investors, the Smithsonian Institution Investment Committee, and the Stanford Law School Fiduciary Education Advisory Board. An active genealogist and writer, she documented French and French Canadian ancestors back to 1625 and English ancestors back to 1835. She was a 10th generation descendant of Antoine Terroux who arrived in Quebec in 1693 from Verdun-sur-Garonne. Her ancestor, Augustin Hebert, one of the first colonists of Montreal, emigrated from Caen in France in 1641. Her Bamford and Latham English ancestors emigrated from Rochdale, England in the 1870s to work in the textile mills of North Andover, Massachusetts. A regular golf and tennis player, she was a member of the Claremont Country Club and the Berkeley Tennis Club. Marian and Harold lived an active and eventful life together with many fond memories including a river rafting trip through the Grand Canyon where the attached photo was taken. Marian is survived by her husband, Dr. Harold P. Smith, Jr. of Piedmont, daughters Natalya Marie Smith of La Jolla, and Erika Bamford Smith of Oakland, and son Harold (Peter) P. Smith, III and his wife Patricia McCoy Smith of Oakland. She is also survived by grandchildren Andrew Smith of Oakland, and Harold Gonzalez and Natasha Gonzalez of La Jolla. She is additionally survived by her sisters Roberta Banan of Longboat Key, Florida, and Jacqueline (John) Moran of Little Compton, Rhode Island, and her brothers, Gilbert (Gail) Bamford of Vero Beach, Florida, David Bamford of Sarasota, Florida and James Bamford of Andover, Massachusetts. She is predeceased by her siblings Edith Welch of Longboat Key, Florida, and Susan Sullivan and Stephan Bamford of Andover, Massachusetts. Burial services will be private. A celebration of Marian’s life will be held at an appropriate time. In lieu of flowers the family requests that donations in Marian’s memory be made to the Oak Tree Foundation, c/o Claremont Country Club, 5295 Broadway Terrace, Oakland, CA 94618. The Oak Tree Foundation is a tax exempt non-profit organization with the mission to provide a financial safety net and educational support for Claremont Country Club employees and their immediate families.

articles.text: Citibank at 333 Highland Avenue and Bank of America at 345 Highland Avenue are temporarily closed to customer traffic. Bank of America has been closed for nearly two years, and CitiBank recently closed. Wells Fargo Bank at 344 Highland Avenue reopened on Tuesday, January 25, after six days of closure due to staffing shortages. A spokesperson for Bank of America, Betty Riess, said that the closure of its branch in Piedmont in March 2020 was due to COVID and “the health and safety of associates and clients. Typically, our temporary closures have occurred in areas where we’re seeing fewer visits, or our staffing is not sufficient for a center to remain open,” she said. ATMs at all three branch banks are operational. Wells Fargo Bank is open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday. Citibank at 333 Highland Avenue and Bank of America next door, remain closed.
articles.title: Wells Fargo reopens, Bank of America and Citibank still closed

articles.text: Three piedmont parent attorneys and two anti-vaccination non-profit organizations filed a lawsuit against the Piedmont Unified School District challenging its policy of requiring all students to be vaccinated against COVID. On January 13 Alameda County Superior Court Judge Brad Seligman temporarily halted enforcement of the Piedmont mandate which would have referred unvaccinated students to online independent study. In a regularly scheduled school board meeting tonight, the district plans to announce the COVID vaccine will be removed from the list of mandatory vaccinations for attendance. “At this time, the District finds no educational value in transferring vaccine-hesitant students into an Independent Study program when we are experiencing a remarkably high vaccination rate across all campuses,” the board document states. As of January 21, 59 students out of a total district enrollment of 2,340 were not yet vaccinated, including four preschoolers not yet age-eligible. The vaccine policy was initially created on September 22, and required students age 12 and older to submit proof of vaccination by November 17. No students were denied access to campus at that time, and the deadline was extended to January 5 for students 12 and older. The deadline for students ages 5-11 was January 14, but judge Seligman’s stay to the order was issued one day earlier. Serving as lead plaintiff’s attorney, Jessica Barsotti, a PHS
articles.title: School district drops COVID from list of required vaccines

articles.text: The American Red Cross announced on January 11 that it is facing a national blood crisis, describing it as “the worst blood shortage in more than a decade.” Dangerously low blood supply levels are creating a risk to patient care across the country, the agency explained in a press release, and is forcing doctors “to make difficult decisions about who receives blood transfusions and who will need to wait until more products become available.” Blood donations are critically needed at this time, especially type O blood donors; however, donors of all types are encouraged to make an appointment now to give in the weeks ahead. “Winter weather across the country and the recent surge of COVID-19 cases are compounding the already-dire situation facing the blood supply,” said Dr. Baia Lasky, medical director for the Red Cross. “Please, if you are eligible, make an appointment to give blood or platelets in the days and weeks ahead to ensure no patient is forced to wait for critical care.” Due to COVID-19 and challenges presented by the pandemic, the agency has seen about a 10% overall decline in donations as well as ongoing blood drive cancellations due to staff shortages. To donate blood at the Blood Bank at 6230 Claremont Avenue in Oakland, call (800) 733-2767.
articles.title: Red Cross announces urgent need for blood donations

articles.text: Do you include God in that mission statement? How does our role in the world relate to how we understand God? When looking at Jesus in the temple, we don’t have much reference about him since his birth. This is inaugural in which he proclaims his personal mission. This is before he goes out to do all the good works. He selects a passage from a scroll. He could have chosen any number of passages, but he selected a passage from the prophet Isaiah. Before I go down that road, I want to discuss what you think of your personal mission statement. A mission statement is something that describes who you are and what you will achieve in the world. At St. John’s we say to manifest the love of God through the Holy Spirit with each other, our community and the world through worship, spiritual growth and Christian service. My question is, do you feel you manifest God’s love through the Holy Spirit? Do you do this with each other here in community, do you do this in the world? Do you do this through worship? Do you dedicate yourself to spiritual growth? What acts of Christian service do you perform? This is what we say at St. John’s, and I am curious if this aligns with your personal mission? I am going to use another passage and see if this aligns. Are you a person embodied in justice for all people and for God’s creation, and you believe in church vitality? Are you rooted in spirituality or transparent and accountable as a leader as you build Inclusive community? I just quoted the Diocese of California. Are you a person who goes out and gives sight to the blind? Do you help heal people and help people see things physically or spiritually? How do you bring good news to the poor? Good news is where you help people have hope and feel love. How have you told others about God and all that God has done for you? If you have done this, your mission might be aligned with Jesus. Carrying out a mission is not easy. We all have a variety of gifts, and they are not all the same. pages.text: 2 Wednesday, January 26, 2022 Opinion Red Cross announces urgent need for blood donations By Allyson Aleksey The American Red Cross announced on January 11 that it is facing a national blood crisis, describing it as “the worst blood shortage in more than a decade.” Dangerously low blood supply levels are creating a risk to patient care across the country, the agency explained in a press release, and is forcing doctors “to make difficult decisions about who receives blood transfusions and who will need to wait until more products become available.” Blood donations are critically needed at this time, especially type O blood donors; however, donors of all types are encouraged to make an appointment now to give in the weeks ahead. “Winter weather across the country and the recent surge of COVID-19 cases are compounding the already-dire situation facing the blood supply,” said Dr. Baia Lasky, medical director for the Red Cross. “Please, if you are eligible, make an appointment to give blood or platelets in the days and weeks ahead to ensure no patient is forced to wait for critical care.” Due to COVID-19 and challenges presented by the pandemic, the agency has seen about a 10% overall decline in donations as well as ongoing blood drive cancellations due to staff shortages. To donate blood at the Blood Bank at 6230 Claremont Avenue in Oakland, call (800) 733-2767. articles.text: Healthcare company Curative has moved its testing location from Vista Avenue in front of City Hall to the Community Hall parking lot at 711 Highland Avenue. Curative has expanded its testing from two days a week, Sunday and Monday, to five days a week, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. Walk-up registration is accepted, but because of high demand, appointments are strongly encouraged. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is currently accepting applications from residents who are interested in serving on City Council on an interim basis. The deadline to apply is Monday, January 31. Piedmont City Council held a special meeting on January 6 to determine the process by which it would fill a vacancy left by council member Tim Rood following his resignation on December 31, 2021. Council members chose to seek applications for appointment to City Council from residents, to serve as interim council member until the results of the general municipal election are certified on November 8. A resident must meet three requirements to apply for the position. First, the person must be a qualified voter in Piedmont; second, the person must not hold any other office or employment with the city; and third, the person must not be rendered ineligible due to the term limits provisions of the City Charter. Interested residents may submit applications electronically, or in-person to the City Clerk’s Office by 5 p.m. on January 31. Postmarks will not be accepted. City Council will interview candidates and applicants will have the opportunity to discuss their candidacy with council members. At a special meeting on February 7, each applicant will be asked to make a brief presentation to council members. Applications are available on the City website at https://piedmont.ca.gov and from the City Clerk’s Office. For more information on the application process, contact City Clerk John Tulloch at (510) 420-3041 or via email at jtulloch@piedmont.ca.gov. “I’ll be in the Counting House, counting all the money.”
articles.title: Jan. 31 deadline for City Council applicants

articles.text: Crews from CF Contracting began working on the San Carlos Avenue retaining wall project on January 15. CF Contracting recently completed work on a retaining wall on Oakland Avenue just above the Oakland Avenue bridge. The City awarded both projects to the same contractor on August 16, 2021, with an total budget of $611,000. The contractor mobilized equipment on Oakland and Sunnyside Avenues on October 11, 2021, and began demolition of the existing retaining wall the next day. Once completed in early 2022, the crews then moved five blocks uphill to San Carlos. The retaining wall on the lower side of San Carlos Avenue is leaning into the roadway. The length of the wall that is currently being replaced is approximately 140 feet. The entire project was expected to take seven weeks but was delayed approximately 30 days due to rain. Work was further delayed due to problems with a PG&E gas line and utility pole anchor, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales confirmed. The construction on San Carlos should be completed by February 23. The retaining wall on the lower side of San Carlos Avenue between Oakland and Magnolia Avenues, is currently being repaired. articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department issued a shelter in place advisory on Saturday morning for the area of Lakeview Avenue and Poplar Way, where multiple trees and wires were down due to high winds. Tree limbs were continuing to fall throughout the day, and Fire Department and Piedmont Police Department staff joined PG&E workers to ensure the safety of pedestrians and vehicles. Piedmont Public Works worked to clear trees in various hot spots throughout the city. Standby crews responded onsite at 9 p.m. Friday night after receiving calls about downed power lines and fallen trees, confirmed Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “Crews placed barricades, signage, and cleared branches where possible. By 5 a.m. they called additional staff and on-call contractors to assist with tree removal and to open blocked roadways,” Gonzales said. At least five city-owned trees fell during the Friday night storm, and many more privately owned trees fell or were severely damaged. By 2 p.m. Saturday, all known roadways were re-opened as Public Works crews, Police Department, and Fire Department finished clearing debris and other hazards. PG&E reported widespread damages and multiple power outages in Montclair and pockets of Piedmont. Wind gusts were reported at nearly 60 miles per hour, according to the National Weather Service.
articles.title: Windstorm

articles.text: The 2021-2022 Piedmont Education Foundation Giving Campaign far surpassed its goal of raising $3 million for Piedmont schools. This year’s campaign generated a record $3.7 million with contributions from 1,200 families, also a record high. The results reflect a deep support of children and schools in Piedmont. This support is critical, as Piedmont schools count on Giving Campaign funds to support essential programs that provide a top-notch education for students. “Piedmont families are showing their gratitude for reopened schools, increased health and safety measures, and a return to the robust curriculum and individualized student attention that set our schools apart,” said Education Foundation Executive Director Heather Frank. The funds will help keep Piedmont’s student/teacher ratios low and will continue to support essential programs including libraries and librarians, art and music, S.T.E.A.M. training, electives, A.P. classes, counselors, and special education support. Funds will be allocated by a committee composed of Piedmont parents and community members, who will meet to learn more about the district’s needs and decide on the allocation of funds. A full report of how the funds will be allocated will be made available to the public. In an informal competition, parents of first grade students won the contest for the highest participation with 81% of families giving. They have won a taco truck party in the spring. The kindergarten parents at Wildwood School had the highest participation level of the year with 93% of families donating to the Giving Campaign. “We really appreciate the community’s support of this year’s Giving Campaign, which makes up about 8% of [the] school district’s annual budget,” said Giving Campaign Co-Chair Christine Wente von Metzsch. The campaign’s success is also due to both the staff at the Piedmont Education Foundation office and a dedicated committee of volunteers that worked for months. This year’s volunteer committee was one of the largest yet, with over 60 parents from across Piedmont’s schools. This year’s campaign team put up banners and signs at the schools, conducted community outreach, wrote letters and made phone calls, organized and spoke at numerous community events, ran mail and e-mail campaigns and text banks, spread the word via weekly messaging in school bulletins, class emails and local news outlets, amplified campaign messaging on PEF’s social media. They also distributed 760 Giving Campaign lawn signs and engaged in personal outreach to hundreds of donors. “The Giving Campaign is truly a community effort. The tremendous success of this year’s campaign is a resounding testament to the ongoing commitment and dedication of volunteers and the donors who consistently put our schools and kids first,” said Nicki Gilbert, Chair of the Education Foundation board. The Giving Campaign leadership team would like to extend their deep gratitude to the team at the Piedmont Education Foundation, the many volunteers who helped with the campaign, and the entire Piedmont community for supporting our schools.
articles.title: Giving Campaign raises record $3.7 Million

articles.text: Schools are reopening after summer break, and it’s time to send your children to school. One has asthma, and the other a history of lung complications. You rest assured that their school is [using] every protective measure possible. Unfortunately. for the majority of non-Piedmont residents, this likely isn’t a safe assumption. The Piedmont Highlander had planned to run a story demanding action on the part of the school district, asking them to mandate the COVID-19 vaccine for all students and staff of Piedmont schools. However, on September 22, the school board satisfied this request before it was made. They ruled that all persons must provide proof of vaccination to attend class on campus. All U.S. public schools must follow suit and mandate the vaccine in the interest of their students and staff. Any attending student or instructing staff member should be held to a basic standard of expectation of consideration and respect. They must protect both themselves and the members of their communities by receiving full inoculation against COVID-19. The current widely implemented policy across California schools directed at teaching staff allows weekly testing as a valid substitute for proof of vaccination. The caveat that unvaccinated people must be tested weekly provides little assurance that those individuals will not be carriers and transmitters of the virus. In the six-day interim period between testing it is highly likely that an individual [can be] infected, remains asymptomatic, and proceeds to interact with others, unknowingly acting as a carrier and transmitting the virus, according to the CDC. According to its August 23 news release, the FDA fully approved the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine for individuals 16 years of age and older. All three vaccines went through four stages of rigorous clinical trial prior to public release, as per the FDA standard, according to the National Institute of Health. Severe allergic reaction to any of the vaccines has occurred in roughly 2 to 5 million cases, according to the CDC. It is important to protect personal freedoms, but not without question. Personal freedoms extend as far as the person to whom they belong. The moment any action extends beyond the bounds of the individual, it becomes the concern of all those the action affects. Vaccination against COVID-19 easily breaches this threshold. Curiosity and caution are important practices, but hesitancy bred by misinformation is exceedingly dangerous, and no public institution should cater to this mentality. The COVID-19 vaccine is safe, and this must be regarded as fact, and policy decisions made accordingly. Even a high vaccination rate within a community [does not] remove all risk associated with exposure to the virus. Having received both doses of the vaccine nearly eliminates the chance of hospitalization in young people; however, it does not guarantee full immunity or prevent transmission, according to the CDC. Young people, upon infection, can become transmitters of the disease, hence posing a serious threat to the more vulnerable individuals they may interact with. It is the duty of able community members to protect their vulnerable counterparts – they rely on the fulfillment of this duty. Piedmont has helped set an important precedent. This article was originally published in the high school newspaper, The Piedmont Highlander, on January 18, 2022. Aryana Fisher, a junior at Piedmont High School, is Editor of Closer Look for TPH.
articles.title: All high schools need vaccine mandates

articles.text: A wide selection of computer classes will be available through Piedmont Adult School in the Spring semester. Classes range from beginning to advanced, and from single, two-hour sessions to multi-session weekly courses and run until June 4. Some classes have started but can still be joined. Long-time Piedmont Adult School teacher Helen Nishikai teaches Adobe Acrobat, Wordpress, Quickbooks Online and selected Microsoft Excel sections. She holds a California Teaching Credential in Adult Education for Computer Technology and Business Management. “I love helping people learn new skills that they can apply directly to their job or personal life,” said Nishikai. New to Piedmont Adult School this school year is Mike Matthews, who teaches popular courses on how to use Apple products. Many of his classes are 2-hour workshops on using specific Apple Apps such as Messages, Notes and Photos. He also teaches an eight-week course on the basics of using your iPhone. For more information visit Piedmontadultschool.org. Classes are open to all adults age 18 and over. Piedmont Adult School offers in-person as well as online classes. In-person classes will be held at Piedmont High School and will follow Piedmont School District COVID-19 guidelines. The Piedmont Adult School office is located at 760 Magnolia Avenue. For information call (510) 594-2655, or e-mail: piedmontadultschool@piedmont.k12. ca.us.

Don’t forget to stop by the planetarium and megadome to experience space and science on the biggest of big screens. See how high, intricate, and stable of a structure you can build while learning about form and design. As always ,Phenna the Fin Whale is out front to climb on. articles.text: As discussed last month, the lasting value of an education in most cases has much more to do with the cognitive skills students develop than the subject matter students remember. The exception to this idea is elementary school where students learn essential skills like reading, spelling and arithmetic. Being able to express oneself in writing is much more important than remembering the enlightened aspects of Macbeth. Learning to solve problems logically is far more important than remembering how to use the quadratic equation. And developing memory techniques for languages is probably more important than remembering the conjugations of estar in the preterite. So, when we examine our students’ classes, we need to examine them in terms of what cognitive skills are being developed. Understanding and logic vs. memorization In high school math and science classes the most valuable skills a student can develop are the ability to build an understanding of a complicated idea as well as logical problem solving. But these will not develop automatically. Students need to focus on developing these skills or they may not gain these skills and might only rely on memory. Understanding is built one piece at a time When trying to understand a complicated concept, it will not come all at once. Complicated ideas have multiple facets and relationships, so we gain each piece a bit at a time. Math is language restricted to quantities Math has two parts, the language that describes quantities and their interactions as well as the logical process of deducing values and relationships. But let’s focus on the language part. Every equation is saying that two different things are the same size. Knowing the Why and How of each step Whenever you take a step in math or science, students need to know why they are allowed to do the step and how it is moving them closer to their goal. If you have an equation, that means two things are the same size. So, for every step in solving an equation, either you have to change both sides the same way, or you have to change the representation of one side, but not the value. Solve logically, not with memory or heuristics There are three approaches to solving a problem, using memory, heuristics or logic. Some students simply try to remember what they have been taught. This requires no understanding and the only skill that is being developed is memory. It is akin to being a trained seal. Heuristics are general problem-solving strategies. Using Heuristics is better than relying on memory, but not much better. The most useful way to solve a problem is to use logic. Next month: How to solve a problem using logic. articles.text: Anna Goldberg, a graduate of Piedmont High School in 2018, was named to the Dean’s List at Lehigh University. This status is granted to students who earned a scholastic average of 3.6 or better while carrying at least 12 hours of regularly graded courses. For more than 150 years, Lehigh University, located in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, has combined outstanding academic and learning opportunities with leadership in fostering innovative research. The school is among the nation’s most selective, highly ranked private research universities. Lehigh’s five colleges provide opportunities to 7,000 students in an academically rigorous environment along with a supportive, engaged campus community.
articles.title: Anna Goldberg named to Lehigh Dean’s List

articles.text: Susan Kuroda, a 2018 graduate of Piedmont High School, was named to the Dean’s List for the Fall semester at Emerson College. The requirement to make Dean’s List is a grade point average of 3.7 or higher for that semester. Kuroda is a senior majoring in Writing and Publishing. Founded in 1880 and located in Boston, Massachusetts in the heart of the city’s Theatre District, Emerson College educates individuals who will solve problems and change the world through engaged leadership in communication and the arts. The College has 3,780 undergraduates and 670 graduate students from across the United States and 50 countries. Supported by state-of-the-art facilities and a renowned faculty, students participate in more than 90 student organizations and performance groups. Emerson is known for its experiential learning programs in Los Angeles, the District of Columbia, the Netherlands, London, China, and the Czech Republic as well as its new Global Portals, with the first program launching this fall in Paris.
articles.title: Susan Kuroda named to Emerson College Dean’s List

Understanding and logic vs. memorization In high school math and science classes the most valuable skills a student can develop are the ability to build an understanding of a complicated idea as well as logical problem solving. But these will not develop automatically. Students need to focus on developing these skills or they may not gain these skills and might only rely on memory. Understanding is built one piece at a time When trying to understand a complicated concept, it will not come all at once. Complicated ideas have multiple facets and relationships, so we gain each piece a bit at a time. Math is language restricted to quantities Math has two parts, the language that describes quantities and their interactions as well as the logical process of deducing values and relationships. But let’s focus on the language part. Every equation is saying that two different things are the same size. Knowing the Why and How of each step Whenever you take a step in math or science, students need to know why they are allowed to do the step and how it is moving them closer to their goal. If you have an equation, that means two things are the same size. So, for every step in solving an equation, either you have to change both sides the same way, or you have to change the representation of one side, but not the value. Solve logically, not with memory or heuristics There are three approaches to solving a problem, using memory, heuristics or logic. Some students simply try to remember what they have been taught. This requires no understanding and the only skill that is being developed is memory. It is akin to being a trained seal. Heuristics are general problem-solving strategies. Using Heuristics is better than relying on memory, but not much better. The most useful way to solve a problem is to use logic. Next month: How to solve a problem using logic. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. articles.text: Mark your calendar for February 4-6, when Piedmont High School students will present the Disney musical Beauty and the Beast. 2022. Directed by Amy Moorhead, the production features over 40 students in the cast and on crew. With choreography by Moorhead, and vocal direction by Amy Belles, the stage musical is based on the Academy Award-winning animated film. The stage version includes all of the wonderful songs written by Alan Menken and the late Howard Ashman, along with new songs by Menken and Tim Rice. The original Broadway production ran for over thirteen years and was nominated for nine Tony Awards, including Best Musical. The classic story tells of Belle, a young woman in a provincial town, and the Beast, who is really a young prince trapped under the spell of an enchantress. If the Beast can learn to love and be loved, the curse will end, and he will be transformed into his former self. But time is running out. If the Beast does not learn his lesson soon, he and his household will be doomed for all eternity. In a tale as old as time, the show is filled with spectacular costumes. It is a great opportunity to bring your entire family to the theater. Performances will take place at Holy Names High School’s theater at 4660 Harbord Drive in Oakland. Tickets are available online at https://www.showtix4u. com/events/pusdbeauty. Cast members of Piedmont High School’s upcoming production of Beauty and the Beast: (front) August Thigpen (Wardrobe, left), Corinn Richards (Chip), Zoe Saldanha (Belle), Holden Temple (LeFou), Aidan Weiss (Maurice); (back) Quincy Munyan (Lumière), Cole Garcia (Gaston), Graham McWeeney (Cogsworth), Scott McKenzie (Beast), and Katherine Stormer (Babette).

articles.text: Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) teen volunteers are currently assisting CityTeam Ministries with the renovation of a century-old building in Oakland that will be used for transitional housing and support for the homeless. PCSC is a youth-led coed service crew with the Piedmont Scout Council led by Ken Li, who created the crew in 2004. Crew members, mostly high school students, participate in several ongoing and recurring service programs, the most recent being assisting CityTeam. “CityTeam Ministries recently started a major upgrade project and put out a call to volunteers to help them with their work in order to keep their costs at a minimum,” said Ken Li. “Through our long-standing relationship with Rebuilding Together Oakland, PCSC heard about this opportunity. We jumped at the chance to make a big impact where our teen members can learn some hands-on skills while helping CityTeam.” Crew members have visited the site twice this month, and last Sunday, January 23, a small group of PCSC teens cut and hung drywall, patched holes in the plaster, and sanded previous coats of drywall. “Young people can have very little experience doing this. Some kids have done drywall work before, but for many it’s very new. We pride ourselves in giving [PCSC crew members] opportunities like this,” said Li. “Service work often revolves around learning a new skill,” Li added, “like cooking, gardening, and home improvement.” The building on Washington Street serves the Oakland community in many ways. At that location CityTeam volunteers offer hot meals every weekday night, and bagged lunches and meals on Saturdays and Sundays. Clean showers are available also. The nonprofit CityTeam helps to relieve the many challenges that low-income Oakland families face. PHS Junior and PSCS crew member Elena Blanco measures drywall. Josh Sachs prepares to install new drywall on a home on Washington Street in Oakland. PCSC crew member Ethan Tran and Elena Blanco carry ladders while assisting in the renovation of a home on Washington Street in Oakland. Ethan Tran “It really is an amazing place, where lives are restored. However, that couldn’t be done without all of the amazing volunteer help,” said Becky McKeen, a Piedmont resident who is an administrative assistant for CityTeam. Ethan Tran, a Piedmont High PCSC crew members Amy Derr and Sara Broach are taught how to safely use power drills. School junior who assisted in last weekend’s service excursion, offered his insight on the experience. “It was a really wonderful experience working at the CityTeam project. I had a great time learning new skills. Learning the backstory of the building inspired me to work harder and hopefully help out again,” he said. “I learned how the leader of the project was formally incarcerated and how this building helped him, and many other people who had fallen on harsh times, move on with their lives.” Li added that his hope is for the Community Service Crew to volunteer at least once each weekend for the next several weeks. To learn more about PCSC, visit https://www.pcservicecrew. org/crew-calendar.
articles.title: Community Service Crew helps renovate historic house

School junior who assisted in last weekend’s service excursion, offered his insight on the experience. “It was a really wonderful experience working at the CityTeam project. articles.text: This treasure of California is among the best winter hikes of the Sierra Nevada Mountains. The abandoned railway at Donner Pass, originally constructed in 1867 for the Central Pacific Railroad’s portion of the First Transcontinental Railroad, is a serene wintertime hike. The trek takes you through hollowed out mountain tunnels and snow sheds through the pass surrounding Donner Lake. Aside from the obvious historic railway, the mountain pass is the same area where the Donner Party met their fate in the fierce winter of 1846 – becoming the namesake of the lake and surrounding state park. The walk through the train tunnels is brief, just 2.1 miles, but it gives you the magic of the Tahoe winter without getting knee deep in snow. It’s a great place for children, families, and beginning snowshoers. During warmer weather, you can walk past the last snow shed and up to Donner Peak. Taking the same route as our 2018 summer visit, we go from McGlashan Point over a Native American petroglyph site The starting point for the trail from McGlashan Point goes up a popular sledding hill to the China Wall and first tunnel. Snow piles into some sections of the Donner Pass trail. TJ Stevko, CFP® Financial Advisor 370 Highland Avenue Suite 201 Piedmont, CA 94611 510-547-4589
