articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team was victorious 4-1 over nonleague opponent Arroyo on Friday, January 21 at Estuary Park in Alameda, but they took a 3-1 loss to Acalanes in Lafayette on Monday, January 24. Piedmont has seven matches left in the season, all against Foothill Division opponents. The six-team league with Berkeley, Castro Valley, Bishop O’Dowd, San Leandro, and Alameda is always a tight race. Piedmont’s cur rent record against league teams puts them in the running for a league title and this year will likely be another photo finish. “Everyone has beaten everyone in the league. We still have games against everyone and still haven’t faced Bishop O’Dowd. It’s really close,” said coach Dan Chubbock, who won his first Foothill banner in 2018. PHS has two matches with Bishop O’Dowd after the first game was postponed due to COVID-19 outbreak at O’Dowd . The teams play one another this Friday, January 28 and again on Monday, February 7. “It’s very, very tight. Friday’s game is probably going to determine whether we have a chance at winning the league title. The result on Friday will have a very big impact on the league. Berkeley just beat O’Dowd, so that puts them in the running,” said Chubbock. Staff Photos Piedmont holds a 4-3-2 record and has seven matches remaining, all against league competition. 3-1 loss to Acalanes Piedmont traveled to Lafayette on Monday, January 24 to face Acalanes, losing 3-1. The Dons compete in Div. 3 in the North Coast Section, while PHS plays in Division 2. The Highlanders trailed 1-0 after seven minutes and conceded a second goal around the 35th minute after the Dons’ forward attempted a cross which arced into the net. Junior midfielder Audrey Lam landed Piedmont’s first goal on a beautiful shot from 25 yards to the top bin to make it 2-1 with 15 minutes left in the game. “It was a great goal. She cut inside from the left and smashed it to the top corner,” said Chubbock. Acalanes went on to score their final goal about five minutes later. 4-1 win over Arroyo Piedmont outplayed Arroyo of San Lorenzo 4-1 in a game at Estuary Park in Alameda on January 21. PHS led 2-0 by halftime and pulled ahead 3-0 in the second half before Arroyo pulled closed 3-1, but Highlanders added one more in the closing minutes. Goals were scored by junior Cameron Lorin had two goals, while Rachael Barton, and Hailey Marshburn also scored. NEXT UP Piedmont (4-3-2 overall, 1-2-0 league) heads to Bishop O’Dowd for a big game this Friday, January 28 at 6:00 p.m. Audrey Lam scored in Monday’s game against Acalanes. articles.text: Staff Photos Trinity Zamora had double-doubles against Alameda, San Leandro, and Freedom. Piedmont’s girls’ basketball finished a busy week, winning three of four games. They beat Alameda 67-43 on the road on Wednesday, January 19, was victorious 83-38 over Las Lomas in Walnut Creek on Saturday, January 22, and beat Freedom 62-24 over Freedom in the Sabrina Ionescu Shootout. One day earlier, PHS sustained a stunning 50-49 loss to San Leandro at the buzzer in front of a homecourt crowd at Binks Rawlings Gym on Friday, January 21. It was the time Piedmont has lost to in the 19 years of the coach Bryan Gardere era. “We didn’t play very well against San Leandro, and still had a chance to get out with a win. We had some players missing on our bench and it was too much to overcome. You can’t beat a good team when you don’t shoot the ball well,” said Gardere Piedmont’s record moves to 12-4. 67-43 win over Alameda Piedmont led narrowly 9-5 by the end of the first quarter and exploded in the second quarter to jump ahead 36-11 by halftime. The Highlanders boosted their lead to 54-21 in the third and closed out well, 67-43. Trinity Zamora scored 15 of her 28 points in the second quarter, including three 3-pointers. Final stats: Zamora had 28 points, 16 rebounds, four assists, three steals and four blocks. Natalia Martinez had 25 points, nine rebounds, four steals, and four assists. Maddie Hill scored eight points, six rebounds, one assist and steal. Aniya Perine had six points and two rebounds. 50-49 loss to San Leandro San Leandro’s mighty 50-49 buzzer-beater upset of Piedmont on January 21 improved the Pirates’ record to 12-3 overall and 2-0 in the Foothill Division of the WACC. The two teams are set to play again in the regular-season Maddie Hill had a double-double against San Leandro with 15 points and 11 rebounds.

articles.text: When writing about the athletic accomplishments of student-athletes at Piedmont High, it becomes more difficult to follow their athletic careers in college. articles.text: San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum is hosting a virtual storytelling program for Lunar New Year to welcome the Year of the Tiger. The family-friendly event will begin at 11 a.m. on Sunday, January 30 and is accessible through Zoom. Tickets are free to this virtual event. Asian Art Museum staff will discuss the significance of the Tiger in relation to the Chinese zodiac; recommended for ages 7 and up, staff will explore why the tiger is the third animal of the zodiac and what the tiger symbolizes in Asian art. Artworks from the museum’s collection will be shown. Tickets for the event and downloadable art activities for children are available at https://calendar.asianart. org/event/lunar-new-year-storytelling/?time=1643569200.

articles.text: Dores André and Lonnie Weeks rehearsing as Mrs. Robinson and Benjamin in Cathy Marston’s new ballet, Mrs. Robinson. San Francisco Ballet will present Program I, a selection of three productions, beginning February 1 and running through February 12. George Balanchine’s masterful Symphony in C, with the music of Georges Bizet, will begin the program and includes more than 50 San Francisco Ballet dancers onstage. Trio, choreographed by Artistic Director Helgi Tomasson, includes the music of Tchaikovsky. The dancers will be adorned in billowing gowns and velvet jackets. The world premiere of Mrs. Robinson will complete the program. With a nod to the iconic American novella and film The Graduate, Cathy Marston’s retelling is from the perspective of the titular seductress. “I immediately thought—this is it,” said Marston after learning the novella is set in San Francisco. “This is the piece that I need to make for San Francisco Ballet.” “In the film, Anne Bancroft is impenetrable. And that’s genius, because it means you project your own feelings onto hers. I suppose that was the inspiration for the ballet. I wanted to get underneath the surface and find out why Mrs. Robinson is as she is, why she does the things that she does, and make specific choices based on those answers,” she added. The music for Mrs. Robinson was composed by Terry Davies, with scenic and costume design by Patrick Kinmonth. inside the auditorium. program-1/. 865-2000.

articles.text: San Francisco Symphony is celebrating the Year of the Tiger with a special Lunar New Year performance at Davies Symphony Hall on February 5. Conductor Yue Bao will make her debut leading the orchestra in traditional Chinese folk music and works by Asian composers. Bao serves as Assistant Conductor of the Houston Symphony alongside Music Director Andres Orozco-Estrada. She has served as both conductor and assistant and has worked with Michael Tilson Thomas, Marin Alsop, Esa-Pekka Salonen and Oslo Vanska. The program includes music from Chen Gang and He Zhanhao’s The Buttery Lovers Concerto, performed by violinist Bomsori, and Tan Dun’s Eternal Vow from Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon performed by Symphony Assistant Principal Cell Amos Yang. The program will also include works by Huan-zhi Li, Texu Kim, Huang Ruo, Tyzen Hsiao, and Liu Yua. The event will mark the 22nd anniversary of the Symphony’s celebration of the beginning of the Lunar New Year, or Spring Festival, one of the most important cultural holidays for many nations in East, South, and Southeast Asia. The annual Blue Moon Banquet will not take place this year due to the surge of the COVID Omicron variant. The concert begins at 5 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2021-22/Lunar-NewYear-Year-of-the-Tiger. Guest Conductor Yue Bao will lead San Francisco Symphony on February 5 for the 22nd annual Lunar New Year Celebration.

articles.text: Christoph Waltz, Robert Pattinson, Reese Witherspoon, and Tai in Water for Elephants. Water for Elephants is a solid adaptation of the 2006 best-selling novel by Sara Gruen. The film opens with an old man (Hal Holbrook), standing out in the rain, watching the circus, now loaded on trucks, preparing to leave and move onto the next town. One of the circus owners brings him inside, and over a glass of whisky, curious about the old guy, encourages him to tell his story. And so the tale begins, told at first by the old Jacob, but then his voice over soon morphs into that of young Jacob (Robert Pattison), who is sitting for his final veterinarian exam. He is called out of the test and told that his parents have just been killed in a car accident. Devastated, Jacob packs his things and leaves, jumping a train, one that turns out to be carrying the Benzini Bros. circus. August Rosenbluth (Christoph p Waltz), the circus ringmaster and boss, hires Jacob as a circus roustabout, at least until he finds out that he is a vet. August’s wife, the lovely Marlena (Reese Withersoon), immediately captures Jacob’s attention. She performs center ring, of course, and the film soon telegraphs that a relationship is in the offing, the only question is how it will secretly evolve. There is much that makes this film more than just passable. One is the setting – a circus in 1931 during the depths of the Great Depression. It was a time when people were desperate for any form of entertainment, anything to take them out of the reality of that stark economic period. The Benzini Circus is replete with all manner of interesting characters. It is a world apart from the ordinary life led by those who live in the towns and bring their children to see the extraordinary. The circus is also a culture unto itself with a language and mores that are more than interesting. Unfortunately, the film only briefly touches on this world, though the opportunity is offered when an old veteran, Camel (Jim Norton), takes Jacob on a tour. He is dazzled and in awe of all that he sees. The circus is vibrant and alive, full of color and magic and music. But there is also a dark side, one that Jacob comes to understand and even fear. August, he discovers, can slip from friendly and welcoming to cruelty that borders on the insane. C h r i s t o ph Wa lt z , t he Oscar-winning actor who starred in Inglourious Basterds, delivers a superb performance, one that is powerful and captivating. He provides an interesting contrast to Pattison’s Jacob. Pattison’s face is not one that emotes. He doesn’t seem capable of changing his expressions from scene to scene, his remoteness ever consistent. It was a quality that worked nicely in the “Twilight” series where he portrayed a stoic vampire; however, in the role of Jacob he is asked to do more. Unfortunately, he seems somewhat at a loss. Witherspoon and Waltz are consummate actors and able to transform themselves. Waltz chews up every scene he is in, as he did in Inglourious Basterds where he convincingly portrayed a malevolent Nazi officer. Witherspoon is resilient and fragile with a touch of trapped desperation. In the aggregate Water for Elephants is fine entertainment. Water for Elephants. Directed by Francis Lawrence. Starring Reese Witherspoon, Robert Pattison, Christoph Waltz, Hal Holbrook and Jim Norton. 2 hrs., 3 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS Water for Elephants – it’s all about the circus life

articles.text: California paella looks spectacular, and nothing could be easier to make. One of the most spectacular restaurants in the world is located not far from Barcelona. It is like eating in Mesa Verde amidst the cliff dwellings in New Mexico. Magnificent vistas and beautiful paella – need I say more? Let your imagination run wild. All of this is yours just about an hour from Barcelona. If you are religious, take the opportunity to visit the Montserrat monastery, then continue driving into the mountains. All the while think of paella. Set your compass to Restaurant El Puig de la Balma in the town of Mura. The location is stunning. It is a crevasse in a sheer mountainside. The restaurant itself was built in the 11th century entirely of rock. Take a look at its website and then study the cliff dwellings in New Mexico. California style paella In honor of Catalonians’ favorite dish, here is a California style paella. It is so simple that you don’t even need a recipe. You can serve any number of people by adjusting the portion of rice – one handful per person. It is best if you have a paella pan, but a large skillet will work just as well. Moisten in the pan with some good quality olive oil and then put in some salt and pepper. Meanwhile, dice some bell pepper, onion, and garlic and put them in the pan to brown. When the vegetables are soft, add the next ingredients. You may put in anything you have in the refrigerator. Some things you might use are artichoke hearts, olives, zucchini or any kind of vegetable, even capers. Anything goes. And you can use any kind of meat. To the lightly browned vegetables add a generous portion of arborio rice, one handful per person. 12 ounces will serve six people. You will need broth. By Chris Honore’ Water for Elephants is a solid adaptation of the 2006 best-selling novel by Sara Gruen. The film opens with an old man (Hal Holbrook), standing out in the rain, watching the circus, now loaded on trucks, preparing to leave and move onto the next town. One of the circus owners brings him inside, and over a glass of whisky, curious about the old guy, encourages him to tell his story. And so the tale begins, told at first by the old Jacob, but then his voice over soon morphs into that of young Jacob (Robert Pattison), who is sitting for his final veterinarian exam. He is called out of the test and told that his parents have just been killed in a car accident. Devastated, Jacob packs his things and leaves, jumping a train, one that turns out to be carrying the Benzini Bros. circus. August Rosenbluth (Christoph p Waltz), the circus ringmaster and boss, hires Jacob as a circus roustabout, at least until he finds out that he is a vet. August’s wife, the lovely Marlena (Reese Withersoon), immediately captures Jacob’s attention. She performs center ring, of course, and the film soon telegraphs that a relationship is in the offing, the only question is how it will secretly evolve. There is much that makes this film more than just passable. One is the setting – a circus in 1931 during the depths of the Great Depression. It was a time when people were desperate for any form of entertainment, anything to take them out of the reality of that stark economic period. The Benzini Circus is replete with all manner of interesting characters. It is a world apart from the ordinary life led by those who live in the towns and bring their children to see the extraordinary. The circus is also a culture unto itself with a language and mores that are more than interesting. Unfortunately, the film only briefly touches on this world, though the opportunity is offered when an old veteran, Camel (Jim Norton), takes Jacob on a tour. He is dazzled and in awe of all that he sees. The circus is vibrant and alive, full of color and magic and music. But there is also a dark side, one that Jacob comes to understand and even fear. August, he discovers, can slip from friendly and welcoming to cruelty that borders on the insane. C h r i s t o ph Wa lt z , t he Oscar-winning actor who starred in Inglourious Basterds, delivers a superb performance, one that is powerful and captivating. He provides an interesting contrast to Pattison’s Jacob. Pattison’s face is not one that emotes. He doesn’t seem capable of changing his expressions from scene to scene, his remoteness ever consistent. It was a quality that worked nicely in the “Twilight” series where he portrayed a stoic vampire; however, in the role of Jacob he is asked to do more. Unfortunately, he seems somewhat at a loss. Witherspoon and Waltz are consummate actors and able to transform themselves. Waltz chews up every scene he is in, as he did in Inglourious Basterds where he convincingly portrayed a malevolent Nazi officer. Witherspoon is resilient and fragile with a touch of trapped desperation. In the aggregate Water for Elephants is fine entertainment. Water for Elephants. Directed by Francis Lawrence. articles.text: Bu Jim Gardner Dear Jim: I have lived in my home for 30 years and all of a sudden, I’m starting to have a bunch of problems. My basement and crawlspaces are flooding, and I’m getting cracks in the walls and ceilings in my house. Why is this happening, and what can I do about it? I have talked to several drainage people, and they have told me The correct solution different things. –Alex S. Dear Alex: Most older homes have inadequate or non-existent drainage systems, that are original to the property or improperly built and are no longer working. Add to that the effects of a changing climate and more substantial rain events, and our homes are no longer able to cope. Cracks, sloping floors and other interior changes are often merely a reflection of drainage-related settlement problems when our foundations are not built to modern standards. Older foundations are shallow, unreinforced, in poor condition and more prone to movement and water infiltration. A dual drainage membrane system helps preserve older foundations. It is crucial to identify the particular type of drainage issue you are experiencing. Water problems can be a function of either surface water, subterranean water, or both. The solutions range from simply attaching flexible pipe to your downspouts to get water away from your house, to digging 10’ deep trenches when French drains are needed for deep drainage issues. Where the drainage work is located, what type of system to use, and the drainage depth are different for every project and are a function of the particular conditions at your home. Hillside homes on steep slopes with water problems in different locations can be a challenge. Unfortunately, many drainage “professionals” offer up cookie cutter solutions that can create more substantial drainage problems in the future if they are not properly designed. What should I do about It? Sometimes the answer is to do nothing. If you are a new homeowner and the problem is not an emergency, I often recommend observing the problems through a full rain cycle. If downspouts are draining up against the house, flexible piping should be attached to them so water is brought away from the house. If the issues are Separate piping for downspouts and the French drain are essential. ongoing or more urgent, I would consult with an experienced drainage contractor. The key is understanding how to design a system that will work long term. Don’t rely on general contractors or landscapers unless they have substantial experience with this work. A poor drainage plan can often make drainage conditions worse and more expensive in the long run. Jim Gardner is a long-time Piedmont resident who has been doing structural repair and basement renovation in your neighborhood since 1983. articles.text: Part 36 in a biweekly series A number of years ago I was designing a new resort in Palm Desert. Because accommodating buyers’ needs and wishes is critical, we had numerous meetings with the real estate agents, the people who actually sold the houses and units. How big should the kitchen be? What amenities are critical? What size do buyers want? Finally, after yet another long discussion, an experienced agent told us that there was one question she got from prospective buyers more than any other: “Do you think we will make friends here?” This was a true epiphany, and something I’ll never forget. She was telling us that the most important thing to buyers is not size, layout, or style – it is the desire to join and be a part of a community. I have come to believe that at the heart of successful cities and towns is how readily the place supports and facilitates community. There are of course many inter-related social, economic, and governmental components to this concept, but they are all tied to the built environment. That is to say, the planning, urban design, architectural, landscape architectural and interior concepts we have been discussing in this column the last couple of years can all work together to enhance and facilitate interaction among people…or, sometimes, unfortunately, to inhibit it. There is room in virtually all development for the inclusion of small incidental public spaces, such as the “flower stand alley” nearby on Piedmont Ave. Note how benches and chairs inevitably start to appear in these natural gathering places. The triangular “plazita” across from the Piedmont Theater is, I think, as close as we come to a town square in the area. It is minimal, but in the right location. Enlivened by shops, restaurants, and the theater, it is well used. Whether we are considering development on vacant land (referred to as “greenfield” development) or, as in Piedmont, adaptive reuse or infill (“brownfield development”), the community enhancement component is critical to success and should be on top of our minds. No matter what type of project or what size, this consideration applies to them all and includes to some degree everything from a sidewalk design to the layout of a large civic building. When the group bid goodbye Kabir Solanki in front of the mural on Martin Levy’s garage. to Martin he told them to look for “Death’s Door,” a gate along Portsmouth Walk. All around the gate and fence are cactuses, broken ceramics, and other fun decorations. At the top of Portsmouth Walk is Annerley Road and a few houses beyond is Robert McNamara’s childhood home, where the walkers stopped for a group photo. The group then reversed their steps and went up Annerley to Harvard Road to find another destination, a hidden path that took them up to a back alley between Harvard and Oakmont. Lois Price lives nearby and said she didn’t know if the alley has a name. The group decided that it should be called “Lois Lane” (pun intended). On the return to the Exedra Sherry Jacobs and Quincy Dong took a quick side trip to see the top of the steep Prospect Drive cul-de-sac while the rest of the group watched from below. It appears to be another alley providing access to garages for the adjacent homes. Maulshree Solanki said her son’s name is taken from the Indian mystic and poet Kabir, who was a disciple of the Hindu ascetic Ramananda. Piedmont’s young Kabir had no problems with the 3-mile walk and he shared observations with his mother to record in his Explorer’s notebook. Besides “Wildwood secret path, fun stones, and mint,” Kabir also noted that there were “zero mushrooms.” The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday, rain or shine, at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. articles.text: Longtime Piedmont resident Nicholas Molnar, a vintner who helped pioneer fine wine in the now-famous Napa County region of Carneros, died on January 11. He was 94. A native Hungarian who fled Budapest after the 1956 revolution failed to overthrow the Stalinist regime, Molnar was an entrepreneurial grape grower, planting numerous vineyards in Napa County in the 1960s and ’70s. Presciently, in 1973 he bought a 100-acre plot in what were then viewed as the marginal southern stretches of the county, abutting the marshlands of San Pablo Bay. The climate there was considered too windy, too cold, too extreme for fine wine. Today, Carneros is renowned as one of California’s premier places for wine grapes, and that vineyard became the foundation for the Molnar family’s Obsidian Wine Co. “He was always an explorer,” said Arpad Molnar, his son. Later in his career, working with his children, Molnar planted a vineyard in another place that was considered marginal, Lake County, and became one of the first to import Hungarian oak barrels into the U.S. As with the Carneros vineyard, these ventures were initially met with skepticism, but ultimately proved influential on the California wine industry. Molnár Miklós was born in Budapest in 1927. He grew up in a politically fraught time, as Hungary faced the Great Depression, then World War II, then Soviet occupation. Molnar’s father was a business owner — he ran a trucking company — and in the late 1940s, like many who were vilified as capitalists, both father and son spent time in prison. He married a gymnast, Andrea Bodo. While she was in Australia, competing in the 1956 Olympics, a revolt broke out in Budapest against the Soviet regime. Molnar participated, taking to the streets in October 1956. When it became clear that the Soviets would crush the revolution, Molnar fled, crossing the Austrian border on his own. He found his way to Melbourne, where he reunited with his wife, who had won a gold medal. Molnar, Bodo and other members of the Hungarian Olympic gymnastics team decided not to return to Hungary, initially remaining in Australia. A new opportunity soon presented itself: U.S. magazine magnate Henry Luce, who had just founded a new publication called Sports Illustrated, offered to host the Hungarian team on a tour of the United States. (The move, Arpad Molnar believes, was politically motivated, publicizing the refugees of a communist regime during the height of the Cold War.) The arrangement proved especially advantageous for Molnar, who had done some work as a journalist in Hungary and was assigned to cover the tour for Sports Illustrated. Just before Christmas 1956, the tour touched down in San Francisco. “Gov. Knight Hails Stateless Group,” reads The Chronicle’s headline on Dec. 25. Molnar and Bodo immediately took to the city and decided to stay. In San Francisco, Molnar worked briefly as a journalist and then sold life insurance. He and Bodo divorced, and in 1967 he married another Hungarian refugee, Catherine de Bokay. They settled in Piedmont. “He had been a patriarch among Hungarian-Americans in the Bay Area, and could well have served as an honorary Hungarian consul here too, ready to answer any query about the old country, the culture or language while producing California wines with relish. I felt privileged to have known him over the past half-century here,” said Piedmont resident Paul Hertelendy, also of Hungarian ancestry. Among his life insurance customers were the Pepi brothers, who had a winery in Napa. (Originally called Robert Pepi Winery, it’s now Cardinale, owned by Jackson Family Wines.) That’s where Molnar got the idea to plant a vineyard, according to his son. He placed ads in newspapers to find investors. Beginning in the 1960s, aided by numerous investors, Molnar bought several undeveloped plots of land in Napa County and planted wine grapes on them. Not all of them worked out, and in several cases he ended up having to sell the properties to meet his obligations to investors. But one parcel, in the southern edge of the county where the Napa River meets the bay, he managed to keep. Before Molnar bought it in 1973, the 100-acre site had been sheep grazing land. Few other vineyards existed in Carneros at the time; it would be 12 more years before Carneros was officially recognized as an American Viticultural Area, the government designation for a wine region. Conventional wisdom held that it wasn’t as well suited to wine grapes as the rest of Napa County. Molnar proved otherwise. He planted Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, grape varieties that thrive in cooler climates. The same year, the French Champagne company Moet Hennessy arrived in Napa, with plans to create a winery – Nicholas Molnar helped pioneer fine wine in the now-famous Napa County region of Carneros. Famed California vintner Nicholas Molnar with wife Catherine. what would become Domaine Chandon – and was looking for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, the grapes used in Champagne. Through 1985, Molnar sold the entire crop from his vineyard to Chandon. Today, the fruit is sold to sparkling-wine producers Schramsberg and Mumm, and also used for the Molnar family’s own Poseidon label. “He was always a bit of an outsider,” said Arpad Molnar. “The wine industry is so insular, and he sort of orbited around that scene, but never wanted to be in that scene. He always felt that when you’re outside of it a little bit, you can think creatively.” In the early 1990s, Molnar and his two sons, Arpad and Peter, became involved in efforts to revitalize Hungary’s economy after the fall of the communist regime. Molnar’s first idea: wild rice. “He read an article about wild rice in the San Francisco Chronicle and how popular it was becoming,” Arpad Molnar said. So he bought some, flew to Hungary, and helped farmers plant it in their fields. He had a similar idea about wine barrels after finding a cooperage in Hungary, called Kádár, that was struggling financially. Though it had once produced wine barrels, during the Soviet occupation it had been forced to make furniture for Russian markets. They decided to help by buying its barrels and importing them into the U.S. “Winemakers told us, no one here is ever going to buy a Hungarian barrel,” said Arpad Molnar. Then as now, California’s wine industry is modeled on France, growing French grapes — like Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir — and aging them in French oak barrels, which many high-end wineries still consider the gold standard. When the Molnars imported their first Hungarian barrels in 1993, their main selling point was that they were cheaper than the French counterparts. At first, their only customer was Gallo. But once again, Molnar was ahead of the curve. The Molnars now sell Kádár barrels to 120 wineries in California and in countries including Australia and New Zealand. The family eventually took an ownership stake in the cooperage, adding an impressive partner — the famous French cooperage Taransaud. Molnar initially called his land in Carneros in 1973 the Chardonnay Vineyard. His children later convinced him to change the name to the less generic-sounding Poseidon Vineyard. Molnar’s last major frontier was in Lake County. By the late 1990s, land in Napa County was getting expensive, and he suspected that there was an opportunity to be had in the areas just north of the county line, where the terroir was similar but the real estate market much softer. Again with investors, he and his sons bought a 100-acre walnut orchard in 1999. The soil was studded with chunky, shiny, black obsidian rocks. They called the vineyard Obsidian Ridge, and soon developed a strong reputation for producing Napa Valley-caliber Cabernet Sauvignons. “None of this struck us until much later, but it was as outthere as planting in Carneros in the 1970s,” said Arpad Molnar. “Everyone said you couldn’t grow great Cabernet in Lake County.” His father would have wanted to be remembered as a pioneer, Arpad Molnar said. “He had this relentless curiosity. He was always interested in what was new, not quite there yet. Sometimes it didn’t work out. And sometimes it did.” Nicholas Molnar is survived by his wife, Catherine; his children Aniko, Peter and Arpad; and his grandchildren Renna, Kyla, Nichos, Gabriel, Eszter and Andreas. This obituary was principally written by Esther Mobley and appeared in the San Francisco Chronicle on January 23, 2022.

He always felt that when you’re outside of it a little bit, you can think creatively.” In the early 1990s, Molnar and his two sons, Arpad and Peter, became involved in efforts to revitalize Hungary’s economy after the fall of the communist regime. Molnar’s first idea: wild rice. “He read an article about wild rice in the San Francisco Chronicle and how popular it was becoming,” Arpad Molnar said. So he bought some, flew to Hungary, and helped farmers plant it in their fields. He had a similar idea about wine barrels after finding a cooperage in Hungary, called Kádár, that was struggling financially. Though it had once produced wine barrels, during the Soviet occupation it had been forced to make furniture for Russian markets. They decided to help by buying its barrels and importing them into the U.S. “Winemakers told us, no one here is ever going to buy a Hungarian barrel,” said Arpad Molnar. Then as now, California’s wine industry is modeled on France, growing French grapes — like Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir — and aging them in French oak barrels, which many high-end wineries still consider the gold standard. When the Molnars imported their first Hungarian barrels in 1993, their main selling point was that they were cheaper than the French counterparts. At first, their only customer was Gallo. But once again, Molnar was ahead of the curve. The Molnars now sell Kádár barrels to 120 wineries in California and in countries including Australia and New Zealand. The family eventually took an ownership stake in the cooperage, adding an impressive partner — the famous French cooperage Taransaud. Molnar initially called his land in Carneros in 1973 the Chardonnay Vineyard. His children later convinced him to change the name to the less generic-sounding Poseidon Vineyard. Molnar’s last major frontier was in Lake County. By the late 1990s, land in Napa County was getting expensive, and he suspected that there was an opportunity to be had in the areas just north of the county line, where the terroir was similar but the real estate market much softer. Again with investors, he and his sons bought a 100-acre walnut orchard in 1999. The soil was studded with chunky, shiny, black obsidian rocks. They called the vineyard Obsidian Ridge, and soon developed a strong reputation for producing Napa Valley-caliber Cabernet Sauvignons. “None of this struck us until much later, but it was as outthere as planting in Carneros in the 1970s,” said Arpad Molnar. “Everyone said you couldn’t grow great Cabernet in Lake County.” His father would have wanted to be remembered as a pioneer, Arpad Molnar said. “He had this relentless curiosity. He was always interested in what was new, not quite there yet. Sometimes it didn’t work out. And sometimes it did.” Nicholas Molnar is survived by his wife, Catherine; his children Aniko, Peter and Arpad; and his grandchildren Renna, Kyla, Nichos, Gabriel, Eszter and Andreas. This obituary was principally written by Esther Mobley and appeared in the San Francisco Chronicle on January 23, 2022.

articles.text: Although the Bay Area has received substantial rainfall recently, Piedmont and the surrounding area of Alameda County are still in a severe drought according to the U.S. Drought Monitor and the East Bay Municipal Utility District. Recent weather has led to Alameda County experiencing an above average amount of rainfall. While recent rains aren’t enough to end the drought, there are ways to collect and utilize rain here in Piedmont. Rainwater is a renewable resource that can be harvested and recycled. Apart from the equipment necessary to catch and use the rain, such as a rain barrel, using rainwater is essentially free. Freshwater from rainfall can reduce the need for supplemental irrigation and contribute to resilient, climate-appropriate gardens. Harvesting rainwater is sustainable and can be implemented by anyone. monters can reduce dependence on municipally treated water throughout the year. During the summer months when water is in peak demand, using rainwater can save treated water for necessities. Rain barrels and rainwater catchment systems are available to purchase at local Bay Area hardware stores in a variety of sizes and styles. Local to the Bay Area, the Urban Farmer Store’s Rainwater Harvesting Resources, Greywater Action’s Presentations and Videos, and Garden for the Environment’s upcoming rainwater harvesting events can help Piedmonters learn about how to prepare their own rainwater harvesting system. Although there are many types of rain barrels and rainwater catchment systems to consider, the best system will vary depending on individual needs. There are a few key factors to consider Piedmont resident Julia Burke utilizes attractive ceramic “rain barrels” in her garden. when setting up a rainwater harvesting system. For example, research shows that the best rain barrels have thick walls that can withstand different temperatures, are opaque to inhibit algae growth, and are securely covered and screened to prevent debris, insects, and objects from falling into or even living in the tank. The barrel or system should be planned so that it is in a safe, stable, and secure spot to prevent erosion from overflow, tipping or movement of the barrel, or water concentrating near structures. Furthermore, for landscape irrigation purposes, the system will need to have an easy outlet nozzle or otherwise accessible hose or connection to a drip irrigation system. For those who already have rainwater harvesting systems, regular inspection, cleaning, and maintenance can prolong the life of your system. Rain gutters and water catchment systems should both be inspected and cleaned twice a year to ensure they are free of debris that may inhibit the harvesting system. When inspecting a rain barrel, make sure there are no cracks or algae inside the barrel and that the screen is capable of keeping out debris and insects such as mosquitos. Rain barrels should be cleaned once a year to prevent the buildup of debris, which can be removed with nontoxic cleaner like vinegar. Rainwater harvesting is just one part of a series of actions that can help conserve water. Other resources for Piedmonters to save water and utilize resources during times of drought include the Piedmont Climate Challenge and the Bay Area Stormwater Management Agencies Association (BASMAA). The Piedmont Climate Challenge highlights water-wise changes including mindful lifestyle changes as well as home appliance upgrades to maximize water efficiency. Similarly, the BASMAA website features Rain Barrel and Rain Garden Fact Sheets. With these actions in mind, Piedmonters can play their part in contributing to a sustainable water management system. To actually be used by people, they must be obvious, convenient, interesting, and energized, and they have to be located and designed so that people want to be there. Further, our development thinking has to go beyond the city limits. To borrow from John Donne, no city is an island entire of itself—especially small cities like Piedmont. We walk to, shop in, dine in and recreate in close by surrounding Oakland neighborhoods; they certainly are a part of our lives in Piedmont. What this means is that in all of our urban design and planning development work, we have to look outward as well as inward to accommodate and appropriately interface with what is around us. articles.text: As of January 14, all elementary students ages 5-11 in the Piedmont School District were required to submit proof of vaccinations against COVID-19 in order to attend classes. Of the 958 students at the three elementary schools, 53 have not yet provided documentation. This represents a 94% vaccination rate. None of the 53 students have been barred from attending school yet, as the school district continues to work with families to help them get vaccinated. “We are in contact with all remaining families and will continue to provide any assistance,” said Director of Communications Brian Killgore. Students aged 12-18 had an initial deadline of November 17 to supply proof of full vaccination to the district. By that date there were 33 unvaccinated students or students who had not yet provided documentation. The deadline was extended to January 5 at the start of the second semester. By that date, all but nine students ages 12-18 were vaccinated. On September 22, Piedmont’s school board announced the requirement for all age-eligible students to get vaccinated from COVID-19. articles.text: The Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) and the City of Piedmont co-hosted the 25th Annual MLK Day Celebration on January 17 honoring the life and legacy of Civil Rights Leader Martin Luther King, Jr. Due to COVID and Omicron, this year’s event was virtual and available via Zoom. The program included five guest speakers: U.S Representative Barbara Lee; Dr. Clayborne Carson, Founding Director of the Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute; Anna Malaika Tubbs, author of The Three Mothers; Assembly member Buffy Wicks; and Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King. The theme of this year’s program was “Changing Souls, Changing Lives, and Creating Community.” Drawing upon a quote from Dr. King, which calls for us to “create a beloved community,” each featured speaker touched on what a beloved community means. The celebration was founded and organized by Piedmont resident Lois Corrin. This year, she was joined by her daughter Camillie Lafayette in moderating the program and introducing program speakers. U.S. Rep. Barbara Lee State Assembly member Buffy Wicks Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King
articles.title: MLK Day celebration on Jan. 17 honors life, legacy of Civil Rights leader

None of the 53 students have been barred from attending school yet, as the school district continues to work with families to help them get vaccinated. “We are in contact with all remaining families and will continue to provide any assistance,” said Director of Communications Brian Killgore. Students aged 12-18 had an initial deadline of November 17 to supply proof of full vaccination to the district. By that date there were 33 unvaccinated students or students who had not yet provided documentation. The deadline was extended to January 5 at the start of the second semester. By that date, all but nine students ages 12-18 were vaccinated. On September 22, Piedmont’s school board announced the requirement for all age-eligible students to get vaccinated from COVID-19. articles.text: Open letter to Piedmont community. Editor: Recently, I was surprised to learn of Piedmont High School’s decision to release the head football coach, Jerome Johnson. I am concerned about the future of the program. Our sons played for three different coaches from 2016-2021 and coach Johnson was outstanding. I was the JV and Varsity Team Parent and worked closely with each coach. I am grateful that Coach Johnson provided stability and leadership during the last three seasons. He was knowledgeable, student-centered, patient, and inspirational. We appreciate Coach Johnson’s dedication to our community and are dismayed with the way he has been treated. Football was truly the highlight of our family’s high school experience and the most valuable growth experience for our sons. They learned discipline, teamwork, leadership, how to overcome disappointment, and humility. Today, a new group of players has the opportunity to play under the lights at Witter Field. Parents have the opportunity to share in the Highlander pride of a 100+ year tradition. We hope that the Piedmont community recognizes the value of the football program to the development of young players – from flag football in middle school to the JV and Varsity teams. Each team is a developmental milestone and players should aspire to play at the highest level for their ability. The thought of discontinuing the Varsity team is not only disappointing to the current upperclassmen but also implies that younger players aren’t good enough to carry on the tradition of sophomores on varsity. Our experience shows that with the right coaching, discipline and physical conditioning, encouraging parents, and a supportive administration the varsity team will continue to teach valuable lessons to our players. I sincerely hope this discussion about the future of the football program moves to the hiring of a head coach, recruiting players, and scheduling an off-season workout schedule. Let’s move forward with confidence and conviction. –Mary Alice McNeil Ed. note: Mary Alice McNeil is a PHS alum and parent of two former football players, Billy McNeil (Class of 2020), and Tommy McNeil (Class of 2021).
articles.title: Let’s get the football program back on track

articles.text: St. Francis is known for that famous saying “preach the gospel, and if you have to, use words.” God is probably less concerned about what we believe and more concerned about the way we act. When we get right down to it, there are simply too many words flying around and not enough meaningful action. And as Christians approach Easter, the celebration of Jesus’ resurrection, it is easy for us to get sidetracked by words in the form of creeds, liturgies and theologies. These provide enough words to suffocate the real story that was all about meaningful action. It’s in that context that I share what I consider to be an Easter Story. A few years ago, Elizabeth Gilbert, author of “Eat, Pray, Love”, wrote about an incident that changed her life. She was riding the midtown bus in New York City in evening rush hour traffic. The weather was the worst January had to offer, complete with sleet and gusting wind. To quote her, “It sucked”. The bus was moving at a crawl, tempting her to get out and walk, but the cold icy world she was staring at through the window paralyzed her. The depression in that mobile metal tomb was palpable. Then something happened. When they arrived at 10th Street, the bus driver turned to address his gathered congregation in the bus. He said: “Ladies and Gentleman, we are now nearing the Hudson River. I’m going to ask you to do me a favor. When you get off the bus, I’m going to hold out my hand. As you walk past me, I want you to drop your troubles into the palm of my hand. I’ll take your troubles for you, and when I drive past the river, I’ll throw them in. The reason I want to do this is because you all seem like you’ve had a bad day, and I don’t want you taking all your worries and sorrows home to your friends and families now, because they deserve better than that, don’t they? So you just leave your troubles here with me to dispose of, and you all go have a wonderful night, OK?” Gilbert recounts: “The whole bus – the whole grumpy lot of us – broke into laughter. articles.text: The American Red Cross announced on January 11 that it is facing a national blood crisis, describing it as “the worst blood shortage in more than a decade.” Dangerously low blood supply levels are creating a risk to patient care across the country, the agency explained in a press release, and is forcing doctors “to make difficult decisions about who receives blood transfusions and who will need to wait until more products become available.” Blood donations are critically needed at this time, especially type O blood donors; however, donors of all types are encouraged to make an appointment now to give in the weeks ahead. “Winter weather across the country and the recent surge of COVID-19 cases are compounding the already-dire situation facing the blood supply,” said Dr. Baia Lasky, medical director for the Red Cross. “Please, if you are eligible, make an appointment to give blood or platelets in the days and weeks ahead to ensure no patient is forced to wait for critical care.” Over the next few weeks, about 54% of donation appointments remain unfilled in the Red Cross’s Northern California Coastal Region. Due to COVID-19 and challenges presented by the pandemic, the agency has seen about a 10% overall decline in donations as well as ongoing blood drive cancellations due to staff shortages. To donate blood at the Blood Bank at 6230 Claremont Avenue in Oakland, call (800) 733-2767. articles.text: The City of Oakland is imposing a proof of vaccination ordinance on February 1, which requires proof of current COVID vaccinations to enter many indoor facilities, including bars, restaurants, clubs, and gyms. The city made the announcement on January 5, and businesses are instructed to post a notice by January 15, two weeks before the ordinance goes into effect. In addition to entertainment venues, restaurants and bars, patrons will be asked to show proof of vaccination to enter senior adult care facilities and city senior programs. To enter Oakland City Hall visitors will be required to show proof of vaccination or a recent negative COVID-19 test within 72 hours of entry. Patrons will be expected to show their vaccination status at large, indoor events at city and privately-owned facilities. The vaccination requirements for private and public indoor events are in place for events with 1,000 or more attendees. The ordinance will be similar to San Francisco’s ordinance that became effective in August 2021, which required businesses in high-contact indoor sectors to verify vaccination status. This does not include shopping establishments, department stores, or grocery stores. Business owners in Oakland may download and print a notice poster of the ordinance at: https:// www.oaklandca.gov/resources/ city-vaccination-mandate-ordinance. articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont launched its Defending Democracy Speaker Series on January 11 with a presentation on Voting Rights by Carol Moon Goldberg, president of the League of Women Voters of California. Upcoming events in this series include Ranked Choice Voting with Rob Richie on February 10, Election Law and the Supreme Court with Erwin Chemerinsky on March 1, International Perspective on U.S. Democracy with Dr. Fiona Hill on March 30, and Election Subversion and Disinformation with Rick Hasen on April 5. The series is co-sponsored by Leagues across the country in Collier County, Florida; Gunnison Valley, Colorado; Oakland, California; The Pikes Peak Region, Colorado; Portland, Oregon; Pueblo, Colorado; Santa Barbara, California; and Solano County, California. Goldberg opened her presentation with a brief history of voting rights in California and in the U.S. that highlighted the country’s expansion of the right to vote beyond white, male property owners. This expansion was marked by the ratification of the 13th, 14th, 15th and 19th Amendments to the Constitution, the 1965 Voting Rights Act, and the Help America Vote Act that provided funding to help The League’s work in California has been instrumental in laws being passed that protect voting rights, including some of those mentioned above and Prop. 7, which restores voting rights to people who are on parole. Many of them are taxpaying, contributing members of society who deserve a voice in their government. Goldberg closed her presentation with a focus on the current federal voting rights legislation and suggestions for how the public can support voting rights. The Freedom to Vote Act protects and expands the right to vote, decreases the influence of money in politics and curbs partisan gerrymandering. The John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act (JLVRAA) effectively restores section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 that was gutted by the Supreme Court in Shelby County v. Holder in 2013. The JLVRAA would require federal preclearance for certain changes to state voting laws and would result in federal voting rights protections to counter racial discrimination. The League is part of a coalition of 230 organizations supporting these federal bills. Residents can support voting rights by visiting the Declaration for American Democracy (https://dfadcoalition. org/), a site representing this coalition, clicking on “events” and taking action. articles.text: Starting on January 24, Piedmont High School will try starting classes at 8:30 a.m. instead of 8 a.m. The pilot schedule will last for four weeks, until February 18. It will also include later dismissal times and the addition of a Homeroom period at PHS. The change comes in preparation for new California Senate Bill 328, which will require public high schools in California to start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. as of fall 2022. The bill also requires middle schools to not start until 8:00 a.m. Piedmont Middle School currently starts classes at 8:20 a.m. PMS is participating in a similar pilot schedule affecting dismissal times and adding a homeroom period. The new bell schedule was explained during a January 14 PHS Parent Club meeting. In the pilot schedule, school will begin at 8:30 a.m. Monday through Friday. On Mondays the last class period will end at 3:25 p.m.; Tuesdays and Thursday will go until 3:35 p.m. On Wednesdays and Fridays class will let out at 2:50 p.m. Piedmont High will remain on a block schedule with 90-minute classes Tuesday through Friday. On Mondays, students will continue to meet with all seven periods in 45-minute blocks. Lunch will continue to be 40 minutes but will start at 11:30 instead of 1:00 p.m.. Studies have shown that at the onset of puberty, the adolescent body does not produce melatonin or begin to feel sleepy until about 10:45 p.m., making an 8:00 a.m. start to school difficult while getting the 8-10 hours of required sleep for teens. On Wednesdays and Fridays the last period of the day will be a 45-minute Homeroom, required for all students. We d ne sd ay Home ro om will have “program” activities, including the mental health BESS survey, student presentations on consent, academic work, and a survey of the bell schedule. On Fridays students will have time to get extra help, make up tests, and complete science labs during Homeroom. Teachers may select students to attend their tutorial and students may request to attend a teacher’s specific tutorial. Homeroom is not a requirePiedmont High will temporarily begin school at 8:30 a.m., well in advance of the state’s requirement set for next fall. ment of the state legislation. “We are trying some things in the pilot [schedule], and we know that we are going to be able to do things a little differently if we commit to [homeroom] year long. Part of this is to keep things manageable [for teacher schedules],” said Littlefield. One logistical complication results from students, especially upper classmen, that have a free Period 7, but have to return to school at 2:05 p.m. on Wednesdays and Fridays instead of being dismissed at the start of lunch period. For these students, the high school is making the library available during 7th period and will also offer PCR COVID testing at that time. A later release time will also affect after-school extracurricular activities. Student athletes will be allowed to leave early to go to games. “There are a lot of different types of scenarios that can happen, and we will discuss them through this process,” said Littlefield. “We are going to try this and then we are going to learn from it and figure out what were the best practices of this and what do we really need to consider and reconsider.” California is the first state in the nation to move back the start time for high school students.
articles.title: Piedmont High to try later start times

articles.text: On January 18 Piedmont School District announced that masks would again have to be worn outdoors on all school campuses. The mandate goes into effect today, Wednesday, January 19 and applies to all students, staff and anyone on campus. “Until indications are that the surge has peaked and the number of COVID cases within the District are in decline, the outdoor masking requirement for secondary students and staff will be temporarily reinstated effective Wednesday, January 19th,” declared superintendent Randy Booker in an email to parents of students in the district. The requirement also applies to family members while on campus during picking up or dropping of their students, or while visiting during the day. The decision will be revisited at the District’s Health & Safety Steering Committee meeting on January 26th. “I am aware this may not be a popular decision with everyone,” Booker acknowledged. “Our goal remains to protect in-person instruction and keep our students and staff on campus. It was the consensus of the Committee that under current conditions, this step back was the best way to continue accomplishing that goal,” he added. On November 1, 2021 the on-campus outdoor mask mandate was lifted by the school district for vaccinated 12-18 years olds. An outdoor mask mandate for elementary students during P.E., recess and anytime on campus remained in place at the time and has never been lifted since the return to school in 2020. No outdoor mask requirement at schools has been required by the California Department of Public Health. The initial decision to require masks outdoors, then their removal for the vaccinated, and now reinstated were recommendations by Booker With advice and consent by the District’s Health and Safety Steering Committee. Wearing masks outdoors has not been an action item by the school board. In the first semester, from August 20 through December 17, 2021, there were 25 student COVID cases reported and 13 among staff. From December 18 to January 10 there were 228 COVID cases reported by staff and students. From January 11-14 there were 33 new COVID cases reported by staff and students. As of Tuesday, January 18, 97% of all students in the school district were fully vaccinated.
articles.title: Outdoor mask mandate reinstated by school district

articles.text: In October 2021 Piedmont City Council approved the allocation of $100,000 in American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds to be used by the school district to hire a temporary, full-time nurse to assist with response to COVID. Since then, the district received no applications for the position, so School Superintendent Randy Booker has now requested to use the funds to hire health clerks. Funds from the American Rescue Plan Act are restricted and generally must be used to support public health response to the COVID-19 emergency. In October the City carved out ARPA funds that were intended to support the school district with a full-time nurse. City Administrator Sara Lillevand noted at the time that it was the school’s most important need. “At that time, the urgent need and request was for a full-time nurse to support [reopening] efforts. Unfortunately, they have not had luck fulfilling that position,” Lillevand told City Council members at a meeting yesterday, January 18. “With this big post-holiday surge [of Omicron], the district is doing a tremendous amount of testing to keep schools open. The [recent] request was to shift that funding for a similar need but different position – for multiple parttime health clerks. This request is very much in line with the intent of [the original] allocation.” School district health clerks provide support to school site operations with specific responsibilities under the direction of nurses or school principals, making the positions eligible for ARPA fund use. The revision was approved unanimously by four council members. “We want to do all we can to support the schools by keeping them open,” Mayor Teddy Gray King said.
articles.title: City Council approves using ARPA funds for PUSD to hire health clerks instead

articles.text: Brooke Hendershott of Piedmont was named to the Dean’s List for the Fall semester at College of the Holy Cross. A junior, Hendershott is majoring in Chemistry. He was among 1,375 students named to the Dean’s List for outstanding academic achievement. To qualify, students must pass four or more letter-graded courses with no failing grades during the semester and earn a GPA of 3.5 or higher. Located in Worcester, Massachusetts, Holy Cross is among the nation’s leading liberal arts institutions. A highly selective, four-year, exclusively undergraduate college of 3,100 students, Holy Cross is renowned for offering a rigorous, personalized education in the Jesuit, Catholic tradition. Since its founding in 1843, Holy Cross has made a positive impact in society by graduating students who distinguish themselves as thoughtful leaders in business, professional and civic life.
articles.title: Hendershott named to Holy Cross Dean’s List

articles.text: Matthias Haggerty, a 2018 graduate of Piedmont High School, was named to the Dean’s List for the Fall 2021 semester at Wheaton College. To earn Dean’s List honors students must carry 12 or more credit hours and achieve a 3.5 grade point average or higher on a 4.0 scale. Wheaton College is a coeducational Christian liberal arts college located in Wheaton, Illinois, a suburb of Chicago, and noted for its rigorous academics, integration of faith and learning. It is consistently ranking among the top liberal arts colleges in the country.
articles.title: Haggerty named to Dean’s List at Wheaton

articles.text: Seven Piedmont parents were selected in an online vote last week to be members of a new committee, the Superintendent Community Advisory Committee. articles.text: “There’s a problem with how we teach math in the United States,” explained Carlos Trujillo, Chair of Bishop O’Dowd’s Math Department. “The standard course sequence dates back to the Industrial Revolution. It’s not setting students up to master the skills they need to succeed in today’s world.” Last year, in accordance with leading-edge research from the Stanford Graduate School of Education, The University of Chicago, and a growing cadre of mathematicians, data scientists, teachers, and education policy leaders, O’Dowd’s Math Department developed a two-year geometry, algebra, and trigonometry sequence – an innovative course remodel designed to prepare students to be problem solvers in today’s tech and data economy. As it stands now, most U.S. math students learn a sequence of Algebra 1 (one year), Geometry (one year), Algebra 2 (one year). “This math track is like learning to play piano one year, switching to cello for another year, then going back to piano as though you never stopped practicing,” Trujillo said. The sequence doesn’t support a true command of fundamental math concepts. “It’s how students get frustrated with math,” Trujillo noted. Second, this sequence usually doesn’t create enough time for students to take multiple upper division courses, like Data Science and Multivariable Calculus. “These are the courses that have Carlos Trujillo, O’Dowd High School Math Chair, teaches Advanced Placement Calculus. a big payoff for students,” Trujillo said. “They start solving real world problems, thinking creatively, and strengthening their college applications.” O’Dowd’s two-year math sequence is focused on students mastering the concepts they need to be successful. “We don’t want students who just know how to do the mechanics.” Trujillo stated. “We want them to gain the technical vocabulary, notational fluency, the analytical skills, and the conceptual thinking that matter for problem solving. It’s like an exponential function. Our students’ mastery will compound and accelerate over four years and put them at an advantage when it comes to pursuing STEM careers.” The shift also opens the pathways for all students to take AP Calculus by their junior or senior year. something less than 10 percent of students were previously able to achieve. “We’re giving students a rock-solid foundation to excel in Pre Calculus, Finite Math, Data Science or even AP Calculus as juniors,” Trujillo emphasized. There are a range of AP courses they can take, even Multivariable Calculus. “O’Dowd is one of only a few high schools in the nation that teaches this,” Trujillo said. Multivariable Calculus lays the mathematical foundation for machine learning and theoretical computer science. “We need to be preparing students to be drivers and innovators of the kinds of systems that Google Maps and Spotify are built on,” Trujillo insists. “They’re going to keep changing the world.” J.D. Childs is President of Bishop O’Dowd High School.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. articles.text: Staff Photos Natalia Martinez led Piedmont with 25 points, 14 points in the second quarter, and nine rebounds in the Highlanders’ 60-43 win over Southern California power Lynwood. Competing in the prestigious 9th annual MLK Showcase, a collection of 24 top ranked teams hosted by St. Mary’s in Stockton, Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team came up big with a convincing 60-43 win against Los Angeles power Lynwood on Saturday, January 15. “Overall, it was a great game. Everybody contributed with effort and toughness, and that’s what you want to see,” said Piedmont coach Bryan Gardere. “We’re playing well and will try to keep that competitive greatness at a high level. We played really tough defense and shut them down going into halftime.” Natalie Martinez had a 14-point outburst in the second quarter, and led her team with 25 points and nine rebounds. Trinity Zamora had a double-double with 21 points and 14 rebounds. PHS jumped out to a commanding 18-11 lead in the first quarter, then turned its vaunted defense loose to hold Lynwood to only three points before halftime. The Highlanders extended the lead to 45-27 in the third and finished out strong at 60-43. In the first quarter, Zamora scored six points on 3-pointers, while forward Kat Melian, a sophomore and first-year varsity starter, had four points and several key rebounds. “Kat Melian is having a good year. She is really tough and always shows high-effort,” said Gardere. Zamora added six more points in the second quarter, and Maddie Hill added five points with a 3-pointer and a pair of free throws. “Maddie is a great leader for us. She had some fantastic on-ball defense,” said Gardere. After halftime it was the Natalie Martinez show. The Trinity Zamora had a double-double with 21 points and 14 rebounds. Gardere had high praise for Maddie Hill’s on-ball defense in the MLK Showcase.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team’s defense led the way to a gritty 2-1 victory over Castro Valley on the road on Friday, January 14, on goals by Rachel Barton and Nina Goldberg. The Trojans controlled ball possession for most of the game, and had opportunities to score on 12 corner kicks, but the PHS defense held strong. “I would say we were the stronger team in the first half, while in the second we were definitely under pressure. They had a ton of [chances], but they didn’t create much to threaten the goal,” said Piedmont coach Dan Chubbock. “They hit us a lot on the counter attack, but [our] girls looked like they were having fun out there.” Rachel Barton scored in the seventh minute to put Piedmont in front, 1-0. Castro Valley tied the match shortly after halftime in the 37th minute. The Trojans’ joy was short-lived when PHS captain Nina Goldberg scored two minutes later on a nifty header assisted by Emily Fitzgerald. Barton has been a standout winger in Piedmont’s attack throughout the season, often maintaining possession against tight defense to create scoring chances. “We have a really solid front line,” said Barton. “Emily is so good at getting those passes down to me. A lot of it is the communication on getting the ball down the field and me booking to try and get it. This year, I’ve worked really hard on crossing and getting my hips around the ball to really angle the ball in front of the goalie.” Making an enormous difference in Thursday’s match was Audrey Lam, Piedmont’s maestro in the midfield. She was instrumental in controlling the ball, creating scoring chances with slick footwork, and tracking back to help out on defense. “Audrey’s work rate getting back and forth is amazing. She had a defensive header that reminded me of LeBron James in the 2016 NBA Finals. She wanted to win this game, it was fun to watch her,” said coach Chubbock. Match Recap The action got off to a fast start with Piedmont’s first shot on goal coming in the third minute. The goal by Barton came after Goldberg sent a long ball to Fitzgerald, who sent a through ball down the right side to Barton. Staff Photos Emily Fitzgerald (left) and Tucker Donahue (right) celebrate with Rachel Barton (15) after Barton’s goal against Castro Valley. Emily Fitzgerald assisted on both Piedmont goals against Castro Valley. Her right-footed shot curled over the Trojans’ keeper to the far post for the goal and a 1-0 lead 7 minutes into the game. CV had a couple of near chances in the following minutes, including a shot going over the net in the ninth minute and another shot skirt wide in the 11th. Castro Valley’s goal came in the 37th minute after goalkeeper Morgan Hunt tried to crash on an approaching forward, who chipped the ball over Hunt into the net. But two minutes later, only one minute before halftime, Piedmont recaptured the lead on a corner kick into the penalty area. The ball skipped toward Fitzgerald, who instinctively volleyed a header back toward Goldberg, who slotted in the goal to make it 2-1. In the second half, Castro Valley controlled the action and opened the first 18 minutes of the final 40 with one shot on target and four corners. Hunt, meanwhile, had a critical diving save in the 71st minute to maintain Piedmont’s tenuous lead. CV had another shot on goal go wide in the 74th and another long shot easily saved in the 76th. Lam had the last scoring chance for Piedmont in the 76th minute with footwork that left Trojans’ grasping at air trying to defend her, but her shot was saved by the Trojan goalie. Castro Valley ‘s frustration led to a red card in stoppage time to end the game. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-2-1 overall) hosts division rival Berkeley tonight at Witter Field, Wednesday, January 19, at 6:30 p.m. Audrey Lam was Piedmont’s maestro in the midfield against Castro Valley, showing flashy footwork to create several scoring chances.
articles.title: Highlanders defeat Castro Valley 2-1 on the road

But two minutes later, only one minute before halftime, Piedmont recaptured the lead on a corner kick into the penalty area. The ball skipped toward Fitzgerald, who instinctively volleyed a header back toward Goldberg, who slotted in the goal to make it 2-1. In the second half, Castro Valley controlled the action and opened the first 18 minutes of the final 40 with one shot on target and four corners. Hunt, meanwhile, had a critical diving save in the 71st minute to maintain Piedmont’s tenuous lead. CV had another shot on goal go wide in the 74th and another long shot easily saved in the 76th. Lam had the last scoring chance for Piedmont in the 76th minute with footwork that left Trojans’ grasping at air trying to defend her, but her shot was saved by the Trojan goalie. Castro Valley ‘s frustration led to a red card in stoppage time to end the game. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-2-1 overall) hosts division rival Berkeley tonight at Witter Field, Wednesday, January 19, at 6:30 p.m. Audrey Lam was Piedmont’s maestro in the midfield against Castro Valley, showing flashy footwork to create several scoring chances.

articles.text: The Australian Open is currently underway, meaning it will be Mackie McDonald season in Piedmont from now through January 30. McDonald won a victory in four sets on Sunday, January 16 over Nikola Milojevic of Serbia, 5-7, 6-4, 6-3, 6-2. Yesterday he faced No. 18 seeded Aslan Karatsev of Russia. Karatsev is the world’s No. 15 ranked player, and McDonald is No. 55. A third round match is scheduled for Friday, January 21. If he defeated Karatsev, he would play the winner of No. 10 seeded Hubert Hurkacz of Poland vs. France’s Adrian Mannarino. The Round of 16 is on Saturday, January 22. When McDonald reached the Round of 16 last year, it marked the furthest he advanced in Grand Slam tournaments since the 2018 Wimbledon. In the match with Milojevic, the world’s No. 139 ranked player, McDonald was successful at the service line with seven aces. He won 79 percent of his first serves, and won 50 of 63 games in which he got his first serve in play. The Serbian won the first set after McDonald led 2-1 including a dominant 40-love win the third game. Milojevic powered ahead 3-2 but McDonald reclaimed the lead 4-3 and eventually held setpoint at 5-4. The Serbian then claimed three straight games to win the first set 7-5. In the second set, Milojevic held a 4-3 lead until Mackie won three straight games to win the set 6-4. McDonald converted three of six break point opportunities. Then in the third at 2-2, McDonald won 40-0 to go ahead Mackie McDonald won his first round match over Nikola Milojevic in the Australian Open on January 16. He faced Aslan Karatsev on Tuesday night. 3-2 and then claimed the next game to jump ahead before winning 6-3. McDonald dominated the final fourth set, 6-2, including two wins as the returner; one in the third game to go ahead 2-1 and another in the fifth 4-1, which was a 40-15 victory. articles.text: Come see Golden Gate Park’s Peacock Meadow as it is transformed into an enchanted forest of otherworldly shapes and ever-changing light. “Entwined,” a public art installation by San Francisco artist Charles Gadeken, creates a whimsical wonderland where visitors can explore paths and sit under a grove of three entwined sculptural trees. A public art installation, “Entwined” is currently located adjacent to the Conservatory of Flowers in Golden Gate Park. “Entwined” by Charles Gadeken Gadeken is an industrial artist who for over 25 years has created monumental interactive public artworks that reimagine the world “post-nature.” His work has been commissioned by Black Rock Arts Foundation, City of San Francisco, Insomniac Events, Coachella, Absolut Vodka, City of Palo Alto, City of Calabasas, City of Los Altos, and Stanford University. Many of his works have been exhibited internationally. “Entwined” is available to view from dusk until 8:30 p.m. Those who visit are asked to wear a mask at all times and practice social distancing. Viewing is free and tickets are not required.
articles.title: Visit “Entwined” in Golden Gate Park now through February 1

articles.text: Celebrate Lunar New Year at Oakland Museum with programs highlighting the Year of the Tiger. Oakland Museum of California is celebrating the Year of the Tiger with a series of Lunar New Year programs beginning January 25. A mix of online and in-person activities will be offered as part of the museum’s 21st Annual Lunar New Year Celebration. This year’s events celebrate the range of Asian cultures and traditions that make up the Oakland community, and display the strength, bravery, and resilience of the Tiger. The festivities will begin on Tuesday, January 25, with a virtual cooking demonstration by OMCA staff member Linda Jia. Jia will demonstrate how to make dumplings, a traditional Lunar New Year dish. You can watch the demonstration on the museum’s YouTube channel by visiting https://www. youtube.com/watch?v=BGhBNZfrS1s. February 1 Families will enjoy a virtual, hands-on shadow puppet art activity on Tuesday, February 1 led by museum staff member Leslie Cheng. She will show audiences how to make shadow puppets, an ancient form of storytelling. Shadow puppet kits can be downloaded from the museum’s website. February 5 On February 5, audiences are invited to visit the museum and participate in story time with famed San Francisco author Oliver Chin. Chin recently launched a new graphic novel series entitled Awesome Asian Americans. A limited capacity, family-friendly in-person celebration will be held at the museum on Saturday, February 5 from 12 p.m. to 3 p.m. Proof of vaccination will be required to attend. For a full schedule of events, visit https://museumca.org/lunarnew-year-celebration-year-tiger.
articles.title: Oakland Museum announces plans to celebrate Lunar New Year

articles.text: FOG Design and Art Fair will be held at Fort Mason Festival Pavilion in San Francisco from January 20 through 23. The fair celebrates current and significant contributors to the worlds of design and visual arts. FOG assembles 45 leading international galleries, showcasing prominent 20th century and contemporary design dealers. 2022 exhibitors include London’s Gallery FUMI, White Cube, Sarah Myerscough Gallery, and David Gill Gallery; New York’s Gladstone Gallery, KARMA, Kasmin Gallery and R & Company; San Francisco’s Friends Indeed Gallery, Crown Point Press, Haines Gallery; and pt. 2 Gallery in Oakland, among others. The event’s Preview Gala supports San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SFMOMA) exhibitions and education programs. Fair hours are Thursday through Saturday, January 20-22 from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. The fair will also be open on Sunday, January 23 from form 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Those attending the FOG Design and Art Preview Gala Photo courtesy of San Francisco Museum of Modern Art A display at the 2016 FOG Fair. will have a preview of the Fair at Fort Mason Center on Wednesday, January 19. Proof of vaccination is required for entry, and mask are required inside the Festival Pavilion when not eating or drinking. Timed ticketing will be observed, and pavilion capacity is reduced in order to observe safe distancing. For a full list of fair programming and exhibitor details, visit fogfair.com. For more information, contact fog@fogfair.com or (415) 745-3315.
articles.title: FOG Design and Art Fair begins at Fort Mason Center tomorrow

articles.text: For mer Music Director Michael Tilson Thomas (MTT) will conduct the San Francisco Symphony in two weeks of concerts live at Davies Symphony Hall. The first concerts, held January 20 through 22, will include Sergei Prokofiev’s Symphony No. 5 and Dmitri Shostakovich’s Cello Concerto No. 2 performed by cellist Gautier Capucon. The second series, January 27 through 29, will include Gustav Mahler’s Symphony No. 1 – a staple in Tilson Thomas’ repertoire – and pianist Yuja Wang performing Franz Liszt’s Piano Concerto No. 1. MTT became Music Director of the San Francisco Symphony in 1995, and for 25 years led the symphony in championing contemporary and American composers alongside classical masters. Though retired, he continues to lead the orchestra in four weeks of concerts annually. Tickets for concerts at Davies Symphony Hall may be purchased at www.sfsymphony. org, or by calling the box office at (415) 864-6000. Davies Symphony Hall is located at 201 Van Ness Avenue in San Francisco. Former San Francisco Symphony Music Director Michael Tilson Thomas
articles.title: MTT conducts series of concerts with SF Symphony Jan. 20-29
