articles.text: Sa n Fr a nci s c o Ba l le t announced the appointment of Tamara Rojo as Artistic Director on January 11. She is the first woman to lead the ballet company and will succeed Helgi Tomasson, who led the company for nearly 40 years, and retires in June this year. Rojo comes to the ballet company from London’s prestigious English National Ballet, where she served as artistic director and lead principal for nearly a decade. “SF Ballet is thrilled that Tamara Rojo will be joining us in San Francisco as artistic director later this year,” said Sunnie Evers and Fran Streets, co-chairs of the search committee. ”She’s had an outstanding international career as a dancer and has been a transformative artistic director over the last near-decade. Classical ballet is evolving from a very ‘traditional’ past, and as a creative visionary, Tamara is the dynamic leader who will change and expand upon how patrons of dance will be able to see and engage with it. She is the voice of the future, and we are delighted she will be here at SF Ballet.” “I’ve long admired San Francisco Ballet as one of the most creative dance companies in America, offering so many different artistic voices the opportunity to create works for some Tamara Rojo wlll lead San Francisco Ballet as its new Artistic Director as of June this year. of the best dancers in the world,” said Rojo. “I’m excited to join SF Ballet to add to the innovative spirit of the company as we reassess what the future of ballet can and should look like, opening the best of what our art form can offer to the widest possible audience. And while internationally recognized both for its performances and training, SF Ballet has a deep, year-round commitment to San Francisco audiences and the community – a dynamic community that my family and I very much look forward to joining and exploring.” Rojo will move to San Francisco with her husband Isaac Hernandez, who was recently appointed as a principal dancer with San Francisco Ballet.
articles.title: SF Ballet names Tamara Rojo as new Artistic Director

articles.text: Marin Theatre Company will present its first production of the year, Pass Over, beginning January 27, with performances through February 20. Pass Over is Antoinette Chinoye Nwandu’s new play, directed by Kevin R. Free. The cast includes Edward Ewell as Moses, LeRoy S. Graham as Kitch, and Adam Roy as Mister. Moses and Kitch pass the time and dream of their version of a promised land when a stranger wanders into their space and disrupts their plans. The play crafts everyday profanities into poetic and humorous riffs. Marin Theatre Company is located at 397 Miller Avenue in Mill Valley; phone (415) 388-5200. Proof of vaccination and masking is required. To obtain tickets, visit https://www.marintheatre.org/productions/pass-over-1#overview Promotional poster for Mari Theatre company’s production of Pass Over.
articles.title: Marin Theatre Company presents Pass Over beginning January 27

articles.text: Emily Blunt stars in The Girl on the Train. Earlier this year I picked up Paula Hawkins’ novel, The Girl on the Train. Written in 2015, it reached the bestseller list and was often compared to Gillian Flynn’s novel Gone Girl, also a mystery-thriller that included multiple points of view. I confess that I read most of Hawkins’ book and then stopped, something I rarely do. Usually, I’ll power through a book despite whatever flaws tempt me to put it down. Caveat phrase: “So little time, so many books.” What caused me to stop reading The Girl on the Train was its unreliable narrator, Ruth Watson. She continually made awful choices, many while in a drunken stupor. I simply came to a point where I didn’t want to spend any more time with her. I share all this to say that I was, therefore, hesitant to see the film. But I know Emily Blunt, who portrays Rachel, to be a gifted actor and was curious how she would interpret the character. decided that Blunt’s portrayal, while maddening at times, was spot on. Though the story is about three women and their points of view, it is Blunt who is the hub of the wagon wheel, so to speak. I am reluctant to share too much of the plot in this review because Girl is a mystery-thriller of a sort, one in which pieces of a puzzle are scattered in front of the audience, using multiple flashbacks, with real-time segments showing Rachel taking a commuter train into Manhattan from Westchester and then returning. While she rides, she sips constantly from a water bottle filled with vodka and all that she sees is seen through a prism distorted by alcohol. What is real and what is fantasy is, at least to her, unknowable. She often spots a couple standing on their second story porch in an embrace, and begins looking for them, willing herself not to look while nurturing the idea that they share a perfect love. With each brief glimpse, as the train passes by, she observes them closely understanding that their companionship wounds her and yet enthralls her. Compounding her pain and fascination is the fact that the house of this anonymous couple is just three doors away from a home that she once shared with her now ex-husband, Tom (Justin Theroux), who lives there with his new wife, Anna (Rebecca Ferguson) and their new baby. He is now living the life she so desperately wanted to share with him. Rachel is a fantasist, damaged and chronically self- destructive. One late afternoon she spots from the train the woman (Haley Bennett) standing on the familiar porch, but she is in the arms of a different man. Rachel reacts with rage, feeling she has personally been betrayed. And then the woman, Megan, goes missing. And so the narrative continues as Rachel staggers into the life of Megan’s husband, Scott (Luke Evans). She tries to reconstruct her connection to Megan, knowing they were strangers yet is certain she knows something about why she has gone missing. But the shroud of alcohol makes any attempt at full recall elusive. The pieces of the puzzle are scattered, and it is up to the audience to fit them together with little help from Rachel who binges into deeper dysfunction. What is also revealed is that Megan and Anna are not who they appear to be either. Especially Megan. This is a film with many twists. I was curious to see how Hawkins would bring all the disparate parts together, and I wasn’t disappointed. As an aside, the cast is remarkable. Emily Blunt’s performance is worthy of an award for best actress. The Girl on the Train. Directed by Tate Taylor. Starring Emily Blunt, Haley Bennett, Justin Theroux. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated R.

Politics and music have always been strange bedfellows, and they have been since the beginning of time. Here are some of the more interesting relationships: The earliest mention of a musical ruler is Biblical King David. But even more sensational is Roman Emperor Nero. You know… The guy who fiddled while Rome burned. There is a lot more to the story than you have been told. Did Nero get a bad rap by historians? All that you hear is that Nero fiddled while Rome burned. One political commentator of the time claimed that Nero was concerned with city redevelopment. Does that sound familiar? Sarcasm aside, Nero can take credit for being the first musical non-biblical political figure. Many followed in Nero‘s footsteps. Nero’s most notorious disciple was Italian dictator Benito Mussolini. He was a real violinist. Being Italian, he loved music and promoted the careers of numerous famous musicians. But anyone who opposed him… look out. Conductor Arturo Toscanini was famously anti-fascist. So Mussolini‘s black-shirt thugs beat him savagely. Toscanini was a deep thinking musician, and he just didn’t like the sound of the fascist anthem. Interestingly, Mussolini‘s violin surfaced not long ago. It was an Amati. The story goes on. Mussolini‘s son turned out to be a famous jazz pianist, who was respected on his own. Former U.S. President Harry Truman practiced the piano every day, and was a supporter of the arts.

articles.text: Disney began its remarkable history of animated stories with a singular mouse, Mickey. So, it’s no surprise that once again the animators have returned to The Great Mouse Detective, based on the children’s book series, Basil of Baker Street, by Eve Titus and Paul Galone. The writers embraced the still budding technology of CGI, realizing that the contemporary audience of kids wanted something a bit more zany. Anthropomorphism alone doesn’t quite cut it. The result is Detective, with a compelling cast of mice and rats, all living in Victorian England in 1897. The tale begins by introducing Olivia Flaversham (Susanne Pollatscheck) and her father Hiram (Alan Young), a master toymaker. Unexpectedly, Hiram, while working in his shop, is kidnapped by a strange bat called Fidget (Candy Candido). He’s a malevolent creature with a broken wing and a peg leg, and bursts in and snatches Olivia’s father. She is at first frantic and at loss as what to do; but then sets out to find the famed mouse detective, Basil of Baker Street (Barrie Ingham), who actually lives in the foundation of the home of Sherlock Homes. When Basil learns that the rogue kidnapper was Fidget, the henchman of his nemesis, Professor Ratigan (Vincent Price), a villain he has pursued for years, he immediately takes the case and sets out to solve the mystery of the missing Hiram. And so the hunt begins, a story filled with schemes by Ratigan, whose ultimate dream is to become the supreme ruler of all of England’s Mousedom. The search even includes Sherlock Holmes’ own Basset Hound, Toby (Frank Welker). The plot is exciting, and involves Olivia being kidnapped, a massive dirigible owned by Ratigan who intends to use it to make last minute escapes. He even manages to crash into the Big Ben tower clock, where, as it turns out, Olivia is being held captive. Kids will enjoy The Great Mouse Detective from the get go. There is not only a mystery to be solved, but offers nonstop action, led by Basil, magnifying glass in hand (naturally), who is in hot pursuit of the villainous Ratigan. At his side, of course, is his trusty assistant Dawson (Van Bettin). The Great Mouse Detective. Disney Animation. Directed by John Musker. 1 hr., 20 min. Rated G. articles.text: Film review by Chris Honoré Benji (2018) is a remake of the popular 1974 family-friendly film that focuses on the love of a stray dog by two latchkey kids, Carter and Frankie Hughes (Gabriel Bateman and Darby Camp) who recently lost their father, and live with their single mom, Whitney Hughes (Kiele Sanchez). The story opens when a mother canine and her small litter are taken to the animal shelter by a malevolent dogcatcher. Out of the shadows appears the face of a pint-sized pooch, watching as the family is carted off. He is a mixed-breed dog who lives on the street, searching for food wherever he can find it. In his travels, he meets up with Carter and Frankie. They try and feed him some strawberries, but he is cautious and timid; however, he quickly realizes that the kids will not hurt him and follows them home. Carter spots the little guy outside, and they decide to bring him inside, though uncertain of their mom’s reaction, and hide him under a pile of stuffed animals. Frankie wants to name him after Benjamin Franklin, which naturally gets shortened to Benji. When Whitney discovers Benji, she insists that the kids take the stray back where they found him. With regret they obey, and leaving Benji to fend for himself they stop off at Mr. Sam’s Pawn Shop (Gralen Bryant Banks). Without their knowing, Benji follows them. To their surprise, they walk into the middle of a robbery carried out by two thugs (Will Rothhaar and Angus Sampson). When one of their masks slips off, they realize that Carter and Frankie can identify them and so they kidnap the kids, forcing them into a van. Benji, who has been outside waiting, sees this taking place and chases after the van, all the way to the robbers’ hideout, a large, decaying plantation house. Watching the kids being taken into the house, and seeing that the men own a mean-looking Rottweiler, Benji hurries back to Grant and Frankie’s home where he tries to convince Whitney and a friendly cop, Lyle (Jerod Haynes), to follow him back to the hideout. Of course, the children in the audience are rooting for Benji, and hoping that the adults will figure out what Benji is trying to say. But Benji never utters a word, and the filmmakers never use voiceover or CGI lip movement. All that Benji urgently wants to say must be conveyed by his facial expressions. This is known as the Kuleshov method: the audience attributes emotions and communication to what is essentially a blank face, which, in this case, belongs to Benji. There are harrowing moments, chases, and the challenge to outwit the bad guys in order to rescue the kids. The children in the audience will be riveted to their seats, and definitely will fall in love with Benji. Benji. Written and directed by Brandon Camp. Streaming on Netflix. Starring Gabriel Bateman, Darby Camp, Kiele Sanchez. 1 hr., 6 min. Rated G.
articles.title: Benji a movie that kids love

The troop’s next adventure takes place January 22-23 at Pinnacles National Park near Hollister, where the Scouts expect to explore caves and hike to the summit to view the 85 resident California Condors soaring overhead on 9-foot wingspans. Any Piedmont youth, boys and girls age 11 to 17, interested in spending time outdoors, going on hikes, and improving leadership and outdoor skills is invited to become a member of Troop 15. articles.text: What is fun? One definition is enjoyment, amusement, or lighthearted pleasure. Piedmont Scouts in Troop 11 got to experience many exciting and engaging things on a recent trip to Dillon Beach on the Sonoma coast that topped the definition of fun. As a new Scout I was blown away by the experience and activities presented for us. I especially enjoyed the sand dunes, where we spent several hours exploring. One memorable moment was launching model rockets. They blasted off into the sky so fast just like the concept of time. In addition, troop members brought bobsleds and we all took turns sliding down the huge dunes. We also buried some members in the thick sand, and some of us even lost our shoes in the endless dunes. When looking into the distance, it was like there was no end. I had a wonderful time playing hide-and-go-seek with my friends as we ran across the deep dunes, smelling sand. It was truly magical. In Scouting, we learn to take responsibility for ourselves, and learn the power of leadership. We had a great opportunity demonstrating our leadership skills in the Troop cooking competition where each Patrol was tasked to make a main dish on a budget. The dish had to include a vegetable and carb balance. Some of the dishes included spaghetti and meatballs, tacos, pizza, and steak. All of the dishes were amazing, but the Mildewed Mangoes Patrol took first place and won the Golden Spatula. The Gremlins Patrol lost by only 1/10 of a point and took second. As part of the Gremlins Patrol, I enjoyed working with my peers to create a delicious dish. The Gremlins made spaghetti and meatballs along with an improvised salad. We all had a chance to go to the beach and see the big sea lions. They were vast like the moon, and their poise was mystical. The next morning each Patrol made their own breakfast. We even had a chance to try some fresh crab that had been caught that morning. The crab was shared amongst the whole troop, and it was delicious. Afterwards some Scouts participated in a beach cleanup, while others stayed back to learn about knife and ax tools and how to build a fire. The beach cleanup group was happy to report there was not as much trash as expected. Although it was quite windy, Troop 11 Scouts learn to fish for crab from the beach. the Scouts learned to build bonfires and got some good flames – at least for a little while. Troop 11 ended its fantastic journey with a closing circle and talking about the roses and thorns of the trip. Everyone described the thrill they had on the sand dunes. And although it was a cold trip, we had a very memorable time with our friends, whether wrestling over shoes, arm wrestling, or watching cheesy skits. What I learned is that black truffles are at their finest harvested in the winter, and that one region in particular, the Dordogne in the southwest, is the mecca of France’s black truffles. I followed a Paris event for a truffle market set up a once-a-year at Courbevoie just west of Neuilly-sur-Seine. articles.text: The Piedmont Avenue library sits on property with an interesting history. The property, a small corner of a large piece originally owned by the Hume Family, was donated by them in the late 1800s so a neighborhood school could be built on it. At that time, a creek ran across the undeveloped area and a number of trees grew in the open spaces. Among those trees was the Giant Sequoia that is located in front of Piedmont Avenue Elementary School. Now, more than 100 years later, it has seen its share of local history and experienced first-hand the change from rural to urban living and the effect of climate change. As well as its age, the street pavement and the concrete sidewalks have all affected the tree’s access to ground water and contributed to its decline. The tree will be removed next week and a coastal redwood, Aptos Blue, will be planted to replace it. This tree has made great contributions to the neighborhood, serving as a landmark and providing shade for those waiting for the school bus or playing in the front school yard. Some people have found its environs a good place for a picnic or playing with youngsters and dogs. Its shade will be missed, indeed. The school and the library will continue, however. Just down the block from the tree but on the same property, the Piedmont Avenue Library serves the community, too, but in a different way. Its services and collections provide something for most everyone. If the library doesn’t have an item in stock, they can probably get it for you. And let’s hope that when they reach the age of that tree they’re still here. The Humes couldn’t have known how the neighborhood would change or what a contribution they were making when they put that little school on that corner of their property. Ruby Long is a Piedmont Avenue neighbor whose work has appeared in local and national publications. articles.text: Sadly, identity theft happens throughout the year – but some identity thieves are particularly active during tax-filing season. How can you protect yourself? One of the most important moves you can make is to be suspicious of requests by people or entities claiming to be from the Internal Revenue Service. You may receive phone calls, texts and emails, but these types of communication are often just “phishing” scams with one goal in mind: to capture your personal information. These phishers can be quite clever, sending emails that appear to contain the IRS logo or making calls that may even seem to be coming from the IRS. Don’t open any links or attachments to the emails and don’t answer the calls – and don’t be alarmed if the caller leaves a vaguely threatening voicemail, either asking for personal information, such as your Social Security number, or informing you of some debts you supposedly owe to the IRS that must be taken care of “immediately.” In reality, the IRS will not initiate contact with you by phone, email, text message or social media to request personal or financial information, or to inquire about issues pertaining to your tax returns. Instead, the agency will first send you a letter. And if you’re unsure of the legitimacy of such a letter, contact the IRS directly at 800-829-1040. Of course, not all scam artists are fake IRS representatives – some will pass themselves off as tax preparers. Fortunately, most tax preparers are honest, but it’s not too hard to find the dishonest ones who might ask you to sign a blank return, promise you a big refund before looking at your records or try to charge a fee based on the percentage of your return. Legitimate tax preparers will make no grand promises and will explain their fees upfront. Before hiring someone to do your taxes, find out their qualifications. The IRS provides some valuable tips for choosing a reputable tax preparer, but you can also ask your friends and relatives for referrals. Another tax scam to watch out for is the fraudulent tax return – that is, someone filing a return in your name. To do so, a scammer would need your name, birthdate and Social Security number. If you’re already providing two of these pieces of information – your name and birthdate on social media, and you also include your birthplace – you could be making it easier for scam artists to somehow get the third. It’s a good idea to check your privacy settings and limit what you’re sharing publicly. You might also want to use a nickname and omit your last name, birthday and birthplace. Here’s one more defensive measure: File your taxes as soon as you can. Identity thieves often strike early in the tax season, so they can file their bogus returns before their victims. To learn more about tax scams, visit the IRS website (irs.gov) and search for the “Taxpayer Guide to Identity Theft.” This document describes some signs of identity theft and provides tips for what to do if you are victimized. It’s unfortunate that identity theft exists, but by taking the proper precautions, you can help insulate yourself from this threat, even when tax season is over. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. TJ Stevko is a financial advisor with Edward Jones in Piedmot at 370 Highland Avenue, tel. 547-4589.

articles.text: Bookmark, the non-profit bookstore in Old Oakland that helps support Oakland Public Library, will celebrate its 30th anniversary throughout the year in 2022. To honor 30 years of support, all books will be 30% off the marked prices every Saturday and Sunday. The Bookmark Bookstore is located at 721 Washington Street in Oakland. All proceeds from the sale of gently used, donated books will benefit the Oakland Public Library. The Bookmark features books of general interest, CDs, LPs, comics, jigsaw puzzles and a selection of collectible books. In addition, members of Friends of Oakland Public Library (FOPL) will receive 30% off the marked price every day the store is open, instead of the usual 20% discount for members. Membership may be purchased in the store or online for $25 per year, $15 for seniors and full-time students. The Bookmark Store is open from 11:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Wednesday through Sunday. The Friends of the Oakland Public Library is a nonprofit organization dedicated to supporting the Oakland Public Library. Through funds raised by operating a used bookstore and through its membership program of nearly 1,000 members, the Friends donated over $1 million to the Oakland Public Library over the past five years. To become a member, call 444- 0473 or click on FOPL.org.

articles.text: Wednesday Walkers stop for a group photo on January 12 at the site of Walter Blair’s house. Pictured are: Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Jim Kellogg, Ken Young, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Wenny Young, Christine Calliste, Priscilla Wanerus, Dena Belinkoff, Quincy Dong, Kat Lang, Aaron Katzel, Helen Dong, Pat Keller, Siow Fang Tan, Lilly Guardia-Labar, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Bob Gustafson, Nadine Guffanti, Stella Houston, Sarah Johnson, Jim Kuo, Melba Yee, Phil Witte, Alicia Rivera, and Dick Carter. The group welcomed Peter Persoff back for his first walk since the pandemic hiatus. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group enjoys learning about Piedmont’s history and also how it relates to the streets they walk. At the start of a New Year it seemed appropriate that the walk on January 12 would have a focus on the early period of the region’s history. So, it was decided that this walk would be about Walter Blair, for whom Blair Avenue is named. A strong showing of 28 walkers and one K-9 best friend were at the Exedra on this sunny, winter morning. Drawing on the research of Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi, the history of Blair was shared with the group. His parents were Vermont farmers of Scottish descent, and he was one of 12 children. He came to California in 1852 during the gold rush and at age 22 he became the first European settler in the Piedmont hills. He was a dairy farmer, capitalist, and founder of the original Blair Park. In 1852 Blair purchased 600 acres in the Piedmont hills for $750. It encompassed most of the land between today’s Moraga, Scenic, Magnolia and Grand Avenues. Blair’s original cabin was where the modern home at 111 Highland Avenue is now located. Blair called his street “Vernal Avenue” because of its lush ferns and shrubs. The back of the house was on today’s Waldo Avenue. The walkers headed off on Highland (not Vernal) Avenue, noting historic homes as they went. They continued to the end of Highland at Moraga Avenue. They looked across the street to the spot where an arched entrance to Blair Park once stood, and more of Blair’s history was told. Blair established Blair’s Dairy at the corner of today’s Blair and El Cerrito Avenues, and his cattle grazed in pastures that went down to what is now Grand Avenue. However, he found real estate and other commercial interests to be also profitable. He built the Piedmont Springs Hotel in 1871, which was at the top of today’s Piedmont Park, and partnered with investors to build a horsecar line from downtown Oakland to Piedmont Avenue. In 1878 Blair decided to build his own line, the Piedmont Railway, which ran from where the Piedmont Avenue line ended at the gates of the Mountain View Cemetery, and went through his grain fields to Vernal Avenue and the Piedmont Springs Hotel. To increase the number of riders, in 1884 Blair developed 40 acres of the land between the cemetery and Moraga Avenue as a picnic park, and named it Blair Park. It offered picnic tables, paths for wandering, a Japanese Tea House, a dancing pavilion, a Venetian canal ride, a bandstand, swings, bridges over waterfalls and a stream, a fountain, a lake, and even hot air balloon ascensions. Many of the picnickers and hotel guests enjoyed the views and climate in Piedmont and stayed to purchase property and build homes. They became Piedmont’s early residents. Blair also opened the Dracena Quarry, which is today’s Dracena Park, to sell crushed rock to pave the streets of Oakland, Piedmont and the nearby Mountain View Cemetery. Blair was only 57 when he died in 1888. He is buried in Mountain View Cemetery. After his death Blair Park was purchased by another train line, but it went into receivership in 1893, and its assets were sold in 1895. In 1901 the park was abandoned, and the land was still vacant in 1913, but in 1917 new homes began to be built on it. A builder, Guy Turner, constructed 11 bungalows on the cemetery side of Moraga Avenue and at least six more a few years later. The walkers made their way down Moraga looking at the homes that Turner built 100 years ago. Pictured are: Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Jim Kellogg, Ken Young, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Wenny Young, Christine Calliste, Priscilla Wanerus, Dena Belinkoff, Quincy Dong, Kat Lang, Aaron Katzel, Helen Dong, Pat Keller, Siow Fang Tan, Lilly Guardia-Labar, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Bob Gustafson, Nadine Guffanti, Stella Houston, Sarah Johnson, Jim Kuo, Melba Yee, Phil Witte, Alicia Rivera, and Dick Carter. The group welcomed Peter Persoff back for his first walk since the pandemic hiatus. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group enjoys learning about Piedmont’s history and also how it relates to the streets they walk. At the start of a New Year it seemed appropriate that the walk on January 12 would have a focus on the early period of the region’s history. So, it was decided that this walk would be about Walter Blair, for whom Blair Avenue is named. A strong showing of 28 walkers and one K-9 best friend were at the Exedra on this sunny, winter morning. Drawing on the research of Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi, the history of Blair was shared with the group. His parents were Vermont farmers of Scottish descent, and he was one of 12 children. He came to California in 1852 during the gold rush and at age 22 he became the first European settler in the Piedmont hills. He was a dairy farmer, capitalist, and founder of the original Blair Park. In 1852 Blair purchased 600 acres in the Piedmont hills for $750. It encompassed most of the land between today’s Moraga, Scenic, Magnolia and Grand Avenues. Blair’s original cabin was where the modern home at 111 Highland Avenue is now located. Blair called his street “Vernal Avenue” because of its lush ferns and shrubs. The back of the house was on today’s Waldo Avenue. The walkers headed off on Highland (not Vernal) Avenue, noting historic homes as they went. They continued to the end of Highland at Moraga Avenue. They looked across the street to the spot where an arched entrance to Blair Park once stood, and more of Blair’s history was told. Blair established Blair’s Dairy at the corner of today’s Blair and El Cerrito Avenues, and his cattle grazed in pastures that went down to what is now Grand Avenue. However, he found real estate and other commercial interests to be also profitable. He built the Piedmont Springs Hotel in 1871, which was at the top of today’s Piedmont Park, and partnered with investors to build a horsecar line from downtown Oakland to Piedmont Avenue. In 1878 Blair decided to build his own line, the Piedmont Railway, which ran from where the Piedmont Avenue line ended at the gates of the Mountain View Cemetery, and went through his grain fields to Vernal Avenue and the Piedmont Springs Hotel. To increase the number of riders, in 1884 Blair developed 40 acres of the land between the cemetery and Moraga Avenue as a picnic park, and named it Blair Park. It offered picnic tables, paths for wandering, a Japanese Tea House, a dancing pavilion, a Venetian canal ride, a bandstand, swings, bridges over waterfalls and a stream, a fountain, a lake, and even hot air balloon ascensions. Many of the picnickers and hotel guests enjoyed the views and climate in Piedmont and stayed to purchase property and build homes. They became Piedmont’s early residents. Blair also opened the Dracena Quarry, which is today’s Dracena Park, to sell crushed rock to pave the streets of Oakland, Piedmont and the nearby Mountain View Cemetery. Blair was only 57 when he died in 1888. He is buried in Mountain View Cemetery. After his death Blair Park was purchased by another train line, but it went into receivership in 1893, and its assets were sold in 1895. In 1901 the park was abandoned, and the land was still vacant in 1913, but in 1917 new homes began to be built on it. articles.text: Civilizations around the world have been celebrating the start of each New Year for at least 4,000 years. Common traditions include attending parties, eating special New Year’s food, making resolutions for the new year and watching fireworks displays. But when the singing, fireworks and champagne toasts are over, many of us become more serious about life. We take stock and plan new courses of action to better our lives. This is best seen in one of the most popular customs of the new year, making resolutions. So why are so many of my friends shunning this custom this year? I was having a discussion about making resolutions with a group of Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living residents the other day. Our residents have had the chance to make many resolutions for each of their new years. After my informal poll, the general consensus was to not make resolutions. Pat said, “In all honesty, I don’t make them, because I never can keep them!” Gloria added, “New Year’s Day is a new chance to try again. Yet, I don’t make resolutions, because each and every day I look forward to doing better!” Another resident added, “I think of each day as a new beginning.” Since many resolutions result in taking something away, I think I will adopt Gloria’s approach. It seems one is more likely to accomplish a goal that is specific and based on doing something each day instead of avoiding Lake Merritt resident Laura McGee considers her New Year’s resolutions. something or taking something away. I always appreciate talking with our residents. There is definitely something to be learned from aging and wisdom. As I’ve travelled through life, I have learned that it’s better for me not to make a New Year’s resolution, than to make one and fail. So my goal to cut down on sugar will result in my buying only one box of cookies from the grocery store each week. My main goal, to resume my exercise regime, will begin after my birthday celebration - which is just around the corner. Our residents seem to be in agreement that the time to set goals is when we are motivated to keep them, not just because the calendar is turned to a new page. I think that with this approach we have a better chance at keeping our resolutions rather than having failure again slap us in the face. Let’s set and keep goals, not just at the New Year, but at any time we feel moved to do so. Welcome 2022. We have the entire year of fresh starts ahead of us. Happy New Year! Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living at 1800 Madison Street in Oakland. Call 510-903-3600 or visit www. thelakemerritt.com.

articles.text: Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I just got a new MacBook Air that is still in the box. I am trying to decide if I should transfer all of my files with Time Machine or just start fresh? I have years of stuff that I don’t use, and I started to have some trouble opening some of my files. Also, some of my applications (on my old laptop) have been shutting down unexpectedly. All I really do these days is use my email, write a few Word files, and take photos. My email is through Gmail. The salesperson at Best Buy suggested that I use Dropbox or iCloud to store and transfer my files. Can you explain how that would be different than transferring everything with Time Machine? –Lissa M., Oakland Dear Lissa: This is a great question. It’s your second sentence that leads me to my answer. Since you are having some application crashes and also have a ton of old files you don’t need, I would recommend setting this up as a new machine. That being said, it would also be possible and even desirable to use Dropbox or iCloud to transfer the files you do want. If you only have a few files that you want to keep, and by “a few” I mean less than a gigabyte or so, I would recommend moving them to a folder in Dropbox before you set up your new Mac. Dropbox is a cloud service. You can think of it as a virtual hard drive. You must have an account, and most likely if you’re going to use it to sync files you already have on your computer, you’re going to want one of their paid accounts. You download the application, sign into your account, and then you would have a folder in finder called, “Dropbox”. Anything that you move into Dropbox; folders, files, pictures, etc. can be synced with other machines that are signed into the same Dropbox account. This gives you the most control over what you want to move over to the new machine. You could create a folder on the desktop of your old machine, called something like “To Be Transferred” or “Keepers”. Then you would simply upload that folder to Dropbox, which is as simple as dragging to the Dropbox icon in Finder. There are plenty of tutorials online about using this application, and their website, www.dropbox.com has very good ones. The nice thing about this is that you can cherry pick things to move over. If you use iCloud to sync your desktop and documents, it will sync everything on your desktop and documents. Anything you don’t want to be stored in iCloud, you have to move out of your documents folder and off of your desktop. This system is great if you want everything to look the same on more than one machine, but not practical if you only want to move a few files over. In your situation, I think Dropbox makes more sense. As far as your photos go, if you haven’t already, I would enable iCloud Photos to sync on your laptop as well as your phone before you set up the new machine. This way, when you sign into iCloud on your new Air, and enable iCloud Photos, all of your photos will come into your photo library. If you have tens of thousands of photos, then make sure to do this well enough ahead of time that the complete library has a chance to upload to iCloud. Since you use Gmail, when you set your email up on the new machine, everything that’s on Gmail’s servers will come into your mail application, so that’s no problem. What won’t come over are any emails you are saving locally; that means folders stored under “On my Mac” in Apple Mail. If this is the case, re-create these folders under Gmail in the folders list in Mac mail, and copy any of the emails in the local folders to Gmail ones. Again, there are lots of tutorials online about how to do this. Here is what makes all of this different than using your Time Machine back up drive to transfer your data. When you use Time Machine, it copies everything on your current computer every hour onto an external drive. This includes everything you see, like documents, files, folders, pictures, your music and photo library, all of your applications, as well as things you don’t see, like preferences, drivers, and files that live in the user and system library. So, if one or more of those files are corrupt, Time Machine still copies it. If you migrate these files to a new computer, it is possible you will inherit any problems you had on your old machine. For this reason, in your case, I would recommend the Dropbox solution. Personally, I use a combination of iCloud and Dropbox. And of course, if you need help, you can contact me, and I can help with the new set up. This article first appeared in the Post on March 31, 2021. Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com and themacmama.blogspot.com.
articles.title: The advantages of using Time Machine for files

articles.text: There are many reasons that someone becomes a caregiver: they have been caring for a family member and discovered their strengths in being compassionate; they are following a path into nursing or related medical field and want some hands-on experience; or they enjoy helping others and developing meaningful oneon-one connections. As caregiving becomes a high in-demand career with more people living longer in the comfort of their own homes, there can also be financial incentives to consider this job. The need for quality caregivers has possibly never been greater. Yet there are reasons that caregiving can be more than just a job. We’d like to share five of them: 1. Transferable skills The skills gained in a caregiving job can apply to all kinds of other roles, including some in the home care agency office. Things like being compassionate, being a good listener, showing patience, and other qualities used to assist people whose abilities have changed due to illness or age can be used in all other personal and professional situations to your benefit. 2. Training At Homewatch CareGivers, caregivers have the opportunity for additional training via the Homewatch CareGivers University which can empower them to grow professionally. These courses may include dementia care, behavioral health, instructions on caring for people who are living with intellectual and developmental disabilities, and much more. Once you start learning, there is no telling how far you can go in a career. 3. Flexibility Caregivers often have scheduling flexibility, much different than a traditional 9 to 5 type of job, which means they have the ability to pick and choose what suits them and their own families while earning money from their career. 4. Making a difference Yes, a smile can change someone’s world. Many people who need in-home care services have become isolated from a life that brought them joy. Symptoms of chronic conditions may limit their abilities to engage in certain activities or socialize as they once did. A friendly caregiver who provides transportation for errands, plays a fun board game, gives medication reminders, and much more, can alleviate their feelings of loneliness, helplessness, and boredom. 5. Each day is new. Caregiving may have challenges and surprises and that can help you to grow personally and professionally, as well as bring laughs and new life skills. Each client is unique and brings their own life story and needs to the relationship, and a chance to learn more. Homewatch CareGivers is locat­ ed at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmon­ ters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com.
articles.title: 5 reasons caregiving is meaningful

Dropbox is a cloud service. You can think of it as a virtual hard drive. You must have an account, and most likely if you’re going to use it to sync files you already have on your computer, you’re going to want one of their paid accounts. You download the application, sign into your account, and then you would have a folder in finder called, “Dropbox”. Anything that you move into Dropbox; folders, files, pictures, etc. can be synced with other machines that are signed into the same Dropbox account. This gives you the most control over what you want to move over to the new machine. You could create a folder on the desktop of your old machine, called something like “To Be Transferred” or “Keepers”. Then you would simply upload that folder to Dropbox, which is as simple as dragging to the Dropbox icon in Finder. There are plenty of tutorials online about using this application, and their website, www.dropbox.com has very good ones. The nice thing about this is that you can cherry pick things to move over. If you use iCloud to sync your desktop and documents, it will sync everything on your desktop and documents. Anything you don’t want to be stored in iCloud, you have to move out of your documents folder and off of your desktop. This system is great if you want everything to look the same on more than one machine, but not practical if you only want to move a few files over. In your situation, I think Dropbox makes more sense. As far as your photos go, if you haven’t already, I would enable iCloud Photos to sync on your laptop as well as your phone before you set up the new machine. This way, when you sign into iCloud on your new Air, and enable iCloud Photos, all of your photos will come into your photo library. If you have tens of thousands of photos, then make sure to do this well enough ahead of time that the complete library has a chance to upload to iCloud. Since you use Gmail, when you set your email up on the new machine, everything that’s on Gmail’s servers will come into your mail application, so that’s no problem. What won’t come over are any emails you are saving locally; that means folders stored under “On my Mac” in Apple Mail. If this is the case, re-create these folders under Gmail in the folders list in Mac mail, and copy any of the emails in the local folders to Gmail ones. Again, there are lots of tutorials online about how to do this. Here is what makes all of this different than using your Time Machine back up drive to transfer your data. When you use Time Machine, it copies everything on your current computer every hour onto an external drive. This includes everything you see, like documents, files, folders, pictures, your music and photo library, all of your applications, as well as things you don’t see, like preferences, drivers, and files that live in the user and system library. So, if one or more of those files are corrupt, Time Machine still copies it. If you migrate these files to a new computer, it is possible you will inherit any problems you had on your old machine. For this reason, in your case, I would recommend the Dropbox solution. Personally, I use a combination of iCloud and Dropbox. And of course, if you need help, you can contact me, and I can help with the new set up. This article first appeared in the Post on March 31, 2021. In an interview with the Post, Rutherford gave his take on the situation. “Knowing what we know now, I don’t think taking two weeks off is a necessary thing to do, unless there are staffing issues driving it or such high absenteeism,” he said. “The original concern about school, two years ago, was that within schools are huge incubators of disease, and it would spread to grandparents. We don’t have lots of evidence of that happening,” Rutherford said. School closures in 2020 extended into 2021 resulting in the school district receiving heavy criticism from the community. This year keeping schools open has been a top priority. “The district has comprehensive plans to keep students and staff in school to the greatest extent possible,” Booker confirmed in a memo dated January 12. Having the teachers, parents and students understanding the school district’s plans has been key as well. Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) President Dr. Elise Marks made the teachTwo important components of this phase are site analysis and programming. “I loved this design concept, and all of the thoughtful detail that has come out of public workshops,” said City Council member Betsy Andersen. “There was a tremendous outpour from the public, [even] during the pandemic. We’ve been without a pool for two years… I’m hopeful we will have this new facility on time to open in 2024. I want to encourage everyone to stay engaged and [provide comment] at meetings.” “This is a huge project to move forward and is unlike [other] projects the city has taken on,” said Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King. “We’re lucky we live in an environment where we have a commitment to aquatics, seeing how complicated and expensive it can be for any city. PUSD teachers are in their classrooms and that is where we intend to stay,” Marks said at the January 12 school board meeting. Teachers were given and required to wear N-95 or KN-95 masks from January 12-21, and Marks estimated that roughly half of the students now wear the N-95 mask in class. Prior to schools’ resumption on January 5, the district received 3,000 COVID test kits from the state, with two tests in each. They helped students and staff prescreen themselves prior to returning to classrooms. The district reported approximately 228 COVID cases among staff and students from December 17- January 10, and 33 cases from January 11-14. Ninety-seven percent of all students in grades K-12 were vaccinated by January 18. Omicron can result in breakthrough cases, but serious cases of COVID have not been common among individuals who have been vaccinated. It has taken a multi-pronged approach through testing, mask-wearing, isolation, vaccination and substitution to keep Piedmont schools open to start the second semester. articles.text: Phase 3 Communications is continuing construction work on Magnolia Avenue between Hillside and Highland Avenues, with an expected completion date by Friday, January 28. Utility work is being done in this section of Piedmont to expand better cell phone and internet access to residents. Crown Castle is the owner of the utility project and Phase 3 Communications is the general contractor installing the new system. Construction in this area began in July 2021, confirmed Phase 3 Communications Vice President Juan Carlos DeZubiria. Recent work on Magnolia Avenue began this week on Monday, January 17, and will continue through January 28. It is situated in the two blocks on Hillside and Magnolia Avenue from the Recreation Department to the Exedra. The company will bore in the street in front of the Recreation Dept. and Dress Best for Less carriage house on Bonita Avenue. The area will not be closed off to vehicular traffic, confirmed Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. Crews and flaggers will be on-site to direct traffic if needed, and work will be conducted from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays. Work will stop daily from 3 p.m. to 4 p.m. to accommodate school dismissals. A January 14 press release from the City of Piedmont noted the high volume of traffic in the area and urged motorists to avoid the area if possible. “The City realizes that this utility work in such a highly congested area adjacent to schools is not ideal,” said City Clerk John Tulloch. “Originally planned for late 2021, the work has been delayed to avoid conflicts in the area, including the School District’s ongoing construction, but unfortunately, it must be completed at this time.” “[Phase 3 Communications] did get approval to work later in the day, so we are hoping they will finish the work quickly,” Gonzales said. nationwide walkout that closed half of the primary schools in France. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is currently accepting applications from residents who are interested in and qualified for serving on the City Council on an interim basis. The deadline to apply is Monday, January 31. Piedmont City Council held a special meeting on January 6 to determine the process by which it would fill a vacancy left by council member Tim Rood following his resignation on December 31, 2021. Council members chose to seek applications for appointment to City Council from residents to serve as interim council member until the results of the general municipal election are certified on November 8. Residents must meet three requirements to apply for the position: 1. Must be a qualified registered voter in Piedmont 2. Must not hold any other office or employment with the city 3. Must not be rendered ineligible due to the term limits provisions of the City Charter Interested residents may submit applications electronically, or in-person to the City Clerk’s Office by 5 p.m. on January 31. Postmarks will not be accepted. Members of the city council will interview candidates at which time applicants will have the opportunity to discuss their candidacy with council members. At a special meeting on February 7 applicants will be asked to make a brief presentation to council members. Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King noted at the January 6 meeting that this is the third time she has assisted in filling a vacancy mid-election. City Council filled vacancies left by former mayor Margaret Fujioka in 2016 and former mayor Jeff Wieler in 2017. The Council also chose to take applications from residents in those appointments. “Both times resulted in finding new talent [for City Council],” said King. Applications are available on the City website at https://piedmont.ca.gov and from the City Clerk’s Office. For more information on the application process, contact City Clerk John Tulloch at (510) 420-3041 or via email at jtulloch@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: The Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) and the City of Piedmont will co-sponsor its 25th annual MLK Day celebration on Monday, January 17, Martin Luther King, Jr. Day, a national holiday. The event will be held via Zoom at 11 a.m. Speakers for the event include Rep. Barbara Lee; Dr. Clayborne Carson, Founding Director of the Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute; Anna Malaika Tubbs, author of The Three Mothers; State Assembly member Buffy Wicks; and Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King. This year’s theme is “Changing Souls, Changing Lives, and Creating Community.” King’s vision for inclusive communities calls on each member to reflect and embrace change. “Our goal is to create a beloved community, and this will require a qualitative change in our souls, as well as a quantitative change in our lives,” he said. Art and literature created by Piedmont youth will be showcased at the event. Students were asked to create art that represents a “beloved community” and to answer two questions: what does a beloved community mean to you? How can we create an inclusive and beloved community in Piedmont? The deadline to submit entries was January 10. PADC is honoring the King legacy with a day of community service at St. Vincent de Paul, an organization that provides support for families in Alameda County who face hunger or live in poverty. The Committee invites residents to sign up for service by visiting https://www. padc.info/mlk2022, where more information of the event, including a Zoom link, can be found. articles.text: Piedmont students started their second semester of classes on Wednesday, January 5, but not all of them were in school, likely due to a surge in Covid-19 cases spurred on by the Omicron variant. Attendance the first three days back was down by approximately 10% through the district compared to the last week of class in December. The district, with an estimated enrollment of 2413 in its six schools, has reported that approximately 228 covid cases were reported among staff and students between December 17 and January 10. An estimated 190 cases were reported to the district prior to the resumption of classes on January 5. In comparison, in the first four months of the school year only 24 student cases and 13 staff cases were recorded. “With the need for testing and backlog of emails and voicemails for our District nurses and Health Clerks, the decision was made to prioritize clearing students and staff to return to campus,” said Communications Director Brian Killgore.” “While we can attribute some of these absences to positive COVID cases, we are aware of families keeping their students home as a precaution,” Killgore said. Students weren’t the only ones missing from campus. There were 27 staff absences on Wednesday, the first day back, 34 absences Thursday and Friday, and 35 on Monday, January 10. “We want to be clear this does not mean every absent staff member has tested positive for Covid. Some may have symptoms and stayed home as a precaution, or were absent for other reasons, such as staying home with a sick child,” Killgore said. With substitutes and other district staff member filling in, all teacher vacancies were covered through Monday this week, January 10. Finding available substitutes has been a problem all year across the country, prompting the Piedmont School District to increase the per diem rate for substitutes in September from $140 to $200 a day. Piedmont updated its policy for returning to class on Thursday December 6 for students and staff that have received a positive COVID-19 test result. “Clearance to Return,” testing is now being provided by the district at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse at
articles.title: A is for absent, O is for Omicron

Right after the French onion soup arrived, things got ugly and fast. Seems like after years of abuse my gall bladder had chosen this moment to go on strike. After a few minutes of considering whether it was just food poisoning, it became evident that I was seriously sick. After a few hours of trying to wait it out back home, and consulting with our neighbors and friends Mike and Drennan, we made our way down to Alta Bates Hospital emergency room. Mike is an EMT and I seriously recommend everyone have an EMT friend down the street. Four hours later they got me in to see the doctor who, after tests, said “You have a gangrenous gall bladder and it needs to come out, now. “I have always been a procrastinator – fast decisions are not my style – but this seemed the time for action. So, despite the fact that my surgeon looked like Ferris Buehler, none of the hospital staff had seen or heard of him, and there was no internet in the emergency room to check any reviews, off we went. Back in my room I met my nurse, a middle-aged man from Nigeria named Gracious, and another nurse, a young lady from Ethiopia named Lovely. They wrote their names on the whiteboard on the wall along with my name and the date. I liked looking up and seeing them. Psalm 23 says “surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life…” Gracious and Lovely is not bad either. Thank God for the miracle of anesthesia. I remember nothing of the surgery except for a few seconds of the surgeon’s choice of 70’s rock and roll as operating music before blacking out. Back in a regular room I was introduced to my roommate, Josh. Usually you would think a private room would be better than a shared one, but not with Josh. My new golden hair-streaked millennial hipster friend was there to show me the ropes. He wanted a sandwich and they declined as it was too close to his surgery time. “Cancel the surgery,” he calmly said. They gave him the sandwich and the surgery. When breakfast arrived and was inedible, he immediately called the nurse and ordered French toast and scrambled eggs. “Make it two” I yelled. When things got a little slow in the evening he called and ordered Door Dash to deliver two milkshakes and 4 cookies from The Creamery. Who knew you could do that? When it was time for his elbow surgery and he put on the backless gown, he asked for pants to go with it. They came immediately. I had no idea there was an alternative to flashing your backside down the hallway. Later I said to Josh through the curtain that divided our beds, “Josh how did you get to know so much about hospitals?” “Four years ago I had leukemia and spent quite a bit of time in them. This one’s OK but I have seen better. You should try the UC Hospitals – their desserts are amazing.” Wherever you are now Josh, thanks. You were a gracious gift and made my one night in the hospital a memorable one. Bill McNabb is the former Senior Minister at Piedmont community Church and a longtime Piedmont resident. articles.text: We are in a battle on many fronts. That much is clear as we begin 2022. Medically, we are in a battle to subdue COVID-19. Politically, we are in a battle to preserve democracy. Religiously, we are in a battle to keep Christ in Christianity. Thus, television series like “The Mandlorian” offer meaningful reflection on the world we live in, raising questions such as how we best wage the battles of our time. One of those questions is, “Are we better off keeping our helmets on or taking them off?” If, like me, you watch the series, then you know that the title character, following the Way of the Mandalores, neither takes off his helmet nor allows it to be removed by others. There are reasons practical (the helmet provides protection) and spiritual (“This is the Way”) for this practice. However, as the story unfolds, it becomes clear that practitioners of the Way are far from united in this practice. Some, like the more fanatical Children of the Watch, forbid the removal of one’s helmet with few exceptions. Others, such as the storied anti-Imperial warrior Bo-Katan, take off their helmet whenever they please. For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. articles.text: The Piedmont Planning Commission discussed aspects of Senate Bill (SB) 9 at a January 10 meeting and how it will apply to the city’s fair housing endeavors. “The state has decided that cities are not processing construction of new housing units fast enough. So [the city] can only provide objective standards, much like a building code is an objective standard, and there can be no discretion in the review. This is a major change,” said Senior Piedmont Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell. SB 9 was signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2021, and the requirements of the bill went into effect on January 1 of this year. It requires local jurisdictions to grant by-right approval of housing developments of one to two units, and urban lot ‘splits’ for single-family zoning districts. “SB 9 is a state law we’re going to have to address in the city zoning code,” Piedmont Planning Director Kevin Jackson confirmed. In Piedmont, single-family zoning districts are Zone A and E. Homeowners in these zones would be eligible to split their lot into a duplex-style, or two properties on one lot, if it involves the demolition of no more than 25% of the exterior walls or structure. The result would be two parcels of approximately equal size. The secondary ‘property’ may be then used for home ownership, or to rent out to a tenant that will occupy the property for more than 30 days. Short-term rentals, like for popular rental websites AirBnB or VRBO, are not permitted. The new structure would not need a design review permit. “That is the crux of SB 9,” said Macdonald-Powell confirmed. Jackson explained that the city will need to develop objective design standards for projects that are eligible for SB 9. Units and subdivisions created under SB 9 would not be reviewed by the Planning Commission, would not be subject to public hearing or right of appeal, and must be reviewed by city staff according to objective standards, not yet created by the city. The law is not specific about whether or not the lots created could also have Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) or Junior Accessory Dwelling Units (JADUs) in addition to those two lots, Macdonald-Powell added.
articles.title: How will Senate Bill 9 affect Piedmont and its housing future?

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council rejected a recommendation to increase the speed limit on Moraga Avenue from 25 mph to 30 mph at a December 20, 2021 meeting. A study done by Kittelson & Associates, Inc. was presented to council members, which included the recommendation of raising the speed limit on Moraga Avenue from Ramona Avenue to Maxwelton Road – its entire length in the city of Piedmont – by 5 mph. The city asked Kittelson & Associates to complete a study on selective roads to ensure compliance with state regulations. Speed limits throughout Piedmont have been established over the years by traffic and radar speed studies. “We get speed complaints on Moraga Avenue, and we’re considering installing [Class II] bike lanes on Moraga around Coaches Field, as well as doing striping modifications. Both of those, we feel, will have a positive impact in reducing speeds through that area,” City Planner John Wanger said. Between 2016 and 2021 there have been 32 collisions on Moraga Avenue. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers added that radar enforcement could not be used for this stretch of Moraga Avenue if the speed limit remains at 25 mph. Bowers confirmed that the department does receive speed complaints, and that the department would address complaints in different ways. The city council adopted all other findings and recommendations in the Speed Zone Engineering and Traffic Study conducted by Kittelson & Associates, Inc., dated August 2021. The survey included 12 non-residential roadway segments in Piedmont.
articles.title: Moraga Ave. speed limit to remain at 25 mph

articles.text: The League of California Cities, a non-profit statewide association that provides education and training services to elected city officials, released a report detailing legislation passed last year and how it will affect cities across the state. The League zeroed in on Senate Bill (SB) 9, which requires local governments to approve housing developments containing two residential units in single-family zones and urban lot splits. The report found that lawmakers introduced 2,421 bills total, far surpassing the totals of 2019 and 2020. Of the 836 bills to reach the governor’s desk, about 92% were signed into law, many of which made a significant investment in the production of affordable housing. However, more than 240 cities joined the League in its opposition of SB 9 before Gov. Newsom signed it into law in September 2021. “SB 9 undermines the ability of local governments to responsibly plan for the type of housing that communities need, while usurping local democracy and the input of local residents,” said Carolyn Coleman, CEO of the League of California Cities. The bill was authored by Senate President pro tempore Toni Atkins (D-San Diego), who said it would “set California’s housing availability on a path of inclusion so that more families can attain the California dream.” It was a critical piece of the Senate’s “Housing Package,” a comprehensive effort to increase the state’s affordable housing stock. Assembly member Buffy Wicks, who represents Piedmont in the State Assembly, said that single-family zoning is an exclusionary policy. She was a staunch proponent of SB 9. “Single-family zoning is rooted in redlining. It has created huge problems, and results in exclusionary housing. At least in this bill, these units can be deed-restricted, should local governments decide - which I think is an important step forward,” Wicks said. “We need to legalize duplexes. This bill will create more housing, and density in a way that doesn’t fundamentally alter the character of the neighborhood.” The bill went into effect on January 1 this year, and Bay Area city planners have already received proposals. The City of Concord received its first application under the new bill on January 5. Piedmont has not yet received an application under SB 9. Lic. articles.text: A deadly apartment-building fire in the Bronx, New York last weekend has prompted communities nationwide to revisit safety concerns surrounding electric space heaters. The commonly used appliance was the source of the fire that killed at least 17 people on January 9. A space heater is an appliance that is used to heat a single, small-to-medium sized living area. Although convenient, they can be dangerous if not used properly. pages.text: Wednesday, January 12, 2022 5 How will Senate Bill 9 affect Piedmont and its housing future? By Allyson Aleksey The Piedmont Planning Commission discussed aspects of Senate Bill (SB) 9 at a January 10 meeting and how it will apply to the city’s fair housing endeavors. “The state has decided that cities are not processing construction of new housing units fast enough. So [the city] can only provide objective standards, much like a building code is an objective standard, and there can be no discretion in the review. This is a major change,” said Senior Piedmont Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell. SB 9 was signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2021, and the requirements of the bill went into effect on January 1 of this year. It requires local jurisdictions to grant by-right approval of housing developments of one to two units, and urban lot ‘splits’ for single-family zoning districts. “SB 9 is a state law we’re going to have to address in the city zoning code,” Piedmont Planning Director Kevin Jackson confirmed. In Piedmont, single-family zoning districts are Zone A and E. Homeowners in these zones would be eligible to split their lot into a duplex-style, or two properties on one lot, if it involves the demolition of no more than 25% of the exterior walls or structure. The result would be two parcels of approximately equal size. The secondary ‘property’ may be then used for home ownership, or to rent out to a tenant that will occupy the property for more than 30 days. Short-term rentals, like for popular rental websites AirBnB or VRBO, are not permitted. The new structure would not need a design review permit. “That is the crux of SB 9,” said Macdonald-Powell confirmed. Jackson explained that the city will need to develop objective design standards for projects that are eligible for SB 9. Units and subdivisions created under SB 9 would not be reviewed by the Planning Commission, would not be subject to public hearing or right of appeal, and must be reviewed by city staff according to objective standards, not yet created by the city. The law is not specific about whether or not the lots created could also have Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) or Junior Accessory Dwelling Units (JADUs) in addition to those two lots, Macdonald-Powell added. Local lawmakers and agencies debate SB 9 By Allyson Aleksey The League of California Cities, a non-profit statewide association that provides education and training services to elected city officials, released a report detailing legislation passed last year and how it will affect cities across the state. The League zeroed in on Senate Bill (SB) 9, which requires local governments to approve housing developments containing two residential units in single-family zones and urban lot splits. The report found that lawmakers introduced 2,421 bills total, far surpassing the totals of 2019 and 2020. Of the 836 bills to reach the governor’s desk, about 92% were signed into law, many of which made a significant investment in the production of affordable housing. However, more than 240 cities joined the League in its opposition of SB 9 before Gov. Newsom signed it into law in September 2021. “SB 9 undermines the ability of local governments to responsibly plan for the type of housing that communities need, while usurping local democracy and the input of local residents,” said Carolyn Coleman, CEO of the League of California Cities. The bill was authored by Senate President pro tempore Toni Atkins (D-San Diego), who said it would “set California’s housing availability on a path of inclusion so that more families can attain the California dream.” It was a critical piece of the Senate’s “Housing Package,” a comprehensive effort to increase the state’s affordable housing stock. Assembly member Buffy Wicks, who represents Piedmont in the State Assembly, said that single-family zoning is an exclusionary policy. She was a staunch proponent of SB 9. “Single-family zoning is rooted in redlining. It has created huge problems, and results in exclusionary housing. At least in this bill, these units can be deed-restricted, should local governments decide - which I think is an important step forward,” Wicks said. “We need to legalize duplexes. This bill will create more housing, and density in a way that doesn’t fundamentally alter the character of the neighborhood.” The bill went into effect on January 1 this year, and Bay Area city planners have already received proposals. The City of Concord received its first application under the new bill on January 5. Piedmont has not yet received an application under SB 9. Lic. articles.text: Piedmont students aged 12 and older were given until the first day of the second semester, January 5, to submit proof of COVID-19 vaccination to the school district. Proof is now a requirement to attend classes. On January 5, only nine students had not complied. The district has not placed any of the nine in Independent Study, and no students left the district for the semester due to their vaccination status. Some homeless students enrolled at Piedmont are not subject to the vaccination policy. “We continue to work with each student and family to find solutions with the shared goal of keeping students in class,” said Communications Director Brian Killgore. January 5 is the second deadline for students aged 12 and older to provide their proof of vaccination. COVID-19 was added to the district’s vaccination list on September 22 by the school board and the deadline for submission was initially November 17. Come November 17, 33 students had yet to provide documentation and the deadline was pushed back to January 5 for them. By November 30 that number was down to 14. January 14 deadline The deadline for showing proof of full vaccination of students aged 5-11 is this Friday, January 14. The district is still waiting for documentation from an estimated 80 of the younger students. Nearly 92% of elementary school students have submitted their proof of vaccination. The FDA gave emergency approval for the Pfizer vaccine in kids aged 5-11 on October 29. Full vaccination is achieved two weeks after the final dose. The outdoor mask policy still applies to all elementary students.

articles.text: As a family, encourage kids’ creativity. I’m sitting here in the midst of the Omicron surge trying to find words for parents and kids out there on creativity and imagination that could be fun, helpful or inspirational, but I’ve got to admit…the page is feeling awfully blank right now. So, to all the parents out there right now feeling tired and worn out, I just want to say, “I see you.” I read a NY Times piece on their app recently about how we should all just prepare to get back to the world of hours and hours of screen time and be ok with it because that’s just where we are, and I definitely wanted to throw my phone across the room. Anyone else experiencing COVID rage? But, time marches forward and our kids still need us and they need creativity and imagination, so here are a few ideas that are just back to the basics for bringing creative play into your home. music!! Try adding variety by playing with genre: classical, rock, pop, musicals, opera, jazz, big band, all the types of music you can think of or search for on Spotify. 2. Dance/Move You know the dance move “the shopping cart”? Well, have you tried “the tooth brushing?” What about “the eating spaghetti” or “the riding your bike?” Any of these normal day-to-day activities can be turned into dance moves with a little fun and rhythm. Just mime the activity and repeat! Challenge your kids to a “dance off” with these silly movements. 3. Crayon Self Portraits Get out the crayons, put everyone in front of a hand mirror and start to draw. If you want to have some fun with older kids, ask them to try to do the project with their non-dominant hand. 4. Cake Decorating Find all of the weird old jars of sprinkles and decorations that you have sitting around the house. Bake a cake (I highly recommend the one from the box), get your kids to frost it with some store-bought frosting and then let them loose with whatever edible decoration you have in the back of your pantry. 5. Read a Good Book Together (or watch a show based on a good book) I love curling up with kids to read aloud. A lot of parents do this at bedtime, but maybe a rainy Saturday afternoon can also become a book moment. What’s a favorite book from your childhood? Share that with your family. Or, if you are too tired, find a show or a movie based on a book and watch that together. Stories are universal and a great way to escape together into imagination. Nina Meehan is CEO of Bay Area Children’s Theatre. For information see Bay Area Children’s Theatre – Sparking Creativity, Inspiring Imagination (bactheatre.org)
articles.title: Thinking Outside The Classroom Creative things for kids to do during the Omicron surge

articles.text: For decades the number one impetus for moving to Piedmont has been its schools. But how well compensated are the teachers? A Special School Board meeting was held last week on Thursday, January 6, at which the school board approved a pay increase of 2.5% for all teachers retroactive to July 1, 2021. Based upon information from 2019, teacher salaries can range from approximately $50,000 for a first-year faculty member to a high of around $109,000 (before benefits or extra pay) for a teacher with more than 25 years of experience. A 2.5% increase would see those amounts increase to $51,250 and $111,725. Data on salaries are available for all school district employees of all California public schools. Piedmont School District salaries are available going back only to 2019. Piedmont teachers have received salary increases as follows: 2018-19 3% 2019-20 2% 2020-21 6% 2021-22 2.5% Veteran Piedmont High School English teacher Dr. Elise Marks took over as president of the Associated Piedmont Teachers (APT) at the end of October 2021. The job of president has seen a significant increase in Seen here teaching remotely, Dr. Elise Marks taught an extra class period of English last year due to staffing shortages and is now the APT President. responsibilities since the start of the pandemic, with changes in work environment, safety concerns and general uncertainty. Marks applauded the recent salary agreement with the school district but has warned that inflation is on track to outpace the raises. “The Legislative Analyst’s Office is predicting inflation of 5.35% for next year, and teachers are very worried. One member told me almost half her monthly income is already going to her $1400 rent, which will increase again in January. Others tell me they don’t know how they’re going to manage to keep paying for daycare for their kids,” Marks said.
articles.title: A perspective on teacher raises

articles.text: Parents have until 5 p.m. tomorrow, Thursday, January 13, to vote for their school site’s representative on the new Superintendent Community Advisory Committee. Elected representatives’ responsibilities include attending their respective school’s Parent Club meetings and reporting on their discussions. One parent for each school site will be elected and two at-large individuals will be included as the next two highest vote getters, totaling eight members. The committee’s formation resulted from a May 2021 recommendation from an independent consultant, Naomi Hunter, who analyzed the District’s Pandemic Response Survey of last year. Along with forming this committee, Hunter also recommended the hiring of a Communications Director (now Brian Killgore) and to continue surveying the community with regular job performance and trust surveys. Sara DeVries, co-president of the PHS Parents’ Club, explained that the committee should give voice to underrepresented parents. “[The District] could have just said ‘We will take the Parent Club President and they will be the representatives.’ But that is not what this is. Most of the people I have seen aren’t people that have a particular role already.” In an email communication, the District said the committee is being formed in an attempt to “[Build] off of the success of a variety of Superintendent com-
articles.title: Voting for new committee of parents closes tomorrow

articles.text: mittees (Facilities Steering, Budget Advisory, Health and Safety Steering, etc.).” The email continues, “The purpose of the committee is to: 1. Strengthen community and positive relationships amongst our various stakeholders. 2. Listen, learn, and better understand one another on the various successes and areas to improve across the District. 3. articles.text: Tickets for “Glowfari,” the beloved annual Oakland Zoo event, are available now through January 20. Advance ticketing is required. “Glowfari” features hundreds of life-size glowing animal lanterns throughout the Zoo and will display all-new light fixtures for the event’s return this year. It takes the place of last year’s “Zoolights,” and features larger light displays, longer hours of admission, and more available dates. The event is appropriate for all ages and invites attendees to take a mile-long illuminated stroll through the campus and ride to gondola to see the remarkable, 65-foot “Queen Ant Tunnel.” Finish the evening with a ride on the express train through the zoo’s winter wonderland.
