articles.text: This Christmas break, my dad decided to entertain the family by renting a house near Lake Tahoe. We hadn’t seen snow for a while, and most of us were excited to do some skiing. It should be noted that the family skiing aptitude is not distributed equally. My dad is a world record holder in high hurdles, so he’s pretty good with keeping his balance. My older sister and her boyfriend (also invited) both played sports in high school. I did cross-country running. It doesn’t help much when it comes to doing cross-country skiing, but it’s something. Lastly, my mother, who hadn’t done any sports before meeting my dad, has skied once or twice – and without much enthusiasm, I should add. On the second day of our stay at Tahoe, the five of us dressed in the ridiculously bulky ski clothes, piled into the car and drove to North Tahoe Cross Country. As we waited for our skis at the rental counter, our anticipation was building. Six years ago we tried skiing and struggled getting our skis on without them falling off when we tried to lift our feet. To get to the trails this winter we struggled up a steep hill – kind of the opposite of what most cross-country skiers expect. But after that, nothing could stop us, at least that’s what we thought. For a while I was in the lead, showing off to the stragglers behind me. But then I got too cocky and fell as I tried to go faster. The real challenge was to get up: after making positions I didn’t even know I could do, I pulled myself up, only to start sliding down the hill. I remembered hearing about the “the pizza method” (also known as the snowplow), in which you point your skis towards each other to slow your descent. That helped me stop, but now I had to go back up the hill. After my less than graceful descent down the first hill, everything was calm. My sister, mother, and I were going steady, while my dad and my sister’s boyfriend were speeding ahead. The forest around us was beautiful; all the evergreens were covered in snow, like a Nutcracker wonderland. In about an hour, we stopped for a water break. Looking at a map of the trails, my dad figured out that the next portion was downhill. I led the charge, and when I saw the sign “To Lodge” I assumed that’s where we were going before anything bad happened (think Donner Party). But instead, the Edel Party decided to push ahead to find a lake my mother claimed she remembered from six years earlier. I, on the other hand, wished them good luck and headed to warmth and safety. After my share of humiliating falls, I just took off my skis and walked, arriving at the lodge in one piece. And there, after making myself comfortable by the fireplace, I began my wait. Thirty minutes went by, then forty, and still no sign of anyone. Finally, I got a call from my dad saying he was almost at the lodge, and could I please ask the front desk to arrange a lift for my mom? I was confused – what happened to my mom and the rest of the family? Arriving in a few minutes, my dad explained that after a bad downhill fall that had wiped out all four of them, my mom lost her confidence, and as the saying goes, it really went downhill for her from there. On her last fall, she had injured her knee, so my dad had gone ahead to get help. Soon, in came the hobbling hero at the lodge on her own, somehow having missed the snowmobile that had been dispatched to rescue her. The three of us settled in the warming hut, my mom in a rather gloomy mood. I finally got a text from my sister. She and her boyfriend were still looking for the lake, whose existence at that point sounded very suspicious. Inspecting the map, I came to the conclusion that the only possible “lake” around there was a scenic lookout with a view of Lake Tahoe. I sent the photo of the map to my sister, who by now was completely lost. She and her boyfriend had to retrace their steps for 45 minutes, then spend another hour skiing to the lodge. When they finally arrived, they were barely walking – or talking. Next came a trip to the pharmacy for ice packs for my mom’s knee, and phone calls to various orthopedists. The weather forecast kept flashing winter storm warnings, and while my sister and her boyfriend did choose to go downhill skiing the next day, my mother packed our bags and reminisced about driving in a snowstorm in the Alps. Her terrifying stories had some effect on my dad. On the morning of our departure, we left the earliest we ever had in the history of the Edel family. Slowly, we made our way across the barely visible Donner Pass on slippery mountain roads. In retrospect, I love being outdoors in the snow, but I think I’ve had my fill of snow for the next couple of years. Larissa Edel is a freshman at Bentley School in Lafayette.

pages.text: Wednesday, January 12, 2022 7 Voting for new committee of parents closes tomorrow By Jay Russell Parents have until 5 p.m. tomorrow, Thursday, January 13, to vote for their school site’s representative on the new Superintendent Community Advisory Committee. Elected representatives’ responsibilities include attending their respective school’s Parent Club meetings and reporting on their discussions. One parent for each school site will be elected and two at-large individuals will be included as the next two highest vote getters, totaling eight members. The committee’s formation resulted from a May 2021 recommendation from an independent consultant, Naomi Hunter, who analyzed the District’s Pandemic Response Survey of last year. Along with forming this committee, Hunter also recommended the hiring of a Communications Director (now Brian Killgore) and to continue surveying the community with regular job performance and trust surveys. Sara DeVries, co-president of the PHS Parents’ Club, explained that the committee should give voice to underrepresented parents. “[The District] could have just said ‘We will take the Parent Club President and they will be the representatives.’ But that is not what this is. Most of the people I have seen aren’t people that have a particular role already.” In an email communication, the District said the committee is being formed in an attempt to “[Build] off of the success of a variety of Superintendent committees (Facilities Steering, Budget Advisory, Health and Safety Steering, etc.).” The email continues, “The purpose of the committee is to: 1. Strengthen community and positive relationships amongst our various stakeholders. 2. Listen, learn, and better understand one another on the various successes and areas to improve across the District. 3. Generate ideas to improve communications, district-wide operations, and the student and staff learning/working environment.” Voting must be done through Google Forms, by clicking the link from the district email sent to parents this week on Monday, January 10. E v e n t C a l e n d a r Last chance to see Glowfari at Oakland Zoo By Allyson Aleksey Tickets for “Glowfari,” the beloved annual Oakland Zoo event, are available now through January 20. Advance ticketing is required. “Glowfari” features hundreds of life-size glowing animal lanterns throughout the Zoo and will display all-new light fixtures for the event’s return this year. It takes the place of last year’s “Zoolights,” and features larger light displays, longer hours of admission, and more available dates. The event is appropriate for all ages and invites attendees to take a mile-long illuminated stroll through the campus and ride to gondola to see the remarkable, 65-foot “Queen Ant Tunnel.” Finish the evening with a ride on the express train through the zoo’s winter wonderland. Tickets to this event are on sale now. “Glowfari” is available to visit from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. In January, the event is only available Wednesday through Sunday. By Jay Russell Children’s Fairyland Fairyland.org 699 Bellevue Avenue, Oakland, 452-2259 Fairyland is a 10-acre fantasy world for young children. The park has a new puppet show, Mae Lin & The Magic Brush, to ignite the imaginations of everyone at the open air Children’s Storybook Theater. Performances are at 10 a.m., 11 a.m., 2 p.m. and 3 p.m. Inspired by an old Chinese tale, this is a story of a young girl who is given a magic brush that makes anything she paints come to life. Fairyland remains open Friday through Sundays from 9 a.m. to 12 noon, and from 1:00 to 4:00 p.m. It will be open on Monday, January 17, MLK Jr. Day. Pacific Pinball Museum Pacificpinball.org 1510 Webster Street, Alameda 769-1349 The Pacific Pinball museum is more than an arcade; it also functions as a must-see museum for art, history and science fans. It is an interactive museum offering a chronological and historical display of rare “bagatelles” and early games, to over 90 pinball machines from the 1940’s to present day available to play. Throughout the museum are hand painted murals, vintage jukeboxes and rotating exhibits. K1 Speed: Go-Cart Racing K1speed.com 160 Beacon St, So. San Francisco 650-942-0765 Why wait until 16 to get the kids driving? Kids taller than 4 feet, can get behind the wheel at K1 Indoor Go-Cart racing, to experience the thrill of the electric go-carts, with speeds of up to 45 mph. Juniors can race other juniors, and there is a Junior race league night February 1. Registration is at 6:00 p.m. and races are at 6:30. Members of the family over 4’10” can all race together in the adult races. K1 also has a location in Dublin, CA. Birthday party rentals are also available. Lindsay Wildlife Experience Lindsaywildlife.org 1931 First Avenue, Walnut Creek (925) 935-1978 The exhibit hall is open from 10 a.m.-5 p.m. Wednesdays-Sundays. My older sister and her boyfriend (also invited) both played sports in high school. I did cross-country running. It doesn’t help much when it comes to doing cross-country skiing, but it’s something. Lastly, my mother, who hadn’t done any sports before meeting my dad, has skied once or twice – and without much enthusiasm, I should add. On the second day of our stay at Tahoe, the five of us dressed in the ridiculously bulky ski clothes, piled into the car and drove to North Tahoe Cross Country. As we waited for our skis at the rental counter, our anticipation was building. Six years ago we tried skiing and struggled getting our skis on without them falling off when we tried to lift our feet. To get to the trails this winter we struggled up a steep hill – kind of the opposite of what most cross-country skiers expect. But after that, nothing could stop us, at least that’s what we thought. For a while I was in the lead, showing off to the stragglers behind me. But then I got too cocky and fell as I tried to go faster. The real challenge was to get up: after making positions I didn’t even know I could do, I pulled myself up, only to start sliding down the hill. I remembered hearing about the “the pizza method” (also known as the snowplow), in which you point your skis towards each other to slow your descent. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont High School made a decision in December to not renew the contract of football head coach Staff Photos Jerome Johnson’s departure means Piedmont will lose former NFL running back Jarmar Julien as its offensive coordinator. Piedmont High School has declined to renew the year-toyear contract with head football coach Jerome Johnson after a season marked by an unusually low turnout of players. Johnson, with 30 years of experience as a football coach, departs after building a 10-14 overall record in three seasons. His team was 5-0 in the shortened spring season of 2021 but witnessed an historic low turnout of players last fall, August 2021. The varsity ended up with barely 20 players, though the JV team had a reasonably healthy turnout of players. But playing a full schedule of games this past fall with a shallow roster meant that the majority of players played a full game on both offense and defense. The overall effect of fatigue led directly to a It has been confirmed that Johnson was let go on December 3, though the school made no announcement. It appears that the first notification to football parents was an e-mail sent by Athletic Director Bradley Smet on January 7 inviting them to a virtual meeting three days later on Monday, January 10. Parents tuning in to the meeting on zoom expressed shock at the decision and the school’s lack of effort to inform them of the decision and the future of the sport at PHS. The school has made no announcement to parents or the public on its plans for the search for new head coach. It also has not confirmed plans for the future in general of football at Piedmont High School. The school was one of the first in the East to establish a football program, dating back to 1921 when the high school was built. Sudden and sometimes inexplicable coaching changes are part of the recent history of the school’s athletic department, and the school has built a reputation among coaches a being unstable. Johnson’s firing is reminiscent of the release of basketball coaches Mike Hudson in 2020, and Chris Lavdiotis in 2018. Hudson is now head coach at Berkeley, and Lavdiotis is head girls coach at Miramonte. The sacking of Jerem Stothers as head coach of the boys’ lacrosse team in 2016 is another example of a successful coach abruptly shown the door. Stothers takes over as Berkeley’s head coach this spring. The PHS varsity football program took a major hit in roster size last fall resulting in a roster of as few as 14 players, as opposed to 35-40 in a normal year. Going into its last game of the season, Piedmont was 2-3 against league opponents based upon a strong defensive unit. But with injuries building up as players had to compensate for a reduced roster by playing both offense and defense, Johnson was placed in an impossible situation. The future looked bright for the JV program, but only five seniors were expected to be available on the team next fall. Johnson came to the school as an assistant under head coach John Trotman in 2019. He was promoted to head coach after Trotman accepted a fulltime job and some job stability with the San Francisco Department of Public Health. Johnson was the Defensive Coordinator at McClymonds when it won the State Championship in 2016. He was a member of the coaching staff at Bishop O’Dowd led by Hardy Nickerson from 2010-2013. He was also Contra Costa College’s director of football operations under Alonzo Carter, now San Jose State’s running back’s coach and assistant head coach. Piedmont posted a 3-7 record in Johnson’s first season at Piedmont with a roster comprised of mostly Junior Varsity call-ups, largely juniors. After a summer and fall without football due to the global pandemic, the same roster returned in the spring of 2021 for its shortened season, going a perfect 5-0. Johnson’s dismissal comes as the latest chapter in what continues to be seen as an incoherent athletic department.

articles.text: Following the news this week of Piedmont High School’s decision on December 3 to not renew the contract of head football coach Jerome Johnson, parents and students are left to ask what the future holds for the sport. Football and track are the oldest sports at Piedmont High, both actively competing since the school’s founding in 1921. But does a 100-year tradition have any meaning? THE SCHOOL HAS NOT The school has not yet announced to the pubic the dismissal of coach Johnson, nor has it announced a plan to hire new coaches, or even plans for the football season next fall. Faced with a drastically low turnout of varsity-level players this past fall, the school seemed to make no attempt to gather parents and students during the season to hatch a plan to have a sufficient number or juniors and seniors interested in playing football come August 2020. Parents of JV payers have been fully supportive of efforts to build the program in the past year and a half. But no effort appears to have been made during the season, nor immediately after its conclusion. No meeting with parents seems to have been scheduled in October or November, and the question of the future of football at Witter Field was barely touched upon at the team’s end-of-season banquet. Many football parents were blindsided by an announcement from Athletic Director Bradley Smet on January 7 that a meeting of parents would be held on January 10. The meeting was ostensibly to discuss the future of the program, but for some parents it was the first time they learned that Johnson was terminated as head coach on December 3, one month earlier. This comes after initial roster numbers suggest 32 players would be available, while other projections propose the number is closer to 38 students spread between Varsity and Junior Varsity. Piedmont’s current options include generating enough interest among student to field a bona fide varsity, settling for a junior varsity team, rebuilding with a Frosh-Soph and a JV team. A Piedmont team would likely play in the Mission Division of the Western Alameda County Conference and compete in the Shoreline Division, the least competitive group of schools. Piedmont would play some favorable teams on the mend, like Irvington, Kennedy, Newark Memorial, San Lorenzo, American, Alameda, and Arroyo. Parents and coaches have speculated that the low turnout of players was based primarily on the concern of parents about the health of their students during a time of COVID and its many implications. Coming by Witter Field on a Friday night, the energy from the football crowd is always more boisterous than any other sport at the school, even inside Binks Rawlings Gym for basketball. The tradition of varsity football at Witter goes back to 1921, a history that is rivaled by few.

articles.text: The last time we visited Sunol Wilderness Regional Preserve’s Little Yosemite in December 2020, the often-ventured creek was nearly bone dry. Now, after the recent rains, the area near Sunol, is lively again and is in its prime stages of activity. The area is among the smaller of East Bay Regional Park District’s parks but is also one of the more popular destinations with its creek and rocky terrain Little Yosemite. It becomes a frequented watering hole in the warmer months, while those seeking a jolt will still find a reason to jump in the water this winter. The location is a bit of a beginners’ course in canyon climbing as you scale over boulders, keeping sharp eyes on where to put feet, hands, and track landing spots. The rocks require proper footwear and grip, given some of the stones have compiled algae and are quite slippery. The walk from the Sunol Regional parking lot is a mellow 1.1 miles from the gate on Ohlone Road. Given its popularity, you’ll see plenty of people. Adjacent to the main trail is a more secluded path along the creek, eventually re-merging with Ohlone Road on your way to Little Yosemite. The path down to the Little Yosemite area is narrow, and depending on the time of the day and year, you will likely be taking your time. On our 1.1-mile hike toward Little Yosemite, we saw 77 other hikers on a Sunday morning, despite using the more secluded portion of the trail for half of the walk. On the walk back on the main trail, we saw 155 other walkers including a large number of families.

articles.text: All four of Piedmont High School’s winter sports have been impacted by the Omicron variant of COVID-19, with 11 games and matches from January 3-10 rescheduled. Postponements were hopeful but not guaranteed and some games may not be able to be rescheduled. Each of the two basketball and two soccer teams has maintained enough players to compete, but other teams in the Western Alameda County Conference and North Coast Section have had to cancel because of incomplete rosters. All Hayward schools were closed on January 3, including frequent WACC competitors Hayward, Tennyson, and Mt. Eden, along with Moreau Catholic. Also, WACC schools St. Joseph of Alameda and Oakland’s Bishop O’Dowd canceled or postponed its soccer and basketball games. Oakland Athletic League also canceled all games, impacting Oakland High and Oakland Tech, which played Piedmont in basketball and soccer earlier this season. terday, January 11, was postponed, though its match at Castro Valley this Friday, January 14, is on. Boys Soccer The PHS boys’ soccer team had two matches rescheduled by its opponents. A January 5 match at San Leandro was pushed to a later date due to an Omicron outbreak on the Pirates’ team. A match on January 7 match with Hayward also will be rescheduled, as all Hayward high schools are currently closed. Girls Basketball Coach Bryan Gardere’s basketball team had its January 3 game against Encinal pushed to January 10. The girls’ squad has done well to limit exposure to Omicron with just one player missing from the lineup this week on Monday. The Highlander have had three games postponed with new dates not yet confirmed: January 5 vs. Berkeley, January 7 with Bishop O’Dowd, and January 12 vs. St. Joseph. Boys Basketball The boys’ basketball team has been able to practice and play games as scheduled, with only two players testing positive. articles.text: Visit Filoli Gardens any day of the week to see what’s in bloom this season. Filoli Historic House and Garden is showcasing its seasonal horticulture with a wide display of winter blooms. Filoli, located in Woodside, is an expansive estate and historical landmark that is considered one of the finest remaining country estates of the 20th century. The estate boasts more than 16 acres of English Renaissance gardens and a 6.8-acre Gentleman’s Orchard. While many botanical gardens are less active during winter months, Filoli’s gardens are alive with colorful winter blooms. “Filoli sits in a location where there are actually lots of plants that bloom in winter,” explained its Horticulture Director Jim Salyards. “This season, magnolias, citrus, hellebores, camellias, and paper whites are blooming as well as less showy flowers like the delicate violets and cyclamen. Winter is a time to make your way through the garden at a slower pace, take in the design of the garden spaces, and observe each plant and flower.” Tropical plants, citrus, and orchids will be on display inside the mansion. “From construction in 1917 and through its modern history, the House at Filoli has had a tradition of bringing nature indoors,” CEO Kara Newport said. “The flower-arranging room was part of the original house plan, and both women of the house, Agnes Bourn and Lurline Roth, had a passion for flower arranging. Today, our talented horticulture staff create arrangements weekly and we bring in an array of tropical houseplants which bring the house to life.” Tickets are on sale now. Advance ticketing is required and can be purchased by visiting www.filoli.org/visit. The estate is open every day from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. In addition, the nonprofit will celebrate the late Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Day by offering a soundscape and reflective space where guests can hear famous oratories of the civil rights movement. The presentation will be Saturday through Monday, January 15-17. Filoli will also welcome the Lunar New Year at the end of this month with a virtual tour that showcases winter orchid and citrus displays, as well as its collection of Asian art in the mansion. A virtual Chinese brush painting demonstration by artist Ming Lee will be presented. Filoli Historic House and Garden is located at 86 Canada Road in Woodside. Call (650) 364-8300 for more information. Free delivery to Piedmont

articles.text: The current exhibition “Mothership” will end at Oakland Museum on February 27. Oakland Museum of California’s exhibit “Mothership: Voyage into Afrofuturism” is on display through February 27. The exhibition uses tenants of fantasy and science fiction as a vehicle to “envision the African Diaspora and Black culture as central in a technically advanced and culturally rich civilization.” Artists featured are from a diverse range of arts, including literature, film, and music. Works from Octavia Butler, Sun Ra, and Kahlil Joseph will be exhibited. Visitors will explore contemporary artworks, including a Dora Milaje costume from the Marvel film “Black Panther,” photography, and other historical objects and artifacts. Purchase tickets by visiting https://museumca.org/exhibit/ mothership-voyage-afrofuturism. Oakland Museum of California is located at 1000 Oak Street.
articles.title: Mothership: Voyage into Afrofuturism exhibit continues at Oakland Museum to Feb. 27

articles.text: FOG Design and Art Fair will be held at Fort Mason Festival Pavilion in San Francisco from January 20 through 23. The fair celebrates current and significant contributors to the worlds of design and visual arts. FOG assembles 45 leading international galleries, showcasing prominent 20th century and contemporary design dealers. 2022 exhibitors include London’s Gallery FUMI, White Cube, Sarah Myerscough Gallery, and David Gill Gallery; New York’s Gladstone Gallery, KARMA, Kasmin Gallery and R & Company; San Francisco’s Friends Indeed Gallery, Crown Point Press, Haines Gallery; and pt. 2 Gallery in Oakland, among others. The event’s Preview Gala supports San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SFMOMA) exhibitions and education programs. Fair hours from Thursday through Saturday, January 20-22, will be from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. The fair will be open from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Sunday, January 23. For early access to the fair, visit Fort Mason Center on Wednesday, January 19 for the FOG Design and Art Preview Gala. Proof of vaccination is required for entry, and masks are required inside the Festival Pavilion when not eating or drinking. Timed ticketing will be observed and pavilion capacity is reduced in order to observe safe distancing. For tickets and a full list of programming and exhibitor details, visit fogfair.com. For more information, contact fog@ fogfair.com or call (415) 745-3315. Photo by Drew Altizer Visit Fort Mason Center and explore works of art and design by contemporary artists.

articles.text: Former Music Director Michael Tilson Thomas (MTT) will conduct the San Francisco Symphony in two weeks of concerts live at Davies Symphony Hall. The first concerts, held January 20 through 22 will include Prokofiev’s Symphony No. 5 and Shostakovich’s Cello Concerto No. 2 with guest cellist Gautier Capucon. Concerts from January 27 through 29 will feature Gustav Mahler’s Symphony No. 1, and pianist Yuja Wang performing Franz Liszt’s Piano Concerto No. 1. Tilson Thomas became Music Director of the San Francisco Symphony in 1995, during a period of significant growth and recognition of the orchestra. He led the symphony in championing contemporary and American composers alongside classical masters and continues to lead the orchestra in four weeks of concerts annually. Tickets for concerts at Davies Symphony Hall can be purchased at www.sfsymphony.org, or by calling the box office at (415) Michael Tilson Thomas 864-6000. Davies Symphony Hall is located at 201 Van Ness Avenue in San Francisco. New health protocols as of February 1 San Francisco Symphony announced updated safety protocols on January 4 for audiences attending live performances at Davies Symphony Hall. Beginning February 1, proof of a COVID-19 booster received at least one week prior to an event will be required for entrances into the symphony hall. The announcement expands the symphony’s already established requirement that all patrons, performers, volunteers, and staff age 12 and up present proof of vaccination against COVID-19 for entry into Davies Symphony Hall and all events held at that venue. Audience members younger than 12 may show proof of vaccination or a negative COVID-19 test. Audience members age 2 to 4 must show proof of a negative COVID- 19 test. PCR tests may be shown within 48 hours of the event, or an antigen rapid test shown within 24 hours of the event.
articles.title: MTT to conduct SF Symphony live Jan. 20-29

They will discuss a new book, aimed at Young Adult readers, entitled “Freedom! The Story of the Black Panther Party.” MoAD docents will then present pairings of art from public-accessible archives and music of the American Civil Rights Era beginning at 2 p.m. Audience members are invited to join the conversation via online chatrooms as docents discuss this period in American history through the lens of visual and audio art forms. articles.text: SF Sketchfest, a comedy and improv festival that was founded in 2001, announced that this year’s event will be postponed to a future date due to the rise of COVID cases in the Bay Area. The festival was originally scheduled to take place January 7 through January 23 at various locations in San Francisco. Festival co-founders Cole Stratton, David Owen, and Janet Varney explained the reasoning for postponement in a festival update listed on the event’s webpage. Many artists have reached out to the co-founders and expressed concern about traveling and performing at a time when the COVID Omicron variant is causing increased positive and breakthrough infections around the country. “We have also had some artists and staff members test positive for COVID,” the announcement explained. “Faced with multiple artists, show, and flight cancellations, we have made the tough decision to postpone the festival to a later date. Our goal is to keep as much of the original lineup intact as possible.” Ticket holders will be contacted directly in the coming weeks with rescheduled dates, details, and options. articles.text: Journalist, essayist and screenwriter Joan Didion died on December 23, 2021, leaving behind an expansive portfolio of work that encompasses decades of California history and culture. Her contributions to the field of journalism ushered in a style of writing known as ‘New Journalism,’ reminiscent of long-form non-fiction. Didion, originally from Sacramento, began her career as a journalist in the 1960’s chronicling huge counter-culture movements of her day - most notably the “Hippie counterculture” movement largely headquartered in San Francisco’s Haight-Asbury district. Didion arrived there at the most opportune time to observe the movement – during the height of the “Summer of Love” in 1967. Her observations were published in the September 23, 1967 edition of Saturday Evening Post. Didion reported on what she called “America’s atomization” – the failure of the American Dream, the things America promised but did not deliver, and proof that things fall apart. The fact that her reportage comes mainly from California, where gilded and optimistic interpretations of the American Dream reigned, was nothing short of ironic. Speaking from nativism and experience, she challenged what her contemporaries thought they knew about California, especially her colleagues and editors in New York City. In Where I was From, she describes the Californians she was observing. “They who came to California were not the self-satisfied, happy and content people, but the adventurous, the restless, and the daring, They were different even from those who settled in other western states. They didn’t come west for homes and security, but for adventure and money. They pushed in over the mountains and founded the biggest cities in the west.” Didion can be considered one of the few examples of writers who succeeded in writing for the screen, the novel, and the newspaper. She and her husband John Gregory Dunne wrote over 20 screenplays together, including The Panic in Needle Park, A Star is Born (which was remade to cast Lady Gaga and Bradley Cooper in 2018), and Up Close and Personal. Didion was so influential as a California letter writer that shortly after the announcement of her death, Gov. Gavin Newsom Joan Didion in 2019. Photo by Brigitte Lacombe Photo courtesy of The New Yorker Joan Didion pictured in San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury district in the 1960s released a lengthy statement eulogizing her as the “requisite voice of California.” “A fifth-generation Californian, Joan was a pioneer of the new journalism movement of the 1960s, capturing in prose the state’s growing counterculture movement that would soon influence the nation,” Newsom wrote. “She was peerless in her capacity to write about life, loss, love and society – easily the best living writer in California. Her ability to put the tapestry of California and the times into words made her a treasure for her generation and generations to come. California belonged to Joan Didion.” For those interested in discovering or revisiting Didion’s work, I would suggest beginning with her debut collection of essays, Slouching Toward Bethlehem. Her novel The Year of Magical Thinking, which won the 2005 National Book Award for Nonfiction, is another must-read. A masterful documentary produced by her nephew Griffin Dunne, entitled The Center Will Not Hold, is available on Netflix. Photo courtesy of New York Times Joan Didion pictured at her house in Malibu with husband John Gregory Dunne, who died in 2003, and their daughter, Quintana Roo Dunne, who died a year and a half later.
articles.title: A dedication to Joan Didion

articles.text: About this time of year, the President delivers the State of the Union address. He tells it like it is – politically. So, what is the state of music? Let me tell you like it is – at least from my standpoint. Almost everyone knows of the Pantheon in Athens. I suggest that we construct a Musical pantheon. And just who should be in our pantheon, you might ask? I suggest that we begin with two surprises from the world of sports. The first person I want in the musical pantheon is the great football coach Vince Lombardi. Why start with coach Lombardi? He was a man of great discipline and integrity. He taught all of his players to be respectful and keep their mind on their business. His famous quote “control the line of scrimmage“ applies very much to music. He did not allow touchdown celebrations. He taught respect. Proof of his success is his winning record and also that his football players went on to lead successful lives after the gridiron. It is good to pattern ourselves after his example. Staying in the world of sports, I select the sports columnist Jim Murray. He didn’t write so much about sports as he saw it. The fact is, he had terrible eyesight. Murray commented on sports more from a philosophical standpoint. His criticism could be biting but it was written in such a way that no one was offended. Modern society has much to learn from people like Jim Murray. Paganini comes next. His accomplishments in music are legendary. He is often considered the greatest violinist of all time. But he was much more than that. He was the prototype for every entertainer who came after him. Without Paganini there would have been no Frank Sinatra, no Elvis, no Beatles, no Mohamed Ali. Paganini invented publicity. I would also include Enrico Caruso, perhaps the greatest tenor of all time. He also had a great work ethic and was a great colleague. Did you know that he was a composer and a famous artist? Jascha Heifetz is in contention as the greatest violinist of all time. Sadly, he is one of the most misunderstood and maligned performers of all time. He was accused of cold and mechanical perfection. This is simply not true. His 100% sincerity was misunderstood as coldness. His mantra was to give his very best at all times or die in the attempt. No performances were identical. He always observed the reactions of the audience. If he felt he was losing the attention of an audience, Green Bay Packers football coach Vince Lombardi. he felt he had to do something out of the ordinary. He said that he deserved to be booed if he didn’t give 100%. Where are artists like these today? Many of the artists of today are far more perfect than those of yesteryear. Violinists of today actually exceed the perfection of Jascha Heifetz. I’ll tell you a little secret; if you listen to some of his recordings, there are places where he really messes up. But he actually wanted those to be included on his recordings. He was human. He had great integrity and sincerity, something I can personally confirm. Today’s players remind me of automatons. They are perfect today, yesterday and ditto tomorrow. Every performance is exactly the same. In the headlong quest for uniform perfection, however, they have lost their humanity. They make up for it with uniformity. Instead of looking within to their souls. We often read in the major newspapers that the musical performer “attacked the instrument”. Attacking the instrument is real big these days. So is “tearing into the instrument”. Loud is good, louder is better, some say. I am reminded of one of the great violinists of the past, Mischa Elman. When he was praised for his powerful tone, Elman always replied the same way: “the violin is not a trumpet. You say I have a big tone. That is only half the story. The other half is that I can play softer than anybody else.” It is that contrast which made Elman so marvelous. How important is nuance to art these days? Unique personalities and national differences made the old performers individual and unique. I much prefer that to the uniformity and predictability of today’s performers. Perfection they have. That is marvelous in its way. But the cost in humanity is lamentable. And so it goes in the world of music.
articles.title: Telling it like it is

articles.text: Gerard Butler and Johnny Wesson star in Chasing Mavericks Chasing Mavericks is a family friendly, classic sports story, reminiscent of those inspirational films that were so ubiquitous in the 70s and 80s. The field of play, however, is not a grassy pitch or an oval track; rather, it’s based on a true story set in a famous surfing spot, just north of Half Moon Bay on the Northern California coast, known for its monster-size 30-foot waves (some peaking over 60 feet) and a dangerous, life threatening undertow. It’s called Mavericks. The focus of the film is a teenager, Jay Moriarity (Johnny Weston), whose dream is to ride the seemingly impossible northern Pacific break. He quickly learns that to ride and survive the El Nino-created waves will require not only extensive training and endurance, but the ability to hold one’s breath for up to four minutes or risk drowning. The narrative opens with 9-year-old Jay attempting to rescue the small dog of his childhood friend, Kim (later portrayed by Leven Rambin), that has fallen into the surf. Jay is saved from the surging waves by a crusty old surfer, Frosty Hesson (Gerard Butler). Two years later he reluctantly agrees to mentor Jay, after Jay persistently tells Frosty his unyielding desire to surf Mavericks. And so the adventure begins with Frosty putting Jay through a rigorous training regime, insisting that he must learn not only the basics of big wave riding, but must practice those skills that will help him survive the harrowing, unforgiving waves if he wipes out and finds himself in the grip of what’s called the “spin cycle.” Frosty also loans Jay his “big gun” long board. Jay’s single-parent mom (Elisabeth Shue) buys him a weather radio for his 16th birthday, allowing him to track the storms that produce the huge surf. Of course, after months of practice, the singular storm arrives and Jay’s opportunity presents itself. Mavericks is ready; however, will Jay be ready, and will he be able to master the mythical monsters that form and crash with a Zen-like intensity that must be seen to be believed? Meanwhile, Frosty and Kim stand on shore and watch Jay paddling toward his destiny. Chasing Mavericks. Streaming on HBO. Directed by Curtis Hanson. Starring Gerard Butler, Johnny Wesson, Elisabeth Shue. 1 hr., 56 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: Though Robert Redford’s film The Conspirator explores a footnote to history, one that is likely unfamiliar to most, it is also an allegory, which, perhaps not surprisingly, parallels recent post 9-11 events. Briefly, after Abraham Lincoln was assassinated at Ford’s Theater in Washington D.C., on the night of April 14, 1865, eight conspirators were eventually captured or killed, the most prominent being John Wilkes Booth, the actual assassin. What is not well known is that one of the people charged as an accomplice was Mary Surratt, a woman who ran a boarding house in Washington in which those accused, including her son, often met. She was accused of being the “woman who built the nest that hatched the plot.” Her trial was not held in a court before a jury of her peers, but before a military tribunal where the rules of evidence were either truncated or discarded altogether. The essence of the film is not the guilt or innocence of Mary Surratt, which remains to this day in doubt, but the fact that the government, reeling from the trauma of having lost a beloved president, was prepared to sacrifice due process and the Constitution in the interest of handing down swift justice. What makes this film compelling is the remarkable performance of Robin Wright as Mary Surratt. She is stoic and unyielding in her insistence that she is innocent, though she readily acknowledges that she is a Southerner who is anguished by the South’s defeat. Wright also manages to create a sense of ambiguity (something Redford surely intended) regarding what she might have known, or even agreed with, as her son and his cohorts planned the assassination. Cinematographer Newton Thomas Sigel captures the inevitability of Surratt’s situation as dust moats float through the thin light, and cigar smoke rises toward the courtroom ceiling. Many of the images are artful and lovely. From the outset the belief of all in the courtroom – the prosecution, members of the tribunal, even her defense attorney, portrayed nicely by James McAvoy – believe that the woman who sits before them is guilty, no matter the very thin circumstantial evidence offered by the government. But what the film also reveals is that most, such as Edwin Stanton, Secretary of War, played convincingly by Kevin Kline, were willing to sacrifice the Constitution while occluding the presumption of innocence, to achieve an end that they judged was in the best interest of the nation – though certainly not in the best interest of Mary Surratt. Of course, the parallels to America’s incarceration of those in the prison at Guantanamo, many held without the right of habeas corpus, the use of military tribunals, even torture, mirror what Redford so carefully creates in this film. The Civil War was concluded 150 years ago, and there are aspects still debated and discussed – which this film does so very well. Cicero said, “In times of war, the law falls silent.” It’s a line quoted by the prosecution while the government prepares Surratt’s final punishment. The Conspirator. Starring Robin Wright, James McAvoy, Tom Wilkinson, Evan Rachel Wood, Kevin Kline, and Danny Huston. Directed by Robert Redford. 2 hrs., 25 min. Rated PG-13
articles.title: The Conspirator – the story of the trial of Booth and others after Lincoln’s assassination

Wright also manages to create a sense of ambiguity (something Redford surely intended) regarding what she might have known, or even agreed with, as her son and his cohorts planned the assassination. Cinematographer Newton Thomas Sigel captures the inevitability of Surratt’s situation as dust moats float through the thin light, and cigar smoke rises toward the courtroom ceiling. Many of the images are artful and lovely. From the outset the belief of all in the courtroom – the prosecution, members of the tribunal, even her defense attorney, portrayed nicely by James McAvoy – believe that the woman who sits before them is guilty, no matter the very thin circumstantial evidence offered by the government. But what the film also reveals is that most, such as Edwin Stanton, Secretary of War, played convincingly by Kevin Kline, were willing to sacrifice the Constitution while occluding the presumption of innocence, to achieve an end that they judged was in the best interest of the nation – though certainly not in the best interest of Mary Surratt. Of course, the parallels to America’s incarceration of those in the prison at Guantanamo, many held without the right of habeas corpus, the use of military tribunals, even torture, mirror what Redford so carefully creates in this film. The Civil War was concluded 150 years ago, and there are aspects still debated and discussed – which this film does so very well. Cicero said, “In times of war, the law falls silent.” It’s a line quoted by the prosecution while the government prepares Surratt’s final punishment. The Conspirator. Starring Robin Wright, James McAvoy, Tom Wilkinson, Evan Rachel Wood, Kevin Kline, and Danny Huston. Directed by Robert Redford. 2 hrs., 25 min. Rated PG-13 Gerard Butler and Johnny Wesson star in Chasing Mavericks By Chris Honoré Chasing Mavericks is a family friendly, classic sports story, reminiscent of those inspirational films that were so ubiquitous in the 70s and 80s. The field of play, however, is not a grassy pitch or an oval track; rather, it’s based on a true story set in a famous surfing spot, just north of Half Moon Bay on the Northern California coast, known for its monster-size 30-foot waves (some peaking over 60 feet) and a dangerous, life threatening undertow. It’s called Mavericks. The focus of the film is a teenager, Jay Moriarity (Johnny Weston), whose dream is to ride the seemingly impossible northern Pacific break. He quickly learns that to ride and survive the El Nino-created waves will require not only extensive training and endurance, but the ability to hold one’s breath for up to four minutes or risk drowning. The narrative opens with 9-year-old Jay attempting to rescue the small dog of his childhood friend, Kim (later portrayed by Leven Rambin), that has fallen into the surf. Jay is saved from the surging waves by a crusty old surfer, Frosty Hesson (Gerard Butler). Two years later he reluctantly agrees to mentor Jay, after Jay persistently tells Frosty his unyielding desire to surf Mavericks. And so the adventure begins with Frosty putting Jay through a rigorous training regime, insisting that he must learn not only the basics of big wave riding, but must practice those skills that will help him survive the harrowing, unforgiving waves if he wipes out and finds himself in the grip of what’s called the “spin cycle.” Frosty also loans Jay his “big gun” long board. Jay’s single-parent mom (Elisabeth Shue) buys him a weather radio for his 16th birthday, allowing him to track the storms that produce the huge surf. Of course, after months of practice, the singular storm arrives and Jay’s opportunity presents itself. Mavericks is ready; however, will Jay be ready, and will he be able to master the mythical monsters that form and crash with a Zen-like intensity that must be seen to be believed? Meanwhile, Frosty and Kim stand on shore and watch Jay paddling toward his destiny. Chasing Mavericks. Streaming on HBO. Directed by Curtis Hanson. pages.text: 18 Wednesday, January 12, 2022 Features By Will Adams Part 35 in a biweekly series We just got back from a couple of weeks in one of our favorite places, Bucerias, Mexico. It is a quiet beach town, an alternative to the crowds, bustle and pressure of nearby Puerto Vallarta, 30 minutes to the south. At least it was. After a two-year COVID absence we were overwhelmed to find new construction everywhere. Not just construction, but radically different development, Development in danger of changing the entire sense of the town. For those who may be familiar with the place, even the beloved landmark Mark’s restaurant closed for good one week before we arrived. Is all lost? Experiencing this, it was impossible not to reflect on change in our built environment. New buildings, bigger buildings, old places of business gone, new ones in place, more traffic, more people – everything changing, like it or not. It is impossible to really keep things as they were in Bucerias, in the Bay Area, or in Piedmont. In fact, I suppose keeping things “the way they are” or “the way they were” is really a misconception. What this thought represents is really only a brief snapshot in time of what in reality is an ongoing continuous evolution. Sooner or later the continuous accumulation of even small changes become recognizable as something truly new and different. One of the great ironies of much development is that often the very things that made a place desirable and valuable in Drawings by Will Adams The 2 meter-wide iconic pedestrian “kissing bridge” in Bucerias. Mexico was used by hundreds of people each day and the magnificent nearby tree must be over 200 years old. On our two-year COVID deferred visit of a few weeks ago we discovered both are now gone. There is certainly a sense of loss, but we must hope they will be thoughtfully replaced by structures and landscaping of a kind that will inspire in the future. The historic town had a scale and aesthetic that exuded a feeling of peace and tranquility, but it couldn’t keep up with its own desirability. The current development will test the architectural, landscape and urban design competence of the Mexican architects, landscape architects and planners. The level of craftsmanship and artistry common throughout Mexico is evident everywhere. The resulting desirability has led to development, as more and more people want to experience the place. As a result, construction is suddenly everywhere. Note the rebar sticking out on top of the building, indicating that it will be yet higher than the drawing indicates. the first place are compromised or even destroyed by incompetent expansion. In other words, what inspired the development is itself lost as a result of the development. But is this always the case? The answer is no, not always. My thinking is that we have to be prepared for this inevitability of change, of development. We must be well-versed and educated enough to be able to judge early in the proposal and planning process what is good and what is bad – where we are going and where we want to go. For our own future environmental, aesthetic and indeed entire life style, we must manage and direct inevitable changes appropriately. articles.text: It was decided on Monday, January 3, that the members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group would not be comfortable sitting outside the Tea House in Piedmont Park in 52-degree weather, so the group’s discussion that afternoon was changed to a Zoom call. In the warm comfort of their homes, there was a good turnout of 15 readers calling in. Participating were Mike Henn, Nancy Henn, Ken Young, Melba Yee, Lois Price, Sarah Johnson, Alicia Rivera, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Phil Witte, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Carol Long and Priscilla Wanerus. The group was pleased to welcome first-time participant Pat McMahon for the discussion of their January read, Hamnet. Maggie O’Farrell’s Hamnet, published in 2020, received strong critical acclaim, and was named one of the five best works of fiction in 2020 by the New York Times Book Review. The book proved to be an excellent selection for the group. It was enjoyed by some readers, but less liked by others, so it made for a thought-provoking discussion. This historical novel takes place in Stratford-upon-Avon mostly in 1596, when Shakespeare’s only son, Hamnet, died at age 11 from the bubonic plague. Interestingly, O’Farrell’s story doesn’t focus on Shakespeare. He is only referred to as “the father,” “the Latin tutor,” or “her husband” throughout the book. Instead, it centers on his wife, Agnes, and their three children. The story initially covers Shakespeare’s unremarkable youth, problems with his family, his courtship of Agnes, her pregnancy, and their required marriage, before focusing on the circumstances and effects surrounding the boy’s death. Hamnet is a novel about the grief associated with the loss of a child and the damage done to those left behind. The novel has two timelines, before and after Hamnet’s death. The first chapters are devoted to Shakespeare’s coming-of-age with his struggle to cope with an abusive, drunkard grandfather and his early career as a teacher; and the chapters covering his years and events in London that are mostly not told to the reader. Maggie O’Farrell’s Hamnet was named one of the five best works of fiction in 2020 by the New York Times Book Review. In these later chapters the father transfers his grief into the creation of his masterpiece, Hamlet, titled with a common variant of his son’s name. Some members of the group thoroughly enjoyed O’Farrell’s work. They felt it was beautifully written and a powerful description of grief associated with loss. They found O’Farrell’s detailed writing captivating. An example of which is a remarkable 10-page passage in which she traces how the plague reached the Shakespeare children, starting with an infected flea on an African monkey in Alexandria, Egypt, and ending with the death of the boy. It was the “ultimate in contact tracing” for the readers. They also found it impressive that the author could make such a complete, imaginative story out of a character and situation where there is so little actual history known. Other readers were less enthusiastic about the book. They saw this as a story of family dynamics with not-very-interesting people. It was an easy read, but they didn’t have an emotional connection with the characters. They couldn’t quite put their fingers on what was missing for them. Some found the manipulation of events going back and forth to be confusing in the first part of the book. There seemed to be agreement that O’Farrell’s ending tied the story together, concluding that people handle grief in different ways. For future reads, the group had previously selected the non-fiction The Boys in the Boat by Daniel James Brown for February and the novel The Midnight Library by Matt Haig for March. Destiny of the Republic by Candice Millard was chosen as their April book. A 2011 bestseller, it is about the little known, but remarkable life of the assassinated President James Garfield. The group’s next discussion will be Monday, February 7 starting at 1:30 p.m. Weather and Covid protocols permitting, the group will meet in person at the Japanese Tea House by the Community Hall in Piedmont Park. If the forecast is for cold or rain, the group will have their discussion via a Zoom call. New readers are welcome to join the group, and there is no fee to participate. The Boys in the Boat by Daniel Registration with the Recreation James Brown was chosen as the Department is required by calling February read. 510-420-3070.

articles.text: January 5 was the first Wednesday of 2022 for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group. It was a 52 degree and overcast morning, but New Year’s resolutions may have been at work as a strong showing of 31 walkers showed up at the Exedra for the group’s normal 10:30 a.m. start. The group had largely achieved its annual goal of walking every safe Piedmont street during 2021, but there were a few that they had not been able to get to. One was the challenging Crest Road, a street that is difficult because it is long and steep. It is also far from the center of town. The walkers may have walked it in years past, but the current group couldn’t remember ever walking on Crest. They thought it would be a good hike and a great way to start 2022. Going on Highland Avenue the long line of walkers looked like a parade. They took their usual route to Hampton Park, going up Sheridan, Wildwood, and Crocker Avenues, and on to Hampton Road past Crocker Park. Crossing Highland to get on Sheridan required a bit of traffic control for this big group. Many of the walkers are also members of the Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group, and some resumed their enjoyable conversation about their discussion on Monday about Hamnet, a best-seller by Maggie O’Farrell in 2020. As the group walked, they also noted discarded Christmas trees at street curbs, and some homes still decorated – happy reminders of the holidays. The walkers were pleased that an inflatable, moving Scoopy Doo and his friends were at the top of Hampton at Sotelo Avenue to wish them a New Year. The walkers continued on to Hampton Park, where members of the group preferring not to climb to the top of Crest were able to return to the middle of town. The group then crossed La Salle and passed through the two, large, white columns on both sides of Hampton that marked the main entrance to the large St. James Woods residential development of early Piedmont times. They noted the sidewalks’ brown tile inlays that marked this neighborhood’s extensive boundary. The walkers quickly came to Crest and started their ascent. The slope of the street’s initial portion is moderate, but it increases significantly over about a quarter mile as it nears Somerset Road. The group turned right on Somerset, but the degree of hike difficulty didn’t diminish. A large, modern, multi-floor, white house with a metal gate blocking a steep driveway caught their attention. The house is high up the hillside and almost looks like a fortress overlooking a valley. The hearty band of walkers pressed on, looking for a path on the right side of the street that an old Piedmont city map said would take them down to Huntleigh Road. The path no longer seems to exist. After another half mile, they emerged on Estates Drive. The cloudy view of Oakland and the Bay was beautiful, and, some felt, maybe even worth the extra walk effort. However, it was time to return to the Exedra. A direct route down Estates Drive to the equally steep upper portion of Hampton Road was taken. The group then retraced their steps from Hampton Park to the center of town. They passed more reindeer, silver bells, and other holiday decorations as they went, and arrived only 10 minutes later than anticipated at the Community Center parking lot. They had covered over four miles of challenging, steep, and little-seen streets, and it was a good Walking on Wednesdays start for 2022. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday, rain or shine, at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Members of Walking on Wednesdays paused at Piedmont Park for a photo before ascending nearby Crest Road. On hand were: Tami DeSellier, Dena Belinkoff, Christine Calliste, Phil Witte, Stella Houston, Jim Kellogg, Siow Fang Tan, Noemi Alvarado, Brenda Ferrero, Mike Henn, Pat Sheehan, Nancy Henn, Alicia Rivera, Renee Goldhammer, Quincy Dong, Helen Dong, Priscilla Wanerus, Lois Price, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Lilly Guardia Labar, Melba Yee, Sherry Jacobs, Adrienne Hamlin, Alan Goldhammer, Harriette Louie, Pat McMahon, Jim Kuo, Pat Keller, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome first time walkers Carol Braves and Aaron Katzel.

articles.text: The first time I ever went to a flea market, I was 22. I was about to graduate from UC Berkeley. I lived on Howe Street in Oakland in the upper flat of a duplex with my boyfriend at the time and his mother. I was waitressing at Skates on the Bay back then to pay for my education and my apartment, while also supporting myself and two of my younger siblings. My boyfriend’s mother, who was beginning to become a mentor, impressed upon me the value of a well-appointed apartment by the way she had decorated it for all of us. I was deeply affected by the feeling she created through her curation. I wanted to know more about this skill she clearly had. So when she invited me to go with her to the Sausalito Flea Market to hunt for treasures, I was an immediate yes. At that time, she and I were looking for things to spruce up our apartment, to reclaim it as a bohemian, feminine bachelorette pad, since by then my boyfriend had moved out. I’ll never forget the thrill I felt when I walked through the gate at the Flea Market that first time. Quality vintage pieces were everywhere. Potters, painters, and woodworkers were selling their one-of-a-kind wares. It was magic. The air buzzed with the energy of treasure-seeking. As I wandered through the aisles I fell into what I can best describe as a trance. The seeds of my future self were planted that day. In today’s column I am sharing stories about a few of my favorite finds over the years. Some I have kept, some I have sold, and some I’ve given away. And every one of them holds a story that is meaningful to me. 1. Twenty-five years ago, I worked with a waiter who told me that whenever I travel, I should get a piece of art or clothing that I will want to keep forever. The cream jar on the shelf in this photo is one such object. I got it in Chicago, the first year I became an interior designer, while on a trip to NeoCon (a huge, annual trade show for the design industry). The potter who made that jar was selling so many beautiful things, I couldn’t decide... until I did. Now I use this jar on photo shoots every so often. (Take a peek at the portfolio on my website, LMBinteriors.com, to see if you can spot the instances of where and how.) 2. While treasure-hunting with Darshan at Remember When, an antique shop in Cayucos, California (near San Luis Obispo), I remember exactly the moment when this lamp caught my eye. I was like, “Wait! Does anyone realize how good this is?” The lampshade was awful, but the body was this uniquely carved ebonized wood. It had quintessential mid-century-modern vibes. I picked up the lamp and carried it across the store to Darshan, to ask if it was really as good as I thought it was. Darshan agreed, “It’s perfect! You should have it

articles.text: Nat Dodge, a resident of Piedmont for more than 50 years and a fourth generation Piedmonter, passed away at home on February 4, 2020. The onset of Covid prevented the family from holding a memorial service at that time. Born Nathaniel S. Dodge III in Oakland on August 10, 1937, he was the son of Elinor and Nathaniel Dodge Jr. and was raised in Orinda when it was still considered “the country.” He attended Orinda Union Grammar School where, in the fourth grade, he met his future wife, Janis Armstrong. Nat graduated from Acalanes High School in Lafayette in 1955 where he was a member of the football team, and track & field team in discus and shot put. He also drew cartoons and illustrations for the school publications. He attended the University of California at Davis where he played football, was on the Student Council, and was President of the Sigma Nu Fraternity. He graduated in January 1960. He and Jan were married six months earlier on June 13, 1959. A member of the Army ROTC, upon graduation he was commissioned as a 2nd Lieutenant in the Army. Before he was posted to the Infantry School at Fort Benning, Georgia, Nat and his bride of six months went on a wonderful three-month driving tour of Europe in their Morris Minor. Nat retired after six years in the Army Reserve with the rank of Captain. Nat and Jan moved to Piedmont in 1966 and raised their two children. Nat worked at the American Rubber Manufacturing Co., a family business which manufactured rubber goods including conveyor belts, and fire and wine hose. In 1984, Nat left the business and started Dodge Co., Inc., a consulting firm specializing in the design and supply of process equipment to the mining industry. The primary focus was on copper and precious metal mines that were expanding around the world. The company participated in projects in Uzbekistan, West Africa, North and South America, Indonesia, and Australia. Associate offices were established in the U.K., Chile, and Singapore to better serve and support clients in remote project sites. Nat was a longtime member of the American Association of Mining Engineers (AIME), the Nevada Mining Association, and the Sociedad Nacional Mineria de Chile. Nat Dodge, a resident of Piedmont since 1966, passed away on February 4, 2020. Nat was an avid outdoorsman. He was a fair wing shot, fly fisherman, horseman, skier, sailor, and a (very) frustrated golfer. He was an accomplished artist, a collector of old and rare books, and a great reader. He enjoyed both classical and country music, good wine, good food, and spirited political conversations. He was a member of Claremont Country Club and served for several years on the club’s History Committee. Over the years he served the City of Piedmont as a member of the Recreation Commission, and coached a number of his son Nat’s youth sports teams. In recent years, Nat and Jan were able to spend more time at the family property in Northwest Sonoma County, which has served as a family retreat and provided the simple beauty and quiet lifestyle he loved so much. The ranch allowed him to pass on to his children and grandchildren an appreciation of the outdoors, and the basics of hard work, responsibility, and the joy of a job well done. Nat is survived by Jan, his best friend and devoted wife of 60 years, and by his two children, son Nat IV and wife Sallie of Boulder, Colorado, and daughter Beth Dodge Weaver and husband Thad of Wilmington, Delaware. He is also survived by five grandchildren, Robert Weaver of Santa Rosa; Jack Weaver of Morgantown, West Virginia; Henry Dodge of Denver, Colorado; Louisa Dodge of New York City; and Nathaniel Dodge of Jackson, Wyoming. A private family graveside service was held at Mountain View Cemetery in Oakland.
articles.title: Fourth generation Piedmonter Nat Dodge dies

articles.text: Dear Abby: Have you heard about the recent thefts of Frenchies? I am worried. I would not want to lose Tank. He is quite the cutie. Have there been any dog thefts in Piedmont? - Jen and Tank the French Bull Dog Dear Jen and Tank: Fortunately, I have not heard of any Frenchies being taken in Piedmont, but I have heard sad stories in San Francisco and Oakland. Our pug was stolen in the East Bay Hills when she was with a dog walker. By the grace of God (and a big reward offered), she was returned. It was agony, and I wouldn’t want it to happen to anyone. Here are some tips to consider for keeping your dog safe: 1. Get your dog chipped. In years past, chip reading was not universal but now it is. Most vets can read any type of chip. 2. Take a lot of photos of your dog (with and without you) and keep them on your phone so you can send them quickly to various dog services. Home Again is one service that sends out alerts quickly of lost pets with photos to shelters and vet clinics. 3. Do not share too much about your walks on social media. Apparently, some people may track you if they want a dog. 4. Always have a collar with tags on the dog. Even though you are watching them, sometimes they can sneak away. A tag can save a lot of anguish. 5. Be aware of your surroundings. If you get the feeling that Tank is being a bit too rambunctious and may get lost while he’s playing, take him home. Or if you feel someone is watching you, don’t dismiss it. 6. Some vets recommend getting your pet ‘tattooed.’ It can be done under general anesthesia when you’re having the dog neutered. The tattoo will be a seven letter and digit combo that will be unique to each pet and placed in the right ear. Apparently, it can be easily traced and is a permanent way to help get pets back to their owners. Sounds a little painful, but if they’re under anesthesia anyway, they won’t feel a thing. Wags to you and Tank. -Abby Dear Abby: We rescued a bleeding white husky on Christmas Day in the rain near the reservoir on Blair Avenue. The dog was very thin, had been skunked and was bleeding from a back paw. After a number of hours, we were finally able to bring him home. After we fed him, we took the dog to emergency care in Berkeley and they said they couldn’t treat him, so we brought him home again, bathed him with Dawn, cleaned his wound, and fed him a bit more. Eventually he fell asleep. He had a collar on but no tags. He looked like he had been loved and was kind and patient with our dog who sniffed and sniffed him. We called several shelters but it was Christmas Day, and posted photos of him on many sites.

articles.text: We Americans may not know our history, but we know our presidential myths. George Washington and his cherry tree, chopped down in the orchard that so inspired the young Anton Chekhov … Abraham Lincoln, who walked hundreds of miles in the snow to return an overdue library book, only to discover it was a non-circulating reference guide to rail splitting ... Andrew Jackson – “Old Hickory Nuts” himself – battling indigenous peoples on what is now the Rose Garden. Yes, the lives of our most famous presidents consist almost entirely of myths. The nineteenth century is generally considered by many thoughtful people to be the Golden Age of Myths. Our presidents of that era are presumably the most mythical. As just one example, James Garfield’s beard was said to be so thick, it could stop a bullet. Sadly, how wrong. Myths, indeed, can kill. Teddy Roosevelt knew the power of myth. He founded the Bull Moose Party, based on a mythical animal comprised of two real animals. Instead of the usual presidential portrait, he commissioned a bust of himself carved onto the face of Mount Rushmore. His critics, known as “bust busters,” attacked him for self-mythologizing, but he, like Muhammad’s mountain (there’s a reference you don’t hear much anymore), would not budge. Three lesser Presidents were added later, diluting the whole effect, but Teddy, a great outdoorsman and an early environmentalist, was pleased with his enormous visage adorning a previously pristine granite cliff, though he was annoyed at himself for neglecting to remove his glasses while sitting for the sculptor. Barack Obama is commonly believed to be this country’s first African-American president. Not so. The first African-American president was Thomas Jefferson’s mistress, Sally Hemings. She briefly served as head of state and commander in chief when Jefferson became incapacitated during a three-day Bordeaux bender. When he came to, he purportedly snarled at her, “Who told you to go and purchase the Louisiana Territory?” George Washington was mythical even before he became president. He threw a dollar across the Washington River, later named the Potomac. How the Nationals could use an arm like that now! Some myths beg exploding. Take the myth of Honest Abe. Lyin’ Lincoln is more like it. He frequently fibbed – to his friends, to his family, to Congress, to people he didn’t even know. When caught in one of his many deceits, Lincoln would smile that big Lincolnesque grin and say, “Just joshin’!” Such a cunning man. “How’s that Gettysburg Address coming along, Mr. President?” “Almost done,” the Great Equivocator would reply. “On page 40 now.” Then he would wait until the last minute and scribble some words on the back of an envelope. Benjamin Franklin was another early American who wallowed in myths – the roller skate key in the thunderstorm experiment, the Poor Richard stories he told to attract a certain type of woman, the coonskin cap that was really a muskrat cap – all helped to create the myth that he was once president. Yet, he never was, losing narrowly in the disputed 1798 election to Alexander Hamilton. Some myths have faded over time. Mention the great Grover Cleveland Cloning Incident of the late 1880s and many people, even school librarians, scratch their heads, and not because of lice. Cleveland, our twenty-second president (“Cleveland 22”), was so anxious that he might not win reelection that he allowed himself to be cloned, so that he could accomplish twice as much and secure a lasting legacy. The cloning procedure, called homo-hectography in those days, was primitive by today’s standards and so time-consuming that Benjamin Harrison became the twenty-third president before the cloned Cleveland (“Cleveland 24”) could take office. Still, the myth persists that both Clevelands were actually the same man. As long as there are presidents and talk radio, there will be myths. As F.D.R. once reportedly said, “We cannot change history. But we can make stuff up.” Ain’t that the truth. Phil Witte is a weekly cartoonist in the Piedmont Post and a humorist, whose writings and cartoons appear in publications in the U.S. and the U.K. www. philwitte.com

Lyin’ Lincoln is more like it. He frequently fibbed – to his friends, to his family, to Congress, to people he didn’t even know. When caught in one of his many deceits, Lincoln would smile that big Lincolnesque grin and say, “Just joshin’!” Such a cunning man. “How’s that Gettysburg Address coming along, Mr. President?” “Almost done,” the Great Equivocator would reply. “On page 40 now.” Then he would wait until the last minute and scribble some words on the back of an envelope. Benjamin Franklin was another early American who wallowed in myths – the roller skate key in the thunderstorm experiment, the Poor Richard stories he told to attract a certain type of woman, the coonskin cap that was really a muskrat cap – all helped to create the myth that he was once president. Yet, he never was, losing narrowly in the disputed 1798 election to Alexander Hamilton. Some myths have faded over time. Mention the great Grover Cleveland Cloning Incident of the late 1880s and many people, even school librarians, scratch their heads, and not because of lice. Cleveland, our twenty-second president (“Cleveland 22”), was so anxious that he might not win reelection that he allowed himself to be cloned, so that he could accomplish twice as much and secure a lasting legacy. The cloning procedure, called homo-hectography in those days, was primitive by today’s standards and so time-consuming that Benjamin Harrison became the twenty-third president before the cloned Cleveland (“Cleveland 24”) could take office. Still, the myth persists that both Clevelands were actually the same man. As long as there are presidents and talk radio, there will be myths. As F.D.R. once reportedly said, “We cannot change history. But we can make stuff up.” Ain’t that the truth. While the Board of Trustees debated the location of City Hall (some wanted it on Highland Avenue), plans progressed for Piedmont’s first public school. The Bonita Avenue School was built in 1909. It had 8 classrooms for 8 teachers who taught 8 grades and 318 students. The Lake School (now the Egbert W. Beach School) on Lake Avenue) was built three years later to provide more classrooms for students. The first school was built on the east side of Bonita Avenue between Oakland and Vista Avenues, hence the name, Bonita Avenue School. When Frank C. Havens died in 1918, the school was renamed in his memory. Albert Farr designed the school in the Spanish Colonial or Spanish Mission design that he would use the following year for Piedmont’s City Hall and the Oakland Avenue Bridge. The school had two large, square Spanish towers with shallow balconies and ornate cupolas on each side of the main building. Classroom wings on each side extended to the front and rear, making the building an H-shape with the school’s entry set between the two wings. Large arched windows flanked the arched entry, and Mission tile covered the roofs and capped the walls to the courtyard entry. Clara Crumpton was the first principal of the Bonita Avenue School and taught first grade. On the occasion of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco in 1915, Miss Crumpton had her students recreate the “Tower of Jewels” in front of the school. She knew the names of each of her 300 students. The 1947 photo shows the school with its courtyard and classroom wings. The long, rectangular building at the rear is a 5-classroom addition completed in 1937 by the Federal government as a Work Projects Administration project. In 1940 the Board of Education contracted again with the WPA to build auditoriums for what by then were three elementary schools.
