The walkers continued down Bonita Avenue, enjoying the many old homes with cedar shake shingles and a beautiful old Victorian home that is one of oldest houses in Piedmont. They also saw a handsome yucca plant, an original Piedmont street lamp, and an inflatable Santa riding in an airplane with a spinning propeller that was making one of its late flights during the holiday season. At the end of Bonita, the group turned left onto Estrella Avenue, where they took a group photo. They walked down Estrella and also enjoyed the lovely homes on it, one with an interesting, cone shaped, terracotta roof above its front entrance. This is a street that gets little traffic because it runs between the more heavily traveled Moraga and Ramona Avenues. At the bottom of Estrella the street merges with Ramona Avenue. They soon found the 107- foot path between 300 and 304 Ramona that goes down to Park Way and Dracena Park. It is one of the old shortcuts that Piedmonters took to get to Key System trains during the first half of the 20th Century. Long time walkers remembered a rainy Wednesday walk about two years ago when fearless tree cutters in the park took down a set of huge, leaning eucalyptus trees that posed a threat to Park Way homes. At the bottom of Park, the street takes a 90-degree right turn and changes its name to Monticello Avenue. At that spot there is another hidden path on the left, a 169-footer that the walkers took downhill to Artuna Avenue and the panhandle of Dracena Park. Once in Dracena Park, the group inspected the surface of the children’s play area for the first time. On past visits the play structure was fully populated with small people and there was never any space for the walkers. But this past Wednesday there was only one caregiver with her charge in a carriage sitting on a nearby bench, so the group had it all to themselves. They were impressed by how soft and bouncy the surface is. They then took the path up through the park and its majestic redwood trees. A number of dogs with owners were also enjoying the beauty. The walkers stopped at Storyteller Bridge and discussed the history of the original version and its recreation by the Becker family as a Boy Scout project was told. The walkers’ weather luck finally ran out and the rain finally arrived and it was time to make a direct return to the Exedra, its starting point. It had been a year full of Walking on Wednesdays experiences, and almost all of them had been excellent, walking Piedmont’s beautiful streets and being with friends. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday, rain or shine, at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. IT’S NOT A JOB . . . “Low price guarantee!” IT’S OUR PASSION Since 1986 Chicken and rice soup for a cold winter’s night. By Deborah Quok Brrrr...This winter is especially chilly, often with a daily temperature range from the high- 30’s to high 40’s and for several days. Snow on the Bay Area’s highest peaks also attest to this fact. This soup can come together using ingredients you may already have on hand. Perfect for a weeknight, or busy weekend, this recipe takes less than an hour from start to table (excluding time if you prepare homemade chicken broth). I save and freeze the carcass whenever I roast a whole chicken, lately about every other week, so, it doesn’t take long before I have enough to make a couple of quarts of hearty broth. If I have immediate plans for the broth, I will season it accordingly: Asian applications will include a hefty dose of fresh ginger, turmeric, or lemongrass; otherwise, I stick with the conventional basics of onion, celery, carrots, garlic and several herbs. Once you have two quarts of broth, homemade or storebought, the rest of the soup pulls together by chopping a few more aromatics, and then simmering all the ingredients for about 30 minutes. We enjoyed our first servings with crusty garlic bread, but this soup will adapt to pretty much any serving situation. A few advance suggestions: It’s soup, so the recipe is flexible to suit your tastebuds. If using prepared chicken broth, you may want to dial up the flavor by adding a bay leaf or pinch of oregano. Greek-Inspired Chicken and Rice Soup INGREDIENTS • 8 cups chicken broth, preferably homemade but a low-sodium, prepared option works too • 1 pound chicken thighs, skinless and boneless • 1/2 cup onion, diced, about 1 • • • • • • • small 1/2 cup celery, diced 3-4 dial cloves garlic, minced 3/4 cup white rice, long-grain 1/2 cup lemon juice, freshly squeezed, or to taste 2 tablespoons olive oil Fresh parsley and/or mint leaves Freshly ground black pepper and salt, to taste INSTRUCTIONS 1. Rinse the rice in a large sieve until the water drains nearly clear. Set aside to drain. 2. Heat 2 tablespoons of olive oil over medium heat in a large Dutch oven or soup pot, at least 4-quart capacity. Add chicken thighs and cook until just opaque on each side, with barely any browning. 3. Move the chicken to the side of the pan and add onion, celery, and garlic. Stir until the onion begins to turn translucent, then add the rinsed and drained rice. Stir all to combine and continue cooking over medium heat until the rice begins to turn opaque, about 3 – 4 minutes. 4. Add the chicken broth, cover with a tight-fitting lid and bring to a boil. Once boiling, reduce the heat to achieve a slow simmer. Let simmer for about 25 minutes until the chicken is cooked through and the rice has become soft and begins to open (bloom). 5. Remove the chicken pieces and coarsely chop or shred. Return the chicken to the soup and add the freshly squeezed lemon juice. 6. Once the soup returns to a slow simmer it is ready! Serve with a generous flourish of chopped fresh parsley and/or mint leaves. A thin slice of lemon atop will signal the lemony burst of flavor. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com. articles.text: Whisky. The very word invites a smile. Go ahead. Try it. Say “whisky” and watch the upward curve of the lips. Whisky is derived from usky, an eighteenth century adaptation of the Gaelic uisage beatha, which was a translation of the Latin aqua vitae, meaning “water of life.” Is it any wonder, then, that distillers proudly tout malt whisky as the result of a trinity of ingredients: barley, yeast and water? On some lighter, younger whiskies, it is possible to nose out and taste the yeasty cereal notes of the base barley. The real cornucopia of aromas and flavors – the baking spices, honey, vanilla, caramel, toffee, almonds, dried fruits, apple, pear, white flowers, chocolate shavings, ripe banana, coconut, and more – comes from the casks used for maturation. Casks open up a realm of options almost as extensive as the list of characteristics they impart. There are choices on the type of oak, size, degree to which the inside of the cask is toasted and what it was previously used to age. Most frequently, the casks used for whisky contained either bourAn inner ring of stills surrounded by an outer circle of stainless steel washbacks at Macallan is poised to help the distillery produce 11 million liters this year at the new facility, which opened to the public in June 2018. Casks, contributing approximately 80 to 85 percent of a whisky’s flavor, are being used in new ways to introduce added dimension and complexity as the “fourth” ingredient. The River Spey flows through, and gives name to, Scotland’s eastern Highland region of Speyside, arguably the country’s whisky heartland. bon or sherry. Proportions from each would be married together to create the whisky. While following the signposts along the whisky trail in Speyside of Scotland’s eastern Highlands, I quickly learned that the lineup of cask alternatives has been expanding. In the early 2000s, UK law permitted alternative casks, such as those used for brandies and fortified wines, for maturing whisky. Maturing, by definition, can be a slow and lengthy process, and we may now be seeing the results of the tinkering that occurred under a more elastic law. Based on stops for tastings, Port pipes and former cabernet sauvignon barrels seem to be the ones making their way into this mix, bringing in shades of richer fruits such as plum and dark cherry. At Dalmore, the King Alexander III is an elixir that pulls in from six different cask types, including bourbon, sherry, Port and cabernet sauvignon as well as Madeira drums and Malaga barrels. To be sure, casks have always played a central role. Many distilleries are quick to cite that 80 to 85 percent of a whisky’s flavor comes from the casks. Macallan rates the importance of the cask so highly that there is an entirely designated position for selecting the individual trees that will be used to make the casks. From the American oak, which grows taller and has smaller leaves, comes hints of butterscotch and caramel as well as lighter amber and yellow color tones. European oak, which takes longer to grow, imparts the “Christmas cake” (a popular catch-all for describing the combination of spices like nutmeg and dried fruits) and deeper red hues. Given the heavy responsibility of the casks in transmuting barley, yeast and water into the full kaleidoscope that we know as whisky, it seems an oversight to exclude them from the list of ingredients. When asked, I’ve found that the good folks working distilleries will give a nod to casks, but it’s hard to budge them on tradition and the lyricism of holding to the three raw materials. These same aficionados will then lean in and whisper the real secret ingredient, the fifth and final one: time. Originally published in the Piedmont Post on August 14, 2019 Kate Fratar is a certified sommelier and founder and editor of ChasingWine.org, a website dedicated to travel, history, and a study of the world’s varietals. articles.text: A Piedmont resident for 48 years, Joyce Hart passed away peacefully on December 18. She was 88. Born Joyce Williams on June 17, 1933 at Peralta Hospital in Oakland, she was the daughter of Chester Williams and Adelaide Robbins Williams. Throughout her entire life Joyce was a true California girl. As a child she split time in both the East Bay and Southern California. She spent her school months in Orinda and Piedmont and many summers either on Mulholland Drive beneath the Hollywood sign or on an avocado orchard in Laguna Beach. Joyce attended Piedmont High School and was graduated in 1951. She moved on to UC Berkeley where she was an active member of Kappa Alpha Theta sorority. She graduated from Cal in 1955 with a degree in Public Health. Putting that education to good use, Joyce worked at Children’s Hospital in Oakland for 35 years. In 1957 Joyce married Richard (Dick) Hart and the couple began a 58 year partnership that produced sons Larry (1960), Joyce Hart, a 48-year resident of Piedmont, died on December 18 at age 88. Christopher (1969), and Jeremy (1971). Joyce was predeceased by son Kevin (1964-1967). The couple made a home on Portal Ave in Oakland until 1973 when they moved to Hillside Ave in Piedmont. The Hillside house was the center of energy and activity and many a mouth was fed over the years. Joyce enjoyed many hobbies and interests. She was a knitter, seamstress, cook, avid reader, decorator, furniture restorer, and traveler. Her two greatest passions however were bridge and Bay Area sports. She and Dick were Life Master bridge players who enjoyed competitions all over the United States and abroad. Sadly, the pandemic drove her to playing online where she was an active player right up to her passing. Joyce loved all Bay Area sports teams but none more than her A’s and Giants. It was not uncommon to see her in the shade of the Coliseum watching the A’s and listening to the Giants game on her bright yellow headphones. She is survived by sons Larry (Renie), Christopher (Anja), Jeremy (Laura), and grandchildren Alison, Gregory, Jake and Nate. She is predeceased by husband Richard (Dick) Hart in 2015 and son Kevin in 1967. Joyce was energy and drive, fierce and loyal, and will be missed by all who knew her.
articles.title: Longtime Piedmonter Joyce Hart dies on December 18

articles.text: Bill Adams, a Piedmont resident for more than 50 years, died on December 4, 2021. He was 93. Bor n William Har rison Adams on February 27, 1928 in Oakland, he was the son of Egbert and Elizabeth Adams. He grew up in Oakland and Piedmont. Two years after his birth he became the older brother of Tommy Adams. The two would remain the closest of friends until Tommy’s death in 2005. Bill attended Crocker Highlands Elementary School, Piedmont Junior High, and graduated from Piedmont High in 1946. He attended Cal (University of California at Berkeley) where he was a member of the Delta Kappa Epsilon fraternity. Until his last days Bill was adamant that people call it California or Cal, never Berkeley. There, as at Piedmont High, he developed friendships that would last a lifetime. He also met the love of his life, Joan Louise Griffith on a blind date. They were married in September 1950 prior to Bill being drafted into the Army. After basic training at Fort Ord in Monterey, Bill and Joan moved to Fort Bliss in El Paso, Texas where he was stationed for the rest of his tenure. In October 1951 their son Griffith H. Adams was born. Upon discharge from the Army Bill and Joan returned to California where they found their first “home” in Parkmerced, near San Francisco State College. In 1954 their daughter Jennifer was born in San Francisco. Bill began a lifelong insurance career, mostly with Marsh McLennan where he handled the San Francisco Giants account. He went into a partnership with John Craig and the J. Ray McKinney Company. In 1966 he and Joan moved back to Bill’s hometown of Piedmont where they resided for more than 50 years. Bill was a lifelong lover of Big Band music, baseball, dogs and family. As a young boy he closely followed the Oakland Oaks and San Francisco Seals until the Giants moved to town. He knew which sidemen were on most recordings of Benny Goodman and Artie Shaw and his other favorite bands. As a young father he taught his son Griff baseball, playing strikeouts in the Parkmerced carports. He arose at 6 a.m. on many Saturdays to take Jennifer Bill Adams, a resident of Piedmont for more than 50 years, died on December 4, He was 93. to her horseback riding lessons. The two of them rarely missed the annual Dog Show at the Cow Palace so they could “pet the doggies.” Trips to the zoo, Candlestick Park and Cal’s Memorial Stadium were regular outings, in addition to summer trips to Tahoe, Newport Beach or Aptos Beach. Bill was never judgmental about his kids’ choices and helped them to become as independent as he was. He and Joan were Anglophiles and traveled to London every summer for almost 30 years. Flower shows, antique shops, museums and pubs were the main attractions. He had a terrific sense of humor and dozens of friends that he saw regularly, a list headed by his kid brother Tommy. He was an Old Guard (40-year) member of the Bohemian Club in Meyerling Camp along with Tommy. Bill is survived by his wife Joan, son Griff Adams and wife Jamie, and daughter Jennifer Kapp and husband Joe. He is also survived by grandchildren Nicholau (Lydia) Adams, Elizabeth (Farquhar) Forbes, Emiliana (Deviyon) Carter, Will (Gina) Kapp and Gabriela Kapp and her fiancée Kiko Alonso as well as nine great grandchildren. He is predeceased by his parents, brother Tommy in 2005, and nephew Jim. A family celebration of life will occur in the new year. The family suggests that memorial donations in his name be made to Wounded Warriors or Guide Dogs For The Blind.
articles.title: Piedmont’s Bill Adams dies on December 4

articles.text: Bob Schaefer, a former resident of Piedmont for 40 years, died on November 8, 2021 after a 10-year struggle with lung issues. Born Robert Paul Schaefer in St Louis, Missouri, he was the youngest of five children of George and Marie Schaefer. He graduated from St Louis University with a degree in business finance. During his college years he was given the opportunity for summer employment as a clerk for Lucky and Safeway stores, experiences that prompted him to move permanently to the Bay Area after college. He spent his career working in the finance field. While living in San Francisco in 1964 he met his wife of 56 years, Nancy Hogan Schaefer. Shortly after their marriage the following year at Corpus Christi Church, they moved to Piedmont to raise their sons, Eric and Matthew. In 2005 they moved to Reno where they enjoyed a wonderful retirement. Fourteen years later with his health deteriorating they returned to the Bay Area to be closer to family who helped Nancy care for him. Bob had a quick smile for Bob Schaefer, a former resident of Piedmont for 40 years, passed away on November 8, 2021. everyone he met and a joke for any occasion. He was a voracious reader and an enthusiastic storyteller. He loved playing games as well as watching them on TV, particularly Jeopardy. He was also an avid Raiders football and Cardinals baseball team fan. Bob is survived by his beloved Nancy, son Eric, and son Matthew and his wife Brenda. He felt blessed to have three wonderful grandchildren, Preston 19, Madeline 18, and Grant 16. In addition, he is survived by numerous family members in the Midwest and in the East and the extended Hogan clan. Memorial services have been held.

Christopher (1969), and Jeremy (1971). Joyce was predeceased by son Kevin (1964-1967). The couple made a home on Portal Ave in Oakland until 1973 when they moved to Hillside Ave in Piedmont. The Hillside house was the center of energy and activity and many a mouth was fed over the years. Joyce enjoyed many hobbies and interests. She was a knitter, seamstress, cook, avid reader, decorator, furniture restorer, and traveler. Her two greatest passions however were bridge and Bay Area sports. She and Dick were Life Master bridge players who enjoyed competitions all over the United States and abroad. Sadly, the pandemic drove her to playing online where she was an active player right up to her passing. Joyce loved all Bay Area sports teams but none more than her A’s and Giants. It was not uncommon to see her in the shade of the Coliseum watching the A’s and listening to the Giants game on her bright yellow headphones. She is survived by sons Larry (Renie), Christopher (Anja), Jeremy (Laura), and grandchildren Alison, Gregory, Jake and Nate. She is predeceased by husband Richard (Dick) Hart in 2015 and son Kevin in 1967. Joyce was energy and drive, fierce and loyal, and will be missed by all who knew her. Longtime Piedmonter Bob Schaefer dies on November 8 Bob Schaefer, a former resident of Piedmont for 40 years, died on November 8, 2021 after a 10-year struggle with lung issues. Born Robert Paul Schaefer in St Louis, Missouri, he was the youngest of five children of George and Marie Schaefer. He graduated from St Louis University with a degree in business finance. During his college years he was given the opportunity for summer employment as a clerk for Lucky and Safeway stores, experiences that prompted him to move permanently to the Bay Area after college. He spent his career working in the finance field. While living in San Francisco in 1964 he met his wife of 56 years, Nancy Hogan Schaefer. Shortly after their marriage the following year at Corpus Christi Church, they moved to Piedmont to raise their sons, Eric and Matthew. In 2005 they moved to Reno where they enjoyed a wonderful retirement. Fourteen years later with his health deteriorating they returned to the Bay Area to be closer to family who helped Nancy care for him. Bob had a quick smile for Bob Schaefer, a former resident of Piedmont for 40 years, passed away on November 8, 2021. everyone he met and a joke for any occasion. He was a voracious reader and an enthusiastic storyteller. He loved playing games as well as watching them on TV, particularly Jeopardy. He was also an avid Raiders football and Cardinals baseball team fan. Bob is survived by his beloved Nancy, son Eric, and son Matthew and his wife Brenda. He felt blessed to have three wonderful grandchildren, Preston 19, Madeline 18, and Grant 16. In addition, he is survived by numerous family members in the Midwest and in the East and the extended Hogan clan. Memorial services have been held. Piedmont’s Bill Adams dies on December 4 Bill Adams, a Piedmont resident for more than 50 years, died on December 4, 2021. He was 93. Bor n William Har rison Adams on February 27, 1928 in Oakland, he was the son of Egbert and Elizabeth Adams. He grew up in Oakland and Piedmont. Two years after his birth he became the older brother of Tommy Adams. The two would remain the closest of friends until Tommy’s death in 2005. Bill attended Crocker Highlands Elementary School, Piedmont Junior High, and graduated from Piedmont High in 1946. He attended Cal (University of California at Berkeley) where he was a member of the Delta Kappa Epsilon fraternity. Until his last days Bill was adamant that people call it California or Cal, never Berkeley. There, as at Piedmont High, he developed friendships that would last a lifetime. He also met the love of his life, Joan Louise Griffith on a blind date. They were married in September 1950 prior to Bill being drafted into the Army. After basic training at Fort Ord in Monterey, Bill and Joan moved to Fort Bliss in El Paso, Texas where he was stationed for the rest of his tenure. In October 1951 their son Griffith H. Adams was born. Upon discharge from the Army Bill and Joan returned to California where they found their first “home” in Parkmerced, near San Francisco State College. In 1954 their daughter Jennifer was born in San Francisco. Bill began a lifelong insurance career, mostly with Marsh McLennan where he handled the San Francisco Giants account. He went into a partnership with John Craig and the J. Ray McKinney Company. In 1966 he and Joan moved back to Bill’s hometown of Piedmont where they resided for more than 50 years. Bill was a lifelong lover of Big Band music, baseball, dogs and family. As a young boy he closely followed the Oakland Oaks and San Francisco Seals until the Giants moved to town. He knew which sidemen were on most recordings of Benny Goodman and Artie Shaw and his other favorite bands. As a young father he taught his son Griff baseball, playing strikeouts in the Parkmerced carports. He arose at 6 a.m. on many Saturdays to take Jennifer Bill Adams, a resident of Piedmont for more than 50 years, died on December 4, He was 93. to her horseback riding lessons. The two of them rarely missed the annual Dog Show at the Cow Palace so they could “pet the doggies.” Trips to the zoo, Candlestick Park and Cal’s Memorial Stadium were regular outings, in addition to summer trips to Tahoe, Newport Beach or Aptos Beach. Bill was never judgmental about his kids’ choices and helped them to become as independent as he was. He and Joan were Anglophiles and traveled to London every summer for almost 30 years. Flower shows, antique shops, museums and pubs were the main attractions. He had a terrific sense of humor and dozens of friends that he saw regularly, a list headed by his kid brother Tommy. He was an Old Guard (40-year) member of the Bohemian Club in Meyerling Camp along with Tommy. Bill is survived by his wife Joan, son Griff Adams and wife Jamie, and daughter Jennifer Kapp and husband Joe. He is also survived by grandchildren Nicholau (Lydia) Adams, Elizabeth (Farquhar) Forbes, Emiliana (Deviyon) Carter, Will (Gina) Kapp and Gabriela Kapp and her fiancée Kiko Alonso as well as nine great grandchildren. He is predeceased by his parents, brother Tommy in 2005, and nephew Jim. A family celebration of life will occur in the new year. The family suggests that memorial donations in his name be made to Wounded Warriors or Guide Dogs For The Blind. READ IT IN THE POST

articles.text: A Piedmont fire engine was sent to Taylorsville. In the background is a giant fire header. It now has become commonplace to have enormous wildfires every summer in California to the extent that summer and fall are called “fire season.” 2021’s fire season may not have seemed as bad as 2020, since last year’s devastation of wooded lands occurred further away from the eye of Bay Area. However, it was one of the most destructive in recorded California history. For Piedmont firefighters, the 2021 fire season again called upon them to lend a helping hand. Piedmont fire crews were deployed to fight the enormous Dixie Fire in Janesville, Lassen County, on July 20. They stayed battling the flames with five crew rotations, each one lasting 7-10 days. Piedmont crews were also sent to Taylorsville to protect the town. The Dixie Fire burned for three and a half months through Butte, Plumas, Lassen, Shasta, and Tehama Counties from July 13 to October 25 and consumed 963,309 acres before rain helped fire crews fully contain the blaze. “As a firefighter in these very intense fire seasons, it is critical that we send available resources throughout the state as there simply aren’t enough people or apparatus to fight every fire. We will absolutely need mutual aid to be reciprocated when we have fires in Piedmont, so we’re proud to be able to serve when called,” said Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. The Dixie fire was the largest single origin (non-complex) fire in California history. Only the August Lightning Complex fire in 2020 was larger with over 1,032,648 acres. The fire was begun by 38 separate dry lighting-induced fires. Yesterady, Cal Fire officials concluded that the Dixie fire was started by PG&E power lines. When a minor power outage was detected July 13 in the Feather River Canyon near Cresta Dam, a single PG&E maintenance worker responded. The worker was delayed by bridge repairs blocking his route. The worker arrived nine and half hours later to find a fallen tree on a live power line that had started a small brush fire. He attempted to extinguish it by himself, but without success. Cal Fire sent aircraft to drop water on the fire but an illegal drone appeared over the fire, endangering the aircraft and forcing a premature halt to helicopter operations which may have “played a major part in the blaze burning out of control after darkness fell,” according to Butte County District Attorney Mike Ramsey. The ongoing drought in California contributed to a total of 8,619 fires during 2021, and resulted in 2,569,009 acres burned. Other 2021 fires include the Monument fire ever in Trinity County which was the 14th largest California fire at 223,124 acres, and the Caldor fire in Alpine, Amador and El Dorado counties with 221,835 acres burned. Last year, 2021, proved to be the second largest fire year in California’s history, and only one year after the all-time largest year of 4,397,809 acres destroyed in 2020. The Dixie Fire burns near Milford in Lassen County on August 17, 2021.

articles.text: An epic snowstorm hitting Lake Tahoe near the end of December has resulted in a record 214 inches of snow – nearly 18 feet – in less than a month. As a favorite vacation destination for Piedmont residents, Tahoe provided a white Christmas, but resulted in road closures of Highways 80. 50, 267 and SR 28 for more than three days. Hundreds of families were unable to return home due to the highway closures. The snow measured at Donner Pass by U.C. Berkeley’s Central Sierra Snow Lab revealed that the total is higher than any other December in 142 years when snowfall was first recorded in Tahoe. The Snow Lab reports that the current snowfall is at 242% of the average snowfall for 2021- 2022. Rains in October helped prepare the Tahoe landscape for potential runoff in the future. At Northstar Ski Resort, 134 inches of snow – more than 11 feet – fell in a 7-day period, from December 22-28. The biggest amount was at Donner Pass with 36 inches in one day – December 27. The record at Donner Pass is 52 inches that fell in one day in 1989. Piedmont residents trying to drive back to the East Bay reported seeing snow to the tops of telephone poles. Snowfall measures the cumulative daily of snow falling, while snowpack differs and is the amount of snow that remains after melting. The snowpack in the Sierras is at 150% of average as of January 4. Climatologist and California Department of Water Resources (CDWR) Officials agree that the current drought is not over. “December alone will not end the drought, clearly,” said Jeanine Jones, interstate resources manager for CDWR. Climatologists are predicting dry conditions for the rest of the season. Models predict the second straight year of La Niña, which deflects storms in the Pacific to the Northwest and can mean drier conditions in the Southwest of North America. California adopted new emergency drought regulations on January 4 to conserve water. The regulations ban using hoses to clean sidewalks and driveways, washing cars without a shutoff nozzle on the hose and watering lawns and gardens after rain. Cars drive slowly through mountainous walls of snow. Travel to and from Tahoe was made difficult or impossible on Highways 80, 50, 267 and SR 28, all of which were closed the days following Christmas. The record for most Tahoe snowfall in a month in the last 30 years was 238 inches in January 2017. December 2021’s storms produced 214 inches of snow, two feet shy of the record.

articles.text: detected in most states and is rapidly increasing the proportion of COVID-19 cases it is causing, according to the Centers for Disease Control (CDC). The agency expects that anyone with Omicron infection can spread the virus to others, even if they are vaccinated or don’t have symptoms. Although Piedmont is one of the most vaccinated populations in the Bay Area, residents are not immune from contracting the highly transmissible variant. On December 31, 2021, Piedmont had the biggest jump of new COVID cases reported within a 7-day period. Between December 26 and December 31, over 40 new cases were reported. According to data provided by the Alameda County Health Department (ACPHD), as of January 3, there were 424 confirmed cases of COVID in Piedmont since the pandemic began more than a year and half ago. “My understanding is that the current testing landscape is a result of a variety of reasons, including how infectious the Omicron variant is, those wanting to get tested before and after holiday travel, those needing to get tested before school resumes, and the natural limitations of what all testing clinics can handle,” Gould said. “It’s a perfect storm and I am grateful that Curative teams across the country are working tirelessly to provide as many tests as possible.” Following the surge in testing, Curative announced that appointment times are generally made available four days before the date of the test. For example, in Piedmont’s case, appointments for tests on Sunday would be available on the preceding Wednesday or Thursday and appointments for tests on Monday would be available on Thursday or Friday. Appointments can be made at cur. tv/piedmont. Appointments for Sunday, January 9 and Monday, January 10 will be available later this week. For further information, contact Curative directly at 888-702- 9042, or visit their website at curative.com. articles.text: NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that Bids shall be uploaded electronically to the BPXpress City of Piedmont planroom via the “Submit Bid Docs” tab on the Project page until the hour of 2:00 p.m. on the 20th day of January 2022 (no bids will be accepted after 2:00 p.m.) for the construction of the following project: FY 2021-2022 Street Tree Pruning Project Complete bid packages, including project plans, technical specifications, bid forms and contract documents may be secured from BPXpress Reprographics by logging on to: www.blueprintexpress.com/piedmont or by calling 510-559-8299 or by email: Richmond@bpxprinting.com There is a non-refundable fee of $55 per set for a printed package, plus shipping and handling. All bidders must purchase a complete set of the documents (hard copy or complete download) from BPXpress Reprographics to be considered responsive and to receive subsequent communications, such as addenda. Bids shall be uploaded electronically to the BPXpress City of Piedmont planroom via the “Submit Bid Docs” tab on the Project page before 2:00 p.m., Thursday, January 20, 2022. Bids will be publicly opened via an online Zoom meeting at 2:30 p.m. on January 20th, 2022. The Zoom meeting login information can be found in the bid documents. Pursuant to the provisions of Section 1770 et seq. of the California Labor Code the Director of Industrial Relations for the State of California has ascertained the current general prevailing rate of wages for employer purposes, in Alameda County, State of California. Not less than the general prevailing rate of per diem wages for work of a similar character in Alameda County and not less than the general prevailing rate of per diem wages for holiday work fixed as provided in the California Labor Code shall be paid to all workers engaged in performing the project. Pursuant to the provisions of Section 1771.1 of the California Labor Code, A contractor or subcontractor shall not be qualified to bid on, be listed in a bid proposal, subject to the requirements of Section 4104 of the Public Contract Code, or engage in the performance of any contract for public work, as defined in Chapter 1 of Part 7 of Division 2 of the California Labor Code, unless currently registered and qualified to perform public work pursuant to Civil Code Section 1725.5. Please note: It is not a violation of Section 1771.1 for an unregistered contractor to submit a bid that is authorized by Section 7029.1 of the Business and Professions Code or by Section 10164 or 20103.5 of the Public Contract Code, provided the contractor is registered to perform public work pursuant to Section 1725.5 at the time the contract is awarded. Any bids submitted without proof that Bidder and any listed subcontractor(s) are currently registered and qualified to perform public work, pursuant to Labor Code Section 1725.5, shall not be accepted by the City. In accordance with California Civil Code Section 1771.4, the project is subject to compliance monitoring and enforcement by the Department of Industrial Relations. In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 3300, a valid class C-61 / D-49 California contractor’s license is required to bid on the project. The City of Piedmont reserves the right to postpone the date and time for the opening of proposals at any time prior to the date and time announced in the advertisement in accordance with applicable law. The City of Piedmont reserves the right to reject any and all bids or to waive any defects or irregularity in bidding in accordance with applicable law. In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20103.8, if the City elects to award a contract for performance of the project, the contract will be awarded in accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20162 and other applicable law to the responsible bidder submitting a responsive bid with the lowest total bid price for the base bid without consideration of the bid price for any additive or deductive items. All bids will remain valid for 90 days after the bid opening. Except as permitted by law and subject to all applicable remedies, including forfeiture of bidder’s security, bidders may not withdraw their bid during the 90-day period after the bid opening. meda County, California.
